en: The Commentary by Śaṅkara.
Salutations to Śrī Vanaśaṅkarī and Vanaśaṅkara.
He belongs to the Bhāradvāja lineage; his Vedic branch is the Bahvṛca; his mother is named Ramā, and his venerable father is known as Raṅgabhaṭṭa. (1)
His elder brother was Narahari, a scholar of the two systems of Mīmāṃsā, who ascended to the position of Jagadguru as Vidyāśaṅkarabhāratī. (2)
Bearing that very name, the lord of the Kāravīra seat shines forth;
he whose family history is thus is Śaṅkara, who possesses the title of Śāstrī. 3.
Having bowed to Dakṣiṇakedāra and remembered the lotus-feet of his guru, this one of meager intellect composes an easy-to-understand commentary on the Bhūṣaṇasāra. (4)

Here, indeed, the wise scholar named Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa, son of Raṅgojībhaṭṭa, desiring to comment upon the *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakārikā* composed by Bhaṭṭojī Dīkṣita for the sake of the comprehension of those wishing to attain it, and considering that every undertaking is pervaded by obstacles, has performed [the following] for the purpose of pacifying the multitude of impediments that obstruct the dissemination and completion of this work concerning the established tenets of Grammar (*vaiyākaraṇasiddhānta*) which he intends to begin.

At the beginning of the work, he composes an auspicious invocation in the form of a hymn to Śrī Lakṣmīramaṇa—the beloved of Śrī and Lakṣmī—who is Gaurī, the creator of the entire universe, for the purpose of instructing his disciples: "Śrīlakṣmīramaṇam. *Śrī* is Sarasvatī; *Lakṣmī* is the beloved of Hari. Their *ramaṇa* (beloved) is he who delights (*ramate*). The suffix *lyu* (ana) is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule for the *nandī*-group of roots. In the mantra "Śrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives," the word *śrī* refers to Sarasvatī and not to Lakṣmī, because Lakṣmī is mentioned separately.

"Is it not true that Viṣṇu is the heart of Śiva, and Śiva is the heart of Viṣṇu? He who speaks of any difference between Viṣṇu and Rudra is indeed a person of deluded intellect"—from such statements as these, since any distinction between Hari and Hara brings about misfortune, one might perceive a difference when praising Kṛṣṇa-Viṣṇu separately from Śiva-Viṣṇu. Therefore, in order to establish non-difference by refuting that notion, he provides a qualifying epithet for the Beloved of Lakṣmī through their identity: "Gaurīramaṇa" (the Beloved of Gaurī).

Gaurī is Pārvatī; her lover is Śiva. The suffix *ini* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), meaning "he who possesses that form as his own essential nature" (*svarūpa*). Others, however, explain it thus: he "fashions" (*rūpayati*) Gaurī’s lover—that is, he displays him as non-different from himself—employing the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) according to the rule *supyajātāv* (Pāṇini 3.2.78).

As for the seed of that [objection]: since the word *rūpa* is listed in the *rasādi* group, the suffix *ini* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 5.2.100, *rasādibhyaśca*, which is intended to exclude other possessive suffixes such as *matup* and *ini-ṭhan*) would be difficult to obtain. By this qualification, the non-difference between Hari and Hara is clearly stated. Thus, the meaning is: "I bow to"—that is, I praise—Viṣṇu, the lover of Lakṣmī, who is non-different from the lover of Gaurī. This is because of the traditional rule of Pāṇini: *ṇu* [is used] in the sense of praising (*stuti*).

Praise (*stuti*) is the presentation [of an object] as possessing the highest excellence. The meaning is: "I present the Beloved of Lakṣmī as possessing the highest excellence. Regarding the term *sphoṭarūpam*: this is an epithet of the Beloved of Lakṣmī. Based on the etymology "that from which the meaning (*artha*) bursts forth (*sphuṭati*) or shines forth (*prakāśate*)," *sphoṭa* is that reality (*tattva*) which illuminates all meanings. And that reality, described in the Vedāntas as the cause of the entire universe, is none other than Brahman qualified by *māyā*; thus, the meaning is that *sphoṭa* is Brahman.

"Of that form" (tadrūpam) means "of that very nature," which is to say, non-different from Brahman, who is the cause of the entire world; the meaning is "the beloved of Lakṣmī" (Lakṣmīramaṇa). Alternatively, it may be an adjective qualifying the world (jagat). In this latter case, "sphoṭa" refers to the expressive word (vācaka-śabda), because from it the objects such as pots and cloths "burst forth" (sphuṭati) or become manifest. "Rūpa" refers to the object (artha), because it is "shaped" (rūpyate) or made known. In the compound formed by the collective dvandva of these two, the singular neuter form is used.

This entire visible world, consisting of the denotable and the denotative (i.e., name and form), evolves from whom; the word "yataḥ" (from whom) takes the suffix *tasi* in the sense of the genitive due to its inclusion in the group beginning with "ādi. The connection is: "that Lakṣmīramaṇa from whom this evolution occurs. It is said to be "everything" because the production of any single entity consisting of name and form could also possibly arise from another, even from an ordinary person (*pāmara*). Evolution (*vivarta*) is defined as an unreal transformation into something else.

And that [appearance] is the manifestation of various unreal forms without abandoning its own prior nature, just like the perception of silver in mother-of-pearl or of a snake in a rope. In these cases, the mother-of-pearl or the rope, without relinquishing its own essential form, appears in another form—namely, as silver or as a snake. The sense is this: where something remains itself unmodified while appearing otherwise, that is *vivarta* (illusory appearance). *Pariṇāma* (evolutionary transformation) is a real change into another state.

Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the becoming otherwise through the abandonment of a prior form. The meaning is that where something, being itself modified, becomes otherwise while remaining the very same substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), that is transformation. For example, the transformation of milk into the nature of curds: here, milk, being itself modified, abandons its prior form and becomes otherwise, transforming into the nature of curds. By this, it is stated that the Blessed Lord, the Beloved of Lakṣmī, is the cause of the entire universe by virtue of being the substratum of manifestation (*vivarta*).

By this, it is indicated that he possesses the most excellent austerity and is thus worthy of praise; furthermore, since Sphoṭa is the object of worship for grammarians, this suggests an auspicious invocation in the form of a hymn to the appropriate tutelary deity. || 1 ||

Now, he praises that distinguished deity who is preeminent as an expounder of the science of grammar (vyākaraṇaśāstra), beginning with the words "śeṣāśeṣārtha": The meaning is: for the sake of obtaining (*lābha*)—that is, for the sake of understanding—all the meanings, whether explicit or implicit, including the denotations (*vācya*) and so forth, which reside in the *Mahābhāṣya* of Śeṣa, the serpent named Śeṣa and author of the *Mahābhāṣya*. The connection is as follows: pray to Śiva, whose ornament (*bhūṣaṇa*) is Śeṣa—the infinite one—as either his decoration or his couch; and [pray] to Viṣṇu, who reclines upon Śeṣa (*śeṣaśāyin*).

Anticipating the objection that one should pray to Śeṣa alone for the sake of attaining all remaining goals, rather than to Śiva and others, he explains his specific distinction with the words "the giver of all fruits" (*aśeṣaphala*). The compound is formed by joining the word ending in the suffix *tṛc* (or *tṛn*)—meaning "the giver"—with the genitive case form of "all" (*aśeṣa*), signifying the entirety of worldly and otherworldly fruits up to and including liberation (*apavarga*).

The fact that the Lord is the bestower of all fruits without exception is well-known in the Śrutis and Smṛtis, such as: "Whatever one does for the gods, the gods do the same for him," and "He obtains from there all desired and beneficial things, exactly as they have been ordained. Now, to dispel the doubt—namely, how there can be the attainment of all goals without remainder when there is a multitude of obstructing sins—he states that qualifying attribute: "in the ocean of existence" (*bhavābdhi*). "Existence" (*bhava*) means *saṃsāra* (the cycle of worldly existence); the compound is formed according to the rule for *mayūravyaṃsakādi* compounds, meaning "existence itself is the ocean."

Alternatively, it is a comparative compound (upamita-samāsa) meaning "existence is like an ocean. The crossing of the ocean of existence requires a boat—that is, a means—therein, according to the Vedic scripture: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow. Thus, the sense is this: if one who is capable of bringing about the cessation of saṃsāra—which consists of a succession of manifold sufferings and cannot be accomplished by any other means—is already so capable, then what need is there to mention that his capacity to remove the obstructing sins is even greater? This is the intended meaning.

And thus, through the removal of obstructing sins, there would be the attainment of all remaining goals without effort; such is the intention [of the author], that his mind does not entertain even a trace of doubt regarding that matter. || 2 ||
Then, he praises his paternal uncle Bhaṭṭojī Dīkṣita—the foremost among all scholars of that time—in order to perpetuate his fame:

I, Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa, for the sake of the completion of this work titled *Bhūṣaṇasāra*—which serves as a commentary on the *Kārikās* composed by my paternal uncle Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita—and for its propagation through study among many people, [salute] that uncle, the brother of my father, upon whose tongue-tip the Goddess of Speech, Sarasvatī, ever rejoices and dances again and again with exceeding intensity due to his attainment of the status of a preeminent scholar who discerns the sweetness of my words.

"I bow" means "I praise. Here, since this Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa praises his paternal uncle Bhaṭṭojī Dīkṣita for the successful completion of his own work titled *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, it is understood that this paternal uncle Bhaṭṭojī Dīkṣita was Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa’s teacher who bestowed knowledge upon him.

The sense is this: because the statement of the learned, "No example of a true guru who bestows knowledge has ever been seen within the belly of the three worlds," makes it clear that the guru who imparts wisdom is superior to all others, it is appropriate to perform the salutation of the paternal uncle before the salutation of the father who bestowed birth. Otherwise, since the father is more worthy of worship than the paternal uncle—both by virtue of granting birth and by being the one who performs the *vratabandha* (the initiation rite) that establishes the status of the twice-born—it would not be consistent to perform the salutation of the paternal uncle before the salutation of the father.

Because the tongue is the organ of taste, the phrase "whose tongue" is used to manifest his mastery over all the essences of Sarasvatī through that very organ. Furthermore, the dancing of the Goddess of Speech upon the tip of his tongue signifies the instantaneous and incessant manifestation of word and meaning in the form of a continuous flow. By this, his extraordinary scholarship and eloquence are proclaimed. (3)

Composing an auspicious invocation consisting of a salutation to the triad of sages beginning with Pāṇini, the founders of the science of grammar, and demonstrating the fourfold preliminary conditions—namely the qualified student, the subject matter, the relationship, and the purpose—in order to ensure the engagement of discerning readers, he announces his intended work so that the students may attend to it: [The author states: "I shall now explain... [etc. (as per the original verse).

Having bowed down to the sages Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali, to his father named Raṅgoji Bhaṭṭa, and to Ḍhuṇḍhi Siddhivināyaka—having performed a supreme prostration characterized by the quality of the eight-limbed (sāṣṭāṅga) gesture—he [addresses] those established doctrines (siddhāntas)—meaning the tenets of the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas), such as that the verbal root alone expresses the efficient force (bhāvanā) and that the verbal suffixes (tiṅ) alone express the agent and so forth—which have been refuted by the exponents of the words of Gautama and Jaimini.

The meaning is: "I shall demonstrate through logical arguments and reasonings; I shall illuminate the logical grounds for the validity of the established doctrines. And the meaning is: "I shall establish that the words of those modern logicians and Mīmāṃsakas who comment on the teachings of Gautama and Jaimini are devoid of logic and are beset by the defect of irrationality."

Salutation (*namaskāra*) is an activity consisting either of the joining of hands and head or the utterance of the word "namaḥ," which is conducive to making known the superiority residing in another as characterized by one's own inferiority. Regarding the phrase "refuted by commentators" (*vyākhyātṛbhir dūṣitān*): by the use of the term "commentators" (*vyākhyātṛ*), it is indicated that there is indeed no contradiction between the sages such as Jaimini and Gautama and Pāṇini and others. This is a *karmadhāraya* compound containing a *bahuvrīhi*: those for whom Pāṇini is the first (*pāṇinir ādir yeṣām*) are "Pāṇini and others," and these are the sages (*munayaḥ*).

The *bahuvrīhi* compound [in the term *dvaitadhvāntavidhvaṃsana*] is of the *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* type, just like [the rule] "sarvādīni" (*Pāṇini 1.1.27*). By this, the fact that Pāṇini himself is also worthy of salutation is obtained. As for the statements of Gautama and Jaimini, they refer to the *Nyāyasūtras* and the *Mīmāṃsāsūtras*. Since his paternal uncle is indicated as the teacher who bestowed knowledge upon him, there might be a suspicion that his own father, Raṅgoji Bhaṭṭa, was not a scholar; therefore, he qualifies him with the words beginning with "dvaitadhvānta... [meaning] "the dispeller of the darkness of duality. Duality (*dvaita*) is that which has come from the two (*dvīta*)—that is, difference (*bheda*)—which has reached [him] by way of being its locus; the knowledge of that is "duality" (*dvaita*).

This means a cognition that penetrates multiplicity. That very thing, because it is obscuring, is "darkness" (*dhvānta*), "gloom" (*tamas*), or "delusion" (*moha*). Its "removal" is its dispelling; she whose first fruit is that—such [is she]. She is the goddess of speech in the form of a man (*puṃbhāvavāgdevatā*); "in the form of a man" (*puṃbhāvā*) means she whose nature or form is that of a man, i.e., one having the appearance of a Puruṣa. And she is the goddess of speech, Sarasvatī; the meaning is "having that as her form."

Because the two terms *vāgdevatām* and *pitaram* possess non-feminine genders (*ajahalliṅgatvāt*), they form a grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇyam*), similar to the expression "the woman is the principal. By this, his unsurpassed proficiency in the Uttaramīmāṃsā, which establishes non-duality (*advaita*), is indicated. The term *ḍhuṇḍhim* is also an epithet of the father; that is to say, he is not only the very embodiment of the Goddess of Speech (*Vāgdevatā*), but also the very embodiment of Mahāgaṇapati. Otherwise, the salutation to Mahāgaṇapati immediately following the salutation to the father would be entirely inconsistent—this is the intended meaning.

By the statement, "I shall reveal [them] through the established doctrines," it should be understood that the subject matter (*viṣaya*) is the established doctrines of the Grammarians; the relationship (*saṃbandha*) between the subject matter and the book is that of the expounded and the expounder; the qualified candidate (*adhikārī*) is one who desires to know them; and the fruit (*phala*) is the knowledge thereof. || 4 ||

Fearing the abundance of obstacles, he again performs an auspicious rite in the form of saluting Gaṇeśa and others; for the sake of perpetuating his own fame, he records his own name and the title of the work he intends to compose: "Having bowed to Gaṇeśa... and so forth.

The meaning is: "of him who is the Lord (Īśa), the controller, of the Gaṇas—the attendants of Śiva. Alternatively, "Gaṇeśa" means one who sharpens (śyati) the desires (gaṇānām iḥ) of the multitude of devotees; here, "desire" is an elliptical term that includes anger and the other members of the group. Thus, he is Gaṇeśa because he whets or attenuates the sixfold group consisting of desire, anger, and so forth. His "lotus-feet" (pādābja) refers to his feet themselves as a lotus; it is expressed in the singular due to their extreme closeness. He is a "Guru" because he destroys ignorance through the instruction of knowledge (gṛṇāti ajñānam). The suffix *ku* is applied according to the Uṇādi rule *kṛgrorucca*.

A *guru* is so called because he utters (*gṛṇāti*) or teaches a hidden meaning. A *sarasvatī* is one who possesses a lake (*saras*) of nectar (*amṛta*). Those who study or know the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*) are *vaiyākaraṇas*; it means that this work is like an ornament (*bhūṣaṇa*), providing beauty for them. Thus, this title of the book is significant to its content.

This means that grammarians who study only the treatises on word-formation (*śabdaprakriyā*) without studying this work which elucidates the formation of meaning (*arthaprakriyā*) do not shine with full perfection, as if they were unadorned. By this, it is indicated that this work is indispensable for those who study the science of grammar.

This very commentary, composed by the great scholar Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa, which establishes the methods of exposition taught by the Naiyāyikas and Mīmāṃsakas and refutes them while being extremely extensive and replete with erudition, is called the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*; however, due to its extensiveness, it is sometimes referred to as the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*.

Considering that [the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*] is beneficial only for those of the highest capacity and not for those of middling or lower capacities, this commentary was composed by extracting the essential doctrines and explaining them concisely for their benefit as well; thus its name, *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, is well-known. According to the maxim "a part of a name may stand for the whole name," it is referred to simply as *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa* in the root text.

It should be understood that in both cases, the kārikās which constitute the subject matter of the commentary are identical, having been composed by one's own guru, Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita; this will become clear further on. || 5 ||

Now, Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita, the author of the *Kārikās* which serve as the foundation for this commentary, performs an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) in the form of remembering his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) to remove obstacles to the composition of his intended work; thus he says, "prāripsita... and so forth. The meaning is: for the sake of the pacification—that is, the destruction—of those evils (*durita*) which act as obstacles to that collection of *kārikās* beginning with "phalavyāpārayordhātuḥ," which is the work desired to be commenced.

Since it has been stated here specifically that [the purpose of *maṅgala*] is "for the pacification of obstacles," the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*), which is established by the authority of the Vedic injunction inferred from the non-secular, unobjectionable conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), does not serve a function toward the completion [of a work]. This is because we observe the completion of the works of atheists even without an auspicious rite, which shows that the auspicious rite lacks utility for completion. Rather, since the absence of obstacles is established as a cause for every effect whatsoever, the utility of the auspicious rite lies solely in the destruction of obstacles.

It is indicated that completion is achieved solely by that collection of means attentive to the composition of the work—namely, the intellect, understanding, and so forth, which possess ever-new blossoming. Regarding the phrase "remembrance of the serpent" (*phaṇismaraṇa*): the meaning is that for the attainment of all the established doctrines contained in the *Mahābhāṣya*, it is entirely appropriate to perform an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) consisting of the remembrance of the serpent, since the author of the *Mahābhāṣya* is an incarnation of Śeṣa, who is known as the Serpent (*phaṇin*). This is the intended sense.

Now, if one asks what the purpose is for placing an auspicious invocation at the beginning of a work, he says: "For the sake of instructing the disciples. When such a composed verse is recited by the disciples at the time of commencing the work, they too [think]: "Indeed, those scriptures which begin with an auspicious rite, have an auspicious rite in their middle, and end with an auspicious rite, become renowned and possess heroic authors as well as long-lived authors; and may the students likewise be endowed with prosperity."

The meaning is that [the author] intends for them to partake in the fruit of the auspiciousness spoken by the author of the *Mahābhāṣya*. "The work he wishes to compose" refers to the treatise in the form of the *Kārikāvalī*. "He promises" means he makes known its necessity as something to be done. The meaning of the verbal root *jñā* (to know) as qualified by the prefix *prati* is an activity conducive to making known the necessity of the work. In this context, the cognition of necessity resides in the work intended to be composed, by virtue of the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā-sambandha*). And the activity conducive to such a cognition resides in the author of the book.
And that activity consists of the employment of words in the form: "I am composing such-and-such a work.

When there is a desire to know the agent of the act of extraction—asking "By whom was it extracted?"—he says: "by us" (*asmābhiḥ*). Since Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita is well-known as the author of the *Śabdakaustubha*, the meaning of "by us" is "by Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita. There—in the *Śabdakaustubha*. Here—in the work consisting of the *Kārikāvalī*.

And thus, since the meaning—that "whatever matter has been determined by [the author] of the *Śabdakaustubha*, that very same matter is here—in this work, the *Kārikāvalī*—stated in brief"—is obtained through proximity (*pratyāsatti*), one understands the identity of the author of the *Śabdakaustubha* and the author of the *Kārikāvalī* work; consequently, it follows that the *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakārikā* was composed by Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita.

By this, through the demonstration of the extraordinary scholarship of the author of the *Kārikāvalī* text, it is indicated that his work, the *Kārikāvalī*, is worthy of being studied at the conclusion [of the study of grammar]. He states the purpose of drawing from the ocean of the *Bhāṣya* as a source for the *Śabdakaustubha* with the passage beginning "stated in the *Śabdakaustubha*" and ending with "for the sake of refutation. He states the result of refuting what has been proposed by moderns with the word "otherwise," meaning in the case of the opposite of what was stated.

The meaning is: "if the refutation of its being a modern invention were not performed. "Rooted in that" means rooted in the *Śabdakaustubha*. "Of this too" refers to the work *Kārikāvalī*. "A modern invention" means invented by a modern person—that is, by someone contemporary or recent. "In the event of its becoming the essence of that" means in the event of its being determined to be the essence of that [the *Śabdakaustubha*]. "For the followers of Pāṇini" means for those who study the science proclaimed by the sage Pāṇini. "The consequence of its being unacceptable" [is the intended meaning].

Thus, the sense is that the very statement regarding the necessity of necessarily adopting [this work] is the result of refuting the notion that it was merely imagined by a modern person. He demonstrates the purpose of stating "it has been determined therein" with the passage beginning with "for this reason also" and ending with "to indicate.

It should be understood that although other deities exist, the fact that the serpent (phaṇin) alone is mentioned here is intended to suggest that, because he is an incarnation of the serpent named Śeṣa and because he is the most venerable teacher who initiated the science of grammar, the Great Commentator (Mahābhāṣyakāra) himself is the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) appropriate to the subject matter being treated in this context. || 1 ||
"Regarding the matter proposed": this means the matter that has been made known as the object to be established. He says—speaks—"of the result and the operation."

The verbal root (*dhātu*) is traditionally held to denote both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*). That is to say, the verbal root expresses the result and the operation, and both the result and the operation are expressed by the verbal root. However, the personal endings (*tiṅ*) are traditionally held to denote the locus (*āśraya*). By virtue of proximity, the *ti* suffixes and so forth are traditionally held to denote the object (*karman*), which is the locus of the result, and the agent (*kartṛ*), which is the locus of the operation. Thus, the meaning is that the object and the agent are expressed by the *ti* suffixes and so forth. As for those *tiṅ* endings whose meaning is the abstract action (*bhāva*), they are not to be included here, because they merely restate the meaning of the verbal root.

The operation (*vyāpāra*) with respect to the fruit (*phala*) is primary. This means that the operation is that which possesses the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by the fruit, while the fruit is its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). As for the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) are, by proximity, qualifiers of the fruit and the operation; the fruit and the operation are the qualificands, and the agent and the object are their qualifiers. Such is the extremely concise meaning of the verse.

One might object: since the statement of the learned authorities—"Whatever gender, number, and case-ending belong to the substantive (viśeṣya), those same gender, number, and case-endings belong to its qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) as well"—establishes a rule that the words expressing the substantive and its qualifier must agree in number, the word *smṛtāḥ* (feminine plural), which has a number different from the number of the word expressing the substantive (*dhātuḥ*), could not be construed with the substantive *dhātuḥ* (masculine singular). To address this, he says: "In the phrase 'the word *dhātuḥ*'... up to "...the construction."

*Vipariṇāma* (transformation) is the postulation of case-endings and so forth that are capable of syntactic connection (*anvaya*), by abandoning those case-endings and so forth whose meanings are not so connected. The meaning here is that *vacanavipariṇāma* (transformation of number) consists in the utterance of a word with a singular ending immediately following a remembered [original] word. It is precisely because of the requirement for the coreferentiality (*samānavacanatva*) of the words expressing the qualificand and the qualifier that there is no cognition of the relation between qualifier and qualificand in cases such as "the white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭāḥ*), where the plural ending on *paṭāḥ* contradicts the singular ending on *śuklaḥ*. Furthermore, the status of being a qualifier and a qualificand does not obtain even when there is a difference in gender or number.

It should not be argued that, according to the maxim "the case-ending for both the qualifier and the qualified is indeed the same," the word *smṛtāḥ* (in the plural) must function as a qualifier for the word *dhātuḥ* (in the singular), just as in examples such as *vedāḥ pramāṇam*. This is because that maxim applies only in cases where there is a necessary intention to express a number that contradicts the number conveyed by the case-ending following the word denoting the qualified object.

For example, in the expression "The Vedas are the means of valid knowledge" (*vedāḥ pramāṇam*), the word expressing the qualificand is "means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇam*). The number conveyed by the case-ending there is singularity; however, since the plurality of "the Vedas"—a number contrary to that—is intended to be expressed there, the definition [of grammatical number] is consistent. In the statement "The Vedas are the means of valid knowledge," it is desired to convey that the Vedas possess a single type of validity. And that [conveyance] would be untenable without intending the plurality inherent in the Vedas; this and more should be seen in the *Laghu-kaumudī* (or *Laghu-manjūṣā*), in the section on the meaning of case-endings (*sub-artha-vicāra*) under the heading "The Remainder" (*śeṣe*).
The sense is that, in the present context, there is no reason to intend the plural number when it is said "they are remembered."

By the use of the dual number in the expression *phalavyāpārayoḥ*, it is indicated that the verbal root (*dhātu*) possesses distinct powers (*śakti*) with respect to the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) separately; it does not mean that there is a single power residing in the operation as delimited by the result. For if that were the case, since there would be no decisive factor (*vinigamanā-viraheṇa*) regarding which is the qualifier and which the qualified, one might as well assume a single power for the result as delimited by the operation. Thus, although the assumption of two powers is equal, it would entail the undesirable consequence of assuming two cumbersome delimiters of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), namely: "being an operation delimited by a result" and "being a result delimited by an operation."

Furthermore, since the fruit (phala) and the operation (vyāpāra) are presented by a single power (*śakti*) that qualifies [the root-meaning], they would each constitute only a part of the word-meaning (*padārthaikadeśa*). Consequently, in sentences such as *taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("He cooks rice"), the rice could not be construed with the fruit, and in *caitreṇa taṇḍulaḥ pacyate* ("Rice is cooked by Caitra"), Caitra could not be construed with the operation. This is because of the maxim that "a word-meaning is construed with another word-meaning" (*padārthaḥ padārthena*), which maintains a rule that where the connection of a qualifier is intended, the object must be known as not being a qualifier of anything else (i.e., not having attained the status of being a qualifier relative to another).

Because the presentation of an object through a single power directed toward a qualified entity occurs only as having entered into a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*), for this very reason, the expression "the pot is eternal" (*nityo ghaṭaḥ*) does not occur when one intends to qualify the potness (*ghaṭatva*)—which is presented by a single power directed toward the pot qualified by potness—with the qualifier "eternal. However, the application of the qualifier "blue" to the pot—which is a part of the referent of the word—does indeed occur, because the pot is cognized as not being qualified by anything else [in that specific context].

Thus, even in the compound *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), there is no connection of the qualifier "prosperous" (*ṛddha*) with the king; this is because the king is known as a qualifier of the man. However, in the phrase *sundaro rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the handsome king's man"), the connection of the qualifier "handsome" (*sundara*) with the man does indeed occur; this is because the man is known as a qualifier of nothing else.

In the sentence "the man of the wealthy king" (*ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), however, because there is an absence of *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning), at the time of the connection with the qualifier, the word "king" (*rājñaḥ*) is understood as not being qualified by anything else; thus, the connection with the qualifier "wealthy" (*ṛddhasya*) occurs in relation to the king. In a sentence, after the separate meanings of the individual words have been presented, the connection occurs through the relationship of qualifier and qualified by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors. In a compound (*vṛtti*), by contrast, the presentation of the word-meanings occurs only as having already entered into the relationship of qualifier and qualified; this is the distinction.

The intended meaning of the Nyāya system is this: a word-meaning (padārtha) connects with another word-meaning, but not with a mere part of a word-meaning. Otherwise, even in the sentence "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), there would be no connection between "king" and "man," because the "man" presented by the single denotative power (*śakti*) directed toward the man qualified by "manhood" (*puruṣatva*) would be a mere part of the word-meaning—this is how it should be understood. In that context, the fruit-portion (*phalāṃśa*) is generally a qualifier of the operation (*vyāpāra*). The relation (*saṃsarga*) is the producer-produced relationship; thus, these two—the operation and the fruit—connect through the relation of qualifier and qualified, as in the expression "an operation conducive to the fruit."

Now, since one does not experience a cognition of mutual relation—either as qualifier and qualified (or locus and located)—between the sun and the lion presented by the word *hari*, and since it is observed that there is no mutual relation of qualifier and qualified between the meanings of the two words "option" (*vikalpa*) and "also" (*api*) presented by the word *vā* according to the lexicon—"*vā* may [be used] in the sense of option, comparison, 'even,' and also in conjunction"—and because one must necessarily accept the rule that relation occurs only between meanings presented by distinct words, [there can be no relation] between those presented by a single word.

If it is argued that the mutual connection between the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) would thus be impossible, and therefore the acceptance of separate potencies is improper—this is not so. For, since we observe the mutual connection between the meaning of the *laṭ* suffix (the effort) and its presentness in the view of the opponent (*paramata*), and likewise between the substratum and number which are the meanings of the *tiṅ* suffix in our own view (*svamata*), such a restrictive rule must be limited. Consequently, due to the diversity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), there is no obstacle to accepting the mutual connection between the result and the operation.

Now, if it is argued that on the view of separate potencies (*pṛthak-śakti-pakṣa*), since the fruit is understood independently from the word "going" (*gamana*), there would be the undesirable consequence of understanding "going" as not being an operation (*vyāpāra*); therefore, to avoid this, one should accept only the view of a single potency (*eka-śakti-pakṣa*)—that too is not correct. Because of its internal nature (*antaraṅgatva*) due to being presented first, the fruit and the operation are first connected by way of the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), and only afterwards with other meanings.

Furthermore, since the fruit (phala) is not presented independently [of the action], the operation itself—qualified by the fruit—is understood as the primary qualificand (viśeṣya) following the word "gamana" (going), and not its opposite; thus, there is no contingency of the cognition that "going is not the operation."

It explains that the "fruit" (*phala*) refers to the portion of the result attained in sequence, such as "softening" (*viklitti*) and so forth. Softening is a state of loosening, a specific kind of separation of parts, or their re-union. And this [softening] is denoted by its specific forms, such as softening and the like, but not by the general form of "fruit-ness. This is because the cognition of it is established by experience only through those respective specific forms; furthermore, even those who do not know [the technical categories] such as "verbal root-ness" (*dhātutva*), such as literary critics (*kāvyajña*) and others, have such a cognition.

For this very reason, when the meaning of the sentence is being demonstrated, the cognition of the result (*phala*) is appropriately stated in its specific forms, such as "conducive to softening" (*viklitti-anukūla*) or "conducive to production" (*utpatti-anukūla*). Although in common worldly usage that which one acts for the sake of is considered the result (*phalatva*), here a technical (*pāribhāṣika*) definition is adopted. Otherwise, since the persistence of hunger—the purpose of cooking—would not be accomplished even after the cooking is finished, the linguistic usage "he cooked" (*apākṣīt*) would be untenable. Likewise, the activities of the virtuous are for the benefit of others.

In cases such as "rivers flow for the benefit of others" (*paropakārāya vahanti nadyaḥ*), since the result in the form of benefiting others resides in a locus different from the operation (*vyāpāravyadhikaraṇa*), even intransitive actions like "setting out" (*pravṛtti*) would incur the status of being transitive. Furthermore, because one observes in the world that an action is undertaken only with some specific aim in view, the conventional distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs would be difficult to maintain.

And the technical definition of being a "result" (phala), which culminates in softening and so forth, is as follows: "In the context of co-occurrence with a suffix denoting an agent, it is that which is the meaning of a verbal root, provided that it is produced by the meaning of that same verbal root and possesses the property of being the locus of the qualifier-nature (prakāratā) as determined by the qualificand-nature (viśeṣyatā) residing in the meaning of that same verbal root."

In the expression "he cooks the rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), the definition [of *phala*] is applicable because the softening (*viklitti*)—which is the meaning of the verbal root *pac*—possesses the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) as determined by a primary objecthood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in such an operation, provided that it is produced by the operation [of heating] which constitutes the meaning of the root *pac*. Similarly, in cases such as "he wards off the boy from the fire" (*agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati*), the status of being a *phala* (result) should be inferred because the definition applies to the absence of an operation conducive to contact—which is the meaning of the root in the sense of an operation conducive to the absence of an operation conducive to contact.

In this context, the phrase "in co-occurrence with a suffix denoting an agent" (*kartṛpratyayasamabhivyāhāre*) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an incidental indicator) and not a restrictive qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*). The point to be understood is that it is not the case that whatever meaning possesses the status of a result (*phalatva*) when in co-occurrence with an agent-suffix must necessarily possess the status of a result when in co-occurrence with an object-suffix as well. Thus, in instances involving object-suffixes—such as *pacyate taṇḍulaḥ* ("the rice is being cooked") or *pakvaḥ taṇḍulaḥ* ("the rice is cooked")—there is no contingency of [the action of] softening (*viklitti*) and so forth failing to be the result, even though they function as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

In this context, if the first part of the definition were stated merely as "being produced" (*janyatve sati*), then undesirable consequences would arise for objects such as the conjunction produced by disjunction (*vibhāgajanya-saṃyoga*) in the case of an action like "falling," because that disjunction is itself produced (by an effort) and thus would result in being a "result" (*phala*). To prevent this, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is specified as a qualifier of "being produced" through the relation of "determinacy" (*nirūpakatā*). The meaning is: "while being produced in a manner determined by the meaning of the verbal root. Since the aforementioned disjunction is not produced in a manner determined by the meaning of the verbal root, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

[Objection: Even so, since separation (*vibhāga*) is produced by some meaning of a verbal root—such as *gam* (to go), which consists of an activity conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location—it remains the case that it would still incur the status of being a "result" (*phala*). [Response: No, because of the qualification "belonging to that [verbal] root. By proximity, the meaning is: provided that there is a state of being produced by the meaning of that specific verbal root, or provided that it has attained the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) relative to the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the meaning of that specific verbal root.

And thus, according to the *Niruktavibhāga*, even though [separation] possesses the status of being a qualifier determined by a primary objectivity (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the connection with the meaning of the root *pat* (to fall), and even though it is the meaning of the root *pat*, it does not have the status of a "result" (*phala*), because it lacks the property of being produced (*janyatva*) in relation to the meaning of the root *pat*. Now, one might object: "In that case, in examples such as 'he goes from Prayāga to Kāśī,' separation would incur the status of a result, since it is produced by the operation (*vyāpāra*) which is the meaning of the root *gam* (to go). This is not so, because of the inclusion of the qualifier "being the meaning of that root" (*taddhātvarthatva*). The meaning is: "the state of being the object of a presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by that specific verbal root."

The meaning of the root *gam* (to go) and similar verbs is an activity conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location (*uttaradeśasaṃyoga*). In this context, since conjunction with a subsequent location is absolutely impossible without a prior disjunction from the previous location, the latter is an inseparable concomitant. Thus, although disjunction is produced by the activity—which constitutes the meaning of the verbal root *gam*—it does not qualify as a "result" (*phala*), because it is not the object presented by the presentation of the verbal root *gam*. This is the intended sense.

If it is objected: "Even so, in the case of 'the leaf falls' (*parṇaṃ patati*), there would be the undesired consequence that the conjunction produced by the disjunction (which is the meaning of the root *pat*) would be a 'result' (*phala*), because it is produced by the disjunction that is the meaning of that root and is itself the meaning of that root"—then, to prevent this, the second qualifier beginning with "residing in the meaning of that root" (*taddhātvarthaniṣṭha*) and ending with "being real" (*satyanta*) is added. Consequently, although the aforementioned conjunction is produced by the meaning of the root *pat* and is indeed the meaning of that root, it is not a result, because it does not possess the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) as determined by the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the meaning of the root *pat*.

And thus, in the meaning of the verbal root *pat* (to fall), the two qualifiers ending in "sat" (being) are included in order to preclude the mutual status of being a result for both disjunction (*vibhāga*) and conjunction (*saṃyoga*). By this, it should be understood that in cases such as "the leaf falls from the tree to the ground," the tree and so forth—the substrata of disjunction—and the ground and so forth—the substrata of conjunction—do not possess the status of an object (*karman*). Furthermore, this is stated according to the view that in some intransitive roots (*akarmaka-dhātu*), the meaning of the root consists of mere activity (*vyāpāra* alone); whereas it is stated with the intention of the general maxim that "the root [denotes] both the result and the activity."

However, it should be understood that if one does not accept that view, the second qualifier—"being true"—need not be included. Thus, the definition of the result (*phala*) is simply: "the state of being the meaning of a verbal root, while being produced by the meaning of that same verbal root. Here, "being produced" (*janyatva*) should be taken as common to both the superimposed (*āropita*) and the non-superimposed (*anāropita*). Consequently, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *īśvaraḥ tiṣṭhati* ("The Lord stands") or *patye śete* ("She lies down for her husband"), because the standing of the Lord and the lying down directed toward the husband are not in fact produced by the meanings of the roots; rather, "being produced" is superimposed upon the standing and the lying down.

The meaning of the root *sthā* (to stand) is an activity conducive to staying. It should be understood that the meaning of the root *śīṅ* (to lie down) is a mental resolve directed toward lying down; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the form *āste* (he sits) is included. Furthermore, in expressions such as *gāṃ payo dogdhi* (he milks the cow for milk), the meaning of the root *duh* is an activity conducive to an activity that is conducive to a separation residing in a liquid substance contained within [the cow].

In this context, the operation (*vyāpāra*) residing in the cow is to be understood as the *phala* (result) because it is produced by the operation denoted by that verbal root, because it has attained the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) relative to the meaning of that verbal root, and because it is the meaning of that verbal root. Furthermore, the separation (*vibhāga*) is also to be understood as the *phala* because it is produced by the operation denoted by that verbal root residing in the cow, and because it possesses both the qualifying and the qualified attributes, such as "residing in the meaning of that verbal root" and so forth. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), examples such as "he leads the goat to the village" (*ajāṃ grāmaṃ nayati*) are included.

If it is argued that, in cases such as "he prevents the boy from the fire" (*agnim māṇavakaṃ vārayati*), the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) itself—just like the absence of an activity conducive to conjunction—would incur the status of a *phala* (result), because it possesses the three characteristics [of being related to the agent, being produced by the activity denoted by the verbal root, and residing in the object], let it be so; for there is no fault merely on that account.

It should not be argued that, since the meaning of the root *nī* (to lead) consists of an operation conducive to an operation conducive to conjunction with the northern region (*uttaradeśa-saṃyoga*), both the village and the fire would incur the status of an object (*karman*)—because the village, like the fire, is the locus of the result in the form of conjunction, which is qualified by being produced by the operation denoted by that root belonging to the goat; for in the definition of the technical term "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*), the result produced by the operation that is the counter-positive of the absence [of the agent's desire] is not taken into account. Otherwise, the rule *vāraṇārthānām* would become an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *kartur īpsitatamam*.

Furthermore, in the case of *māṇavakam* (the boy), the accusative case would likewise not apply; for in examples such as *taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice"), the technical designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) has already served its purpose. In cases such as *paśya mṛgo dhāvati* ("see, the deer runs"), although the running and so forth possess the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) determined by the primary qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the meaning of the root *dṛś* ("to see"), they do not constitute the "result" (*phala*). This is because they lack the quality of being produced (*janyatva*) in relation to the meaning of the root *dṛś*, and because they do not themselves constitute the meaning of the root *dṛś*. Moreover, since the status of being an object that conforms to the principal [action] is more powerful, the deer would not have the status of an "agent" (*kartṛ*).

Thus, in cases such as "one binds a horse in beans" (*māṣeṣvaśvaṃ badhnāti*), when a horse is tied in a bean field specifically for the purpose of eating beans for the sake of nourishment, then because the eating is not produced by the meaning of the verb "binds" (*badhnāti*) and because it is not the meaning of "binds," it does not possess the status of a *phala* (result). Consequently, it should be understood that even though the beans are the locus (*āśraya*) of the eating, they do not possess the status of an *object* (*karman*).

Having thus defined the result (*phala*), he defines the operation (*vyāpāra*) with the words "the operation, however... The definition of an operation is: being denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu*), while simultaneously being the generator of the result denoted by that same verbal root. The meaning is that in cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), because [actions like] blowing and so forth generate the result denoted by the root (such as softening) and are themselves denotable by the root, they possess the status of an operation. If one were to state merely "being denotable by the root," there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the result itself, such as softening, would also be an operation; therefore, the qualifier "while being the generator of the result denoted by the root" is included.

If only that much [the property of being an operation] were stated, then in cases such as "he cooks rice with wood," since the fire-ignition residing in the wood and the softening-responsiveness (mārdavārhatva) residing in the rice would both be operations—because they produce the fruit of the verbal root-meaning, which is the state of being cooked (*viklitti*)—they would incur the status of being operations (*vyāpāratva*). Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*anāpatti*) that the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) and others would not apply. Therefore, the term "denoted by the verbal root" (*dhātuvācyatva*) is added as a qualifier. Thus, by intending that the operation consisting of blowing (*phūtkāra*), etc., residing in Devadatta is what is denoted by the verbal root, there is no fault, because the actions residing in the wood and so forth lack the status of being denoted by the verbal root.

However, when there is an intention to express that actions residing in wood and so forth are denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), they indeed possess the status of an operation (*vyāpāra*). For this very reason, such expressions as "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*) and "the pieces of wood cook" (*kāṣṭhāni pacanti*) are logically consistent; the point is that only the substratum of the operation denoted by the verbal root possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛ*). And thus, it should be understood that the meaning of a verbal root is an operation conducive to a result (*phala*).

One might object: "If, to the question 'What does he do?', the answer is 'He cooks,' whereas there is no such answer for 'He exists,' then verbs like *asti* (to exist) would not be expressive of action. This is not so; for it is with this very intention—that an operation conducive to a result (*phalānukūla-vyāpāra*) is designated by the word 'action' (*kriyā*) in the *Mahābhāṣya* and other works—that the author of the *Bhūṣaṇasāra* stated the definition of action as: "Action is that which is denoted as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena abhidhīyamānā*), namely, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)."

The author will also state that "the operation (*vyāpāra*) is precisely *bhāvanā*; it is generation (*utpādanā*), and it is action (*kriyā*). Thus, the operation itself possesses the nature of action. The word *bhāvanā*—derived from the causative form of the root *bhū* (meaning "to arise") by the rule *ṇyāsa-śrantho yuc* to denote the abstract state (*bhāve*)—expresses an operation conducive to arising. The word *abhidhā*, however, by the etymology "it expresses (*abhidadhāti*) [or] produces (*janayati*) the result," denotes an operation that generates a result.

In this context, the suffix *ka* is applied to the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *abhi* according to the rule *ātaścopasarge*. Thus, the meaning is that "activity" (*vyāpāra*) is a function whose essence consists of an object being denoted as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), which is synonymous with what is termed "productive activity" (*bhāvanā*). Here, the mention of "denotation of productive activity" (*bhāvanābhidhā*) is intended to dispel the misconception that, although the function is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it is specifically the particular sense expressed by words such as "productive activity" that constitutes the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārthatva*).

It should be understood that the statement "it is called action" (*kriyā*) is intended to demonstrate that the root *bhū* when ending in the causative suffix (*ṇic*) has the same meaning as the simple root *kṛ*. Nor should it be argued that, even if the operation that is the meaning of a verbal root is thus declared to be "action," the previously mentioned difficulty regarding the impossibility of "action-ness" for roots such as *as* (to be) remains as it was; for, through the relationship of question and answer based on the distinction between general and particular, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and thus the "action-ness" of the operations that are the meanings of *pac* (to cook) and so forth is established. However, this does not apply to *as* and the like.

When asked "What does he do? regarding someone who is about to perish, the answer "He exists" (*asti*) is universally accepted; therefore, it is easily established that verbs such as *asti* are indeed actions (*kriyā*). Furthermore, since the ground for applying the term "action"—namely, "being perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) without depending on the co-occurrence of another word"—is present in *asti* just as it is in *karoti*, the status of these as actions is proven without effort.

In this context, "being the object of accomplishment" (*sādhyatva*) should be understood as that which is established intrinsically (*svataḥ-siddha*) and independently of the meanings of other words, because that which depends on the meanings of other words is secondary (*gauṇa*). Thus, the definition of "activity" (*vyāpāratva*) is simply the state of being perceived in the form of an object of accomplishment even without the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of another word. The inclusion of the phrase "even without [the co-occurrence of] another word, etc. is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to objects such as a jar in sentences like "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), where the jar is also perceived as an object of accomplishment due to its co-occurrence with the verb "to make."

However, when not used in conjunction with "karoti" and so forth, jars and the like are perceived as already established (*siddha*). It is only through the employment of "karoti" and so forth that the jar is perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), because "karoti" itself is perceived as already established. The meaning is that it is only through the employment of "karoti" and so forth that the jar is perceived as something to be accomplished, whereas "karoti" is established even by its own nature.

The point is that the status of [the action] as the aforementioned operation (*vyāpāra*) remains intact, because the entire collection of actions beginning with placing [the pot] on the fire and ending with taking it off the fire is perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), even in the absence of the employment of other words [to express it]. To refute the claim that the stated meaning is baseless, he says "And it has been said," and so forth. The word "as far as" (*yāvat*) means "entirely. He explains the very meaning of the word "entire" with the passage beginning "established" (*siddha*), and so forth. Thus, the meaning of the word "entire" consists precisely in this twofold nature.

The meaning is as follows: whether a thing already established—as in "he cooked" (*apākṣīt*)—or one not yet established—as in "he cooks" (*pacati*) or "he will cook" (*pakṣyati*)—is called "action" (*kriyā*) when it is expressed in its nature as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and in that specific manner. If it is asked whether this is a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the word "action" for such an object (which is perceived as being inherently to be accomplished), he says "no," and explains: "that which has resorted to a sequence."

The sequence that is resorted to is "resorted-to-sequence" (*āśritakrama*); that which has this very sequence as its form is "having the nature of resorted-to-sequence" (*āśritakramarūpā*). The state of being such is "the nature of having resorted-to-sequence" (*āśritakramarūpatva*); because of that, it is designated as "action" (*kriyā*). For the essential nature of action is that wherein its constituent parts arise sequentially; that is to say, it is the nature of an aggregate of parts arising in succession. This is the intended meaning: the phrase "because of having the nature of resorted-to-sequence" is a demonstration of the referent of the word "action. And thus, it is called "action" (*kriyā*) because it is "being done" (*kriyate*).

In this regard, when the inquiry arises as to "by what is something done" and "what is done," the meaning is that—by way of proximity and through the successive production of its constituent parts—that object which is produced or accomplished in the form of a whole (*samūha*) is called "action" (*kriyā*). In other words, the very nature of action is an object consisting of a whole that is to be accomplished through the successive production of its parts. By this, it is demonstrated that action has the nature of a sequence based on its substrates.

The statement by the learned that "action is successive" is also consistent precisely because action consists of a sequence of dependent stages. Furthermore, it should be understood that it is precisely because action consists of a sequence of dependent stages that its cognition as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is established. Since the constituent parts, beginning with placing [the pot] on the fire and ending with taking it off, arise in succession, the nature of action—defined as the aggregate of operations expressed by verbal roots such as *pac* (to cook)—remains intact.

Where there is no operation involving the sequential production of parts—as in the case of the substratum (āśrayatā) and so forth—one must effect a superimposition (āropa) of the state of having sequential parts upon it. Even in the case of the result (phala), there is a superimposition of the possession of sequential parts belonging to the operation that produces it. For this very reason, the status of being a giver (dātṛtva) based on action is established for that which expresses the mere result. And thus, it is proven that "action" (kriyā) is a collection of operations.

Now, one might object: "Granted that the collection of operations constitutes action (*kriyā*), even so, what is the proof for its cognition in the form of being something-to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*)? In response to this inquiry, [the author] states "pacati," "pākaḥ," and so forth, in order to establish that cognition in the form of being something-to-be-accomplished by means of the evidence consisting in the observation that in some cases there is an expectancy for another action, while in other cases there is no such expectancy.

In the case of *pacati* ("he cooks"), although there is an identical cognition of the verbal root-meaning—the activity conducive to softening—from both the root *pac* and from the suffix *ghañ* in *pāka*, once the action is understood through the word *pacati*, there is no further expectancy for an action; therefore, "sādhyatva" (the state of being an end-in-process) is defined as that form residing in such an action which prevents the arising of expectancy for another action. Thus, he says "tathā ca" and so forth, referring to that which is established as the delimitor of the capacity to obstruct the arising of expectancy for another action.

The meaning is that the specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*) is that very nature which constitutes the state of being an object to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*). This alone is the delimitor of the capacity for connection with the factors of action (*kāraka*), and it is co-locative with the property of having successive parts. It is precisely this established specific universal that is designated by the term "heterogeneity" (*vaijātya*). Whether that heterogeneity is an additional entity or resides solely within words such as *pacati* (he cooks) is another matter. And that state of being an object to be accomplished is everywhere expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*).

Even in forms such as *pāka* ending in the suffix *ghañ*, the action (*kriyā*) is denoted by the root *pac* precisely as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*). For this very reason, in the expression *odanasya pākaḥ* ("the cooking of rice"), the genitive case in the word *odana* is established by the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.65) to denote the object (*karman*). Otherwise, since there is a rule that kārakas can only connect with an action perceived as something to be accomplished, that [genitive] would not be possible. However, by means of *ghañ* and other such suffixes, the action is denoted as something already accomplished (*siddhatvena*), because when "cooking" (*pāka*) is mentioned, there arises an expectancy for another action, such as "it comes into being" or "it has perished."

And *siddhatva* (the state of being accomplished) is the defining characteristic (*avacchedaka-rūpa*) that gives rise to the expectancy for another action. The meaning is that it is the nature of a specific genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*, i.e., *vaijātya*) which, by virtue of being the delimiting factor for the arousal of expectancy for an action, is established as such. And thus, depending on whether there is a connection with the meaning of the verbal root *pac* (to cook), the usage is "a beautiful cooking" (*śobhanaḥ pākaḥ*), or, when connected with the meaning of the suffix *ghañ*, it is "a beautiful act of cooking" (*śobhanaḥ pākaḥ*); in this way, the usage is determined by the distinction between the state of being a goal (*sādhyatva*) and the state of being accomplished (*siddhatva*).

And the author himself will state this further on: "In that context [of words like *pāka*], action is based on the verbal root (*dhātu*) by virtue of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*); however, that aspect of its being an already established entity (*siddha-bhāva*) is based on suffixes such as *ghañ*. The word "there" (*tatra*) means in words ending in *ghañ* and other such suffixes, such as *pāka*. The specific details will be explained later. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the usage of indeclinables (*avyaya*) such as *hiruk* as being "predominantly action" (*kriyā-pradhāna*), which is made in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *taddhitaśca*, would be untenable because their meanings do not appear as things to be accomplished (*sādhya*). This is because [the term "predominantly action"] refers to those [indeclinables] whose meanings are indeed intended as things to be accomplished.

Such usage [of adverbs] is based on their being qualifiers of action alone, because they function like words ending in the suffix *ktvā* and others which denote the meaning of that [suffix]. Just as the meaning of words ending in *ktvā*, prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning "connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusaṃbandha*), serves as a qualifier of action alone—as in the case of "he goes" (*vrajati*)—in the same way, the meanings of indeclinables such as *bahir* and *gā* serve as qualifiers of action alone. By the word "alone" (*mātra*), the exclusion of being a qualifier determined by the meaning of a noun-base (*nāman*) is intended. Thus, the sense is that the usage there is merely figurative (*gauṇa*).

Because the meanings of words such as *hiruk* (separately) lack the status of an action perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena pratīyamāna-kriyātvābhāva*), there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with a *kāraka* (participant in an action) therein; for it is a rule that *kārakas* connect only with an action perceived as something to be accomplished. This is because the meanings of *hiruk* and so forth lack the status of an action perceived [as such], since they possess the quality of not requiring another action to complete their sense (*kriyāntarākāṅkṣāsattva*).

[Objection: But surely, if *api* is excluded by a form that does not give rise to an expectancy for another action (*kriyāntara*) based on its verbal root (*dhātu*), then in the sentence "If one should bow to Kṛṣṇa, one would attain happiness," there would be no connection between the actions of bowing and attaining happiness as cause and effect due to the absence of such an expectancy. [Response: This is not so, because the expectancy is aroused through the assistance of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word *cet*. Others, however, maintain that being an end to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) is simply the state of being produced (*niṣpādyatva*), since it is established by experience that the cognition occurs precisely in that form.

This is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *suṭ‌kātpūrvaḥ*. For there, after stating that "the operation between a verbal root and a prefix is internal (*antaraṅga*)," it is said: "This is not the essence; rather, first the root is joined with its grammatical factor (*sādhana*), and afterwards with the prefix. For the factor brings about the action, and the prefix qualifies that [action]."

The *sādhana* (means of accomplishment) is the suffix (*pratyaya*) that makes it known; it brings about the action by making it known as characterized by the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*). Therefore, the elders have stated that the grammatical operation (*kārya*) prompted by that [suffix] occurs first. On the authority of this *Bhāṣya*, the manifestation [of the action] as something to be accomplished is accepted. Thus, when the meaning of roots such as *pac* is known as something to be accomplished, there necessarily arises an expectancy for its means of accomplishment (*sādhanākāṅkṣā*); consequently, "being something to be accomplished" (*sādhyatva*) is precisely the possession of that form which delimits the capacity to arouse the expectancy for a means of accomplishment.

For this very reason, in expressions such as "having eaten rice, he goes" (*odanaṃ bhuktvā vrajati*), there occurs a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the act of eating and its factors (*kāraka*s), such as the rice. Otherwise, since the suffix *-ktvā* is prescribed in connection with a verbal root (*dhātu*), and because the act of eating would possess an expectancy for an action such as "going," it would not appear as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—that is, by means of a property that does not give rise to an expectancy for another action—and consequently, the connection of factors like "rice" would not be possible therein. Furthermore, the act of eating would not have the status of being the meaning of the verbal root.

Because there is a rule that the connection of *kārakas* (factors of action) occurs only with an action (*kriyā*) that is perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*). The phrase "of such [an action]" means "of an action perceived as something to be accomplished. This is also because such an action alone constitutes the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Thus, they say that in cases such as "If one should bow to Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇaṃ namet cet*), since the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) raised by the word *cet* is seen even though the aforementioned state of being perceived as something to be accomplished does not manifest, defects such as over-extension (*ativyāpti*) certainly occur. He states that "the state of being characterized by that form" (*tadrūpavattvam*) is precisely this aforementioned state of being something to be accomplished, which is the nature of non-substantiality (*asattvabhūtatva*).

The intention is as follows: once it is established that there exists a distinct class (*vaijātya*) residing solely in the operation (*kriyā*) inherent in the verbal root (*dhātu*), it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to accept that this very [class] constitutes the nature of non-existence (*asattva*), rather than postulating some other [property] such as the lack of connection with gender, number, and so forth. However, that aforementioned distinct class is indeed co-locatable (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the lack of connection with gender and the rest.

"Etadeva" (this very thing) means precisely by keeping in mind that state of being non-substantial (*asattvabhūtatva*), which is non-different from the previously mentioned state of being an object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatva*). "And the state of being non-substantial" (*asattvabhūto bhāvaśca*): the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*); the meaning is "the state of being [only] substantial" (*bhāva eva*). By the restrictive particle "eva," there is the exclusion of a state of being substantial (*sattvabhūta-bhāva*). "By *tiṅ*-words" means by words ending in *tiṅ*-suffixes. Regarding the phrase "is denoted" (*abhidhīyate*), the ellipsis is "primarily" (*prādhānyena*), and so forth. Thus, the meaning is that the state of being non-substantial, indeed, is denoted primarily by *tiṅ*-ending words such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), and so on.

Therefore, even when denoting a state that has not yet attained substantial existence (*asattvabhūtabhāva*) by means of words ending in primary suffixes (*kṛdanta*) functioning as qualifiers, there is no deficiency whatsoever. And the phrase "this [action]" means that it consists of an action perceived as being in the state of being accomplished (*sādhyatvena*). The meaning is that it is the denotable object (*śakya*) of roots such as *pac* (to cook) in its various specific forms, such as the nature of blowing (*phūtkāratva*) or the nature of heating from below (*adhaḥsaṃtāpanatva*). He states the reason for this with the passage ending in "...because it is established by experience (*anubhava*) in such cases as 'he cooks' (*pacati*)."

For this very reason, once a verbal cognition has arisen from expressions such as "he cooks" (*pacati*) in its specific forms—such as the nature of blowing (*phūtkāratva*) and so forth—the doubt "Does he possess this blowing or not? does not arise. However, if the cognition were in a general form, the occurrence of doubt would be unavoidable due to the absence of certainty regarding either alternative; such is the meaning.

Now, if it is admitted that, by the force of such experience, from expressions like "he cooks" (*pacati*) there arises a cognition of specific forms such as "spitting" (*phūtkāra*) and so forth, then—since the delimiters of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), such as "spitting-ness" (*phūtkāratva*) and the rest, are manifold, and since it is impossible to speak of a single [unitary] power—the consequence would follow that roots like *pac* have multiple meanings (*nānārtha*). For multiplicity of meaning consists precisely in the possession of a single property that serves as the delimiter of the relatum of the power, while the delimiters of the power itself are manifold properties.

As stated in the lexicon: "The word *hari* [denotes] Viṣṇu, Indra, a frog, a lion, a horse, and the sun," the word *hari* possesses a primary expressive power (*śakti*), known as denotation (*vācyatā*), with respect to lions, horses, and the sun, in the form of the properties of being a lion, being a horse, and being the sun. And that [power] is delimited by various properties such as "lion-ness" (*siṃhatva*) and so forth.

The word *hari* is the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of such a power; the property that delimits the determinateness (*nirūpakatāvacchedaka*) residing in that [power] is the phonetic sequence *harī-* (the letters *ha*, *rī*, etc.). Since that [sequence] is one and the same, the state of possessing such a single property exists in the word *hari*; thus, the application of the definition—that the word *hari* has multiple meanings—is established. The point is that this remains unimpaired in the case of words such as *pac* (to cook). To avoid the contingency of [words like *pac*] having multiple meanings, he says: "by the principle of *tadādi* (and so forth)."

Although objects such as pots and cloths are understood from words like "that" (tat) and so forth by way of their respective specific properties such as "pot-ness," they are nevertheless not called "multivalent" (anekārtha) in the same way that words like "hari" are. This is because, by way of a single property consisting in being the object of a recurring cognition delimited by various properties such as pot-ness, multiple objects possessing those various properties are understood from them.

Furthermore, a word that conveys objects possessing various properties by means of a single, recurring property as its primary qualifier does not possess multiple meanings. This is like the word "substance" (*dravya*), which conveys objects such as pots and cloths by virtue of their commonality as substances. For a word is considered to have multiple meanings only when it possesses a single property that serves as the delimiting factor for the denotative power (*śakti*) as it is determined by various non-recurring, distinct properties.

Now, one might object: "In that case, since it is appropriate for that very form by which [an object] is cognized to be the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), and since the delimitor of denotability is the object of the apprehension of the word's power (*śakti*), it would follow that 'being an object of cognition' (*buddhiviṣayatva*)—just like 'pot-ness' (*ghaṭatva*)—would appear in the verbal cognition produced by words such as *tad* (that) and so forth. Consequently, the cognition desired from words like *tad* in its specific forms such as 'pot-ness' would not occur. If this is argued, we say: no.

Since being the object of cognition (*buddhiviṣayatva*) functions as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), and since a secondary indicator—by virtue of not being the object of the apprehension of a word’s denotative power (*śakti*)—does not appear in verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), there is no fault. Furthermore, being a secondary indicator consists in not being the object of the apprehension of a word’s denotative power by way of being the object of the cognition produced by that word. As stated by the authors of the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*: "The apprehension of the denotative power of words such as 'that' (*tadādi*) is precisely this: 'The word "that" and so forth has its denotative power residing in those things which possess pot-ness and the like, presented under the form of being objects of cognition, and which possess the delimitors of being objects of cognition.'"

"The state of being an object of cognition (*buddhiviṣayatva*) is merely a common feature (*anugamaka*) in the case of presentation (*upasthiti*), but there is no denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to that [common] aspect. This is the principle of *tad-ādi* (words like "that" and so forth). Similarly, in the present case as well, since there exists a specific cognition—such as the cognition having blowing (*phūtkāra*) and so forth as its object—which serves as the sub-stratum of the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakāvacchedaka*) and acts as a common feature for the delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) such as "blowing-ness" (*phūtkāratva*) and so on, [the word denotes them] by way of that specific cognition which has become a mere qualifier (*upalakṣaṇa*) in the form of being an object of cognition.

The point is this: since it is possible to accept that verbal roots such as *pac* (to cook) have their denotative power (*śakti*) restricted by a specific cognition—characterized by being the object of a cognition—that serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), there is no contingency of polysemy (*nānārthatva*). This is because, even though the delimiters of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) are multiple, there can still be a single delimiter for those delimiters themselves. The cognition functions as the delimiter of denotability through the relation of "objectness" (*viṣayatā-sambandha*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the state of being the object of a specific cognition is included.

In this regard, some, in order to avoid the fault of polysemy (*nānārthatva*), postulate a specific universal (*jāti*) called "action-ness" (*kriyātva*), which is common to all these [instances such as blowing], co-referential with the denotability of the verbal root, and which is established as the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word *kriyā*, just as "water-ness" (*jalatva*) is established as the delimitor of the denotative capacity of the word *jala*. They argue that since blowing and so forth are perceived under the form of action-ness, verbs such as *pac* do not possess polysemy at all. This is not correct.

Because there is a rule that the capacity for cognition belongs only to that form which serves as the delimitor of possibility (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*), it follows that cognition would not occur through those various specific forms. Nor should it be argued that cognition occurs in its specific form by virtue of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words such as *pac* (to cook); for this would entail the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) due to postulating a cognition in both general and specific forms simultaneously. Furthermore, it is not accepted that verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) proceeds by taking a property (*dharma*) that is merely being postulated as its primary basis.

Otherwise, since the property of being a horse or salt would have to be postulated as the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) for words such as *saindhava*, there would be the consequence of assuming a single common property residing in both horses and salt; consequently, the status of such words as having multiple meanings (*nānārtha*) would be abolished. If it is argued that no assumption of an additional property is appropriate in those cases because the cognition [of the object] occurs through the property of "horseness" (*aśvatva*) and so on, as is established by experience—then here too, the cognition occurs through the property of "blowing" (*phūtkāratva*) and so on, as is established by experience.
