Therefore, just as in the case of the word *hari* and others, the multiplicity of meaning (*nānārthatva*) for verbs such as *pac* (to cook) is indeed accepted.

Others, however, maintain that since words such as *tad* (that) have cognition as their object, they convey meaning only through the general form of the universal (*sāmānya*), as is evident from the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *śeṣe* and other sources. Regarding the phrase "in the case of the verb, there is unity of action" (*ākhyāte kriyaikatve*), the intended meaning is as follows: an aggregate of operations (*vyāpārasamūha*) composed of parts produced in succession is called "action" (*kriyā*).

In this regard, since the operations of the constituent parts are manifold, momentary, and sequential, they cannot exist simultaneously; thus, because a collection [of such parts] is impossible, it is impossible to say that "one action" is expressed by the verb on the basis of an intended unity residing in that collection. Consequently, when the established rule that "one action is conveyed by the verbal suffix" appears untenable, the author establishes that very rule with the words beginning "vyavasthāpi" (the establishment also). The term "establishment" (*vyavasthā*) refers to the restriction that "there is one action"; the particle *api* (also) is a conjunctive particle used here to include the avoidance of the consequence of having multiple meanings.

Regarding the term *avacchedaka*: the operations beginning with placing [the pot] on the fire and ending with taking it off are the capacities (*śakyāḥ*). The properties residing in those [operations], such as "being the act of placing on the fire" (*adhiśrayaṇatva*) and so forth, are the delimiters of capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). The meaning is: having grasped the unity of that specific mental state (*buddhiviśeṣa*) which is the delimiter of those [properties]. That property by which there is capacity is the delimiter of capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

The sense is as follows: since the capacities (śakyatāvacchedaka) such as "placing on the fire" (adhiśrayaṇa) and so forth possess their status as capacities by virtue of being objects of a single cognition (buddhiviṣayatva), the cognition itself—acting as the substrate—is the property that delimits the delimitation of the capacity (śakyatāvacchedakatāvacchedaka-dharma) through the relation of objecthood (viṣayatā-sambandha). And since that cognition is one and of the nature of a collective apprehension (samūhālambana), the unity residing in such a cognition is superimposed upon the operations of placing on the fire and so forth; thus, there is the established conclusion that "the action is one. Alternatively, the meaning is: "having grasped the unity belonging to the collection residing in such a cognition."

He cites the *Vākyapadīya* as an authority for his own stated position, beginning with the words "And it has been said," etc. Regarding the phrase "by those that have become subordinate": a collection is designated by the term "action" (*kriyā*) when it consists of a group of operations—such as placing [the pot on the fire] and so forth—which, though existing in the intellect and arising in a sequential order, are subordinated to the aggregate; that is, they are joined with constituent parts appearing in their respective forms such as blowing [on the fire], and this group, whose nature is non-difference, is conceptually constructed (*prakalpita*) by a unifying cognition (*saṃkalanātmikā buddhi*) which takes unity as its object (a cognition consisting of a collective apprehension). Such a group is what is conventionally termed "action."

This is the meaning. Here, since the term *guṇabhūtaiḥ* would result in tautology if it meant "being constituent parts" (*aṅgabhūtaiḥ*), the word *guṇa* refers to a property (*dharma*). The word *bhūta*, according to the maxim "those [roots] which have the sense of reaching (*prāpti*) have the sense of knowing (*jñāna*)," and because the root *bhū* is said to mean "to reach," is a past passive participle (*kta*) ending in the present sense and thus refers to knowledge. Therefore, it means "appearing in those respective forms. It is stated that they perceive the "aggregate" (*samūha*) due to proximity. Since an aggregate of real entities is impossible for things that perish in a moment, it is stated that they perceive it "by means of the intellect" (*buddhyā*).

Thus, the meaning is that the conventional usage of a "collection" (samūha) is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by the intellect, and not something real. As stated by Patañjali: "Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is that which follows upon verbal cognition and is devoid of a real object. Its meaning is as follows: it is a "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) because it has the nature of following after mere verbal cognition within the intellect and is devoid of an external object; it is "constructed" (*kalpyate*) specifically [by thought]. In this context, it is clearly understood that there is a sequence based on the parts and a unity based on the whole.

The intention [of this statement] is that it serves to indicate the commonality (*anugamaka*) of the delimiters of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), such as the state of being a "Buddha" (*buddhasthatva*). Now, an objection might be raised: "If the operation (*vyāpāra*) consists of a collection (*samudāya*), then the usage 'the pot cooks' (*stālī pacati*) would be impossible, since it refers to each individual act such as placing [the pot on the fire] (*adhiśrayaṇa*) and so forth. This is not so; for even in each single constituent part, there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of the nature of a whole (*samūhatva*), and thus the usage is justified. And regarding this superimposition, the very cognition of such a thing is the proof (*pramāṇa*). For this very reason, it was stated by Bhartṛhari: "The verbal roots *pac* and others [denote] either a single part or the collection of operations."

"They proceed by way of their own nature, relying upon a common form. Regarding the phrase "common form," the meaning is that these elements (dhātus) are endowed with a common, non-different nature; thus they are non-distinct. By this, it is clearly stated that because the cognition "he cooks" persists everywhere, there is a superimposition of the entire aggregate—which is not yet complete in every single part—upon each individual constituent part.

In reality, even an action such as placing [the pot] on the fire does not consist of a single moment; for it possesses constituent parts such as the stretching out of the hand, the taking up of the vessel, and the joining with the stove. Thus, it too must be understood as being essentially a collection. It should be understood that the grasp of the relationship—namely, the expressive power (*śakti*)—of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) occurs only through an action that has been apprehended via superimposition (*adhyāsa*). For this very reason, one does not say "he cooked" (*apākṣīt*) merely because the act of blowing has passed away while other operations are still in a present state; this is because the pastness and other temporal qualities are connected with the entire aggregate. This is how it should be known.

Objection: Since it is denotable in its specific form, the verbal cognition would have to be "the blowing and so forth conducive to softening," and not "the operation conducive to softening" in a general form. Reply: This is not so. Because roots have multiple meanings (*anekārthatva*), it is accepted that sometimes they convey [the action] in a general form as "action-ness" (*kriyātva*). In that case, whatever is present in the speaker's mind at that time is what is denoted; at that very time, its substratum is the agent (*kartṛ*). As stated by Hari: "When the action has been expressed by the root, agency is always intended for the *kāraka*."

For this very reason, expressions such as "the wood cooks" (*kāṣṭhaṃ pacati*) and "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*) are logically consistent. By this same principle, the expression "he cooks with that wood" (*etena kāṣṭhena pacati*) is also not untenable; for in that case, the operation of the wood is not intended to be expressed as the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Thus, the objection that "if the action of the wood were denoted, the instrumental case would not occur, and if it were not denoted, the nominative case would not occur," and so forth, is refuted. In this context, the delimitor of the capacity (*śakti*) is the state of being a cook (*pacitva*) and so on, which consists in specific sequential orders (*ānupūrvī*), and not the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*).

The point is that since that [property of being a verbal root] exists even in the case of *gacchati* and so forth, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasakti*); and that which is over-extended cannot serve as a delimitor of expressive power (*śaktatānavacchedaka*), because only a property that occurs neither less nor more than [the relevant set] can function as a delimitor.

Having thus briefly defined the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), he begins to speak [on the next topic] with the words "But regarding the locus" (*āśraye tu*). Although, between the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*), the operation is generally primary, because the locus of the result—the object (*karman*)—was mentioned first in the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca* and in the root-text (*mūla*) as "the giver of the result and the operation," he speaks accordingly: "in the locus of the result," "the locus of the result is the object," and so forth.

The meaning is that, according to the principle of the artificial (*kṛtrima*) and the non-artificial (*akṛtrima*), it is appropriate for the terms *karman* (object) and *kartṛ* (agent) to refer only to the substratum of the operation toward the fruit and the substratum of the operation itself, and not to the worldly [notions] of motion and the possession of volition (*kṛti*). This is because the rule *svatantraḥ kartā* (P. 1.4.54) prescribes the technical designation *kartṛ* for one who is independent and is the substratum of the primary operation denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*). The point is that if the designation *kartṛ* were prescribed only for one possessing volition (*kṛtimat*), then in cases such as *ghaṭo bhavati* ("the pot comes into being") or *kāṣṭhāni pacanti* ("the pieces of wood cook"), the designation would not apply to the pot and so forth.

In this regard, since the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are obtained through the verbal root (*dhātu*), the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) has no denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to those two parts; rather, its power resides in the substratum (*āśraya*) alone. This is stated by the words beginning with "tatra" (in that case). The phrase "because they are obtainable from another" follows the maxim that "only that which cannot be obtained otherwise is the meaning of a word. The sense is that once the result and the operation are already obtained by the verbal root itself, to postulate a further denotative power for the finite verb in respect to them would lead to unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Now, if one accepts that the power [of the finite verb] resides in the substratum, then "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*) must be stated as the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). And "substratum-ness" is simply the state of being a locus (*ādhāratva*).

And that [agency] is differentiated according to the differences among its qualifiers (*nirūpaka*) and so forth. Thus, because the nature of substratum-ness (*āśrayatva*) is manifold, there would follow a plurality of powers (*śakti*); therefore, he says "that-that" (*tattad*). The meaning is that the nature of the power of agency and so forth is partless (*akhaṇḍa*). Although it must necessarily be admitted that even the power of agency and so forth is manifold due to the difference among its qualifiers.

Otherwise, in the case of "Having eaten today, he will eat in two days" or "after two days," even if the word *akāraka* (non-agent) in the rule *saptamīpañcamyau kārakamadhye* refers to capacity (*śakti*), there would be an impossibility of using the seventh or fifth case endings after the word *dvyaha* (two days)—which denotes time situated between two capacities of agency—because the capacity of agency is unitary.

The point is this: although there is no inconsistency in the agency-power (*kartṛtva-śakti*) being distinct from the two acts of eating—the present act of eating and the subsequent act of eating—nevertheless, since that [agency] is subsumed under the nature of being a substratum (*āśrayatātva*), it is the delimiting factor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Consequently, defects such as the multiplicity of powers (*śaktinānātva*) do not arise. Now, what is the proof for the claim that both the substratum of the result and the substratum of the operation are denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta* = *tiṅ*)? It might be argued that when one says "he cooks" (*pacati*), the cognition of a substratum arises, and this would lead one to postulate the denotative power of the suffix in that regard. However, this is not so.

It must be said that just as the cognition of an object possessing a conch-shaped neck and so forth, arising from the word "jar" (ghaṭa), leads one to postulate a denotative power (śakti) in the word "jar" for such an object—on the basis of the logical principle that "whatever is cognized from something is the denotation of that thing"—because it is only a cognition that cannot be accounted for otherwise that serves as a valid means of knowledge (māna). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating a denotative power even in the word "Gaṅgā" for objects such as the riverbank.

If it is argued that the explanation is achieved through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone, the author, intending to show that the same can be explained otherwise even in the present case, asks with the words beginning "But as for these two," etc. This doubt is raised according to the Mīmāṃsaka view; for they maintain that the fruit is the meaning of the verbal root, while the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is *bhāvanā* (the activity conducive to the fruit). He explains the cognition [of the substratum] arising when one says "he cooks" (*pacati*) by providing an alternative interpretation. The phrase "from the cognition" means from the cognitions of both the substratum of the fruit and the substratum of the activity.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here is with the phrase "due to its arising" (*asyāḥ saṃbhavāt*). He demonstrates this arising by saying "by means of indication" (*lakṣaṇayā*). The sense is that, just as the bank of the Gaṅgā is apprehended from the word "Gaṅgā" through indication, so too is its substratum apprehended from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), which denotes the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). An objection is raised: if there were indication of the substratum in the verbal suffix, the cognition of the productive activity would not occur.

To avoid the necessity of postulating a power (*śakti*) for the verb in the sense of productive activity (*bhāvanā*), it would be impossible to resort to indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the substratum (*āśraya*), because of the contradiction of two simultaneous functions (*vṛtti*). Furthermore, even if one were to resort to indirect indication in the substratum of the productive activity by way of being its locus, the productive activity would not be perceived as primary. Moreover, there would be the consequence of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) if one were to resort to indirect indication in the qualified entity. For these reasons, he says "by implication" (*ākṣepāt*). In the Mīmāṃsā system, "implication" (*ākṣepa*) means presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); however, in the Tārkika system, it is inference (*anumāna*).

Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is as follows: when something is not possible without another thing, that [other] thing is postulated on its account. For example, in the case of "The fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," since his fatness—which is not produced by practices such as yoga—is not possible without eating, eating is postulated; and because of the prohibition "he does not eat during the day," this postulation culminates in the conclusion that he eats at night. Similarly, in the present context, since the mental modification (*bhāvanā*, i.e., the operation) is not possible without an agent, it postulates its own substratum in the form of an agent. This is the intended meaning.

In the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), however, the meaning is as follows: taking *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) as the subject (*pakṣa*), its possession of an agent is established by the inference "because it is an effect, like a cloth. This [inference] entails the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, which is what is meant by "entailment" (*ākṣepa*). Likewise, since even a result (*phala*) is untenable without its own substratum, that substratum would be entailed by it. Since it is accepted that even what is obtained through entailment can be an object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), there is no contradiction in the cognition of *bhāvanā* within the verbal cognition produced by a verb ending (*ākhyāta*).

Now, since the recollection of word-meanings produced by words is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), it is improper to claim that what is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*) can be an object of verbal cognition. Furthermore, if the agent and so forth were merely implied, there would be the impossibility of the number denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) co-referentially connecting with them; for the agent and so forth would not be presented through a linguistic function (*vṛtti*). This is according to the maxim: "A linguistic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is fulfilled only by a word."

Because the [objection] that [the agenthood] is precluded by the establishment of the object of verbal cognition is raised, he says "or from a word ending in the nominative case" (*prathamāntapadāt*) out of dissatisfaction with that meaning. The intended sense is this: since the apprehension of the substratum (*āśraya*) is possible from the very first-case-ending word such as "Devadatta" which is co-occurrent with [the verb], the cognition [of the substratum] is not a proof for postulating a denotative power (*śakti*) of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) toward the substratum. Therefore, he says "here it is replied" (*atrocyate*), and so forth. He cites the Pāṇinian sūtra *laḥ karmaṇi ca* as an authority for the view that the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) have denotative power toward both the substratum of the result and the substratum of the operation.

One might object: "Does this sūtra not cause one to grasp the capacity [of verbal suffixes] for the *karman* (object), rather than for the *kartṛ* (agent), because no word denoting an agent is heard therein? Anticipating this doubt, he says "atra hi" and so forth. By the word "ca" (and), the word "kartari" ending in the locative case from the preceding sūtra (*kartari kṛt*) is drawn over into the present sūtra; this is the meaning. One might grant that there is such an attraction of the word "kartari," yet this sūtra would only cause one to understand the capacity of the *lakāras* themselves for the sense of the agent and so on. To this he replies: "bodhakatārūpām" and so forth.

The meaning is "in the form of being the producer of understanding. "The capacity residing in *tiP* and so forth" means the capacity located in *tiP*, etc. This is the underlying idea: since only *tiP* and other suffixes are heard at the time of usage, and since the comprehension of meaning arises from them alone, it is more parsimonious to superimpose upon the *l*-suffix—which is postulated as the substitute for *tiP* and others for the sake of systematic derivation—the capacity residing in *tiP* and so forth, which consists in being the producer of meaning. Thus, by this rule (*Pāṇini 3.4.69*), the *l*-suffixes are prescribed in the sense of the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*). This is the intended purport.

The sense is that the teacher Pāṇini has explicitly stated by his own voice that the finite verbal suffix (tiṅ), which is denoted by the term "verb" (ākhyātapada), possesses a denotative power (śakti) with respect to its locus (āśraya). Now, an objection may be raised: since the understanding of meaning is already established from the suffixes *ti* and so forth, and because the letter *l* is never heard in actual usage, let the suffixes *ti*, *tas*, and so on, be prescribed independently by the rule "tiptasjhi... without mentioning *la*.

If it is argued that one should instead formulate the rules by placing the term *tiṅ* in the position of *laṭ*—according to the sequence "the *tiṅ* [suffixes] are used for the present tense" (*vartamāne tiṅ*) and "the *śatṛ* and *śānac* [suffixes] are used when not coreferential with a word ending in a non-first-case *tiṅ*" (*tiṅaḥ śatṛśānacāvaprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe*)—and then prescribe the times such as the present by way of restating *tib* and so on, we say no. This is because it would result in the inconsistency of rules such as "the *ṭi* of the *ātmanepada* suffixes following a *ṭit* [lakāra]" (*ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere*), which prescribes the substitution of *e* for the *ṭi* of those *ātmanepada* suffixes prescribed in place of a *ṭit* *lakāra*.

[Objection: Since there is no such thing as a *tiṅ* suffix ending in *ṭ*, one might argue that by formulating rules such as "in the present tense, *tiṅ* [is used]" (*vartamāne tiṅ*) or "in the recent past, *tiṅ* [is used]" (*anadyatane tiṅ*), one could attach those respective indicatory letters (*anubandhas*) to the *tiṅ* suffixes expressing those specific times. In this way, rules such as "for the *ātmanepada* endings ending in *ṭ*" (*ṭita ātmanepadānām*) would not be inconsistent. [Response: Even so, rules such as "for *liṭ*, *ta* and *jha* become *eś* and *irec*" (*liṭastajhayoreśirec*) and "for the first person of *luṭ*, *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*" (*luṭaḥ prathamasya ḍāraurasaḥ*) would become inconsistent. Since composing alternative formulations for each of those cases would lead to excessive complexity (*gaurava*), let us leave the matter at that.

Regarding the superimposition (*āropa*) upon the imagined substituendum (*sthānin*) of the expressive power residing in the substitute (*ādeśa*), he provides an illustration: in cases such as *rāmān* and *rāmaiḥ*, since the respective meanings are understood from the nasal *n* and the visarga (*visarga*) themselves, there is a rule that the expressive power residing in those [substituenda] belongs only to the substituendum when it possesses meaning within the context of the relation between substituendum and substitute. Thus, by superimposing [that power] onto the aggregate formed by that substituendum, the suffixes *śas*, *bhis*, and so on, are prescribed for the purposes of the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*). This is the intended sense. He raises a doubt regarding the subject matter of the sūtra *laḥ karmaṇi ca* with the words "na cet" (if not).

In the sūtra *laḥ karmaṇi*, the terms *karman* (object) and *kartṛ* (agent) signify the properties (*dharma*) of objecthood and agenthood respectively. This is because the reference is "predominant in its abstract state" (*bhāvapradhānanirdeśāt*). [The meaning of this is: from the utterance of the word [the suffix], there arises a cognition in which the abstract property—defined as the qualifier (*prakāra*) produced by the base—is predominant, that is, the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and where [that property] is primary. The intended sense is that [the words] generate a cognition through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), wherein the natural qualifier functions as the qualificand and the [actual] qualificand functions as the qualifier.

Just as "potness" (ghaṭatva) is that which resides in the pot, so too the word "pot" has the potness as its qualificand; this is also because of parsimony (*lāghava*). If, however, the word were taken to refer to the substratum (*dharmin*), then one would have to postulate a denotative power (*śakti*) for the word "pot" not only in the pot qualified by potness, but also in the object qualified by the state of being an object (*karmatva*), and in the agent qualified by effort (*kṛti*). Consequently, one would have to accept an infinite number of fruits and efforts as the delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), which results in extreme prolixity (*gaurava*).

The meaning is that, however, since the capacity [of the action] resides in the effort (*kṛti*), and because "effort-ness" (*kṛtitva*) is a single universal (*jāti*), there is simplicity (*lāghava*) due to the unity of the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Agency (*kartṛtva*) is effort, and objecthood (*karmatva*) is the result. Now, if it is asked whether agency and objecthood are inherently of the nature of effort and result respectively, it is said in reply: the word *kartṛ* (agent), which is derived from the root *kṛ* (meaning "exertion") with the suffix *tṛc* in the sense of the agent, expresses the meaning "one who possesses exertion."

The suffix following that [verbal root], however, is a non-relational suffix (*apratyaya*) and denotes the effort (*yatna*) which serves as a qualifier for the cognition produced by the verbal base (*prakṛti*). Since effort is action (*kṛti*), it is established that agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in the nature of action. Furthermore, because the term "object" (*karman*) is technical (*pāribhāṣika*), referring to the substratum of the result (*phala*), and because the suffix following that [verbal root] conveys the result which functions as a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal base, it is established that objecthood (*karmatva*) consists in the nature of the result. This is the meaning.

The meaning is that since both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are already conveyed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself, it is utterly improper to postulate a further denotative power (*śakti*) for the suffix (*lakāra*) in that regard; thus, this sūtra does not intend to teach that the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) possesses a denotative power for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). "According to the method of another system" (*darśanāntarīyarītyā*): "another system" (*darśanāntara*) refers to a different philosophical view, namely the Mīmāṃsā system; the phrase means "according to its method. "Because it is not the meaning of the root" (*dhātvarthatvābhāvāt*): The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the result alone—such as the softening of rice (*viklitti*)—is the meaning of the root, while the operation is the meaning of the suffix.

Because it is more parsimonious (lāghava) to postulate the expressive power (śakti) for a few suffixes such as *ti* and others in that regard, rather than postulating the power for many verbal roots (*dhātu*) in their operation; and because the analysis of *pacati* as "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*) shows that the fruit (*phala*) is the meaning of the root; and because the analysis of the verb ending *ti* by means of the root *kṛ*, which signifies productive activity (*bhāvanā*), establishes that it is the suffix (the verb ending) alone that has the meaning of productive activity (*vyāpāra/bhāvanā*). This is because it is an established principle that the analyzed term and its analysis must have the same meaning.

And in that case, since the [action] would not be obtainable from the verbal root (*dhātu*), the prescription of the *l*-suffixes for the action (*vyāpāra*) would be possible. If it is argued that even though the result (*phala*) is obtainable from the verbal root, the prescription of the *l*-suffixes would apply to "objecthood" (*karmatva*) in the form of being the locus of that result, then the *kṛt* suffixes such as *ṇvul*, *tavyat*, and so on—which are prescribed for the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) and others—would also fail to denote the agent and the object. This is because one would have to admit that the words "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "object" (*karman*) found in sūtras such as *kartari kṛt* and *tayoreva*, like the words "agent" and "object" in the sūtra *laḥ karmaṇi ca*, refer to the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) and the state of being an object (*karmatva*).

If, out of a mere partiality for parsimony, it is accepted that the words *kartṛ* and *karman* occurring in the sūtra *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69) denote the properties of agency (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*), then it is equally appropriate to accept that the words *kartṛ* and *karman* occurring in sūtras such as *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67) also denote the properties of agency and objecthood; for the words *kartṛ* and *karman* in the sūtra *laḥ karmaṇi...* are intended to signify the properties consisting of agency and objecthood, whereas in the sūtras such as *kartari kṛt*... [they are likewise intended to signify those same properties].

The meaning is that there would be a lack of uniformity (*vaiṣamya*) in this way, as the [suffixes] would be intent upon the property-possessor (*dharmin*) qualified by the property (*dharma*). Thus, the intention is that while being a "blowing" (*phūtkāratva*) and so forth would be the delimitor of the denotatum (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) for suffixes such as *ṇvul*, whereas being "softening" (*viklittitva*) and so forth would be the delimitor of the denotatum for suffixes such as *tavya*, but not "substratumness" (*āśrayatva*). "Equal in fortune and misfortune" (*tulyayogakṣema*) means that its "yoga-kṣema"—that is, its capacity to convey the meaning—is equal.

[Objection: Surely, in the case of "Devadatta is a cook," the denotation of the agent and so forth by the word [ending in] *-pācaka* must necessarily be accepted on the strength of the experience of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) with Devadatta; however, the acquisition of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) will be established through implication (*ākṣepa*). Similarly, since non-difference is observed here in "Devadatta cooks," let it be that verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) denote the agent; let there be no denotability (*vācyatva*) of the *bhāvanā*, as its acquisition through implication is possible. To this, he says: "Moreover" (*api ca*), etc. "Of the Mīmāṃsakas"—the word "in the opinion" (*mate*) is to be supplied.

Now, if verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) denote the agent, how is it that the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is understood from them? To this, he says: "Of the productive activity itself," and so forth. "That being the case" means: if [the productive activity] were obtainable through implication (*ākṣepa*). "It would not be" means: because the productive activity would not be directly expressed by the verbal suffix, it would lack primacy; for the principle is that only the directly expressed meaning appears as primary. Otherwise, in cases such as "Bring the fire," there would be the undesirable consequence of even the implied vessel appearing as primary.

He refutes the aforementioned undesirable consequence with the words "if it be said—no. He establishes that even in verbal forms such as *ghaṭam ānaya* ("bring the jar"), the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), though obtainable through implication (*ākṣepa*), possesses the status of the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣyatva*).

The meaning is as follows: once it has been determined—through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and through parsimony (*lāghava*)—that the word-meaning (*padārtha*) is the universal (*jāti*), then because it is impossible for a universal, which is formless (*amūrta*), to be connected with actions such as "bringing," one must accept that the individual (*vyakti*) which is the substratum of that universal and is implied by it is primary, on the strength of experience. In the same way, it is possible to establish that the primacy of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), which is implied by the agent denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), is established by experience.

The sense is that by this, the deviation from the rule that "only the expressed meaning (vācyārtha) is primary" has been demonstrated. According to the grammatical injunction *anekam anyapadārthe* ("many [words] [form a compound] when another word's meaning [is intended]"), the analysis *piṅge akṣiṇī yasyāḥ* ("she whose eyes are tawny") shows that the correctness of the *bahuvrīhi* compound is established precisely in the sense of a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) which is primary. And by the term "genitive meaning" (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*), it is understood that the relation itself—the meaning of the case-ending—is what is intended, having the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) as its subordinate element.

And it has been stated in the *Āruṇādhikaraṇa*: "This *bahuvrīhi* compound is prescribed in the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*). And the possessive suffix occurs when there is a relation expressed as 'this belongs to that'. Thus, although the possessive suffix *matup* is prescribed in the sense of a primary genitive, in cases such as "bring the cow-possessor" (*gomantam ānaya*), one observes the bringing of the person [who owns the cows]. Therefore, by the force of the experienced predominance of the substratum (the possessor) implied by the relation, the rule that "the denoted meaning alone possesses predominance" is clearly subject to deviation; this is the intended sense. [The example] "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*)...

If it is argued that *bhāvanā* (the causal efficiency) is denoted by the verbal suffix because it is explained by the root *kṛ*, which has the sense of *bhāvanā*—then [we reply that] since an agent (*kartṛ*) is also explained by the verbal suffix in the word "karoti" (*he does*), [the same would apply to] the [agent] in "pacati" (*he cooks*).

The meaning is that there would be uncertainty as to whether the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) or in the agent (*kartṛ*). Regarding the analysis of the agent: the analysis performed by the root *kṛ* (meaning "productive activity") upon the verbal suffix in the word *pacati*—namely, its analysis as having "productive activity" as its meaning—is an analysis of the meaning of the word itself. However, the analysis of the agent performed by the verbal suffix in the word *karoti* is not an analysis of the meaning of the word; rather, it is intended so that the cognition of the agent may arise from the word *pacati*.

The point is this: since the agent, who is obtainable through implication (*ākṣepa*) as the intended object of the purport (*tātparya*), is merely being explained [by the verb], it is determined that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has its power (*śakti*) in the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) alone; thus, there is no occasion for the aforementioned lack of certainty. Regarding the statement that "the explanation of the agent is an explanation of what is not the literal meaning of the word," he provides an example: "cooking" (*pākam*).

The meaning is as follows: although the verbal root *pac* denotes only the act of softening (*viklitti*), one observes the use of the accusative case in "pākam" (cooking) with respect to the object; thus, while the status of that [object] as an "action" (*karma*) is explained through the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), it is not an explanation of the literal lexical meaning (*śabdārtha*). Now, an objection is raised: since the accusative in "pākam" explains a "karmatva" that is not the literal lexical meaning, and since we observe the explanation of even a relation (*saṃsarga*) that is not the literal lexical meaning, one might ask why this is considered an explanation of something other than the literal lexical meaning. To address this, he provides another example, beginning with "itaretara-".

The meaning is as follows: just as in the case of "dhava-khadirau" (the Dhava and Khadira trees) and similar compounds, the element of conjunction (*samuccaya*)—which is not directly denoted by the words constituting the *itaretarayoga* dvandva compound—is explained by the two *ca* particles present in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*). Thus, the meaning is that explaining a word-meaning which is not [explicitly] part of the word's own referent does not determine the meaning of the verbal root (*ākhyāta*).

The meaning is as follows: if it is maintained that such an explanation serves to determine the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), then—even though *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) is not the literal denotation of the word—it can still be established through implication (*ākṣepa*) because it constitutes the intended object of the speaker's purport; thus, while the explanation would be justified, your desired position that *bhāvanā* itself is the denotation of the verbal suffix would fail, and instead, the agent alone would be the denotation. To show that the denotation of the agent alone is necessary, he says: "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*).

The meaning is as follows: just as in cases such as "Caitra cooks," it is established by experience that there is a cognition of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) with Caitra, and thus it is necessary for verbal suffixes (*kṛt*) to denote the agent and so forth; likewise, in cases such as "Devadatta cooks," because there is a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*)—namely, "an activity conducive to softening, occurring in the present, whose agent is non-different from Devadatta"—and because there is an experience of a cognition of non-difference with Devadatta, it is also necessary for verbal endings (*ākhyāta*) to denote the agent and so forth.

And thus, the idea is that it would be all the more difficult for *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) to be expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Now, an objection may be raised: there is a rule that non-difference (*abheda*) is construed only where the words expressing the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) possess identical case-endings (*samānavibhaktikatva*). Furthermore, having identical case-endings means that the word expressing the qualifier possesses a case-ending belonging to the same class as the case-ending following the word expressing the qualified. This "belonging to the same class" (*sājātya*) is to be understood through properties such as being first-case (*prathamātva*), second-case (*dvitīyātva*), and so forth, which are subsumed under the category of case-ness (*vibhaktitva*).

For this very reason, there is no fear that the sentence "the blue [is] the pot" (*nīlo ghaṭam*) would result in a cognition of identity (*abhedānvaya*); this is what is meant by the passage beginning with "nor [is there] identity... and ending with "...that is not present here. The phrase "that" (*tat*) means: "the state of having the same case-ending (*samānavibhaktikatva*), which is the regulator for the cognition of identity. The phrase "here" (*atra*) means: "it is not present in cases such as 'Devadatta cooks' (*devadattaḥ pacati*)," because there is no homogeneity (*sājātya*) between the nominative case-ending (*prathamāvibhakti*) and the verbal suffix (*tiṅvibhakti*) due to their being distinct properties subsumed under the categories of *sup* (nominal endings) and *tiṅ* (verbal endings).

The point is this: since there is no rule governing the cognition of non-difference (abhedānvaya), and because the cognition of non-difference is thus impossible, it is not logical that the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) denotes the agent (kartṛ) and so forth. To demonstrate an exception to the rule regarding the requirement of identical case endings (samānavibhaktikatva), he says: "By Soma... (someneti).

In this context, the Mīmāṃsakas have determined in works such as the *Nyāyaprakāśa* that, since it is untenable for *soma* to serve as the means of sacrifice (*yāgārthatva*) without secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and since its syntactic connection as non-different (*abhedānvaya*) [with the sacrifice] would otherwise be impossible, there is no risk of the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*). This is because the word *soma*—through secondary indication in the sense of "possessing soma" (*matvarthe*)—enjoins a qualified injunction: "One should effect the desired end by means of a sacrifice possessed of soma. However, in that case, because the third-case suffix (*tṛtīyā*) and the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) lack homogeneity (*sājātya*) by virtue of a property subsumed under being a nominal suffix (*sup*), there could be no cognition of their syntactic connection as non-different.

The meaning is that since the Mīmāṃsakas indeed accept that [the fruit is the object], the difficulty of avoiding the counter-example (vyabhicāra) to the rule regarding the requirement of identical case endings remains unavoidable. As for the example *stokaṃ pacati* ("he cooks slightly"): even though the fruit is not the primary object, it possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*) by virtue of being designated as such through the principle of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), because it is the locus of the fruit. For this very reason, one should understand that the second case ending occurs in *stokam*, which is in grammatical apposition with it. Here, the non-difference relation (*abheda*) of the referent of the word *stoka* with the fruit produced by the operation denoted by the verbal root is quite clear. In this case as well, the violation of the aforementioned rule should be inferred in the same manner as before.

Now, one might object: according to the statement of the learned that "there is non-difference (abheda) in the relation between the meanings of two nouns having the same case-ending," it is only in the case of the non-difference between the meanings of two nouns that having the same case-ending is the restrictive condition, and not elsewhere. To this, he says: "rājapuruṣa" (the king's servant). Here, the word *rāja* (king) refers, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), to that which possesses ownership belonging to the king. There is a relation of non-difference between such an object denoted by the word *rāja* and the person (*puruṣa*). This is because the resulting cognition is: "a person who is non-different from that which possesses ownership as defined by the king."

In this case, because the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is not heard in the first word, there is an absence of the qualified (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) caused by the absence of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). However, in the first two examples, although the case-endings are present, the absence of the qualified is caused by the absence of the homogeneity (*sājātya*) that serves as the qualifier; this is the distinction.

The point is that even if the rule regarding the requirement of identical case endings (samānavibhaktikatva) were restricted to the domain of two nominal meanings (*nāmārtha*), its violation would be all the more unavoidable. Thus, since the cognition of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) in cases such as "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*) is entirely unimpeded, the conclusion is that the denotative power (*śakti*) of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) must necessarily fall upon the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, in order to account for the cognition of non-difference.

One might object: "Let it be that in cases such as 'Devadatta cooks' (*devadattaḥ pacati*), it is the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) alone that is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). However, the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the meaning of the word 'Devadatta' and the meaning of the verbal suffix—which arises [in experience]—would otherwise be inexplicable; thus, the verbal suffix must be taken as having a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for the agent. With this intention, the author raises the objection with the words "na cet" (if it be said). Coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists in two words conveying a single substratum (*dharmin*). Thus, the point is that since the cognition of identity can be accounted for through secondary signification alone, it is pointless to accept that the verbal suffix has a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for the agent.

When the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is maintained by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since the agent is expressed [by the suffix], [the author] says: "The word *piṅgākṣī* and so forth are derivative (*yaugika*). "Derivative" (*yoga*) means the power residing in the parts [of a compound]; the meaning is: of those words that function to denote an object by prioritizing that [etymological] power. Regarding the phrase "because they would not result in denoting a substance": the meaning is that since the cognition of a substance would be accomplished through indication alone, these words would not possess the status of being "denoters of substance" (*dravyavācin*). Rather, the sense is that it would be more appropriate for them to be "denoters of a relation" (*saṃbandhavācin*). This applies as well to other such secondary derivatives (*taddhita*).
The point is that even the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) forming compounds such as *vaiśvadevī* would not denote a substance.

He clarifies that etymological (*yogika*) words denote only a relation by stating "anekamanyapadārthe" and so forth. According to the meaning of the stated rule—"several [words] ending in the nominative case, when functioning in the sense of another word, are compounded; that is a *bahuvrīhi*"—and because of the analysis shown as "she whose eyes are tawny" (*piṅge akṣiṇī yasyāḥ*), it follows that the *bahuvrīhi* compound derives its grammatical correctness only from the primary genitive sense presented by the word "yasyāḥ" (of whom). This is the meaning.

Since a genitive relation, which has the meaning of the base (prakṛti) as its subordinate element, is understood precisely through a word ending in the genitive case—as in "of whom" (*yasyāḥ*)—the compound *piṅgākṣī* functions by incorporating that external referent (*anyapadārtha*). Therefore, the intended meaning is that the grammatical validity (*sādhutva*) of the *bahuvrīhi* is obtained only when it expresses a relation with the principal member. And it is stated in the Vārttika on the *Āruṇādhikaraṇa*: "This *bahuvrīhi* compound is prescribed in the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*); and the possessive suffix occurs in the sense of a relation expressed as 'this belongs to that'."

Even in the case of a taddhita suffix denoting a deity, since in the analytical explanation (vigraha)—"the Viśvedevas are the deity of this"—one observes that the relationship expressed by the genitive case is indeed predominant, it is determined that the relationship itself is what is signified by the compound formation (vṛtti).

If it is argued, "Let it be that, according to the stated method, the relation of the primary genitive sense alone is what is expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound and so forth; what is the loss?", he replies: "And thus," etc. "Because no substance is mentioned in the sentence beginning with 'aruṇayā'": the meaning is that, according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, the word *aruṇa* (red) has its power (*śakti*) postulated only for the quality of redness, and because, according to the aforementioned method, the power of words such as *piṅgākṣī* (tawny-eyed) is postulated only for the relation of the primary genitive sense, no substance is mentioned. "In its own sentence": "its own" refers to the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) of the purchase (*krayaṇa*).

The meaning is that this would result in the abolition of the *Āruṇādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the "red cow"), which establishes that the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) is construed only with the substance denoted by the compound *piṅgākṣyaikahāyanī* ("the reddish-eyed one-year-old female") occurring within such a sentence as "with a reddish-eyed one-year-old" (*aruṇayā piṅgākṣyā ekahāyanyā*). This is because, according to the opponent's view, the redness would instead be construed with the entire class of substances denoted by the word "cow."

Thus, regarding the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard [in scripture]: "One purchases Soma with a reddish-brown, yellow-eyed, one-year-old cow. Here, the word *aruṇā* (reddish-brown) is the *prakṛti* (verbal root/stem) portion; the verbal root *krī* (to buy) is the denotative *śruti*; the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) in *krīṇāti* is the injunctive *śruti*; and the third-case suffix (*tṛtīyāpratyaya*) in *aruṇayā* is the applicatory *śruti* in the form of a case ending. However, the word *aruṇā* denotes only the quality of redness due to parsimony (*lāghava*), and does not denote a substance qualified by the quality of redness.

If one were to accept that the word *aruṇā* (red) has a primary denotative power (*śakti*) toward an object qualified by the quality [of redness], it would result in the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), because the meaning of a word consists precisely in what cannot be obtained through other means. Furthermore, the substance which serves as the substratum can be obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*). Thus, in this context, the instrumental suffix in the word *aruṇayā* (by means of the red one) indicates, through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), that the quality of redness—the meaning of the verbal root—is an instrument for the purchase of Soma. However, that is untenable; for "purchase" (*kraya*) is defined as the taking of some object after giving another object.

Giving and receiving are possible only for corporeal objects such as clothing, gold, and the like, but not for that which is incorporeal, such as a mere quality (*guṇa*); for it is impossible to give or otherwise dispose of a quality by extracting it from the substance (*dravya*) that serves as its substratum. Therefore, since the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) lacks the power to enjoin application (*viniyojakatva*), it must be stated that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is what effects the application here. And the context assigns the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) to all substances, including the cups (*graha*), the bowls (*camasa*), and so forth. In this regard, the construction of the words is as follows: "aruṇayā" (with the red one) constitutes a separate sentence.

In this regard, having raised the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position that—by means of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*), all the instrumental substances (*sādhanadravya*) belonging to the context are referred to (*anūdya*), and the quality (*guṇa*) is enjoined by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—such that "all those instrumental substances which belong to the Jyotiṣṭoma must be made red"; [the reply is given]: because the words *piṅgākṣī* and *ekahāyanī* denote a substance (*dravya*) through the *bahuvrīhi* compound prescribed for the sense of another word (*anyapadārtha*)—namely, "she whose eyes are tawny" (*piṅge akṣiṇī yasyāḥ*) and "she who has one year" (*ekaṃ hāyanaṃ yasyāḥ*)—and because the substance here is the cow (*go*).

This is because of the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "I shall purchase [the cow] with a cow. Furthermore, in the two words *piṅgākṣyā* (with the reddish-eyed one) and *ekahāyanyā* (with the one-year-old), the hearing of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) makes known that the substance is the instrument for the act of purchasing. Likewise, the hearing of the instrumental case-ending in *aruṇayā* (with the red one) also makes known that the quality of redness (*āruṇya-guṇa*) is the instrument for the purchase. Since that [instrumentality] is not possible without the mediation of a substance, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), there occurs what is called "delimitation by a substance," which is the grasping of the substance as the locus of its own [quality]. By the word "own" (*sva*), the quality is grasped.

And thus, by the word "quality" (guṇa), the substance serving as the locus of such qualities is to be understood; it is postulated that [the quality] serves to delimit the substance. Furthermore, in this context, the substance is specifically the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) mentioned in its own sentence, because of its proximity. Consequently, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) stated—that the meaning results in "one purchases Soma with a one-year-old cow qualified by the quality of redness"—would be inconsistent. This is because, according to the aforementioned reasoning, words such as *piṅgākṣī* (tawny-eyed) signify a relationship with the primary genitive sense, and therefore they lack the status of denoting a substance.

In this regard, the following should be understood: although in a compound such as *yasya* (of whom), the genitive relation—which is subordinate to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*)—is perceived as the primary element within the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), nevertheless, in the *bahuvrīhi* compound *citragur devadattaḥ* (Devadatta, who has brindled cows), the base-meaning is made primary with the genitive relation as subordinate, in accordance with grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the inherent nature of linguistic power (*śabdaśakti*). Thus, by postulating a reversal of the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇabhāva-vyatyāsa*) within the formation of the compound, the denotation of a substance (*dravyavācitva*) for *bahuvrīhi*s such as *piṅgākṣī* is established. This is also the view of the author of the *Mīmāṃsā-vārttika*.
"In all cases, it is the substance (*dravya*) alone that is denoted by derivative words (*yaugika-śabda*);

for it is not possible for the relation (*saṃbandha*) to be the denotable meaning, because that would entail excessive complexity (*atigaurava*)," so they say. This is the underlying point: a relation is indeed established by experience to be defined by its two relata and distinct from those two relata. In that regard, in expressions such as *citraguḥ* ("one who has brindled cows"), the denotability of the relation must be postulated as a relational object (*sāṃsargika-viṣayatā*) in accordance with the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*).

Thus, in this case, although one relatum—the form of a cow—is expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), since a relation is defined by two relata, it cannot be manifested without the manifestation of the other relatum; consequently, the expressibility of the second relatum must also be postulated. Because this results in the assumption of two distinct powers (*śakti*), which entails excessive complexity (*gaurava*), it is not possible for the Bahuvrīhi compound to have the mere relation as its denotation. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, since the cognition of the relation is established through the implication of the relata themselves, it is impossible for the relation to be denoted [by the word], as it would then be something obtainable from another source. As it has been said: "If the relation can be understood through the relata alone, who would then attribute a denotative power to the word for that [relation]? Thus, in this manner, one must necessarily accept that derivative words such as *piṅgākṣī* (tawny-eyed) and *vaiśvadevī* (belonging to the Viśvedevas) denote substances according to the reasoning stated above.

Therefore, "the owner of variegated cows" (*citragosambandhī*) is the meaning of the compound (*samāsa*), while "he whose cows are variegated" (*yatsambandhinyaś citrā gāvaḥ*) is the meaning of the analytical expansion (*vigraha*). Since it has been stated that there is a reversal of the relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) in the compound, even in the sentence "he to whom variegated cows belong" (*citrā gāvo yamya*), which is imagined for the purpose of demonstrating the meaning of the compound, the meaning remains "the owner of variegated cows" due to that same reversal of the qualifier-qualified relationship. It is precisely to demonstrate this reversal of the qualifier-qualified relationship that the elders employ the formulation "he whose [cows] are variegated" (*citrā gāvo yasya saḥ*).

Therefore, it should be understood that Nāgeśabhaṭṭa stated in the *Laghumañjūṣā* that there is no contradiction between the unity of meaning (*samānārthatva*) of the derivative formation (*vṛtti*) and its analytical expansion (*vigraha*).
Likewise, although incorporeal redness (*āruṇya*) cannot be a direct means for purchasing, it can be a means for purchasing indirectly through the substance that serves as its substratum.

Just as the feminine suffix in the word *aruṇā* indicates the femininity residing in the substance in the form of a cow—which is the substratum of the quality of redness—and thereby makes known, through a mediated relationship, the connection between the quality of redness and femininity; so too, the third-case suffix in *aruṇayā* indicates that the substance in the form of a cow, which is the substratum of the quality of redness, is the means for purchase, and thereby makes known, through a mediated relationship, that the quality of redness is the means for purchase. Thus, there is nothing at all inconsistent in this.

Regarding the phrase "by the fundamental reason" (*mūlayuktyā*): the meaning is that there exists a fundamental reason—that is, a unique reason—proving that [the word] denotes a substance; namely, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This coreferentiality is established by experience in cases such as *piṅgākṣī gauḥ* ("the brown-eyed cow") and *vaiśvadevī āmikṣā* ("the curd for the Viśvedevas"), because it is possible to account for it through implication and other means.

And thus, for the words *piṅgākṣī* and so forth used by the Yogins, as well as for the suffixes contained within terms such as *vaiśvadevī*, there is nothing whatsoever that proves their denotation of a substance (*dravya*), since the cognition of such a substance is established through implication (*ākṣepa*) and other means; therefore, they would not possess the quality of denoting a substance. This and other points have been investigated in detail in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*; it should be understood from that very source.

Now, since Pāṇini’s sūtra *laḥ karmaṇi* states that the *lakāra*s possess the power (*śakti*) to denote the agent and other roles, the statement *“but the *tiṅ*s [denote] the substratum”* is untenable; therefore, he says: “as the capacity to cause cognition. This means that the power consists in being the generator of cognition. Regarding the phrase *“only in the *tiṅ*s”*: the meaning is that this power resides solely in the *tiṅ*s because, at the time of usage during actual linguistic practice, only *tiṅ*s are present, and it is established by experience that the cognition of the agent and other roles arises from them alone.

Since the knowledge of word-meanings is the cause for the knowledge of the sentence-meaning, he first demonstrates the logical connection by stating that the word-meanings must be defined; then, in order to define the sentence-meaning as the qualificand, he says: "The operation is primary with respect to the result. This means that with respect to the result—such as the softening of grain—the operation is the primary element, i.e., the qualificand. The meaning is that the operation possesses primacy as defined by the result, while the result is its qualifier. Regarding the phrase "but with respect to the substratum": this refers to both the substratum of the result and the substratum of the operation.

Since the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are obtainable from the verbal root (*dhātu*), their meaning is merely the locus (*āśraya*), according to the maxim that "the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained otherwise. Thus, being the locus itself is the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Regarding the term *tiṅ*: this status as a communicator [of meaning] is attributed to the *tiṅ* suffixes by taking the meaning of the substituend (*ādeśin*), the *lakāra*, as their own meaning; or else, it is with the intention that the power (*śakti*) resides in the *tiṅ* suffixes themselves, because it is established by experience that the understanding of meanings such as the agent (*kartṛ*) arises from *tiP* and so on alone, since the *lakāra* is absent in actual usage. Regarding the phrase *tiṅartha* (the meaning of *tiṅ*): [it refers to the agent, etc.]...

[The categories are] agent, object, number, and time. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it means among the meanings [of the suffixes], such as the agent and so forth. The agent (*kartṛ*) is a qualifier of the operation (*vyāpāra*), in the sense that the agent possesses a state of being a qualifier as determined by the operation through the relation of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). This is because there arises the cognition: "the operation resides in the agent. Similarly, the object (*karman*) is a qualifier of the result (*phala*), in the sense that the object possesses a state of being a qualifier as determined by the result. This is because there arises the cognition: "the softening (*viklitti*) and so forth reside in the rice and so forth. As for "number" (*saṃkhyā*):...

The meaning is that when used in conjunction with an agentive suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*), number (*saṃkhyā*) is construed as a qualifier of the agent; when used with a patientive suffix (*karma-pratyaya*), number is construed as a qualifier of the patient (*karman*). Now, one might object: since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), consisting of both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*), is presented by the base (*prakṛti*) itself and is thus equally proximate, why does number not construe as a qualifier of that [meaning] instead?

Furthermore, since number is the meaning of the suffix, and because it is logical that its connection occurs with the meaning of the verbal root—which is the meaning of the base (prakṛti)—and because we observe that the number belonging to the meaning of a nominal suffix connects only with the meaning of the base, one might raise the doubt that the number belonging to the meaning of a verbal suffix should likewise connect only with the meaning of the verbal root. Dispelling this doubt, he states the reason for the connection of number with the agent and so forth: "because they are expressed by the same suffix" (*samānapratyayopāttatvāt*). This means that by the very same suffix which expresses the meaning of the agent or the object, the meaning of number is also expressed.

The meaning is that, in view of the sense of the verbal root (*dhātu*), because of the superior proximity (*pratyāsatti*) between the agent and the object, it is logically correct that number (*saṃkhyā*) should apply only to them. Thus, since the direct statement of a single case-ending (*samānābhidhāna-śruti*) is stronger than a sentence consisting of mere co-occurrence (*samabhihāra*), it is pointed out that it is utterly improper for the Naiyāyikas to apply the application of number to the meaning expressed by the nominative case-ending (*prathamāntārtha*) instead of applying it to the meaning conveyed by the single suffix (*ekapratyaya*).

And thus, the nature of the causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) as it bears fruit is indicated by the phrase "the number of the meaning of the verb" (ākhyātārthasaṃkhyā). The term *ākhyāta* is used by the Mīmāṃsakas and others to refer exclusively to verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), whereas it is used by the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas) to refer to words ending in such suffixes, as seen in the Bhāṣya in the passage: "a verb [is connected] with a verb."

A finite verb (*ākhyāta*) is that which possesses *tiṅ* suffixes; its meaning is number (*saṃkhyā*). In a cognition where that [number] is the qualifier (*prakāra*), the cause is the presentation of the agent or object—generated by the finite verb—which stands in the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*). Thus, the causal relationship (the state of being cause and effect) is established: such a presentation is the cause of that cognition. This means that the number conveyed by that suffix is construed with the meaning in the form of the agent or object conveyed by that same suffix. In this context, the portion "having the agent or object as the qualificand" (*kartṛ-karma-viśeṣyaka*) must also be included.

Thus, it should be understood that the delimitors of the effect (kāryatāvacchedaka) are the state of being a cognition whose qualificandum is the agent in the form of an object qualified by the number of the meaning of the verb, and the state of being a cognition whose qualificandum is the object in the form of an object qualified in that same way. The delimitors of the cause (kāraṇatāvacchedaka) are the state of being the presentation of the meaning as the agent produced by the verb, and the state of being the presentation of the meaning as the object in that same way. It should be noted that the relation serving as the delimiting relation for both the effect-ness and the cause-ness is inherence (samavāya).

In this context, if one were to state only that [the cause] is "with respect to the cognition having the agent or object as its qualificandum" within the scope of the delimitor of the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason in cases such as *pakta* (the cooker) and *pācaka* (the cook), because of the absence of the presentation of the agent or object generated by a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Consequently, the intended cognition having the agent or other [roles] as the qualificandum would not arise through an agent-suffix (*kartṛpratyaya*). Therefore, the component "having the number denoted by the verbal suffix as its qualifier" (*ākhyātārthasaṃkhyāprakāraka*) has been inserted therein.

And thus, since the presence of the agent or object brought about by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is a cause for a cognition whose qualifier is the number denoted by that suffix, in cases such as *pakta* (the cooker) and *pācaka* (the cook), a cognition having an agent as its qualificandum and some meaning (namely, the activity denoted by the verbal root) as its qualifier arises without impediment. The term "number" (*saṃkhyā*) has been included [in the definition] to prevent the unwanted consequence of a cognition having time, which is the meaning of the verbal suffix, as its qualifier.

If it is objected: "In cases such as *paktrā* (the agent of cooking), since the cognition having the operation (*vyāpāra*) as its qualifier is established merely by the phrase 'having number as its qualifier' (*saṃkhyāprakāraka*), what is the purpose of the qualification 'number is the meaning of the verbal suffix' (*ākhyātārtha*)? We reply: No. Because, in the absence of the presentation of the agent or object produced by the verbal suffix—as in the case of *ghaṭaḥ* ("pot") and so forth—there would be no cognition having the number (such as singularity) denoted by the nominal suffix (*sub*) as its qualifier.

For there is a rule that such an apprehension [of the meaning] is necessary for a cognition whose qualifier is the number belonging to the meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*), but not for a cognition whose qualifier is the number belonging to the meaning of a nominal suffix (*sub*); thus, that [rule] serves its purpose. If, in the scope of the delimiting condition of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), one were to omit the words "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "object" (*karman*) and simply state that "the apprehension produced by the verb is the cause," then—under the view that the *laṭ* and other suffixes prescribed by rules such as *vartamāne laṭ* denote time such as the present—the time itself would also be an object of the apprehension produced by the verb. Consequently, in the case of [the sentence] *pacati*, [there would be a problem regarding] the number belonging to the meaning of the verb.

The temporal factor (*kāla*) would have to be construed as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*) [of the agent or object]. To prevent this, the phrase "agent and object" (*kartṛkarman*) is provided as a qualification for that which is presented through the relation of being the object (*viṣayatayā*). Thus, the intended meaning is that although time is indeed the object of the cognition generated by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), it lacks the nature of an agent or an object; consequently, the number denoted by the verbal suffix does not conjoin with it as a qualifier.

Now, in such cases as "Devadatta cooks rice" (*devadattas taṇḍulaṃ pacati*) and "Rice is cooked by Devadatta" (*devadattena taṇḍulaḥ pacyate*), would not the number—one—which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)—be construed as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*) with respect to the object, namely the rice? Likewise, would the number denoted by the verbal suffix not be construed as a qualifier with respect to the agent, namely Devadatta? This is because the meanings of those two [the rice and Devadatta] are already presented by the words *taṇḍula* and *devadatta*. And if that were so, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the rule.

To prevent this [undesired consequence], the condition of being "generated by the verbal suffix" (ākhyātajanyatva) is provided as a qualifier for the agent and the object. Consequently, in the aforementioned usage, the number—whether singular or plural—expressed by the verbal suffix does not relate as a qualifier to the object and agent presented by other words such as *taṇḍula* (rice) and *devadatta*; rather, it relates only to the agent and object presented by the verbal suffix itself.

In the sentence "He cooks rice with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), because the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) does not produce a cognitive relation (*anvayabodha*) where the agent or instrument (*karaṇa*)—qualified by its own number—is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the phrase "having the agent or object as the qualificand" (*kartṛkarmaviśeṣyaka*) is included in the definition of the effect-determiner (*kāryatāvacchedakakoṭau*) in order to avoid deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Thus, the meaning is that the presentation of the agent or object generated by the verbal suffix is the regulator of the cognition in which the number denoted by the suffix is the qualifier and the agent or object is the qualificand. Here it should be understood that "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*) refers to the breakdown of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāvabhaṅga*).

Deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is of two kinds: deviation in positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*) and deviation in negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*). Among these, the first occurs when the effect is absent despite the presence of the cause; the second occurs when the cause is absent despite the presence of the effect. In the sentence "He cooks rice with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ taṇḍulam pacati*), there is deviation in positive concomitance because, although the cause—the presentation of the agent and the object produced by the verbal suffix—is present, the effect—the cognition of a relation in which the number denoted by the verbal suffix is the qualifier and the instrument is the qualificand—is absent.

In cases such as *paktā* (the cooker) and *pācaka* (the cook), although there exists an effect in the form of a cognition having the agent (*kartṛ*) as its qualificand due to the agentive suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*), there is nevertheless a negative deviation (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) because of the absence of the cause, which is the presentation of the agent or object produced by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). To avoid the aforementioned deviation in both instances, the respective qualifiers have been provided; this is another point.

Having thus established the relation between cause and effect according to our own school, [the author] says "of the Naiyāyikas and others" in order to demonstrate the complexity (gaurava) inherent in the causal theory of the Naiyāyikas. According to the view of the logicians (tārkika), verbal cognition has the meaning of the nominative case as its primary qualificand; therefore, the number expressed by the verb (ākhyāta) is construed with the nominative case alone. The meaning is that just as the action (kṛti) conveyed by the verb is construed with the nominative case, so too is the number conveyed by the verb.

And thus, the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) must be stated as follows: "The cognition having the number of the meaning of the verb as its qualifier has as its cause the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case. "That too" means that even the aforementioned causal relation [is not established]. "Like the moon," etc.

In the cases "the face is seen like the moon" (*candra iva mukhaṃ dṛśyate*) and "Maitra goes after eating" (*bhuktvā vrajati maitraḥ*), since the moon and the act of eating denoted by the suffix *ktvā* would possess the status of being the referents of the nominative case, it would follow that they are related as qualifiers (*prakāratayā*) to the number denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha-saṃkhyā*) in the words "is seen" (*dṛśyate*) and "goes" (*vrajati*). However, this is not desired, because we never experience the number denoted by the verbal suffix as applying to the moon or the act of eating. Now, if it is asked how that which ends in *ktvā* can have the status of a nominative referent, the answer is as follows: [The answer continues: It is said that [the *ktvā*-ending] functions as a qualifier for the agent (*kartṛ-viśeṣaṇatva*). Just as in the sentence "He goes having bathed" (*snātvā gacchati*), the act of bathing is understood as a qualifier of the agent of going; similarly, here too, the act of eating is understood as a qualifier of the agent of going. Therefore, the agent of eating, being identical with the agent of going, is expressed by the single nominative case-ending (*ekavibhaktyā*) and thus possesses the status of being a primary referent (*pradhāna*). Consequently, the number denoted by the verbal suffix applies to that very agent. Thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, it is not the case that the number denoted by the verbal suffix applies to the act of eating, because that act is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the act of going. Nor does it apply to the moon, because the moon is merely a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) for the face. Therefore, the application of the verbal number is restricted solely to the agent. This is the established conclusion. As stated: "The verbal number applies to the agent, and the agent is expressed by the same case-ending. This is the view of the venerable Patañjali. Alternatively, one may say that the verbal number applies to the object (*karman*) and so forth, depending on the specific context. Thus, the rule is: "The verbal number applies to the agent, the object, and so on, according to the speaker's intention. This is the correct position. Therefore, the verbal number applies to the agent alone. Hence, there is no fault whatsoever. Thus, the meaning of the *sūtra* is established. This concludes the discussion. In this context, regarding two actions whose agents are identical, the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ*—which means that the suffix *ktvā* is applied after a word denoting that meaning which is temporally prior among the two—does not apply when there is a desire to know the agent of that action. This is because of the introduction of the Vārttika, "The indeclinable *kṛt*-suffixes denote the abstract state (*bhāva*)," which establishes that the meaning of the *ktvā* suffix is exclusively the abstract state. Furthermore, that [abstract state] is indeed insentient (*asattvabhūta*), since, as in the case of *pāka* and similar forms, there is no perception of gender or number.

And thus, because the action expressed by the suffix *ktvā* is of the nature of a non-substance (*asattvarūpa*), there is no cognition of duality and so forth; consequently, there is no dual number and so on, but rather only the singular number. This is because the singular is the default (*autsargika*) and does not depend upon [the presence of] a number. Furthermore, since that [singular] is the first to be presented, it belongs to the nominative case alone. As for its elision (*luk*) in cases such as "from an indeclinable" (*avyayādāva*), that is another matter. Now, if it is accepted that the suffix *ktvā* expresses merely the abstract action (*bhāvamātra*), then in expressions such as "I, having eaten, am going" (*ahaṃ bhuktvā vrajāmi*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of the third case ending after the word *asmad*.

Nor should it be argued that [the agent] is not expressed because it is already expressed by the finite verb (*tiṅanta*); for even though the agent who is the referent of the finite verb is expressed, the agent who is the referent of the suffix *ktvā* is not. If this is said, we reply: no, because the Bhāṣya accepts that when the power (*śakti*) relative to the action denoted by the principal finite verb is expressed, the power relative to the subordinate action denoted by the *ktvā*-suffix is also expressed. As it has been said: "Where there are two actions belonging to a single substance, one principal and the other subordinate, and their powers are distinct, the power residing in the subordinate follows the principal."

And likewise, because the action denoted by the base of the *ktvā* suffix qualifies another action, the agenthood (*kartṛtva*) relative to the principal action is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Since that [agenthood] is expressed, the agenthood relative to the action which serves as its qualifier is also expressed; therefore, when [the agent] is already expressed, only the nominative (*prathamā*) occurs. In this way, since both "moon" (*candra*) and "eating" (*bhojana*) are objects of the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case, in order to prevent a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that regard, the qualification "not having attained the status of being qualified by another" (*itara-viśeṣaṇatvānāpanna*) is added to the phrase "in the presentation generated by a word ending in the nominative case."

It must be given [as a rule]. And its meaning is that it is not occupied by a qualifierhood (viśeṣaṇatā) as determined by a qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) residing in a meaning other than that which ends in the nominative case (prathamānta). Thus, the meaning is that there would be excessive complexity (gaurava) in having to state: "With respect to a cognition whose mode (prakāra) is the number denoted by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta), the cause is the mental presence (upasthiti) produced by a word ending in the nominative case, provided that such a word has not attained a qualifierhood as determined by a qualificandhood residing in a meaning other than that [of the verb]."
