In the expression "the face is like the moon" (*candra iva mukham*), there arises the cognition that "the face possesses a similarity as defined by the moon"; thus, because the moon has attained the status of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) relative to the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the similarity—which is the meaning of the particle *iva*—it is so. Likewise, in the expression "having eaten, he goes" (*bhuktvā vrajati*), there arises the cognition that "there is a going at a time subsequent to eating, performed by the same agent who performed the eating"; therefore, [the action] of the base-meaning of the *ktvā*-suffix [is related] to another action.

Because the act of eating functions as a qualifier—specifically, because it has attained the status of a qualifier relative to the qualificandumhood residing in the act of going, which is the meaning of the finite verb (*tiṅanta*)—the aforementioned defect does not arise in the two cases [of "The moon is seen" and "He eats"]; namely, the undesirable consequence that the number expressed by the verbal suffix would be understood as a qualifier of both the moon and the act of eating. [This is rejected] on the grounds of excessive complexity (*atigaurava*).

In the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), with respect to a cognition whose qualifier is the number belonging to the meaning of a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the cause is the presentation of the agent or object produced by that verbal suffix. Since neither the moon nor the eating possesses the status of being the meaning of a verbal suffix, a cognition of number-connection with them does not arise; therefore, it is unnecessary to include the condition "not being a qualifier of another" [in the definition], which results in parsimony (*lāghava*). However, in the other system (the Naiyāyika view), that condition must be included, which results in excessive complexity (*gaurava*). This also refers to the aforementioned complexity in the other system.

Alternatively, the meaning is that even within our own system, there is brevity (lāghava) when compared to the views of others. That is to say, it serves as the proof for the point that even opponents must accept that the agent and the object are expressed by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta-vācyatva), in order to avoid the fault of prolixity (gaurava).

Having thus established that the agent, the object, and number—being included within the meaning of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*)—function as qualifiers, he now establishes the same for time as well, beginning with the words "But time... The meaning is this: time, known by the names past, future, and present, possesses the status of a qualifier relative to the activity denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), and the activity is the qualificand. To demonstrate the authoritative evidence for time being a qualifier of the activity, he says "For instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth. From the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "of the verbal root," the word "of the verbal root" is understood [in the subsequent context].

Furthermore, the word *dhātoḥ* (from the root), by virtue of the definitions of meaning such as *bhū sattāyām* ("the root *bhū* is in the sense of existence") and the authority of the *bhūvādi* sūtra, presents the meaning of the root as consisting of both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*). Because it is perceived as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the cognition produced by the root, it presents only the operation. The phrase *vartamāne* (in the present) is a qualifier of the operation which is the meaning of the root. Thus, the meaning of the rule *vartamāne laṭ* ("*laṭ* [is used] for the present") is: "*laṭ* [is used] after a root that denotes an operation (*kriyā*) which is present."

The term *laṭ* signifies that which indicates the present tense. Thus, according to the maxim "qualities (guṇas) exist for the sake of another," words denoting time such as "present" are not qualifiers of the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*), but rather qualifiers of the primary action itself. Consequently, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in the case of *pacati* ("he cooks") is: "an action conducive to cooking, having a single locus, occurring at the present time"; and in the case of *pacyate* ("it is cooked"), it is: "an action occurring at the present time, conducive to that softening (*viklitti*) which has a single locus."

According to the Prācīna (ancient) view, in cases where there is co-utterance with words such as *taṇḍula* (rice), the object presented by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is construed as non-different from the rice and so forth; likewise, in cases of co-utterance with words such as *Caitra*, which denote the agent, the agent presented by the verbal suffix is construed as non-different from Caitra and so forth.

And likewise, in the case of "he cooks rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), the understanding is that there is an activity, residing in the agent denoted by the suffix *laṭ* (which is non-different from Caitra), which is contemporaneous and conducive to the softening (*viklitti*) residing in the rice. In the case of "the rice is cooked by Caitra" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacyate caitreṇa*), the understanding is that there is an activity, residing in the object denoted by the suffix *laṭ* (which is non-different from the rice), which is contemporaneous and conducive to the softening residing in that which is non-different from the rice, and which resides in Caitra.

In this root text, by stating "due to predominance" (*prādhānyāt*), it is indicated that in the case of an object-verb (*karmākhyāta*), because the result (*phala*) is predominant, the connection with the present time (*vartamānatva*) applies to the result. Thus, in the sentence *taṇḍulaḥ pacyate caitreṇa* ("The rice is being cooked by Caitra"), the understanding is: "There is a softening (*viklitti*) residing in the object denoted by the suffix *laṭ*, which is non-different from the rice, produced by an activity residing in Caitra, and existing at the present time. However, this appears to be incorrect; for later [the text] states: "Nor is there an understanding of softening in the result."

However, this [view] does not appear correct. For, having begun with the statement "nor is there its connection with the fruit," according to the aforementioned reasoning, since the fruit is yet to come and thus non-existent at the time the operation has commenced, it is impossible for the present tense to connect with it; consequently, the form *pacyate* would be untenable, while *pakṣyate* would instead result. Therefore, even in the case of the passive (karmākhyāta), the connection with the present time belongs to the operation alone.

This is because, as is well-established, the presentation of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) generated by the verbal root (*dhātu*)—in relation to the cognition of time—is a cause for the cognition of time, just as it is for the cognition of a *kāraka* (participant), through the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*). Thus, in the sentence "He has gone to the village" (*grāmaṃ gataḥ*), the connection with the present time occurs precisely with respect to the activity (*vyāpāra*) which serves as the qualifier of the agent (*kartṛ*), the meaning of the suffix *-kta*. Consequently, the resulting cognition is: "The softening (*viklitti*) residing in the object denoted by the suffix *-laṭ* (the rice), which is non-different from the rice, is produced by an activity residing in Caitra that is present."

Others, however, hold that when something is predominant, it is at that time that there is a connection with [the temporal] time (*kāla*). Since predominance is observed in both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*), there is no room here for a restrictive rule such as "the cognition of time as a qualifier [occurs only] through the root *i* (to go)," etc. When the result has not yet arisen but the operation exists, the term "is cooking" (*pacati*) is used because the state of being present is superimposed upon the result; thus, there is no inconsistency. The meaning is that just as one uses the expression "he cooks" even at the time of placing the pot on the fire—due to the superimposition of the form of the whole upon each individual part—so it is in this case as well.

They say that in cases of superimposition (*āropa*), common consensus (*pratīti*) alone is the refuge. And thus, it should be understood that when the result (*phala*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the connection with time occurs precisely there. In this view, the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) signifies time only by way of being an indicator (*dyotaka*). It should be understood that in the alternative view—that the *laṭ* suffix occurs in the sense of the present, meaning the *laṭ* expresses the present time—the signification of time by the verbal suffix is through its denotative capacity (*śakyatā*).

Now, since the very same verbal suffix by which the meaning consisting of the agent or the object is conveyed also conveys the number such as singularity and so forth, there is a single expressive word for both meanings; thus, by the principle of "identity of expression" (*samānābhidhāna-śruti*), just as the connection of number with the agent or the object is accepted, so too, when time is connected with the aforementioned agent or object, he states the refutations according to the perspective of those who rely solely on the literal sense (*lakṣyaikacakṣuṣka*): "The past," etc.

The *bhāvanā* (efficient force) that culminates in softening (*viklitti*) and is conducive to it has passed away, meaning it is completed. If such an agent were still present, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the form "pacati" (he cooks), because the agent would still exist even when the activity has ceased. This is because, on the view that time is construed with the meaning of the agent and so forth, the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.69) forms a single syntactic unit [with the definition of the present tense], which implies that the suffix *laṭ* occurs after a verbal root whose agent exists at the present time.

In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the connection (*anvaya*) [of the suffix] is with the operation (*vyāpāra*) of time; thus, the suffix *laṭ* (the present tense marker) is desired only when the operation residing in the agent (*kartṛniṣṭhavyāpāra*) is present. And it is precisely in that case that the usage "he cooks" (*pacati*) occurs. Likewise, regarding an agent whose productive activity (*bhāvanā*) has passed, the intended usage "he cooked" (*apākṣīt*) would not be possible, because the agent would still be existing [according to your view]. Similarly, when the operation conducive to softening (*viklitti*) has not yet commenced, even though the agent exists, the intended usage "he is cooking" (*pacati*) would not be possible.

However, because this view is beset by refutations such as the consequence that one would have to use the expression "he cooks" [even when the action has ceased], the theory that time is construed with the agent or the object is not tenable. Now, one might argue: "Let the construction of time be with the result itself; in that case, there is no room for the aforementioned refutation. Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words "Nor with the result," and so forth. If one accepts the construction of time with the result, then at the stage when the result in the form of softening (viklitti) has not yet arisen, even if the activity is present, the expression "he cooks" would not occur, because the result itself is not present.

The meaning is that in the usage "syāt ca pakṣyati" (it might cook tomorrow), there would be the loss of what is desired and the occurrence of what is undesired. Having stated the objections when the time denoted by the suffix *ākhyāta* (the verbal suffix) is construed with the agent, the object, or the result, he begins to state the fault even when the time is construed with the operation (*vyāpāra*), starting with the words "na cāmavāta... and so forth. *Āmavāta* is a specific type of disease.

Consequently, for a person whose body has become inert like a piece of wood—devoid of movement, lacking any pulsation in the limbs such as the hands and feet—even though there is no possibility of the result [of rising], the verbal usage "he rises" would apply, because the activity consisting of an effort conducive to conjunction with a higher location exists in that person.

And thus, since the objection applies equally to all positions regarding the connection of the time denoted by the verb with the agent or the object, as well as with the result or the operation, it is improper to adopt the position that the connection of time is only with the operation (*vyāpāra*). The opponent's intention is that if the connection of time were admitted with the result (*phala*), then because the result has not yet arisen at that moment, such an [undesired] usage would not occur. To ward off the possibility of such an undesirable usage, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) says: "of the effort of another" (*parayatnasya*).

Because effort (*yatna*) is an internal quality residing in the self (*ātman*), it is more proximate [to the speaker] than that which resides in another; since such effort cannot be known by another through perception, no such usage occurs. The meaning is that when one employs a word with the desire to convey a particular meaning, the knowledge of that meaning is necessarily required.

One might object: "Even if the effort residing in another is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), once that effort is understood through inference (*anumāna*), the undesirable consequence (*prayogāpatti*) that 'he stands up' would be unavoidable. Anticipating this, the author refutes it by accepting the objection as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), beginning with the words "some movement" (*kiṃ cicceṣṭā*). The meaning is: by means of an action located in parts of the body such as the hands and feet; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), his writing and so forth are to be included. The formulation of the inference (*anumānaprayoga*) is as follows: taking the movement residing in Caitra as the subject (*pakṣa*), its being produced by an effort is established as the probandum (*sādhya*), because it is a movement (*ceṣṭātva*), like my own movement.

Alternatively, [the argument is]: "This person, though rendered inert (jaḍībhūta), possesses an effort conducive to rising, because he possesses an action of a different kind, like myself. Thus, [one says] "this person rises. The meaning is that although he possesses an effort conducive to rising, the result consisting of conjunction with an upper location is not produced due to a lack of capacity—that is, due to the absence of the auxiliary cause in the form of capacity; for this is established by common worldly experience. Therefore, regarding a person paralyzed by rheumatism (āmavāta), the linguistic usage "he rises" is indeed accepted. "And thus," etc.

The meaning is: "and because the aforementioned arguments must necessarily be accepted. It should be understood that all four meanings of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) are indeed qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), while the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), namely the activity (*vyāpāra*), alone is the primary element (*pradhāna*) and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). By the restrictive particle (*eva*) in the phrase "only qualifiers," the status of being the qualificand is excluded from the meanings of the suffixes. By the restrictive particle in the phrase "only [the] activity," it should be understood that the result (which is also a meaning of the suffix) and the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth are excluded.

An objection is raised: "If *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth are denoted by the suffix (*tiṅ*), then it follows that *bhāvanā* must be a qualifier with respect to the meaning of the suffix, according to the grammatical maxim that 'the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix [stand in a qualifier-qualified relationship]'; to this, he replies with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*).

In cases such as *paktā* (cook) and *pācaka* (one who cooks), because one experiences the cognition that [the agent] is the substratum of an activity conducive to softening (*viklitti*), the predominance of the meaning of the suffix over the meanings of the base and suffix is observed; likewise, there is an objection that in cases such as *pacati* (he cooks) as well, the agent and so forth—the meanings of the *tiṅ*-suffix—should be predominant, and the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvanā*) should be its qualifier. To this, he provides the answer: "Nevertheless, the action is predominant" (*tathāpi bhāvapradhānam*). The sentence ending with "verbal suffixes" (*ākhyātām*) is intended to set forth the definition of a verb (*ākhyāta*).

In this context, the relationship between the subject and the predicate must be understood as follows: "the verb (ākhyāta) is that which has the action (bhāva) as its primary meaning. Otherwise, because it appears first, "that which has the action as its primary meaning" would be the subject (uddeśya), and "verb" would be the predicate (vidheya). Consequently, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to nouns (nāman) such as *tvayā*, *mayā*, and *anyaiḥ* in expressions like *tvayā edhanīyam* ("it is to be kindled by you"), since these nouns also primarily signify the action.

In cases involving the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), it is a general rule (*autsargika*) that there is an appearance of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) by the delimiting property of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) with respect to the predicate. Accordingly, it is understood that in a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), which is delimited by the property of being a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*), there resides the quality of denoting the primary meaning of the action (*bhāva*). In the present context, *ākhyātatva* is the delimiting property of the subject, and it is the pervaded (*vyāpya*). The quality of denoting the primary meaning of the action is the delimiting property of the predicate (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*), and it is the pervader (*vyāpaka*). A verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is that which ends in a *tiṅ* affix.

Regarding the statement "a verb [is connected] with a verb," the *Bhāṣya* establishes that the word *ākhyāta* (verb) denotes only that which ends in a *tiṅ* suffix. Furthermore, its primacy (*prādhānya*) is determined in relation to the meanings of the stem and suffix that express it, as these are understood through implication. By the term "itself" (*sva*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—namely, the productive activity (*bhāvanā*)—is intended. The verbal root such as *pac* (to cook) is that which expresses this. The suffix derived from that root is the *tiṅ* suffix in forms such as *pacati*. Its referent is the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth. It is in relation to these that the primacy should be understood.

The meaning is that a *tiṅ*-ending word generates a cognition in which the primary qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) resides in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), as determined by a modehood (prakāratā) residing in the meaning of the *tiṅ* itself. In other words, the delimiting factor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is simply the state of being a *tiṅ*-ending form. The term "bhāvapradhāna" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which the *bhāva* is predominant. Here, *bhāva* refers to action (*kriyā*). And this action conveys both the operation (*vyāpāra*)—by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "that by which something is done" (*kriyate 'nena*) using the instrumental sense—and the result (*phala*)—by the etymological derivation as "that which is done" (*kriyate*) using the objective sense.

Consequently, in the case of a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), there is primacy for both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*); therein, the term *kartṛvācya* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which the agent is denoted. And the referent of the other member (*anyapadārtha*) is the verbal suffix itself; thus, the meaning is "in a verbal suffix that denotes the agent. This should be understood similarly for the term *karmavācya*. The distinction is that in the case of what is denoted as the agent (*kartṛvācya*), the operation (*vyāpāra*) has primacy, whereas in the case of what is denoted as the object (*karmavācya*), the result (*phala*) has primacy. Regarding the phrase "those in which substance is predominant" (*sattvapradhānāni*): here too, the construction of the relationship between the subject and the predicate is "the nouns (*nāmāni*) are those in which substance is predominant."

Otherwise, if "nominality" were prescribed with reference to the capacity to generate a cognition whose qualificand-ness resides in a substance (*sattva*/*dravya*) according to the literal sense [of the definition], there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that it would apply to finite verb endings (*tiṅanta*) such as *pacati*, since these generate a cognition whose qualificand-ness resides in a substance such as the agent (*kartṛ*), which is itself qualified by a number residing in the locus (*āśrayatva*).

The meaning is that [words] convey an object which possesses a primary status as a qualificand (mukhyaviśeṣyatā) characterized by a mode (prakāratā) residing in gender and so forth—this being based on the analysis (*vigraha*) "that in which substance (*sattva*), which is the substratum of gender and so forth, is predominant. And this very thing is the definition of a noun (*nāman*). The delimiting property of being defined (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is "noun-ness" (*nāmatva*), consisting in the fact of being the basis for the prescription of suffixes such as *su* and others. Regarding the rule *bhūvādi-* (Pāṇini 1.3.1), there is indeed the following commentary (*bhāṣya*) on that rule: "Verbs such as *pacati* and others are the agents of the action of 'becoming' (*bhavati*)."

By this, it is clearly understood that the action of "becoming" (*bhavati*), which has the actions such as "cooking" (*pacati*) as its agent, possesses primacy. Otherwise, according to the rule that "the base and the suffix express the meaning together," the action denoted by the verbal root would already be restricted as a qualifier of the agent and so forth expressed by the finite verb (*ākhyāta*). Consequently, since it would lack expectancy for connection with another word-meaning, the demonstration by the author of the *Bhāṣya*—that the actions such as "cooking," which are themselves qualifiers of the agent and so forth expressed by the finite verb, are connected to the action of "becoming"—would be inconsistent.

It may be so. Therefore, the meaning is that the primacy of the action denoted by the verbal root (dhātvartha-kriyā) is understood as being determined by the mode-of-being (prakāratā) residing in the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyātārtha). And thus, from the Nirukta statement "the [sentence] has the action as its primary element" (bhāvapradhānam), and from the commentary on that Nirukta which states "pacy- and other [roots] denote actions," it is established that the bhāvanā, which constitutes the meaning of the verbal root, possesses primacy even in relation to the meaning of the suffix.

Thus, by virtue of both the previously cited etymological treatises (*nirukta*) and the authoritative commentary (*bhāṣya*), one must necessarily accept a restriction—specifically, an abandonment—of the rule that "among the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), the meaning of the suffix is predominant," in the case of verbal endings (*tiṅanta*). Otherwise, the implication is that you yourselves, who maintain the predominance of the suffix-meaning, would contradict the *Nirukta* and other such works. Furthermore, he states another objection regarding the lack of restriction in the rule that "among the meanings of the base and the suffix, the meaning of the suffix is predominant," beginning with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).

In expressions such as "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), since the agent is the primary meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), there arises an understanding of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) in the form: "the agent, who is the meaning of the suffix, is non-different from Devadatta. Consequently, even the referent of the nominative case, such as Devadatta, would attain primacy. This would result in an inconsistency with the unity of sentence (*ekavākyatva*) demonstrated by the Author of the Bhāṣya in the example "Look, the deer runs" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*), which takes the form: "the act of seeing has as its object the running whose agent is the deer."

If the root-meaning (*dhātu*) were to express the process (*bhāvanā*), and the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth were to be expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), then according to the rule that "the meaning of the base and the suffix [are related as qualifier and qualified]," the deer—which is the substratum of the action of running and is denoted by a word ending in the nominative case—would necessarily be construed as the object (*karman*) of the action of seeing. Consequently, since the sentence "paśya mṛgaṃ dhāvati" (see the deer running) would only be possible in the sense "you are the substratum of the act of seeing whose object is the deer which is the substratum of the act of running," such a sentence would effectively be rendered obsolete. This is the intended meaning.

It should be understood that by the passage beginning with "mūle prathamānta" and ending with "dvitīyāpatteḥ," the reason for the impossibility of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) within the theory that maintains the predominance of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārthaprādhānyavāda*) has been established. Here, it should be understood as follows: the form *dhāvati* is derived either from the root *dhāv* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) with the present tense suffix (*laṭ*), or from the root *sṛ*, which denotes swift motion, through the substitution of *dhau* before a suffix marked with *ś* (i.e., a *śit* suffix). Running (*dhāvana*) is defined as an activity (*vyāpāra*) characterized by intense velocity, conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location. The meaning of the suffix *laṭ* is the agent (*kartṛ*).

In that context, there is a coreferential relation (*anvaya*) with the deer through non-difference (*abheda*). Thus, according to the Vaiyākaraṇa school, the verbal cognition has the primary action as its principal qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*), being understood as: "the more intense activity, conducive to conjunction with a specific location, which resides in the agent—that is, the meaning of the suffix *laṭ*—which is non-different from the deer. Similarly, in the case of *paśya*, there is the second-person singular middle voice ending (*loṇmadhyamapuruṣaikavacana*) and the substitute *paśya* for the root *dṛś*. The meaning of the root *dṛś* is an activity conducive to visual perception (*cakṣurjñāna*).

And thus, there is a distinct cognition: "An operation, which is the object of an injunction and is conducive to visual perception, resides in an agent whose meaning is non-different from the meaning of the second-person imperative suffix. The relation between the meanings of two words appears through the capacity of syntactic connection (*saṃsargamaryādā*) within a single word-meaning; there is no requirement for a word expressing that relation itself. Therefore, when the action of running performed by a deer is construed as the object of the action of seeing, the cognition arises through a single sentence as follows: "An operation, which is the object of an injunction and is conducive to visual perception, has as its agent an agent whose meaning is non-different from the meaning of the *laṭ* (present) suffix [denoting] the deer."

In that context, since "running" (dhāvana), which serves as the object of the act of seeing, is denoted by a verbal root (dhātu), and since a verbal root lacks the designation of a nominal stem (prātipadika), there is no possibility of a second case ending (*dvitīyā*) arising from it. This is because the *Bhāṣya* accepts the relation of action and factor (*kriyākārakabhāva*) between two actions in such instances as "the act of cooking exists" (*pacati bhavati*)—meaning "the act of cooking comes to be"—and "the future act of cooking exists" (*pakṣyati bhavati*)—meaning "the future act of cooking exists in a subtle form. By the same logic, the intention is that even in the sentence "Look, the deer is running" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*), the understanding of the connection between two actions is admitted.

According to the view of those who maintain that the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya) is predominant, there would arise the cognition: "The deer possesses an activity characterized by velocity conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location. In such a cognition, the deer—which serves as the qualificand—would have to be construed as the object (*karman*) of the act of seeing (*dṛśi-kriyā*). However, this is not possible. Since the deer, being the object, is the primary meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*), it is not denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) in the word *paśya*; consequently, its construction would result in the occurrence of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) by the rule *anabhihite karmaṇi dvitīyā* ("the accusative is used for the object when it is not already expressed [by another means]"), which contradicts the intended usage.

The point is this: the deer is the substantive (viśeṣya) with respect to the act of running, and it is the direct qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) with respect to the act of seeing; furthermore, the act of seeing is the primary element here. Thus, since the agent in the form of the deer is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) in the word *dhāvati* ("is running"), the rule "the nominative case applies when [the agent] is already expressed" (*abhihite prathamā*) would result in the nominative case after the word *mṛga*. At the same time, because it is the object (*karman*) defined by the act of seeing, the accusative case would also apply after that word. Between these two, the nominative is more immediate (*antaraṅga*), because it is based on the single sentence *mṛgo dhāvati* ("the deer is running").

The second [case-ending], however, is *bahiraṅga* (external), because it depends on both sentences, as seen in the example "paśya mṛgo dhāvati" (see, the deer runs). Consequently, setting aside the second case, the first case must occur first due to its being *antaraṅga* (internal) by virtue of being presented first. Therefore, even though there is a connection with the action of seeing, there is no possibility of the second case occurring, because—according to the maxim "one who has already eaten"—it is improper to subvert an internal grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) that has already been produced.

If it is argued that, because they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), the meaning would be "the seeing has the deer as its agent and running as its object," which would result in the collapse of the usage *paśya mṛgo dhāvati* ("see, the deer runs"), we reply: although the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) due to its dependence on the extrinsic action of seeing, nevertheless, because the action of the root *tṛ* (to cross) is primary, and because in common worldly usage it is observed that an operation determined by the primary [element] is everywhere more powerful, the accusative—conforming to the primary action—would prevail, overriding even the nominative (*prathamā*), which is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*).

However, this fault does not apply to the view that holds that the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) has the primary object (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) as its focus on the activity (*vyāpāra*). This is because, since the deer is an internal factor (*antaraṅga*) by virtue of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the running, the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the nominative case (*prathamā*) that has already arisen is not sublated. In the view of the Logicians (*Tārkika*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the activity conducive to the result (*phala*). Due to parsimony (*lāghava*), the expressive power (*śakti*) of the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) resides in the effort (*kṛti*). Furthermore, the effort connects with the referent of the nominative case through the relation of substratum (*āśrayatā-sambandha*). And the verbal cognition has the referent of the nominative case as its primary object.

And likewise, in the view of the Naiyāyikas, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) of the sentence "Look, the deer runs" is as follows: "The deer possesses an effort conducive to an activity conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location. Regarding the word "look," having supplied the object "him" (*tam*), the meaning is: "You"—the referent of the second-person pronoun—possess an effort conducive to an activity conducive to visual perception; this meaning is indeed distinct [from the first], and not part of a single syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of a second-case ending (*dvitīyā*) following the word "deer. Anticipating the objection that there would be the occurrence of a second-case ending, he refutes it with the words beginning with "And not thus" (*na caivam*). "Thus" (*evam*) means...

The meaning is that [the suffix] *dvitīyā* (accusative) would apply after the word *mṛga*. Since the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau* prescribes the substitution of *śatṛ* and *śānac* for *laṭ* when it is in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with a word ending in a case other than the nominative (*apramathamānta*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*) that *śatṛ* would necessarily replace *laṭ* during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*) in the case of *dhāvati*, following the word *mṛga*, which would require the accusative case. Thus, the intention of the objector is that the accusative case will not be employed precisely out of fear that the personal endings (*tib-ādi*) would fail to occur.

The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin), however, maintains that the occurrence of the present participle suffix *śatṛ* is not an obstacle to the application of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*). Rather, it is the fact that the object (*karman*) has already been expressed (*abhihitatva*) that constitutes the obstacle. For even when the *śatṛ* suffix occurs, there is no expression of the object, because the present tense (*laṭ*) pertains to the agent (*kartṛ*). Consequently, since the state of the object being unexpressed remains as it was, the application of the accusative case would be unavoidable; reflecting on this, he says: "Even so" (*evamapi*). The meaning is: "even though the *śatṛ* suffix has occurred."

Since the deer is construed as the object (*karman*) in the act of seeing, and because the accusative case suffix (*dvitīyā*) must necessarily apply after the word "deer" (*mṛga*)—as the object has not been expressed by another grammatical element—the sentence "Look at the running deer" (*dhāvantaṃ mṛgaṃ paśya*) alone is appropriate; thus, the usage "Look, the deer runs" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*) is altogether impossible. This is the meaning.

Anticipating the objection that the usage "paśya mṛgo dhāvati" (see, the deer runs) might be possible because there is no application of the second case ending after the word "mṛga," [the author] refutes it with the words beginning "na ca paśya ity atra. The meaning of the intention [of the objection] is as follows: the deer is not construed as the object (*karman*) of the act of seeing expressed by "paśya"; rather, the word "tam" (him), as an independent object, must be supplied there. Thus, since the meaning would be "see that deer which is running," the usage "paśya mṛgo dhāvati" would be possible. [The response is: such a supply (*adhyāhāra*) is not tenable.

The meaning is that, if that were the case, there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) consisting of a split in the sentence structure, whereby "the deer runs" would be one sentence and "see him" a second. Furthermore, because it is established by the experience of all people that from the sentence "See, the deer runs," there arises a single unified cognition—namely, that the act of seeing has as its object the intense running residing in the deer—it is intended to demonstrate that the intense running residing in the deer is indeed construed with the act of seeing through the relation of being its object (*karmatā*).

And this [explanation] is properly established in the view of the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas), who maintain that the cognition has the primary action as its qualificand. For in the case of the word "he runs" (*dhāvati*), there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the intense running—which is the qualificand perceived from that word and which resides in the agent denoted by the sense of the present tense (*laṭ*), namely the deer—as the object (*karman*) of the act of seeing, [the structure being]: "intense running, not distinct from the deer, residing in the agent, which is conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location."

This [explanation] is not tenable either in the view of those who maintain that the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth are denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), as held by proponents of the primacy of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārthaprādhānyavādin*), nor in the view of the logicians (*tārkika*) who maintain that the verbal cognition has the word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*) as its primary qualificand. This is because, from the arising of the verbal cognition—"the seeing which has the deer as its object and is the locus of an effort conducive to an operation conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location"—there would be the contingency of the accusative case after the word "deer" (*mṛga*); therefore, to avoid this, the object "him" (*tam*) is supplied (*adhyāhāra*) in relation to the act of seeing.

In that context, although the word "him" (tam) may refer either to the mere deer or to the deer as the locus of the action conducive to running, it is impossible for the intended meaning—that the perception has as its object the intense running residing in the deer—to be understood from that sentence.

But surely, when there is a reference by that word to a deer qualified by the action of running intensely, according to the maxim—"Injunctions and prohibitions transfer to the qualifier when there is a contradiction regarding the qualificand"—just as in the case of "The crested one has perished," where the connection with perishing is abandoned in favor of the crested one (the qualificand) and results in the connection with perishing being finalized in the crest (the qualifier), so too here, since the connection results in the action of intense running residing in the deer itself being understood as the object, [there is no fault].

If it is argued that the intended meaning of the etymology is untenable, we say no, because of the disparity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). To explain: in the example "the crested one has perished" (*śikhī dhvastaḥ*), since the connection with destruction is sublated by perception in the case of the person qualified by the crest—who is the substantive (*viśeṣya*)—it is logical that the connection with destruction culminates in its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), namely, the crest.

In the case of the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*), consider the sentence "the deer runs" (*mṛgo dhāvati*). Here, since there is no sublation (*bādhā*) of the status of being the object of the act of seeing with respect to the deer, which serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), it is appropriate that the deer itself—the qualificand—is construed with the act of seeing through the relation of being its object. It should be understood that it is entirely improper for the act of running intensely, which serves as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of that deer, to be construed as the object of the act of seeing, because such a construction lacks any basis in authoritative cognition (*aprāmāṇika*). He concludes the present topic with the words "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*).

The meaning is: in the view that accepts a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) where the agent and so forth denoted by the verb (ākhyāta) are the qualificand, as well as in the view that maintains a cognition where the meaning of the nominative-ending word (prathamāntārtha) is the qualificand, there is the inevitability of the fault consisting in the impossibility of the syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) sanctioned by the author of the Bhāṣya.

The causal relation between the cognition and its presentation as stated by the Naiyāyikas—that "the presentation of the meaning generated by a word ending in the nominative case, functioning as the qualificand, is the cause of a cognition in which there is a manner (prakāra), i.e., a specific operation of the verbal root (dhātvartha) distinct from number, time, and so forth"—is not to be accepted, because it is afflicted by the aforementioned defects. This is the meaning. He states his own established conclusion with the words "But rather... (kiṃ tu).

The causal relationship between the cognition and the mental representation (upasthiti) is to be understood as follows: when a cognition is to be produced that has the agent (kartṛ)—which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (tiṅ) denoted by the verb—as its qualifier, the mental representation of the productive operation (bhāvanā) arising from the verbal root (dhātu) is the cause, related [to that cognition] by way of the relation of being the qualificandum (viśeṣyatā). This is because it is established by experience that from the sentence "Devadatta cooks rice" (devadattas taṇḍulaṃ pacati), there arises the cognition: "the operation conducive to the softening of the rice, which resides in that agent who is non-different from Devadatta, who is the meaning of the present indicative suffix (laṭ)."

Although this operation (*vyāpāra*) is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) in its specific forms such as *phūtkāratva* (the nature of blowing), nevertheless, because verbal roots possess multiple meanings, it may sometimes be denoted by the root even in its general form. For this very reason, at the time of demonstrating the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), it is stated that the cognition occurs in a general form as "an operation conducive to softening" (*viklittyanukūlo vyāpāraḥ*), rather than being specified in a particular form as "blowing, etc., conducive to softening" (*viklittyunukūlaḥ phūtkārādiḥ*); thus, [the theory] is consistent.

Thus, in the original [definition], the qualification stated for the linguistic cognition produced by a verbal root—that it must have "the state of being an efficient force" (*bhāvanātva*) as its delimiting objective—should be understood with the intention that a verbal root sometimes produces a cognition where the state of being an efficient force is the qualifier. Similarly, one must also accept the following causal relation: in order to produce a cognition where the object denoted by the *tiṅ* suffix is the qualifier, the linguistic cognition produced by the verbal root is the cause, related to it through the relation of being the qualificandum residing in the fruit [of the action].

Now, since it is observed as a rule that the meaning of the verbal root—the activity—is a qualifier only with respect to the meaning of a *kṛt* suffix and not with respect to the meaning of a *tiṅ* suffix, one must necessarily accept a causal relation between the cognition and its presentation, such that the presentation produced by a *kṛt* suffix is the cause for generating a verbal cognition in which the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is the qualifier. And thus, a verbal cognition in which an action is the qualifier and another action is the qualificand—such as [the one supposedly arising] from "pacati bhavati" (cooking exists)—is absolutely impossible.

Anticipating the objection that there is an absence of the semantic presentation (*upastiti*) produced by a *kṛt* suffix—which serves as the cause for a verbal cognition where the mode (*prakāra*) is an action—he refutes it with the words "having the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) as the mode. Just as in cases such as "the goer" (*gantṛ*), a verbal cognition is universally established by experience as having the meaning of the suffix as its primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*), namely, "the substratum of an activity conducive to conjunction with another location"—in such a cognition to be generated, [the relation] is that of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by the modality (*prakāratā*) residing in the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) which is the meaning of the verbal root.

Just as the causal relation between cognition and its object is accepted—namely, that the presentation of the object of an action (*kṛti*) is the cause of the cognition [of that action]—in the same way, when a cognition having the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) as its qualifier is to be generated, the following causal relation must also be postulated: the presentation of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) derived from the verbal root is the cause, related to the effect by the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by the qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in the productive operation denoted by the verbal root. He states the proof for postulating the aforementioned causal relation with the example, "Look, there is a deer," and so forth.

The meaning is that in cases such as *pacati bhavati*, the understanding (bodha) where the bhāvanā is the qualificand and the bhāvanā is the qualifier—based on their being a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*)—is supported by the Bhāṣya and other authorities. Regarding the phrase "the direction" (*dig*): the mention of *atiṅ* in the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* was intended to prevent the elision of accent (*nighāta*) for a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) following another finite verb, as in *pacati bhavati*. If there were no single-sentence status (*ekavākyatva*) in such instances, then because the condition of being within the same sentence (*samānavākyasthatva*) would be absent, the elision of accent would not apply anyway; thus, the mention of *atiṅ* would be redundant. Therefore, single-sentence status exists even for a collection of finite verbs.

The meaning is that this indicates what is intended by the author of the Sūtra. Alternatively, the sentence "the deer runs" (*dhāvati mṛgaḥ*), which denotes a qualified object—namely, a deer possessing an effort conducive to running—is construed with the act of seeing (*darśana*) through the relation of being its object (*karmatā*). In that case, since the relation between the referent of a noun and the referent of a verbal root occurs as non-difference (*abhedena*), there is no contradiction with the rules of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*). This is because the sentence itself is not the referent of a noun (*nāmārtha*). Nor does it follow that the accusative case-ending would apply, because a sentence is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatvāt*).

The meaning is that even though syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is possible through the principle that the status of being the object of the act of seeing (*darśanakarmatva*) ultimately results in [the object] running, due to the force of the intended purport (*tātparya*), the Naiyāyikas cannot avoid the contradiction with the statement "the action is the primary element" (*bhāvapradhānam*), which has its meaning established by the Bhāṣya. And thus: *Itthaṃ ca...* (And so... [follows].

The meaning is as follows: when the agent and so forth, which are the meanings of the suffix, function as qualifiers of the verbal root meaning; when the number, which is the meaning of the suffix, functions as a qualifier of the agent and so forth which are the meanings of the suffix; or alternatively, when the presentation of the verbal root meaning—the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)—is the cause for generating a cognition whose qualificand is the agent which is the meaning of the verbal suffix, and when the presentation of the verbal root meaning—the result—is the cause for generating a cognition whose qualificand is the object which is the meaning of the verbal suffix. In the case of *pacati*, the form of the cognition is: "There is an activity conducive to the softening [of the rice], occurring at the present time, having a single agent."

"Verb is that in which the state (bhāva) is predominant; verb is that in which the action (kriyā) is predominant"—this is in accordance with the commentary on the *Nirukta*. Likewise, even in the case of a transitive verb such as *pacyate* ("it is cooked"), according to the view of the ancients, the form of cognition should be understood as having the operation (*vyāpāra*) as its primary qualificand: "the operation, occurring at the present time, which is conducive to that softening (*viklitti*) which has a single object."

The moderns, however, argue that since in cases such as *pakvastandulaḥ* (cooked rice), where a kṛt-affix occurs, the understanding is that "the rice is the locus of the softening (*viklitti*) brought about by the operation," the primacy of the result (*phala*) with respect to the operation is observed; therefore, they maintain that even in cases ending in a karmatiṅ-affix, it is logical that the result alone should be the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*). Precisely because the result is the primary qualificand even in the case of tiṅ-antapadas, there is no abandonment of the rule that [the meaning of the suffix] must be construed as a qualifier of the meaning of its own base (*prakṛti*).

In the case of *pacyate* ("it is cooked"), the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)—the result delimited by an operation—is related to the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), namely the object (*karman*). Since the result, which is the softening (*viklitti*), is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) there, the definition [of the object] is satisfied through its connection with that [result] by way of the relation of substratumhood (*āśrayatā-sambandha*). This is because the cognition [produced] is: "The softening, produced by an operation, has as its substratum an object non-different from rice. In the case of verbal suffixes expressing the abstract action (*bhāva*), since they merely restate the meaning of the root, the abstract action denoted by the root alone is the primary qualificand.

Nor should it be argued that the present time (*vartamānatva*) would not be conveyed there by the *laṭ* suffix and others; for the *tiṅ* suffixes function as indicators (*dyotaka*) of the present time because it serves as a qualifier of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*), which is the activity (*vyāpāra*), as is experienced in actual usage. Even in the view that they are denoters (*vācaka*), one must accept its status as a qualifier of the verbal root's activity due to the lack of any other recourse and in accordance with experience. If it is asked: "In that case, how is the cognition of number (*saṃkhyā*) also possible there?", the answer is: no.

For in the case of the *bhāvalakāra* (the impersonal passive), since neither the agent nor the object—which would otherwise be connected with number—is perceived, the number pertaining to them remains unconnected. Nor should it be suspected that number might instead be connected to the *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) itself, just as it is to the present tense; for the *bhāvanā* is presented by the verbal root precisely as something not connected with gender or number. It is for this very reason that its nature is said to be non-substantial (*asattvarūpatva*).

However, since it is a rule that neither the base (*prakṛti*) alone nor the suffix (*pratyaya*) alone should be employed, the singular number is used solely for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). Even in that case, there is no requirement for the number one (*ekatva-saṃkhyā*), because of the established conclusion of the *Bhāṣya*: "The singular shall be applied as the general rule (*utsarga*). The underlying idea is this: the formulation of the sūtra is to be broken down as "the singular [is used] for one" and "the dual for two," while "the plural for many" remains exactly as it stands.

In that context, since there is a rule governing the dual and plural endings for duality and plurality respectively, it follows that in cases where those two do not apply, the singular ending is used by disregarding number; such is its meaning. However, in instances where there is co-utterance with words like "Caitra" which denote the agent, there is a syntactic relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the agent presented by the verb and Caitra and the others. Thus, in the sentence "Caitra cooks rice," the understanding is as follows: the verbal root expresses a softening (*viklitti*) residing in the rice; the suffix expresses a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) residing in an agent non-different from Caitra, which is singular, and which is present in time. This is the cognition derived from "Caitra cooks rice."

Thus, even when there is co-utterance with words such as "rice" (*taṇḍula*) which denote the object (*karman*), because the object presented by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is construed as non-different from the rice and so forth, the understanding in the sentence "Rice is being cooked by Caitra" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacyate caitreṇa*) is that the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is conducive to a softening (*viklitti*) which has a single Caitra as its locus and has a single rice-grain as its non-different locus; with this intention, he says: "But when words such as 'Devadatta' are employed," [and] "by the agent, etc., which are the meanings of the verbal suffix. This is because non-difference is construed only between the meanings of two nouns that possess the same case-ending.
The point is that [the derivation of meaning] is flawed because it is subject to deviation in cases such as "one should sacrifice with soma," "he cooks a little," and "the king's servant."

It has been stated that, for the generation of a cognition whose qualifier is the agent (kartṛ) denoted by the verb, the cause is the presentation of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) produced by the verbal root (*dhātu*), through the relation of objective content (*viṣayatā*). However, it is not observed that every verbal root alone expresses *vyāpāra* (activity), because in cases such as *naśyati* ("perishes"), no cognition of activity is experienced. Thus, with the intention of pointing out the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the aforementioned causal relationship in such instances, he says: "In the case of 'the jar perishes' (*ghaṭo naśyati*)," etc. The point is this: the meaning of the root *naś* is not merely destruction (*nāśa*).

However, since the root *ṇaś* is listed in the *dhātupāṭha* as meaning "non-perception" (*adarśana*), its meaning is an operation conducive to that non-perception. And that operation is the conjunction of the causal complex for destruction (*nāśasāmagrī*) together with the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*). Here, the coexistence of the causal complex for destruction with the counter-correlativity should be understood by way of the relation of "determiningness" (*nirūpakatā*). Thus, the meaning is that the operation is precisely the conjunction of that causal complex for destruction which determines the counter-correlativity residing in the jar.

The causal complex for destruction (*nāśasāmagrī*) consists of the gradual, sequential disintegration of parts and so forth. Thus, because the understanding arises that [destruction] is an operation conducive to non-perception (*adarśanānukūla-vyāpāra*) having a substratum non-different from the jar, there is no violation of the relationship between cause and effect; this is the meaning. For this very reason—that is, precisely because the root *naś* signifies an operation conducive to non-perception—[it is said]: "when that [complex] exists," meaning when the causal complex consisting of the gradual disintegration of parts and so forth is present.

The meaning is that [the action] perishes until the point when there exists an operation conducive to the manifestation of its parts and its existence; once the operation has ceased, it is said to have "perished," and if the operation is yet to come, the usage "it will perish" (*naṅkṣyati*) is justified. Regarding sentences such as "Devadatta knows" (*devadatto jānāti*) or "he desires" (*icchati*), he explains the understanding of the sentence-meaning as "having a locus non-different from Devadatta," and so forth. That is the meaning of "and that operation. Finally, it is simply the state of being the locus (*āśrayatā*).

The meaning is that, when an investigation is carried out to its ultimate conclusion, the very state of being the locus (*āśrayatā*) as determined by knowledge, desire, and so forth, is itself the operation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to that [result]. Since knowledge, desire, and the like are not perceived apart from their locus, the state of being the locus itself is the operation by virtue of being the generator of their perception. The meaning is that those operations which bring about the state of being the locus, through the superimposition (*āropa*) of them, constitute the cognition of the locus; and because they exist prior to and subsequent to [the result], they possess the nature of an operation. It should be understood, however, that in reality, even the contact between the self and the mind (*ātma-manaḥ-saṃyoga*) can be the operation conducive to knowledge, desire, and so forth. || 2 ||

Now, as an introduction to stating what determines the intended meaning—given the contingency of asking where the substratum-connection resides in the fruit and where the operation resides—the author sets the stage with the words beginning "nanvākhyātasya" (But surely, of the verbal suffix...). By the statement "tiṅs are traditionally held to denote the substratum," it is asserted that the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), when standing alone, possesses the expressive power (*śakti*) for both the agent and the object. Consequently, from the *tip* suffix in the word *pacati*, there would follow the cognition of both the agent and the object, because the expressive power exists in both cases; such is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "A word uttered once conveys its meaning only once; and according to the maxim that 'it is improper for a word to have multiple meanings without evidence,' there can be no simultaneous cognition of two meanings. To this, he replies: "Just as in the case of the cognition of the agent alone (*kartṛmātrabodhavat*). By the word *mātra*, the object of the action (*karmārtha*) is excluded. [In the phrase] "of the object alone" (*karmamātrasyāpi*), the word *mātra* excludes the meaning of the agent. [The result would be] the contingency of such a cognition (*bodhāpatti*).

The point is as follows: just as from a word such as *hari*, which has multiple meanings, there arises at one time the cognition of a lion alone and at another time the cognition of a horse alone because the indicators of intention (*tātparya*), such as context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, are equal [in their influence], so too in the case of *pacati*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition of the object alone, since the expressive power (*śakti*) is the same. Regarding the term "indicator of intention" (*tātparyagrāhaka*): it means that which generates a grasp of the intention (*tātparya*), which consists in being uttered with the desire that a particular cognition of a specific meaning should arise.

This means that [the rule] captures the intended meaning as established by the experience of the teachers who founded the grammatical system (*śāstra*). Consequently, although a modern person might intend to convey the agent in the expression *pacyate* ("it is cooked"), there is no cognition of the agent because the teachers such as Pāṇini did not intend that; rather, there is only a cognition of the object (*karman*). Therefore, he says "phalavyāpāra" (the result and the operation). The word "tatra" (therein) has the sense of "tayor" (of those two); thus, the meaning is "between those two, namely the result and the operation."

Now, if *taṅ* were to indicate the coreferentiality (*anvaya*) with the substratum (*āśraya*) of the result, then in cases such as *edhate* and *niviśate*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) that the substratum of the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-artha*) would have to be coreferential with the result; therefore, in this context, *taṅ* must be understood as that which has arisen specifically from roots marked with *parasmaipada*, being qualified by the absence of being prompted by a prefix (*upasarga*). That is to say, it refers to *taṅ* when used in conjunction with *yaK* and so forth. Consequently, there is no fault in instances such as those cited in the *Nirukta*. As for *yaK*: [it refers to the passive suffix].

Now, one might object that in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *sukhyati* and *duḥkhyati*, which end in the *ya*-affix of the *kaṇḍvādi* class, the *ya* should be understood as that which occurs in co-occurrence with the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings; yet even so, the fault remains in forms such as *kaṇḍūyate*. To exclude this, the *ya* here must be understood as specifically that prescribed by the rule "the *ya*-affix [is applied] when a *sārvadhātuka* ending follows. Similarly, *ciṇ* must also be understood as specifically that prescribed by the rule "the *ciṇ* affix [is applied] in the sense of the impersonal (*bhāva*) or the passive (*karman*). Consequently, there is no over-extension in forms such as *adīpīt*, where the *ciṇ* ending follows the roots *dīp*, *jan*, etc., as in the rule "after *dīp*, *jan*, etc. The phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the *iṭ* augment prescribed as being like *ciṇ* (*ciṇvadiṭ*).

Just as in examples such as *yathā kāriṣyate ghaṭaḥ* ("as the pot will be made"), so too, in the case of [the suffixes] *śyan* and *parasmaipada* prescribed by the rule *kuṣirañjoḥ prācām o* (Pāṇini 3.1.90), these two are also indicators (*dyotaka*). For example, in cases such as *rajyati ghaṭaḥ svayameva* ("the pot colors itself"). Even in the case of the *liṅ* and other suffixes, context and the like should be understood as indicators according to the aforementioned method. The conventional usage—that *taṅ* and other [ātmanepada] suffixes indicate the object (*karman*), while *śa* and other [parasmaipada] suffixes indicate the agent (*kartṛ*)—is established by the passage beginning with *phalānvayyāśrayasya* and ending with *samudāyārthaḥ*.
"Causing one to grasp the intended meaning" (*tātparyaṃ grāhayanti*) means: producing the cognition of those respective meanings. || 3 ||

The phrase "it implies" (ākṣipati) refers to its function as a grasper of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the etymological derivation (*nirukta*). The sense is that [the suffixes] such as *taṅ* indicate the connection with the substratum (*āśraya*) in relation to the fruit (*phala*), while those such as *śap* indicate it in relation to the operation (*vyāpāra*). "Deviation" (*vyabhicāra*) means the breakdown of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

The meaning is that in cases such as *abodhi saḥ* ("he was awakened") and *pacyate odanaḥ svayameva* ("the rice cooks by itself"), although the suffix *yaK* and others are present, there is no connection of the substratum (*āśraya*) with the result; and although the suffixes *ŚaP* and others are absent, there is a connection of the substratum with the operation (*vyāpāra*). Thus, there arises a positive deviation (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*), which is the absence of the effect despite the presence of the cause, and a negative deviation (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), which is the presence of the effect despite the absence of the cause. To clarify this very deviation, he explains the process of establishing it with the words "when the object [becomes] the agent" (*karmaṇaḥ kartṛtve*).

When, in order to highlight the extreme ease [of the action], the activity of the agent—the person—is not intended to be expressed, but rather only the activity residing in the object such as the rice (*odana*), which is intended as being conducive to softening (*viklitti*) and so forth, then, although the suffixes *yaK* (passive marker) and *ātmanepada* endings occur because the rule "like the object [is the agent]" (*karmavat karmaṇā*) prescribes an extension of grammatical operations to the agent when the *L*-suffixes are formed from the root *pac*, the understanding derived from the verb (*ākhyāta*) pertains only to the agent. Therefore, the meaning is that the connection occurs only with the activity that serves as the locus (*āśraya*) of the meaning of the verb, and not with the result (*phala*).

Similarly, in the case of *abodhi* as well, from the root *budh* in the *luṅ* tense, with the substitution of the third person singular *ātmanepada* ending in its place, and the application of *ciṇ* by the rule *dīpajana...* etc., and subsequently the elision of that *ciṇ* substitute by the rule *ciṇo luk*, even here there is no connection of the substratum (*āśraya*) with the fruit; rather, it is connected only with the operation (*vyāpāra*). Therefore, he says: "This is a general rule," and so forth. [The term] "agent" refers to the *kartṛ*.

In examples such as *pacyata odanaḥ svayam eva* ("the rice cooks by itself"), and—by the force of the word "etcetera"—in cases like *kramād amuṃ nārada ity abodhi saḥ* ("gradually he was recognized as Nārada"), the previously stated point—that the *taṅ*-suffixes (*ātmanepada*) indicate the object (*karman*) and the *śa*-suffixes (*parasmaipada*) indicate the agent (*kartṛ*) due to their reversal—is an *utsarga*. By the etymology "that which is abandoned" (*utsṛjyate*) or "that which is set aside" (*tyajyate*), it is a general rule because it exists in many instances; however, the meaning is that it is common (*prāyika*) rather than universal (*sārvatrika*). Therefore, because the aforementioned point is not universal.

"Appropriate" (yathocitam) means that even if something is not explicitly followed [in the text], it is appropriate because it conforms to linguistic proficiency; the sense is that one must accept the expressive power [of words] solely in accordance with tradition (āgama), that is, following the scriptures. To clarify this very point by describing the verbal cognition (śābdabodha), he says: "For here... He states "Nārada" in order to demonstrate the verbal cognition of the one who has understood [the verse]. He then says "sāmānya... [to explain the nature of that cognition].

It should be understood that within the sequence of cognitions—first "a mass of light," then "an embodied being," then "a person," and finally "Nārada"—each preceding cognition is a general (sāmānya) cognition, while each succeeding one is a specific (viśeṣa) cognition. Regarding the term *ekanārada*: it means the cognition whose object is that single Nārada. Here, because the object is already expressed by the particle *iti*, the accusative case does not follow the word *nārada*.

In the view of Bhaṭṭanāgeśa, however, the cognition to be understood is that [the action] is conducive to the knowledge having the form "Nārada" (i.e., *nārada iti jñānam*), and so forth. In that case, because the word "Nārada," ending in the nominative case, is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatvāt*), there is no possibility of applying the accusative case either. They do not accept the view that [the accusative applies] "in some cases through a particle" (*kvacinnipātena*), because the Bhāṣya enumerates only finite verbs (*tiṅ*), primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*) [as governing the accusative]. As for what was stated [earlier], "according to the tradition" (*yathāgamaṃ*), he states its intended meaning with the words beginning with "sakarmaka" (transitive), and so on.

The meaning is as follows: the suffixes *ya*, *ciṇ*, *yak*, and so forth—which are prescribed by rules such as *sārvadhātuke yak* and which are co-occurrent with a verbal root that denotes a result residing in a locus other than the operation (*vyāpāra*)—are the indicators (*dyotaka*) of the agent and the object common to both the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). In cases such as *odanaḥ svayameva pacyate* ("the rice cooks by itself"), if one adopts the position of "transference of grammatical rules" (*śāstrātideśapakṣa*), there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the very result itself. This is because, under that view, the *ya*-suffix and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) prescribed by rules common to the abstract state (*bhāva*) would be present, and thus the requirement for the relation of the substratum (*āśraya*) to the operation would have to apply to the result alone.

To avoid that [over-extension], the qualifier ending with "samabhivyāhṛta" (co-occurring) has been provided, beginning with "sakarmaka" (transitive). Thus, the meaning is that since a root in the sense of a reflexive object (*karmakartṛ*) is generally intransitive (*akarmaka*), the *yaṅ* and *ātmanepada* endings occurring therein do not denote the object, because they lack co-occurrence with a transitive root. In cases such as "abodhi śrīkṛṣṇaḥ" (Śrī Kṛṣṇa was awakened), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because the *ciṇ* suffix co-occurs with a transitive root; to prevent this, the qualifier beginning with "bhāvasādhāraṇa" (common to the abstract state) is applied to the *yaṅ* and other suffixes.

Furthermore, regarding the term *ciṇ* in the expression "it was not understood" (*abodhi*), since it is prescribed by the rule *dīpajanabudha...* [Pāṇini 3.1.61], it is a general prescription for the abstract action (*bhāva*) and lacks the capacity to indicate an object (*karman*). This is the meaning. For one who lacks knowledge of the specific grammatical rules that prescribe *ciṇ*, *yaṅ*, and so forth, context and other such factors are the sole indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*). The same should be understood for the optative (*liṅ*) and other suffixes as well. Otherwise, in a case such as *pece* (he cooked), since both agent and object would be identical, the lack of any indicator of the intended meaning would lead to the undesirable consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

By this, the following [objection] is refuted: "Since the verb possesses the capacity (*śakti*) for the states of object (*karman*), agent (*kartṛ*), and so forth, just as the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is understood in all instances such as *pacati*, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that the states of object, agent, and so forth are also understood everywhere, because the capacity for them exists. This is to be understood as being refuted by the statement that the *yaṅ* suffix and others serve to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). (4)

Now, in order to strengthen the previously stated general view that a verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes an operation (*vyāpāra*), he prepares the ground with the words "evam" and so forth. The meaning is: having first defined the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) according to the method of the *Nirukta*, namely, "the *tiṅ*-suffixes denote the substratum (*āśraya*)," and so on. One might object: "After stating the general denotation of the root as an operation, it would have been more appropriate to establish that [denotation] at the outset through supporting and refuting arguments (*sādhaka-bādhaka-yukti*) by way of contextual sequence (*avasara-saṃgati*), rather than describing the sentence-meaning. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The maxim of the needle and the frying-pan (*sūcī-kaṭāha-nyāya*). [This means that one must first attend to the most difficult point before proceeding to the easier ones.]

This is the "needle-and-pot" maxim (*sūcīkaṭāhanyāya*). For instance, when a blacksmith first encounters the task of making a pot—which, though already required—is abandoned because it requires great effort, and subsequently performs first the task of making a needle—which, though encountered later, is accomplished with little effort—this is the "needle-and-pot" maxim. Even in worldly practice, it is well known that when two tasks arise simultaneously, the easier one is performed first and the more difficult one later.

Thus, according to this logic, because the misconceptions (*vipratipatti*) of the opponents whose views are to be refuted are few and not difficult to understand, the meaning of the sentence is easily established and easily comprehended through their refutation; therefore, that [the meaning of the sentence] alone was described first, and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) was not determined. It should be understood that in that case, because the misconceptions of the opponents to be refuted are numerous and because it would be difficult to grasp at that time due to its being entangled in various kinds of complex and obscure arguments (*tarka-jāla*). [The phrase] "ending in *laṭ* etc. refers to this.

Here, the word *anta* (end) signifies "proximity to what follows. The term *laḍādirantaḥ* is an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound, meaning "that which has *laṭ* and so forth as its final element [in proximity]. Thus, the phrase *laḍādyantaḥ* means "in a verbal root (*dhātu*). The purpose of this statement is directed toward the Prābhākaras and others who assert that, by the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) "the non-expressiveness of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) resides in the verbal root," there is an absence of expressibility (*vācyatva*)—as defined by a denotative power residing in the verbal root—with respect to the productive activity.

Alternatively, the meaning is as follows: "The absence of denotative power (vācakatva), which is defined by the state of being denoted (vācyatā) by that which culminates in productive activity (bhāvanā), resides in the verbal root (dhātu). Their intention is this: if productive activity were denoted by the verbal root, then according to the maxim that "the meaning of the suffix is predominant," the predominance of that [activity] would be untenable; therefore, they maintain that it is not denoted by the verbal root. By the term "Prābhākara and others," the Naiyāyikas are included.

Although the Naiyāyikas maintain that the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an operation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to a result, even so, such an operation is not designated by the term *bhāvanā* in their system. Thus, with reference to the Mīmāṃsakas, [the author] states "the operation is *bhāvanā*" in order to establish, through arguments for and against, that *bhāvanā* is denoted by the verbal root, and for the Naiyāyikas, to confirm that the operation which is the meaning of the root is what is expressed by the word *bhāvanā*.

The meaning of the first half of the verse is this: whatever object is expressed by the word "operation" (*vyāpāra*), that very same object is designated by the words "bringing into being" (*utpādanā*) and "action" (*kriyā*).

If it is asked, "What kind of object is designated by the term 'operation' (*vyāpāra*)?", it is stated in accordance with the verses of Harika: It is that collection of operations—such as placing [the pot on the fire] and so forth—which arise in succession, reside in the intellect, and consist of the non-difference constructed by a synthesizing cognition (*saṃkalanātmikā buddhi*), while being joined with parts appearing in their respective forms such as "blowing" (*phūtkāratva*) and the like.

The word *pada*, which denotes such an operation (*vyāpāra*), is explained by words such as *bhāvanā* and so forth; thus, because the explained term and its explanation possess the same meaning, it is established that the verbal root (*dhātu*) expresses *bhāvanā*. This is the sense, based on the statement that "the verbal root [denotes] both the result and the operation. In the phrase "that very [operation] is *bhāvanā*," the division of words is *sā eva*. The meaning is: "That which is the operation is precisely *bhāvanā*. For it has been stated by the learned: "A pronoun (*sarvanāman*), which brings about identity between the subject and the referent, partakes of the gender of either one of them."

It is like the expression *yatkarma ṇā cetsa kartā* ("if that which is the object by means of the instrument is the agent"). Alternatively, let there be the masculine designation *sa eva* ("that very same"); the meaning is that the operation (*vyāpāra*) is itself the efficient force (*bhāvanā*). The intention is that this is grammatically correct because of the elision of the nominative suffix *s-* in *saḥ*, according to the rule *so'ci lope cet pādapūraṇam*.

Now, it might be argued that all that was previously stated would be logical if the verbal root (*dhātu*) were established as denoting an activity (*vyāpāra*); however, when the question arises as to what the proof for this is, [the author] demonstrates that the very analysis of roots such as *pac* (to cook) by means of the root *kṛ* (to do), which signifies activity—since it will be stated later that "therefore, *karoti* (he does) shall be the explanation of the root"—is the proof itself, namely: "He cooks produces the cooking," and so forth. Thus he says: "He cooks produces the cooking," etc.

Now, one might ask: since it has been stated in the verse that "the operation (*vyāpāra*) is indeed *bhāvanā*," and that "whatever is action (*kriyā*), that itself is *bhāvanā*, and that itself is production (*utpādanā*)," the status of action as *bhāvanā* is already established; for what purpose, then, was the term "operation" (*vyāpāra*) inserted? To this, he says: "And the term 'operation'... Regarding the phrase "of those [actions] not consisting of effort": the term "operation" is employed so that even those operations such as blowing (*phūtkāra*) and the like—which are distinct from the effort denoted by the word "volition" (*kṛti*)—may be established as being denotable by the term *bhāvanā* in their respective specific forms.

The point is this: by using the word *kriyā* (action), which is derived from a suffix (*śa*) denoting "being" (*bhāva*) and thus signifies "effort" (*yatna*)—just like the word *kṛti*—one would obtain that only effort residing in a conscious being alone is denoted by the term *bhāvanā*, and not the operations common to both conscious and unconscious entities. And the purpose of the word *kriyā* is to indicate that such operations are denotable by verbal roots (*dhātu*) as well as denotable by the word *kriyā*. "For this very reason" means: precisely because the operation, in its various forms, is denotable by the verbal root.
