The meaning is that awareness (*bodha*) is established for all; thus, the denial of awareness—which is established by the experience of everyone—in its specific form is improper. Likewise, because the operation (*vyāpāra*) is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) in its specific form, at the time of the cognition produced by the sentence "Caitra cooks," the doubt "Does Caitra possess [the action of] blowing and so forth, or not? does not arise. However, in the case of a cognition in a general form, since there is no ascertainment of either alternative—namely, "it exists" or "it does not exist"—doubt is unavoidable; this is the intended sense.

Now, a bystander raises an objection—establishing that the root expresses effort (*kṛti*) by means of the rule accepted by the Naiyāyikas—arguing that it is improper to accept *phūtkāratva* (the state of blowing) and so forth as the delimiters of the denotation (*vācyatāvacchedaka*) because they are cumbersome and manifold; rather, since it is simpler and unitary, it is more appropriate to accept *kṛtitva* (the state of being effort) alone as the delimiter of the root's denotation. This objection is presented with the words "And not thus... up to "...is correct. The word "thus" (*evam*) refers to the aforementioned manner in which the operations such as blowing and so forth would be the denotations of the root.

"Of these," namely blowing (*phūtkāra*) and so forth. The ellipsis to be supplied is "provided that their status as the delimitors of capability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*) is accepted. Regarding "due to heaviness": the meaning is because they are cumbersome and because they are manifold. "Only the nature of effort (*kṛtitva*)" means that, in comparison with blowing and so forth, the nature of effort—specifically the nature of activity (*pravṛttitva*)—is a particular universal (*jāti*) established as the delimitor of the effectness (*kāryatā*) determined by the cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*). The meaning is that this is due to its lightness and its unity as a universal. By the word "only" (*eva*), blowing and so forth are excluded. "The delimitant of that" [refers to the nature of effort].

The meaning is that the delimitor (avacchedaka) of what is expressed by the verbal root must be stated. Thus, the intention of the objection is: "Let the meaning of the verbal root be an action (kṛti) conducive to softening (viklitti). And action is nothing but effort (yatna). Now, if action is indeed the meaning expressed by the verbal root, how can the experience of everyone—which is well-established—be accounted for, namely the cognition of "operation" (vyāpāra) and so forth in cases like "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*), where effort is precluded in an insentient object such as a chariot? To this, he says: "In cases such as 'the chariot goes'... [and] "of 'he knows' (*jānāti*)," the supplement is "Devadatta," and so forth.

The phrase "and so forth" (ādi) includes [verbs such as] "desires" (icchati) and "perishes" (naśyati). The phrase "because of being an operation" (vyāpāratvāt) and so forth includes [the properties of] being a substratum (āśrayatva) and being a counter-correlate (pratiyogitva). And that [is understood] through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā); such is the meaning. This is the method of the Naiyāyikas.

The meaning is as follows: Just as the Naiyāyikas—who maintain that the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) have their primary denotation (*śakti*) in the action (*kṛti*) due to parsimony (*lāghava*), and not in the agent (*kartṛ*), because positing the denotation in the agent (who is defined as one possessing an action) involves complexity (*gaurava*)—have established the usage "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*) by accepting a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for either the operation (*vyāpāra*) or the substratum (*āśrayatva*); in the same way, I, Śaṅkuka, am able to establish [my position] even though the action is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

It should be understood here that the Naiyāyika method is followed by the neutral observer solely for the purpose of supporting the view that the action is the meaning of the verbal root, and not for the sake of any other support.

For such a rule regarding the status of a delimiting factor (avacchedakatva) is possible only when a simpler [property] exists, whereas it is absent when a more complex one does; that is, when a simpler property established by another means of knowledge can serve as the delimiting factor, a more complex property should not be postulated as such.

The meaning of this is as follows: just as the delimitingness (*avacchedakatva*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absence of smoke that is a cognizable object (*prameya-dhūma-abhāva*) is accepted only in "pure smokeness" (*śuddha-dhūmatva*), which is co-extensive with "cognizable smokeness" (*prameya-dhūmatva*), and not in "smokeness qualified by cognizability" (*prameyatva-viśiṣṭa-dhūmatva*), because both the light and the heavy properties are established by other means of knowledge consisting of the power of words (*śabda-śakti*); it does not mean, however, that even when a light property is accessible through another means of knowledge, it must be accepted merely out of regard for parsimony (*lāghava*).

Furthermore, although "being an action" (*kṛtitva*) is a simpler property than "being a blowing sound" (*phūtkāratva*) and so forth, it cannot be known through other means of knowledge; moreover, since it is possible to accept a complex property as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) by the force of examples, the aforementioned restriction does not apply in the present case. With the intention that such a doubt from an outsider is therefore unjustified, he says: "Even of the state of being a delimitor of capability... (*śakyatāvacchedakatvasyāpi*).

The meaning is as follows: just as in the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), where the property consisting of being the bank of the Gaṅgā—which is presented through indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—is accepted as the delimitor of the indicated object (*lakṣyatāvacchedakatva*), so too there is no obstacle to accepting the property of being a puff of breath (*phūtkāratva*) and the like as the delimitor of the denotable object (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*), even though they are heavy properties. [This addresses the objection regarding] the disparity between those two.

The sense is that the view of the "neutral observer" (taṭastha), who suspects that the root denotes effort (*kṛti*), is entirely untenable; for there is no evidence to justify the distinction that both power (*śakti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—since they are equally of the nature of the relation between a word and its meaning—possess the property of being the delimitors of the indicated object (*lakṣyatāvacchedakatva*), whereas the delimitors of the denoted object (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*) do not reside therein. Furthermore, this is incorrect because such an experience does not arise for those who have actual experience, namely, that from the word *pacati* one understands "an effort conducive to the softening [of rice]" (*viklitti-anukūla-yatna*).

Now, it might be objected: "Is it not the case that the status of *kṛtitva* (the nature of being an effort) as the delimitor of what is denoted by the verbal root was not proposed merely out of consideration for parsimony (*lāghava*), but rather on the basis of parsimony accompanied by the possibility of its being cognizable through other means of knowledge? Thus, he raises the possibility of its being cognizable through other means of knowledge with the words 'And it is not... The underlying intention is this: the fact that the root *kṛñ* has "effort" (*yatna*) as its meaning must necessarily be accepted. This is because we observe the linguistic usage "the cloth is made" (*paṭaḥ kṛtaḥ*) only at the time when there is a reflective awareness (*anusaṃdhāna*) of its being produced by effort.

However, in the absence of the consideration that [the sprout] is produced by effort (*yatnajanyatva*), one observes the usage of the term "made" (*kṛta*) in the sense that "the sprout was made," whereas one observes the usage of the term "unmade" (*akṛta*) in the sense that "the sprout has arisen. Furthermore, since the verbal root *pac* contained within the expression "he cooks" (*pacati*) is explained by means of the verb *karoti* (meaning effort) as "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), and because the answer "he cooks" to the question "What does he do?"—which concerns effort—is otherwise inexplicable unless it possesses the meaning of effort, the intention of the doubt is that effort alone is the meaning of the verbal root; and this effort is nothing other than volitional action (*kṛti*).

This might be possible if it were easy to maintain that the root *kṛ* has "effort" (*yatna*) as its meaning; however, since that itself is difficult to establish, the claim that the verbal root possesses the meaning of effort is far from being tenable—this is the intention behind saying "the chariot" (*ratha*). In this context, if the word "chariot" were not employed, there would be no loss of such usage because an effort conducive to motion exists in sentient beings such as Caitra; therefore, the word "chariot" is specifically mentioned.

If one were to state merely that "the sprout was made" (*kṛta*), the aforementioned usage would be justified by taking it to mean being produced by the effort of Īśvara—a term synonymous with "exertion" (*yatna*). Therefore, it is said "by the seed, etc. (*bījādinā*). Thus, since effort is entirely precluded in the case of insentient things like chariots and seeds, such usage would otherwise be inconsistent; consequently, the root *kṛ* does not denote effort. Rather, it denotes activity (*vyāpāra*), for without this, the aforementioned usage would be untenable. It should not be argued that because *kṛ* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for activity, its denotation of effort is not thereby destroyed.

Since it is improper to assume a figurative meaning when the primary meaning is possible, and since the root *kṛ* is frequently observed to denote activity (*vyāpāra*), it is appropriate that the expressive power (*śakti*) of *kṛ* resides in activity itself. Thus, because the verbal root is explained by the verb *karoti* (which has such a meaning), and because there is a rule that the explainer and the thing explained must have identical meanings, the intention is that the denotation of the verbal root as activity must necessarily be accepted. Furthermore, "explanation" (*vivaraṇa*) is the statement of a word's meaning by means of another word having the same meaning.

It should be understood that the phrase "he cooks" (*pacati*) has its meaning explained by another expression having the same sense, such as "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*). Now, the author prepares the introductory context (bhūmikā) for the second half of the verse beginning with "Furthermore, because *kṛñ* would result in being intransitive" (*kiṃca... akarmakatāpatter iti*), using the words "Furthermore" (*kiṃca*) and so on. Regarding "of the productive activity" (*bhāvanāyāḥ*): this refers to productive activity in the form of an operation (*vyāpāra*). "If it were not denoted" (*avācyatve*) means: provided that there is an absence of being denoted as expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*), and an absence of being denoted as expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).

Consequently, since the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is ultimately reduced to the mere result (phala), the definition of the object (karmatva) must be stated as either "being the locus of the result of the verbal root's meaning which resides in a different substratum from the operation that produces that [result]," or simply "being the locus of the result of the verbal root's meaning. Here, the word "self" (sva) refers to the result.

And thus, when the suffix *ṇic*—which expresses an operation conducive to the meaning of the root *bhū* (to become) in the sense of "origination"—is applied, as in the case of *ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati* ("he brings about a pot"), the word *ghaṭa* takes the accusative case because the pot is the locus (*āśraya*) of the fruit of the verbal root's meaning, which consists of origination. Similarly, in the case of *ghaṭo bhavati* ("the pot becomes"), the same logic would apply: since the pot would be the locus of the fruit of the verbal root's meaning consisting of origination, it would follow that the word *ghaṭa* should take the accusative case. This is the point to be understood here.

In the case of a causative (*ṇijanta*) construction, the first definition of the object (*karman*) applies when [the action] has its own producer as the agent, while the second applies to the pure causative (*śuddhe ṇijante*). One might raise the objection that in the sentence "The pot comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), a dative case would erroneously follow the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*); however, this is raised to prevent such an occurrence. [The author] counters with the phrase "because of the sublation of the designation 'object'" (*karmasaṃjñāyā bādhāt*).

The opponent’s intention is as follows: since in the expression "the jar comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), the jar is perceived as the agent (*kartṛ*), even though it is the locus of the fruit consisting of its own arising, the designation of "object" (*karman*) is set aside by the designation of "agent," and thus there is no occurrence of the accusative case. To this, [the author] says "anugata... (in the verse), meaning that what was stated—that the jar possesses agency—is not possible; for since you are unable to state a definition of agency that applies to both sentient and insentient entities alike, the jar lacks agency, and consequently, the occurrence of the accusative case is unavoidable.

He establishes that the jar (*ghaṭa*) is indeed not an agent by stating "of being the locus of the effort," and so forth. If agency is defined as being the locus of an effort conducive to the fruit of the meaning of various verbal roots, then—since effort, which is synonymous with volition (*prayatna*), is a property residing only in sentient beings and is therefore absent in insentient things—there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "the jar exists. [This applies to] the "set of causal factors" (*kārakacakra*).

If it is argued that [the definition] is "being the initiator of a collection of factors (kāraka) capable of being connected with the action inherent in the primary substratum," then there is indeed an over-narrow application (avyāpti) in cases such as "the pot cooks" (sthālī pacati) or "the sword cuts" (asiś chinatti), because an insentient object like a pot lacks the capacity to initiate the entire cycle of factors. The point is that because a jar is insentient, it lacks both the status of being the locus of volitional effort (kṛti) and the status of being the prompter of the cycle of factors.

And thus, since the designation "agent" (kartṛ) has been stated to apply only to that which possesses an action (*kṛti*) and so forth, in the absence of such an action, the designation "agent" cannot be obtained; consequently, because the designation "object" (*karman*) would not be an exception [to the agent], the occurrence of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would be unavoidable—this is the meaning. In my view, however, there is no fault, because the status of being an agent exists by virtue of being the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*); therefore, the first case ending (*prathamā*) alone occurs, and not the second.

Having thus refuted the view of the Naiyāyikas—who do not maintain that the verbal root (*dhātu*) expresses the operation (*vyāpāra*)—he now addresses the Mīmāṃsaka, who asserts that the fruit (*phala*) is the meaning of the root and the operation is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), by stating: "conducive to the meaning of the root" (*dhātvarthānukūla*). The intended sense is as follows: according to the rule *svatantraḥ kartā* ("the independent one is the agent"), independence (*svātantrya*) consists in being the locus of the operation conducive to the fruit expressed by the root-meaning. Since this [independence] is indeed uncontradicted in the case of a jar (*ghaṭa*), owing to the presence of the operation conducive to its production (*utpatti*), I consider such independence alone to be agency (*kartṛtva*).

That too is not correct, because it is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*); thus he says: "merely a factor of action" (*kārakamātra*). The word "merely" (*mātra*) signifies totality. Since the status of being a substratum of some action conducive to the fruit of the respective verbal root-meaning exists in all factors of action (*kāraka*s), such as the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*), there would be an over-extension. The meaning is that the definition of a *kāraka* is simply "that which produces an action."

Now, although independence—in the form of being the locus of an activity conducive to the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha)—exists in all kārakas, it is understood from the formulation of the rule *svatantraḥ kartā* that the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) applies only to that whose independence is intended to be expressed as being the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Otherwise, because the designation "agent" would sublate [all others], the designations such as "ablative" (*apādāna*) and so forth would become devoid of scope.

Consequently, in such expressions as "he cooks rice in a pot with wood," there would be a total disappearance of the employment of kārakas such as the instrument (karaṇa). For this very reason, Nāgeśabhaṭṭa stated in the *Laghumañjūṣā* during his investigation into the meaning of case-endings (*sub-artha*): "Because all [kārakas] produce the action independently through their respective operations, they possess the status of the agent (*kartṛ*) kāraka."

Here, the meaning of the word *svātantrye* (in independence) is "precisely with the intention of [denoting] independence. Therefore, when there is an intention [to specify] such things as "by whom," "what," or "how does one cook," the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth certainly occurs by virtue of their respective functions. This has also been stated by Hari: "The status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) exists in every case simply in the accomplishment [of the action]; the possibility of being an instrument and so forth arises when there is a requirement for distinctions among functions."

For example, even though both parents are agents (*kartṛ*) in the birth of a son, when there is a desire to express the distinction—"Who [is the agent] in relation to whom, and who [is the agent] from what?"—the conventional usage "This person produces this son from her" is likewise justified. This is also stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *kāraka*: "When the effort residing in the cooking pot is being described, the pot is independent (*svatantra*). The meaning of that is: it possesses independence as intended by the speaker.

And thus, since independence (*svātantrya*) depends upon the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), there is neither an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) nor the undesired application of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) in the expression *ghaṭo bhavati*. This is because, by intending independence for the very operation conducive to the result of the verbal root as residing in the jar, the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) is unavoidable; therefore, he says "and moreover," etc., [concluding with] "it would be cut off."

The meaning is that if *bhāvanā* in the form of an operation were not denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu*), then the distinction between "this root is transitive" and "this root is intransitive" would be entirely impossible to establish. He states the definition of a transitive root as accepted in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) with the words beginning "svārthaphala... (the fruit of its own meaning). By the word "sva" (own), the verbal root is to be understood.

And thus, if a verbal root expresses an operation that has a different locus (vyadhikaraṇa) from the fruit denoted by that root, then that root is called "transitive" (sakarmaka). The qualification "having a locus different from its own expressed fruit" is added as a modifier of the operation in order to avoid over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to intransitive roots such as *bhū* and others. Therefore, the meaning is that an intransitive root like *bhū* is not transitive because it expresses an operation that has the same locus as the fruit expressed by itself.

[Objection: But surely, since the roots *bhū* (to become) and others also denote operations that have a locus distinct from the result of the meaning of roots such as *pac* (to cook), the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains exactly as it was. [Response: This is not so, because of the provision of the qualification "having its own meaning as the result" (*svārtha-phala*). The meaning is: "that which has a result whose locus is distinct from its own meaning. Therefore, although the operation of *bhū* and other roots has a locus distinct from the result of the meaning of roots like *pac*, there is no fault, because it lacks the quality of having a locus distinct from the result of its own meaning.

Objection: In sentences such as "Caitra goes to the village," since the result of the verbal root's meaning—namely, conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—resides in both [the agent and the object] due to its being "doubly located" (*dviṣṭha*), it exists in both the village and Caitra. Consequently, because the activity residing in Caitra does not have a different locus from the result of the verbal root's meaning, there would be no pervasion (*avyāpti*). And thus, the verbal roots like *gam* (to go) would not possess the property of having an object (*sakarmakatva*). If this is argued, we say: No.

And "having a different locus from the fruit" (phalavyadhikaraṇatva) is intended to mean: residing in something other than the locus of any fruit whatsoever belonging to the meaning of that verbal root, as delimited by the relation that defines the nature of that fruit. The meaning of this is that, between the two—the locus of the fruit and [the locus of] the operation—it is the operation that resides in something distinct from whichever one among those two is the locus of the fruit. In short, what is to be understood is that the operation resides in something distinct from the locus of some fruit, and not that it must reside in something distinct from the loci of all fruits.

And thus, although the operation (*vyāpāra*) of roots such as *gam* (to go) does not reside in a locus distinct from the entire substratum of the result, there is no failure to include *gam* and other such roots among the transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*). The meaning is this: between the village (*grāma*) and Caitra—the two loci of the result consisting of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) which is the meaning of the root *gam*—that one which is the locus of the result is the village; and since the root expresses an operation residing in Caitra, who is distinct from that [locus], there is no non-inclusion of *gam* and others among the transitive verbs. Furthermore, in the case of "the pot comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), the meaning of the root *bhū* is an operation conducive to origination (*utpatti*).

In this regard, one might raise the objection that there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of a transitive verb (*sakarmaka*) to intransitive verbs such as *bhū* (to become), because the operation (*vyāpāra*) resides in the pot while the result (*phala*), consisting of its coming into being, resides in time through a temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*); thus, these verbs would be considered transitive since they denote an operation whose locus is distinct from the locus of their own meaning’s result. This objection is avoided by specifying "by means of the relation that delimits the status of being a result" (*phalatāvacchedaka-sambandhena*). Thus, the intended meaning is that the operation is meant to reside in something distinct from whatever serves as the locus of the result by means of that very relation which delimits the status of being a result.

The point is this: in expressions such as "the jar comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), although the action of the root *bhū* (to be) exists in a jar that is distinct from the time of the locus of the result by virtue of a temporal relation, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). This is because, by means of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*)—which serves as the delimiting condition for the status of being a result—the action resides in the jar that is the locus of the result consisting of origination (*utpatti*), and thus it does not reside in a locus different from that of the result.

If it is argued that, based on the understanding from "he lives" (*jīvati*) and similar forms that "he sustains the vital breaths," the meaning of the root *jīv* is an activity conducive to the sustaining of the vital breaths—in which case the activity resides in Devadatta or another agent, while the result consisting of sustenance resides in the vital breaths, and sustenance means maintaining them in their proper state—then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to intransitive roots like *jīv*, because they denote an activity whose locus is distinct from the locus of the result of their own meaning. To this, it must be added as a qualification that the result of the root's own meaning must have its locus not included within the denotation of the verbal root itself.

The definition begins with "that which has as its fruit its own meaning, whose locus is not included within the meaning of the verbal root," and so forth. The meaning of this is: that fruit whose locus (āśraya) is not included—that is, not contained—within the meaning of the verbal root. Thus, the intention is that there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) here, because the vital breath (prāṇa), which is the locus of the fruit consisting of the action of holding (dhāraṇā) denoted by the verbal root, is itself included within the meaning of that verbal root. In the same way, the property of "not having an unintended object" (avivakṣitakarmakatvābhāva) must also be provided as a qualifier for "its own meaning."

To define transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) by another method, since it cannot be defined through the distinction of verbal roots (*vivigamanā*), [the author] states "svārthavyāpāra... and so forth. "Its own meaning" (*svārthaḥ*) means the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); that is to say, what is expressed by the verbal root. The meaning is: transitivity consists in being the denoter of a result (*phala*) that resides in a locus different from such an operation (*vyāpāra*). Furthermore, "residing in a locus different from the operation" should be understood as "subsisting in a substratum that is not the substratum of the operation."

The operation such as blowing (phūtkāra) denoted by the verbal root [√dhmā], its locus is Devadatta and so forth, while that which is not its locus is the rice and so forth; because [roots] such as √pac denote results such as softening (viklitti) residing in the latter, the definition is applicable to them. The inclusion of the relation that delimits the resulthood (phalatāvacchedaka-sambandha) and so forth should be understood as before.

"It is impossible" means that since the status of being transitive (sakarmakatva), as accepted in the established doctrine (siddhānta) and explained etymologically, cannot be accounted for otherwise, it must necessarily be admitted that the verbal root (dhātu) denotes *bhāvanā* in the form of an operation (*vyāpāra*). This is the intended meaning. Having raised the objection that the status of being transitive could be established by another method, he refutes it with the words "being one of those [others] is its essence," and so forth.

If it is argued that "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*) consists in being one of those verbal roots (*dhātu*) which are intended to be transitive—having first enumerated each of them individually in its specific form and then taking the property of being a constituent of that collection as the very essence of transitivity—this is not correct. [The phrase] "of one and the same" means "of that which is delimited by a single sequential order" (*ekānupūrvyavacchinna*). [The word] "because of being observed" (*darśanāt*)...

The sense is that, just as in the expression "the river flows" (*nadī vahati*), the root *vah* is intransitive (without an object) in the sense of flowing, whereas in "he carries a load" (*bhāraṃ vahati*), it is transitive (with an object) in the sense of conveying; so too, if *vah* were listed among the group of transitive roots, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to its intransitive sense of flowing. Conversely, if it were not listed there, there would be the fault of non-extension (*aprasaṅga*) to that very same transitive sense of conveying. Thus, the point is that this is seen as a case of observing such faults of over-extension and non-extension. This is what is meant by "tadetad" (this very thing).

Having considered the collection of faults [raised] in the *Nirukta*, he says: "The root *kṛ* (to do/make) is intransitive. Now, being transitive (*sakarmakatva*) consists in denoting a result that resides in a locus different from the operation that produces itself. By the word "itself" (*sva*), the result is to be understood. Thus, the meaning is: denoting a result which subsists in a locus other than that of the operation which generates such a result. And such transitivity is easily established for the root *kṛ*.

For instance, effort (*yatna*) resides in the jar and so forth, related by the relation of objective content delimited by the result; however, the operation (*vyāpāra*) that produces it resides in Devadatta and consists of the self's conjunction (*ātma-saṃyoga*). Thus, since the root *kṛ* denotes a result that is non-co-referential with its own productive operation, it follows that it would be intransitive. Furthermore, being intransitive is defined as being distinct from those [roots] characterized as transitive as described above. Since this [definition] cannot be stated in the case of the root *kṛ*, the consequence of *kṛ* being intransitive is inconsistent; thus he says, "The meaning is this. [He explains: "merely the result" (*phalamātra*).

Since the inclusion of the word *mātra* (only) excludes the operation (*vyāpāra*), one must accept that in cases such as *karoti* ("he does"), the expressed meaning of the root *kṛ* is merely effort (*yatna*), which stands in the place of the result (*phala*). And thus, "like the root *yati*": just as the root *yati*, whose meaning is effort, is well-known to be intransitive (*akarmaka*), so too would the root *kṛ* incur the status of being intransitive. This is because both *yati* and *kṛ* are identical in their denotation of effort, which stands in the place of the result.

Therefore, the intention is that it is not appropriate to assert the transitivity previously mentioned—namely, that [the root] has an object consisting in the operation upon its own progenitor (svajanakavyāpāra) and so forth; rather, one must accept the transitivity as stated in the root text according to our own system, namely, that it consists in the fruit being for its own sake (svārthaphala) and so on.

Otherwise, if one disregards the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) and accepts only the transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) as stated by [the opponent] himself, then even the verbal root *yat* (to strive) would incur transitivity—since its effort (*yatna*) also resides in objects such as a jar through the relation of "objective-determining-ness" (*phalatāvacchedaka-viṣayatā*), because it occurs in a locus that possesses the operation (*vyāpāra*) of mental contact (*manaḥ-saṃyoga*) which produces itself. Consequently, the point is that if *kṛñ* were to denote effort alone, the transitivity accepted in the established doctrine would be impossible, and thus the resulting status of intransitivity (*akarmakatā*) would be unavoidable.

One might object: "Is it not the case that the very basis for the conventional designation 'intransitive' (akarmaka) is the expression of an operation (vyāpāra) that resides in the same locus as its fruit (phala)? Since this is absent in the root *kṛ*, how can there be the consequence of it being intransitive? To this, he says: "by the aforementioned method. This means: by the method implied in the statement of the final doctrine (siddhānta), namely that "intransitivity" consists in being a verbal root distinct from those roots designated as transitive (sakarmaka).

Otherwise, if *bhāvanā* in the form of an operation (*vyāpāra*) were not denoted by the verbal root, then since the definition of "intransitive" (*akarmaka*)—namely, being expressive of an operation that has the same locus as its fruit (*phala*)—would become impossible to maintain, even the verb *yat* would fail to be classified as intransitive; for it would lack the quality of expressing an operation co-locus with its fruit. This is the intended meaning. Thus, the point is that effort (*yatna*) is not accepted as the meaning of the root *kṛ*, because it is subordinate to the fruit.

[Objection: "But if every verbal root (*dhātu*) expresses only an operation (*vyāpāra*), then since it would be possible for every root to be intransitive (*akarmaka*), the specific mention of the root *kṛ* (in the rule) is inappropriate. [The author] says: "Regarding the word *kṛñaḥ*. The meaning is that the word *kṛñ*, by means of a non-exclusive indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*), includes all roots, both those denoted by its primary power (*śakya*) and those indicated by its secondary power (*lakṣya*). "Regarding 'intransitivity' (*akarmakatā*): If every root expressed only the result (*phala*) and did not express the operation, then all roots would necessarily be intransitive. "Regarding 'transitivity' (*sakarmakatā*): [This refers to the case where they express the operation as well.]

The meaning is that if "having an object" (*sakarmakatva*) consisted merely in denoting a result (*phala*), then all verbal roots would necessarily have objects, and consequently, the distinction between transitive (*sakarmaka*) and intransitive (*akarmaka*) roots would be destroyed. Thus, it is not proper for every root to denote only the result; rather, it must be admitted that they also denote the operation (*vyāpāra*). This is the underlying intention. Now, with the words "Or else" (*athavā*) and so forth, he prepares the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) to introduce the root text stating that the root *kṛ* is intransitive by another method. He says "having established" (*prasādhyeti*).

The meaning is: by means of explaining the first half [of the verse] as "bhāvanā is vyāpāra" (the efficient force is the operation), he establishes that it is necessary for every verbal root (*dhātu*) to denote an operation (*vyāpāra*). Regarding the word "tat": while demonstrating that it is also necessary for the aspect of the result (*phalāṃśa*) to be denoted by every verbal root, he uses the example of roots such as *jānāti* (he knows) and *karoti* (he does). The sense is: in the case of roots whose meanings consist of cognition, desire, or volition, the Naiyāyikas have stated that these roots denote only the action of knowing and so forth, excluding the aspect of the result; he speaks of the root *kṛñ* in order to refute that [position].

The word *mātra* (only) is for the purpose of excluding the result [from the denotation]. Generally, transitive verbs denote both the result and the operation; however, verbs such as *jānāti* (he knows) and *karoti* (he does) denote operations such as cognition (*jñāna*) and effort (*yatna*). Some Naiyāyikas maintain that all intransitive verbs do not denote a result, because no result is experienced from them; rather, they denote only the operation. This is the meaning.

Now, one might raise the following objection: even if, according to the aforementioned method, [the root *kṛ*] does not denote the fruit (*phala*), it is still possible for it to possess transitivity (*sakarmakatva*)—defined as denoting an operation that has a locus distinct from the fruit—since it denotes an operation (such as effort) that is non-different from the effort which has a locus distinct from fruits such as origination (*utpatti*). Thus, how can *kṛñ* be considered intransitive? To resolve this doubt, he says: "The meaning is this. [He explains: "The meaning of the verbal root... (*dhātvartha iti*).

The meaning is that even if every verbal root (dhātu) expresses an operation (vyāpāra) whose locus is distinct from some result (phala), since the result itself is not the meaning of the root in all cases, the definition of "transitive" (sakarmaka) stated in the established doctrine—namely, "having its own meaning as the result"—would be destroyed. Furthermore, the transitivity just mentioned cannot be adopted, because it would be over-extensive (ativyāpti), applying even to roots such as *yat* and *syandi*, which express operations whose loci are distinct from some result not expressed by the root. This is the intended sense.

Now, one might object: in accordance with the conventional usage of "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*), let it be that for roots such as *pac* ("to cook"), even the aspect of the result (*phala*) is denoted; however, for roots such as *kṛ* ("to do"), there is only the denotation of the mere operation (*vyāpāra*) consisting of effort (*yatna*) and the like. In that case, the conventional usage of "transitivity" [for *kṛ*, etc. is merely figurative (*gauṇa*), based on the fact that their meaning is connected with an object (*karman*).

Thus, anticipating the objection that even in the absence of primary objecthood—defined as possessing a result delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha)—a figurative objecthood consisting in the nature of being an object (*viṣayatva*) might still be possible, he states the passage beginning with "And [it is] not [the case] in the case of *kṛñ* etc. and ending with "is appropriate. The phrase "even though it is secondary" (*bhāktatve 'pi*) means "even though it is figurative" (*lākṣaṇikatve 'pi*). The reason given is "because of impossibility" (*asaṃbhavāt*); this means that according to the maxim that when a primary application is possible, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) is understood to apply only there and not to a secondary one, the personal endings (*lakāra*) cannot occur in a secondary object.

He clarifies this very point by means of an illustration with the words "for not" (*na hi*). Even though the word *gaṅgā* has its secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the bank, the meaning of that [indicated sense] cannot accomplish such actions as bathing or drinking; this is the sense. He states "and thus" (*evaṃ ca*) because the aforementioned fault does not apply if the root *kṛ* denotes an effort conducive to production. By the phrase "mere effort" (*yatnamātram*), the result consisting of production is excluded.

Thus, while the Naiyāyika-accepted denotation of mere effort is rejected, the intended meaning of an effort conducive to the result consisting of production is precisely what he himself desires; this is the underlying thought. || 5 ||

"Exactly for this reason" means that it is because it is undesirable for the root *kṛ* to have the meaning of "mere action" (*vyāpāramātra*). [Objection: If so, then what kind of meaning is intended for the root *kṛ*? To this he says: "but rather, production" (*kiṃ tūtpādanam*). Since the word "production" (*utpādana*) has the meaning of effort (*yatna*) and so forth conducive to arising (*utpatti*), the meaning intended for the root *kṛ* is effort and the like, accompanied by the result which is arising. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "effort and so forth," activities other than effort are also included, in accordance with such usage as "a sprout is produced by a seed."

The sense is that since effort (*yatna*) is sublated in the case of insentient things such as seeds, even when that [effort] is abandoned, there is still the cognition of an activity distinct from effort by virtue of *śakti* (potency) alone. Regarding the term "being denotable" (*vācyatve*): the meaning is that it is necessary for the result (*phala*) to be denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu*). Regarding "another argument" (*yuktyantaram*): the meaning is another reasoning; the sense is that it is a compound according to the rule for the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-class. He clarifies that very other argument with the words beginning with "therefore" (*ataḥ*).

The meaning is: because the meaning of the root *kṛ* is not merely effort (*yatna*) residing in the agent's operation, but rather effort conducive to production (*utpatti*) and so forth; for this reason [the rule applies]. "It should be like the object" (*karmavat syāt*): thus, since the result, which consists of production, resides in the object (*karmastha*), the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) arises by the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*. Consequently, in cases such as *kriyate ghaṭaḥ svayam eva* ("the pot is made by itself"), the application of *yaṅ* and other affixes is also justified; this is the sense of the further favorable point.

If the meaning [of the root] were merely effort situated in the operation (*vyāpāra*), then the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) would not occur; for effort situated in the operation is precluded in the case of a jar (*ghaṭa*) and such things. However, if the result in the form of production (*utpatti*) is accepted, then just as "the rice is cooked by itself" (*pacyate odanaḥ svayameva*) is valid, so too "the jar is made by itself" (*kriyate ghaṭaḥ svayameva*) is justified—this is the intended sense. "The rule is observed" (*sūtraṃ lakṣyate*) means that what is prescribed by the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* (Pāṇini 3.1.87), which contains the word *karmavat*, is observed.

For this very reason, the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) with "the *ya*-class [suffixes] and so forth prescribed by the Sūtra" is justified. If the Sūtra itself were the object being characterized (*lakṣya*), it would not connect with the phrase "the *ya*-class and so forth"; rather, the intention is that the Sūtra would remain entirely unconnected with "the *ya*-class and so forth. Here, it should be understood that under the view of the extension of operations (*kāryātideśa*), the status of being prescribed by the Sūtra "as the object, like the object" (*karmavat karmaṇā*) applies to the *ya*-class suffixes directly; however, under the view of the extension of rules (*śāstrātideśa*), it applies through a mediated succession. [The opponent says: "That would not be possible."

The meaning is that since the root *kṛ* does not denote a result (*phala*), and because its meaning—an effort (*yatna*)—is absolutely non-existent in insentient objects like a jar due to contradiction [with their nature], the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* (Pāṇini 3.1.87)—which signifies that an agent becomes like the object when there is an action equal to the action residing in the object, or an action consisting of an operation having the same locus as the result—is not applicable here. One might object: "In that case, the absence of the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) is simply what we desire. To this, we say: no.

[Otherwise], there would arise a contradiction with the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *karmavat karmaṇā*, which provides the example *kriyate ghaṭaḥ svayam eva* (the pot is being made by itself) as an illustration of the treatment [of the agent] like the object (*karmavadbhāva*). Now, one might argue that although effort (*yatna*) does not exist in the pot or similar objects by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), its existence in the pot is nonetheless uncontradicted by way of the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*).

For this very reason, in the expression "he knows the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ jānāti*), just as the cognition has the status of an object (*karmatva*) because it resides in the jar through the relation of objective content (*viṣayatā*) which delimits the result, so too the effort (*yatna*)—residing in the jar through the relation of objective content—possesses the status of an object; thus, the usage "he makes the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*) is justified. Nor should it be argued that, by this logic, one could also say "he exerts effort toward the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ yatate*).

This is because effort (*yatna*) present in the agent (*kartṛ*) is not treated as a "result" (*phala*) by virtue of being its object (*viṣaya*); thus, it is not accepted that "objecthood" (*viṣayatā*) is the delimitor of resulthood (*phalatāvacchedaka*). And so, even if the root *kṛñ* denotes mere effort alone, the example of the application of the *karmavat-bhāva* (the treatment of the subject like the object) stated in the Bhāṣya—"the pot is made by itself" (*kriyate ghaṭaḥ svayameva*)—is indeed justified. If this is argued, we say no. For, on that basis, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of such usages as "the pot is seen by itself" (*dṛśyate ghaṭaḥ svayameva*). With this intention, he says: "just as 'the pot is seen' (*yathā dṛśyate ghaṭaḥ*)," [and] "because it does not reside in the pot" (*ghaṭāvṛttitvāt*).

The meaning is as follows: since the act of seeing (*darśana*), which is knowledge (*jñāna*), does not reside solely in the pot, it lacks the quality of having its action situated in the object (*karmasthakriyakatva*); therefore, the status of being treated like an object (*karmavadbhāva*)—as in the expression "the pot sees itself"—does not occur. Similarly, although the root *kṛ* (to do/make) can be explained in phrases such as "he makes a pot" when it signifies mere effort (*yatna*), since that effort also does not reside solely in the pot, it lacks the quality of having its action situated in the object; thus, the status of being treated like an object—as in the expression "the pot makes itself"—would not occur. This is the intended sense.

The point is this: regarding the rule "that which has an action equal to that of the object is treated like the object" (*karmavatkarmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*), it is an established tenet (*siddhānta*) that this treatment as the object applies only to those [roots] whose action resides in the object (*karmasthakriyaka*), and not to those whose action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyaka*). That in which the result (*phala*) occurs solely in the object is one whose action resides in the object; for example, in cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks") and *bhinatti* ("he splits"). For softening (*viklitti*) or being split into two (*dvidhābhavana*) and so forth can never reside in the agent.

However, where the result (phala) resides in both the agent and the object, that is a verb whose action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyaka*). For example, in cases such as "he sees the jar" (*paśyati ghaṭam*) or "he goes to the village" (*gacchati grāmam*). This is because the result of the verb *paśyati*, which consists of visual cognition, resides in both the agent and the object through the relations of inherence (*samavāya*) and the objecthood relation (*viṣayatā*). Likewise, the result of the verb *gacchati*, which consists of conjunction with a location in front, resides in both the agent and the object through the relation of inherence.

In this way, it should be understood that laughter (*hāsa*), which is a particular modification of the mind (*cittavṛttiviśeṣa*), likewise resides in both [the agent and the object] through the relations of inherence (*samavāya*) and objective content (*viṣayatā*). And thus, just as in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), because the fruit of the act of seeing—namely, knowledge (*jñāna*)—resides in both [agent and object], the action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyatva*) and lacks the quality of residing in the object (*karmasthakriyatvābhāva*), so that the status of being "like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply; similarly, in the case under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*), because effort (*yatna*) resides in both through the relations of inherence and objective content, the action resides in the agent and lacks the quality of residing in the object.
The ultimate point is that the status of being treated like a verbal root (*karmavadbhāva*) would not at all apply; this will be explained further below. (6)

Having raised an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he prepares the ground for its refutation with the words "In this way" (*evam*). The meaning is as follows: since the definition beginning with "having a fruit in a different locus from its own object" (*svārthaphalavyadhikaraṇa*) is accepted by the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) as the very basis for the conventional usage of "transitivity," then, in order to establish the status of being "like an object" (*karmavadbhāva*) in the case of the sentence *kriyate ghaṭaḥ svayameva* ("the jar is made by itself"), one must admit that the root *kṛ* denotes an effort accompanied by the fruit consisting of origination (*utpatti*). The phrase "of *kṛñ* and so forth" includes roots such as *pac* and others by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). The phrase "even of *jānāti* and so forth" [is included].

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), objects such as those to be reached (*gamya*) are included. "Having as its fruit the destruction of the veil delimited by the object" means that the fruit consists in the destruction of the veil residing in the object, by way of the relation of delimitation (*avacchedakatā*). By the phrase "destruction of the veil etc.," conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth are also understood. "Otherwise" means in the opposite of what has been stated; that is to say, in the case of not denoting a fruit such as the destruction of the veil. [The phrase] "because there would be no [such] consequence" (*anāpatter iti*)...

The meaning is that the conditions for the conventional usage of a verb as "transitive"—beginning with the requirement that the fruit of its own purpose (*svārthaphala*) reside in a locus other than the agent—are absent in that case. And as for the phrase "tathā ca" (and so too): it means "given that it expresses a fruit such as the removal of an obstruction (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*). Regarding the question "what would not be [the case]? (*kiṃ na syāt*): the meaning is that just as in the sentence "the pot is produced by itself" (*kriyate ghaṭaḥ svayameva*), the pot is the substratum of the fruit consisting of origination (*utpatti*), so too it is the substratum of the fruit consisting of the removal of an obstruction; therefore, why should it not be understood that "the pot [is produced] by itself"?

The hidden intention [of the author] is that, in this way, it is improper to accept even the transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) in the form of "having its own meaning as the fruit" (*svārthaphala*), though it is accepted in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). Furthermore, suspecting that there would also be the fault of the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of such usage as "the village is being gone-to by itself" (*gamyate grāmaḥ svayameva*), he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "nirvartye ca" and so forth: one might ask, "What is the reason that the *karmavadbhāva* (the treatment of an object as if it were the agent) applies to objects that are produced (*nirvartya*) or modified (*vikārya*), but not to objects that are merely reached (*prāpya*)? To this, he says: "The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is here. This means that in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* (Pāṇini 3.1.87), the word "dhātoḥ" (of a verbal root) is understood to carry over from the preceding rule *dhātor ekācaḥ*. For in that context, the word "dhātoḥ" indeed follows from *dhātor ekācaḥ*.

The meaning is that the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) has been determined as follows: since the rule states "one whose action is equal to the action denoted by the verbal root" (*dhātor vācyayā kriyayā tulyakriyaḥ*), this implies that even though the operations of the sword and the pot actually exist during their respective states as instrument (*karaṇa*) and locus (*adhikaraṇa*), those operations are not denoted by the verbal root. Consequently, in examples such as *asiś chinatti* ("the sword cuts") and *sthālī pacati* ("the pot cooks"), there is no over-extension (*atiprasakti*) of the definition to the agent who possesses an action equal to that of the instrument or the locus. Therefore, the phrase "by [an action] equal to that of the object" (*karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*)—which is added [to the definition]—is intended to define an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyā*). This is the sense of the established conclusion.

Since the state of having an action whose locus is the object (*karmasthakriyakatva*) is possible only when the object is distinct from that which is reached (*prāpya*), the author says "that which is desired" (*īpsitam*) in order to demonstrate the nature of the object distinct from that which is reached. The meaning is that the object (*karman*) is that which is most desired by the agent, and it is of three kinds. Therefore, there is no fault even if there is an excess of objects distinct from those that are desired. Regarding "the state of being reached" (*prāpyatva*): the author himself will explain the definitions of the first two types in the section determining the meaning of case-terminations (*subarthanirṇaya*). Regarding "not perceived as qualified by a distinction produced by the action" (*kriyākṛtaviśeṣa*): the meaning is the state of not being perceived as characterized by a distinction produced by the action.

Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which no change produced by action (*kriyākṛtaviśeṣa*) is perceived. The inversion of the qualifier [to place it first] follows the rule for the *rājadanta*-group. Thus, the result is that an object is "attained" (*prāpya*) when, in relation to the action of a particular root, no change produced by action is generally perceived; such is the object of that root's action. As for the phrase "it will be stated," the meaning is: by the sentence in the *Vākyapadīya* beginning with "of the changes produced by action," and so forth.

In order to clarify that "having an action residing in the object"—defined as having the sense of an activity that produces a specific change in the object—is the cause for the application of the *karmavat* rule, [the author] demonstrates its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words beginning with "nahi" (not). Where a certain specific change produced by the action, residing in the object, can be perceived simultaneously with the perception of the object itself, such an object is either *nirvartya* (to be brought into being) or *vikārya* (to be modified). In examples such as "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), the specific change consists in the attainment of its own nature.

In cases such as "he presses the *soma*," however, it should be understood that the specific change consists in its being reduced to a powder. But where, by observing the action, not even the slightest change produced by the action can be perceived on the part of the object, that is an "object to be reached" (*prāpyakarma*); therefore, it has been stated by some that it is "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*) by one and "gone to" (*gata*) by another, meaning it is entirely impossible to know [the change] through the observation of the action.

Thus, the application of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) here is as follows: where a change produced by the action (*kriyākṛta-viśeṣa*) is observed in the object (*karman*), there is the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*); but where it is not observed at all, there is no such status. This is what [the author] states with the words "of a jar, etc., in the case of seeing, etc. By the word "etc. in *ghaṭādeḥ*, the village (*grāma*) is included; by the word "etc. in *dṛśyādau*, the root *gam* (to go) is included.

And thus, the meaning is that because the object in the form of a jar, as determined by the meaning of the verbal root *dṛś* (to see), and the object such as a village, as determined by the meaning of the verbal root *gam* (to go), are both "attainable objects" (*prāpyakarman*). "No over-extension [of the rule] occurs" means that there is no occurrence of the status of being treated like an object (*karmavadbhāva*). He states another argument of others to prove that verbal roots denote the result (*phala*) with the words "of verbal roots" (*dhātūnām*). If verbal roots did not denote the result, they would ultimately result in denoting mere activity (*vyāpāra*) alone.

Furthermore, because the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the verbal root *gam* (to go) is the regulator for the manifestation of the result consisting of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and the co-occurrence of the verbal root *tyaj* (to abandon) is the regulator for the manifestation of the result consisting of disjunction (*vibhāga*), there is no possibility of understanding disjunction in the sentence "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), nor is there the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of understanding conjunction in the sentence "he abandons the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ tyajati*). The phrase "of *tyaji* and *gami*" (*tyajigamyor*) is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of all verbal roots that possess such meanings. [The objection] "the consequence of synonymy" (*paryāyatāpatti*) arises because there is no difference in their being denoters of action; the meaning is that there is no difference between *tyaji* and *gami* in their being denoters of a single class of action.

The point is this: when the delimitors of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) are identical, it is precisely the difference in the delimiters of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) that constitutes synonymy (*paryāyatā*). That is to say, because a single action produces both conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*), the verbs *tyaji* (to abandon) and *gami* (to go) would result in being synonyms. Consequently, there would be no distinction between the expressions "he goes" (*gacchati*) and "he abandons" (*tyajati*). This means that the usage "he abandons" (*tyajati*) would result in the sense of "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), and the usage "he goes" (*gacchati*) would result in the sense of "he abandons the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ tyajati*).

[Objection: Is it not accepted that the roots *tyaji* (to abandon) and *gam* (to go) have as their meaning an activity characterized respectively by separation (*vibhāga*) and conjunction (*saṃyoga*)? Consequently, the previously mentioned fault of "lack of distinction" does not apply; therefore, [the author] says: "Even though the result is a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*)," etc. Being an "indicator" means not being an object of the primary denotative power (*śakti*), while still being an object of the cognition produced by that word. [The phrase] "of the very same action," etc., is because of its being the generator [of the result].

And thus, since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) are equally produced by the operation that constitutes the meaning of the verbal roots *gam* ("to go") and *tyaj* ("to abandon"), there is no determining factor (*vinigamaka*) to establish that conjunction alone is the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the operation denoted by *gam*, while disjunction alone is the indicator of the operation denoted by *tyaj*. Consequently, if one were to accept that both are indicators for the operations of both roots, the aforementioned undesirable consequence (*niruktāpatti*) would be unavoidable. Therefore, the sense is that the verbal root must necessarily be admitted to have its power (*śakti*) directed toward the result (*phala*) as well.

Concluding the argument that the verbal root (*dhātu*) expresses the result (*phala*), he says "therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is that, based on the aforementioned reasonings, it must necessarily be accepted that transitive roots (*sakarmaka-dhātu*) express the result. He says "without dispute" (*nirvivādam*); the meaning is that the state of being intransitive (*akarmakatva*), which consists in expressing an operation (*vyāpāra*) that is coreferential with its own result, is impossible without the admission that the root expresses the result. He says "the root *bhū* [is used] in the sense of existence" (*bhū sattāyām*).

The meaning is that, because only the result (phala) is specified in the *bhvādi* group, and because the cognition of existence (*sattā*) and so forth from [roots] such as *bhū* is established by the experience of everyone; and "for this very reason" means precisely because all verbal roots denote the result; and "it is consistent" [means it follows logically].

In the expression "he cooks rice-grains into porridge" (*taṇḍulānodanaṃ pacati*), because of the understanding that "by moistening the rice-grains, he brings about the porridge," it is intended that the rice-grains possess the status of an *object as a modification* (*vikāryakarma*) and the porridge possesses the status of an *object as a product* (*nirvartyakarma*). To justify this, the Bhāṣya states, "the root *pac* has two meanings," meaning that it signifies two results consisting of production and modification. This is because a single operation produces both aforementioned results. The sense is that if [the root] were intended to signify two distinct operations, the inconsistency would be obvious. The word "dig" (direction) [indicates that this is merely one aspect].

The intended meaning is as follows: it is necessary that even intransitive roots denote a fruit (*phala*). Otherwise, the mention of fruits such as *sattā* (existence) among verbal roots would result in futility; for, by the very nature of the general power of verbal roots, an understanding of the operation (*vyāpāra*) is possible for *bhū* and others just as it is for *pac* and others. Furthermore, in order for roots such as *jñā* (to know) to be transitive, one must admit that they denote an operation conducive to cognition (*jñāna*) and so forth. And if that were the case, one could also say "the eye knows" (*cakṣur jānāti*), because even in the case of the eye, there exists a contact between the eye and the mind (*manas*) conducive to cognition. [To this objection] the answer is: no, for this would be met with the consequence of an undesired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), just as in the case of "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*). This is the underlying intention. || 7 ||

Having thus established, by means of the arguments just stated, that both the fruit (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are denotable, [the author] sets forth the introductory framework (*bhūmikā*) to raise and refute the view of those following Maṇḍana Miśra—that "the *bhāvanā* is indeed denoted by the *tiṅ* suffix"—with the words beginning "Let it be so established," etc., up to "denotability."

The point is this: although it has been established by the aforementioned arguments that the operation (*vyāpāra*) is the object of the cognition produced by a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), there remains uncertainty as to whether it is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*). This is because, in the case of *pacati*, we observe an analysis (*vivaraṇa*) into two words—*pākam* and *karoti*—corresponding respectively to the base and the suffix; thus, it is possible to assert that the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is denoted by the finite suffix (*tiṅ*) as well. [The phrase] "not by the root" [is used].

The meaning is as follows: because of the rule that "the operation (vyāpāra) understood as primary—such as 'the productive activity (bhāvanā) conducive to cooking' from the word *pacati*—is the meaning of the suffix," it is more appropriate to state that this [activity] is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta* / *tiṅ*) alone; therefore, it cannot be said to be expressed by the root (*dhātu*). He states "for when that [suffix] is added" (*tad-āgame hi*) because the rule that "the meaning of the suffix is primary" is subject to deviation in the case of number and so forth, since the number conveyed by the suffix is construed as a qualifier of the agent also conveyed by that same suffix.

In the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), the singularity conveyed by the singular suffix does not connect with the action as its instrument; rather, it connects with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). This is because one accepts the grammatical maxim that "suffixes convey their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base. If this were accepted, since singularity would lack the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, the sacrifice would remain unimpaired even in its absence; thus, the opponent's prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that singularity is simply not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). To this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached: "The singularity is indicated in such a way that it becomes something expressed by the word 'that' (*tadartha*)," just like the word *tu* (which serves to distinguish). Thus, singularity is indeed an intended factor.

For when its singular number is heard upon its arrival [in the context], its status as an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) is perceived, just as it is for other qualifiers such as the redness of the animal (*paśu-lauhitya*). Thus, the sense is that since the qualified entity is understood to be an auxiliary by virtue of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), it is logical that this qualifier—which is conveyed by the word—should also possess the status of an auxiliary, just like the word's denotation of the animal itself.

And thus, just as unity is observed there [in the case of "he cooks"] from the occurrence of the singular number, so too, when a verb such as *pacati* is heard, because an activity (*vyāpāra*) is understood, its status as having that [activity] as its meaning must be accepted; otherwise, it would result in a contradiction with the aforementioned reasoning—this is the intended sense.

[Objection: But in that case, the previously stated distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs would be destroyed, because the *vyāpāra* (operation) would not constitute the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Furthermore, since it would be difficult to define "agency" (*kartṛtva*) as consisting in being the substratum of the operation expressed by the verbal root, the suffix [denoting the agent] would not occur in cases such as *devadattaḥ pacati* ("Devadatta cooks"), where Devadatta is the agent. Therefore, he states "In this way" (*evañ ca*) to explain that transitivity and so forth are of a different nature. The phrase "if the operation were denoted by the *tiṅ*-suffix" means: if the operation were the meaning expressed by the *tiṅ*-suffix. The phrase "connected with itself," etc., follows.

One's own "prakṛti" (verbal root) is the base; that which is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) joined with it is its meaning. The state of being a transitive verb (*sakarmaka-dhātutva*) means having the capacity to denote a result (*phala*) that resides in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) from the operation (*vyāpāra*) which constitutes the meaning of that [denoted suffix]. Now, one might object: since the operation denoted by the suffix in verbs such as *pacati* (he cooks), when joined with roots like *pac*, denotes a result that resides in a different locus from that operation, it would follow that these are transitive verbs even when used intransitively. This is not so, because the term "joined with it" (*svayukta*) is provided as a qualification for the suffix in the definition. Thus, the objection does not hold.

Alternatively, that verbal root whose transitivity (sakarmakatva) one intends to express must be understood by its own term (svapada). In this context, it is intended to establish the transitivity of roots such as *bhū* (to become). Thus, the meaning is that because [roots like *bhū*] denote a result that is coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the operation denoted by the verb ending associated with them, and lack the quality of denoting a result that is non-coreferential with the operation denoted by such a verb ending, roots such as *bhū* do not possess transitivity. Furthermore, "being conjoined with" (*svayuktatva*) means occurring immediately after [the root].

Therefore, in cases such as *caitraḥ pacati* ("Caitra cooks") and *bhavati ghaṭaḥ* ("the pot exists"), even though the verb following the root *pac* is immediately preceded by the verbal root *bhū*, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because it does not occur immediately after the verbal root *bhū*.

However, if one were to include merely the property of "occurring after" (*svottaravartitvamātra*), then in the sentences "the pot exists" (*ghaṭo bhavati*) and "Maitra cooks" (*pacati maitraḥ*), there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the verbal suffix following the root *bhū* (in *bhavati*). This is because the verbal suffix following the root *pac* occurs after the root *bhū*, and since it denotes an action (*vyāpāra*) that has a result (*phala*) residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) from that action, it would incorrectly apply to the root *bhū*. It should be understood, however, that if the element of "immediacy" (*avyavahitatva*) is included, there is no such over-extension; for the verbal suffix following *pac* does not occur immediately after the root *bhū*. Regarding the term "agency" (*kartṛtva*): [this follows].

The meaning is that agency (*kartṛtva*) must be defined as the state of being the substratum of that activity which is the referent of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*). This is the case, for example, with Caitra and others in sentences such as "Caitra cooks. In cases such as "Caitra causes Maitra to cook," both the instigated (*prayojya*) and the instigator (*prayojaka*) possess agency because they are the substrata of the activity denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇij*) and the verbal suffix. Furthermore, in instances such as "It is cooked by Devadatta" or "Devadatta stands," Devadatta’s agency should be understood from his being the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix. The phrase "and so forth" [indicates further examples].

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of these two: (1) that the state of being intransitive (*akarmakatva*) consists in denoting a result that is coreferential with the operation expressed by the verb associated with the [agent] himself; and (2) that the state of being an object (*karmatva*) consists in being the locus of the result produced by the operation expressed by the verb associated with the [agent] himself. Regarding the phrase "one who considers himself a Mīmāṃsaka": the suffix *khaś* is applied according to the rule *ātmamāne khaś*. Thus, he addresses one who considers himself a Mīmāṃsaka while speaking in such a manner, and replies: "Therefore, the root *kṛ*" and so forth. He says "of the intention" (*abhiprāyasya*) because the reason had not been stated previously.

The meaning is that the word *tasmāt* (therefore) refers back to what has been established in the mind (*buddhistha*). "The consequence of the cognition 'the village possesses motion' (*gamanavān*)" means that since the object denoted by the word *gamana*—which ends in the suffix *lyuṭ* and expresses the sense of an action—is the result in the form of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), the usage "the village possesses motion" would be grammatically correct, just as one says "the village possesses conjunction," because conjunction exists in the village. "Because it is the substratum of conjunction" [is said] because no one ever uses the expression "cooking occurs" when the result has not yet arisen; therefore, he says "when the operation (*vyāpāra*) exists."

He says "there is no fault" (*anāpatti*) in accordance with the view of those who hold that the sole eye is the object-to-be-reached (*lakṣyaikacakṣuṣka*). The sense is that whether the result arises or not, at the stage of engaging in the activity, the application [of the rule] that "cooking occurs" is desired by everyone. "Cessation of activity" means the destruction of the activity. And as for the phrase "otherwise there would be a fault": since no one accepts that cooking exists when the activity has ceased, he says "provided the result exists."

The sense is that even when the operation has ceased, one would have to conclude that "cooking exists" because the fruit [of the action] still persists, since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is understood to be the fruit alone. He removes the aforementioned objection with the words "yad... (as for...). Regarding the phrase "bhāvapratyayasya": the meaning is that suffixes such as *tyuṭ* and *ghañ*, which are prescribed in the sense of "being" (*bhāva*), are accepted as denoting the operation conducive to the fruit of the verbal root's meaning. As for "nānupapattiḥ" (there is no inconsistency): the meaning is that since the operation denoted by suffixes such as *lyuṭ* and *ghañ* does not exist in the village, there is no undesirable consequence of using the expression "the village possesses going" (*grāmo gamanavān*).

Thus, because the operation conducive to softening (*viklitti*), which is denoted by the suffix *ghañ*, is construed with "becoming" (*bhavati*) and so forth through the relation of agency (*kartṛtā-sambandha*), there is no occurrence of either non-occurrence (*anāpatti*) or over-extension (*āpatti*); this is the meaning. To refute this, he says: "This is not so. Now, if the mere result (*phala*) is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), then it would be more appropriate for the *ghañ* and other suffixes prescribed for abstract action (*bhāva*) to denote only the mere result; how then can they be said to denote the operation conducive to the result? To this, he replies: "Like the active voice (*kartṛ-ākhyāta*)."

The meaning is as follows: just as in the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca*, the term *kartari* (which is carried over from a previous rule) refers to "agency" (*kartṛtva*)—either by the logic of the *ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* section or because the reference is primarily to the state of being—an agent being defined as "one who is the substratum of activity" (*vyāpārāśrayaḥ kartā*). Furthermore, since the suffix following the word *kartṛ* denotes the activity that serves as the qualifier in the cognition produced by its base, it is accepted that the suffix itself denotes activity. Thus, by the rule *laḥ karmaṇi*, the introduction of the *lakāra* suffixes is established with respect to activity.

The meaning is that the Mīmāṃsakas accept [this], because it would follow that there is a contradiction with the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "in the sense of state" (*bhāve*), since it would be possible to prescribe [the suffixes] *lyuṭ*, *ghañ*, and so forth even for the agent by the very rule "kṛt [suffixes] in the sense of the agent" (*kartari kṛt*). For in that [Bhāṣya], it is stated: "The meaning of *ghañ* and other [suffixes] is a state that has become a substance" (*sattvabhūto bhāvo ghañāderarthaḥ*). However, if *kṛt* suffixes were prescribed for the action (vyāpāra) by the rule "kṛt [suffixes] in the sense of the agent," then *ghañ* and the others would denote an action that has not become a substance (*asattvabhūta*), just like the verbal endings (*lakāra*).

The point is that, consequently, the contradiction with the previously cited commentary is indeed evident. Regarding the phrase "and because of the occurrence of contradiction," the word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason; it should be understood that if one were to construe it as "since there is futility, therefore there is the occurrence of contradiction," nothing more than a mere stylistic variation of expression would have been established.

Since the phrase "there is a contradiction with that Bhāṣya" is cited as a pratīka in Mā-ma-hari’s commentary named *Kāśikā*, it is inferred that the same reading existed in the manuscript of the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra* used by him; enough said on this point. Regarding the expression "this must be accepted": the meaning is that even if one were to exert an effort exceeding mere labor—by the force of the word "api"—and were to concede that "the fruit is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)" and "effort (*yatna*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*)," [the following would occur]. Regarding the phrase "attainment of all operations": [it refers to the result of such an admission].

The meaning is that, due to the lack of a decisive factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), effort (*yatna*)—and by the word "also" (*api*), even the operation (*vyāpāra*)—is accepted as being denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu*). Regarding the term "gaurava" (complexity): the meaning is that the expressive power (*śakti*) of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) may reside in number, time, and so forth, but not in effort; for since effort can be obtained through other means, it is improper to postulate an expressive power there, which would result in complexity.

The meaning is as follows: precisely because the verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes an operation common to both sentient and insentient entities, it is consistent with the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* that the personal endings (*tiṅ*) express the agent and the object; and it is likewise consistent with the rule *kartari kṛt* that even primary suffixes such as *ghañ*—just like those beginning with *ṇvul* and *tṛc*—would result in expressing the agent, which necessitates the prescriptive teaching *bhāve* (in the sense of the abstract action) for the purpose of overriding that [agentive denotation]. By the passage ending with "gauravam," the collection of reasons residing in the intended meaning, indicated by the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*), has been clarified.

He states "of the word *pacati*" in order to show that the explanation and analysis of the verbal root *pac* and so forth is derived solely from the aforementioned collection of reasons, and not from the *tiṅ* suffix contained within words such as *pacati*. Regarding the phrase "of the word *pacati*": in the word *pacati*, there are two parts—the verbal root *pac* and the suffix *tip* that follows it.

Regarding the analysis performed by the two words "pākam" and "karoti," the pair consisting of "pākam" and the verbal root *kṛ* is an analysis solely of the root *pac*, which is a constituent of the word "pacati"; it is not an analysis of the suffix (*pratyaya*) contained therein. Thus, the meaning is that even the activity (*kṛti*), which is the meaning of the root *kṛ*, is expressed by the verbal root as something possessing an operation (*vyāpāra*). As for the phrase "that too": even the analysis of "pacati" as "pākaṃ karoti" (he performs cooking) is not sufficient to establish that the *tiṅ* suffixes have as their meaning an operation in the form of productive activity (*bhāvanā*).
