The *Nyāyasamuccaya* maintains that by the use of the word "api," the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) holds primacy over the meanings of both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix. The sense is that even this rule is not sufficient to establish that *bhāvanā* is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), because that [position] will be refuted later. Regarding the term "sublating argument" (*bādhaka*): it refers to the objection stated by the Mīmāṃsakas that if *bhāvanā* were the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), it would contradict the rule concerning the base and the suffix. "That view" refers to their opinion.

The meaning is that the Mīmāṃsaka position is that the analysis (*vivaraṇa*) of the root *pac* contained within the word "pacati" is "pāka" (cooking), while the suffix *ti* following it is analyzed as the root *kṛ*. He refutes this by pointing out the flaw, beginning with the words "But this is not... (*na tv asau*). The meaning is that this root *kṛ* is not the analysis or explanation of the *tiṅ*-suffixes. His intention is that the analysis of those [suffixes] is rather the suffix *ti* contained within the word "karoti. He provides the reason for the root *kṛ* not being an analysis of the *tiṅ*-suffixes in the passage beginning with "In cases such as 'pakvavān'... (*pakvavān ityādau*).

In the Siddhānta (the established conclusion), in the case of *pakvavān* ("one who has cooked"), the meaning of the verbal root *pac* is not the objective factor (*karman*), but rather it is purely of the nature of an action (*kriyā*). The objective factor, however, is the rice (*taṇḍula*). In order to preserve the rule that between the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), the meaning of the suffix alone is predominant, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that in instances involving verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*), the suffix itself possesses the meaning of the operation (*vyāpāra*). Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), however, hold that the rule regarding the meanings of the base and the suffix is not a restrictive one, but rather a general statement (*utsarga*).

If it were maintained that comprehension occurs everywhere solely by following the conventional derivation (*vyutpatti*), then the objection would be raised that in the case of *pakvavān*, there would result the impossibility of syntactic connection (*ananvayāpatti*). He clarifies that very impossibility of connection with the words beginning "This is the point" (*ayaṃ bhāvaḥ*). "They express the sense of 'together' (*saha*)": they cause the understanding of a connected meaning. When the question arises as to which of the two meanings is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and which is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), he says "Of those two" (*tayoḥ*).

Between the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), the meaning of the suffix—that is, the meaning expressed by the suffix—is primary; this means it possesses a "subjecthood" (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a "modehood" (*prakāratā*) residing in the meaning of the base. He demonstrates, through words, the causal relationship established by the previously mentioned grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*), stating: "by way of subjecthood. The meaning is that, for the production of a cognition in which there is a modehood residing in the meaning of the base, the cause is the presentation of the meaning of the suffix following such a base, related [to the effect] by the relation of subjecthood (*viśeṣyatā*).

In the word *pakvavān*, [the author] demonstrates that both the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) possess the status of a *kāraka* (participant in action), which is the factor that necessitates their mutual syntactic connection. He states: "The act of cooking (*pāka*) is the object (*karman*) *kāraka*. The meaning is this: the act of cooking is the "fruit-portion" (*phalāṃśa*). Because it is produced by an operation (*vyāpāra*), and because the fruit itself—by virtue of being treated as if it were the primary entity (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*)—is the locus of that fruit, it possesses the status of an object (*karman*). Regarding "the agent (*kartṛ*) *kāraka*": according to the grammatical rule *kartari kṛt* ("the *kṛt*-suffixes denote the agent"), the meaning of the suffix *-ktavatu* is the agent *kāraka*.

Regarding the impossibility of mutual syntactic connection (*parasparānvaya*) between two factors of action (*kāraka*), he states the solution according to the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* and according to our own view. In the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, concerning the passage "He buys Soma with a ruddy, yellow-eyed, one-year-old [cow]," it is established that the instrumental factor (*karaṇakāraka*) denoted by the three words beginning with *aruṇayā* is connected individually to the productive activity of purchase (*krayabhāvanā*). Thus, there is a purchase accomplished by a productive activity which has redness as its instrument, yellow eyes as its instrument, and being one-year-old as its instrument; and by means of such a purchase, one acquires the Soma.

The understanding is that one should meditate [upon them as identical]. It has been stated that the subsequent realization—that the cow qualified by the quality of ruddiness is the very same one possessing reddish-brown eyes, and that she is likewise qualified by the state of being one-year-old—arises through the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Thus, it is clearly established that the factors of action (*kārakas*) are connected only with the action, and not with one another. Furthermore, based on the etymological derivation "that which performs (*karoti*) an action" or "that which produces (*janayati*) an action," the word *kāraka* refers to that which generates an action.

The meaning is as follows, according to the method to be explained in the *Subarthanirṇaya*: when it is known that [the agent] is a producer of action (*kriyājanaka*), there arises a desire to know "What is that action? due to the rule that a producer necessarily requires an object to be produced (*janya*). Furthermore, since the action itself—as that which is to be produced—requires a producer, there is a fitness for the mutual connection between those two alone, namely the action and the factor of action (*kāraka*). This serves as the proof for the rule that factors of action are connected only with the action, as will be stated in the determination of the meaning of case-endings (*subarthanirṇaya*).

"Non-occurrence of syntactic connection (*anvaya*)" means that, according to the two aforementioned methods, a mutual connection among the factors of action (*kārakas*) is not possible in any way. Here, this distinction should be understood: in the Mīmāṃsaka view, in such cases as "one buys Soma with a one-year-old reddish-brown cow," all the qualifiers and the qualified are connected to the action, whereas their mutual connection is subsequent and mental; however, in the Vaiyākaraṇa view, it is the qualified object as characterized by its qualifiers [that is connected to the action].

For this very reason, in cases such as *nīlotpalam* ("blue lotus"), the formation of a compound is justified by implication (*sāmarthyāt*). Regarding the phrase "because of the impossibility of the rule itself": since, in your view, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) consists merely of the action (*phalamātra*), there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in instances such as *pakvavān* ("one who has cooked"); thus, because the rule that the base and the suffix meanings must be construed together is impossible, where would the previously mentioned causal relationship—which indicates the predominance of the suffix meaning—be applicable? The word *kva* (where) indicates that such a relationship is utterly impossible. This is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "Even if, according to the manner previously stated, there is no possibility of mutual syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the factors of action (*kāraka*s), a connection might still be possible according to the method taught by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda. To this, he replies: "And not merely a relation" (*na ca sambandhamātram*). In the word *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice"), by means of the direct statement (*śruti*) consisting of the single word—namely, the direct statement of the verbal root and so forth—there is a connection between the meaning of the root and the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), that is to say, between the fruit and the operation (*vyāpāra*).

Only the relation—that is, the general category of relation—was mentioned; since there is an absence of the third and subsequent case-endings there, and because it is impossible for [the word] to connect in a specific form such as instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) and so forth, its connection is established through the general relation. Regarding the "entry into one part" of that general relation—that is, the entry into, or the communication of, that specific relation such as instrumentality which constitutes one part of that general relation—the "operation" (*vyāpāra*), meaning the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of this scriptural statement (*śruti*), does not exist—it is not present. This is the meaning.

Likewise, in the present case as well, the syntactic connection (anvaya) "the agent is related to the cooking" is possible; thus, the intention of the objector is that it is only when there is a cognition [of the agent] in its specific form as an object (karman) and so forth that there is a requirement for an action (kriyā). [The author] replies, "due to the absence of compatibility" (yogyatāvirahāt), meaning that such a connection is impossible because the result (phala) is incompatible with being a factor of action (kāraka). Now, one might object: "Compatibility is the non-sublation of the meaning"; since such compatibility exists here, the statement regarding the "absence of compatibility" is incorrect. To this, [the author] says: "because [compatibility] consists in possessing the nature that serves as the cause for syntactic connection."

The meaning is as follows: the state of possessing such a nature—that which serves as the cause (*prayojaka*) and the reason (*hetubhūta*) for the connection (*anvaya*) with the factors of action (*kāraka*)—is precisely what constitutes "suitability" (*yogyatā*). Now, since there is a rule that such a nature belongs to the factors of action only through their connection with the action (*kriyā*) presented by the verbal root (*dhātu*), that very [action] is the suitability; this is the intended sense. This has been stated in the root-text from "for it is indeed the state of being an action... up to "...will be explained. By the term "that which causes the connection" (*anvaya-prayojaka*), the delimiting factor of the connected entity (*anvayi-tāvacchedaka*) is denoted.

For it should be understood that whatever is delimited by a property under which a relation occurs, that very thing possesses the status of being the delimitor of the relatum (*anvayitāvacchedakatva*). Since there is a rule that case-factors (*kārakas*) relate only to what is delimited by "action-ness" (*kriyātva*), the intended meaning is that action-ness alone is the delimitor of the relation with case-factors. "This very [fact]" means: that which is the cause for the non-mutual relation of case-factors. "By way of explanation" means: by means of another word having the same meaning as that [original term], through the statement of its meaning.

The phrase "he has cooked" (*kṛtavān pākam*) demonstrates that the meanings of the base and the suffix in *pakvavān* are respectively the object and the agent. The intention behind stating "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) is that there is no lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) in *pakvavān*, because it is possible for the act of cooking (*pāka*) to be construed as the object within the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) implied by the agent of the suffix *-ktvā*. Regarding the statement "the meaning of the suffix is primary," he explains that the form of the restriction here can be twofold, according to the distinction between the subject and the predicate, namely: "that which is primary" and "that which is the meaning of the suffix."

He states the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) even regarding the two-fold rule in the passage beginning with "ajā-aśva," etc. Regarding the first rule, "that which is the meaning of the suffix" (*yaḥ pratyayārthaḥ*), since the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) such as *aja* (goat) is not the meaning of the suffix, it would lack predominance (*prādhānya*) due to this deviation; rather, predominance would result for the meaning of the feminine suffix itself. Regarding the second rule, "that which is the meaning of the suffix" (*yaḥ pratyayārthaḥ*), he states the deviation in the passage beginning with "chāgyādeḥ" (of the goat, etc.).

The point here is that even if "femininity" (*strītva*) were the meaning of the suffix, there would still be no deviation from the rule because the meaning indicated by it necessarily appears as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*), and furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (*anāpatti*) that the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) would not attain primacy. Thus, since this [rule] is beset by such objections, the principle that "the meaning of the suffix is the primary one" is not a universal rule (*niyama*), but rather a general statement (*sāmānyavacana*). Consequently, it is not possible to maintain—on the strength of that [rule]—that the activity (*vyāpāra*) is the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārthatva*). This is the intended sense.

How, then, is there an understanding of the operation (*vyāpāra*) as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in cases such as "he cooks" (*pacati*)? To this, he says: "by way of being the qualificand, etc. [The phrase] "in accordance with linguistic usage" (*vyutpattyanurodhāt*) means: *vyutpatti* is the apprehension of the power (*śakti*) of words to convey meaning; "in accordance with that" means in accordance with the apprehension of the power to convey the sentence-meaning, which is to say, the verbal cognition has the operation as its qualificand.

And thus, the point is this: it is the very apprehension of the capacity to convey meaning (*arthāvabodhaka-śaktigraha*)—which has the specific operation as its qualificand—that regulates verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), and not [factors] such as being the meaning of a suffix. Therefore, even though the *bhāvanā* is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), there is no inconsistency in its being the primary element. For, according to the experience of the learned, cognition follows linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), but linguistic convention does not follow cognition.

The Mīmāṃsakas, however, observing that the *bhāvanā* (productive urge) holds primacy in the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence, postulate—following that lead—that it is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*). This [opponent's] objection—that such a postulation of grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) based on [their own] cognition is utterly improper because it contradicts the experience of the learned—is refuted by the phrase "for this very reason. He demonstrates that cognition follows grammatical derivation with the words "only as having the nominative-terminated [subject] as the qualificandum" (*prathamāntaviśeṣyaka eva*). That is to say, the Naiyāyikas accept that verbal cognition has precisely that as its object, being based solely on the apprehension of the capacity to generate the cognition of such a meaning, and specifically as having the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) as its qualifier.

Since the rule holds that whatever form enables the comprehension of the intended meaning (śakyārtha) is necessarily the delimitor of that capacity (śakyatāvacchedaka), the theorists of poetics (ālaṃkārikas) accept that in instances such as "The hamlet is on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) and "A creeper has grown on the mountain" (*jātā latā hi śaile*), the cognition of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) occurs precisely through the forms of "Gaṅgā-ness" (*gaṅgātva*) and "creeper-ness" (*latātva*). Consequently, the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) arising from the cognition of extraordinary coolness, sanctity, and so forth, as well as the "contrariety" (*vaiparītya*) expressed by the inverted words, are both logically consistent. Thus it is said.

The Naiyāyikas, however, say that when one ought to say "a hamlet on the bank of the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgātīre ghoṣaḥ*), the cognition of qualities such as coolness and purity arises precisely from the force of saying "a hamlet in the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*). Regarding the example "the pot is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*): "in reverse" (*viparyayeṇa*) means by way of inversion. For those who are proficient (*vyutpannānām*), this refers to those who possess the apprehension of the capacity to generate a cognition—where the pot is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the state of being the object (*karmatva*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)—through the relation of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), even in a sentence composed of unrelated words such as "the pot," "the state of being the object," and "bringing. This refers to the view of the modern Naiyāyikas.

In the *karmadhāraya* compound *naiyāyika*, the word is derived from the analysis "one who studies or knows *nyāya*"; since it is thus a verbal derivative (*kriyāśabda*), its position as the first member is not fixed, similar to words such as *pāṭhaka* (reader) or *pācaka* (cook). The nature of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is defined as: "the incapacity of a single word to convey a relation [with another] unless that other word is present. In the phrase "of the word" (*padasya*), the meaning of the genitive case is "residing in" (*niṣṭhatva*); thus, the sense is "residing in the word."

And likewise, those who, observing that the word *ghaṭa* possesses a lack of capacity to produce a cognitive relation (anvayānanubhāvakatva) when the word *karmatva* is absent, accept that verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) arises from such a sentence, employ the term "navya" (modern) for the purpose of specifying them. Thus, for them, the understanding of the meaning arises even from such a sentence; however, it does not arise for those who lack such a linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*). As it has been said: "For others, it is simply devoid of expectancy (*tannirākāṅkṣam eva*). The meaning is that it is "devoid of expectancy" with respect to a verbal cognition whose relation is that of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*).

The sense is that everything stated in such passages as these is consistent. "For this very reason" means: because cognition follows from linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). Regarding the statement "the primary meaning is the meaning of the suffix": this refers to the position established by the natural force (*svarasa*) of the sūtra, namely, that whatever is the primary element is the meaning of the suffix. The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: here the word *āśiṣyam* (to be taught) is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). Thus, the statement "the primary meaning is the meaning of the suffix" need not be made. He states the reason for this: "because the meaning [is determined] by something else."

"Because, according to worldly linguistic convention (*lokavyutpatti*), it is established that the meaning is the qualificand and so forth, while the cognition [of it] is [the qualifier]. "Even this being the case" means: even though the cognition of the operation as the qualificand is established in accordance with linguistic convention. "The statement 'the primary element is the action' (*bhāvapradhānam*) itself... [is the point].

The sense is this: by the restrictive particle *eva*, there is an exclusion of the phrase "of the meanings of the base and the suffix," because that [phrase] is general and universal, whereas this [present rule] is a specific exception (*apavāda*). Therefore, even though the activity (*vyāpāra*) is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), it is to be respected as the primary object (*viśeṣya*) in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) as the authoritative means of knowledge. In this context, the word "verb" (*ākhyāta*) denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), based on the etymological derivation: "that by which the meaning, being the most prominent in every respect, is expressed (*ākhyāyate*). This is because only verbal bases such as nouns (*nāman*) and so forth are the subjects of the [preceding] rule.

Furthermore, from the *Nirukta* statement, "Names are born from verbal roots" (*nāmānyākhyātajāni*), it follows that a name cannot possibly be produced by a suffix belonging to a verb, nor can it be produced by that which ends in such a suffix. For this very reason, the *Mahābhāṣya* records the sentence, "Everything that is a name is said to be born from a root in grammar, as is the case with the offspring of a cart," which conveys the same meaning as the previously cited *Nirukta*. Thus, the definition of a verbal root (*dhātu*) is established as that which expresses the primary meaning within a sentence relative to all other elements.

The mention of "predominance" (*prādhānya*) is intended to clarify that the cognition arises precisely with that [agent] as its primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and not to include it within the definition; this is the path accepted by the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa*. However, the modern grammarians (*navya-vaiyākaraṇa*) hold that in this context the word "verb" (*ākhyāta*) refers to a finite verbal form (*tiṅ-anta*), because in the rule "a verb [is used] after a verb," the meaning is understood in exactly that way, and because the treatise begins with: "There are four classes of words: nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*). According to them, there are four meanings of a verb: the state (*bhāva*), time (*kāla*), the factor of action (*kāraka*), and number (*saṃkhyā*).

Regarding the statement "therein, the action (bhāva) is predominant": *bhāva* refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The meaning of the verbal root should be understood as either the result (*phala*) or the operation (*vyāpāra*). "Predominant" means the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Thus, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: that in which the action is predominant. A verb (*ākhyāta*), ending in a *tiṅ* suffix, generates a cognition in which either the result or the operation is predominant. Nouns (*nāman*) are nominal stems (*prātipadika*). They are "predominant in substance" (*sattvapradhāna*); "substance" (*sattva*) here means a thing (*dravya*) which is the locus of gender and number.

The meaning is that cognitions which have those [verbal suffixes] as their primary element—that is, which have them as their qualificands—generate cognitions consisting of syntactic integration (*anvaya-bodha*). For example, they say that in the case of *pacati*, the cognition has the activity (*vyāpāra*) as its primary element; whereas in the case of *pacyate*, the object to be understood is a result (*phala*) such as softening (*viklitti*), which has that [result] as its primary element, and so forth.

Having thus demonstrated that the view "the meaning of the suffix is the primary [element]" is not to be respected, he states "For when that is introduced," etc., in order to show that even the maxim "for when that is introduced" (*tadāgame hi*) is not to be respected regarding the sense that "whatever is the meaning of the suffix, that is the primary. Regarding the term *ativyāptam*: the compound *ativyāptaścātivyāptaṃ ca* (both "over-pervasive" and "that which is over-pervasive") is a neuter singular residual compound (*ekaśeṣa*) formed according to the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena*, since it consists of a masculine and a neuter noun. It is also in the singular number. *Ativyāptam* means "over-pervasive," "too widely applicable," or "deviant"—that is to say, it is inconstant.

He clarifies the very fact of deviation [from the literal meaning] by stating: "What was done here? is the question; "Cooked" is the answer. Thus, the explanation takes the form of a question and answer. In that context, from the understanding of the meaning of the question "What was done?"—namely, "What object did the operation have?"—it is understood that the object of the operation is what is desired to be known (*jijñāsya*). In the word "cooked" (*pakvam*), the suffix *kta* denotes the object (*karman*), and the neuter gender is used in its general sense.

And thus, because the object of inquiry is not understood from the word *pakvam* (cooked), it cannot logically follow as a subsequent [element]; therefore, if its capacity to convey an operation (*vyāpāra*) is accepted, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since that [operation] is not the meaning of the suffix—this is the sense. By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "*pakvam apīti*," the case of *pakvavān* (one who has cooked) is included; for even there, although the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is cognized through implication (*ākṣepa*) and so forth, a deviation is possible because it is not the meaning of the suffix. This applies even in the case of *pakvam*.

Just as in the case of "he cooks" (*pacati*), because the verbal root *pac* is explained by the word "cooking" (*pāka*) and the suffix *tip* is explained by the root *kṛ*, which signifies the sense of productive activity (*bhāvanā*), the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denotes activity—also known by the synonym *bhāvanā*—and that its explanation by the root *kṛ* is primary and that activity is understood; likewise, in the case of "cooked" (*pakva*), there is also an explanation of the suffix *kta* by the root *kṛ* signifying *bhāvanā*, and thus there is a cognition of *bhāvanā*. Therefore, even in the expressions "the possessor of what is cooked" (*pakvavān*) and "the cooked" (*pakvam*), *bhāvanā* is present.

The sense is that there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) both of the maxim "for when that [element] is present" (*tadāgame hi*)—which implies that the meaning is expressed by the suffix—and of the explanation provided by the root *kṛ*. Now, one might object: "Just as it has been accepted that the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is the meaning of the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) because of the explanation by the root *kṛ* and the application of the maxim 'for when that is present,' let it likewise be admitted that this [force] is the meaning of primary nominal suffixes (*kṛt*) as well; and thus, there will be no over-extension. To this, he says: "Even (*api*). By the word "even," another point is added. He reveals that very other point with the words: "And so... (*tathā ca*).

The point is this: it is beyond dispute and accepted by both the proponent and the opponent that the cognition of *bhāvanā* (efficient force) occurs in both cases—namely, in verbal forms ending in *tiṅ* such as *pacati*, and in verbal forms ending in *kṛt* such as *paktā* and *pakvavān*. Regarding the inquiry as to whether that *bhāvanā* is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) or by the suffix (*pratyaya*), if one were to say it is by the suffix, there would be the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) because multiple suffixes exist, necessitating the postulation of multiple powers (*śakti*). Therefore, it must be understood that it is expressed by the verbal root.

Since the root *pac* is one and the same in both cases, there is great parsimony (*lāghava*) by postulating a single power; with this intention, he says "ubhayasādhāraṇya" and so forth. The meaning is that because the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is perceived as following both the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) and the primary derivative suffix (*kṛdanta*), its existence [is established]. Regarding "the root alone": it is more appropriate to postulate that the root itself—which enters into both as a constituent—is the denoter of the *bhāvanā*, due to the parsimony of having only one [denoter]. He states another objection as well: "and the consequence of [the *bhāvanā*] being the primary [meaning]."

The point is this: if verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) were denoters of *bhāvanā* (efficient force), then since the cognition of the object and the agent could be obtained through implication by the *bhāvanā* itself, the *bhāvanā* would be primary as the meaning of the suffix—just as the Mīmāṃsakas assert. Similarly, if kṛt-suffixes were also denoters of *bhāvanā*, the same consequence of the primacy of *bhāvanā* would follow. Consequently, there would be no possibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in cases such as "the rice is cooked" (*pakvastandulaḥ*) or "Caitra is a cooker" (*paktā caitraḥ*), and the aforementioned over-extension (*ativyāpti*) could not be avoided. This is the sense. || 8 ||

Demonstrating another proof for the claim that the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone expresses the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), he says: "What is to be done? (*kiṃ kāryam*). Here, the word *kim* does not have the sense of a question; rather, because it was introduced previously, it is employed merely to complete the number of syllables required by the Vedic meter. For this very reason, the commentator omits it and explains: "What is to be done" (*kāryam*). The remainder of the thought is that the suffix *ṇyat* is prescribed in the sense of the object (*karman*) by the rule *ṛ-halor ṇyat*. Regarding the form *anīya*: [it is derived from the same root with the suffix *anīyar*].

In examples such as *pacanīyam*, the suffix *anīyar* is prescribed for the object (*karman*) by the rule *tavyattavyānīyaraḥ*; [and] *ṇiniḥ* [is prescribed]. Regarding the sense of the past (*bhūte*), under the heading [of the section on kṛt suffixes], the suffix *ṇiniḥ* is prescribed after the root *yaj* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*) by the rule *karaṇe yajaḥ*; this means that *ṇiniḥ* is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) in the past tense. These suffixes, beginning with *ṇyat*, express meanings such as the object and so forth; they do not exist without connection to an action (*kriyā*).

Since only those things connected with an action (kriyā) can be *kārakas*, if a verbal root (*dhātu*) does not denote an action in the form of an operation (*vyāpāra*), there can be no connection with an action, and thus the status of being a *kāraka* is impossible. And if that is impossible, then because the technical designations (*saṃjñās*) such as "object" (*karman*) and so forth—which are prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "with respect to a *kāraka*"—would also be impossible, the meaning is that [the factors] do not exist, i.e., they are non-existent, in the sense of being objects and so forth. This refers to the phrase "its denotability" (*tadvācyatām*).

And thus, the meaning is that the rules prescribing suffixes such as *ṇyat* for the sense of the object (*karman*) and so forth indicate—just as the impossibility of [the boy’s] being fat otherwise indicates his eating at night—that the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is indeed denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), since it would otherwise be impossible. Having reflected on this, he says: "without an action," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility of being a *kāraka*": since being a *kāraka* consists precisely in being connected with an action, the meaning is that without an action, the status of being a *kāraka* is impossible.

One might object: "Is this prescription of the *ṇyat* suffix and others with the sense of the object (*karman*) and so forth not a proof for the fact that a verbal root denotes an action in the form of an operation? For the status of the *ṇyat* suffixes as having the sense of the object and so forth can be established by other means as well; and only that which cannot be explained otherwise (*anyathānupapanna*) constitutes proof. Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution with the words "And not... [and] "The Bhaṭṭa method."

The point is as follows: having stated that *kṛt* suffixes denote the agent, the object, and so forth—on the basis of the experience of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in cases such as "Devadatta is a cook" (*pācako devadattaḥ*) and "the rice is cooked" (*pakvastandulaḥ*)—one might raise the objection that, since the verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes only the result (*phala*) and there is no [root] denoting action (*kriyā*), there would be no cognition of action in instances involving *kṛt*-derived forms; and in the absence of such a cognition, their status as a *kāraka* (participant in action) and so forth would also not be possible. Anticipating this objection, [it is argued that] because the status of being a *kāraka* is impossible without action, in that case...

The meaning is that the Bhaṭṭa position—that action (*kriyā*) is implied by the factors of action (*kārakas*) such as the agent and the object solely for their own acquisition of status, and that the status of being a *kāraka* and the application of suffixes denoting *kārakas* are established only through connection with that implied action—is not tenable. Demonstrating its untenability because it contradicts the method established elsewhere, he says: "Even in the case of the verb" (*ākhyāte 'pi*). In the context of finite verbal forms (*tiṅanta*), the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) in the form of an operation is not denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*).

If that were the case, there would be no cognition of it as the primary element; rather, it is expressed solely by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) designated as *tiṅ*. This is because it is perceived as the most predominant factor in the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Furthermore, the predominance of the meaning of the suffix over the meanings of the base and suffix is established in grammatical treatises (*pāṭhaka*) in examples such as *aupagavaḥ* ("the son of Upagu"), and because its status as being expressed by the verbal suffix is determined by the maxim "for when that [suffix] is introduced... (*tadāgame hi*). As it has been said: "The base and the suffix always express the meaning of the suffix together."

"Because of its predominance, the meaning of the suffix is determined to be *bhāvanā* (the efficient force). Nor should it be argued that in such a case there would be no cognition of the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*), due to the absence of words denoting them; for *bhāvanā* is an activity (*vyāpāra*), and an activity is always necessarily possessed of a substratum (*sāśraya*), since an activity without a substratum is impossible.

And likewise, if there were no substratum (āśraya) at all, then the efficient force (bhāvanā) would not even attain existence; thus, in order to obtain its own essential nature as a self, the bhāvanā necessitates an agent. Since the comprehension of both the agent and the object is possible through this very necessity, why should the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) be postulated as having the function of denoting them? It is in this manner that the Mīmāṃsakas have established, on the basis of its predominance, that the bhāvanā is the meaning expressed by the verbal suffix.

This being the case, if the aforementioned Bhāṭṭa method were adopted, then the meaning would be "even in the case of *ākhyāta*," that is, even in the case of a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) designated as *ākhyāta*. Regarding the phrase "in the event of such a consequence": it means that once one accepts that even those verbal suffixes designated as *tiṅ*, which are included within the category of *kṛt* suffixes, denote the agent and the object, and having accepted this, one takes the action implied by those agents and objects for the sake of their own realization—then, given that the denotation of agent and object by the *tiṅ* suffixes is thus established. Regarding the phrase "there too": [it refers to the same situation].

The meaning is that even in the case of a verbal suffix (ākhyāta) designated as *tiṅ*, the expressibility (*vācyatva*) of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), that is, its being expressed by the *tiṅ* suffix, would not at all be established. Thus, because it would contradict the well-established doctrine [of the school] elsewhere, the aforementioned Bhaṭṭa position is not fit to be adopted in cases such as "kāryam" (it is to be done); this is the sense. [Regarding the phrase] "liṅga-saṃkhyā-anvaya" (the connection with gender and number).

The meaning is as follows: since verbal cognition arises in cases such as *pakvavān* (the cooker), *pakvavatī* (the female cooker), and *pakvastandulaḥ* (cooked rice) in the form "Caitra, who possesses a non-different activity conducive to softening, qualified by masculinity and singularity," one must necessarily accept that the agent, object, and so forth are denoted by the *kṛt* suffixes (*kṛt-pratyaya*) in order for gender (masculinity, etc. and number (singularity, etc. to be construed [with those terms].

If it is thought that the cognition of the agent and the object arises through the implication of the operation (vyāpāra) by means of that [number], which serves to define its own nature, then even in the case of a verbal suffix (ākhyāta), since there is the cognition that "the substratum of the operation is qualified by oneness and so forth," the agent and the object would have to be denoted in order for the number such as oneness to be construed with them. Furthermore, in accordance with the cognition in cases such as *pakvavān* ("he who has cooked")—namely, "an operation belonging to Devadatta as agent and occurring at a past time"—the denotation of the productive activity (bhāvanā) itself would also be required in order to provide the locus for the construction of time and the factors of action (kāraka) as qualifiers of the operation.

The meaning is that expressibility (*vācyatva*) must necessarily be accepted. By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even in all [cases]," he demonstrates another reason for the necessity of the verbal root denoting the operation (*vyāpāra*), beginning with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). Regarding the example "split by the claws": the meaning of the root *bhid* is the splitting (*dvidhābhavana*) produced by an operation; the suffix *kta* denotes the object (*karman*); and the instrumental case in "by the claws" (*nakhaiḥ*) denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "Hiraṇyakaśipu is the locus of the tearing apart produced by an operation whose instrument is the claws."

In this regard, since the term *kāraka* is understood through its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "that which performs" or "that which produces an action" (*kriyā*), and since an action requires another action to be produced, there is a mutual syntactic connection (*parasparam anvaya*) based on semantic competency (*sāmarthya*). Consequently, according to the grammarians' school (*vaiyākaraṇamata*), the compound *nakhabhinna* ("nail-pierced") is formed. In the same way, the formation of the compound *haritrāta* ("protected by Hari") is also to be explained.

In the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, however, since only the *tiṅ*-suffixes denote the operation (*vyāpāra*) which is the nature of productive activity (*bhāvanā*), there is an absence of such an operation here due to the absence of a *tiṅ*-suffix. Consequently, according to the principle of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*, factors of action (*kārakas*) must connect only with an action; because they lack mutual connection in the absence of that [action], there would be no syntactic competency (*asāmarthya*), and thus no compound could occur between the instrument and object *kārakas* "nakhaiḥ" (by nails) and "bhinnah" (split). This is the meaning. To demonstrate the absence of the compound along with its reason, he provides the example: "puruṣo rājñaḥ" (the man of the king), and so forth.

The meaning is that just as there is no compound in the expression "the king's wife" when the intended connection is between the man and the king, and between the wife and Devadatta—because they lack the semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) due to not being mutually connected—likewise, there would be no compound in cases such as "split by nails. To establish this semantic competency, he raises an objection with the words: "And it is not [the word] 'nails' that is supplied... (*na cādhyāhṛteti*).

The meaning is as follows: according to the logical principle that "that which is impossible without something else is implied by it," the word *nakhaiḥ* (by means of nails) functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) kāraka; since being a kāraka consists in being a generator (*janakatva*), and generation is impossible without that which is generated (*janya*), one must grasp the action of "doing" (*karoti-kriyā*) which is implied by that instrumental kāraka as that which defines its own nature. Regarding the term *sāmarthyam* (capacity), it means having the form of semantic compatibility (*anvaya-yogyatva*).

And thus, the meaning is that the capacity [of the compound] must be established by taking recourse to an implied verb, because the verbal cognition "it is split by means of nails" (*nakhaiḥ kṛtvā bhinnaḥ*) arises from [the compound] being the locus of a division produced by the operation whose instrument is the nails. While demonstrating an example for establishing this capacity by taking recourse to an implied verb, he says: "like *dadhyodana*," etc. *Dadhnā odanaḥ* (rice with curd) becomes *dadhyodanaḥ*. This is a third-case *tatpuruṣa* compound, following the rule *annena vyañjanam*.

The meaning of that sūtra is indeed this: a word denoting a substance qualified by an action (saṃskāraka-dravya-vācaka) ending in the third case is compounded with the word *anna*. Here, because the connection of the third-case instrumental *dadhnā* as a qualifier with the word *odana* is blocked—since there is a rule that the syntactic factor (*kāraka*) expressed by a case-ending must be understood as subordinate to an action—the compound is justified by accepting a semantic relationship (*sāmarthya*) through the act of sprinkling (*upaseka-kriyā*), which is implied by the instrumental factor of the case-meaning that would otherwise be inexplicable without an action.

Thus, in this context, the meaning of the term *adhyāhāra* (supplying an ellipsis) is precisely an objection based on logical inconsistency (*anupapatti*). For if one were not to accept that the establishment of semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) occurs here by means of a supplied verb, then it would be quite clear that no compound could take place due to a lack of competency. The point is that, similarly, in cases such as *nakha-bhinna* ("nail-pierced"), the establishment of competency by means of a supplied verb is necessary. By the phrase "tatra vidhyānarthakyāt" and so forth, he refutes the view that the establishment of competency in cases like *nakha-bhinna* by means of a supplied verb is not tenable according to reason.

The point is this: since the grammatical rule *annaṃ vyañjanam* ("condiment with rice") is a *padavidhi* (a rule concerning words), the governing maxim (*paribhāṣā*) *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* ("a word-rule applies to words that are semantically connected") comes into play. Consequently, for words such as *dadhi* ("curd") which, by their mere form, lack semantic connection unless an intermediate action is supplied, the formation of a compound via the aforementioned sūtra is otherwise impossible. Thus, although one must accept a compound in cases like *dadhyodana* ("rice with curd") by establishing semantic connection through the mediation of an implied action due to the lack of any other recourse, even in the Mīmāṃsaka view, this would apply to cases such as *harikṛtam* ("done by Hari").

Since the verbal root *kṛ* denotes an operation (*vyāpāra*), agency (*kartṛtva*) as defined by that operation exists directly in Hari (Viṣṇu). Thus, according to the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the third case ending—which expresses the agent or instrument relative to the action presented by the verbal root that serves as the base for the *kṛt*-suffix—is compounded with the word ending in that *kṛt*-suffix. Consequently, because the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā* finds its purpose through this direct connection with the meaning of the verbal root—having brought forth the action (*kriyā*) by implication—the rule is fulfilled.

The sense is this: because the application [of the rule] in examples such as *haritrātaḥ* is impossible—given that it would have to rely on a series of relations consisting in being produced by actions whose agents and so forth are implied by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for [the status of] being an agent—it follows from the very meaning that the adoption of a secondary (*gauṇa*) sense is appropriate only when the primary (*mukhya*) sense is absent, and not otherwise. This is addressed by the phrase "not in a single [instance]" (*na caikasyām*), which anticipates the objection regarding the establishment of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) in cases such as *nakhabhinnaḥ* according to the Mīmāṃsā method.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that when two words are connected as the object (*karman*) and so forth within a single action (*kriyā*), their *sāmarthya* (semantic competency) consists precisely in that fact of being connected to the same action. For this very reason, compounds such as *nīlotpalam* ("blue lotus") are established. If, however, one did not rely on this competency characterized by connection to a single action, then in cases like *nīlotpalam*, no compound would be possible due to a lack of *sāmarthya*. To illustrate: through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the word *nīla* is understood to denote the quality of blueness.

The word *utpala*, however, refers to a substance qualified by the property of being an *utpala*. Alternatively, let that word also refer to the universal (*jāti*) of *utpalatva* according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*. In either case, because the mutual connection between the words *nīla* and *utpala*—through their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—is sublated, there is a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*), and thus a compound does not apply. [For instance,] in the expression "the lotus exists" (*utpalam asti*), the lotus is connected to the action of existence as its agent; and since the blue color resides in such a lotus, the blue is likewise connected to the action of existence through its substratum.

Alternatively, let it be that "existence" (*sattā*) is predicated with reference to the lotus, and then the quality "blue" is predicated as its substrate with reference to that very existence; thus, since the words "blue" and "lotus" possess the capacity for composition—consisting in their connection to a single action through their status as factors (*kāraka*) or through the relationship of the subject and the predicate within a single act of being—it is unobjectionable that the compound is formed. Homage be to those Mīmāṃsakas who speak in this manner!

And likewise, in the present case as well, there is no connection between those two [words] through the aforementioned indirect succession; rather, the capacity (*sāmarthya*) consists solely in their being connected to a single action. And that [capacity] exists because *nakhaiḥ* (with nails) is connected to the action of "doing" (*karoti*) as its instrument (*karaṇa*), while *bhinnaḥ* (split) is connected to that very same action as its object (*karman*)—in the sense of being the generator of a splitting residing in itself. This is the intention of the objector, and the meaning is that there is no impossibility of compounding. He refutes this with the words beginning "asūryampaśyāḥ" (those who do not see the sun).

Regarding the rule *asūryalalāṭayordṛśitapoḥ*, its meaning is this: when *asūrya* and *lalāṭa* are used as object-words (*karma-upapada*), the suffix *khaś* is applied after the roots *dṛś* (to see) and *tap* (to heat). Thus, when the word *asūrya* is the object-word for *dṛś*, the suffix *khaś* is added; because of the marker *śit*, the root *dṛś* undergoes the substitution *paśya* according to the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭdrśaḥ śaḥ*. Then, by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya mum*, the augment *mum* is inserted after the first member of the compound, resulting in the formation of *asūryampaśya*. The understanding [of the term] is: "those who possess the absence of seeing the sun."

The meaning is that in the expression *asūryampaśyā rājadārāḥ* ("the king's wives who do not look at the sun"), because there is an understanding of the mere absence of the act of seeing, the word *sūrya* lacks syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). Consequently, this compound is considered by the author of the Bhāṣya and others to be an "unfit compound" (*asamarthasamāsa*). [The phrase] "because there would be no such fault" means that in your view, that status of being an unfit compound would be undermined.

The meaning is that, in the sense of "not seeing the sun," because the negative particle (*nañ*)—functioning as a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation)—is construed with the action of seeing (*darśana-kriyā*), the sun (*sūrya*) is also construed within that very action as its object (*karman*). Thus, the condition of "capacity" (*sāmarthya*), defined as the connection to a single action, is present. By the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*), examples such as *aśrāddhabhojī* ("one who does not eat at a funeral feast") are to be understood; for in the sense of "he does not eat a *śrāddha* meal," that too is an instance of an *asamartha-samāsa* (compound of non-coordinated members).

If it is argued that there is no loss [to our position] because *asūryampaśya* and similar compounds can be considered *samartha-samāsa* (compounds based on semantic connection) since both members are connected to the very act of seeing, [the author] replies: "Even if this were accepted, [the following would occur]. In the sense of "everything was made from clay," there would result the undesirable formation of the compound *sarvamṛttikaḥ* from *sarva* and *mṛttikā*. This is because the word *mṛttikā* is connected to the meaning of the root *kṛ* as the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the referent of the word *sarva* is connected to it as the object (*karman*); thus, the condition of "semantic connection" (*sāmarthya*)—defined as being connected to a single action—is present.

In our view, however, the meaning is that since clay functions as the instrument (*karaṇa-kāraka*), and there is a rule that a *kāraka* must necessarily connect with an action (*kriyā*), the word *sarva*—lacking the status of a verbal action (*kriyā-śabda*)—is unfit for connection and thus lacks the required semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*); therefore, no compound can occur. Precisely because of this lack of semantic capacity, it is stated in the rule *sarvacarmaṇaḥ kṛtaḥ khakhañau* that a compound occurs by means of a formal exception (*nipātana*) in the sense of "made from the whole hide" (*sarvacarmaṇā kṛtaḥ*).

Now, one might raise the objection: "Even though both types of clay possess the capacity [to produce a jar] by virtue of being connected to the same action, since the rule *kartṛ-karaṇe kṛtā* prescribes a compound of a word ending in the instrumental case denoting an instrument with a *kṛdanta* (a word ending in a primary suffix), and since the word *sarva* is not a *kṛdanta*, the rule prescribing the compound would not apply; thus, there could be no compound. Anticipating this, he says: "And not here. One should not think that there is an absence of a rule prescribing the compound in the case of *sarvamṛttika*.

The meaning is that although the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā* does not apply because the word *sarva* lacks a *kṛt* suffix, the rule *saha supā* itself exists as its prescriptive authority. If one asks, "What would be the loss if *saha supā* were not a prescriber of compound formation? he says in response, "Otherwise... it would not occur. The implication is that, in that case, the statement by the author of the Bhāṣya and others—that this is an "asamartha-samāsa" (compound of non-coordinated words)—would be inconsistent.

But surely, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the rule *saha supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4) is not resorted to here because it is a "recourse of last resort" (*agatikagati*) and because it falls within the scope of the *samartha-paribhāṣā*. Otherwise, the formulation of various compound rules such as *dvitīyā śrita-* (Pāṇini 2.1.24) would be rendered useless. Furthermore, one would have to assume that the *samartha-paribhāṣā* does not apply to the rule *saha supā*. As for the statement that this is an "asamartha-samāsa," it must be explained as being intended to mean that the compounding occurs by virtue of an irregularity (*nipātana*).

Furthermore, with the intention that a compound such as *sarvamṛttikaḥ* would not be possible either due to the absence of an agent (*vidhātṛ*) or because [the object] is not denoted [by the verbal root], he says: "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*). Regarding the example *ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati* ("he brings about the jar"): if the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), then the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is restricted to the result alone. Thus, the meaning of the root *bhū* is "origination" (*utpatti*), and the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is "activity" (*vyāpāra*). This activity is construed with origination through the relation of "conduciveness" (*anukūlatā*). The meaning is therefore: "an activity conducive to origination."

And so, just as in the case of "he causes the pot to be" (*bhāvayati ghaṭam*), where the pot receives the designation of *karman* (object) because it is the locus of the arising produced by the operation denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), and thus the second case ending occurs for the object; likewise, in the case of "the pot comes into being" (*bhavati ghaṭaḥ*), the meaning of the root *bhū* is "arising," and the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is "operation. When these are construed through the relation of favorability (*anukūlatā*), the resulting sense is "an operation conducive to arising."

And likewise, since the pot (ghaṭa) would be the locus of the arising produced by the operation signified by the verbal suffix (tiṅ), it would receive the designation of "object" (karman); consequently, when the accusative case ending arises, instead of the form *bhavati ghaṭaḥ*, one would have to say *bhavati ghaṭam*. Regarding the phrase *dhātvarthaphala* (the fruit which is the meaning of the root): in both cases, the objection that the pot receives the designation of "object" because it is the locus of the fruit consisting of arising—which is the meaning of the root *bhū*—is raised as a doubt, [which is then addressed] with the words *na cākhyāta* (and not by the verb).

The point is this: in the causative (*ṇijanta*), the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*), and it is that very operation which is restated by the *tiṅ* suffix following the causative; the operation of the prompted agent (*prayojya-vyāpāra*) is not expressed [by the *tiṅ*]. However, in the non-causative form, the operation of the prompted agent is denoted by the *tiṅ* suffix. Thus, there is a disparity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the case under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*). Consequently, in the expression "he causes the jar to come into being" (*ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati*), since the jar lacks the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*), its status as an object (*karmatva*)—defined in relation to the operation signified by the causative suffix—is beyond reproach, and thus the accusative case ending occurs.

Regarding the statement "the jar becomes" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), the meaning is that the jar does not possess the status of an object (*karmatva*) because its agenthood (*kartṛsaṃjñā*)—based on being the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārthavyāpāra*)—sublates [the application of the term "object"]. The Grammarian refutes this as follows: "regarding the activity denoted by the verbal suffix. The meaning is: agenthood belongs to that which is the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix when it is uttered in conjunction with a root in its non-causative (*aṇyant*, i.e., simple) form. For example: *pacati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta cooks") is the non-causative state; *pācayati viṣṇumitram* ("He causes Viṣṇumitra to cook") is also a non-causative state. However, *pācayati devadatto viṣṇumitreṇa* ("Devadatta causes [Viṣṇumitra] to cook by means of Viṣṇumitra") is the causative (*ṇyant*) state.

In that regard, although Viṣṇumitra possesses the status of agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of being the locus of the activity denoted by the verb in the state of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), in the case of a causative construction, the activity expressed by the verbal suffix belongs exclusively to the instigator (*prayojaka*)—the activity signified by the *ṇic* itself. Consequently, agency would belong only to the instigator Devadatta, who is the locus of that specific activity denoted by the verbal suffix, and not to the prompted (*prayojya*) Viṣṇumitra, because he lacks the status of being the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix as co-occurrent with the causative verbal root.

And thus, since Viṣṇumitra lacks the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would not apply according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā*; this is the meaning of the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*). In my view, however, there is no fault. The meaning of the root *pāci* (causative of *pac*) is an operation conducive to an operation that is itself conducive to softening (*viklitti*). In that context, because Viṣṇumitra possesses the status of agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of being the locus of the operation expressed by the root *pac*, which is the base of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the application of the third case is easily justified. As in the example: "He causes [him] to go to the village" (*grāmaṃ gamayati*).

In the case of a causative (*ṇijanta*) construction, according to the previously stated reasoning, since the prompted agent (*prayojya*), Viṣṇumitra, lacks the status of being the agent (*kartṛ*), the designation of "object" (*karman*)—which is prescribed by the rule *kartur īpsitatamam* for that which is the substratum of the result produced by the activity residing in the agent—would not apply even to the village, which is the substratum of the result produced by the activity residing in Viṣṇumitra.

Just as in the case of *grāmaṃ gacchati viṣṇumitraḥ* (Viṣṇumitra goes to the village), where according to the Mīmāṃsaka view Viṣṇumitra receives the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) because he is the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix, and the village receives the designation of "object" (*karman*) because it is the substratum of the fruit—conjunction—denoted by the root which is produced by the activity residing in such an agent, and thus the village possesses the status of being the object of the action of going; likewise, in the case of the causative form (*ṇijanta*), even though the village is the substratum of the fruit—conjunction—denoted by the root which is produced by the activity residing in Viṣṇumitra...

The status of being the object of the root *gam* (i.e., being the locus of the result consisting of conjunction produced by the operation residing in the agent) would not occur; for at that time, Viṣṇumitra lacks the designation "agent" according to the method previously stated. Consequently, the meaning is that the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) would not follow the word *grāma*. Now, one might object: even in the Grammarian’s system, it must necessarily be admitted that in the rule *kartur īpsitatamam* ("that which is most desired by the agent"), the word *kartṛ* does not refer to the technical designation "agent," but rather refers merely to that which is independent (*svatantra*).

Otherwise, in the sentence "Devadatta causes Viṣṇumitra to go to the village," since the prompted agent (Viṣṇumitra) would be designated as the *karman* by the rule *gati-buddhi-* [Pāṇini 1.4.52], he would lack the designation of *kartṛ* (agent); consequently, the village could not receive the designation of *karman*. If it is argued that this fault does not apply even in my view because the prompted agent Viṣṇumitra possesses independence (*svātantrya*), defined as being the locus of the activity conducive to the conjunction that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root, we say: no.

In your view as a Mīmāṃsaka, the meaning of the term "independence" (svātantrya) is precisely the state of being the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix; for it must be understood that since the activity conducive to the fruit of the root-meaning exists in every *kāraka*, the independence you have defined would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to objects (*karman*) and the rest. Now, it might be argued that when a verbal suffix is used in conjunction with a causative (*ṇyanta*) root, it is accepted as denoting the activities residing in both the instigated (*prayojya*) and the instigator (*prayojaka*).

Furthermore, since both the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*) are the substrata of the operation denoted by the verbal root, the agency (*kartṛtva*) of both is established. Consequently, in the sentence *pācayati viṣṇumitram* ("He causes Viṣṇumitra to cook"), because Viṣṇumitra possesses agency, the instrumental case is correctly applied to him as the agent. Likewise, in the sentence *grāmaṃ gamayati* ("He causes [Viṣṇumitra] to go to the village"), the status of the village as the object of the motion (*gamikarmatā*) is established, because it is the substratum of the result—namely, conjunction—which is the meaning of the verbal root and is produced by the operation residing in Viṣṇumitra, the agent of the instigated action. If this is argued, [we reply]: no.

In the expression *ghaṭaṃ bhāvayati* ("he brings about a pot"), since the pot—which is the object to be brought about (*prayojya*)—is also the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha-vyāpārāśraya*), it would incur the status of an agent (*kartṛtā*) just like the potter. Consequently, the technical designation "object" (*karman*) would be sublated, and by virtue of its higher priority, the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) alone would apply. Thus, just as in *ghaṭo bhavati*, there would be the nominative case in *bhāvayati ghaṭaḥ* instead of *bhāvayati ghaṭam*, because in both instances the pot possesses agency due to being the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix. This is the meaning.

Nor should it be argued that the village possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*) by virtue of being the locus of the fruit—namely, the conjunction produced by the root-meaning which is itself generated by the causal agent’s operation denoted by the suffix *ṇic*—and that it is for this very reason that the accusative case ending is justified. For if that were the case, even though the village would be the object of the causative form (*ṇijanta*), its lack of being the object of the root *gam* (to go) would remain as it was. This is the intended meaning. If one asks, "What is the loss if the village lacks the status of being the object of the root *gam*? the author replies with the words beginning "And thus... (*tathā ca*). [The consequence is that] even the following [usage] would not occur: "ity api na syāt" (even this would not be possible).

The meaning is that in the expression *grāmāya gamayati* ("he causes [him] to go to the village"), even if the village does not possess the status of being the direct object (*karmatva*) of the act of going, the dative case would still not occur after the word *grāma* if it were not for the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi*. He states the reason for the absence of the dative after the word *grāma* by citing the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi*. The meaning of that sūtra is: "When there is volitional effort (*iṣṭā*), the accusative and dative cases are used for the object of a verb meaning 'to go' that is distinct from a path (*adhvan*)."

In your view, the state of being the object of a verb whose meaning is motion must be stated as either (1) the state of being the locus of the result produced by the activity denoted by the verbal suffix, which resides in an agent who is the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal suffix co-occurring with a verbal root whose meaning is motion in the form of conjunction; or (2) the state of being the object of desire, characterized by being the locus of that result. It must be stated.

The roots *gam* (to go), *śal*, *hul*, *pat* (to fall/go), *aṭ*, and *paṭ* (to move), as well as *ragh* and *lagh*—these and others are roots whose meaning is "motion. A verbal form (*ākhyāta*) associated with such a root, which consists of a *tiṅ*-suffix, has as its meaning an operation (*vyāpāra*). The agent (*kartṛ*) is the locus of that operation. The object of motion (*gatyarthakarma*) is that village or similar location which is the desired locus of the fruit of the root-meaning—in the form of conjunction—which is produced by the operation residing in such an agent. In other words: when a verb denotes an action of going, the agent is the substratum of that action. The object of the action of going is that place, such as a village, which is intended as the locus of the result of the action (conjunction), which results from the operation inherent in that agent. This is what constitutes the "object" in the case of roots meaning "to go."

The meaning is "according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas. And thus, although the second case ending is justified because the village (*grāma*) is the object of the causative (*ṇijanta*) verb—being the locus of the result, namely conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is the meaning of the root *gam*, as prompted by the activity (the meaning of the suffix *ṇic*) residing in the instigator (*prayojaka*)—nevertheless, since the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) co-occurring with the causative denotes the activity (the meaning of *ṇic*) residing in the instigator who is the agent (*kartṛ*), [the action] of the one being prompted (*prayojya*)...

The meaning is that, because there is an absence of agency, the state of being the object (*karmatā*) of the root *gam*—which consists in being the locus of the result (conjunction) produced by an operation residing in an agent who is essentially the locus of such an operation denoted by a verbal suffix—is not possible for the village; therefore, the dative case prescribed for the object of a verb meaning "to go" would not occur at all in that instance.

In this regard, the following should be understood: although the village is the locus of the result—conjunction—which is produced by the operation residing in Viṣṇumitra, Viṣṇumitra lacks the status of an agent (kartṛ). Consequently, just as there is no such usage as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*) for a person devoid of the operation residing in the agent, [so too the village cannot be the object]. By the phrase "by this" (*etena*), the meaning is: by the justification of the dative usage in *grāmāya*. By the phrase "both," the meaning is: the two operations residing in both the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*). By the phrase "refuted" (*apāstam*), [it is meant that the objection is dismissed].

The point is this: although the verb *gamayati* is stated to be formed from a root with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), it lacks connection with a root whose primary meaning is "motion. Consequently, the prompted agent (the horse) does not possess the status of being a "agent of motion"—defined as being the locus of the activity denoted by the verb associated with a root meaning "motion. Since the status of being an "object of motion" is thus unattained, the grammatical anomaly of the fourth case ending remains unresolved.

Furthermore, even if one accepts that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in a causative construction (*ṇijanta*) denotes the operations of both the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*), thereby establishing Viṣṇumitra’s status as the agent, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would still be absolutely impossible there; for since the agenthood residing in him is already expressed by the verbal suffix, the nominative (*prathamā*) alone would be required after the word "Viṣṇumitra" just as it is after the word "Devadatta."

Furthermore, regarding the sentence "Devadatta causes Viṣṇumitra to go to the village," the *Bhāṣya* states that although the designation of *karman* (object) for Viṣṇumitra—the agent (*kartṛ*) under the causative (*ṇic*)—is already established by the rule *kartur īpsitatamam* ("that which is most desired by the agent"), the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇikartā sa ṇau* is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). This is because the *sūtra* prescribes the *karman* designation for the agent of the root when it follows a causative suffix (*ṇic*), specifically in the case of roots meaning motion (*gati*), cognition (*buddhi*), eating (*pratyavasāna*), those having sound as their object (*śabdakarman*), and intransitives (*akarmaka*). Thus, the rule serves to restrict the application of the *karman* designation to these specific categories.

In this regard, one might raise the following objection: by adopting the objective predominance (*ārthaprādhānya*) characterized by being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*), Viṣṇumitra would acquire the designation of *kartṛ* (agent) because he is the substratum of the primary action denoted by the verbal root *gam* (to go). Simultaneously, he would also acquire the designation of *karman* (object) according to the rule *kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*. Between these two, since the designation of *karman* is subsequent (*para*), it would supersede the designation of *kartṛ*; therefore, the rule *gati-buddhi-* would be necessary to prevent that supersession. Consequently, it is argued that it is improper to claim that the rule has the purpose of excluding [the application of the *kartṛ* designation].

Since the activity of the prompter (*prayojaka*) possesses both objective predominance (*ārthaprādhānya*), characterized by its independence from others, and verbal predominance (*śābdaprādhānya*), the designation of "object" (*karma-saṃjñā*)—which applies by virtue of such predominance—is more powerful; thus, the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) does not apply at all. Consequently, as there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the rule *kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma* (P. 1.4.49) is established without exception, and it has been concluded that the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi...* (P. 1.4.52) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).

The point is this: such being the case, since the causative (*ṇij*) affix denotes the operations of both the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*), both would equally be the substrata of the operation expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Consequently, it would be illogical for the instigator to hold primacy over the instigated. Furthermore, according to the rule *hetumati ca*, it is understood that the operation of the instigator is what is denoted by the causative affix; therefore, it is illogical for that operation to be denoted by the verbal suffix as well. This is the intended meaning.

Now, one might object that the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.12) has been rejected in the Bhāṣya by establishing the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) in the sense of "she lies with her husband" (*patye śete*), just as in other examples; thus, there would be no harm even if the village were not the object of a verb meaning "to go. To this, he says: "Furthermore... and "In that usage... and so forth.

It must necessarily be stated that the status of being an agent (kartṛtva) belongs to the substratum of the activity denoted by the verb only when both the verb and its meaning—the activity and its substratum—occur within the same sentence; otherwise, in the case of "the pot exists" (*ghaṭo vidyate*), one would incur the undesirable consequence of a nominative case-ending after the word "pot" (*ghaṭam*) in the sentence "he makes the pot" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), by taking the status of being the substratum of such an activity as present there.

Furthermore, in a sentence such as "Devadatta cooked" (*devadattaḥ paktā*), which lacks a finite verb (*ākhyāta*), Devadatta would not possess the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*) because the agent denoted by the primary suffix (*kṛt-pratyaya*) lacks the support of the activity denoted by a finite verb residing in the same sentence. Thus, the intention is that the definition of agency as "the locus of the activity denoted by a finite verb" suffers from the flaw of being over-narrow (*avyāpti*) when applied to the agent denoted by a primary suffix. Now, one might object: even in cases devoid of a finite verb, the addition (*adhyāhāra*) of a finite verb-ending is necessary in accordance with the requirements of the nominative case (*prathamā*).

Otherwise, the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the nominative case prescribed by the rule "the nominative occurs when coreferential with a finite verb" (*tiṅ-samānādhikaraṇe prathamā*) would not be established. If it is argued that in such cases—as in *devadattaḥ paktā* ("Devadatta is a cooker")—the agenthood of Devadatta is possible through the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of a verb such as "exists" (*asti*), we say no. Even if the agenthood relative to the root *as* (to be) were thus established, the agenthood relative to the root *pac* (to cook) would remain unestablished; consequently, the suffix *tṛc* could not occur after the root *pac* in the form *paktā*.

Is it not the case that the meaning of the rule *kartari kṛt* is accepted as being merely this: "A *kṛt* suffix occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) with respect to that referent which has been apprehended as the locus of the activity that constitutes the meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*) derived from that root"? In the sentence *devadattaḥ pacati*, since Devadatta has been apprehended as the locus of the activity that constitutes the meaning of the verb derived from the root *pac*, the suffix *tṛc* occurs after the root *pac* with respect to such a referent as Devadatta; such is its meaning.

Alternatively, it is accepted that the operation (*vyāpāra*) is also the meaning of a *kṛt* suffix. The meaning is that *kṛt* suffixes denoting an agent (*kartṛ*) or an object (*karman*) express both the factor (*kāraka*) and the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). Thus, agency (*kartṛtva*) consists precisely in being the substratum (*āśraya*) of the operation which is the meaning of the suffix; for example, in "Maitra cooks" (*maitraḥ pacati*), Maitra and so forth [are agents]; and in "Devadatta causes Caitra to cook" (*devadattena caitraḥ pācayati*), both [Devadatta and Caitra] are agents because they are the substrata of the operation expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), respectively.

Likewise, in cases such as "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ paktā*), it is established that Devadatta and others possess the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) by virtue of being the substratum of the activity that is the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix. Thus, one might argue that in expressions like "Devadatta cooks" which lack a finite verb (*ākhyāta*), there is no resulting loss of Devadatta's agency. To this, he replies "no," and says "the direction [is clear]" (*dig iti*).

The intended meaning is as follows: regarding a cognition whose qualificand is *bhāvanā* (efficient force) and which has as its relation the suitability for the result denoted by the verbal root, the Mīmāṃsakas must accept that both the sequence of the verbal root and the suffix (*ākhyāta*) and the sequence of the verbal root and the primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*) are causes. However, the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas), on the other hand, need only accept that the sequence of the verbal root alone is the cause of such a cognition; thus, there is parsimony (*lāghava*). And so, due to this parsimony, it is more appropriate that *bhāvanā* is the meaning of the verbal root itself rather than the meaning of the suffix—this is the underlying point.

Furthermore, he provides an introduction to the second half of the verse beginning with "kiṃca kriyā" by stating "sūtrānupapatti" (the inconsistency of the Sūtra). The meaning is that he demonstrates the inconsistency of the Sūtra as a proof for the view that the verbal root's meaning is an operation (*vyāpāra*). The phrase "svotprekṣitatvam" means "being imagined by one's own fancy"; that is to say, the claim that the verbal root expresses an operation residing [in the agent] is baseless. He refutes or rejects this by saying "kiṃca" (furthermore).

Is it not the case that the rule *bhūvādayaḥ* (P. 1.3.1) means, by way of a *bahuvrīhi* compound—namely, "those for which *bhū* is the first"—that *bhū* and the subsequent items are designated as verbal roots (*dhātu*), and not that those words recited in the *bhv-ādi* list which denote action are designated as verbal roots, because there is no word to indicate that [latter] meaning? How then is the term *bhūvādayaḥ* explained? It is through a *nipātana* (an irregularity), where the augment *va* is added for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). For the author of the Vārttikas has stated: "This *va* is employed after *bhūvādayaḥ* for the sake of auspiciousness. "For the sake of auspiciousness" means indicative of auspiciousness.

The meaning is that just as in the world the acquisition of something previously unobtained, such as curd and so forth, is indicative of auspiciousness, so it is here. Thus, in order to dispel the doubt that the Sūtra would otherwise be untenable, he states the meaning of that Sūtra with the words "In that regard, earth and speech," and so on. Regarding the phrase "of the two expressing the manner of determination" (*vyavasthā*): *vyavasthā* is a primary sense that necessarily requires a limit; that which has nothing prior to it and has something subsequent to it is called "first."

When it is said "this is the first," there is necessarily an expectancy for a limit (avadhi) as to what it is first in relation to; therefore, the meaning is that the root *bhū* is the first in relation to the collection of verbal roots listed in the *bhv-ādi* group. "Type" (*prakāra*) means similarity. Thus, between the two words *ādi* having the aforementioned meanings, there is a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of those that are identical in form (*sarūpa*). Then, the compound *bhūv-ādayaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi*: "those whose beginnings are *bhū* and *v*."

In this context, there is a correspondence between the word *ādi*, which denotes "classification," and the word *bhū*, as well as between the word *vā*, which denotes "kind," and the word *bhū*; this is a connection according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). Consequently, he states what the meaning of the aphorism (*sūtra*) becomes: "the earth and so forth," and so on.
