In that regard, the word *bhū* is twofold: one signifying "earth" and the other signifying "existence" (*sattā*), etc.; thus, there is a connection with the word *vā* according to their respective order. And consequently, he states what the meaning of the aphorism becomes: "the earth and so forth," and so on.

In this context, the word *bhū* is of two kinds: that which has the meaning of "earth" (*bhūmi*) and that which has the meaning of "existence" (*sattā*), etc. Likewise, the word *vā* is also of two kinds: that which has the meaning of "option" (*vikalpa*) and that which has the meaning of "motion" (*gati*), etc. Among these, because both types of the word *vā* denote meanings that do not conform to gender and number, they signify non-substance (*asattva*). Due to its association with them, the word *bhū* is understood here as signifying existence, etc., rather than earth; and that [word *bhū*] becomes expressive of action (*kriyā*). Due to its association with that, the word *vā* is also understood as having only the meaning of motion, etc.

With the intention that this similarity consists precisely in being expressive of an action, the author says in the root-text: "And this. The meaning is: "and this similarity. Regarding the phrase "by way of being expressive of an action": according to the traditional rule (smṛti), "the root *vā* [is used] in the senses of going and smelling," just as it possesses expressiveness for actions in the form of going and so forth, so too do roots such as *bhū* possess expressiveness for actions in the form of existence (*sattā*) and so forth; thus, there is a similarity between them. If similarity were grasped merely by virtue of being a word (*śabdatva*), then since that property would not serve to differentiate, the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the term *vādi* would result in redundancy.

If similarity were accepted on the grounds that the root *vā* belongs to the *adādi-gaṇa* (the class beginning with *ad*)—either by virtue of being *adādi* or by virtue of having the meaning of "motion"—then there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*), as this would include all roots of the *bhvādi-gaṇa*. Therefore, the intention is that similarity must be understood solely through the capacity to denote action (*kriyāvācakatva*), as established by the commentary. Furthermore, the similarity in the case of the root *vā* should be understood according to the difference in usage: just as the word *vā* within the form *vāti* denotes action, so too does the word *vā* within the form *vātaḥ*.

The meaning is that this follows from the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that there is a difference in words with each utterance. Consequently, the word *bhū*, which has the sense of "earth," and the word *vā*, which has the sense of "option," do not possess the status of verbal roots (*dhātu*).

Otherwise, since the word *bhū* (meaning "earth") would be a verbal root (*dhātu*) and the particle *vā* (meaning "optionally") would not be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), they would lack the status of being nominal stems; consequently, the case endings (*sup*) would not apply, and the status of being a "word" (*pada*) would not be attained. As a result, in expressions such as *bhūstiṣṭhati* ("the earth stands") or *vā gacchati* ("or goes"), the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*—which prescribes that a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) following another finite verb is unaccented—would fail to apply to the finite verbs *tiṣṭhati* and *gacchati*. Furthermore, the case ending *sup* would not arise after the word *bhū*, because the words *bhū* and *vā* would lack the status of being "words. This is the intended meaning.

In the case of the example *evaṃ bhūstvā vā mā vā na pātayiṣyati*, the application of the rule *tvāmau dvitīyāyāḥ* would not occur, because the words *bhū* and *vā* lack the status of being *pada*s (independent words). This is how it should be understood. Thus, he refines the actual meaning of the sūtra as it results from its formulation by stating "provided that [the word] denotes an action" (*kriyāvācakatve sati*), and so forth. In this refinement, if one were to define a verbal root (*dhātu*) merely as that which denotes an action—omitting the condition of being listed in the *bhvādi* group—there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to words such as *hiruk* and *nānā*, which denote actions like avoiding or separating. To prevent this, the condition of being listed in the *bhvādi* group has been included.

In reality, however, since the meanings such as "exclusion" (varjana) understood from indeclinables like *hiruk* possess a requirement for another action (*kriyāntarākāṅkṣā*), they lack the property of being perceived by way of a form that does not give rise to a requirement for another action; therefore, they do not even possess the status of being actions (*kriyātva*). As for the conventional usage of these as denoters of action, it is stated previously that this is figurative (*gauṇa*) because they serve merely as qualifiers of an action and because they do not admit connection with gender and other such attributes. With this intention, he says: "in cases such as 'ity-ādau'."

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of forms such as *śiśye* (the third person singular perfect middle), where the suffix *taṅ* has the sense of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*); as well as *āṇavayati* and *vaṭṭayati*. Regarding *śiśye*, if the vowel *e* were designated as a verbal root (*dhātu*), then by the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śitī* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), the substitution of *ā* would apply. However, since that which ends in a *tiṅ* suffix is not subject to the designation of "instruction" (*upadeśa*), the application of *ā* does not arise for the whole; thus, it should be understood that the application of *ā* would have occurred specifically for the vowel *e*. Furthermore, the application of the *taṅ* suffixes does not occur here, because their meaning has already been expressed—this is how it should be understood.

If it is argued: "Surely, even in the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), just as in the *paryudāsa* (exclusion) view, the very capacity for being followed by a *śit* suffix is the cause for the application of *ātvam*; therefore, since that capacity is absent here, there is no possibility of *ātvam*," then the fault would be the undesired consequence (*āpatti*) of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) for forms such as *āṇavayati* and *vaṭṭayati* due to their falling within the scope of the rules defining verbal roots (*dhātu-saṃjñā*). The meanings of *āṇavayati* and *vaṭṭayati* are, respectively, "he commands" (*ājñāpayati*) and "he turns" (*vartayati*). || 9 ||

If it is argued: "In that case, let it simply be said that the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) consists in being listed in the *bhv-ādi* group; there is no need for the qualification 'denoting an action' (*kriyāvācakatva*)," [the author] replies with the words "of pronouns, *yā* and so forth. The point is this: if one were to state merely "being listed in the group," then even a pronoun such as *yā* would have the status of a verbal root. This is because the pronoun *yā* has a form identical to a verbal root since it is listed in the *bhv-ādi* group, and there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) [of its status as a pronoun] when it occurs in the *bhv-ādi* list. [The opponent might say: "Let it be a verbal root; what is the harm? To this, [the author] says: "Since it is a verbal root, [it would fall under] *ātaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.84] and *śn* [Pāṇini 3.1.78]; the combination of these two is *ścam*. The suffix *ṭac* is applied at the end of the compound according to [Pāṇini 5.4.106], *dvandvāccudaṣahantāt*. 11.11.ś. ca. ca. The compound *ścam* is formed by the conjunction of these two. The suffix *ṭac* is added to a *dvandva* compound ending in *cu*, *da*, *ṣ*, or *ha*. (Note: The text contains a scribal error regarding the specific rule number and the term *śn*; the intended reference is likely to the rules governing the substitution of *śn* for the root *as*.)

Therefore, it should be understood that the seventh case singular ending is [intended] by the word "śce". The meaning is that if the elision of the vowel *ā* were applied by the rule *dhātoḥ*, then in the sense of "whom you see" (*yāḥ paśyasi*), the undesirable form *yaḥ paśyasi* would result. This undesirable consequence is to be understood as following the perspective of one who looks only at the actual linguistic usage (*lakṣyaikacakṣuṣka*). Regarding the phrase "because it is technical" (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*): here, the word *lakṣaṇa* refers—by virtue of a partial application of power (*ekadeśa-śakti*), similar to the words *bhāmā* or *satyā*—to the *lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā concerning that which is taught by a specific rule versus that which is taught by a general rule).

The meaning is that the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied in the sense of "he/she/it deserves" (*arhati*) by the rule *tadarhati*; this is because [the word *yā*] falls under the scope of the technical paribhāṣā concerning "that which is taught by its specific form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*). Thus, only the word *yā* taught by its specific form (as part of the root *yā* in the *bhvādi* class) is grasped by the term *bhvādi*, and not the pronoun *yā*, because the latter possesses a nature established through the consideration of the application of grammatical rules. Therefore, in that first case, the occurrence of that [suffix] is not possible; for [in the case of the pronoun], when followed by a consonant (*jhal*), the anusvāra and the fifth letter [nasal] arise from the letter *na* within verbal roots (*dhātu*).

A *śakāra* arising from a *sakāra*, or a *śakāra* followed by a *cakāra* or *chakāra*, is born from the *ṣṭavarga*; likewise, a *ṭavarga* following a *repha* or a *ṣakāra* is born from the *tavarga*. Among verbal roots (*dhātu*), the *anusvāra* and the fifth letter [of each varga] following a *jhal* consonant are born from the *nakāra*. For example: *asraṃsu*, *añcu*, and so forth. A *śakāra* followed by *śa* or *ca* is born from a *sakāra*. For example: *hariśśete*, *vraścū*, and so forth. A *ṭavarga* following a *repha* or a *ṣakāra* is born from the *tavarga*. For example: *ūrṇuñ*, *ṣṭhā*, and so forth. Thus it is stated by the learned authorities.

And thus, even for those [grammarians] who hold that the nature of a word is its being the object of a cognition occurring subsequent to the cognition of its formal derivation (*lakṣaṇa*), the designation *dhātu* (verbal root) is established by the force of its inclusion in the *dhātupāṭha* (list of roots). This is because the paribhāṣā "that which is taught by a rule and that which is taught as a specific form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*) does not apply to the prescription of the *dhātu* designation. Even in the second case [of their view], the application of that [designation] is impossible; for otherwise, forms such as *paśuṣaḥ* would result in being unestablished. To explain: in the analysis *paśum sanoti*, when the suffix *viṭ* is applied by the rule *janasanakhanakramagamaviṭ*, the substitution of *ā* for *o* occurs by the rule *viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt*.

Consequently, by the rule *āto dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.140), when the vowel *ā* is elided, the form *paśuṣaḥ* is established. However, if in the rule *ato dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.140) only that vowel *ā* which is explicitly mentioned (*pratipadokta*) were taken, then because the *ā* in *ṣā* would be merely derivative (*lākṣaṇika*), its elision would not occur; thus, *paśuṣaḥ* would not be established. The meaning is that this paribhāṣā applies only to that derivative form whose existence is impossible without the application of a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇapravṛtti*).

But even so, for the sake of establishing forms such as *ktvāḥ śnaḥ*, the author of the Vārttika modified the rule by changing *ātaḥ* to *ātaḥ anāpaḥ*; how then can there be the possibility of elision of the vowel *ā* in *yāḥ paśyasi*? To this, he says "or" (*vā*) and so forth. The meaning is that there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the indeclinable *vā*. This is what is meant by "over-occurrence" (*atiprasaṅga*).

The meaning is as follows: since the particle *vā* signifying option (*vikalpārthaka*)—which is similar to the *vā* designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*)—is read in the *bhvādi* class [of roots], there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that this indeclinable *vā* is also a verbal root (*dhātu*), due to the lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) when choosing between them. As for what the loss would be if it were a verbal root, he says: "the usage *vāti* [meaning] 'optionally' would result. Thus, while the usage *vāti* with the sense of motion (*gati*) and so forth is accepted, such a usage with the sense of option is not desired; this is the intended point.

And this is an illustration, as he says: "in *vā* etc. By the word "etc.," the prefix *su* is included; *mā* and *māṅ*, as well as those beginning with vowels (*svarādi*), are also comprised. Although *ṣu* is listed among the verbal roots (*dhātu*), nevertheless in actual usage the word *su* alone is the root. Thus, it should be understood that just as the usage *savati* meaning "to produce" and so forth is established, the usage *savati* meaning "to shine" would be undesirable. However, if [the definition] is stated as "being expressive of action" (*kriyāvācakatve sati*), then no fault arises.

One might object: "Even if it is stated that [the particle] *vā* expresses action only when it is a verb, in cases such as 'he wavers' (*vāti*), an action in the form of wavering is indeed perceived from the indeclinable *vā*, just as it is in 'he deliberates' (*vikalpayati*). If this is argued, the answer is no. It should be understood that while the meaning of "option" (*vikalpa*) is perceived from the indeclinable *vā*—just as it is from particles such as *hiruk* or *nānā*—it lacks the status of an action because it is not perceived through a form that possesses the capacity to give rise to an expectancy for another action (*kriyāntarākāṅkṣānutthāpakatāvacchedaka-rūpa*). Since it does possess an expectancy for another action, it is not an action. Thus it must be understood.

Now, if it were intended that both *vā*—the indeclinable and the non-indeclinable—are verbal roots (*dhātu*), then there would be no purpose for the mention of their meanings; for since that [mention] was made, it is understood by the very force of that fact that only those which possess the mentioned meanings can be verbal roots. Anticipating the objection that the indeclinable *vā* in the sense of "option" cannot be a verbal root because its meaning is not specified in the list [of roots]—just as the meanings of "motion" and "smelling" are specified—the author provides the following resolution, beginning with the words "na ca gatigandhana... and so forth.

Regarding the term "niyāmaka" (restrictive): by the force of the specification of meaning, only that *vā* which has the specified meanings of "going" (*gati*) and so forth receives the designation of a verbal root (*dhātu*), and not the *vā* used in the sense of option (*vikalpa*) whose meaning is not specified. In this manner, it should be understood that the specification of meaning acts as a restrictor for the designation of a verbal root; otherwise, such a specification of meaning would be purposeless—this is the intended sense. He refutes [the claim of] restrictiveness with the words "tasya" (of that), meaning: of the specification of meanings such as "existence" (*sattā*) and so forth. [The reason is] "because the meanings are not specified."

The meaning is that there is no mention of the existence (*sattā*) of the meaning and so forth by the name "beginningless" (*anādi*). Regarding the phrase "in the Bhāṣya": it means in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *muṇḍamiśra*. Regarding the phrase "because it is obtained as being modern": the meaning is that the indication of the meaning was recited by modern [grammarians] such as Bhīmasena and others; for Bhīmasena and others indeed indicated the meaning. It is clear from both the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika that the teacher Pāṇini, however, did not recite [the words] *bhavedha* and so forth.

For this very reason, the Vārttika and its Bhāṣya in the *Dhātusaṃjñā-sūtra* are consistent: "The mention of 'measure' (*parimāṇa*) must be made; it should be stated that 'this much [extent] receives the designation of root (*dhātu*'); for why is it that the word *bhū* receives the designation of root, and not the word *bhū-vidha*? The phrase "because there is no teaching of meanings" (*arthānādeśanāt*) means "because there is no teaching of meanings in all cases."

For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *namovarivaścitraḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.19): "Indeed, for this purpose the Teacher teaches [the roots] in various ways; in some cases he prescribes meanings, and in others he does not. For this same reason, the statement that the particle *eva* in the rule *karda, khurda, gurda, guda krīḍāyāmeva* (Dhātupāṭha 1.286) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding the fact that roots have multiple meanings becomes consistent. Therefore, it is established that a root (*dhātu*) is that which denotes an action (*kriyā*). 10.

Now, one who cannot tolerate that a verbal root (*dhātu*) expresses an operation (*vyāpāra*), and who considers that the meaning of a root—which is included within the very definition of being a root—is only the action (*kriyā*) as the result (*phala*) itself, and that there is no such thing as an "operation" distinct from that; and who thus raises the Mīmāṃsaka objection that the rule *na bhūvādayaḥ* would otherwise be untenable, thereby serving as proof for a root's expression of an operation—this person is addressed and refuted by the statement: "If being the meaning of a root were the same as being an action (*kriyātva*)."

In this introductory section, with the intention that the objector accepts the definition of "action" (*kriyātva*) as being simply "the state of being the meaning of a verbal root" (*dhātvarthatva*)—by means of the statement "and action is nothing but the meaning of a verbal root"—the author says: "If the state of being an action is indeed the state of being the meaning of a verbal root. Having thus accepted the definition of action, he demonstrates the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), which obstructs the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, starting with the words "then," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: for the cognition of *dhātutva* (the nature of being a verbal root), the cognition of *kriyātva* (the nature of being an action) in the form of "being the meaning of a verbal root" (*dhātvarthatva*) is the cause; and for the cognition of *kriyātva*, the cognition of *dhātutva* in the form of "denoting an action" (*kriyāvācakatva*) must be stated as the cause. Thus, due to mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), no understanding of the meaning whatsoever could arise from the statement "action-ness is the meaning of a verbal root. [In the commentary: "in the apprehension of *dhātutva*" means "in the cognition of *dhātutva*"; "its meaning-ness" (*tadarthatva*) means "the meaning-ness of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthatva*); and "delimited by that" (*tadavacchinna*), etc., refers to the same.

The meaning is that the knowledge of *dhātutva* (the status of being a verbal root) consists in the property of being a denoter residing in that which denotes an object whose nature is action (*kriyā*), as delimited by the universal *kriyātva*. Regarding the phrase "the word *graha*": the meaning is that one should supply the word *graha*, which has the sense of "knowing" (*jñāna*). Regarding the phrase "as heard [in the text]": the meaning is that there is no supplying of the word *graha*. Regarding the phrase "in the case of origination": for example, in the origination of a seed and its sprout, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*); however, that is resolved by the fact that the series is beginningless (*anāditva*), which is another matter.

Or, for example, just as it is impossible for Devadatta to arise from Yajñadatta and for Yajñadatta to arise from Devadatta—that is to say, in a mutual arising, it is impossible for either one to be the cause of the other. Or "in the case of *graha*": that [term] is well-known in the rule *halantyam*.

For example, once the meaning of the word *it* is known, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "consonant" (*hal*) is established by the rule *ādir antyena*; and once the designation of "consonant" is established, the meaning of the word *it* is established by the rule *hal antyam*. Thus, because these two rules—*hal antyam* and *ādir antyena*—are mutually dependent, comprehension cannot occur due to circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*). It is not possible for one to be the cause of the other's cognition when they are mutually dependent.

The meaning is that causality belongs only to that which is invariably and immediately antecedent to the effect; and since this [condition] is not possible for both Devadatta and Yajñadatta, nor for both the word *it* and the word *hal*, there is an obstacle to their mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) regarding both production and apprehension. This is because it would lead to a lack of logical consistency (*asaṃgati*).

The earth is the locus (*ādhāra*) of the flow of water in a river and the like, while water is the locus of the earth; thus, there is a mutual relationship of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) between earth and water. Or, just as from the two-fold common usage "the cloth is in the threads" and "the threads are in the cloth," the existence of threads and cloth is seen to be established through a mutual relationship of locus and located, so too in the present case, since there is no obstacle to the verbal root-meaning being the action (*kriyātva*) or to the state-of-being-an-action (*kriyātva*) being the verbal root-meaning, the objection raised regarding the defect of non-comprehension (*abodha*) in the aforementioned instance is untenable.

The point is that in cases other than the arising of a [linguistic] apprehension (*graha*), mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) does not act as an obstacle and is therefore not a defect. He raises a doubt in order to avoid this mutual dependence by saying, "nor is it being one of several" (*na cānyatamatvam*). I consider the nature of a verbal root (*dhātutva*)—which consists in being one of as many things as are conventionally designated by the term 'verbal root'—to be the *dhātutva* contained within the phrase "the meaning of a verbal root is action-ness" (*dhātvarthatvaṃ kriyātvam*). And thus, he thinks, there is no possibility of mutual dependence. He rejects this very point by saying, "because it would result in futility" (*vaiyarthyāpatteriti*).

"Any one of those" (*tadanyatama*) means "any one of those that are conventionally designated by the term *dhātu*. If it were accepted that being "any one of those" (*tadanyatamatva*) constitutes the state of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*), then the grammatical rule "the roots begin with *bhū*" (*bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*) would be rendered useless. This is because in rules such as "from a root expressing an action" (*dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ*), the desired result is achieved simply by taking that which possesses the state of being a root in the form of "being any one of those. Nor should it be argued that the phrase "conventionally designated by the term *dhātu*" is necessary for the purpose of defining the meaning of the word *dhātu* contained within that very phrase.

Since it is impossible to understand the meaning of the sentence "bhū-vādayaḥ" (the roots beginning with *bhū*) without [the roots] denoting action in the form of an operation (*vyāpāra*), it is impossible to know the referent of the term "root" (*dhātu*); consequently, even the Preceptor of the Gods (*suraguru*) would be unable to recognize "root-ness" as consisting in being one or another of those [entities]. It is for this very reason that he says, according to his intention: "Let it be as it may. Regarding the phrase "a series of operations" (*vyāpārasantāna*): the meaning is that the entire collection of operations, starting from placing [the pot] on the stove and ending with taking it off the stove, is what is denoted by the word "action" (*kriyā*).

In this way, in all roots beginning with *bhū*, the collection of operations expressed by the verbal form is to be inferred; for it has been stated that "the root [denotes] both the result and the operation. Thus, the definition of being a root (*dhātutva*), as supported by the Bhāṣya, is simply: "being listed in the *bhū* class and so forth while denoting such an action"—this is the meaning. Regarding the subject matter of the rule *bhūvādayaḥ*, he raises an objection: "Now, [regarding] 'existence' and so forth. The meaning is: "Rootness consists in being listed in the [verbal] classes while denoting any one of those portions of the result, such as existence (*sattā*), softening (*viklitti*), and so on."

Regarding the term "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*): the meaning is that it consists of the sense of the sentence produced by the sūtra *bhūvādayaḥ*. The intention is that the word "or" (*vā*) is understood as being similar [to the verb] because it denotes a result such as existence (*sattā*), and not because it denotes action (*kriyā*). The point is that if one adopts the formulation "denoting any one of the components of the result," even the suspicion of the sūtra's redundancy does not arise. Now, how is the usage in the Bhāṣya—"a root (*dhātu*) is that which expresses action"—to be reconciled, given that the component of the result lacks the nature of action? To this, he says: "because it is the meaning of the root."

If it is argued that even the fruit of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*) is conventionally treated as "action" (*kriyā*) in a secondary sense—because it is the fruit produced by an action consisting of an operation (*vyāpāra*) culminating in something specific—the author replies, "This is not sound," with the words beginning "among one or another. The point is this: since we observe the usage *vikalpayati* (he conceptualizes), where *vikalpa* has the sense of "option" (*vikalpa*), it is necessary for *vikalpa* to be included among "one or another" (*anyatama*). Consequently, because of its similarity to the word *vā* (or) listed in the [gaṇa] list, it is necessary to include the particle *vā* when it has the sense of option within the *bhvādi* class; thus, the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of "verbal root" (*dhātu*) to that case is unavoidable. || 11 ||

He raises an objection with "nanu" (but surely), [referring to] "asyaiva" (of this very thing). The meaning is: if being a verbal root (*dhātu*) consists solely in denoting an action while being listed in the *bhvādi* class, etc., then—by the use of the particle "eva" (only)—the status of denoting merely a result is excluded. [The reason given is] "because there is no cognition of an action. From forms such as *asti*, *bhavati*, and *vidyate*, only the cognition of a result in the form of existence (*sattā*) arises, and not of an action in the form of an operation (*vyāpāra*) distinct from that.

For this very reason, when asked "What does he do?"—as in the case where "he cooks" (pacati) is the answer—the reply "he exists" (asti) is not appropriate; the meaning is that from the word "exists," there is no cognition of an action (*kriyā*). Regarding the phrase "the consequence of [them] not being verbal roots" (*adhātutvaprasaṅga*): since verbs such as *asti* lack the expression of an action, they would not possess the status of a verbal root (*dhātutva*). Consequently, the suffixes *laṭ* and so forth would not apply; therefore, he says "in the case of *asti* and so on. "The part of the substratum" (*dharmibhāga*) means the aspect of the substratum (*dharmin*) consisting of existence (*sattā*) and the like. The substratum is an object constituted by properties whose nature is the result, such as existence.

In the case of transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*), the substratum (*dharmin*) is the object (*karman*), such as rice and so forth. However, in the case of intransitive verbs (*akarmaka*), since the result resides in the agent (*kartṛ*), the substratum to be understood is the agent himself, such as Devadatta and so forth. Since that which exists as a real entity does not necessarily produce the cognition of *bhāvanā*, he says: "as that which is to be brought about" (*bhāvyatvena*). This means: by way of being accomplished through the operation whose nature is *bhāvanā*. "Intended" (*vivakṣita*) means: when there is a desire to speak [of it].

The resulting meaning is that there is a desire to know the activity that brings about the result. To demonstrate that very locus of inquiry, he says: "Has he gone from there or not? Here, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) according to the rule *gatyarthākarmaka...* (Pāṇini 3.4.72), because the root *gam* signifies the sense of going. This is understood from the cognition: "Does he possess an activity conducive to separation, which is the meaning of the root *gam*, or does he not possess such an activity? regarding the specific location of that separation.

And thus, in response to this question, he provides the answer—"it exists with great effort"—in order to dispel the desire to know regarding the operation (*vyāpāra*) that is being perceived here by means of stating an operation conducive to existence (*sattā*). By the inclusion of the word "effort" (*yatna*) here, since it is stated that existence is produced by effort, the meaning of the verbal root *as* is understood to be an operation conducive to existence; such is the sense. Since the desire to know is satisfied by the final determination of the meaning as "not non-existent," the word "exists" (*asti*) serves as the answer to the question. This is all the more so [as follows]: [The text continues: "Sutarām" (all the more so). This refers to the fact that the desire to know is indeed removed by the statement of the operation conducive to existence, which is the meaning of the root *as*, through the employment of the term "effort. Thus, the status of "exists" as an answer to the question is established. Furthermore, because the word "effort" is employed, it is understood that the meaning of the root *as* is an operation conducive to existence, and not merely the state of being. Therefore, the removal of the desire to know occurs through the final determination of the meaning as "not non-existent," and "exists" functions as the answer to the question. This is even more evident.

The implication is that when there is an intention to express meanings such as "origination" (utpatti), it is certain that verbs like *asti* (to be) denote an activity (*vyāpāra*). This is because the cognition of an activity conducive to origination is established by the universal experience of all people in those cases. The use of the suffix *-tavant* (in the word *dhrauvyam*) is intended to emphasize that while the cognition of activity occurs only occasionally when the meaning is "existence" (*sattā*), the cognition of activity occurs in every instance when the meaning is "origination" and so forth. By the phrase "origination and so forth" (*utpattyādi*), the defeat (*parābhava*) expressed in "he is defeated" (*parābhavati*) is included.

If *asti* and other such verbs have the sense of "origination" (*utpatti*), the usage in the *Rāmāyaṇa* serves as proof; the meaning of *āsīt* and *abhavat* is "it originated. If they had the sense of "existence" (*sattā*), there would be a contradiction with experience; the point is that in genealogical records (*vaṃśāvalī*), only the sense of origination is established by experience. Furthermore, he provides another proof for the view that *asti* and others denote an operation (*vyāpāra*) co-located with existence, stating: "Moreover... [and] "the distinction between the *laṭ* [present tense] and so forth would not be possible."

The meaning is that if [the verbal root] *asti* and so forth do not denote an operation (*vyāpāra*), there would be no systematic application of verbal suffixes such as the present tense marker *laṭ*, the aorist *luṅ* for the past, or the future *lṛṅ*; for it is by the rule "in the present, *laṭ*" and so on that *laṭ* and the others are prescribed when there is the intention to express existence within the present time and so forth. Since the states of being present and so on are established by universal experience as residing in time, the words "present" and so forth denote specific divisions of time. By the particle *eva* in the phrase "of that very [intention]," the [actual] result is excluded.

The sense is that the non-connection of [temporal properties] such as presentness with the fruit has already been established. Regarding this very point, he provides the proof with the words "for the sake of distinguishing actions" (*kriyābhedāya*), etc. The dative case in *bhedāya* should be understood as expressing purpose (*tādarthye*), or alternatively, as being used in the sense of the suffix *-tum* (according to Pāṇini 2.3.15). The meaning is that time, which is conveyed by the *laṭ* (present tense) and other suffixes, serves to differentiate an action qualified by presentness and so forth from other actions. Since the principle "the entire sentence is [one unit]" implies that the expression "for the sake of distinguishing actions" is restrictive, the time conveyed by the *laṭ* and other suffixes is a differentiator of the action alone.

Therefore, the connection with time occurs only with respect to action (*kriyā*). As for the number denoted by suffixes (sup) and verbal endings (tiṅ), it is the differentiator of everything—the meaning of both verbal roots and nominal stems—such is the meaning of the *Vākyapadīya*. It is also stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *bhūvādi* sūtra: "Without action, the times of past, future, and present are not manifested; yet even by means of [verbs] such as *asti* ('is'), the times of past, future, and present are manifested. The sense is that this is because specific times are understood through [the forms] *asti*, *abhūt*, and *bhaviṣyati*.

Therefore, it should be understood that if action (*kriyā*) were not present there, then the *laṭ* [present tense] suffix and others would likewise not exist. Thus, the intention is that the very experience of the author of the *Bhāṣya* and others serves as the proof for the fact that roots such as *as* (to be) denote action. He raises an objection with "nanu" in order to introduce the second half of the verse, "anyatrāśeṣabhāvāt. "Evam" means "if the root denotes action. Regarding "aśeṣabhāvāt": *śeṣabhāva* means separation (*pṛthagbhāva*).

The meaning is as follows: "residing in different substrata" refers to the state of residing in distinct loci, while its absence is "residing in a single locus"; therefore, the point is that there is co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) and its fruit. That *bhāvanā* consists of an activity (*vyāpāra*). It does not manifest clearly in that way. Regarding the phrase "in its clear manifestation": this means the clear appearance of the *bhāvanā*. Regarding the term "defect" (*doṣa*): thus, just like distance and so forth, the co-occurrence of the fruit and the *bhāvanā* acts as an obstacle to the clear cognition of the *bhāvanā*, which consists of an activity.

"Regarding the term *praśna* (question): the meaning is a question concerning a specific action (*vyāpāraviśeṣa*). 'Like the answer *pacati* (he cooks)': the meaning is that since it is well-known that the verbal root *pac* denotes a specific action, its status as an answer to such a question is appropriate. 'The answer might also be [the case]': the intention of the objector is that even though verbs such as *as* (to be) denote an action, the word *asti* (he is) is not accepted as an answer [to a question about a specific action], because it denotes action in general; how much less so, then, when it does not denote an action at all?"

The proponent (siddhāntin) states "because it is accepted" (*iṣṭāpatter*) to show that even though [the verb] denotes action in general, its status as a subsequent [element] is indeed desired. He demonstrates the very locus of this acceptance with the passage beginning from "one whose destruction is imminent" (*āsannavināśam*) up to the end of "because the subsequent is agreed upon by all. Thus, the sense is that the denotation of action by verbs such as *asti* ("is") is necessary. Regarding the other case—that which is different from one whose destruction is imminent—it is determined to be in a state of stability.

The meaning is that when there is a certainty regarding an action conducive to existence, the question "What does he do? is restricted to not having anything else as its object; therefore, the answer "He exists" (*asti*) is not [appropriate]. || 12 ||

He raises an objection with "nanu" (now, an objection). "In this way" means: if [roots] such as *as* (to be) and others denoted a *bhāvanā* consisting of an operation (*vyāpāra*). "Because of being restricted to a result" means: since the operation conducive to a result is what is expressed by the single term *bhāvanā*, and because the result is included within the scope of the meaning of the word *bhāvanā*, the *bhāvanā* is necessarily restricted to a result. "Because of being an object" (*karmatvāt*) means: [because it is] the substratum of the result brought about by the primary operation conveyed by the root in question. "In the case of denoting an action" (*kriyāvācakatve*).

The meaning is that even for intransitive verbs, there is the denotation of an operation conducive to a result. Anticipating the objection that all verbs—whether transitive, intransitive, or both—would consequently become transitive (like *pac* and others) because they denote an operation conducive to a result, he says: "Of the result and the operation."

Now, one might object: if the fact that the result and the operation reside in the same locus is the determinant of intransitivity (*akarmakatā*), then in cases such as *grāmaṃ gacchati* ("he goes to the village") and *vṛkṣaṃ tyajati* ("he leaves the tree"), since the result—consisting of conjunction and disjunction produced by the operation—also resides in the agent (the *kartṛ*), the result and the operation would not reside in different loci. Consequently, verbs like *gam* and others would also incur the status of being intransitive. Anticipating this, the author says: "The state of residing in one [locus] alone. The meaning is: "residing in one alone" means residing in one while not residing in anything other than that one.

He states the resultant meaning applicable to the present context regarding the term *ekamātra* (only one): "having different substrata" (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*). That is to say, when the fruit (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) do not reside in different substrata. By the inclusion of the word *mātra*, he shows that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to roots such as *gam* (to go) and others, because they lack the aforementioned definition of an intransitive root (*akarmaka-dhātu*). He illustrates the intransitive root defined by the stated characteristic with the example "such as *bhū* (to be)," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "when there is a difference in the substratum" (*dharmibhede*), [the meaning is as follows].

The fruit (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are the two properties (*dharma*); the entities that serve as their substrata (*āśraya*) are the subjects (*dharmin*). When there is a difference between these two—that is, when the substrata of the fruit and the operation are distinct—the root (*dhātu*) is transitive (*sakarmaka*); this is the meaning. The point is that the distinction between the substrata of the fruit and the operation is the cause for the conventional designation of a root as transitive. Consequently, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *gam* (to go), even though the substrata of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and its corresponding operation are one and the same. He cites the *Vākyapadīya* as authority for the view that the root *as* denotes an operation conducive to a fruit: "the self by means of the self."

The meaning is as follows: by "non-existence of the self" (*ātmanasattām*), [it is meant] by the self itself (*ātmanā svena*). That which possesses an activity conducive to existence (*sattānukūlavyāpāravān*) is designated—that is, conventionally expressed—as "it exists. Furthermore, according to Pāṇini’s rule, "the root *bhṛ* (√*bhṛ*) signifies supporting and nourishing," it is understood here that there is an activity conducive to its own support (*svadhāraṇānukūlo vyāpāraḥ*). And in this context, "self-ness" (*svatvam*) is simply existence itself (*sattaiva*). The point is that, just as in the case of the verb "to die" (*mriyate*) one clearly perceives an activity conducive to the abandonment of existence, here one clearly perceives, by contrast, an activity conducive to the maintenance of existence.

Anticipating the objection that "in this way, the verb *ās* (to sit) would become transitive," he refutes it with the words "by that object" (*tena karmaṇā*). The meaning is that one should not speak of *ās* as being transitive on account of an object that serves as the locus for the result consisting of self-supporting. He states the reason for this with the words "by a portion of the result" (*phalāṃśena*). The meaning is that both the result, which consists of self-supporting, and the activity conducive to that result reside solely in a single agent.

Now, one might raise the objection that in such cases as "he knows himself" or "he desires [himself]," since the result—consisting of knowledge, desire, and so forth—resides solely in a single agent, it is impossible for these verbs to be transitive (*sakarmaka*). Anticipating this and seeking to refute it, the author says, "There are two selves," and so on. The underlying idea is this: although the self is one, a distinction between two selves is postulated; one is delimited by the body, while the other is delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). By the passage beginning with "therein, the inner self," he demonstrates their respective status as object (*karman*) and agent (*kartṛ*).

The *antarātmā* (inner self) is that which is delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); the meaning is that it is the agent (*kartṛ*) and the locus of activity (*vyāpārāśraya*). The *śarīrātmā* (bodily self) is that which is delimited by the body; the meaning is that it is the locus of the fruits of action (*karmaphalāśraya*). Thus, by taking into account this difference based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhika-bheda*), one understands that there is no impossibility of [the verb] having an object (*sakarmakatva*), nor does it follow that it would be intransitive (*akarmakatva*), because the [respective] results and activities are established as residing in different substrates.

Thus, in the case of the statement "he kills himself by himself" (*ātmānam ātmanā hanti*) or "he creates himself by himself" (*sṛjaty ātmānam ātmanā*), one should understand that because there exists a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is neither the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) nor over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the definitions of transitive and intransitive verbs. However, this point must be noted: if this were the case, then verbs such as *jīvati* ("he lives") and *nṛtyati* ("he dances") would incur the status of being transitive. This is because the results consisting of the maintenance of life or the movement of limbs would exist in a locus distinct from the operation conducive to them.

The meaning is that since retention (dhāraṇa) resides in the vital breath (prāṇa), distraction (vikṣepa) resides in the limbs (gātra), and the activity (vyāpāra) resides in Devadatta, who is distinct from them, the result (phala) is located in a different locus (vyadhikaraṇa) from the activity. Therefore, the definition of transitivity (sakarmakatva) must be stated as follows: "being expressive of an activity whose locus is distinct from the locus of the result, while not being expressive of the substratum of the result."

Furthermore, although roots such as *jīv* (to live) denote an operation whose locus is distinct from its result—given the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) that "the root *jīv* means 'to sustain life' (*prāṇadhāraṇa*)," "the root *nṛt* means 'to move the limbs' (*gātravikṣepa*)," and "the roots *sraṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu* mean 'to fall down' (*adhaḥpatana*)"—these roots do not possess an object (*sakarmaka*). This is because they denote the substrata of the result, namely the vital breaths, the limbs, and the lower regions [of the body], yet they lack the denotation of those [substrata] as being the objects of the action. For this very reason, it should be understood that although the root *ās* (to sit) signifies an operation conducive to self-sustenance, it is not transitive (*sakarmaka*), because it denotes the substratum of the result in its own nature (*svarūpa*). || 13 ||

Regarding the view that the operation (*vyāpāra*) is denoted by the verbal root, he raises an objection with the word "nanu" (but). The phrase "asattvabhūtā" (not being an entity) means that when the operation, which is of the nature of an action, is presented by the verbal root in the form of a "state-to-be-accomplished" (*sādhyatva*)—a specific generic property (*vaijātya*) that does not give rise to an expectancy for another action. The phrase "pākaḥ" (cooking) refers to instances such as those ending in the suffix *ghañ*. The phrase "tatpratyaya" means the undesirable consequence of its being perceived in that form of a state-to-be-accomplished. If it is argued that such a perception is indeed desired in the case of words ending in *ghañ*, he replies: "And this is not an acceptable consequence."

To provide the reason for the [alleged] non-arrival at a conclusion, he says: *kṛdabhihita* (expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix). The meaning is as follows: the "action" (*bhāva*) denoted by a *kṛt* suffix—the meaning of the verbal root—manifests or appears as if it were a substance (*dravya*), being similar to a substance in its possession of the property of a substance, namely, the state of being established (*siddhatva*) characterized by a specific generic quality (*vaijātya*) that serves as the delimiter for the arousal of an expectancy for another action. Regarding the phrase "because of contradiction with the Bhāṣya": one might raise the objection that, based on the aforementioned Bhāṣya, an action expressed by a *kṛdanta* word denoting a "state" (*bhāva*) is understood precisely as being established (*siddhatva*) in the sense of being capable of syntactic connection with gender, number, and so forth. Anticipating this, he says: "*ākhyātaśabda*" (the word ending in a verbal suffix).

He provides the explanation of the term *ākhyātaśabda* with the example "Look, a deer! (*paśya mṛgaḥ*) and so forth. Thus, *ākhyātaśabda* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Furthermore, it should be understood as having a dual ending, meaning "that in which there are two words in the form of a verb" (*ākhyātarūpau śabdau yasmin*). This is because we see the explanation of the word *bhāgābhyām* as "by the two [words] ending in *tiṅ*. And the sentence (*vākya*) is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), precisely because two finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) can occur therein. For this very reason, it is indicated that even though it would be more concise, it is not a *karmadhāraya* compound.

And thus, the phrase "in a verbal form" (ākhyātaśabde) means "in a collection of non-finite elements" (atiṅantasamudāye). Regarding the term "misinterpretation": having accepted a *karmadhāraya* compound in "ākhyātaśabde," the interpretation of "by the two parts" as "by the two parts consisting of stem and suffix" is incorrect. "Because of the existence of two parts" means that even in a word such as *pacati*, there exists a pair of parts consisting of stem and suffix.

The point is that, just as in the case of the word *pāka* ("cooking"), in the case of *pacati* ("he cooks") as well, there would be the undesirable consequence of the action being perceived as already established (*siddha*); furthermore, since neither part [of the verb] would denote the action, the analogy would become inconsistent. Others, however, maintain that this analogy is intended merely to illustrate the cognition [of the action] by way of its being either something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) or a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

Just as in the case of *pacati* ("he cooks"), where in a verbal form (*tiṅanta*) the meaning of the root (*prakṛti*) is understood as the object to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*), while its own meaning in the form of the means (*sādhanatva*) is expressed by the suffix (*tiṅ*), so too in the case of *pāka* ("cooking"), the action is conveyed by the root as something to be accomplished, while it is conveyed by the suffix in the form of being already established (*siddhatvena*). They say that this very explanation is seen in the work of Helārāja. This refers to the state of being the object to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment (*sādhyasādhanarūpatā*).

The meaning is that, respectively, the nature of the object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*) is established by the portion [of the verb] "see" (*paśya*), and the nature of the means-of-accomplishment (*sādhana*) is established by the portion "run" (*dhāvati*), as they are conceived in the grammatical treatises. In this regard, "being the object-to-be-accomplished" is defined as that which does not give rise to an expectancy for another action, and so forth. "Being the means-of-accomplishment," however, is the state of being construed as a *kāraka* (participant in an action). This is the underlying point: in the case of "see" (*paśya*), there is the status of the action as something to be accomplished, the construal of *kārakas* within itself, or the absence of its own construal elsewhere as a *kāraka*.

The status of "runs" (*dhāvati*) as an instrument (*sādhana*), however, consists in its own connection with another [action] by way of being a *kāraka* (participant). In this same manner, even in cases such as "he cooks and [that] exists" (*pacati bhavati*), the understanding is that there is a present cooking action having a single agent, and a present action of existing having that same single agent; this should be inferred there as well. And thus, in cases such as "look, the deer runs" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*), the cognition is that the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is conducive to that seeing which is the means for achieving the desired end, and which has as its object the present action of running whose locus is non-different from a single deer.

Objection: If the action denoted by the verb is admitted to possess the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*) or an object (*karmatva*), then its insentient nature (*asattvarūpatva*)—defined as the inability to be construed elsewhere as a *kāraka*—would be lost. Response: This is not so. It should be understood that this very [inability to be construed] is what constitutes its insentient nature: "An action is not joined with gender, other actions, or *kārakas* that do not serve as its substratum; this alone is to be determined as its insentient nature."

The meaning is this: since it has been stated by Hari that "the *liṅga* (gender) and those things which do not serve as the substratum for action (*kriyā*) are not connected with action," one obtains the sense that "the state of being non-existent (*asattvarūpatva*)" consists in not being connected [with action] in a form subsumed under the status of being a *kāraka* other than agenthood (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*). Therefore, even if the action presented by a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) were to accept agenthood and objecthood, there would be no violation of its state of being non-existent. This refers to the phrase "that [is the case] in the case of *ghañ*-suffixes and so forth."

The meaning is that in examples such as *pāka*, the action is understood through the base (*prakṛti*) as being in the state of being accomplished (*sādhya*), whereas through the suffix (*pratyaya*) it is understood as being in the state of being an instrument of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Now, one might object: "In *dhāvati* (he runs) and *paśya* (see), the two actions do not correlate with gender and number, whereas in *pāka*, they do correlate; since there is thus no similarity between the two cases, how can there be the relationship of example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*)? To this, he says: "This much [is the difference]. [The phrase] "presented by the *ghañ*-suffix etc. means "the action. [The objection continues: "It is not so."

The meaning is that an action presented by a suffix such as *ghañ* is not of the same nature as an action presented by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Thus, the point is that because of this disparity, the relationship between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*) is untenable. For it is not an absolute rule that similarity in every respect is required for the relationship of example and subject of the example; otherwise, even the comparison of the moon and the face would not exist, as they lack similarity in all respects. Furthermore, if there were similarity in every respect, the very relationship of example and subject of the example would collapse.

For it is not the case that "pot" is like "pot," or "cloth" is like "cloth. Rather, similarity is required only in some respect, and that [similarity] exists even in the present context; thus he says, "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). Just as an action presented by a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) connects elsewhere as a *kāraka*, so too an action presented by a primary derivative suffix such as *-ghañ* connects elsewhere as a *kāraka*. Therefore, the relationship between the example and the illustrated case should be understood through the property of connecting as a *kāraka*.

Now, one might ask: what is the proof that action is perceived in the form of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) from the verbal root which constitutes the base in expressions such as *pāka* (cooking)? To this, he says: "Because of the evidence [provided by] 'the cooking of rice' (*odanasya pākaḥ*)," meaning because of the existence of the genitive case used for the object (*karman*).

The intention is as follows: since the suffix *ghañ* denotes the action only in its state of completion (*siddhāvasthā*) by virtue of being a *ghañ*-prakṛti root, there is a rule that the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the factors of action (*kārakas*) must occur only with an object that is perceived as something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Consequently, because "rice" (*odana*) would not be a *kāraka* [in that case], it is impossible for it to have the technical designation "object" (*karman*), which is subsumed under the category of *kāraka*. Thus, the genitive case in the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.65) would be untenable; this very untenability serves as proof that the root which is the *prakṛti* of the *ghañ* suffix expresses the action in its state of being to be accomplished (*sādhyāvasthāpanna*). To justify the use of the genitive case, he raises an objection: "Nor is it supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*)."

The meaning is that the genitive case would indeed occur because of the indirect connection (*paramparā*)—namely, "of the action in its state of being to-be-accomplished (*sādhyāvasthā*) as presented by the verbal suffix (in *adhyāhṛta*)," [then] "of the cooking (*pāka*) by means of the cooking," and [finally] "of the cooking by means of the boiled rice (*odana*). If it is argued that this is not so, because even though the action in its state of being to-be-accomplished is not perceived from the root in a word ending in a *ghañ*-suffix, it is not proper to assume that such a root denotes an action in its state of being to-be-accomplished on the basis of a genitive case that is otherwise justifiable, [the author] says: "Only with a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix."

The meaning is that the genitive case is prescribed for the agent and the object by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* only after a word that denotes the agent or object as determined by an action presented by a verbal root which serves as the base (*prakṛti*) for a *kṛt* suffix. Thus, the point is that such a genitive of the object would be impossible unless the verbal root serving as the base for the *kṛt* suffix denotes an action in its state of being yet to be accomplished (*sādhyāvastha*).

Indeed, since there is a connection between a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix and a verbal action in the state of being a *sādhya* (to be accomplished) presented by an implied finite verb (*tiṅanta*), there is also a connection with such an action mediated through the *kṛt*-suffix; thus, with this intention, he says "na lokāvyaya... [Pāṇini 2.3.69]. And regarding "niṣedhācca": the meaning is that the genitive case is prohibited when there is a connection with an action presented by a verbal root (*dhātu*) which is the base of an implied substitute for a finite verb form (*lādeśa*).

It should also be understood that even the genitive compound *odanapākaḥ*—which is prescribed by the rule "the genitive [case-ending] connected with a *kṛt*-suffix is compounded"—would not be possible here, because a genitive [ending] connected with a *kṛt*-suffix is impossible; this is due to the lack of semantic connection (*sāmarthya*), as the word ending in the genitive does not relate to the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Nor should one suspect that the sentence and the compound could exist through the genitive characterized as "residual" (*śeṣalakṣaṇa*); for in cases such as *nalapākaḥ* (Nala’s cooking) or *śuṇṭhīpākaḥ* (ginger’s cooking), this would result in the dissolution of the comprehension established by common experience, which takes the form of Nala being the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth.

Therefore, the very impossibility of a genitive of object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*) in the case of a *kṛt*-suffix serves as the proof that, in such instances, the verbal root signifies an action in its state of being to-be-accomplished (*sādhya-avasthāpanna*). Now, one might object: "If the verbal root which is the base of a *kṛt* suffix denoting the abstract state (*bhāva*) expresses an action in its state of being to-be-accomplished, then since instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is possible just as much as objecthood (*karmatva*) relative to that [action], the expression ‘pākaḥ kāṣṭhaiḥ’ (‘cooking with wood’) would also be possible. Anticipating this objection, he replies—stating that this is indeed acceptable—with the passage beginning with “in this manner” and ending with “is indeed desired.”

The Mīmāṃsakas, maintaining that the bhāvanā in the form of an activity is denoted by the verbal suffix (tiṅ-pratyaya) precisely because it has attained the state of being something to be accomplished (sādhya), consider the usage "cooking with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pākaḥ*) to be undesirable. "In this way" means: just as in the expression "cooking" (*pāka*), the activity in its state of being something to be accomplished is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) for the sake of establishing the status of the rice-gruel (*odana*) as the object (*karman*), so too the factor of the result (*phalāṃśa*) is also expressed by the verbal root only as something in the state of being something to be accomplished.

The state of being the object of accomplishment (*sādhyāvasthā*) itself is called the state of non-existence (*asattvāvasthā*) by the grammarians. "For this very reason" means: precisely because even the result (*phala*), having attained the state of non-existence, is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*). "Just like 'he cooks little' (*stokaṃ pacati')" [is the example].

The meaning is as follows: even though the result (*phala*) is of the nature of softening (*viklitti*), because it possesses a designation [as a primary object] and is the substratum of the result, it is an *object* (*karman*). Consequently, just as the accusative case occurs after words such as *stoka* when they are in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [result], so too in the expression *stokaṃ pākaḥ*, since the result of the verbal root's meaning is presented as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the word *stokam* takes the accusative case due to its coreferential connection with that result. Thus, it is justified.

The point is this: if the fruit-portion (*phalāṃśa*) were presented as being established as an existent entity (*sattvāvasthāpanna*), then—given the rule that the factors of action (*kāraka*) must necessarily connect with an object perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—there would be no connection with the object presented as something to be accomplished even when there is a connection through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); consequently, the expression "stokaṃ pākaḥ" (a small cooking) would not be possible. If it is asked: "How can a single meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) appear simultaneously as both a contradictory state of being to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*) and as an already-accomplished state (*siddha*)?"—the answer is: No.

The meaning is as follows: just as a single person possesses both the status of fatherhood and sonship due to the difference in their respective relations, so too, because both [the agent and the object] can occur in the very same thing due to the difference in their related factors (*saṃbandhin*) such as the *kāraka* (participant in action) and gender, there is no contradiction between them. However, when the connection is with the operation (*vyāpāra*), the form is simply "stokaḥ pākaḥ" (a small cooking), because since the operation is not an object (*akarmatā*), the accusative case is not applicable to its qualifier. Furthermore, one should not suspect that the genitive case prescribed by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* would apply here, overriding the accusative, in the case of a connection with the result (*phala*).

The meaning is that this has been established in the *Laghumañjūṣā*, because by virtue of its association with the agent (*kartṛ-sāhacaryeṇa*), only that object which is construed as distinct from the verbal root-meaning is understood there. || 14 ||

"Etadeva" (this very thing) means that there is simply the manifestation of a single action as both the state of being to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*) and the state of being already-accomplished (*siddha*). Regarding "the action as something to-be-accomplished": the word "therein" (*tatra*) refers to [words] ending in *dhā* and other suffixes; the word "is perceived" (*pratīyate*) is to be supplied. To explain how the action is perceived as something to-be-accomplished, he says "having the form of a verbal root" (*dhāturūpā*). This means that for which the form of the verbal root is the basis or cause. That is to say, by the inherent nature of the power of words, the action denoted by the verbal root (consisting of the result and the operation) is perceived as something to-be-accomplished.

The term *kriyā* (action) is used as a common designation to indicate that both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are perceived as things to be accomplished (*sādhya*). This is because, according to the technical grammarians (*tāntrika*), the words for "action" are conventionally applied to both the result and the operation. The phrase *siddhabhāvas tu* means "but the perception [of them] as already established (*siddhatvena pratītiḥ*). The expression *ghañādi* means "that which has the suffixes such as *ghañ* as its basis or cause. The meaning is that the action (i.e., the result and the operation) expressed by the suffixes beginning with *ghañ* is perceived as something already established.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), suffixes such as *ktvā*, *tumun*, and *ktin* are to be understood. Anticipating the objection that there is no evidence for the understanding of the activity and the result as being accomplished (*siddhatva*) through [suffixes] such as *ghañ*, he refutes it with the passage beginning with "nor... and ending with "...because it is a means of valid cognition" (*mānatvāt*). [The phrase] "when 'cooking' (*pāka*) is said" is used.

The meaning is as follows: upon hearing words such as "pāka" (cooking), even though there is a non-difference relation (*abhedānvaya*) between the meaning of the verbal root and the action denoted by the suffix *ghañ*, there still exists an expectancy for another action to be accomplished by that cooking—such as "it must be done," "it must be destroyed," "it remains," "it arises," or "it is perceived"—and this very expectancy serves as the proof [for the existence of the action]. Regarding the phrase "in that which is presented by the verbal root": this refers to instances such as "he cooks" (*pacati*). This is because the impossibility of that [non-difference relation] has already been stated.

The meaning is that when it is said "he cooks" (*pacati*), since no further expectation for another action arises once the action has been understood, it has already been stated that such an expectation for another action is impossible. The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "because it possesses a nature that does not give rise to an expectation for another action," which is the definition of being a "thing-to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*). The point is that because an object presented under a nature that does not give rise to an expectation for another action cannot be construed with another action, an expectation for another action is impossible. [This is the reason for] the phrase "there being no such consequence."

The point is that if the suffix *ghañ* were to denote only an action (*kriyā*) that has reached the state of being accomplished (*sādhyāvasthāpanna*), then because such an action would not possess gender, words like *stoka* (small), which express qualifiers of such a verbal meaning (*dhātvartha*), would also lack masculine gender; consequently, the rule "the neuter is used for the general" (*sāmānye napuṃsakam*) would be the only applicable outcome.

However, when the action is understood as being established in its accomplished state (*siddhāvasthāpanna*), such an action is connected with gender, number, and so forth; consequently, since words such as *stoka* (a little) are in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with that [action], they too are connected with gender and number. Thus, in the expression *stokaḥ pākaḥ* ("a slight cooking"), both singularity and masculinity are logically justified. He clarifies this very point with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Regarding "connection with the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthānvaya*): when there is connection with the fruit of the verbal root's meaning, the accusative case and neuter gender apply to words such as *stoka*.

In the case of connection with *bhāvanā*—which consists of the operation (*vyāpāra*) that is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—even though the nominative case (*prathamā*) would be impossible (as in "one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma with devotion"), there is at least the neuter gender. However, when there is connection with the operation that is the meaning of the suffix *ghañ*, since the operation lacks the status of being an object (*karmatva*), the accusative case does not apply; consequently, by the rule *prātipadikārtha-* [Pāṇini 2.3.46], the nominative case applies and the masculine gender is used. Furthermore, because the fruit (*phala*) which is the meaning of *ghañ* is only a part of the word-meaning (*padārthaikadeśa*), words such as *stoka-* do not connect with it.

The intention [of the author] is as follows: even though the fruit of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) constitutes only a portion of the word-meaning (*padārtha*), the connection with other word-meanings still occurs therein; otherwise, forms such as *taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice"), *stokaṃ pacati* ("he cooks a little"), and *stokaṃ pākaḥ* ("a little cooking") would be unaccountable. "The denotative power (*śakti*) belongs to the *ghañ*-suffixes, etc. means that their meaning is the operation (*vyāpāra*) which is connected with gender, number, and so forth. "By this" means by accepting that *ghañ*-suffixes and the like denote an operation existing in a completed state (*siddhāvasthāpanna*). "Merely for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutāmātra*)"—this is the sense.

By the word "only" (*mātra*), the meaning is that [the suffix] excludes the function of denoting an object and signifies merely the grammatical correctness of the usage. "Is cast aside" (*apāstam*) means it is refuted. Now, the author of the *Kātantra-Parīṣiṣṭa* holds the view that the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the suffix *ghañ* is not admitted to reside in the operation in its accomplished state, but rather in the word ending in *ghañ*; thus, since the connection occurs with the meaning presented by the power of the *ghañ*-ending form, the expression "a small cooking" (*stokaḥ pākaḥ*) is indeed justified. Anticipating this view, he rejects it with the words "nor [is it] the *ghañ*-ending," etc. [He says] "by the sequence of the *ghañ*-ending," etc.

The meaning is as follows: if one were to accept that the composite form ending in *ghañ* has a power (*śakti*) with respect to an object whose operation has reached the state of accomplishment (*siddhāvasthāpanna*), then there would be the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) because both serial orders (*ānupūrvī*)—namely, "cook-ness" (*pākatva*) and "sacrifice-ness" (*yāgatva*)—would have to be accepted as the delimiters of the power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). Therefore, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*) and in accordance with the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) "in the sense of the action itself" (*bhāve*), it is more appropriate to accept that the power resides in the suffix *ghañ* itself with respect to such an object, and thus to maintain that the property of being *ghañ* (*ghañatva*) alone is the delimiter of the power.

Surely, even you must admit the existence of a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*). Otherwise, due to the absence of meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) would not apply; for it is a settled doctrine that the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is understood to carry over from the rule *kṛt-taddhita-*. Furthermore, since the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya-artha*) is construed only with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti-artha*), in the absence of a collective power, the construal of the number and other properties expressed by the case-endings (*vibhakti-artha*) would also be impossible. Thus, although a collective power is necessary, the power of the suffix *ghañ* itself is also indispensable by virtue of the grammatical injunction (*anuśāsana*).

Otherwise, even the suffix *ṇvul* and others would not be established as having denotative power (*śakti*). If it is argued that since the understanding of meanings such as "agent" in words like *paktṛ* ("cook") is possible through the power of the word-form as a whole (*samudāya-śakti*) alone, it is accepted that *ṇvul* and others lack independent power—this is not so, because it contradicts grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*) such as "the *kṛt*-suffixes denote the agent."

In the analysis (*vigraha*) "janamejayati," if one were to derive the form from the root *ej* with the causative suffix *ṇic* followed by the suffix *khaś*, then although *khaś* would be treated as a *sārvadhātuka* due to its being marked with *ś*, the suffix *śap* would not be applied because it does not denote the agent. Consequently, the form *janamejaya* would be unestablished, and furthermore, since *khaś* is marked with *ṅ*, there would be the undesirable consequence of prohibiting *guṇa*. Therefore, the capacity for the suffix *ghañ* must indeed be accepted. For this very reason, the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "the state [of an action] expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix," becomes consistent; thus, there is no contradiction. With this intention, he says: "iti dag" (thus, *dag*). 15.

Now, one might object: "If there were a rule that the relation (*anvaya*) among factors of action (*kāraka*) consists solely in their activity (*vyāpāra*), then only on that basis—by virtue of the requirement for the genitive of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*) in expressions such as *odanasya pākaḥ* (the cooking of rice)—would it be established that the verbal root denotes activity; otherwise, it would not. But what is the proof for such a rule? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says "nanu" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "ending in a vocative": it means "of that which ends in a vocative," i.e., of the meaning of that which ends in the vocative case-ending.

The meaning is that just as the linguistic usage of a word’s being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) and so forth is mediated by its referent (*artha*), so too is the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of a word ending in a vocative case suffix mediated by its referent—or rather, [the connection] belongs to that very word ending in the vocative. Regarding the phrase "in the action" (*kriyāyām*): the meaning is that the connection occurs with the activity expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*), which is the object of the instigation (*pravartanā*). As for the example "Speak, Devadatta": the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) here is that in the vocative case-meaning, Devadatta—the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)—is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) relative to the vocative itself, while he is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) relative to the act of speaking expressed by the word "speak" (*brūhi*).

"Whatever is a vocative word is an adverbial modifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the action; for if that were so, there would be a *nighāta* accent in 'vrajāni devadatta' (I am going, Devadatta)," according to the *Vākyapadīya*. He states the reason for treating the vocative as an adverbial modifier of the action with the words "because of the requirement of the *nighāta* accent. Regarding the definition of a sentence as "a verb together with its modifiers," the phrase "together with its modifiers" means accompanied by whatever modifiers it has, whether directly or indirectly.

By the inclusion of the phrase "through that succession," the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) of the statement "there is a fish in the deep river" is established. Thus, since the vocative word "Devadatta" can only be justified as part of a single sentence through its connection with the verbal action "speak" (*brūhi*), the rule "of a vocative" (*āmantritasya ca*)—which prescribes the *nighāta* (the unaccented tone)—is established; it would not be so otherwise. Now, one might ask: why is the *nighāta* not established even in the absence of syntactic unity? To this, he says: "in a single sentence" (*samānavākye*).

The meaning is: "provided that the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittika*) reside in the same sentence. In the case of the address "Devadatta," since the address itself relates to the action, Devadatta is connected to the action through a mediated relationship consisting in being the object of an address related to him; thus, the cause and the effect reside in the same sentence—this is the intended sense. And so, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) of the sentence "O Devadatta, you speak" is: "the act of speaking, whose agent is non-different from you, has as its object an address related to Devadatta."

Similarly, in the case of "vrajāni devadatta" ("O Devadatta, let me go"), the cognition is that the act of going, performed by me, has as its object the address directed toward Devadatta. However, some maintain that since that which ends in the vocative case is the subject of what is being restated (anuvādya), and since what is restated requires something to be enjoined (vidheya), and since that which is enjoined is of the nature of an action, this meaning—that the vocative is necessarily connected to the enjoined action—is established by the very nature of the linguistic system. As it was said by Bhartṛhari: "They know that the vocative is merely the bringing about of presence in one who is already established."

For that which has attained presence (*abhimukhya*) is indeed employed in actions. The meaning of this is as follows: "of the established" (*siddhasya*) refers to that which is established by way of the form that delimits its status as the object of address (*saṃbodhyatāvacchedaka-rūpa*), such as "Devadatta-ness" and so forth. Prior to the act of addressing, the existence of the form that delimits its status as the object of address is necessarily required; by this, the seed for [its] being the objective (*uddeśyatva*) is demonstrated. The point is that in common worldly usage, that which is established is well-known as the objective. "The state of being present" (*abhimukhībhāva*) is what constitutes addressing (*saṃbodhana*).

Making [the person] face [the speaker] (*abhimukhīkaraṇa*) consists in producing a state of attentiveness toward the grasping of an unknown object understood through a word employed by oneself, and the operation conducive to the attainment of that attentiveness takes the form of employing a word ending in the vocative case. By the phrase "merely facing [the speaker]," the result is indicated; when the person to be addressed is inferred to possess such a result through the turning of their face and so forth, then the action is enjoined. Thus he says: "when [the person] has attained the state of facing [the speaker]."

He by whom the state of being attentive has been attained—that very person is the "object" (*artha*), whose self is full of meaning, who is to be addressed, and who is the substratum of an activity conducive to awakening, to be employed in actions that are to be well-informed through his own established function. Thus, he is "employed," meaning he is set in motion. And so, by the phrase "is employed," it is clearly indicated that the meaning of the term ending in the vocative case is construed only with an activity that is the object of the instigation; this is their intended meaning.

Thus, it is established that the meaning of the vocative case is an operation conducive to an operation that is conducive to the cognition of an unknown object to be understood by means of a word uttered by oneself. In the example "O Rāma, protect me," the application of this definition is as follows: the word "self" (*sva*) refers to a certain devotee of Rāma who is the speaker of the utterance "O Rāma, protect me."

The word employed by him—such as "O Rāma, protect me"—has as its object a meaning that is yet unknown, namely the sense of "protect me. The operation residing in Rāma, which consists of being oriented toward [the petitioner] and the attainment of attentiveness, is conducive to the cognition of that meaning. The operation residing in the devotee, consisting of the utterance of the words "O Rāma, protect me," is conducive to that [operation of Rāma].
