There is a mutual relationship between the operation—which is the object of the instigation directed toward the referent of the vocative case—and [the instigation itself], in the form of the relation between the subject (uddeśya) and the predicate (vidheya).

The understanding is: "Protection having me as its object, which is the content of an instigation directed toward Rāma who is becoming favorable. Others, however, maintain that in such a cognition of an unknown object, the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed by way of the relation of inherence (*samavetatva*); and it is precisely in such a cognition of the object that the action is construed by way of the relation of objectivity (*viṣayatā*). Thus, they describe the verbal cognition as: "Protection having me as its object, which is the content of a request, and which has as its object the cognition of an unknown object inherent in Rāma."

"Protection" (*rakṣaṇa*) means "safeguarding" (*trāṇa*); that is, performing assistance toward the attainment of what is desired, meaning an activity conducive to the accomplishment of my desired end preceded by the avoidance of the undesired. Since it is stated that [the agent] is "set in motion" (*pravartyate*) toward actions, it is understood that the referent of the vocative case is construed only with the action that is the object of the instigation (*pravartanā*), and that this alone is the cause for the *nighāta* (elision of the accent).

And likewise, in the case of "vrajāni devadatta" ("Go, Devadatta"), since going (*vrajan*) is not the object of the instigation (*pravartanā*), how can it be stated here that the accomplishment of the prohibition is the result? If it is argued that—since there is the *loṭ* suffix by the rule "in cases of command (*praiṣa*), permission (*atisarga*), and [indicating] the time has arrived (*prāptakāla*") when one intends to express the arrival of the time suitable for going—the meaning understood from "vrajāni" is "the time for going performed by me has arrived"—this is not so.

In this context, because the word "jānīhi" (know/understand) is supplied [as the verb], there is no impairment to the status of a single sentence, since the act of understanding—which is intended as the object of the instigation—is construed with "going" as its direct object and "Devadatta" as its intended recipient (*uddeśya*). Thus, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) arising from this is as follows: "The object of the instigation is a cognition whose intended recipient is Devadatta who is facing [the speaker], whose agent is 'I', and which has as its object the going that is appropriate for the occasion."

It should not be argued that, because the rule "na ca jānīhi" (and you do not know) involves the ellipsis [of an object], the sentence composed of two finite verbs lacks the status of a single-sentence unit (*ekavākyatva*) as defined by Pāṇini's paribhāṣā; and that, in the absence of such *ekavākyatva*—which is necessary for the application of the *nighāta* accent—the *nighāta* would fail to be established. For the meaning of the entire collection, "vrajāni devadatta jānīhi" (Go, Devadatta, and know), is present within the portion "vrajāni devadatta," according to the maxim of the "part of a sentence" (*vākyaikadeśanyāya*).

And thus, since the understanding of such a meaning arises from that which is actually heard, the intention is that the *nighāta* (tonal suppression) is not established because the sentence consists of only one *tiṅ*-ending word being heard. Indeed, "Enter, [eat] the cake" (*praviśa piṇḍīm*) is an illustration of the maxim of the "part of a sentence" (*vākyaikadeśanyāya*). In that case, the word "enter" (*praviśa*), which is a part of the sentence, is used in the sense of the sentence "Enter the house" (*praviśa gṛham*); likewise, the word "cake" (*piṇḍīm*), which is a part of the sentence, is used in the sense of the sentence "Eat the cake" (*piṇḍīṃ bhakṣaya*).

And thus, from the single word "enter" (*praviśa*) as it is heard, the understanding of the sentence-meaning "enter the house" (*praviśa gṛham*) arises. This alone is the meaning of the word supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). However, the direct use of the words "house" (*gṛham*) or "eat" (*bhakṣaya*) is not necessary there. In this way, there is no contradiction with the Vārttika cited in the Bhāṣya which states that "a sentence consists of a single finite verb" (*ekatiṅ vākyam*). In the case of "Devadatta cooks, [he] exists" (*pacati bhavati devadattaḥ*), the remainder (*śeṣa*) is "know [this]" (*jānīhi*).

[Objection: Since the technical rule (paribhāṣā) "nanvekatiṅ" applies only to a sentence as such, then in the case of *pacati bhavati devadattaḥ*, because it consists of two finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) and thus lacks the status of a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*), the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*) would not apply to the word *devadatta*. To this, he says: "according to the method stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya. This means: according to the method stated in the Bhāṣya on the *bhūvādi* sūtra—"Verbs such as *pacati* become the agents of the action expressed by the verb *bhavati*"—and according to the method stated in the Bhāṣya on the *samartha* sūtra—"A sentence is a verb (*ākhyāta*) together with its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*)."

"Because of the existence of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*). The meaning is this: in the sentence "Know that," since Devadatta is the objective (*uddeśya*) of the act of knowing—which is the object of the instigation (*pravartanā*)—and the state of being the agent of the act of cooking is the object (*karman*) [of the act of knowing], there exists syntactic unity even in a collection composed of multiple finite verbal forms (*tiṅanta*). The definition "a sentence consists of a single finite verb" (*ekatiṅ vākyam*) is useful only for specific grammatical operations within our own system, such as *nighāta* (the suppression of accent). However, the principle "a verb with its qualifiers [is a sentence]" (*ākhyātaṃ saviśeṣaṇam*) is common to both grammar and the world; this is the intended sense.

In cases such as "He cooks and becomes" (*tena pacati bhavati*) or "Look, the deer runs" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*), where many finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) are combined, there is no deficiency even in the absence of the requirement that there be only one finite verb; for the status of a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*), which is established by universal experience in those instances, is justified by the statement in the Bhāṣya on the *Samartha* Sūtra: "A verbal form (*ākhyāta*) [may be] accompanied by its qualifiers. This is indeed so.

The meaning is that by the rule *āṣṭamikena 'āmantritasya ca'* (Pāṇini 8.1.19), the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) prescribed for a vocative standing within the same sentence after a word [ending in a case-suffix] would indeed apply to "Devadatta. For the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) arising from this is as follows: a knowledge which has as its object an instigation (*pravartanā*), whose content is the act of cooking, and whose objective (*karman*) is the coming-into-being of Devadatta who is being addressed.

Having thus demonstrated the commentator's (Bhāṣyakāra) agreement regarding the status of a collection composed of multiple finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) as a single sentence (*ekavākya*), he says "tiṅṅatiṅaḥ," etc., in order to demonstrate the agreement of the author of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra). The meaning of that [sūtra] is that a finite verb following another non-finite verb (*atiṅanta*) is suppressed (i.e., loses its accent).

In this regard, the inclusion of the term *atiṅ* (not being a finite verb) was made to prevent the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) of the word *bhavati*, which follows the other finite verb (*pacati*) in the collection of two finite verbs in the expression "pacati bhavati. The fact that this [restriction] is rendered unnecessary in the case described by the *Nirukta*—where there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*)—indicates that even a collection of finite verbs constitutes syntactic unity according to the intention of the author of the *Sūtra*. Consequently, in the view of both the author of the *Sūtra* and the author of the *Bhāṣya*, there would be *nighāta* in the sentence "pacati bhavati devadattaḥ."

However, according to the view of the *Vārttika*, [a sentence] would not be so; thus he says, "according to the rule *ekatiṅ vākyam*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is one *tiṅ* (verbal suffix), i.e., a *tiṅanta* (verb). Thus, the meaning is that a collection composed of exactly one *tiṅanta* is a sentence. Now, if a collection composed of exactly one *tiṅanta* constitutes a single sentence (*ekavākya*), then in the case of "tiṣṭhati devadattaḥ, pacati caitraḥ" (Devadatta stands, Caitra cooks), since "devadattaḥ" and "pacati" would form a single sentence, the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* would result in the loss of accent (*nighāta*) for the latter. To this, we say: no.

The qualification "having as its meaning an action qualified by a qualifier" must be included. This means [the compound] must consist of a single finite verb (*tiṅanta*) that has as its meaning an action qualified by a qualifier. The point is that because "devadattasya" connects with "tiṣṭhati" and "pacati" connects with "caitreṇa," the two words "devadattaḥ" and "pacati"—which reside in separate sentences—lack the quality of having as their meaning an action qualified by a qualifier; consequently, it would be impossible for them to incur the loss of accent (*nighāta*) due to being part of a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*). Thus, [the author says], "but not in the other view."

The sense is that, according to the view of the author of the Vārttika alone, there would be no *nighāta* (anudātta accentuation); thus, there is a difference of opinion (*matabheda*). Intending to show that when a consensus of views is possible, a difference of opinion is not logical, he says: "In reality, however" (*vastutastu*). "Having a single finite verb as its qualificand" (*ekatiṅaviśeṣyakam*) means: where there is one finite verb (*tiṅ*), i.e., a word ending in a *tiṅ*-suffix, which serves as the qualificand—that is, the primary conveyer of the meaning of the qualificand. Thus, the meaning is that a collection (*samudāya*) composed of a single finite verb which expresses the meaning of the primary qualificand is a sentence (*vākya*). "Of that intention" (*tadabhiprāyasya*).

The meaning is: "according to the intention of the *vārttika* 'ekatiṅ'. [As stated] by us in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*: "Even when there are many finite verbs (*tiṅanta*), if they are expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*), there is a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*). Thus, the prohibition of the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*) after finite verbs becomes meaningful. The meaning is that even when there are many finite verbs, provided they are expectant—that is, capable of syntactic connection—there exists a single sentence therein. For example: *pacati bhavān akṣīyat*, *hataśāyikāḥ śayyante*, *paśya mṛgo dhāvati*, and so forth.

The meaning is that because there is indeed sentence-unity (*ekavākyatā*) among many finite verbs (*tiṅanta*), there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) for a finite verb following another finite verb. This is because Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa stated in the aforementioned passage of the *Vākyapadīya* that [the rule] is meaningful in this sense. According to his view as well, it certainly occurs; that is to say, in the case of the collection "pacati bhavati devadatta jānīhi," since it consists of a single finite verb (*tiṅanta*) expressing the primary predicate (*mukhyaviśeṣya*), even according to the view of the Vārttika, the *nighāta* of "devadatta" certainly occurs.
The sense is that there is no difference of opinion among the authors of the Sūtra, Vārttika, and Bhāṣya regarding this matter.

Regarding the term *kṛtvorthāḥ*: here, the word *kṛtvaḥ* stands for anything similar to *kṛtvas*; the compound is formed like *uṣṭramukha* (camel-faced), meaning "those whose referents (*artha*) are similar to *kṛtvas*. The intended meaning is "the suffixes beginning with *kṛtvasuc*. Regarding the phrase "counting the repetition of an action" (*kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇane*): in the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇane kṛtvasuc*, *abhyāvṛtti* means birth or, in other words, production (*utpatti*). The sense is that due to the influence of the prefix (*upa*), the root *vṛt* (meaning "to turn") takes on the meaning of production (*utpatti*).

The meaning of "the counting of the repetition of actions" (*kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇanam*) is the enumeration—that is, the calculation—of the birth or arising of actions. Furthermore, only actions that have a single agent and belong to the same class are required; for one does not experience the cognition of repetition in the case of actions performed by different agents or belonging to different classes. Thus, the sense of the rule is that the suffix *kṛtvasuc* occurs in its own sense when words expressing number are used to denote the counting of the repetition of actions.

In the example "he eats five times," the occurrences produced by the repetition of a single act of eating—whose internal distinctions have ceased—are counted as five. The meaning is that, desiring a multiplicity of results in the form of contact with the lower part of the throat-cavity caused by repetition, one performs five repetitions of the production of the act of eating; just as one who desires the result in the form of softening (digestion) performs activities such as blowing [on the food] conducive to that end, so it is here.

The meaning is that the act of eating (*bhujikriyā*) is an operation conducive to the conjunction [of the tongue] with the lower part of the palate. And thus, because of the natural force of the statement "the counting of the repetition of an action" (*kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇana*), the word *pañca* has as its primary referent the production of the number five; the suffix, however, indicates that [repetition]. Furthermore, since it is appropriate for the production of the number five to be construed only with the action mentioned in its own immediate context, the intention is that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of suffixes such as *kṛtvasuc* is obtained only when there is a connection with an action.

Thus, the understanding is that the act of eating is characterized by the number five, occurs in the present time, and has a single agent. In the same way, this should be inferred for cases such as *sakṛt pacati* ("he cooks once") and *dvis pacati* ("he cooks twice"). It should be understood that suffixes such as *kṛtvasuc* are grammatically correct only when connected with an action; therefore, expressions like *dvirghaṭaḥ* ("two jars") do not occur, as in the case of *dvau ghaṭau* ("two jars"), because there is an absence of the counting of an action.

"Kārakāṇi" (the factors of action) means the sixfold set of *kārakas*, beginning with the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). To show that the word "kāraka" refers to action (*kriyā*), he states its etymological meaning: "it performs the designations of agent, object, and so forth. The meaning is that the technical terms such as "agent," "object," and so on, are indeed defined solely in relation to an action, as in: "this is the agent of this action," "this is the object," or "this is the instrument. Thus, these designations apply only to those things that are connected with an action.

The intended meaning is as follows: since the word "kriyāyām" (in an action) is carried over into the subsequent sūtra, "dhruvam apāye," and because that [action] requires a generator (*janaka*), when the phrase "that which is fixed (*dhruvam*) upon departure (*apāye*)" is connected with it as the generator, the sense "the generator of an action" is achieved. Consequently, because a generator requires an object to be generated (*janya*), it is logical that the generator's relation occurs only with that which is generated. Thus, the technical designations such as *apādāna* (ablative) apply only to those things related to the action.

Others, however, observe that based on the etymological derivation *karoti kriyāṃ nirvartayati* ("it performs, it brings about the action"), the status of being a *kāraka* consists in being the producer of an action. And this [status] belongs to all six [factors], beginning with the agent (*kartṛ*). In that case, once it is known that something is a producer of an action, an expectancy arises as to "what is that action?", and since the action itself likewise possesses an expectancy for a producer, it follows by the rule that "whatever is expected by something, it connects with that very thing" that connection [of the *kāraka*] is properly established only there [with the action]. However, the definition that "the status of being a *kāraka* is the state of being connected with an action" is not [correct].

Otherwise, the principle that "the factors of action (kārakas) are connected with the productive operation (bhāvanā)" would result in an inconsistency, since it would imply—by way of logical necessity—that those already connected with the action are [again] connected with the action. In this context: the agent (kartṛ) is the substratum of the operation expressed by the verbal root in question; the object (karman) is that which is intended as the goal by virtue of being the substratum of the fruit of the action expressed by the verbal root in question, which is itself prompted by the primary operation; the instrument (karaṇa) is that which, prompted by the operation residing in the agent, produces the fruit without being separated by any other operation residing in itself; and that which is intended as the goal for the action so that it may connect with all the objects of the action...

They say: "The recipient [of a gift] is that; the ablative (apādāna) is the locus of the separation not expressed by the verbal root of the action in question, which inheres in its respective agent; and the locative (adhikaraṇa) is the substratum of the operation and the result mediated through the agent and the object."

The suffix *vati* is the first [of those introduced by this rule]. It is added after a word ending in the third case when there is an equality of action (*kriyā*). The word "equality" (*tulyam*) is an adjective qualifying "action. It is neuter because it refers to the general category [of action]. The meaning of the rule is: the suffix *vati* shall occur after a word ending in the third case in the sense of "equal to that," provided that which is equal is an action. An example is *brāhmaṇavad adhīte* ("he studies like a Brāhmaṇa"). Here, the word *brāhmaṇa* refers to the study performed by a Brāhmaṇa; the resulting cognition is: "the study performed by a Kṣatriya is equal to the study performed by a Brāhmaṇa."

In that context, it was stated that there is a "first *vat*" because the meaning of the suffix *vat*—namely, "like that"—cannot be construed with a verb. In the example "Maitra is as handsome as Devadatta," the verb "is" (*bhavati*) must be supplied; otherwise, the phrase "if [the similarity] is with respect to an action" (*kriyā cet*) in the Sūtra would be entirely redundant. Thus, since the action alone is the substratum for the similarity expressed by the meaning of *vat*, the grammatical correctness of the first *vat* is obtained only when there is a connection with an action. This refers to the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the connection with verbal roots (*dhātu-sambandha*).

Regarding the rule *dhātusaṃbandhe pratyayāḥ* ("suffixes [occur] when there is a connection with a verbal root"): since a word that is a verbal root cannot possibly have a connection with another word that is a verbal root, the term "verbal root" (*dhātu*) here indicates the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, because a connection resides in two things, the meaning is that there is a connection between two meanings of verbal roots. Thus, by virtue of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "when there is a connection with a verbal root," the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of suffixes prescribed under that heading is obtained only when they are joined with an action (*kriyāyoga*).

In the expression *yathāyāhi yāti* ("as he goes, so he goes"), the root *yā-* takes the imperative (*loṭ*) in the sense of frequent repetition (*kriyāsamabhihāra*). According to the rule "in the case of frequent repetition, there is reduplication" (*kriyāsamabhihāre dve*), the word *yāti* is doubled; however, this doubling is not applicable here [in the sense of the present tense]. In this context, because the meaning of the imperative form *yāhi yāhi* is construed with the action presented by the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) *yāti* through the relation of general and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*), the resulting cognition is: "that which is going repeatedly or intensely, being non-different [from the action], having a single agent, and occurring in the present time."

Regarding the statement "seeing thus, he went" (*evaṃ paśyan yayau*), the meaning is that the act of going has the same agent as the act of seeing performed in the past. In the *Bṛhad-bhūṣaṇa*, however, the example "he cooks in order to eat" (*bhoktuṃ pacati*) is cited. Although the suffix *tumun*—which is prescribed by the rule *tumun-ṇvul-au*—is not specifically ordained for cases involving a connection between verbal roots (*dhātu-sambandha*), nevertheless, since it is ordained only when there is a subordinate word (*upapada*) denoting an action, its status as being conditioned by a connection between actions remains intact; thus, one should understand that there is no inconsistency in the example.

[Objection: Since we observe that in cases such as "bring a non-brāhmaṇa" (*nanv-abrāhmaṇam ānaya*), the negative particle (*nañ*) connects even with something other than a verb, [the author] says "the non-compounded *nañ*. The ellipsis to be supplied is "it connects only with a verb. [Objection: But then, in a case like "this is a jar, not a cloth" (*ghaṭo 'yaṃ na paṭaḥ*), because the non-compounded *nañ* does not connect with a verb, the stated rule would result in an inconsistency; with this intention, he states the intended meaning of the phrase "non-compounded *nañ*" by saying "that which is unfit for composition. He clarifies precisely what it means to be unfit for composition by saying "prasajya-. The compound *prasajya-pratiṣedha* is formed according to the rule *sup-supā*.

*Prasajyāpādya* means a negation that follows after having applied [the action]. This is because it is stated in the *Mañjūṣā*: "It effects a cessation only after having first applied the action and its qualities. Therefore, in the sense of "one who deserves that," the suffix *cha* (forming *tadarhati*) is applied, meaning "fit for connection with an action. This is because it is stated: "But *prasajyapratiṣedha* is that where the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with an action. The point is that that which is connected with an action presented by a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is in every respect unfit for composition (*samāsa*), since composition with a verbal suffix is prohibited.

Otherwise, even in cases such as *abrāhmaṇa*, where the negative particle (*nañ*) is construed with the meaning of the subsequent member of the compound, there would arise the contingency of a deviation from the rule that [the negative] must necessarily be construed with the action, because in some instances—due to the optionality of compounding—it remains uncompounded. Bearing this intention in mind, he says: "because it is impossible to accept [the term *nañ*] according to its literal form. And thus, in order to avoid this deviation, the intended meaning of the phrase "the uncompounded *nañ*" must be understood as "that which is construed with the action presented by a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). This is the underlying point.

Now, in the case of "there is no jar on the ground," it is indeed the absence of the jar itself that is perceived as the very act of existence (*asti-kriyā*) performed by the jar's absence, and not the absence of the act of existence performed by the jar. Nor should it be argued that the negative particle (*nañ*) expresses merely the absence of the existence of the jar, which has the ground as its locus and the jar as its agent.

With the intention that—since on a ground where there is an absence of connection with a jar delimited by the present time, the existence (sattā) residing in that ground at the present time is unestablished, it is impossible to convey the absence of such existence, and because this would contradict experience—one who raises the objection says: "And not 'uncompounded'... up to "...lack of proof. He provides the solution: "...but 'you do not cook'... and so forth. This is because there is a cognition of the negation of the action itself.

The meaning is that there arises the cognition: "the absence of the act of cooking, which is present in time and resides in an agent whose referent is non-different from the referent of 'you' (yuṣmad) etc., as expressed by the suffix *laṭ*. And thus, the point is that such a cognition itself is the proof for the connection of the uncompound *nañ* (negation) with the action. Precisely because the absence, which is the meaning of *nañ*, is connected to the action by way of being its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), there exists grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—consisting in the fact that 'you' and so forth denote the same case-role (*kāraka*) denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Consequently, the first and second persons, as well as the singular and dual numbers, are logically justified.

The point is this: if the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) were construed as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) with the referent of "you" (*yuṣmad*) and so forth, then just as in the case of "your absence exists" or "my absence exists," in expressions such as "you do not cook," there would be no co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—defined here as the negative particle expressing the same grammatical participant (*kāraka*) expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Consequently, the second and first persons would be untenable, dual and plural numbers would be impossible, and the first person would result. He states the reasoning for why this is not the case when one perceives the negation of an action in "the pot is not born" with the words "for this very reason."

The meaning is that there is simply the cognition of the absence of the act of being born (*jananakriyā*). "Even when the jar exists" means even during the state of the jar's existence. The point is that since it is impossible to convey the absence of a jar while the jar is present, one must necessarily admit that in such a case, what is being conveyed is the negation of the action. "Such an usage" means an expression such as "the jar is not being born."

The point is that at the time when a jar exists, there is the absence of an operation conducive to its own production within the jar itself. The intention [of the opponent] is that if the negation (*nañ*) were to connect with the meaning of a noun as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absence that is not part of a compound, then such usage would never occur; for in the case of the "absence of a jar," there is simply a lack of an operation conducive to production residing in the jar. "And thus" means: since, according to the aforementioned method, it is necessary that in expressions such as "you do not cook," the negative particle conveys an absence whose counter-positive is the action. "Only the absence of existence" [is what is meant].

The meaning is that there is simply an absence of the existence of the three factors [agent, object, and action] involved in the pot. By the particle *eva*, the absence of the pot itself is excluded. Now, one might object: "Even if we accept the cognition of an absence whose counter-positive is an action—on the grounds of the inconsistency in previously mentioned cases such as 'the pot is not being produced'—in instances like 'the pot does not exist,' let us simply accept the cognition of the absence of the pot, as there is no subverting evidence [to the contrary]. Thus, the rule that the negative particle (*nañ*) must invariably connect with an action would be violated in that very case. Anticipating this objection, the author demonstrates the subverting evidence against accepting the cognition of the absence of the pot: "For [in the case of] 'the pot...'"

By the phrase "it is not born" (*na jāyate*) and so forth: in one case, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an operation conducive to production; in the other, it is an operation conducive to existence. Between these two, the only distinction is the difference in the meaning of the verbal root; there is no distinction whatsoever beyond this. Even if there is a distinction, it is of no consequence for the conceptualization of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of the absence (*abhāva*) which is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). Thus, in both cases, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is of a single form: namely, an absence whose counter-positive is the action (*kriyā*).

This is because of the statement of the learned masters established by reasoning: "When a single uniform nature is possible, a difference in form is indeed a flaw. This being the case, if one were to postulate a difference in the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of the absence denoted by the negative particle (*nañ*) without any cause, then the uniformity of cognition would be destroyed and a discrepancy (*vairūpya*) would arise; it is precisely this discrepancy that constitutes the objection to accepting the cognition of the absence of a jar in the case of "the jar does not exist. This is the intended meaning.

[Objection: But surely, in the sentence "There is no jar on the ground," which lacks the utterance of a verb, it is the absence of a jar residing on the ground that must be understood; and thus, the rule regarding the necessity of the connection with a verb is violated in that very case. To this, he replies: "And so, 'on the ground, not [is]'—the word 'is' (asti) is to be supplied. This is because of the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "The root *as* (to be), when followed by the present tense (*bhavantī*), is not used even though it exists. The term *bhavantī* is a designation for the present tense (*laṭ*); the meaning is that the verbal root *as* should be employed when followed by the present tense. This is the intended sense.

He states the seed for the [necessary] ellipsis as "by way of the relation of being a qualifier" (*prakāratā-sambandhena*). The meaning is that such a causal relationship has already been established: the presentation of the bhāvanā (efficient force) generated by the verbal root is the cause with respect to the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) delimited by its own nature, by way of the relation of being a qualifier as determined by the qualificandum-ness residing in the absence which is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*).

In this context, it should be understood that the effect (*kārya*) is the generation of a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in which the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) resides in the absence denoted by the negative particle (*nañ*), and this absence is qualified by some specific mode (*prakāratā*). Furthermore, the effect is the generation of a verbal cognition in which the qualificand-ness resides in the absence denoted by the negative particle, and this absence is qualified by such a mode. The cause (*kāraṇa*) is the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*)—in the form of an operation (*vyāpāra*) produced by the verbal root—which is delimited by a relation consisting of the mode-ness residing in that [absence] as its qualificand. The phrase "because it is established" (*klṛptatvāt*) means "because it is necessary" (*āvaśyakatvāt*).

The point is that otherwise, the rule that the absence, which is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), must necessarily connect with the verb would not be tenable. Regarding the phrase "the rest": it means that since the state of being superimposed (*āropitatva*) expressed by the negative particle is manifold, there is an absence of the dual and plural numbers due to the restriction to the singular number, and so forth. || 16 ||

Likewise, regarding the rule *yasya ca bhāvena*: the intention is that by the phrase *yasya ca bhāvena*, a sūtra consisting of these three words is indicated, and by the phrase *ṣaṣṭhī ca*, a sūtra consisting of these two words is indicated. With this in mind, he says: "In the case of *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*," and "and [the genitive] in *ṣaṣṭhī cānādare*. Here, both instances of the word *bhāva* refer to the action expressed by the verbal root (*dhātuvācyakriyā*). The meaning is that the locative case is used for that [agent] whose action characterizes another action.

The word *tataḥ* means "from that which expresses the locus of the action of indicating. Since this [quality] exists in both the words *goṣu* and *duhyamānāsu*, the locative case is applied to both. The meaning of the locative is "the state of being an indicator" (*jñāpakatva*); and because it is stated that this relates to the "characterization of an action" (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*), its connection is only with an action. Thus, the grammatical correctness of the locative absolute (*satisaptamī*) is obtained only when there is a connection with an action, as in: *goṣu duhyamānāsu gataḥ* ("He went while the cows were being milked").

Although both the status of being an indicator (*jñāpakatva*) and the status of being indicated (*jñāpyatva*) of the cows being milked are understood from the words in relation to the action of going, nevertheless, the action of milking residing in the cows is directly the indicator, while the cows are such by virtue of being its substratum. This is because an action whose time is already known serves as an indicator of another action whose time is not yet known, by making known that the latter occurs at the same time as its own locus. Thus, in the verbal cognition "one who possesses the act of going is indicated by cows characterized by the present act of milking," the resulting meaning is: "He went at the time of the milking of the cows."

The same applies to the subsequent sūtra as well; thus, in examples such as *rudati rudato vā* ("while [he] is weeping"), it should be understood that a disregard directed toward the son or others is expressed as the predominant factor. Its "nature" (*svarūpa*) refers to its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). The phrase "it will be explained" implies that this will occur during the occasion of the commentary on the verse *asādhuranumānena*. Regarding the expression "by the action alone" (*kriyayaivaiva*), the particle *eva* serves to exclude non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). Non-connection is the absence of relation; its exclusion is its cessation. Thus, the meaning is that for the aforementioned eightfold group, grammatical correctness exists only through connection with an action, and not otherwise.

One might object: since the word *kriyā* (action) is well-established as denoting merely the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and since the eightfold grammatical correctness [of the suffixes] is established through their connection with the result (*phala*), the rule that they must necessarily connect with *bhāvanā* (productive activity) is not proven; thus, one cannot conclude—on the basis of that rule—that *bhāvanā* is the meaning expressed by the verbal root in cases such as *pāka* (cooking). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The point is this. In sūtras such as *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ* ("*bhū*, *vā*, etc., are verbal roots"), the word *kriyā* is used predominantly to refer to *bhāvanā* in the form of an operation (*vyāpāra*); therefore, the word *kriyā* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) to denote *bhāvanā*.

The meaning is that the word *kriyā* (action), by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), conveys *bhāvanā* (productive activity). With the intention that the evidence for the conventional status of the word *kriyā* in the sense of *bhāvanā* is simply the observation of its frequent employment in that sense, he stated, "mostly by the word *kriyā*. An objection might be raised: "But the word *kriyā* is also seen to be used in the sense of the result (*phala*); how then can it be said that the conventional power of the word *kriyā* belongs exclusively to *bhāvanā*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the aspect of the result, [its use] is occasional."

In the word *kriyā*, the suffix *śa* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) by the rule *kṛñaḥ śa ca*. Thus, through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that which is made (*kriyate*)"—meaning produced by the activity in the form of *bhāvanā*—this word *kriyā* is etymologically (*yaugika*) applicable to the result (*phala*). Furthermore, that [word] is employed in the sense of the result only occasionally. By the term "occasional" (*kvācitka*), the absence of frequent usage is indicated. By this, it is stated that there is no conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) for the word *kriyā* with respect to the factor of the result. It is called "etymological" (*yaugika*) because it has arisen from the connection between the meanings of the root and the suffix (*prakṛti-pratyaya-artha-sambandha*).

*Rūḍhi* is that which conveys meaning solely through the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*), without being assisted by the powers of its constituent parts (*avayava-śakti*); *yoga-śakti* is that which conveys meaning through the power of the constituent parts, independent of the power of the whole.

Because the etymological meaning (*yogārtha*) depends upon the consideration of the meanings of the individual word-components (*avayavārtha*), its presentation is delayed and thus it is "external" (*bahiraṅga*); whereas the conventional meaning (*rūḍhyartha*), not depending on the consideration of the meanings of the components, is presented quickly and is thus "internal" (*antaraṅga*). Consequently, based on the principle that "conventional meaning is stronger than etymological meaning" due to this relationship between the internal and the external, it is necessary to understand by the term *kriyā* (action) only the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) in the form of an operation. Therefore, it is established that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the eight [imperatives] occurs only when they are construed with an action in the form of productive activity (*bhāvanā*).

The meaning is that it is not [determined] by connection with the result (*phalānvaya*). Regarding the phrase "of the technical term" (*saṃjñāśabdasya*): the meaning is "of that which is conventional" (*rūḍhasya*). Regarding the phrase "without regard" (*anapekṣya*): the meaning is "without taking into account the meanings of the constituent parts consisting of the base and the suffix. He cites a section of the *Mīmāṃsā* as an authority for the fact that a technical term is stronger because its application proceeds without regard for the meanings of the base and the suffix; this is expressed by the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). [This is stated] because of the predominance of the technical term (*saṃjñāśabda-prābalyāt*).

The meaning is that a word whose operation is independent is stronger than a word whose operation is dependent. "It was determined in the ninth [book]" means that in the fifth section (adhikaraṇa) of the second quarter (pāda) of the ninth chapter, it was determined that the *rathaṃtara* should be sung upon the two verses (*ṛc*) recited in the *uttarā-grantha*.

For that [rule], namely "He sings it on the *yoni*; he sings it on the two *uttarās*," has been undertaken for the purpose of determining the adoption of the word *uttarā* that conveys a meaning independent of other words, from between two instances of the word *uttarā* that convey meanings respectively dependent and independent upon other words. There are two treatises, *Chandas* and *Uttarā*, which exist for the purpose of reciting the *ṛc*s of the *Sāmaveda*.

In that work named *Chandas*, the *ṛc*s that serve as the source (*yoni*) for various *sāmans* are recited. In the *Uttara-grantha*, however, the *sūktas* consisting of triplets (*tṛca*) are recited. In a single triplet, the *ṛc* belonging to the *Chandas* is the first—the source *ṛc*—while the other two are the subsequent ones (*uttare*). This being the case, regarding the statement "he sings on the two subsequent ones" (*tad-uttarayoḥ gāyati*), when it says "he sings on the two subsequent *ṛc*s of the *rathantara*-source," two kinds of "subsequent ones" are possible.

In the *Chāndogya-grantha*, the verse "abhi tvā śūra" is recited as the source (*yoni*) of the *Rathantara* Sāman; following that, verses such as "tvām iddhi havāmahe" are recited as the sources for the *Bṛhat* and other Sāmans. However, at the end of the *Uttarārcika*, in the hymn "abhi tvā śūra," the verse "na tvāvām anye" is recited after that [first] verse, though it does not serve as the source for any Sāman.

In this regard, according to the *Chandoga* texts, the two verses that follow the *rathantara*’s own source (*svayoni*) are the two verses of the *bṛhat* and other *sāmans*. According to the *Uttaragrantha*, the second and third verses within the triplet (*tṛca*) are the ones following the *rathantara*’s own source.

In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether, by the word "uttara" (subsequent) in the phrase "taduttarayoh," one should take the two verses beginning with "tvāmiddhi havāmahe" as the source-verses (*yoni*) for other *sāmans* such as the *Bṛhat*—which follow the subsequent [verses] to the *Rathantara-yoni* according to the *Chandoga* texts—or whether, according to the *Uttaragrantha*, one should take the second and third verses of the triplet beginning with "na tvā vāṃ anye," which are the source-verses for some *sāman* following the *Rathantara-yoni*. Such being the doubt, there are two types...

In this context, the word *uttara* has two meanings: one denotes "subsequent" in a temporal or sequential sense (*vyavasthā*), and the other denotes a "specific part of a text" (*granthaviśeṣa*). That which denotes "subsequent" is necessarily expectancy-laden (*nityasākāṅkṣa*) with respect to its limit (*avadhi*). This is because when it is said "of the two subsequent [verses]," an expectancy for a limit invariably arises in the form "from what? Therefore, this word conveys its own meaning only by depending on another word that expresses the limit; if it were independent of another word, it would be entirely meaningless.

This has been stated in the Śābara-bhāṣya in this very section: "For all words that denote relations do not express any meaning at all without depending on another word; therefore, another word is required. Otherwise, a sentence whose meaning is incomplete would be non-expressive of any meaning whatsoever. Words denoting relations are always dependent upon another related term."

Since the word *uttarā* is employed in Vedic usage as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for a specific type of literary work, when it is grasped in that sense, it is independent of other words; thus, by mere hearing, it conveys its own complete meaning. This has also been stated in that very same work: "In the case of the apprehension of a name and the named object, one does not require another word; for when things are grasped through direct audition (*śruti*) with their meanings complete, the proximity of another word need not be expected."

Thus, because the word *uttarā* in the case of the *bṛhat* and other *yoni*-verses depends upon a preceding Ṛk, its application is etymological (*yaugikī*), and therefore their presentation is delayed. In the *Uttaragrantha*, however, it functions as a conventional name (*saṃjñā*), which is synonymous with a technical term (*rūḍhi*); thus, the book [itself] is presented immediately. Consequently, since the word *uttarā* brings about the immediate presentation of only those verses recited in the *Uttaragrantha*, it is established that the *rathaṃtara* should be sung there alone, and not in the *bṛhat* and other *yoni*-verses.

And thus, just as in that case a relative term is weaker because its application depends upon the cognition of its respective correlate and therefore has a delayed presentation, whereas a technical name (saṃjñā-śabda) is stronger because its application is independent and thus has an immediate presentation; so too here, the sense is that the technical name is stronger than the etymological (yaugika) term, since the former functions independently of the cognition of the etymological meaning, while the latter functions dependently upon it.

One might object: "Since even the *phala* (result) is treated by the term 'action' (*kriyā*) in the sūtra *karmavat karmaṇā*, and since existence (*sattā*) and the like are perceived as being in the state of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in verbs such as *asti*, *bhavati*, and *vidyati*, there is no obstacle to including the result under the term 'action' as well. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Furthermore, even the portion that is the result... The meaning is that it is a qualifier of the operation (*vyāpāra*). The intention is that it has been stated: "In the case of the result, the operation is primary. [The phrase] "in some cases, they are of such a nature" refers to this.

The meaning is that these are qualifiers of the operation (*vyāpāra*). The intention is that in examples such as *caitras taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("Caitra cooks the rice"), it is observed that in the case of verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) denoting the agent, the factors of action (*kāraka*) serve as qualifiers of the operation. In the case of primary derivative suffixes (*kṛdanta*) such as *paktrā* ("the cooker"), it has been stated "in some cases" because the factors of action function as the qualificands (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the operation. This is expressed by the words "and of qualities" (*guṇānāṃ ca*).

"And because qualities are for the sake of another, there would be no connection due to their equality"—this is the meaning: since qualities (*guṇas*), which are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇas*), exist for the sake of another—that is, because they serve to assist the qualified (*viśeṣya*)—and because of their equality, that is, because they possess the common property of assisting the qualified, there would be no mutual connection or syntactic relation (*anvaya*) among them by way of the relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*).

And thus, just as the result (phala) is construed only with the operation (vyāpāra)—which is the qualificand (viśeṣya)—because it assists that qualificand, so too the factors of action (kārakas) are construed only with the operation, whether directly or indirectly, because they assist the qualificand; they are never construed with the result, since there is no difference in their status as qualifiers and because [the result] lacks expectancy (nirākāṅkṣatva). The point is that, since the nature of being a *kāraka* consists in being a generator of an action, these factors possess expectancy only toward the portion of the action that is to be produced. He himself provides an example consistent with this principle: "All the servants... [etc.].

The meaning is this: just as servants who have not entered into a relationship of mutual subordinate and principal status primarily serve the king alone, so too the *kārakas*, being independent of one another, accept only the operation (*vyāpāra*) as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and not the subordinate portion consisting of the fruit (*phalāṃśa*); therefore, there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with that [fruit].

Furthermore, since factors of action (*kāraka*) are eternally dependent, when there is a requirement for a qualificand (*viśeṣya*), even though the portion consisting of the fruit of the verbal root-meaning is capable of such a connection, one must nevertheless accept its connection only with the *bhāvanā*—which consists of activity (*vyāpāra*) and is capable of fulfilling the requirement for a qualificand for that [fruit] which is itself dependent. To demonstrate this worldly principle, he says: "For not [even] a beggar... and so forth.

For just as it is observed in worldly convention that a beggar does not beg from another beggar when there is a donor other than the beggar, so too the causal factors (*kārakas*), being themselves subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), do not accept the subordinate portion of the fruit (*phalāṃśa*) as their primary object (*viśeṣya*). This means that they do not do so while the primary productive activity (*vyāpāra-pradhāna-bhāvanā*), which is not subordinate and is fit to be accepted as the primary object, exists. Thus they "think" [it].

The meaning is that, according to this principle, even the Mīmāṃsakas consider that the factors of action (*kāraka*) are connected not with the result, but exclusively with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). "And thus" means: and when there is such a rule—that the causal factors are connected only with the productive activity in the form of an operation. He demonstrates the resulting nature of the causal relationship by saying "as the qualificandum," etc. "Causal factors, etc."—by the word "etc.," time and result are included.

The meaning is as follows: when a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is to be produced in which the agent (*kāraka*) and so forth function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), the cause is the presentation of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) generated by the verbal root (*dhātu*), occurring through the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by the qualifierhood (*viśeṣaṇatā*) residing in the agent and so forth. In the sentence "Caitra cooks rice" (*caitras taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), the application of this definition is as follows: Caitra is connected to the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix *laṭ*, by way of the relation of identity (*abheda*).

The agent denoted by the *laṭ* suffix is construed with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) through the relation of residence (*niṣṭhatva*), and the time denoted by the *laṭ* suffix is also construed with that very operation through the relation of temporal connection (*kālika-sambandha*). Likewise, the object consisting of rice is construed with the result consisting of softening (*viklitti*) through the relation of residence, and the result is construed with the operation through the relation of being conducive (*anukūlatā*). With respect to Caitra, the agent denoted by the *laṭ* suffix is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), while with respect to the operation, it is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Likewise, with respect to the rice (*taṇḍula*), the result (*phala*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and with respect to the operation (*vyāpāra*), it is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Thus, the meaning is that there arises a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in which the operation is the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣyaka*), namely: "an operation residing in an agent non-different from Caitra, which is conducive to the softening (*viklitti*) residing in the rice, and which belongs to the present time. In this view, the agent-factor (*kartṛkāraka*) is directly connected to the operation; however, the object-factor (*karmakāraka*) is connected to the result, and since the result is directly connected to the operation, the object is connected to the operation through a mediated sequence (*paramparayā*).

Just as the locus-factor (*adhikaraṇakāraka*) is connected to the action through the medium of the agent or the object, so too it should be understood that the object is also connected to the action itself through the medium of the result (*phala*), and not directly to the result.

Now, one might object: "In cases where the operation (*vyāpāra*) is perceived as primary—such as in finite verb forms like *pacati*—let the factors indeed accept the operation as their qualificand (*viśeṣya*) according to the aforementioned principle; however, where the operation is subordinate, how could the factors accept the operation as their qualificand? To this, he says: "Even in cases such as *paktr-*," and so forth.

In instances such as *paktr-* (the cooker), where suffixes like *tṛc* express the agent (*kartṛ*), the agent is predominant according to the maxim that "between the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix [the latter is predominant]. Consequently, the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) consisting of an operation, which serves as a qualifier for that agent, is also predominant there. Following the aforementioned relationship of cause and effect, the connection of the *kārakas* occurs only with the productive activity that has become the qualifier. For example, in the expression *odanasya paktṛ-* (the cooker of rice), the connection of the object (*karman*)—which is the rice—occurs only with the operation itself, and not with the result.

The meaning is that by the word "in that very [context]" (*tasyām eva*), the connection with the result is excluded. Furthermore, if the connection of the *kārakas* were with the result of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the section concerning the *Vājapeya* sacrifice (*vājapeyādhikaraṇa*) would be inconsistent. For that is the sixth section in the fourth quarter of the first chapter; [it holds that] the result is the meaning of the verbal root, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), and the connection of the verbal root's meaning is with the efficient force by way of being its instrument (*karaṇatva*).

This being the case, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: In the injunction "One desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the *vājapeya*," the word *vājapeya* prescribes a material substance (*guṇa*). Based on its etymology—as that which is "drinkable" (*peya*) "of *vāja*" (i.e., food)—the word *vājapeya* refers to gruel (*yavāgū*). Thus, just as in the injunction "One should sacrifice with *soma*" a material substance in the form of *soma* is prescribed, here a material substance in the form of gruel is prescribed.

It should not be argued that a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) must be accepted in the word *vājapeya* for the sake of obtaining the sense "one should effect self-sovereignty by means of a sacrifice possessing the quality of *vājapeya*. This is because, when the sacrifice is connected simultaneously (*tantra*) with both the *vājapeya* quality and the fruit of self-sovereignty, the sense obtained is simply "one should strive for self-sovereignty by means of the *vājapeya* substance. [Objection: If the sacrifice is connected with the quality, then the sacrifice would become the objective factor (*karmakāraka*), such that the meaning would be "one should perform the sacrifice by means of the *vājapeya* quality."

Likewise, in the case of "one should bring about sovereignty through sacrifice" (*yāgena svārājyaṃ bhāvayet*), the sacrifice possesses the status of an instrumental factor (*karaṇa-kāraka*) in its connection with the fruit. If it is asked how there can be a connection with both [the fruit and the bhāvanā], the answer is no; for since the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is common to both, it is possible for it to possess both forms. In the word *yajeta*, the sacrifice is expressed by the verbal root *yaj*, and the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is expressed by the suffix. From their co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*), however, only a general relationship is understood; and that is common to both the status of being an object (*karman*) and the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*).

In that context, no specific case-ending expressive of either objecthood (*karmatva*) or instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is heard. Therefore, when the common root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is simultaneously connected with both [the substance and the result], the particular relationship appropriate to each respective instance is established there. Thus, by accepting this simultaneous connection (*tantra*), since the meaning "one should perform the sacrifice by means of the *vājapeya* substance" is obtained, there is no need for the figurative indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) even if it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that if one were to admit both connections simultaneously through a single syntactic unit (*tantra*) in the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), there would arise the contingency of two sets of three contradictory properties (*viruddha-trika-dvaya*). To explain: one set consists of the three properties of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*), being the subject of restatement (*anuvādyatva*), and being the primary element (*mukhyatva*); the other set consists of the three properties of being the thing to be taken up (*upādeyatva*), being the thing to be enjoined (*vidheyatva*), and being the subordinate element (*guṇatva*). These two sets of three are mutually contradictory in their respective order. In the word *yajeta*, the result of self-sovereignty (*svārājya-phala*) is the goal (*sādhya*) of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) expressed by the verbal suffix; the sacrifice (*yāga*) is the means (*sādhana*).

In this context, the first triad—consisting of "being the object of reference" (*uddeśyatva*) and so forth—is centered on the fruit of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), which is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). The second triad—consisting of "being that which is to be undertaken" (*upādeyatva*) and so forth—is centered on the sacrifice, which is the means (*sādhana*). The sacrifice is undertaken with a view toward the fruit; the sacrifice is enjoined by restating the fruit. The fruit is the primary and principal element, while the sacrifice is the subordinate and secondary element. "Being the object of reference" for the fruit means being the objective of a mental intention. "Being that which is to be undertaken" for the sacrifice means being the state of being performed. Both of these are properties conditioned by the adjuncts of mind and body, respectively.

The properties of being the subject (*anuvādya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), however, are adventitious attributes (*upādhi*) of words. To state what is already known is *anuvāda* (restatement); to state what is unknown as something to be performed is *vidhi* (injunction). Since the fruit and the sacrifice possess the respective natures of the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*), they stand in the relationship of primary and subordinate. This being so, when one reflects upon their inherent nature—the fruit and its means, namely sovereignty (*svārājya*) and the sacrifice—the fruit possesses the triad of properties beginning with "being the object of reference" (*uddeśyatva*), while the sacrifice possesses the triad beginning with "being that which is to be undertaken" (*upādeyatva*).

Likewise, upon examining the relationship of means and end between the sacrifice (*yāga*) and the *vājapeya* [sacrifice], it results that the triad of properties beginning with "object-to-be-intended" (*uddeśyatva*) pertains to the sacrifice, while the triad beginning with "to-be-adopted" (*upādeyatva*) pertains to the *vājapeya*. Consequently, in the present case, if one accepts the simultaneous and collective connection of the sacrifice—both as a means and as an end—with the *bhāvanā* denoted by the suffix, then the three properties beginning with "to-be-adopted," which are rooted in its being a means, must be admitted for the sacrifice.

Furthermore, because it is at that very time and in that very sacrifice that [the sacrifice] is the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the three properties beginning with being the objective (*uddeśyatva*) would follow. However, due to their contradiction with the properties beginning with being the thing to be enjoined (*upādeyatva*), those three properties beginning with being the objective cannot be admitted there at that very time. Therefore, it is impossible to state that the sacrifice has a simultaneous, unified connection with the productive energy (*bhāvanā*) by way of two modes—both as the means (*sādhana*) and as the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

In this section, once the sacrifice—which is the fruit of the verbal root’s meaning—has been construed with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) as its instrument (*karaṇa*), it is stated that the fault of the "occurrence of two sets of three contradictory factors" (*viruddhatrikadvayāpatti*) arises if another case-factor (*kāraka*) is subsequently construed with that very same sacrifice. The underlying sense is that if another case-factor were to be construed with the fruit of the verbal root’s meaning while it serves as a qualifier, then the presentation of the fault consisting in the occurrence of two sets of three would be irrelevant.

Therefore, with the intention that one must necessarily accept that the connection of *kārakas* (factors of action) does not occur with the fruit of the verbal root-meaning—which has become a qualifier—but rather with the operation (*vyāpāra*) itself, which is the qualificand, [the author] states: "This has been elaborated upon in the *Bhūṣaṇa*. And thus, it is established that for the sake of establishing the connection of *kārakas* such as "of the rice" (*odanasya*) in expressions like "cooking" (*pākaḥ*), it is necessary that the *bhāvanā* (productive activity) in the form of an operation be denotable by the verbal root even when the suffix *ghañ* is present.

Establishing the rule that the functions of the *kārakas* are necessarily connected through another perspective, he states "some, however" (*kecit tu*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the comprehension of the connection and the cessation of expectancy" (*anvayabodhākāṅkṣānivṛttyoḥ*): the meaning is "of the comprehension of the connection and of the cessation of expectancy. Regarding the word "because it is not observed" (*adarśanāt*).

Although the syntactic cognitions "the locus non-different from the ground" (*bhūtalābhinnam adhikaraṇam*) qualified by singularity for the sentence *ghaṭo bhūtale* ("The pot is on the ground"), and "the object non-different from the pot" (*ghaṭābhinnaṃ karma*) for the sentence *devadatto ghaṭam* ("Devadatta [sees] the pot") are possible, nevertheless, according to the maxim that "every sentence is completed by a verb," in both sentences there must sequentially be a verb such as *asti* ("is") or *paśyati* ("sees") without which all the word-meanings constituting the sentence [would remain incomplete].

The meaning is that because there is no mutual understanding of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*), even the cessation of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is not observed. Regarding the phrase "without that" (*tadvyatirekeṇa*): the meaning is that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the two aforementioned sentences cannot be obtained without supplying a verb such as "existence" (*sattā*) or "perception" (*darśana*). By the words "they say" (*āhuḥ*), a lack of satisfaction (*asvarasa*) with their statement is indicated; and this [lack of satisfaction] pertains to the aspect of its being ungrammatical (*asādhutva*).

If, however, grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) were not admitted for a sentence that requires an action, then statements from the *Bhāṣya* such as "when 'the cow' is uttered, the agent and the action are not specified" would result in being incorrect. The intention is that the mutual connection of all word-meanings within a sentence and the satisfaction of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) must be accomplished by the implicit supply (*adhyāhāra*) of a suitable action. The sense is that one must consider how, by this much alone, the rule that case-factors (*kārakas*) are invariably connected with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is established. || 17 ||

"By itself," and so forth. Having stated the argument for the correctness [of the suffix] only when it is connected with a verb (*kriyā*), he now states that same argument in the form of a *pratibandī* (reductio ad absurdum) regarding its lack of connection with a verb: "If, even in the case of the *pakṣa*, there is the meaning of the suffix *-vat*. The meaning is as follows: if the Naiyāyikas maintain that the meaning of the suffix *-vat*—namely, similarity (*sādṛśya*)—is connected [as a qualifier] even in the case of the *pakṣa* (such as a mountain, which possesses the probandum in a state of doubt), and that a *kāraka* such as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is connected [as a qualifier] in the case of *nañ* and other particles within the absence denoted by *nañ*, and that it is connected to the referent of another noun; then [the same logic would apply here].

The meaning is that, in that case, the Naiyāyikas would maintain that [the word] "anveti" (is connected) applies both to the flowers and to the referent of the other noun [the mountain]. The concise point is that, in order to establish the fourth case (*caturthī*) as a *kāraka* in the expression "puṣpebhyaḥ," the assumption you have made regarding the employment of the verb *spṛh* must be abandoned. As for the example "parvato vahnimān" (the mountain possesses fire): by the rule stating "that which is similar to that" (*tena tulyam*), there is no fixed rule that the suffix *vati*, prescribed when similarity is expressed through action, must necessarily connect only with an action.

In the example "like a kitchen" (*mahānasavat*), by the rule *nirukta-sūtra*, the meaning of the suffix *-vat*—namely, similarity—is construed with the mountain itself, not with the action. This is because, through the explanation "just as the kitchen possesses fire, so too does the mountain," one understands the meaning "the mountain is similar to the kitchen"; thus, it is observed that the similarity expressed by the suffix *-vat* is construed with the mountain alone.

Likewise, the restriction that the meaning of the locative case and others prescribed by rules such as *saptamy adhikaraṇe ca*—namely, the kāraka of locus and so forth—is construed only with the action, is also not observed.

The meaning is as follows: in the case of "there is no jar on the ground" (*bhūtale na ghaṭaḥ*), the cognition of the meaning is either "the jar is that which lacks existence on the ground," or "the absence of the jar exists on the ground. Consequently, since the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) prescribed under the heading of *kārakas* is understood to connect only with the absence that is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), whereas in the case of "the jar is on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭaḥ*), the cognition of the meaning is "the jar is that which has the property of being located in the ground," or "the jar exists on the ground," the locus *kāraka* results in its connection with the referent of the nominal stem (*nāmārtha*) itself.

If you disregard the grammatical rules governing the similarity of meaning expressed by the seventh case (locative) and the locative kāraka, and instead accept the connection between the meanings of nouns [as primary] while asserting the correctness of those two [usages], that is utterly improper; thus he says: "Let it be abandoned. Regarding the dative case, [the rule is] "spṛhī" (Pāṇini 1.4.36).

When only the dative ending form *puṣpebhyaḥ* is employed, it is understood that the word *spṛhayati* must be supplied for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) according to the rule *spṛher īpsitaḥ*, which prescribes the dative case; however, neither a word formed from another root with the same meaning nor a mere semantic supplement (*arthādhyāhāra*) should be supplied by the Naiyāyikas. This is because the contradiction with the grammatical injunction (*anuśāsana*) is equal in both cases. Regarding the term *ardhajaratīyam*: *ardhajaratī* means "half-old woman" (the half of an old woman), and *ardhajaratīyam* means "resembling that."

They explain that the suffix *cha* is applied after a compound in the sense of "in that manner" (*it-tham*), provided the compound refers to that [quality]. However, it must be considered here how this can apply to the sense of the object, as in the case of the *ekadeśi-samāsa* (partitive compound) *ardha-jaratī*.

Even if one explains that after forming an *ekadeśisamāsa*, the suffix *cha* is applied in the sense of "belonging to this" (*idamarthe*) because the word belongs to the *gahādi* class, there would still be a problem: since an *ekadeśisamāsa* is dominated by the meaning of the first member, the resulting sense would be "this belongs to half of the old woman," which is not desired. Rather, what is intended is the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word "half" and the word "this," in the sense of "this is half of the old woman. Therefore, a simultaneous application of the two operations (*yugapadvṛtti*) must be performed, as in the case of *śivabhāgavata*.

In this context, if the *karmadhāraya* compound were formed first between the words *śiva* and *bhagavat*, and then the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix applied, the result would be *śaivabhagavataḥ*. Alternatively, if one first establishes *bhāgavata* through the secondary derivative and subsequently intends a compound with *śiva*, there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between *śiva* and the referent of the word *bhagavat*, because the referent of *bhagavat* would be a mere part [of the whole] due to being included within the derivative, according to the maxim that "the meaning of a word connects with the meaning of a word."

Therefore, when two simultaneous functions (*vṛtti*) are applied there to the words *śiva* and *bhagavat*, as well as to the sense of "offspring of Bhagavat," the resulting sentence that makes known the meaning of those functions is: "the offspring of the Lord Śiva. Similarly, when two simultaneous functions are applied with the intention of expressing a relationship between the half of the old woman (*jaratī*) and this [other] half, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words "half of the old woman" and "this half" is established in the sentence that makes known the meaning of those functions: "this is half of the old woman."

The term *jaratīyam* means "this belongs to an old woman" (*jaratyā idam*). When the *karmadhāraya* compound "half and that [which belongs to an old woman]" (*ardhaṃ ca tajjaratīyaṃ ca*) is formed, it is intended as "that which is related to an old woman"; thus, the meaning understood is "that half. In this way, even according to the etymological method, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the words *ardha* (half) and *idaṃ* (this) can be established. Consequently, just as it is improper to say "he desires this half of an old woman, but not this [other half]," so too the notion that Pāṇini’s rule is followed in some instances and abandoned in others is utterly improper, being similar to the "half-old-woman" maxim (*ardhajaratīya*). This is the intended sense. || 18 ||

"Thus" (*evam*) means: just as there is a connection with an action for the aforementioned *aṣṭaka* suffixes, so too [is there a connection] here. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in this context, the inclusion of *ktvā*, *tumun*, and so forth is intended. Regarding the mention of "those whose meaning is being" (*bhāvārtha*): by the word "etcetera" here, the inclusion of *ktvā*, *tumun*, and so forth is intended. "By the action alone" (*kriyayaiva*): the meaning is "by the action alone, even though it is subordinate. The particle "alone" (*eva*) serves to exclude the substance (*dravya*) which possesses gender, number, and so forth, as that which is connected [to the action]. "Connection" (*anvaya*) means relation. Thus he says: "Those such as 'gone' (*gata*) and so forth are without grammatical analysis" (*avigrahā*)."

"Without being distinguished" (*vivicya*) means without attaining the status of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*); that is to say, without being a qualified object (*viśeṣyatayā*). "Of which there is no apprehension" (*na grahaṇaṃ yasyāḥ*) is the meaning. He states the result of this as "become subordinate" (*guṇībhūta*), meaning having attained the status of a qualifier for something else. In the example "he went to the village" (*grāmaṃ gataḥ*), the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *gam* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule *gaty-arthākarmaka-*. Between the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), the meaning of the suffix *kta*—the agent—is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is the meaning of the base: the activity conducive to conjunction with the location in front (the village).

The meaning is: "the locus of an activity conducive to conjunction. In that context, because the village—which is the object (*karman*)—is the locus of the conjunction produced by the activity that serves as a qualifier of the agent (which is the meaning of the *kta* suffix), its connection occurs precisely with the activity that functions as its qualifier. This is because it is an established principle that, in generating a cognition where [an object] has a case-role (*kāraka*) as its mode (*prakāra*), the presence of the productive force (*bhāvanā*) derived from the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the cause, related through the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "Caitra is the locus of an activity conducive to a conjunction residing in the village. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) [refers to this].

The meaning is as follows: just as in the expression "he has gone to the village" (*grāmaṃ gataḥ*), the action of going—which serves as a qualifier with respect to the agent who is the meaning of the *kta* suffix—is connected with the object in the form of the village; likewise, in the expression "one who has previously made" (*kṛtapūrvī*), the action expressed by the root *kṛ*, which serves as a qualifier with respect to the agent who is the meaning of the suffix *in*, is connected with the object in the form of a mat (*kaṭa*). Regarding the term *kṛtapūrvī*: the popular etymological analysis (*laukikavigraha*) is "by whom a mat was previously made. In that context, the word "previously" (*pūrvam*) qualifies the action.

The compound *kṛtapūrva* is formed by the rule *sup-supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4). When the word *anena* is understood as a governing term (*anuvṛtti*), the suffix *ini* is applied to the word *kṛtapūrva* by the rule *pūrvādiniḥ sapūrvācca* (Pāṇini 5.2.86) to denote the agent. In that context, because the mat (*kaṭa*) is the object with respect to the action of making (*karoti*), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used, resulting in *kaṭam*. Now, an objection might be raised: in the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) "the mat was made previously by him" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ pūrvamaneneti*), a compound between the word *kṛta* and the word *pūrva* is not possible. This is because the word *kṛta* lacks semantic independence (*sāmarthya*) due to its dependence on the word *kaṭa*. And since the compound does not exist, the suffix *ini* would likewise be impossible.

Furthermore, one might object: "Since the mat (*kaṭa*) as the object (*karman*) is already expressed by the suffix *-kta* in the word *kṛta*, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would not apply to it. If this is argued, we say no. In the non-grammatical (alaukika) analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) *kṛtam pūrvam*, because the mat is not present there, it cannot be construed as the object; consequently, at that time, the root *kṛ* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), and thus the suffix *-kta* cannot occur in the sense of an object (*karmani*). Instead, the suffix *-kta* occurs in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) according to the rule *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ*. Since the word *kṛta* then has no requirement for the mat (*kaṭa*), the compound and the suffix *-ini* are both valid.

[The two words] are not in apposition (*nirbādha*), because the object (*karman*) has not been expressed [by the suffix]. Consequently, in the case of *kṛtapūrvī*, which ends in the suffix *in*, the meaning resolves to "one who was previously an agent of the action," i.e., "one who did [it] before. Then, when there is a desire to express the status of being an object—arising from the inquiry regarding the object, "What did he do?"—the word *kaṭa* takes the second case ending because it is the object with respect to the action of "making. Furthermore, the status of being an object residing in the mat (*kaṭa*) is not expressed by the suffix *kta*, since that suffix is prescribed in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). Nor is it expressed by the suffix *in*, since that is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

One might object: "In the case of *kaṭam*, shouldn't the genitive prescribed by *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* take precedence over the accusative, since there is a connection with a *kṛt*-suffix? Nor should it be argued that the genitive would not occur simply because of the prohibition regarding connection with a *niṣṭhā* (past participle) suffix; for the prohibition of the genitive in connection with a *niṣṭhā* does not apply here, due to the Vārttika statement: "The genitive is to be added [by way of] an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) when used in connection with a *kta* suffix in the neuter sense of an abstract action. If this is the objection, we reply: no.

In that context, by the force of the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes], it is accepted that the genitive case is the motivator for a connection with a *kṛt* suffix only when that connection has not entered into another grammatical formation (*vṛtti*). In the present case, however, because the word *kṛta* is included within a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) formation, its connection does not motivate the genitive. Thus, in the absence of the genitive, since the object is not already expressed [by another suffix] according to the aforementioned reasoning, the accusative case is easily obtained.

And thus, just as in the case of "he made a mat" (*kaṭaṃ kṛtavān*), there is a connection with the verb "to make" (*karoti*) precisely as it functions as a qualifier of the object "mat," according to the causal relationship defined by the rule beginning with "for the sake of a cognition whose mode is a *kāraka*. The understanding derived from the expression *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat") is: "the agent of an action occurring prior to [the present time] that is conducive to the production residing in the mat"; that is, "one who possesses an activity conducive to that production which has a locus non-different from a single mat. This is what is meant by the phrase "by means of [suffixes] such as *ini*."

The construction is as follows: [the action] is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) with respect to the agent and so forth who perform the act of going (*iny-arthakartr-ādi*). That is to say, the action of "doing" (*karoti-kriyā*), being subordinate with respect to the agent of the act of going, is connected with the object "mat" (*kaṭa-karmaṇā*).
