Alternatively, it should be explained that the action of "doing," being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇabhūtā*) with respect to the meaning of the *kta* suffix which is the base expressing itself, is connected with the agent of the act of going.

The meaning is as follows: "one's own action" (*svakriyā*), the verbal root *kṛ* which denotes it, the suffix *kta* derived from that root, the abstract state (*bhāva*) which is its referent, and that state—which is endowed with gender, number, and so forth—wherein the action of "doing" (*karoti-kriyā*) is subordinate to it; such is the consistency of the definition. In other words, the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) belongs to that which is qualified by the action of "doing," which itself is the qualifier defined by the abstract state (*bhāva*) that is the referent of the suffix *kta*. By this, the sense is that the introduction stating, "the suffixes *ini* and others, prescribed [after roots] in the sense of the agent and so forth, are construed only with the action," becomes consistent with the text.

One might object: "In expressions such as *gata* (gone), since there is a *kṛt*-derivative formation (*kṛdvṛtti*), and since one must accept that in such a formation there is a collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) consisting of 'integration of meaning' (*ekārthībhāva*), it is difficult to explain the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of objects such as the village with the act of going, which is but a single part of the meaning of the word *gata*; for in that case, the act of going is merely a part of the word-meaning. To this, he replies with the words beginning with "And not... (*na ca*). Regarding the phrase "in all formations" (*vṛttimātre*): according to the lexicon (*kośa*) stating that "the word *mātra* signifies entirety (*kārtsnya*) or restriction (*avadhāraṇa*)," the word *mātra* here has the sense of "entirety. Thus, the meaning is "in all [types of] formations. This is because it will be explained below.

The meaning is as follows: by the statement "in a compound (*samāsa*), indeed, there is a distinct power (*śakti*)," the term *samāsa* is used as an indicator for all types of complex formations (*vṛtti*). Since it will be explained that in all five types of formations—namely, primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), compounds (*samāsa*), elliptical formations (*ekaśeṣa*), and verbal roots with prefixes (*sanādyanta*)—there exists a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) consisting of the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), [the question arises: "How is there syntactic connection (*anvaya*) therein? The sense of the objection is that, according to the rule that "a word-meaning (*padārtha*) connects with a word-meaning, and not with a part of a word-meaning," how can there be a connection of the object "village" (*grāma-karman*) with a part of a word-meaning?

Thus, the sense is that this presentation of an example is inconsistent. He provides the resolution with the words "nityasāpekṣeṣu" and so forth. Even when there are words that are always dependent on another related term and function as subordinate members within a compound, the connection of a qualifier such as Devadatta occurs precisely with those [words] which constitute a single part of the compound; for even in the case of partial connection, they generate the cognition of the meaning "Devadatta’s teacher" or "his family."

And thus, the obstacle to partial connection (*ekadeśānvaya*) consists in its failure to produce a cognition of such a meaning; for example, in the case of *ṛddhasya rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king's man of wealth"), even though "wealthy" (*ṛddha*) connects with "king" (*rājan*), it does not produce a cognition of the meanings "the king who is wealthy" or "the king of the wealthy," because the cognition produced there is simply that "the man who belongs to the king is related to the wealthy one. And this obstacle does not exist in the case of those [words] that are invariably dependent (*nityasāpekṣa*). This is the meaning.

As it has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "Every relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*) that is dependent [on another] is always compounded; for that mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), which exists in the sentence (*vākya*), is not lost even in the compound (*vṛtti*)."

For, in the sentence "the family of Devadatta’s teacher" (*devadattasya guroḥ kulam*), the mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) or requirement [for syntactic connection] is not lost even when there is a compound formation (*vṛtti*); it does not cease. Therefore, a word that is invariably dependent (*nityasāpekṣa*) is compounded, and within that compound, the application of the qualifier occurs; furthermore, there arises the comprehension of the meaning "the family of him who is Devadatta’s teacher," because the expectancy is resolved only after such comprehension of the meaning has occurred. Having reflected upon all this, he says: "Devadatta’s teacher’s family."

Since "heaviness" (gurutva) is untenable without a disciple, the teacher is invariably dependent upon the disciple as a constituent element. Here, Devadatta is the disciple; when he is construed with the teacher, who is a part of the referent of the compound, the understanding of the required meaning arises. Thus, the intention is that the rule "a word-meaning [is construed] with a word-meaning" concerns cases other than those involving an invariably dependent element. Some older Naiyāyikas do not accept a primary denotative power (*śakti*) in a compound, nor do they admit secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the prior member of the compound.

However, regarding the term *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), they maintain that the word *puruṣa* refers to a person related to the king, while the word *rāja* functions as a "tātparyagrāhaka" (indicator of the intended meaning); thus, they assert that there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the latter member of the compound. According to that view, since the teacher (*guru*) is not a part of the referent of the word [in the phrase "the teacher is coming"], the connection of the qualifier [with the whole] occurs naturally; therefore, this is not a valid example. Consequently, he presents another example: *caitrasya naptā* ("Caitra’s grandson"). The referent of the word *naptṛ* ("grandson") is a body produced by a body that was itself produced [by Caitra].

Caitra is the grandfather; his son is Vaiśākha; his son is Jyeṣṭha. In this context, the body produced by Caitra belongs to Vaiśākha, and the body produced by Vaiśākha belongs to Jyeṣṭha; thus, Jyeṣṭha is the *naptṛ* (great-grandson) of Caitra, meaning he is his *pautra* (grandson). In that case, within the referent of the word *naptṛ*, which consists of the "body produced" (*janya-śarīra*) and the "body produced by that" (*janya-śarīra-janya-śarīra*), the property of being produced (*janyatva*)—which is one part of the referent—is construed with the meaning of the genitive ending in "Caitra's" (*caitrasya*) through a relation such as being its own counter-correlative (*svanirūpitatva*).

The meaning is that the body is produced by the body, just as [the body] is produced by Caitra. Now, one might object: here too, the referent of the genitive case in "Caitrasya" (of Caitra) does not connect with the "being-produced-ness" (*janyatva*) which is a part of the referent of the word *naptṛ* (grandson); rather, it connects with the body itself, which is the substantive of the word *naptṛ*, through the relation of "being produced by what is produced by oneself. The meaning is that the genitive case signifies the relation of "being produced by what is produced [by the possessor]. Thus, the cognition is: "the body is that which has the property of being produced by what is produced by Caitra. To this, he says: "in such cases," etc.

By the phrase "and so forth," examples such as *ghaṭād anyaḥ* ("different from the pot") and *ghaṭāt pṛthak* ("separate from the pot") are included. In the case of *anya* ("different"), the meaning of the word ending in the ablative case—the pot—is construed with "difference" (*bheda*), which is one constituent part of the referent of the word *anya*. The sense is: "possessing a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the pot. Similarly, in the case of *pṛthak* ("separate"), the meaning of the word ending in the ablative case—the pot—is construed with "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*), which is one constituent part of the referent of the word *pṛthak*. The resulting cognition is: "possessing a distinctness delimited by the pot. Although it is stated in the Bhāṣya that in all such cases the construction occurs through a mediated relationship (*paramparā-sambandha*) involving a constituent part, [this is the analysis].

This has been stated by Hari: "Those things which have a connection with a whole, such as a teacher's family (*gurukula*) and so forth, they, having come into contact with the parts, are joined with that which possesses those parts. The meaning is this: those objects which have a connection with a whole in the form of a teacher's family and so forth—(by this it is indicated that the object consisting of a connection through a series, namely the state of being composed of a part, is the referent of the genitive case following words like *devadatta*)—those objects also, having come into contact with and connected to the parts such as the teacher and so forth, are joined with the whole possessing those parts, such as the teacher's family.

This is because of that meaning. By saying "having touched the parts," even in this view, it is indicated that the parts obtain a specific relation. Nevertheless, in the aforementioned instance, since expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) exists only for a single part, and in accordance with experience, the view of partial connection (*ekadeśānvaya*) alone has been accepted.

For this very reason, the non-arising of doubts such as "Is the teacher Devadatta's or not? or "Is the state of being produced Caitra's or not? immediately after the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) generated by sentences like "Devadatta’s teacher’s house" is easily accounted for.

The intention is this: just as in the aforementioned examples from the *Nirukta*, the connection of a qualifier such as Devadatta with a part of the word-meaning—namely, the teacher and so forth—is accepted, so too there is no obstacle to accepting the connection of objects such as the village with the *bhāvanā* itself, which is subordinate to the word-meaning. He extends this stated principle elsewhere by saying "evam" (thus).

Just as in the case of "going to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), where the objects such as the village are construed with the action (*kriyā*) which is a subordinate part (*guṇabhūta*) of the meaning of the verbal root (*gatipadārtha*), so too in expressions like "cooking in order to eat" (*bhoktuṃ pākaḥ*), the suffix *tumun* is construed with the non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*) subordinate action within the meaning of the word "cooking. This is because the term "cooking" (*pāka*) here functions as a *kṛt*-derivative (*kṛdvṛtti*). The meaning is that the suffix *tumun*—prescribed by the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.10)—is grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) precisely because it is enjoined only when there is a connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*), and thus it construes with the action presented by a verbal root (*dhātu*) denoting a non-substantial entity. In "cooking in order to eat," the *tumun* suffix is prescribed by the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyām*. Since its injunction is restricted to the context of a connection with an action, its correctness follows from its construing with the action presented by a verbal root that denotes a non-substantial entity.

Regarding the expression *bhuktvā pākaḥ*: by the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.21), which prescribes the suffix *ktvā* for two actions having the same agent where the action denoted by the suffix relates to the earlier time, the status of being a verbal noun (*bhāva*) is to be understood. Here, because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) *dhātusaṃbandhe*, the phrase "of two actions" is obtained. Furthermore, according to the Vārttika *avyayakṛto bhāve*, the meaning of suffixes such as *tumun* and others is exclusively the abstract state (*bhāva*). In this regard, it should be understood that in forms ending in *ghañ* such as *pākaḥ*, two actions—one characterized by non-existence and one characterized by existence—are conveyed through the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), standing in a relationship of qualifier and qualified.

Action (*kriyā*) is of a non-substantial nature (*asattvasvabhāvā*) by virtue of its base-meaning (*prakṛtibhāga*), and it is of a substantial nature (*sattvasvabhāvā*) by virtue of its suffix-meaning (*pratyayabhāga*), as in the cases of *bhoktum* ("to eat") and *bhuktvā* ("having eaten"). In these instances, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between the two actions—the action of the base and the action of the suffix—is identical. However, just as in the word *pākaḥ* ("cooking"), a distinction characterized by the possession of gender, number, and so forth—that is, a substantial nature—is perceived in the action which is the meaning of the suffix, such a distinction is likewise perceived in *bhoktum* and *bhuktvā*.

The distinction is that [the action] is not perceived as performing a causal function (*arthakriyā*) with respect to its own conditions. Thus, the meaning of suffixes such as *tumun* is precisely the nature of non-existence (*asattvasvabhāva*) of the entity. Therefore, in cases such as *pāka* ("cooking"), one should understand that even in expressions like *kṛtapūrvaḥ kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat"), the suffixes denote the agent and so forth, by taking the action—which is of the nature of an operation (*vyāpāra*)—as a constituent part of the verbal root (*dhātvaṃśakriyā*), just as in the case of case-endings denoting object, instrument, and so on.

Others, however, maintain that expressions such as *bhoktuṃ pākaḥ* ("cooking for the purpose of eating") and *bhoktuṃ gataḥ* ("gone for the purpose of eating") are indeed incorrect. This is because where there is a mention of a word denoting an action (*kriyāvācaka-śabda*) in relation to an effect (*kārya*), only that which denotes an action existing solely in its state of being accomplished (*sādhyamātra-avasthā*) is primarily intended. However, where the meaning in the form of an action itself is mentioned, even that which denotes an action existing as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*) is included. For this very reason, they say that in connection with words like *gata* and *pāka*, the case endings (*kāraka-vibhakti*), the suffix *kṛtvasuc*, and the suffix *ktvā* are grammatically correct.

His intention is as follows: in the rule *tumunṇvulau*, although the attainment of "only that action which has another action as its purpose" is already established by the feminine designation in the word *kriyārthāyām*, the further mention of the word *kriyā* (action) indicates that the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* apply when there exists a verbal root (*dhātu*) that expresses an action existing solely in the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyamātrāvasthā*) as the primary element. Thus, the meaning is: "the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* [occur] after a verbal root when [it denotes] such an action."

And likewise, in the case of [the word] *gata* ending in the *kta* suffix in the sense of the root meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*), since the suffix-meaning is predominant in a *kṛt*-derived form, the word *gata* denotes a substance (*dravya*). Consequently, because it lacks the capacity to denote an action (*kriyā*), the suffix *tumun* is not applicable there. Similarly, although the suffix *ghañ* in the word *pāka* expresses the abstract state (*bhāva*), one should understand that the word *pāka* also denotes a substance, because—as stated in the Bhāṣya—"an action expressed by a *kṛt* suffix manifests like a substance"—and thus the word *pāka* assumes the properties of a substance, such as being connected with gender and number.

If it is argued that in cases such as *gata-śabda* (the word "gone"), since the verbal root denotes an action in its purely potential state (*sādhyamātrāvastha*), the suffix *tumun* should apply there on that basis—then you are mistaken. This is because, in the rule prescribing *tumun*, the technical designation *upapada* is necessary for the meaning "that which has another action as its purpose" (*kriyārthopapada*). Consequently, by virtue of this great technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*), the meaning of the rule *tumunṇvulau* necessarily requires a word that expresses an action whose fruit is another action.

And thus, the suffix *tumun* is prescribed after a word that denotes an action whose nature is purely to be accomplished (*sādhyamātra-svabhāva*). The point is that although a verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes an action whose nature is purely to be accomplished, it does not [trigger the application of *tumun*] because it lacks the status of being a "word" (*pada*). Furthermore, such a word is necessarily one ending in a finite verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). For this very reason, in this rule (*sūtra*), there is no mention of the meaning "action" (*kriyārūpa-artha*), but rather a mention of the word "that which denotes an action" (*kriyāvācaka-śabda*). The point is that the technical designation "governing word" (*upapada-saṃjñā*) resides in words that possess the technical designation "word" (*pada-saṃjñaka*).

As for the objection that is raised—that because the *kta* suffix in the neuter gender expresses the action merely in its state as something yet to be accomplished (*sādhyamātrāvasthā*), it denotes an action in its purely potential stage; and therefore, when joined with such a word, the *tumun* suffix in the expression "he went to eat" (*bhoktuṃ gataḥ*) would be unavoidable—it must be replied: if one were to raise this doubt by taking the verbal root (*prakṛti*) as denoting an action in its purely potential stage, such a doubt is impossible, because the root lacks the status of a word (*pada*), and because its meaning is subordinate as a qualifier.

If it is argued that, because the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix is predominant, and because the *kta* suffix primarily denotes an action in its state of being merely to-be-accomplished (*sādhyamātra-avasthā*), and because that which ends in such a suffix is a word (*pada*), there might be a suspicion of the application of the *tumun* suffix in connection with it—that too is not the case. For, according to the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "An action expressed by a *kṛt* suffix manifests like a substance," even the word "gone" (*gata*) does not denote an action; for it is said, "The root *han* [denotes] 'striking,' and the root *vac* [denotes] 'speaking.'"

The meaning is as follows: just as the root *vac* is not employed by authoritative grammarians (*śābdika*) in the sense of "they speak" in the word *antiparakādvaceḥ* because the meaning of "speaking" is not perceived there, so too, because the meaning consisting of the counting of the production of actions is not perceived, expressions such as *triḥ pākaḥ* ("threefold cooking") should not be used. Now, one might object: since the power (*śakti*) of the verbal root *vṛt* is restricted by the force of the prefix (*upasarga*) in the rule *abhyāvṛttigaṇane*, the word *abhyāvṛtti* has the meaning of "repeated occurrence," which is to say, "birth" (*janma*).

And that birth is not one, because a single thing is incapable of being counted; rather, it is many, because only a plurality is fit for counting. Thus, the counting of repeated births is a calculation of recurrence (*abhyāvṛtti-gaṇanam*). In that regard, for substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*), which are established by their own nature, there is no capacity for counting through repeated birth, since their production occurs only once. However, in the case of action (*kriyā*), since it is perceived as having its distinctions already resolved through the verbal root (*dhātu*), there is a repeated production, yet no recurrence.

Furthermore, by the term "repetition" (*abhyāvṛtti*), birth is expressed as that which is fit for repeated occurrence, due to the inherent force of the two prefixes *abhi* and *ati*. Since it is action alone—and not substance or other categories—that is fit for repeated birth, once action is obtained simply through the mention of "repetition," the explicit mention of "action" (*kriyā*) here serves to indicate that only action in its state of being something yet to be accomplished (*sādhyamātra-avasthā*) is intended.

In cases such as *pāka*, the action presented by the suffix *ghañ* does not possess the aforementioned nature; therefore, there is no occurrence of the suffix *suc* in forms like *dvistriḥ pāka*. With this intention, [the author] says "some, however," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in *pāka* and so on, such [an action]," the meaning is that in the word *pāka*, the action presented by *ghañ* does not have the nature of being merely something to be accomplished (*sādhyamātra*).

Nor should it be argued that even if the action denoted by the *ghañ*-affix (*pacana*) lacks that [sādhyatva] nature, the suffix *su* (the nominative case-ending) would still be unavoidable because the action denoted by its root (*pac*), being of the nature of a mere *sādhya* (to-be-accomplished), remains intact as the cause for its application. This is because the intention is that, in the case of a *kṛt*-derived word, the meaning of the suffix is generally observed to be predominant; thus, by the action denoted by the *ghañ*-suffix—which is the predominant factor—the effect occasioned by the mere *sādhya* nature inherent in the action that serves as a qualifier of its own root-meaning is overridden, just as by the self itself.

[Objection: "In this manner, even forms such as *dvirvacanam* (the act of doubling) and *dviḥprayogaḥ* (twofold usage) would not be possible; what then is the status of such usages? To this, he says: "*dvirvacanam iti ca*," etc. The meaning is that because such usages are employed by the authors of the Bhāṣya and others, and because of the technical indication (*nirdeśa*) in the rule *dvirvacane'ci*, it is signaled (*jñāpyate*) that the suffix *suC* occurs after the word *dvis* by taking the action (*kriyā*) presented by the verbal root (*dhātu*) which serves as the base for an affix denoting the abstract state (*bhāvārthaka-pratyaya*) contained within such usages.

And thus, since the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of words denoting frequency (*kṛtvo'rtha*) is obtained only in those cases where the favor of the authors of the Sūtras and others is observed upon the formation of *su*-suffixes and the like by taking the action as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), everything is well-established. Here, by the phrase "some, however" (*atra kecit tu*), a lack of approval is indicated. But that [disapproval] is merely because it is more logical to understand that the action must be understood somehow or other through the indication in the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* (P.

1.1.59). It should be understood that Kaiyaṭa and others have clearly stated that the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) in the rule *kriyābhyāvṛtti* (P. 8.1.4) is either for the sake of clarity or for the sake of what follows. || 20 ||

[Objection: But surely, just as in the case of a verbal root (*dhātu*), the capacity to convey *bhāvanā*—in the form of being the denotator—is equally present in the verb (*ākhyāta*) as well, since for the Mīmāṃsakas, the cognition of *bhāvanā* arises from the *tiṅ* suffix. And so, how is it determined that *bhāvanā* is denoted by the verbal root alone and not by the *tiṅ* suffix? Thus he raises the doubt with the words "But [this is] the established conclusion" (*nanu siddhānta iti*). Regarding the phrase "the apprehension of the power of the verb": the meaning is [it refers to] those such as the Mīmāṃsakas who hold that the power to convey *bhāvanā* exists in the verb, i.e., in the suffixes such as *tiṅ*. [The word] "from the cognition" (*bodhāt*)...

The sense is that because the cognition of *bhāvanā* arises from suffixes such as the *tib* and others, it is necessary for the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) to possess the power to convey *bhāvanā*. Thus, in response to the doubt that the determination of *bhāvanā* as being denoted belongs to the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone, he provides the solution with the words "the distinction of the relation between the qualified and the qualifier" (*bhedya-bhedaka-sambandha*). Here, "the qualified" (*bhedya*) is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), and "the qualifier" (*bhedaka*) is the attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*); the "relation" (*sambandha*) is the connection between these two. The "distinction" (*bheda*) refers to the specific difference (*viśeṣa*) consisting of such a relation; "based upon that" (*tannibandhana*) means caused by that.

The meaning is that grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is based on the relationship between a qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). This is the underlying idea: when a particular word, with a specific sequence of sounds (*ānupūrvī*), is declared correct by any one of the authors of the Sūtras, Vārttikas, or Bhāṣya in relation to a particular qualificand as connected with a particular qualifier, that word is correct in that context; elsewhere, it is simply incorrect. For this very reason, the word *aśva* with a dental *s* in the middle is not correct when referring to a horse, but is correct when referring to a poor man. Likewise, the word *aśva* with a palatal *ś* in the middle is correct when referring to a horse, but not when referring to a poor man.

If the agent expressed in this manner were not denoted [by the suffix], and if the verbal root did not denote the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), there would be nothing but ungrammaticality; for grammar teaches grammaticality precisely in that way. Now, one might object: grammar is merely an explanatory account of what is already grammatical, and not a means for grasping linguistic capacity (*śakti*). For this very reason, it was stated in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "Now begins the instruction on words."

In the *Vākyapadīya* as well, it is stated that "this grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) has as its object the knowledge of correctness (*sādhutvajñānaviṣayā*)," and not that it conveys meaning. Dispelling this doubt, he says: "This is the meaning," and so forth. The meaning is that the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇaśāstra*) establishes the correctness of words by teaching that, in the context of the occurrence of a vowel (*ac*), a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) is to be pronounced, and that which is composed of a semi-vowel is correct. Regarding the phrase "in that very [context]": the meaning is "only among correct words. Regarding the term "as a delimiting factor" (*avacchedakatayā*): [it means] by way of being the defining characteristic.

The meaning is as follows: according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, who maintain that "power" (śakti) is precisely that property which is postulated as the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) for the capacity to produce the comprehension of meaning. Regarding the phrase "only one and the same": since there is a rule that the capacity to produce must be delimited by some property, it is necessary to postulate a property as its delimiting factor; therefore, it is logical that grammatical correctness (sādhutva) itself constitutes the state of being expressive (śaktatva). Thus, the meaning is that the state of being expressive and grammatical correctness are one and the same, not two different things.

The point is that since it is accepted that the comprehension of meaning arises only from correct words (*sādhuśabda*), and since *śakti* (denotative power) resides exclusively in correct words, being endowed with *śakti* is itself what constitutes correctness (*sādhutva*). "In that manner" means: in the manner of the etymologists (*niruktaka*) and the Mīmāṃsakas. Thus, the determination of correctness is itself the determination of *śakti*.

The meaning is as follows: since grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is mentioned first among the means of grasping word-power (*śaktigraha*) in the statement of the learned, "Grammar, analogy, etc.," and since the science of grammar is established without obstruction as the determiner of word-power—functioning to teach the correctness (*sādhutva*) of various words by setting forth their respective meanings—the use of the *tiṅ* suffix with the intention of denoting *bhāvanā* is simply incorrect, due to its contradiction with grammatical rules such as "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69).

One might object: "Correctness (*sādhutva*) is not the same as expressive power (*śaktatva*), because we observe that meaning is understood even from incorrect words (*asādhu-śabda*). Rather, correctness is something distinct from that [expressive power]. For this very reason, the usage 'the correct word is expressive' (*sādhuḥ śaktaḥ*) is consistent; for if the two were identical, their simultaneous employment would be untenable. With this intention, he says: "Even in the theory of a distinct expressive power (*atirikta-śakti-vāda*)."

The meaning is as follows: correctness (*sādhutva*) consists in being non-corrupt (*anapabhraṣṭatva*) and so forth, whereas expressive power (*śakti*) is either a particular kind of intention (*icchāviśeṣa*) or a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*). Thus, even in the view that expressive power is something additional to correctness, [the following holds]. Regarding the statement "in the eternal relation between word and meaning," it was said that while the comprehension of meaning is the same whether by means of a correct word or an incorrect one, a restriction regarding religious merit (*dharma*) is established—namely, that one should speak with correct words and not with incorrect ones, just as one may go to a place that is accessible but not to one that is inaccessible. In this context, it is clear that expressive power is something additional to correctness. [The phrase] "it would indeed be so" [is used].

The meaning is as follows: although grammar (*vyākaraṇa-smṛti*) is undertaken for the purpose of making known the correctness (*sādhutva*) of words, since correctness is based on the presentation of specific respective meanings, its capacity to determine verbal power (*śakti*) arises precisely from the force of the collection of meanings. Therefore, due to contradiction with grammar, the use of the suffix *tiP* and so forth in relation to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) would indeed be incorrect—just as the use of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*), such as "by fire" (*agninā*), is incorrect when the dative case (*caturthī*), such as "to Agni" (*agnaye*), is required by the rule *agnaye svāhā*.

The intended meaning is as follows: the established doctrine of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) is that the sentence-sphoṭa (*vākyasphoṭa*) alone is primary. By the etymological derivation "that from which the meaning bursts forth or is manifested," *sphoṭa* means the signifier (*vācaka*). Thus, the term "sentence-sphoṭa" means that the sentence itself is the signifier. Since the venerable Pāṇini, who is foremost in grasping linguistic capacity (*śakti*), first grasps the capacity [of a word] within the sentence through the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), and since it is the sentence alone that generates the comprehension of meaning in the world; and because one perceives the fulfillment of the meaning through the knowledge of the meaning derived solely from the sentence—which is itself free of expectancy—the sentence-sphoṭa possesses primacy.

In this regard, because sentences are infinite due to differences in place, time, and agent, it is absolutely impossible to grasp the linguistic convention for every individual sentence; furthermore, since it is impossible to provide a grammatical exposition of all sentences by means of a simple method, teachers such as Pāṇini and others, having divided the words therein through conceptualization and having further postulated the division between stem and suffix within those words, established the distinction between the meanings of the word, the stem, and the suffix by means of imagined positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).

Therefore, in a sentence such as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), the meaning of the word *ghaṭa* is that which possesses a conch-like neck and so forth, and the meaning of *ānaya* (bring) is an action conducive to conjunction with the location near me; this is to be inferred similarly for sentences such as "lead the horse" (*aśvaṃ naya*) and "tie up the cow" (*gāṃ badhāna*). Thus, according to the aforementioned method, by means of the imagined positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the word *aśva*—which has the palatal *ś* in its middle—is established as being correct (*sādhu*) when it denotes a horse, but incorrect (*asādhu*) when it denotes a poor man, because the expressive power (*śakti*) of the word *aśva* is postulated solely for the purpose of denoting a horse.

Now, he says "in the sacrificial ritual" (yājñe karmaṇi) to show that it would indeed be improper [to hold such a view]. Just as an expiation has been prescribed for the use of an incorrect word in a sacrificial rite, so too, for those who maintain that the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) possesses the power to denote *bhāvanā*, when a verbal suffix is employed in a sacrificial rite with the intention of denoting *bhāvanā*, they would incur the expiation resulting from the transgression of the prohibition, "One shall not speak untruth."

The point is that since the authors of the Sūtras and others have not taught the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) as denoting *bhāvanā*, but rather have prescribed it as having the agent and so forth as its meaning; [one might object]: "But surely the Smṛti of Pāṇini should be discarded because it contradicts the Sūtras of the great sage Jaimini, owing to its weakness. This is not so; for regarding the matter of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), the Smṛti of Pāṇini alone is more authoritative, because the grammar of Pāṇini was composed precisely for the purpose of determining correctness. This is the intended sense.

In reality, even if there were a contradiction with the statements of the commentators on Jaimini’s Sūtras, not even a trace of contradiction with the literal words of the Sūtras would arise in the Pāṇinian Smṛti. For instance, the Sūtra of the sage Jaimini in the section concerning the meaning of verbal roots (bhāvārthādhikaraṇa) states: "Words denoting action have the sense of becoming; from them the action is understood, for it is this [becoming] that is enjoined as the object."

Verbs such as *dadyāt* (one should give) and *juhuyāt* (one should sacrifice) have the sense of "becoming" (*bhāvārtha*), meaning they primarily denote action, according to the Nirukta’s statement: "A verb has becoming as its primary sense. Therefore, from these [verbs], action is understood—that is, it is understood primarily. For this reason, because of this primacy, it is precisely this object in the form of action that is enjoined, and not one in the form of a substance.

Since an action perishes very rapidly, it is impossible for it to produce a result that occurs at a later time; therefore, the meaning is that an *apūrva* (a latent potency) must be postulated as an intermediary. Let the wise discern that from the literal meaning of this sūtra, it is established that the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), and that the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth are by no means its meaning.

The commentators, such as the authors of the *Vṛtti* and others, have explained that very *sūtra* of Jaimini as follows: "Those whose purpose (*artha*)—that is, their aim—is the determination (*pariccheda*) of the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), which consists of the sense of productive activity (*bhāvanā*). The point is this: once the general sense of productive activity has been presented by the verbal suffix, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), in the form of a sacrifice, serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) by distinguishing it from other productive activities, such as giving (*dāna*). Thus, those verbal roots which function as the delimiting factors are what are meant by the term "action-words" (*karmaśabda*).

From those [words], the action (*kriyā*) and the *apūrva* would be understood—that is, known—because this is the meaning that is enjoined; for it is that very [action] which is enjoined by virtue of being heard in a single word (*ekapadaśruti*). There is an invariable concomitance (*vyāpti*) such that whatever is enjoined is connected as the instrument (*karaṇa*) of that [result]. Thus, one should understand that there is a contradiction with the words of the commentators, but no contradiction with the literal syllables of the Sūtra, by those who know the secret of Jaimini’s system.

Now, regarding the prohibition of speaking untruth stated in the section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*)—namely, "One should not speak untruth"—there arises a doubt as to whether this injunction is intended for the person or for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices themselves. Upon deliberation, by means of the authority of *prakaraṇa* (context), which consists of the mutual requirement between the two, this prohibition pertains to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

For instance, since the prohibition of false speech (*anṛtavādana*) is of the nature of a non-existence (*abhāva*), it cannot be grasped by a requirement for a "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*). Therefore, in order to establish that [prohibition], one must postulate an action therein, such that the meaning becomes: "one should effect [the result] by maintaining the prohibition of false speech. Since no specific fruit is indicated here, there arises an expectancy for something to be benefited, namely: "What should one effect here? Similarly, in the statement "One should effect heaven by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargaṃ bhāvayet*), there exists an expectancy for a benefactor, namely: "How should one effect it?"

Therefore, through mutual expectancy and syntactic unity, this prohibition of untruthful speech is enjoined as part of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; by fulfilling the requirement of maintaining the prohibition against speaking untruth, one should effect the attainment of heaven. Consequently, throughout the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, untruthful speech is to be avoided everywhere.

In that regard, when, after telling the Adhvaryu priest, "A sacrificial cake made of rice is to be prepared," one says, "I shall have rice for my own meal; let [the cake] be made of barley instead," then there is certainly no observance of the prohibition. This is because the latter statement differs from the former statement, and thus constitutes false speech (*anṛtavāda*). For it is well known in the world that he who speaks a reply contrary to his previous statement is a speaker of falsehood.

However, at the time of performance, if one acts in contradiction to what was previously stated, the previous statement becomes false. Thus, a prior intention in the form "a sacrificial cake made of rice (*vrīhi*) must be prepared" itself becomes a falsehood, because the performance of a sacrificial cake made of barley (*yava*) contradicts that intention. Consequently, there would be both a deficiency in the sacrifice and a transgression of a prohibition. Therefore, one should not speak that which is contradictory.

Thus, when beginning the optional performance characterized by either the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup, the Adhvaryu priest or others, having resolved upon one alternative, must not subsequently speak falsely by adopting the other alternative; for through false speech, there arises both a deficiency in the sacrifice (*kratuvaiguṇya*) and the incurrence of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) due to the transgression of a prohibition. However, when one performs the rite at the time of its execution strictly in accordance with the prior resolution, then he maintains the prohibition against false speech.

Just as when one resolves upon making an offering of barley, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is made of barley alone, and in this very case the prohibition is perfectly observed; because the performance of the barley cake is in accordance with the prior resolve, there is neither deficiency in the sacrifice nor transgression of the prohibition, and thus there is an absolute absence of the need for expiation (prāyaścitta).

And thus, when the benefit for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices is accomplished by observing the prohibition against speaking untruth, it is thereby established that the very fruit to be produced by the principal rites—the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices—which is the form of heaven, is itself the fruit of the subsidiary element, the prohibition against speaking untruth.

In this manner, the status of the prohibition against speaking untruth as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the section concerning the agent (*kartradhikaraṇa*). With the intention that this would contradict the view of the Grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*), who asserts that the agent is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the Mīmāṃsaka raises an objection beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*). "In your view" means: in the view of the Grammarian who maintains that the agent is denoted by the verbal suffix (the *tiṅ* ending). "Only for the sake of the sacrifice" (*kratvartha eva*)... [refers to the prohibition].

The meaning is that the prohibition "one should not speak untruth" would not even be established as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice (*kratu*) consisting of the Darśapūrṇamāsa. He states the reason for the failure of this prohibition to be established as an auxiliary of the sacrifice with the words beginning "by the verb" (*ākhyātena*) and ending with "is sublated" (*bādhyate*). The underlying idea is as follows: according to the Vaiyākaraṇa school, based on the authority of sūtras such as *laḥ karmaṇi* [Pāṇini 3.4.69], the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*, i.e., *tiṅ* etc. has the agent, the object, and so forth as its meaning; and the verbal root (*dhātu*) has the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) conducive to the result as its meaning.

The doubt-raiser’s assumption is that the agent possesses primacy because of the status of the suffix (*pratyaya*). Thus, by the direct audition (*śruti*) of the verbal suffix in "vadet" (he should speak), the person as the agent is expressed; and by the verbal root (*dhātu*), the act of speaking is expressed. This being the case, since the injunctive direct audition (*viniyoktrī śruti*)—which consists of a single word—communicates a relationship of mutual subsidiary and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) between the two meanings conveyed by its constituent parts, namely the stem (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), it follows that when the verbal suffix denotes the person, the meaning of the stem, which is speaking, is understood to be for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) and as a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*), by virtue of its connection with that person.

Furthermore, since the counter-positive—false speech—is a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*), its prohibition must likewise be enjoined as a property of the person; thus, it possesses the status of being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatva*). And so, regarding the prohibition "one should not speak falsely," the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*)—consisting in being an auxiliary to the ritual—is obtained through the means of proof known as *prakaraṇa* (context), which takes the form of mutual expectancy; whereas the status of being for the sake of the person is obtained through the means of proof known as *śruti* (direct statement).

In that case, because direct statement (śruti) is stronger than context (prakaraṇa), the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice—which is not obtained through context—is set aside; thus, by the prohibition "one shall not speak untruth," there would be only the status of being for the sake of the person (puruṣārthatva), consisting in its being a benefit to the person.

And likewise, when a person's inclination toward speaking untruth arises due to passion, hatred, and so forth, then, by means of the prohibition against speaking untruth, once there is non-engagement in that act, no sin is produced from speaking untruth; consequently, there is neither the experience of misfortune such as falling into hell caused by that sin, nor is there any obstruction to the experience of the fruits produced by meritorious karma in the form of speaking truth.

In this manner, the non-engagement in speaking falsehood results in benefit for the person, and its fruit is precisely the prevention of undesirable consequences such as hell that would otherwise arise through that act; thus, the prohibition of false speech is established as being solely for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), not for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Consequently, when a person speaks falsely, the sin (*pratyavāya*) accrues to the person alone and not to the sacrifice. Therefore, the meaning is that if one were to speak falsely during a sacrifice, it would contradict the practice of all ritualists and Mīmāṃsakas, who maintain that one must perform the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) for a sacrificial defect (*kratubhreṣa*).

If it is asked, "What is the authority for setting aside the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice—which is established by the context—when that is contradicted by the direct scriptural statement 'one shall not speak untruth'? it is replied: there are six authorities, beginning with direct scriptural statement (śruti), which serve as auxiliaries to the applicatory injunction (viniyoga-vidhi) that makes known the relationship between the subsidiary and the primary.

In that regard, when two mutually contradictory means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are presented together regarding a single object, their contradiction precludes their simultaneous application; thus, it must be stated that one sublates the second. And it is well known in the world that this occurs such that the stronger sublates the weaker. Therefore, when there arises a desire to know which among the six—*śruti*, *liṅga*, *vākya*, *prakaraṇa*, *sthāna*, and *samākhyā*—is stronger and which is weaker, [Jaimini] composed the aphorism: "When there is a conflict between *śruti*, *liṅga*, *vākya*, *prakaraṇa*, *sthāna*, and *samākhyā*, each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding because of its remoteness from the purpose."

The Blessed One, the great sage Jaimini, [states that] among the six means of proof (*pramāṇa*)—such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and others—which serve as applicators (*viniyojaka*), when two contradictory ones meet in a single instance, there is a relative weakness: each subsequent one is weaker than each preceding one; the preceding one sublates the subsequent. The reason for this is "due to remoteness of meaning" (*arthaviprakarṣāt*); the meaning is that because the subsequent means of proof is dependent upon the preceding means of proof, there is a remoteness or delay in determining the application—that is, the determination of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*aṅgāṅgitva*).

Here, by stating that each subsequent [means of proof] is weaker, it is indicated that each preceding one is stronger. Among these, *śruti* (direct assertion) is an independent statement. "Statement" (*rava*) means sound (*śabda*). When a certain thing is to be employed for a certain purpose, that word which does not depend on any other means of proof as its employer is called *śruti*. For when something is to be employed for a certain purpose, it does not depend on any of the five subsequent means of proof, such as *liṅga* (indicative mark), and so forth.

The five means of application (*viniyojaka-pramāṇas*), beginning with indicative power (*liṅga*), effect their application only in dependence upon all the preceding means of knowledge. Therefore, in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to these [subsequent means] such as indicative power, the word "independent" (*nirapekṣa*) is stated in the definition of direct assertion (*śruti*). In that regard, an example demonstrating the superiority of direct assertion when there is a conflict between direct assertion and indicative power is presented: "One worships the *Gārhapatya* fire with the *Aindri* [verse]."

"O Indra, you are never neglectful; O Indra, you are never a destroyer for the donor. Rather, you take pleasure in the sacrificer who has offered the oblation"—this is the meaning. This is a verse addressed to Indra (*aindrī ṛk*). It is called *aindrī* because Indra is its deity (*devatā*). In this scripture, the capacity to illuminate the meaning in the form of Indra is observed.

By means of that indicative mark (*liṅga*), one infers the scriptural statement (*śruti*) "With this *aindrī* [verse], he worships Indra," and through such an inferred scripture, the application of this *ṛc* to the worship of Indra would be possible by the authority of the indicative mark. However, because the application of this *ṛc* to the worship of Gārhapatya has already been established by the direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) "With the *aindrī*, [he worships] Gārhapatya," and because direct scripture is more powerful than an inferred scripture, its application is to the worship of Gārhapatya.

In the mantra "kadācana starīrasi," the word *indra*—in accordance with the meaning of the verbal root *idi* (to possess supreme sovereignty)—should be understood as denoting the *gārhapatya* fire either by virtue of its connection with the quality of supreme sovereignty or by virtue of being a means for the sacrifice. Here, the word *aindrī*, the word *gārhapatya*, and the verbal root *sthā* preceded by an upasarga should be understood as the expressive [words]. Thus, the word *aindrī*, the word *gārhapatya*, and the verbal root *sthā* preceded by an upasarga constitute the expressive *śruti*.

The word *aindryā* is an instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*), and *gārhapatyam* is an accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*); these two constitute the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) that assigns the function. Therein, by means of the instrumental case, the status of the *aindrī* verse as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the worship (*upasthāna*) is established. And by means of the accusative case, the status of the *gārhapatya* fire as the principal element (*aṅgin*) of the worship is made known. The *gārhapatya* fire is so called because it is connected with the householder (*gṛhapati*). According to the rule "the suffix *ñya* is added after the word *gṛhapati* when it is connected [with the sense of the fire]," the suffix *ñya* is applied to the word *gṛhapati*.

This being the case, when the authority of *liṅga* (indicative power) is sublated by the authority of *śruti* (direct statement) here, the following reasoning is observed: among the six authorities that enjoin application, *śruti* alone is the direct injunctive authority. Therefore, *śruti* is treated by all as the preeminent authority. The five authorities beginning with *liṅga*, however, are not direct injunctives. That which possesses the capacity to illuminate the meaning is called *liṅga*.

For example, the mantra "kadācana starīrasi" possesses the capacity to reveal its meaning as having Indra as its referent; however, as long as the injunctive scriptural statement (*śruti*)—"one worships with the *aindrī* [mantra] facing Indra"—which functions as the application based on that very capacity, is not known, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is entirely ineffective.

Therefore, when the expectancy arises as to where the mantra "kadācana starīḥ" is to be employed, it stimulates the inherent power of application (*prakalpakatva*) existing by nature in the *liṅga* (indicative power) that serves as the means for employing the Aindra mantra in some ritual act. Thereupon, that *liṅga* postulates a *śruti* (direct scriptural injunction) conducive to itself, such as: "With the Aindra [mantra], one worships Indra."

And since the application (*viniyoga*) occurs there by means of that direct statement (*śruti*), the authority of indicative power (*liṅga*) is an indirect applicator through the medium of the direct statement. Thus, the direct statement, having conveyed its own denotation, applies [the mantra] in the very second moment; whereas the indicative power first causes the words of the mantra to convey their own denoted meaning, and only thereafter is the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the mantra ascertained.

It is understood that the name-mantra (*nāmamantra*) is a means for accomplishing an action directed toward Indra; subsequently, by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), the Vedic revelation (*śruti*)—in the form of case endings—is postulated, consisting of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā vibhakti*) expressing the instrumentality (*sādhanatva*) as "with the mantra dedicated to Indra" (*aindreṇa mantreṇa*), and the accusative case (*dvitīyā vibhakti*) expressing the object (*sādhyatva*) as "Indra" (*indram*). And that revealed text (*śruti*) enjoins the application (*viniyoga*) in the form: "One worships Indra with the mantra dedicated to Indra. Thus, there is a delay until the fourth moment.

This being the case, in the instance of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), there are no intervening operations of determining capacity (*sāmarthya*) or inferring a partial statement (*kṣutika*) between the establishment of the word's own meaning and its application (*viniyoga*). Thus, the application arising through the authority of *śruti* occurs directly and is therefore immediate (*avyavahita*). However, the application arising through the authority of indicative power (*liṅga*) occurs by first postulating a *śruti* and then through that medium; thus, it is separated by one step (*ekāntarita*).

Thus, an application (*viniyoga*) arising from a means of knowledge such as syntactical connection (*vākya*) is produced by first postulating an indicative mark (*liṅga*) and then a direct statement (*śruti*); this is to be understood by analogy for two, three, or more intervening steps. To the extent that there is an increase in the mediation between a means of knowledge and its application, to that same extent its weakness is established. It is established by logic itself that a means of knowledge which applies [the element] with speed is stronger than a means of knowledge which applies it with delay.

For, having sequentially postulated as many prior means of knowledge (pramāṇas) as there are in relation to itself, the *liṅga* (inferential mark) and so forth cause the application (*viniyoga*) to be understood through them. Consequently, when multiple means of knowledge converge upon a single object, the subsequent one sublates the prior. The "understanding" of the subsequent means of knowledge consists precisely in its non-operation with respect to that [prior] object.

Since a subsequent authoritative statement (*vākya*), having postulated the previously arisen collection of means of knowledge (*liṅga* and *śruti*) relative to itself, proceeds to apply a certain meaning to a certain place, at that time—prior even to the attainment of its own essential form by that previously arisen collection of means of knowledge (*liṅga* and *śruti*)—that meaning is applied to a certain place by the preceding means of knowledge (*liṅga* or *śruti*).

Once the application (*viniyoga*) has arisen, the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to "where is the application? ceases; consequently, the capacity of the subsequent means of knowledge (the sentence) to produce [an application] through indicative power (*liṅga*) and so forth becomes obstructed. Thus, because its operation has entirely ceased, that [sentence] does not apply there.

Thus, although the application (*viniyoga*) of the *aindra* mantra for the worship of Indra would have to be established through the means of inference (*liṅga*)—which consists in the capacity to manifest the meaning of "Indra"—by way of postulating a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), this very power of inference to produce such a statement is actually obstructed. This is because the application of the *aindra* verse to the worship of the *gārhapatya* fire has already been accomplished by the explicit third-case *śruti*: "With the *aindrī*, [one worships] the *gārhapatya*. Since this occurs even before the inference of a scriptural statement such as "with the *aindra* mantra, [one worships] Indra" could take place, the power of inference to generate a *kalpya* (to-be-postulated) rule is indeed set aside.

Because direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is more powerful, it sublates indicative mark (*liṅga*). Thus, in the present case regarding the rule "one should not speak untruth," since the agent is denoted by the direct statement of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-śruti*), the application of the phrase "not untruth" to the agent—the person—has already been established by the direct statement consisting of the single word "should speak" (*vadet*). Therefore, while one might otherwise attempt to apply it to the entire context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices by means of the syntactical connection (*vākya*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and direct statement (*śruti*)—all of which would have to be inferred through the evidence of the context (*prakaraṇa*) consisting of mutual expectancy—where could such an application possibly take place? It has already been effected.

Since the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) has thus been satisfied, the capacity of the sentence to project the indicators (*liṅga*) and so forth—which would otherwise result in the authority of the context (*prakaraṇa*)—is obstructed. Therefore, because the direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful, it sublates the authority of the context. Consequently, one might raise the objection that since the understanding arises that the agent is the locus of the prohibition against speaking untruth, the prohibition "Do not speak untruth" must pertain solely to the person (*puruṣārtha*) and not to the ritual (*kratvartha*). Anticipating this, he says: "If this is argued, it is not so."

The point is that, according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, since the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the agent (*kartṛ*)—the person—is not perceived through direct audition (*śruti*). Consequently, in the absence of any conflict with *śruti*, the prohibition "one should not speak untruth" (*nānṛtam*) pertains solely to the ritual (*kratvartha*) by means of the authority of context (*prakaraṇa*) alone. Now, even if in the Vaiyākaraṇa view the agent—the person—is denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the prohibition "one should not speak untruth" cannot possibly pertain to the person; this is stated in the passage beginning with "But the meaning of the *tiṅ*," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: although the agent is denoted by the verbal suffix (such as *ti* etc. on the authority of grammatical rules such as "the [suffix] *la* is used in the sense of the object" (*Pāṇini 3.4.69*), that agent does not possess primacy. The term "bhāva" refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), consisting of either the result (*phala*) or the activity (*vyāpāra*). The compound "pradhāna-yatra" is a *bahuvrīhi*, meaning "that in which [the bhāva] is primary. And the word ending in a *tiṅ*-suffix is the referent of the other member of the compound.

And thus, from the statement of the *Nirukta*, "The verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning," which signifies that a finite verb generates a cognition characterized by a subject-ness residing in the meaning of the verbal root, which is itself determined by a qualifier-ness residing in the meaning of the finite suffix, it is understood that the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) in the form of activity is primary, while the agent and other meanings of the suffix are subordinate qualifiers. Consequently, one must necessarily accept a restriction of the general rule that "between the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), the meaning of the suffix is primary."

And thus, since it is a general rule that between the meaning of a verbal root (*prakṛti*) and the meaning of a suffix (*pratyaya*), the meaning of the suffix is predominant, this principle does not apply to forms ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). Consequently, because the agent denoted by the verb is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) consisting of the activity expressed by the verbal root—and because a qualifier is dependent upon the qualified (*viśeṣya*)—there arises no expectation for a further qualifier such as "What is my qualifier? Therefore, according to the maxim, "Since subordinate elements (*guṇa*) exist for the sake of another, there can be no mutual connection between them on the grounds of parity," [the agent] is not [connected to the prohibition], and thus [the statement] "one should not speak untruth" [remains valid].

He states that "it is not [connected] as a subordinate factor" (*na hi guṇabhūtaḥ*) because a connection with the prohibition as a subordinate element (*aṅgatva* = *viśeṣaṇatva*) is impossible for the agent who has become a subordinate qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Since it is logical that being the principal (*aṅgitva*) belongs only to the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), if the prohibition were connected to the agent—who is a qualifier—as its subordinate element, two contradictory states, namely primacy and non-primacy, would result for that single entity (the agent). Therefore, it is not appropriate to effect a connection of another word-meaning with a qualifier by way of subordination.

Regarding this, they say that the agent, being subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), is neither able nor capable of grasping the prohibition as its own subordinate element. This is because it is contradictory for something already present as a qualifier of another to be further construed as a qualifier of yet another entity. Thus, in the case of "one should sacrifice with *soma*," once the sacrifice has been construed as a qualifier within the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the verbal suffix—as in "one should effect [the result] by means of the sacrifice"—the Mīmāṃsakas reject any further construction of *soma* as the qualificand in that very same context, such as "one should effect the sacrifice by means of *soma*."

Now, one might object: how can the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the verbal root itself apprehend a negation, since it too is connected with the agent who is the meaning of the verbal suffix? To this, he says: "But the *bhāvanā*... and "the primary [element]... Since the *bhāvanā* is the primary element—the qualificand—with respect to the agent who is the meaning of the verbal suffix, there is no obstacle to its connection with the negation denoted by the particle *nañ* as its qualifier; therefore, it is indeed capable of apprehending the negation.

The meaning is as follows: in the word *vadet* ("one should speak"), with respect to the act of speaking which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the agent—which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅartha*)—is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and the act of speaking is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Thus, the cognition is that "the act of speaking resides in the agent. The term *anṛtam* ("untruth") is a qualifier of the speaking; the meaning is "the act of speaking untruth. Such an act of speaking untruth, being the primary element, is construed as a qualifier of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*).

Thus, when the meaning is established as a prohibition of the act of speaking untruth residing in the agent, the question arises: "For what purpose is this prohibition? In response to this inquiry regarding the purpose (*kaimarthyākāṅkṣā*) of the prohibition, one must—by means of the context (*prakaraṇa*) as a valid means of knowledge—infer the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the direct statement (*śruti*), and through those, because the prohibition is applied within the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*) alone is established; such is the meaning.

But if this were the case, then prohibitions such as "one should not harm any living beings" and "one should not eat *kalañja*" would also not have the person as their purpose (*puruṣārthatva*) according to the Vedic text (*śruti*), because the agent presented by the *śruti* would be a mere qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the action.

If, however, it is argued that in prohibitions such as "one should not eat *kalañja*," because no other principal (*aṅgin*) is possible, the prohibition of the agent—who is a qualifier—is itself an auxiliary (*aṅga*), then the previously stated rule—that an object presented as a qualifier of another does not connect with other meanings as a qualifier—would be violated; consequently, in the case of "one should not speak untruth," the prohibition would also become an auxiliary of the agent. Therefore, he says: "Let it be [a duty] of the person engaged in the sacrifice, such as the knowledge of the Vedas (*vedya*)," etc. This means it is a duty of the person associated with the ritual.

If the verb denotes the agent, then by virtue of the direct word (*padaśruti*), the prohibition "one should not speak untruth" would result in being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatva*), whereas by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it would be for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*). In that case, when two means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) have both been reached for the purpose of enjoining a single thing in a particular instance, if their non-contradiction is possible, then it is improper to assume a contradiction. For when there is a contradiction, one must effect the sublation of the weaker by the stronger through an investigation of relative strength; thus, there is no need for such complexity (*māhagaurava*).

However, there is no contradiction, for there is economy (lāghava) in the coexistence of both when one is not sublated by the other. In the present case, between the direct statement (śruti) and the context (prakaraṇa) which are applicable to enjoin the prohibition "not false," the direct statement enjoins it with respect to the person, while the context enjoins it with respect to the sacrifice; thus a contradiction appears. Nevertheless, that [contradiction] is merely apparent.

Since even in the case of a ritual (*kratu*), there is no contradiction between the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*) due to the presence of the person, it is understood from both that the prohibition is a duty pertaining to the person as connected to the ritual; that is to say, through the syntactic unity of the scriptural statement and the context, the person connected to the ritual is presented as a subordinate factor (*aṅgin*) within the prohibition. Thus, from the understanding that the prohibition concerns the speaking of untruth by a person engaged in a ritual, the prohibition is directly a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) of the person, whereas for the ritual, the prohibition is a subordinate factor by way of a mediated succession.

The meaning is as follows: just as a servant who himself is subordinate considers the king to be the principal, and furthermore considers even that which belongs to the king—such as his son, wife, and so forth—to be his own principal, so it is in this case.

Now, one might object: "If this prohibition were for the sake of the person connected to the sacrifice (*kratuyuktapuruṣārtha*), then, since the agent in the sacrifice is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the prohibition against speaking untruth would apply specifically to him; thus, the prohibition against speaking untruth would have to be observed by the sacrificer alone, and not by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others. Consequently, there would be an inconsistency in the performance [of the rite]. Anticipating this, the author says: "Because there is no difference in the performance."

Because the person is qualified by being "engaged in a sacrifice" (*kratuyukta*), the meaning is that there is a prohibition of false speech uttered by that person who is engaged in and connected to the sacrifice. Consequently, just as the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is connected to the sacrifice, so too is the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and others; since there is no difference in their connection to the sacrifice, false speech must be avoided by the priests and others just as it is by the sacrificer—thus, there is no distinction in the performance of the rule.

If, however, the word "proper" (*yukta*) were replaced by the term "agent" (*kartṛ*), such that the prohibition against speaking untruth were stated as "the prohibition against untruth-speaking whose agent is the person who is the performer of the sacrifice"—meaning the prohibition applies to the untruth-speaking of that sacrificer who is the agent of the rite—then, since the prohibition against untruth-speaking would not apply to officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others distinct from the sacrificer, a distinction in practice would arise: namely, that the sacrificer must avoid untruth-speaking while the other priests need not. Considering precisely that such a distinction should not occur...

The author of the *Bhūṣaṇasāra* intends that the phrase "the person connected with the sacrifice" (*kratuyuktapuruṣa*) refers to the "root" (*mūla*). One should understand his intention to be this: by establishing the lack of contradiction between two conflicting authorities that would otherwise apply to the same individual when separated from the ritual context, he supports the view that [the act] is a duty of the person connected with the sacrifice. To provide an example favored by the Mīmāṃsakas for this argument, he cites: "One who is yawning should recite... (*jañjabhyamāno 'nubrūyāt*). This is heard in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*): "One who is yawning should recite: 'In me, skill and wisdom' (*mayi dakṣakratū*). In the word *jañjabhyamānaḥ*, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied to the root *jabh* to express contempt for the action, and from that, the suffix *śānac* is added to denote the agent.

According to the rule of Pāṇini, "jabhī jṛbhi gātravināme," the meaning is "one whose mouth is opened by the stretching of the limbs. In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether this mantra-text is enjoined with reference to a person or with reference to a sacrifice. Upon deliberation, it is understood through the authority of the sentence (*vākya-pramāṇa*) that this is a duty (*dharma*) of the person who is yawning, because the agent is denoted as the primary factor by the *śānac* suffix, which is a *kṛt* affix.

However, by means of the evidence of context (*prakaraṇa*), it is understood as being an auxiliary to the sacrifice; yet, syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than context. Therefore, having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that this is a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) was reached in the fifth section (*jañjabhyamānādhikaraṇa*) of the fourth quarter of the third chapter of Jaimini’s work—that, through the two non-contradictory factors of syntactical connection and context, this is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) by way of purifying the person who is engaged in the sacrifice.

Nor should it be argued that, having inferred the indicative power (*liṅga*) and the syntactical connection (*vākya*) from the context (*prakaraṇa*), and having inferred the direct statement (*śruti*) from those two, the application (*viniyoga*) must be effected by that *śruti* in the fourth moment; for since the application would have already been accomplished by the *śruti*—having inferred both the *liṅga* and the *śruti* from the *vākya*—in the very third moment, the determination that [the act] is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) would eliminate any further expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to "where the application lies," and thus no connection with the sacrifice (*kratu*) could be established. If that were the case, there would be a contradiction between two means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, when there is a conflict, the weaker [evidence] must be sublated by the stronger; however, that [sublation] is not logical. This is because of the maxim: "When a matter can be established without sublation, sublation is improper. Therefore, regarding this recitation of mantras which is enjoined by the authority of syntactical connection (*vākya*) as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the person who is yawning, it is demonstrated—through the assistance of the authority of context (*prakaraṇa*)—that the person yawning, who is the primary factor (*aṅgin*), is not to be understood as unrelated, but rather as one connected to the sacrifice (*kratu*).

Thus, by the absence of contradiction, the coexistence of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established due to the absence of sublation (*bādhā*). And so, having understood that the recitation of the mantra is performed by a person who is engaged in a sacrifice while yawning, it is demonstrated that the recitation of the mantra serves both the purpose of the person and the purpose of the sacrifice—through the medium of the person; such is the intended meaning.

Thus, the intention is as follows: just as in the case of a statement being repeatedly contradicted by *vākya* and *prakaraṇa*—which are not in conflict with each other—the recitation of mantras is understood to pertain to the person engaged in the sacrifice (*kratuyuktapuruṣārtha*) due to the consideration of relative strength and weakness; so too here, it is proper that the prohibition against speaking untruth (*anṛtavadana-niṣedha*) pertains specifically to the person engaged in the sacrifice, because of the non-contradictory *śruti* and *prakaraṇa*. As it has been stated by Bhaṭṭapāda: "Even [acts] such as approaching women, eating meat, and so forth, though pertaining to the person, are dependent [on the ritual context]."

"The prohibition is intended as a subsidiary (aṅga) of the sacrifice because it relies upon the context (prakaraṇa). Regarding the phrase 'eating [of] food, etc. (*bhakṣādīti*), which ends in a neuter accusative: the meaning is that the prohibition stated with reference to objects such as eating meat by means of women—which, although based on the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), is nevertheless accepted as a subsidiary of the sacrifice due to its reliance upon the context. From this statement by Bhaṭṭa, it should be understood that the rule—that a qualifier does not connect with anything other than the thing qualified—is not universal.

The meaning is that because the person connected to the sacrifice is understood as the absence of speaking untruth by that agent, the sacrifice is a qualifier with respect to the person, and the person is a qualifier with respect to the act of speaking.

If one intends for the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) to have the meaning of *bhāvanā* (productive activity) when employing it, then because that [suffix] would be grammatically incorrect (*asādhu*) in relation to that [bhāvanā], there would be no cognition of *bhāvanā* from the verbal suffix; for the knowledge of grammatical correctness is a cause for verbal comprehension. Therefore, he says: "even in its absence," etc. The meaning is that even if the verbal suffix is grammatically incorrect with respect to *bhāvanā*, the cognition of *bhāvanā* certainly arises from the verbal suffix. "Like an Apabhraṃśa word" means:

The meaning is as follows: just as corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) are indeed expressive despite the delusion that they are correct, so too, even if they express *bhāvanā* due to the delusion that they are correct, the suffixes such as *tiP* and others would certainly remain incorrect within that *bhāvanā*. One might object: "Since the grammatical injunctions of Pāṇini and others lack any basis of authority, the correctness of *tiP* and other suffixes in expressing *bhāvanā* remains entirely unimpeded. This is not so.

This is because of the authority of the Vedic scripture cited by the author of the Mahābhāṣya: "The Veda with its six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) should be studied and understood by a Brāhmaṇa without [any other] motive," as well as the authority of the Parāśara Upapurāṇa and others: "The great treatise of Pāṇini, which defines the correctness of words, is beneficial to all; it should be grasped in its entirety, and nothing from it should be discarded."

Now, one might object: since we observe the arising of verbal comprehension even in the absence of knowledge of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), it follows that knowledge of correctness is not a cause of verbal comprehension. Nevertheless, because we do not observe the arising of verbal comprehension when there is knowledge of ungrammaticality (*asādhutva*), it must be admitted that knowledge of ungrammaticality acts as an obstacle to verbal comprehension. Consequently, since grammarians possess the cognition that the suffix *tiP* and others are ungrammatical with respect to the sense of "efficient force" (*bhāvanā*), how can *tiP* and the like convey the sense of "efficient force"? To resolve this doubt, he says: "In reality," and so forth.

"By its absence" (*tavdyatirekeṇa*): the meaning is that it refers to the absence of correctness (*sādhutva*), as well as the determination thereof; that is to say, the cognition of incorrectness (*asādhutvajñāna*). The ellipsis "is not an obstacle" (*na pratibandhakam*) is indeed present. Regarding the phrase "we shall explain":

since the arising of comprehension from words such as *gagarya* is established by the experience of everyone—even for those devoid of the cognition of correctness and possessed of the cognition of incorrectness—it will be explained later in the section on the determination of expressive power (*śaktinirṇaya*) under the verse beginning with "the incorrect [is known] through inference" (*asādhuranumānena*) that the cognition of correctness is not the cause [of comprehension], nor is the cognition of incorrectness an obstacle to it. All is auspicious. 21.
Thus ends the first section, the determination of the general meaning of verbal roots and finite verbs, in the commentary on the Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra known as the Śāṅkarī.
In the composition of Śaṅkara, the son of Raṅgabhaṭṭa, the determination of the meaning of verbal roots and finite verbs is complete in the Sārīya commentary. || 1 ||
Now follows the determination of the specific meanings of the *lakāra*s.
