Since there is a rule that the desire to know a specific meaning is necessarily preceded by knowledge of the general meaning, once the general meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has been determined, he begins the determination of the meanings of the specific verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) through the connection of "opportunity" (*avasara-saṃgati*). Thus he says: "Each one" (*pratyekam*). This means "of each one. The sense is that in the *avyayībhāva* compound formed with repetition (*vīpsā*) as "toward each one" (*ekaikaṃ prati*), the genitive case ending is replaced by the form *am*. "Of the ten suffixes" (*daśalakārāṇām*) means "of the ten *lakāras*"; this is a compound according to the rule *dik-saṃkhye saṃjñāyām*.

The meaning is that this [designation] for *laṭ* and the others is like that of the "Seven Sages" (*saptarṣi*). The genitive case in *lakārāṇām* is used in a general sense of relation; it connects with the word *pratyekam* (each one). The sense is: "of each one among the ten *lakāras*. Regarding the word *artham*: it is a singular used for the genus (*jāti*). He explains [the meaning], i.e., he sets forth [the sense]: "in the present," "in the remote past," and so on. With the words "the *laṭ* and others," etc., he states the full meaning of the verse (*kārikā*). He provides the authority for the fact that the state of being present (*vartamānatva*) is the meaning of *laṭ*: "In the present, *laṭ*" (*vartamāne laṭ*).

The term "presentness" (*vartamānatva*) is defined as "the state of being characterized by an action that has begun but not yet been completed. The meaning is: "the state of time characterized by an action that has commenced and remains unfinished. The intention is that presentness, as residing in time, is established by the universal experience of all people. The literal sense of the words is: "the state of time which is the locus of such an action—one that is both begun and not yet finished."

In the Bhāṣya it is stated: "But this present tense [usage] is logical because the action has not yet reached its completion; for one who is necessarily eating, he also laughs, talks, drinks, and blinks. Because these [other actions] are inseparable [from the primary action], they do not constitute an interruption; thus, the usage "he eats" (*bhuṅkte*) is justified even during the state of laughing and so forth. Furthermore, during the time of studying a text that requires many days to complete, various activities such as eating and walking do not constitute an interruption [of the act of studying].

For this very reason, the usage "Devadatta is reading the *saṃhitā*" is appropriate throughout the period from the beginning of the study of the *saṃhitā* until its completion. For this reason as well, he states a simpler definition: "past" (*bhūta*) and so forth. Thus, the meaning is that "presentness" (*vartamānatva*) is the state of being a time distinct from past and future times. In that context, "pastness" should be understood as the state of being a time that is the locus of an action which is the counter-positive of a present destruction; whereas "futurity" is the state of being a time that is the locus of an action which is the counter-positive of a present prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).

And "presentness" (vartamānatva) in the case of destruction (dhvaṃsa) consists in its occurring within the time that serves as the locus for the current usage; in the same way, presentness should also be understood in the case of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva). Furthermore, the time serving as the locus for the current usage—consisting of a watch (prahara), a day (ahna), and so forth—is to be specified according to each particular instance, as it resides in the mind. He applies the definition to the examples, such as "he cooks" (pacati), etc., by stating "from placing [the pot] on the fire," and so on.

"Adhiśrayaṇa" is placing the pot upon the hearth; "ādi" (beginning) refers to that [act]. "Adhaḥśrayaṇa" is removing the pot from the vicinity of the hearth; "anta" (end) refers to that. When two *bahuvrīhi* compounds are thus formed, they constitute a *karmadhāraya*. The referent of the compound (*anyapadārtha*) is the collection of actions. Even in a *karmadhāraya*, that very collection is the substantive. The meaning is "in the midst of such a collection. That is to say, within the interval between the moment the activity conducive to each respective result begins and the moment it concludes.

The meaning is that because the state of being present (*vartamānatva*) in the form described above exists, there is the use of the suffix *laṭ* (the present tense). Now, one might object: "In cases such as 'the self exists' (*ātmāsti*) or 'mountains exist' (*parvatāḥ santi*), the use of *laṭ* is untenable; for since the activity conducive to the self's maintenance is eternal, there is no beginning (*prārabdhatva*), and thus the state of being present—defined as being begun but not yet completed—is impossible. Anticipating this objection, he provides the resolution with the words beginning "the self" (*ātma*).

Because the activities—such as governance and so forth—of the various kings of the past, future, and present are impermanent, being characterized by origination and destruction, there occurs the origination and so forth of the operation conducive to the maintenance of the self as qualified by those [activities]. Taking into account the temporal distinctions of the times of their origination and completion, one superimposes upon the operation conducive to the maintenance of the self residing in the self and so forth the quality of possessing origination and so forth belonging to the royal activities qualified by those respective times; thus, the nature of being commenced but not yet completed [is established].

The state of being present (*vartamānatva*) is to be established by the operation conducive to the maintenance of the self (*ātma-dhāraṇānukūla-vyāpāra*). This is the meaning: although the operation conducive to the maintenance of the self performed by an agent such as a mountain is eternal and thus devoid of origination and so forth, it is nonetheless possible to easily establish its state of being present—in the form of being commenced but not yet completed—because that aforementioned operation, when qualified by royal actions belonging to past, future, and other times, possesses origination and so forth.

Regarding the statement "the self exists," although the self is eternal and devoid of origination and so forth, since the body possesses origination and the like, one may justify the employment of cognitions expressing existence and so forth by postulating origination and the like for the self as qualified by such a body. Thus, even though origination and the like do not exist in the sense of the mere activity conducive to the maintenance of the self, their existence in that [self]—qualified by the aforementioned attributes—is by no means untenable through the medium of those qualifiers; this is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, in the phrase "of that which is qualified by that" (*tadviśiṣṭasya*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers to "impermanence" (*anityatva*), because it immediately precedes it. Thus, the meaning is that the suffix *laṭ* (present tense marker) has that [impermanence] as its referent by superimposing upon it such properties as "presentness" (*vartamānatva*) belonging to the impermanent action. To provide authority for this point, he cites the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *vartamāne laṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.123), stating: "For it has been said: 'The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the root *sthā* [is expressed by the present suffix]'."

Since royal activities are qualified by time through the relation of being located therein (*ādheyatā-sambandha*), the meaning is that time, which is the locus of such activities, is the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) for the activity of staying (*sthiti*) residing in mountains and the like. In other words, there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of the time that is the locus of the king’s activities onto the activity of staying in the mountains and so forth, by means of the relation of being located therein.

In this regard, Kaiyaṭa explains *apathi* as follows: "The stability of kings is differentiated by distinctions such as past and so forth, whereas the stability of mountains and the like is eternal; thus, their nature as action and their connection with the three times are logically established. The meaning is that the nature of being an action and the connection with the three times are established for the stability of mountains and the like.

Otherwise, since the states of remaining [static] such as mountains possess similar constituent parts, it would follow that they could not be considered actions in the sense of being a collection of parts arranged in a temporal sequence (pūrvāparībhūta). Furthermore, because their distinctions would be difficult to discern, a distinction in time would be untenable; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "it is differentiated by another" (*parato bhidyate*): this refers to everything, such as its own existence (*ātmasattā*) and so forth—in other words, the general category of the meaning of verbal roots like *pac* (to cook) and the like. "It is differentiated by another" means it is differentiated precisely by another; that is, it is differentiated by another factor, such as "presentness," in relation to itself.

The self (*ātman*), however—meaning the existence of the self (*ātmasattā*) and so forth—is not differentiated; it does not possess internal differentiation by itself. That which establishes difference must be distinct from the self-existence and so forth, because the difference within that [existence] is difficult to ascertain due to its having similar constituent parts. Since the second [moment] begins immediately after the attainment of the first, and the third after that, the distinction across the three times is well-established through such ascertained differences. The intention is that this is not the case for the existence of the self and so forth.

Therefore—the meaning is precisely because the existence of the self and so forth cannot, by their own nature, establish difference. Regarding the phrase "mountains and so forth" (*parvatādī*): by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the self and others are included. "By the form of another" (*pararūpeṇa*) means that [the mountain] differs by way of the form—that is, the property—of another, such as the king, which consists of an action like [the act of ruling], namely, by its possession of origination and so on. This connects with the statement, "so it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*."

An objection is raised: "In such Vedic passages as 'Darkness existed, enveloped by the unmanifest void,' 'Verily, Nārāyaṇa alone existed,' and 'I alone was first, I exist, and I shall exist,' since the referents of words such as 'darkness' exist eternally, they lack the nature of being past—defined as being the substratum of an action that is the counter-positive of a destruction existing at the present time. Therefore, the use of verbal suffixes denoting past time is untenable. Anticipating this, the author provides the following resolution: "Thus... (evam).

The intended meaning is this: the meaning of the verbal root *pac* (to cook) is a collection of activities in the form of a continuum, delimited by the result of cooked rice, beginning from placing [the pot] on the fire and ending with taking it off. This applies everywhere. And that duration of time in which the activity is completed is the "present. Because of its connection with that, the meaning of the verbal root is "present.

By this, the doubt that there is no "present" because there is no other category apart from the "past" (the completed object) and the "future" (the uncompleted object)—since what is completed is past and what is not yet completed is future—is dispelled.

One might object that since [statements] such as "the mountains stand," "the self exists," and "the rivers flow" involve the standing of mountains and so forth which exist at all times, there is an absence of the past and future; consequently, because the present—which is the opposite of those two—is also absent, the *laṭ* suffix would not apply. Anticipating this doubt, [the author states: the actions of kings existing in the three periods of time—actions such as protecting the realm, which are differentiated by their being past and so forth—are what differentiate the standing of mountains and the like.

Furthermore, since the present existence of the mountains and other things is distinguished by the specific actions of the kings of the present day, and by adopting this principle, the past and future times are also established—such as "the mountains stood in the time of Nala, Duṣyanta, and others," and "the mountains will stand in the time of Kalki and Viṣṇu"—then, just as the state of being past and so forth was proven regarding the stability of the mountains and such, one must likewise prove the state of being past regarding the existence of darkness (*tamas*) and the like.

Now, is it that presentness and so forth are indicated (*dyotya*) by suffixes such as *laṭ*, or are they expressed (*vācya*) by them? Regarding this, the second alternative is not tenable. For if presentness and so forth were indeed expressed by suffixes such as *laṭ*, then since meanings such as the agent (*kartṛ*) are already fulfilled by other *lakāra*s (such as *loṭ* and *liṅ*), presentness and the like would become sublaters (*bādhaka*) of those meanings. This is because a particular [meaning] sublates a general one. Consequently, suffixes such as *laṭ* would not be denoters of the agent and so forth, precisely because the particular sublates the general.

Furthermore, the *laṭ* and other [tense-affixes] would not denote the agent and so forth. Consequently, in cases such as *caitramaitrau pacataḥ* (Caitra and Maitra cook) and *maitrāḥ pacanti* (the Maitras cook), because the agent is not expressed, the duality and plurality residing in that agent would not be perceived, and thus the dual and plural endings would not occur. Moreover, the *śap* and other [augmentative suffixes] would not appear. Since the *laṭ* and others denote [time] such as the present, they would lack the capacity to denote the agent and so forth; consequently, due to the absence of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with [pronominal bases] such as *yuṣmad*, the systematic arrangement of the persons (*puruṣa*) would not be established.

In the sentence *caitraḥ pacati* ("Caitra cooks"), since the agent is not denoted by the suffix *laṭ*, there would arise the undesirable consequence of a third-case ending for the agent due to its being "unexpressed" (*anabhihita*). Therefore, it is more appropriate that presentness and so forth are merely indicated (*dyotya*) by the suffixes *laṭ* and others. Indication (*dyotakatva*) consists in being the indicator of the power residing in the word with which it is co-uttered (*samabhivyāhṛta*). If presentness and so forth were the denotable meanings (*vācya*) of the suffixes *laṭ* and others, the justification would be as follows: the meanings such as the agent are not sublated by the meanings such as presentness, because there is no mutual contradiction between them.

Because two distinct meanings are possible due to the difference in the delimiters of the denotative capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). To explain: in the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* ("*la*-suffixes [denote] the object"), the use of the plural form "*laḥ*" includes all *lakāra* suffixes; thus, even for the *laṭ* and other suffixes, the agent and so forth would become their meanings. Consequently, the delimiter of the denotative capacity for the meaning of the agent and so forth is the property of being a *lakāra* (*lakāratva*), whereas for the meaning of present time and so forth, it is the property of being a *laṭ* (*laṭtva*) and so on—this is the intended sense.

Furthermore, the point is that *lakāratva* (the property of being a verbal suffix) is the delimitor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) with respect to meanings such as the agent, whereas *laṭtva* (the property of being the present tense suffix) and so on are the delimiters with respect to meanings such as present time. Moreover, [if the suffixes were the denoters], the agent and so forth would have no scope; nor could the optative (*liṅ*) and other suffixes serve as their scope, because just like present time and so on, injunction (*vidhi*) and the rest are also expressed by the optative and other suffixes. Thus, although both positions are established in the Bhāṣya, under the view that the suffixes are the denoters, there arises the undesirable consequence that present time and so on would be primary, since they are the meaning of the suffix.

For that reason, one must assume a restriction of the maxim "of the meanings of the base and the suffix" to cases other than those ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). However, under the view that [suffixes] are *dyotaka* (indicative), since there is a rule that the meaning indicated by the suffix is a qualifier, the rule "the meaning of the suffix is primary"—which concerns the meaning expressed by the suffix—does not apply here; thus, there is no occasion for the restriction of the rule. With the intention that the *dyotakatā* (indicative) view is superior due to its parsimony (*lāghava*), he says "And that," etc. The meaning is "presentness" and so forth. It is "indicated."

The suffixes beginning with *laṭ* are indicators (*dyotaka*). Indication consists in being that which awakens the expressive power residing in a verbal root as co-occurring with *laṭ* and the others. And that [awakening] is not possible without the verbal root having expressive power (*śakti*) regarding the present time and so forth. Thus, raising the objection that if one were to postulate the expressive power of many roots there, it would result in the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*), and therefore only the few suffixes themselves should be the denoters (*vācaka*) rather than indicators, he says: "of action in general" (*kriyāsāmānya*).

The meaning is that because time is the substratum of everything, there is a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) of the verbal root—which expresses an action residing in time in general—toward an operation qualified by a specific time such as the present. This qualification of the operation is to be understood through the relation of "being located" (ādheyatā), which is determined by the locus-ness (adhikaraṇatā) residing in times such as the present. Regarding the phrase "by way of indicating the intended meaning": the sense is that in this specific indication, the very function of indicating the intended meaning is what constitutes the expressiveness (dyotakatva) of the suffix *laṭ* and others in the present context.

And thus, since *tiP* and other suffixes are substitutes for *laṭ* and so forth, they indicate the present time and so on; consequently, in cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks") and *apākṣīt* ("he cooked"), there is no cognition of a past action or a present action [as denoted by the suffixes themselves]. Having accepted the position that [suffixes] are denoters (*vācakatā*), he says "anvaya" (positive concomitance). Positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is the presence of B when A is present; negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is the absence of B when A is absent.

Just as the production of a jar is observed when a staff exists and the production of a jar is not observed when a staff is absent—thus, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the staff is established as the cause of the jar—likewise, when the *laṭ* and other suffixes exist, the cognition of "presentness" and so forth arises, as in "he cooks," "he will cook," and "he cooked. Thus, by means of positive and negative concomitance, that form—the form of presentness and so forth—is the meaning expressed by the *laṭ* and other suffixes; this is the sense.

This means that the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*). The signifier is the *laṭ* suffix and so forth. The delimitor of signifierhood (*vācakatāvacchedaka*) is *laṭ*-ness, *liṭ*-ness, and so on; this too is established by experience (*anubhavasiddha*) in the substitutes (*ādeśa*) such as *tiP* for *laṭ*. And it should be understood that, solely by the force of experience, that *laṭ*-ness and so forth is superimposed upon the substitutes such as *tiP*. For this very reason, even in the suffix in the word *yajeta*, there are two parts: the nature of being a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*) and the nature of being an optative (*liṅtva*).

In this regard, the Mīmāṃsā treatise is consistent in stating that verbal cognition (*śābdībhāvanā*) is expressed by the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) through its aspect as an injunctive suffix. This means that there are two aspects, which are the two delimiters of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*) also maintain that in roots such as *pac* (to cook), there are two delimiters of denotative power: the state of being *pac* (*pacyāditva*) and the state of being a root (*dhātutva*). Among these, by virtue of their general form as roots (*dhātutva*), roots such as *pac* express an action (*kriyā*) consisting of an operation conducive to production (*utpattyanukūlavyāpāra*).

However, they say that [grammarians] speak of the action (*kriyā*) as consisting of specific operations such as blowing upon the fire, which result in specific effects such as the softening of rice; this is because otherwise, if the relationship between the signifier and the signified were not determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it would lead to the undesirable consequence of its total disappearance. Furthermore, even in cases such as *pakta* (a cooker), there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the substratum of the agent's operation. Nor is there any pointlessness in rules such as "the *kṛt* suffix denotes the agent" (*kartari kṛt*).

The sense is that, since it is possible for rules such as *kartari kṛt* to function as indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*) when there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of such a meaning in the verbal root (*dhātu*), this would apply everywhere; consequently, the denotative power (*vācakatva*) of suffixes would never be established, and thus the very doctrine [of their denotative power] would be destroyed.

Regarding the rule *parokṣe liṭ* ("the suffix *liṭ* is used for what is beyond the senses"): from the preceding rule *anadyatane laṅ*, the term *anadyatana* (not of today) is understood by anuvṛtti; *bhūte* (in the past) is the governing heading. Furthermore, "being beyond the senses" (*parokṣatva*) is an attribute of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). This word *parokṣa* is well-known as denoting that which is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). Its etymological derivation is as follows: *paraḥ akṣṇaḥ* = *parokṣam*; the compound is formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-class. The suffix *ac* is added at the end of the compound according to the rule *akṣṇo 'rśanāt*.

In this context, the word *akṣi* denotes all the sense organs (*indriya*) and is not a synonym for the eye alone; otherwise, an object perceived by another sense organ would become "indirect" (*parokṣa*). Thus, the meaning of the rule is that the suffix *liṭ* occurs after a verbal root denoting an action that occurred at a time other than today—that is, an indirect action belonging to a past time distinct from the present day. Consequently, in this view, the *liṭ* suffix indicates a past time other than the current day. In the alternative view, however, it is expressed by the *laṭ* suffix.

In this manner, both the indicative (*dyotakatva*) and expressive (*vācakatva*) functions should be understood for all verbal suffixes (*lakāras*). However, regarding the *liṅ* and other suffixes which are devoid of temporal specification, both their indicative and expressive functions are clearly stated in the root text itself. As for the distinction between the "present" (*adyatana*) and "non-present" (*anadyatana*) time: one view holds that the day consisting of the latter half of the past night together with the former half of the coming night is the "present," while that which differs from this is the "non-present."

The second [definition] is that the current day consists of the last third part of the past night together with the first two thirds of the coming night; that which is distinct from this is "non-current" (*anadyatana*). The third [definition] is that the period from sunrise to sunrise is the current day, and that which is distinct from this is "non-current. Regarding the acceptance of any one of these [definitions], the determination is made according to local custom. As for "remoteness" (*parokṣatva*), some say it is occurring a hundred years ago; others say it is occurring a thousand years ago; and others say it is occurring two or three days ago.

Others [hold that] it is being separated by a wall, a mat, or the like; these positions are established in the Bhāṣya. Among them, it should be understood that "remoteness" (*parokṣatva*) is universally agreed upon as being the state of not being within the range of the speaker's senses, because not being within the range of the senses is an unfailing characteristic in all cases. He states the exclusions for each of the three qualifiers—"not today," "in the past," and "remote"—in sequence with the words beginning with "therefore, in the case of today. Thus, [the usage] "He went this very morning" is not [an instance of the remote past].

In this case, although the action of going occurred in the past and was beyond the range of the speaker’s senses, the *liṭ* (perfect) is not used because the past time is considered "recent" (*adyatana*). For example, one does not say *śvo jagāma* ("He went yesterday"). Here, although the action of going is recent, it is not expressed in the *liṭ* because it occurred in the future relative to the time of speaking, and thus lacks the status of being a past event. Furthermore, one does not employ the *liṅ* (conditional) in the sentence *adrākṣamahy ahaṃ gate 'hni prātareva sa jagāma* ("I saw that he had already gone early this morning on the day after yesterday"). Here, although the action of going occurred in a past time that is not recent, the *liṅ* is not used because the action was witnessed by the speaker and thus lacks the quality of being "out of sight" (*parokṣa*).

He defines *parokṣatva* (remoteness from the senses) with the words "I perceive directly" (*sākṣātkaromi*) and so forth. That which possesses an objectivity expressible by such a word as "I perceive directly"—namely, the absence of being the object of such a cognition—is [the definition]. And the cognition is intended here as residing in the speaker. Consequently, the result is that *parokṣatva* is simply the state of not being within the range of the senses of the speaker. Regarding the statement that the word "remote" (*parokṣa*) is a qualifier of the root-meaning, he raises an objection with the words "not indeed" (*na ca*) and so forth. He says: "What is called an action... (*kriyā nāma*).

That collection which is denoted as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), whose constituent parts are subordinate, and which is apprehended by a single cognition that takes as its object the production of a single result from multiple successive operations, is called "action" (*kriyā*) by the experts in the system. Regarding the phrase "this [action]": since this action consists of a collection of multiple successive operations, it is "entirely unseen by another"—that is, it is not an object of knowledge produced by the means of perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). Regarding the phrase "formed into a whole" (*piṇḍībhūta*): [it refers to the fact that these operations are unified].

The intention of the objection is as follows: since the *Bhāṣya* states that [the action] is beyond the range of the senses (*indriyāgocara*) because the parts perish so rapidly that there is no such thing as a "massed whole" (*piṇḍībhāva*) which could serve as an illustration, the qualification "beyond the senses" (*parokṣa*) is redundant. Regarding the term "non-excluding" (*avyāvartaka*): if, however, some action were perceptible (*pratyakṣa*), then the qualification "beyond the senses" would indeed be meaningful for the purpose of excluding such actions from the scope of the optative suffix (*liṅ*).

The sense is that, since all action is imperceptible (*parokṣa*), such [a rule] would be ineffective because there is nothing to be excluded. He provides the solution with the words "of that which has become a mass" (*piṇḍībhūtāyāḥ*) and so forth. Because the parts are momentary, their combination is absolutely impossible; thus, since a "mass" (*piṇḍa*) does not exist at all, it is impossible to point to it as a "mass. Nevertheless, although each individual part can be the object of such worldly cognition as "I perceive [this]," in order to exclude the use of the optative (*liṅ*) for an action perceived by the speaker through its parts, [the rule applies].

The sense is that [the whole] is therefore meaningful. He states the proof for the perceptibility of the parts with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). This means that in the opposite case of what was stated, there would be no perceptibility even for the parts. In the expression "Look, the deer is running," the act of running performed by the deer would not possess the status of being the object (*karman*) of the act of seeing. And thus, in such a usage, the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatva*) accepted in the *Bhāṣya* would be untenable; this is the sense. Now, one might object: even the parts delimited by moments (*kṣaṇa*) are indeed imperceptible.

Since, just as with the subtlety of an object, the fact of being delimited by subtle time must also necessarily act as an obstacle to perception, direct perception is impossible. Furthermore, the meaning of the Bhāṣya statement "never seen before" (*atyantāparadṛṣṭa*) is simply that it has never been perceived by the means of direct perception, either in its form as a whole or in its form as individual parts. Therefore, like the motion of the sun, every action is to be inferred solely from its effects, such as conjunction with a subsequent location.

In the expression "paśya mṛgo dhāvati" ("see, the deer runs"), since the root *dṛś* is accepted as having the general sense of cognition (*jñāna-sāmānya*), and because the running is inferred from the observation of its successive conjunctions with different locations, Nāgeśabhaṭṭa has stated in the *Laghumañjūṣā* that running is there merely an object of inference (*anumiti-viṣaya*). Following that, he demonstrates the meaningfulness of the word *parokṣa* (indirect) by saying: "of those [actions] characterized by the operation (*vyāpārāviṣṭānām*)."

In this context, what is intended by "remoteness" (pārokṣya) is precisely the remoteness of those means conducive to action that are qualified by an operation; thus, the qualification "remote" applies to the factor of action (kāraka) as qualified by its operation, and not to the action which is the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha). This is because that [action], being beyond the senses, is unfit for perception produced by the external senses, just like an atom.

Therefore, the meaning of the rule *parokṣe liṭ* ("the suffix *liṭ* occurs when there is something beyond the range of sight") is as follows: the suffix *liṭ* occurs after a verbal root that denotes an action residing in someone like Devadatta who is characterized by such an operation (vyāpāra) belonging to the past time other than the current day (*anadyatana-bhūta-kālika*) and who is not within the range of sight (*parokṣa*). Consequently, even though Caitra—who is not engaged in the operation of cooking—is perceptible, there is no inconsistency in the usage "Caitra cooked" (*caitraḥ papāca*), because the one engaged in the operation of cooking is beyond the range of sight; this is the intended sense. Thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply.

The meaning is that since the word *parokṣa* (past tense marker) serves the purpose of precluding the usage "this [Devadatta] cooked" when the agent—such as Devadatta—is directly perceived as being engaged in the activity (*vyāpāra*) of the means of action, there is no fault of its being non-excludent (*avyāvartakatva*). He states the purpose of the phrase "engaged in the activity" with the example "this cooked. The point is that the *liṭ* suffix is desired only when the one engaged in the activity is perceptible, and not when the one not engaged in the activity is perceptible.

Thus, the use of the *liṭ* suffix (the perfect tense) in the expression "Caitra cooked" (*caitraḥ papāca*) occurs only in cases where the agent is not an object of the speaker's direct perception. For when the speaker has directly perceived the agent of a past action—such as the act of going—prepared with a horse and so forth, with his girdle fastened and ready to depart, he does not use the form "He went" (*jagāma*), because the goer, being occupied with the activity and having his girdle fastened, lacks the quality of being beyond the speaker's direct perception (*parokṣatva*).

But when one perceives the agent of such actions as going and so forth as being directly present, yet not permeated by that action, then the suffix *liṭ* (the perfect tense) occurs, as in "he went" (*jagāma*). The intended meaning is that this is because the goer, while permeated by the action, is [otherwise] beyond the range of perception.

Although action (*kriyā*) is not a [direct] means of cognition (*pratyaya*), since the knowledge of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is a cause for the knowledge of the qualified (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), it is indeed difficult to establish the perception of a means (*sādhana*) qualified by such an action, because that action, being a qualifier, lacks perceptibility; and thus its futility remains as it was. Nevertheless, it should be understood that this stated fault does not apply, because at the time of the qualification by actions such as blowing (*phūtkāra*) or hissing (*sītkāra*), what is intended is the imperceptibility (*parokṣatva*) of the means at the time of the performance of the rite.

Where the substance that serves as the substratum for the power of the means (sādhana-śakti)—characterized by hissing, sighing, and so forth, and possessing an excited form—is perceptible, there ordinary people have the misconception (*abhimāna*) that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) itself is perceptible. This misconception is a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*); it is for the purpose of excluding this that the term "imperceptible" (*parokṣa*) is employed. This is the sense. Furthermore, it should be understood that in the view of the ancients, imperceptibility is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root, whereas in the view of the moderns, it is a qualifier of the means to the meaning of the verbal root. Between these, the first view alone is appropriate.

Because, if one were to resort to a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) for the governing rule *yataḥ dhātoḥ*, the relationship would be "being denoted by its own [verbal] root"; whereas if one were to resort to a figurative indication of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the relationship would be "being a means of accomplishment denoted by its own [verbal] root"—this latter view is more cumbersome. Furthermore, the claim that "all action is beyond perception" (*parokṣā*) is not a valid differentiator, because even if the aggregate is beyond perception, each individual constituent part is not.

For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* specifically demonstrates that "being congealed (*piṇḍībhūtā*) cannot be illustrated," showing that it is precisely that which is congealed that cannot be pointed out. For this same reason, in the sentence "Look, the deer is running" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*), it is universally established that the action of running alone functions as the object (*karman*) of the act of seeing. Nor should it be argued that each [moment] individually lacks the nature of an action; for even by that much, its status as the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) remains unimpaired. Furthermore, even a result (*phala*) possesses the nature of an action through the superimposition of temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*) belonging to the operation (*vyāpāra*) that produces it.

For this very reason, in expressions such as *taṇḍulaḥ svayameva* ("the rice cooks by itself"), its designation as a verbal root (*dhātu*) is established when it denotes the mere result (*phala*). It appears that even "imperceptibility" (*parokṣatva*), as stated in the Bhāṣya, is compatible with action (*kriyā*). An objection is raised: "If that is so, how can the periphrastic future (*liṅ*) be justified when the action, or the means (*sādhana*) qualified by the action, is perceptible? This refers to the example: *udayanaḥ kiraṇāvalīṃ vyātene* ("Udayana composed the *Kiraṇāvalī*"). The meaning is "he spread out" (*vitastare*), based on the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) that the root *tanu* signifies expansion (*vistāra*).

He states the reason for this with the words "of its own action" (*svakriyāyāḥ*). The meaning is that since the agent Udayana—who is the performer of the act of rising—is necessarily perceptible, there is no lack of direct perception (*pārokṣya*) regarding the act of rising; therefore, the use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is inappropriate. Alternatively, in the view that the indirectness pertains to the means (*sādhana*), the reason should be understood as follows: because the means as qualified by the action is directly perceived by oneself.

But surely, even when one's own activity is not personally recollected due to distraction or attachment to another object during its present state, the *liṭ* suffix still occurs when that activity is inferred from its effect—as in: "I indeed spoke much before him while intoxicated."

If it is argued that—just as in the previous case there is a remoteness of the action due to the mind being absent because of excessive joy and so forth, so too here, due to distraction in the form of wandering toward other objects, it is possible for the activity performed by Udayana and the instrument qualified by that activity to possess a "remoteness" consisting in their not being objects of Udayana’s direct perception; therefore, there is no inconsistency in the use of the *liṭ* (perfect tense)—we say: no. Even if one could somehow establish the remoteness of one's own activity, it is impossible to establish therein both its non-recentness (*anadyatana*) and its pastness (*atītatva*); thus, the *liṭ* remains indeed inconsistent. This is what he states in the words: "bahutaramanaḥpraṇīti" (due to the leading of the mind elsewhere).

The meaning is that it is entirely impossible to establish both the state of being "non-recent" (*anadyatana*)—defined as a time that is the locus of an action whose destruction is not contemporaneous with today—and the state of being "past" (*bhūtatva*)—defined as a time which is the locus of an action whose destruction is contemporaneous with the present—within the act of composing a work consisting of a collection of sentences intended to produce a determination of the meaning of the scriptures, which is achieved through an intense mental application (*manas-praṇidhāna*), that is, the one-pointedness of the mind. Therefore, the use of the *liṭ* (perfect tense) in the word "vyātene," which signifies non-recent past time, is indeed inappropriate. This is because [such a composition] is impossible.

The intention is that [the use of the perfect tense] is impossible because there is an absence of non-difference from the present day—due to its being delimited by an activity conducive to the expansion of the *Kiraṇāvalī*—and because there is an absence of connection with past time. However, forms such as *vyātene* (he spread) are justified through the superimposition (*āropa*) of the properties of pastness, non-present-tense-ness, and non-evidentness (*parokṣatva*). The purpose of this superimposition, however, is to convey that the work is very easy to compose and can be quickly completed.

The fruit of that [study] is the joy experienced by students who are eager to understand this treatise, which has the ascertainment of the true nature of categories (*padārtha*) as its result; this and more should be kept in mind in the *Mañjūṣā*. In cases where roots such as *kṛ* (to do) and *bhū* (to become) are not employed, the meaning of unapplied *kṛt* and *bhū* roots is "action in general" (*kriyāsāmānya*), which is to say, the substratum of the general property of action-ness (*kriyātva*). However, for the base of the suffix *ām*, the meaning is each specific action (*kriyāviśeṣa*). There is a relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the general and the particular.

And thus, in the case of *edhāṃcakre*, the understanding (*bodha*) should be known as follows: "An action non-different from growth, which has as its locus a single Caitra who is not different [from the agent], which is based on past non-contemporary time, and which possesses indirectness (*pārokṣya*). Alternatively, the understanding is: "An action non-different from growth, which has as its locus a Caitra qualified by singularity and indirectness, and which is based on past non-contemporary time. He states the meaning of the suffix *luṅ* [as] "in non-contemporary [time], *luṅ*," according to the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.111]. From the rule [Pāṇini 3.3.3], "In the future, *gam* and so forth," the word "future" (*bhaviṣyati*) is carried over [as an anuvṛtti].

The term *dhātoḥ* (from a verbal root) is understood as a governing heading (*adhikṛtam*). The phrase "future not belonging to the current day" (*bhaviṣyadanadyatane*) is construed with the action denoted by the verbal root (*dhātvarthakriyā*). Thus, its meaning is: *luṅ* [the aorist suffix] occurs after a verbal root that denotes an action occurring at a time in the future not belonging to the current day. The meaning of the word "not belonging to the current day" (*anadyatana*) has been explained previously in the sūtra on *liṭ* [the perfect tense]. Future-ness (*bhaviṣyattva*), moreover, is the state of being a time that is the locus of an action which is the counter-positive of the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of the present. An example is: "The jar will exist tomorrow" (*ghaṭaḥ śvo bhavitā*).

In this context, since the existence residing in the jar (*ghaṭaniṣṭhasattā*) is to occur on a future day, there exists today the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of such existence; thus, the action which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of that present prior non-existence—namely, the existence residing in the jar—is "future-ness," defined as the temporality (*kālatva*) consisting of the day on which such existence has its locus. The resulting cognition is: "existence having as its locus a single jar, which is not distinct [from the jar], and which has as its substratum a time other than the current day."

Now, an objection is raised: it is incorrect to say in the *kārikā* that "it will happen tomorrow" (*śvo bhāvinī*), because the meaning of the word "tomorrow" (*śvas*) is the immediately following day; thus, since the usage of forms such as *paktā* (the cooker) is accepted even for cooking and other acts occurring on the third day or beyond, the essential meaning of "it will happen tomorrow" is stated to be "it will happen at a time not belonging to the current day. In this way, the intention is that the mention of "tomorrow" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for any non-current day.

And thus, in the case of "caitraḥ taṇḍulaṃ pakṣyati" (Caitra will cook the rice), the understanding is that there is an action which resides in the rice, is conducive to its softening (*viklitti*), has a locus non-different from Caitra alone, and pertains to a future time not belonging to the current day. Regarding the meaning of the suffix *lṛṭ*, he says: "future in general. This means simply futurity pertaining to both the current and the non-current day. He states the authority for this: "lṛṭ śeṣe ca" (Pāṇini 3.3.13). The term "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) is supplied by context. The recurring term "future" (*bhaviṣyati*) is construed with the action, which is the meaning of the root.

In the preceding sūtra, there was a specification of meaning (*arthanirdeśa*) stating "when [another] action is for the sake of an action. Consequently, the term *śeṣa* (the remainder) refers to cases where such an action for the sake of another action is absent; however, by virtue of the word *ca* ("and"), it is understood that it also applies when such an action is present. Thus, the meaning is: the suffix *lṛṭ* occurs after a verbal root denoting an action occurring in the future time, whether or not there is an action for the sake of which that action exists. An example is *ghaṭo bhaviṣyati* ("the pot will be"). The cognition [arising from this] is: an act of becoming (*bhavanakriyā*) occurring in the future time, whose locus (*āśraya*) is non-different from a single pot.

"And *tattvam*" means "and the state of being future. This should be understood as follows: even for the non-remote future (*anadyatana-bhaviṣyat*), when there is merely a desire to express "futurity" in general, only the suffix *lṛṭ* is used. For example: "You will become a Manu named Sāvarṇika on earth," and so forth. Similarly, even for the remote past (*anadyatana-bhūta*), when there is merely a desire to express "pastness" in general, the suffix *luṅ* is used. For example: "There was a king named Suratha," and so forth. [Objection: Let the rule simply be "lṛṭ"; let "śeṣe ca" not be stated.

If it is argued that the rule *bhaviṣyadarthāddhātor lṛṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.15) alone is sufficient for the establishment of the *lṛṭ* suffix—whether or not there exists an action intended for the sake of another action—this is not so. For in cases such as *śayiṣyata iti sthīyate* ("He stays [thinking], 'He will lie down'"), since there is an action intended for the sake of another action, the *lṛṭ* would be superseded by the *tumun* suffix according to the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyām...* (Pāṇini 3.3.10). Nor can it be said that the *lṛṭ* is established by the rule of "optionality regarding dissimilar forms" (*vāsarūpavidhi*), because the application of the *vāsarūpavidhi* is prohibited in the case of *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and affixes having the sense of *khala*.

In the expression *śayiṣyata*, the suffix *lṛṭ* denotes the abstract action (*bhāve*). The word *iti*, however, indicates the connection between the two [the action and the agent]. Thus, the understanding is: "a state of remaining, performed by me, which has lying down at a future time as its result. He states the authority for the fact that the *liṅ* (optative) and other moods have the sense of injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth by saying: "The *leṭ* occurs in the sense of the *liṅ*. Now, even if the *leṭ* is prescribed in the sense of the *liṅ*, how can it have the meaning of injunction and so forth? To this he says: "And the sense of the *liṅ* is injunction and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of invitation (*nimantraṇa*) and the others mentioned in that sūtra.

He states the meaning of the *loṭ* [suffix] as "prayer" (*prārthanā*). This is a partial citation (*pratīka*) for the rule beginning with "prārthanādau. Intending to show that the term is used both as a *tatpuruṣa* compound—meaning "the beginning of prayer"—and as a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that which has prayer as its beginning"—he says, "by 'ādi' [is meant] injunction (*vidhi*), etc., and benediction (*āśis*). He provides the authority for this point by citing "in the sense of benediction, the *liṅ* and *loṭ* [are used]," and so forth. "From such understanding" means from the understanding that the *loṭ* has the senses of injunction, etc., and benediction. He gives an example concerning benediction: "May there be for you the grace of Śiva."

*Āśis* (benediction) is a desire in the form of a wish (*āśaṃsana*) directed toward an auspicious object such as happiness; it resides in the speaker of the word ending in the *loṭ* or *liṅ* suffixes. Such a desire is construed with the action qualified by its *kārakas* through the relation of objective content (*viṣayatā*). Thus, the cognition is: "The coming-into-being [of you] is the object of a desire in the form of a wish, whose agent is the person desiring an auspicious object such as happiness, and which has Śiva—related to you—as its agent and grace as its agent. Since the meanings of terms such as *vidhi* (injunction) have not yet been determined, it should be understood that no examples of them are presented here.

[Objection: But if injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth are not determined, how can the meanings of the *leṭ* and *loṭ* [moods] be determined? To this he says: "Of these two. The meaning is that the meaning of the *liṅ* itself is the meaning of the *leṭ* and *loṭ*. [Regarding the phrase] "by its determination": the meaning is that by the very determination of the meaning of the *liṅ*, the determination of the meanings of the *leṭ* and *loṭ* will come about. The intention is that the determination of the meaning of the *liṅ* will be carried out in the sūtra prescribing the *liṅ* for injunction, invitation, and so forth. (22)

Regarding the phrase "laṅ-ādi" (the *laṅ* and others): by the word "others" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *liṅ*, *luṅ*, and *lṛṅ* is intended. Regarding the term "of those having the marker *ṅ*" (*ṅitām*): this means of the four [tenses] beginning with *laṅ* that have the phoneme *ṅ* as their technical designation (*itsaṃjñaka*). Demonstrating the meaning, he says: "in the sense of yesterday, in the past, in instigation, and so forth. Since the meaning of the word "yesterday" (*hyaḥ*) is the immediately preceding past day, if one intends to express that meaning, the *laṅ* would not be desired even when the action occurred two or more days ago; therefore, with the intention that it serves as an indicator for the remote past (*anadyatana-bhūta*), he says: "in the remote past" (*anadyatane bhūte*).

He states the authority for [the term *bhūta*] being an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) by citing the rule "the *laṅ* suffix is used for the non-current past" (*anadyatane laṅ*). Here, the terms "from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) and "past" (*bhūte*) are supplied as governing rules (*adhikṛta*). "Non-current" (*anadyatana*) is a qualifier of "past" (*bhūta*), and "past" (*bhūta*) is a qualifier of the action denoted by the verbal root. Thus, the meaning is that the *laṅ* suffix occurs after a verbal root that expresses an action occurring at a time within the non-current past. And "pastness" has already been defined as "the time which is the locus of an action whose counter-positive is a present destruction. He provides an example: "his son is... (*asya putraḥ*).

And when *laṅ* is employed, it is appropriate that the action—having occurred on the very day prior to the birth of the son due to its being fully accomplished—is situated in the non-remote past time (*anadyatana-bhūta-kāla*), which consists in its being the counter-positive of a destruction existing in the present. Thus, the cognition [resulting] is: "An operation conducive to birth, pertaining to a non-remote past time, having as its locus a single son not different from this [subject]. Regarding the fact that *vidhi* (injunction), *nimantraṇā* (invitation), and so forth are the meanings of the optative (*liṅ*), he states the authoritative source: "Injunction, invitation," etc. (*vidhi-nimantraṇā-ityādi*).

The meaning is that when meanings such as injunction (*vidhi*) are to be indicated (*dyotya*) or expressed (*vācya*), the *liṅ* suffix should occur after a verbal root; this is the sense of the phrase "for the sake of that" (*tadarthāt*). Both positions—that injunctions and so forth are indicated or that they are expressed—are established in the *Bhāṣya*. Regarding the position that they are indicated, the justification is as follows: it is inappropriate for injunctions and so forth to be the expressed meaning of the *liṅ* suffix. For if that were the case, since the meanings of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth are already fulfilled by other tense-suffixes (*lakāra*) such as the *laṭ*, injunctions and the like would become sublated [by those other suffixes].

Furthermore, the *liṅ* suffix would not denote the agent and so forth. Consequently, in cases such as "Caitra and Maitra should be" (*caitramaitrau bhavetām*), because the agent is not manifested, there would be no cognition of the duality residing therein, and thus the dual and plural endings would not occur. Since the *sārvadhātuka* affix would lack the sense of the agent, the addition of *śap* and other markers would be untenable. And since the *liṅ* denotes meanings such as injunction (*vidhi*) rather than denoting the agent and so forth, there would be no fixed rule for person (*puruṣa-vyavasthā*), as the pronouns *yuṣmad* and others do not denote the grammatical participant (*kāraka*) expressed by the verbal suffix.

Furthermore, in the examples from *Nirukta*, the absence of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) and others—which would otherwise be required by the state of being "struck" (*abhihata*)—would not be established; therefore, it is more appropriate that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth signify [the agent and other grammatical relations]. If, however, they were the expressed meaning (*vācya*), the justification would be as follows: the agent and other factors are not sublated by the optative suffix and the like, because there is no mutual contradiction between them, and because both meanings are possible due to the difference in the delimiters of their expressive capacities (*śaktatāvacchedaka*).

For instance, in the rule *laḥ karmaṇi*, by the use of the plural form *laḥ*, all *lakāra*s are included; thus, even for the *liṅ* [optative], the meanings such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth would indeed be applicable. Consequently, the intended sense is that while *lakāratva* (the property of being a *lakāra*) is the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) with respect to the meanings of the agent and so on, *liṅtva* (the property of being a *liṅ*) is the delimitor with respect to the meanings of injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth. Furthermore, the meanings such as the agent are themselves without scope [elsewhere]. Nor can the *laṭ* and other [present tense] suffixes be considered their scope; this should be understood because, just like injunctions and the like, the present time (*vartamānatva*) and so forth are also denoted by the *laṭ* and other suffixes.

Furthermore, in cases such as *atha api bhavet*, the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*), being the meaning of the suffix, would have the status of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Consequently, the method of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*)—in which the meaning of the verbal root is the primary qualificand, namely: "the coming-into-being (becoming) which has as its locus a single Caitra who is non-different [from the agent], and which is the object of the injunction"—would be untenable. This is because the consequence of the suffix-meaning being the qualificand applies equally to the agent (*kartṛ*) and other such factors as well.

If it is argued that in verbal forms (*ākhyāta*), the general rule—that the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is primary and the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is a qualifier—is set aside in accordance with the *Bhāṣya* statement "the verb has action as its primary meaning" (*bhāvapradhānam ākhyātam*), then one should note that for this very reason there is no fault. He explains the meanings of the words "injunction" (*vidhi*) and so forth with the word "therein" (*tatra*). This means "among those [categories], such as injunctions. "Instigation" (*preraṇā*) means "impelling" (*pravartana*). And impelling is an operation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to activity.

Just as the instigation of a lowly servant or the like by a master toward what the master desires is precisely an *ājñā* (command); whereas the instigation of one who has not yet acted—toward an end desired by him but for which the means are unknown—is *upadeśa* (instruction), such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," and so forth, or the words of a trustworthy person, "Go by this path. That too is indeed a *vidhi* (injunction). In the former case, heaven is the desired object.

The meaning is this: for an agent such as Devadatta who has not yet begun to act, that which is desired—namely heaven—is the object to be attained; and regarding the means to attain that [heaven], which is unknown, there is the sacrifice (*yāga*). This sentence effects the instigation of Devadatta toward such a sacrifice, which serves as the means for attaining heaven; thus, this too is an injunction (*vidhi*). In the latter case, the attainment of Kāśī and so forth is the desired end, and the rest should be inferred accordingly. Regarding the phrase "of an inferior person such as a servant": the mention of "inferiority" is stated in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases where one instigates persons who are equal to or superior to oneself.

And thus, the sense is that there is no status as an injunction (*vidhi*) in those cases. To indicate that being inferior is intended by virtue of being one who is commanded, the phrase "of a servant, etc. is used; therefore, the instigation of a servant who is older than oneself constitutes precisely an injunction (*vidhi*). "Carrying out a commission" (*niyogakaraṇam*) means the incitement of a grandson (*dauhitraka*) or similar person toward a necessary task such as eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony, which is desired by oneself. "Entreaty" (*āmantraṇam*) means the incitement of a grandson or similar person toward something desired by oneself, where they may proceed according to their own will. Thus ends the section on "entreaty."

The meaning is: the instigation of one who is to be prompted to act according to his own desire regarding what he himself wishes for. And this "acting according to one's desire" belongs solely to the one being prompted. This very thing is the permission to act according to one's desire (*kāmacārānujñā*). Permission is the statement that prompts the one being employed—who has already begun acting—by preventing his withdrawal, for the sake of his welfare; it takes such forms as "I am having you do what has been started," or "Act in such a way that it is beneficial. This is merely an illustration of all such forms of address. Regarding the term *adhīṣṭa* (request/respectful command): it means preceded by honor.

The meaning is: engaging someone in a great task that is appropriate for them after having honored them. For example: "Teach the drummer. This is precisely what is meant by *abhyarthanā* (entreaty). *Prārthanā* (petition), however, is a statement that prompts the giving of a desired object and so forth. *Saṃpraśna* (inquiry) is deliberation; it is the desire for a decision regarding one of two alternatives. For example: "O sir, shall I study the Vedas or logic? These four [are the types of *ākṣepa*].

Among the four—starting with injunction (*vidhi*) and ending with authorization (*adhīṣṭa*)—that which is woven through and follows them all is the nature of being an instigation (*pravartanātva*), a generality residing in instigation. It must be accepted that the denotability of these four is by means of that very form, because there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in its being the delimiting factor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*); it is not, however, by way of their respective specific forms such as "injunction-ness" (*vidhitva*) and so on, because there would be prolixity (*gaurava*) in their being the delimiting factors of denotability.

The point is as follows: although it is established by the experience of all people that the injunctions and so forth are understood from prescriptive sentences such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), there is complexity (*gaurava*) if these are held to be denotable in their respective specific forms, because the denotability-restrictor (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) would then be manifold due to the multiplicity of those specific forms. However, if they are denotable as "impulsion" (*pravartanātva*), since impulsion-ness is a single entity, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating that as the denotability-restrictor. Therefore, it is appropriate that the injunctions and so forth are denotable precisely as impulsion.

In order to demonstrate the conformity with the *Vākyapadīya* regarding this point, he says: "And it has been stated. This means: in the verse of Bhartṛhari (*Harikārikā*). "Of the nature of instigation" (*pravartanārūpam*) means: the form of instigation, that is, the state of being an instigation (*pravartanātva*).

Since the property of being an instigation (*pravartanātva*) is present in all four [categories] beginning with injunction (*vidhi*), it is therefore appropriate—according to the literal reading—to enjoin the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as possessing that very property of instigation; for according to the principle of the section on generic form (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*), the expressive power resides in the property itself. As for the phrase "what is the use of the distinction?": the meaning is that there is no purpose whatsoever in wishing to express a distinction based on their mutual separateness in terms of their respective specific forms.

On the contrary, the intention is that the desire to express a distinction is itself burdened by the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*). Now, if this is so, why did the author of the Sūtras take the four [categories] separately? He states their underlying intention: "for the purpose of explaining the principles" (*nyāyavyutpādanāya*). "Principle" (*nyāya*) refers to the specific grounds for the application of each respective term, such as injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth; the meaning is that it is for the sake of understanding those. In other words, it is for the purpose of making known the distinctions within the process of instigation (*pravartanā*). But one might object: "Could that not be understood through worldly usage alone? To this he replies: "for the sake of elaboration" (*prapañcārtham*).

The meaning is that while the understanding of instigation (*pravartanā*) through worldly convention is easily accessible for those of superior capacity, it is difficult to comprehend for those of middling or lower capacity; therefore, the four [authorities] are mentioned in the Sūtra so that they may have a clear comprehension. Regarding the term *pravartanātva*: the word *pravartanā* is derived from the root *vṛt* with the prefix *pra*, followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*, and then the suffix *yuc* according to the rule *ṇyāsa-śrantho yuc*; its meaning is a specific activity conducive to engagement (*pravṛtti*).

Since that specific operation is not observed to produce activity by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), it must be stated that its capacity to produce activity occurs only through the mediation of the knowledge that the object of activity is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatvajñānatva*). Otherwise, if the object of activity were not known to be a means to a desired end, activity would be impossible. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: *pravartanātva* (the state of being an instigation) is precisely that form which serves as the delimiting property (*avacchedakatva*) of the objective content (*viṣayatā*) belonging to the knowledge that generates activity.

"And that" (tacceti) means: and being the delimitor of the objectness (*viṣayatāvacchedakatva*) belonging to the cognition that generates activity. "That alone" (tadeveti) means: only the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). By the word "alone" (*eva*), the state of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and so forth are excluded. The phrase "is to be known as the meaning of the injunction" (*vidhyartho jñeyaḥ*) is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). If it is argued: "One must necessarily admit that the cognition of being achievable through effort is also a cause of activity, just like the cognition of being a means to a desired end; for this very reason, the absence of activity toward such things as the bringing of Mount Sumeru—which cannot be achieved by effort—is logically accounted for," [the author] says: "Even though... (*yadyapi...*) and so on. "This" (*etad*) refers to...

The meaning is: "being the delimitor of the objecthood of the ignorance that generates activity. The phrase "of [the property of] being achievable by effort" is also [to be understood]; the word "exists" is the ellipsis. He states the reason for its existence: "of the knowledge of that" (tajjñānasya). The meaning is: because activity is observed even from the knowledge of being achievable by effort. He refutes the view that the knowledge of being achievable by effort is the cause of activity: "nevertheless" (tathāpi). [This is known] "from common worldly experience alone" (lokata eva).

The meaning is: [the knowledge of the means to an end] arises solely from worldly means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) known as inference (anumāna), such as "sacrifice is achievable by my effort, because it is not pervaded by any property that is incompatible with being achievable by my effort. Regarding the phrase "it is understood": the meaning is that in every case, such as sacrifice, the state of being achievable by effort is understood through inference. However, the fact that sacrifice and the like are means for achieving a desired end, such as heaven, cannot be understood through worldly means of valid cognition; rather, it can only be understood through the Veda. Therefore, the point is that the postulation of [Vedic] potency (śakti) is necessary for you.

Others, however, maintain that the cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) is not the motivator; for there is no activity toward what is ascertained to be unachievable through effort, because—due to the absence of the desired object—one feels aversion toward it as being a cause of futile exertion. Thus, since the property of being achievable through effort is obtainable from other sources, it cannot be the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), according to the maxim that "the meaning of a word is that which is not obtainable otherwise. This is the intended sense.

[Objection: Surely, in order to prevent activity toward such things as eating food mixed with honey and poison, it must be postulated that the cognition of not producing a powerful undesirable result is also a cause of activity; and thus, in that case as well, the denotative power of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is necessary. To this, he says: "balavadaniṣṭa... and so forth. The meaning is: "the cognition of not producing a powerful undesirable result. "Is not the cause" means: "is not a cause of activity."

Now, one might object: since even sacrifices, cooking, and the like produce undesirable suffering as an unavoidable concomitant (nāntarīyaka), how could there be any inclination toward them? To this it is said: "powerful" (balavat). Thus, although sacrifices, cooking, and so forth may produce some slight undesirable effect such as minor pain, because they lack a greater degree of suffering than pleasure, there is indeed an inclination toward them due to their not producing a powerful undesirable result. The point is that a "powerful undesirable result" is defined as suffering that exceeds pleasure.

He states the reasoning for the fact that the cognition of not producing a powerful undesirable result is not a cause of activity: "because it is otherwise established by the absence of aversion. The meaning is this: it must necessarily be admitted that the absence of an obstacle is a cause with respect to every effect; otherwise, the non-occurrence of the production of a jar—even when the entire collection of required causes, such as the wheel, the staff, and the potter, is present—would be inexplicable.

If, however, the absence of an obstacle (*pratibandhakābhāva*) is the cause [of action], then in that case, because the potter has suddenly been afflicted by a specific disease such as flatulence (*āmavāta*), there is the presence of an obstacle in the form of his body becoming inert; thus, the non-perception of the production of the jar is logically accounted for. In the case of eating food mixed with honey and poison, since there exists an excess of suffering in the form of death—which outweighs the pleasure of satiety—there is an absence of inclination due to the presence of an obstacle in the form of aversion toward such suffering.

However, where there is an absence of such an obstacle, activity certainly occurs. For example, in the case of sacrifices and the like—which are accomplished through great effort, expenditure of wealth, and so forth—although they produce a great deal of suffering, since there is no deficiency in that suffering relative to the pleasure of heaven, there is an absence of aversion; and because of this absence of aversion as an obstacle, activity proceeds without hindrance.

And thus, since the occurrence of activity is established through the absence of aversion (i.e., the absence of an obstacle), it need not be accepted that the cognition of "not producing a powerful undesired result" (*balavadaniṣṭājanakatvajñāna*) is the cause of activity. The point is that because this [cognition] is otherwise accounted for by the absence of an obstacle—since its purpose is already served—one should not postulate the cognition of "not producing a powerful undesired result" as a separate cause of activity. Furthermore, the relationship of cause and effect is determined by experts through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

The meaning is as follows: although there is no deviation from the positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*), there is a deviation from negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*). This is because we observe that even when there is the cognition that an action produces a powerful undesirable result such as falling into hell, a lustful believer who is blinded by passion may still engage in sexual intercourse with another's beautiful wife due to the intensity of his desire; this is seen through the postulation of an absence of aversion (*dveṣābhāva*). Thus, due to this deviation from negative concomitance—wherein the effect exists despite the absence of the cause—it is impossible for the cognition that "the act does not produce a powerful undesirable result" to be the cause of engagement (*pravṛtti*).

The positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is that the existence of activity occurs precisely when there is the cognition that [the action] does not produce a powerful undesirable result. The negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is that in the absence of the cognition that [the action] does not produce a powerful undesirable result (i.e., when there is the cognition that it *does* produce a powerful undesirable result), there is an absence of activity. It should be understood that "deviation in the negative concomitance" (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) consists in the presence of the effect despite the absence of the cause; for instance, in the case of desiring another's beautiful wife, although the cause—the cognition that it does not produce a powerful undesirable result—is absent, the effect—activity—is present. Thus, there is deviation.

By the use of the term "believer" (*āstika*) here, it is indicated that there must necessarily be the presence of the knowledge that approaching another's wife is a cause for hell. By the phrase "with intense desire," it is indicated that the absence of aversion in that case is merely an error. By this, the following [objection] is refuted: "Where there is the knowledge that something produces a powerful undesirable result, there aversion is certain; however, where there is an absence of aversion, activity is rightly explained by the presence of the knowledge that it does not produce a powerful undesirable result—thus, there is no deviation from the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*)."

The meaning is that, in that case, the absence of aversion would itself be of the nature of an error. And thus, since in reality there exists the cognition that [the act] produces a powerful undesirable consequence, even though the cause—which is the cognition that it does not produce a powerful undesirable consequence—is absent, we observe the activity of a believer in approaching another's beautiful wife; therefore, the intention is that there is a firm instance of deviation in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*).

And thus, since the state of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) is understood through inference, and since the state of not producing a powerful undesirable result (*balavadaniṣṭājanakatva*) is of no use for initiating action, he states "Therefore," etc., that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is simply the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). Regarding "incitement" (*pravartanā*), the meaning is "the meaning of the optative suffix and so forth. To provide authority for the claim that the state of being a means to a desired end alone is the denotable meaning of the optative suffix and so forth, he cites the statement of Maṇḍana Miśra: "And it has been said," etc., beginning with "For men [there is] no desire... and so on.

"Being the means to what is desired" (*iṣṭābhyupāyatva*) means being the instrument for accomplishing a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). "Other than that"—meaning other than [being the means to the desired], such as not producing a powerful undesired consequence (*balavadaniṣṭājanakatva*)—is not the motivator (*pravartaka*) of men toward actions such as sacrifice; that is to say, it is not the object of the cognition that generates the inclination to act. Rather, the meaning is that only "being the means to the desired" is the object of the cognition that generates the inclination to act. The word *ca* (and) indicates a reason (*hetau*). For [this reason], they state that the meaning of the term *pravartanā* (instigation) is a property (*dharma*) that is the cause of inclination—that is, a property delimited by being the object of the cognition that generates the inclination to act.

The meaning is as follows: the word *pravartanā*, derived from the verbal root *vṛt* preceded by the prefix *pra* and followed by the suffix *ṇic* and then *u*, denotes an activity conducive to engagement (*pravṛtti*). And such an activity is nothing other than the cognition that sacrifice and the like are means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). For it is observed that even when one hears "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), it is only when one knows "this sacrifice is a means to my desired end" that one engages in the sacrifice and not otherwise.

And thus, the knowledge inherent in the performer of a sacrifice (yāga) has a corresponding objective content (*viṣayatā*) directed toward that which is non-different from the sacrifice and is a means to my desired end; and that which delimits such objective content—by the maxim that "when a light property can serve as a delimitor, a heavy property should not be postulated as such"—is simply the state of being a means to the desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) due to its brevity. Therefore, that alone is the meaning of the word *pravartanā* (incitement), and that alone is the denotation (*śakya*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers. This has been explained in detail.

The meaning is as follows: since the knowledge that something is achievable through effort is understood by means of worldly instruments of valid cognition (*laukikapramāṇa*), and since the knowledge that an action is not followed by a powerful undesirable result (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) is of no use for initiating activity, the status of the knowledge that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) alone as the cause of activity is determined by refuting [the causality of] the other two. It should be understood that the detailed elaboration has already been shown, in brief, by the manner of explanation just described.

"By 'and so forth' (ādineti)": the meaning is by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the verse at the point where it says "in instigation and so forth" (*preraṇādau*). "Of cause and effect" (*hetuhetumatoḥ*): the meaning of that sūtra is that the *liṅ* suffix occurs after a verbal root denoting an action that is the cause and after a verbal root denoting an action that is the result, [indicating] the future. "The state of cause and effect" (*hetuhetumadbhāva*): the meaning is cause, effect, and inclination (*āśis*). Among these, an example for the case of inclination (*āśis*) has been stated. Now, he states an example for the state of cause and effect, beginning with "he who [threatens] a Brāhmaṇa," etc. "Threatening" (*avagoraṇa*) means the raising of a staff or similar object for the purpose of killing.

Regarding the term *brāhmaṇāya*, according to the Vārttika rule "that which one aims at through an action [is the recipient]," it functions as a *saṃpradāna* (recipient), and thus takes the dative case, just as in the expression *patye śete* ("she lies down for her husband"). Consequently, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is as follows: whoever performs such an act—that is, whoever acts with a Brāhmaṇa as the intended object—by means of "threatening," which is the activity of brandishing a staff or the like; for that person who is the agent of such an act, the King shall cause "punishment by a hundred," meaning torments administered by the messengers of Yama for a duration of one hundred years. This is the resulting verbal understanding.

In this context, there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the action qualified by its factors—namely, the action of raising a staff or the like directed toward a Brāhmaṇa as the object and performed by a particular agent—and the action consisting of torment (*yātanā*), expressed by the verb "he should cause to suffer" (*yātayet*), through the relation of cause and effect; however, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) does not itself possess the meaning of cause and effect. This is because it has been stated previously that the meaning of the rule [Pāṇini 3.3.161] is that the optative suffix occurs after a verbal root that denotes an action standing in a cause-and-effect relationship.

Since the sūtra is purposeful by virtue of its function in apprehending the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) regarding the cognition of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) through such a connection, the postulation of a further denotative power (*śakti*) for the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in that context is refuted by the principle of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
