He states the meaning of the *luṅ* [suffix] as "mere past" (*bhūtamātra*). With the intention that the word *mātra* serves to restrict the meaning, he says "in the general past" (*bhūtasāmānye*). This means: in that which is delimited by the general property (*sāmānyadharma*) of being past, and not by a specific property (*viśeṣadharma*). He provides the authority for this from the sūtra: *bhūte luṅ*.

The meaning is that the suffix *luṅ* is prescribed after a verbal root with reference to the word "in the past" (*bhūte*), which is delimited by the common property of being of the nature of having occurred. In this context, "in the past" (*bhūte*) is an adjective qualifying the action denoted by the verbal root; its meaning is that *luṅ* occurs after a root expressive of an action belonging to the past time. Regarding the word "here" (*atra*): the meaning is that it refers to the governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*) "in the past" (*bhūte*). He states what "pastness" (*bhūtatva*) is: "present... [and so forth].

Although two types of compounds are possible—namely, *vartamāne* (locative) or *vartamānaḥ* (nominative) *dhvaṃsaḥ*—since they result in the same meaning, the intended sense is as follows: "pastness" (*bhūtatva*) is the state of being a time that serves as the locus of an action which is the counter-positive of a present destruction—that is, a destruction of a past action. Since such an action exists as the counter-positive of that present destruction, it follows that "pastness" is the state of being a time that is the substratum of an action counter-positive to a present destruction. With this intention, he says: "And that is unimpeded with respect to the action."

The meaning is that the state of being the counter-positive of a present destruction (*vartamānadhvaṃsapratiyogitva*) remains intact even in the case of an action that has passed away. Consequently, even though a jar exists at present, because the operation conducive to the production residing in the jar has been completed, the expression "the jar was" (*ghaṭo 'bhūt*) is justified as conveying the understanding of an operation conducive to production belonging to past time, having a substratum non-different from a single jar. By the phrase "counter-positive of a present destruction," its belonging to past time is demonstrated. This is what is meant by "this [is] here."

This [topic], being present by virtue of its establishment in the Buddhist system, will be explained [below]. The word "compendium" (saṃgraha) is to be connected with the word "should be seen" (draṣṭavya). Regarding the term "first" (ādya): the meaning is "belonging to today," that is, "of the current day. Regarding the phrase "due to the distinction": thus, in the first case, all three types of usage are observed—namely, *pacati* (he cooks), *pakṣyati* (he will cook), and *apākṣīt* (he cooked). Regarding the term "last" (antya): the meaning is "non-current-day," that is, distinct from the current day. [The examples are] "past" (*bhūta*) and "future" (*bhaviṣyat*).

The meaning is that "past" (*bhūta*) is that which is delimited by the general property of pastness (*bhūtatva*), and "future" (*bhaviṣyat*) is that which is delimited by the general property of futurity (*bhaviṣyattva*). Regarding the phrase "mere pastness" (*bhūtatvamātra*): the word *mātra* has the sense of restriction. The meaning is that when there is an intention to express [the action] solely through the general property of pastness, the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix is used. However, when there is an intention to express pastness as qualified by the specific property of non-recent time (*anadyatanatva*), the *laṅ* (imperfect) suffix is used. In that same case, when there is an intention to express remoteness (*parokṣatva*), the *liṭ* (perfect) suffix is used. Regarding "mere futurity" (*bhaviṣyattāmātra*): [the same logic applies].

Here too, the word *mātra* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). When there is the intention to express [future time] by means of the general property of being future (*bhaviṣyattva*), the suffix *lṛṭ* is used; but when there is the intention to express it by means of the specific property of being future delimited by non-recentness (*anadyatanatva*), then *luṭ* is used. Regarding the phrase "due to the relation of cause and effect, etc.": by the word "etc.," there is the inclusion of the conditions for the suffix *liṅ*, such as the use of *liṅ* and *loṭ* after verbs meaning "to desire" (*icchārtha*), and *liṅ* after the root *śak* ("to be able"), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of these two":

The meaning is: "by the general property (*sāmānyadharma*) consisting of the state of being past or the state of being future, with reference to the intended past and future times. Regarding the term *lṛṅ*: since the *lṛṅ* (conditional mood) is prescribed by the two rules, "when there is a cause for the *liṅ*" and "also in the past," it occurs when the past or future time is intended to be expressed through that general property. He states the meaning of *lṛṅ*: "When [the non-occurrence] exists," etc. The meaning is: when the non-accomplishment of an action is understood, and when there exists a cause for the *liṅ*, such as the relation of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*), in either the past or future time, the *lṛṅ* occurs.

Regarding this point, he states the authoritative proof: "from the Sūtra. The meaning is that according to the sense of that Sūtra, the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* occurs when a verbal root denoting an action—characterized by being the cause or the effect—is intended to express a past or future time through the general property of "pastness" or "futurity. An example for the future sense is: "if there were good rain," and so forth. Here, the occurrence of good rain is the cause (*hetu*), and the occurrence of an abundant harvest is the effect (*hetumat*).

Having observed here that the occurrence of good harvests follows the occurrence of good rains on numerous previous occasions, one understands through inference that the future occurrence of good rains is also a cause for the occurrence of good harvests. Likewise, one understands the non-occurrence of an action (*kriyātipatti*) due to the presence of an obstacle or the deficiency of a means. An example of the presence of an obstacle is as follows: if the Sun should be situated between Mercury and Venus when they are nearby, it constitutes an obstacle to rain.

As it has been said: "When Mercury and Venus are situated nearby, they make the earth appear full of water; the sun, situated between them, might even dry up the ocean. Such is an obstacle. The means [to overcome it] consists of: an ascendant with water (sajala-lagna), the tenth house being with water, the presence of benefic planets such as the Moon and Venus in the watery ascendant with full aspect and so forth, the conjunction of male and female planets (strī-puruṣa-yoga), the conjunction of the Moon and the Sun, and the conjunction of vehicles fond of water such as elephants and buffaloes, and so on. The deficiency of these factors is their absence.

Thus, when it is understood that the action of good rain has not been accomplished due to an obstacle or the absence of the means, the non-accomplishment of the action of there being an abundance of food is understood precisely through that [non-accomplishment]. Because the non-accomplishment of two actions [is meant], there is a compound of the word ending in the dual number, namely *kriyātipatti*. Having thus understood the causal relation (*hetuhetumadbhāva*) and the non-accomplishment of the action (*kriyātipatti*) from other means of knowledge, the speaker employs the sentence: "If there had been good rain, there would have been an abundance of food."

In this context, from the sentence, the realization of the cause and the effect—namely, the occurrence of good rain and the occurrence of abundance, both pertaining to the future time—is understood. And thus, the cognition is as follows: "The occurrence of abundance, which has a locus non-different from that of the future time and is based on the occurrence of good rain (as its cause), has taken place."

When used in conjunction with the conditional suffix *lṛṅ*, the meaning of the verbal root may also be its non-existence; in that case, the activity denoted by the root is construed as being absent, and the two absences are further construed through a relationship of instigator and instigated (*prayojya-prayojaka-bhāva*). With this intention, he provides another example: "If fire had blazed," and so forth. In this view, he clarifies the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) as follows: "Non-different from fire," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: [the absence of the activity conducive to softening] residing in a locus non-different from rice is caused by the absence of that activity conducive to burning which resides in a locus non-different from fire. Here, the mention of a "caused-causer" (prayojya-prayojaka) relationship between the two absences is for the purpose of demonstrating the "cause-effect" (hetu-hetumat) relationship between the two counter-correlates of those absences—namely, the burning of the fire and the cooking of the rice. This is because of the rule: "That whose absence is dependent on the absence of another is produced by that [other]."

The meaning of the rule is this: the absence of the cooking of rice (*odanapāka*) is dependent upon the absence of the ignition of fire (*vahni-prajvalana*); therefore, that cooking of rice is produced by that [ignition], meaning it is produced by the ignition of fire. Consequently, once it is understood that the absence of the cooking of rice is dependent upon the absence of the ignition of fire, the comprehension of the causal relationship (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) between their respective counter-correlates—the ignition of fire and the cooking of rice—becomes easy; such is the intended sense.

An example of this even in the past tense is: "If Caitra had not existed, then the cooking of rice would not have occurred," and so forth. However, Kālidāsa has demonstrated a very excellent example of the past conditional (*bhūta-lṛṅ*) in the *Raghuvaṃśa*: "If this pair, whose mutual splendor was desirable to one another, had not been joined together, then the Creator’s effort in fashioning their beauty would have been in vain. This is the indication of the meaning.

The meaning is that the sense of "present time" and so forth is demonstrated by the rule *vartamāne laṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.123) and others. "An illustration" means that it is a demonstration of only one part of the meanings of *laṭ* and the other suffixes. "Even in other meanings" means that since *laṭ*, *loṭ*, and others are seen to occur even in the past tense and in the sense of "proper time" (*prāptakāla*) by rules such as *laṭ sme* (Pāṇini 3.2.118) and *sme loṭ* (Pāṇini 3.3.165). According to the system of other schools, the denotative power (*śakti*) of *laṭ* and the other suffixes resides in the sense of present time and so forth because these are well-known; however, in other meanings, there is merely indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for *laṭ* and the rest.

In the view of the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas), however, it should be understood that for every expressed meaning, there is only the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the *laṭ* and other suffixes, and not figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In connection with this topic, he states the rule governing the sequence of *laṭ* and the others: "of these" (*eteṣām*), which means "of the ten tenses and moods" (*daśalakārāṇām*). "Only the sequence of the indicatory letters" (*anubandhakrama eva*) means "only the sequence of the indicatory letters such as *a*, *i*, and so forth. As for the *laṅ* and others, however, the sequence of indicatory letters such as *a* and *i*, assisted by the indicatory letter *ṅ*, is the regulator.

Since Pāṇini first designated the *ṭi*-marked verbal suffixes (lakāras) by stating "the *laṭ* [is used] in the present tense" (*vartamāne laṭ*) and so forth, the Mīmāṃsakas' conventional usage of the term "the fifth *lakāra*, the *leṭ*" becomes consistent. Thus, the meaning is that the sequence of *lakāras* stated by Pāṇini is also accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas. As for the phrase "this is the direction" (*digiti*), its sense is as follows: where neither the suffix nor the base is heard, there it must be assumed that the suffix which is actually heard conveys the meaning of what is not heard.
For this very reason, the traditional maxim—"that which remains denotes the meaning of what has been elided"—becomes consistent; such is the intended meaning. || 23 ||
Thus ends the determination of the meanings of the specific verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) in the *Śāṅkarī*, a commentary on the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*.
This concludes the determination of the meaning of the verbal suffixes in the *Bhūṣaṇa* commentary composed by Śaṅkara, the son of Raṅgabhaṭṭa. (2)
Now begins the determination of the meanings of case-terminations.

"Sub-artha" (the meaning of the suffixes) means the meanings of the *svādi* suffixes which have nominal stems (*pratipadika*) as their base. He explains this by saying, "The locus (*āśraya*), the limit (*avadhi*)," etc., and "the locus is the meaning. Now, one might object: since we observe grammatical rules such as "the second case (*dvitīyā*) is used for the object (*karman*)," and "the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*"), it follows that the second and other cases have the object, instrument, and so forth as their meanings; they do not have the locus as their meaning, because there is no rule stating "the second case is used for the locus," "the third case is used for the locus," and so on. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "For instance," and so forth. And "that [is]... (referring to *tac ca*).

The word *ca* (and) has the sense of *tu* (but/rather). "That action" (*tat-karma*) means "that which is the object (*karman*) as defined in the rule *dvitīyā*. Regarding the phrase *kartur īpsitatamam*: from the root *āp* (to obtain), in the sense of connection, the suffix *san* is added; from that *sannanta* form, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) in the present tense according to the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaś ca*. Because of its connection with that [suffix], the genitive case *kartuḥ* is used for the agent (*kartṛ*) by the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*. Thus, the meaning is: "that which is desired to be connected with by the agent. And the agent is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the activity denoted by the verbal root with which it is co-occurrent.

When the inquiry arises as to what the agent desires to obtain, the meaning "by means of a result produced by an operation that qualifies the referent of the word 'agent'" is obtained by implication, because that [result] is the most proximate factor. The point is that there is no basis for authority (pramāṇa) in abandoning what is proximate to postulate something not proximate. Thus, since the final conclusion is that "the most desired" is the locus of the result brought about by such an operation, he says: "the locus of the result produced by the action."

One might object: since the suffix *san* in the word *īpsita* (desired) conveys the sense of desire, the term *īpsitatama* (most desired) already captures the intended object (*uddeśya*) by virtue of its possessing such a result; therefore, the mere mention of "that which possesses the result" seems redundant. To this he replies: "by virtue of possessing a result produced by the action," [referring] to "the object (*karman*) itself. This means: precisely that which is the substratum of such a result. "Because of being most desired" means: because it is the object of an intensified desire.

The intention is that being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) by virtue of possessing such a result is useful only for the technical designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*), but it is not included within the scope of what is directly expressed (*vācyakoṭi*). He states the reasoning for why the aspect of being the object of desire is not included in the scope of the expressed meaning with the words: "And likewise, [it is] so connected. By the rule *tathā yuktam cānīpsitam* (Pāṇini 1.4.50), the designation of "object" is prescribed for things that are disliked or indifferent; likewise, by *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇikartā sa ṇau* (Pāṇini 1.4.52), the agent of the base verb is designated as the "object" when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied; and by *adhiśīṅsthāsa ādhāraḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.46), the locus is designated as the "object."

If, however, the definition of the object (*karman*) is accepted as including the element of being the object of desire—that is, being the locus of a result produced by an operation—then there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*); for although the quality of being the locus of an operation-produced result exists in objects such as those one hates, the definition would fail to apply due to the absence of being an object of desire.

Since the status of being an object (*karman*) exists even for those who are objects of hatred and the like, in order to ensure that the definition of an object applies to them as well, it is appropriate to define an object simply as "that which is the substratum of a result produced by an action" (*kriyājanyaphalāśraya*). By this, even those who are objects of hatred and so forth are included within the definition of an object. Thus, the state of being intended (*uddeśyatva*), in the form of being the object of a desire, does not enter into the denotative scope of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*), but rather serves only to trigger the application of the technical term (*saṃjñā*). Therefore, he says: "In this very way, it is logical."

The meaning is that it is logical for the definition [of the object] to be precisely that which is not constituted by being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*). Now, if the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) were to denote merely the substratum of the result produced by the action, then in examples such as *taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice"), there would be no cognition [of the rice] as being "most desired" (*īpsitatama*) and so forth; therefore, he says: "desired, undesired," etc. This means: "the states of being the object of desire and the object of non-desire," i.e., the states of being the object of volition and the object of non-volition. "Due to the absence of evidence" means: because it is universally experienced by all people that there is no cognition [of the object] as having the state of being the object of volition and so forth.

The point is this: just as in the case of "Hari rests on Vaikuṇṭha" (*yathā'dhiśete vaikuṇṭhaṃ hariḥ*), the understanding derived from the cognition—"the resting, whose agent is Hari, has Vaikuṇṭha as its locus"—is established by universal experience as consisting solely of Vaikuṇṭha’s status as a locus (*ādhāra*). It does not consist in [Vaikuṇṭha] being co-occurrent (*samabhivyāhṛta*) with the roots *adhi-śī* (to lie down) and so forth. Thus, the co-occurrence with *adhi-śī* and so forth is useful only for assigning the technical designation "object" (*karman*) to the locus, but it does not enter into the category of what is directly expressed (*vācya*). This is because no one experiences it in that way, and therefore no one accepts a cognition [of the locus] as being "that which is most desired to be reached" (*īpsitatama*) or the like.

One might object: "In this manner, let there be no inclusion of the locus [of the action] within the category denoted by the accusative suffix because it is the object of desire; and let its utility for the application of the technical term *karman* remain intact. Nevertheless, according to the meaning of the Nirukta-sūtra, it follows that the meaning of the accusative suffix is only the locus as qualified by the fruit produced by the action, and not the locus alone. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). This means: provided that the locus of the fruit produced by the action is the meaning of the accusative suffix.

Action (*kriyā*) is the operation (*vyāpāra*); the result (*phala*) is [the state of] being softened (*viklitti*) and so forth; and the substratum (*āśraya*) is the locus, such as rice grains. Among these three meanings, only two—namely, the operation and the result—are expressed by the verbal root alone, because it has been stated that "the result and the operation are denoted by the verbal root. Consequently, since those two meanings are already obtainable from other sources, it would entail the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate a further expressive power (*śakti*) for them; therefore, they cannot be the primary meanings of the word—that is to say, they are not the meanings directly denotable by the word itself. In other words, they are not what is expressed by the accusative case ending.

The meaning "substratum" (*āśraya*), however, has not been stated by anyone [else as the primary meaning]; therefore, that alone is the word-meaning—the meaning directly denotable by the word, which is to say, it is what is expressed by the accusative case. The underlying intention is based on the maxim: "The meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained otherwise. Although the substratum is indeed obtained through words such as *taṇḍula* (rice), it is not obtained specifically as a "substratum"; thus, that alone is the directly denotable meaning (*śakya*). Consequently, it should be understood that the meaning of the accusative case is the mere substratum itself, and not something qualified by an effect produced by an action (*kriyājanyaphala-viśiṣṭa*).

And by the word "substratum" (āśraya), that which possesses the capacity of being a substratum is expressed. Now, if it is argued that since neither the state of being desired (īpsitatva) nor the state of being undesired (anīpsitatva) appears in verbal cognition—because such is not experienced—then let the sūtra simply be "the substratum of the result produced by the action is the object" (kriyājanyaphalāśrayaḥ karma). By this much alone, there would be a comprehensive inclusion of all illustrative examples, such as "he cooks rice," "while going to the village he touches grass," and "he eats poison. [This renders unnecessary] the rules "that which is most desired by the agent is the object" (kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma) and "likewise that which is connected [with the action] though undesired" (tathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam).

If it is asked, "What is the purpose of mentioning *īpsitatama* (the most desired) and *anīpsita* (the undesired) separately?", the answer is: No. For if one were to state simply that "the substratum of the result produced by the action is the *karman*," then the rule *vāraṇārthānām* would become an exception (*apavāda*) to this [definition of *karman*], because it is a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*). Consequently, in the sentence *agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati* ("He keeps the boy away from the fire"), the boy (*māṇavaka*) would not receive the designation *karman*. This is because, when verbs meaning "to ward off" are employed, the designation *apādāna* is prescribed for the object that is intended to be avoided.

The rule *vāraṇārthānām* (Pāṇini 1.4.27) is utilized for the prescription of the technical designation *apādāna* (ablative), but the status of being "for the purpose of warding off" (*vāraṇārthatva*) does not appear in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). This is because one does not experience a cognition [of the object] by virtue of its being for the purpose of warding off. Furthermore, "desirability" (*īpsitatva*) consists, by proximity, in being the locus of the result produced by the operation (*vyāpāra*) presented by a verbal root whose meaning is warding off. And that [desirability] remains unimpaired both in the case of fire and in the case of the dog.

The meaning of the root *vṛ* (in *vārayati*) is an operation conducive to the absence of an operation favorable to conjunction and so forth. This being the case, the general rule—"the locus of the result produced by an operation is termed *karman* (object)"—which signifies that whatever is the locus of the result produced by an operation presented by the verbal root becomes designated as an object (*karman*), would apply [to the boy]. Furthermore, there is the rule which signifies that "the locus of the result produced by an operation presented by a root having the sense of warding off (*vāraṇa*) is termed *apādāna* (ablative point)."

By the specific rule (*viśeṣasūtra*) "vāraṇārthānām," the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) is also applicable. Between those two [designations], in cases such as "he cooks rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), the designation of *karman* (accusative) has its own scope; therefore, it would set aside the designation of *karman* obtained by the general rule (*sāmānyasūtra*). Consequently, because it is specifically prescribed by the rule "vāraṇārthānām," the designation of *apādāna* would apply to both "fire" (*agni*) and "the boy" (*māṇavaka*). As a result, the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) would not occur for "the boy" (*māṇavakam*), and the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) would occur even for "the boy," just as it does for "fire."

To exclude that [undesired application], it must indeed be stated: "The object (*karman*) is that which is most desired by the agent. And "being most desired" (*īpsitatamatva*) consists in being the locus of the result of the action denoted by the root, which result is produced by the primary operation (*vyāpāra*) presented by the root in its current context. In this case, the primary operation presented by the root whose meaning is "warding off" is the second operation (the act of preventing). The result of such an operation, as denoted by that root, is the absence of activity; the locus of that result is the boy (*māṇavaka*). Thus, setting aside the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) which would otherwise apply to the boy, the designation of "object" (*karman*) prevails due to his status as the "most desired," because it is a subsequent rule.

In the case of *agni* (fire), although it is "desired" (*īpsita*) because it is the substratum of the result produced by the operation brought about by its own constituent parts (*prakṛtadhātu*), it does not receive the technical designation of "object" (*karman*) because it lacks the status of being the "most desired" (*īpsitatama*)—that is, the substratum of the result produced by the primary operation. Consequently, it receives the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) instead. Thus, it is established that the designation "ablative" applies to anything merely "desired," whereas the designation "object" applies only to that which is "most desired. Since the status of being "most desired" is precisely what triggers the designation of "object," the designation "object" would not apply to that which is "not desired" (*anīpsita*); therefore, the intention is that the rule "and likewise that which is not desired" (*tathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam*) must indeed be stated separately for that purpose.

Now, one might object: if the substratum (*āśraya*) is accepted as the denotable meaning (*śakya*), then "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*) must be admitted as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, "substratum-ness" is simply "the state of being a locus" (*ādhāratva*). Since that [locus-ness] is infinite—because it differs according to the various relations defined by the fruit (*phala*), the operation (*vyāpāra*), and so forth—and because of that infinity, there would be an infinity of powers (*śakti*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "And its nature... (*tattvaṃ ca*). The meaning is: "and substratum-ness. He says: "indivisible" (*akhaṇḍa*). The meaning is: it is the nature of power (*śakti*), which is a property (*dharma*).

And that reality (*dharma*) is indivisible; its indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) consists in being devoid of difference as induced by differences among its qualifiers (*nirūpaka*), even though such qualifiers may differ. Because it is devoid of difference, it is one; and because it is one, it is eternal. This means, in effect, that it is of the nature of an unconditioned, specific universal (*jāti*).

The point is as follows: just as, although the individual cows presented by the word "cow" (go) are infinite, the universal "cowness" (gotva) residing in them is one and undivided—being devoid of the distinctions caused by the differences among the individuals—and is not delimited by other properties such as "cowness-ness" (gotvatva), so too, "substratum-ness" (āśrayatva) is also one, being devoid of the distinctions caused by the differences among its relata (nirūpaka), and is not delimited by other properties such as "substratum-ness-ness" (āśrayatvatva). This is because substratum-ness is the very nature of the substrate itself, not constituted by any property other than "substratum-ness-ness" and the like.

And thus, since the substratum-hood (*āśrayatva*) which serves as the delimitor of the power (*śakti*) is one, the power of the accusative case and others resides in those substrata that are subsumed under it; therefore, there is no infinity of powers—this is the intended meaning. If, on the other hand, even substratum-hood were delimited by another property such as "substratum-hood-ness" (*āśrayatvatva*), meaning it would possess a further defining characteristic, then there would follow the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and moreover, the absence of non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition would result—this is the sense.

Just as in the position that the denotation of a cow-individual qualified by cowness (*gotva*) occurs, it is logical that when a cow-individual qualified by cowness is presented upon hearing the word "cow" in a sentence such as "Bring the cow," that cow-individual becomes connected with actions such as bringing; nevertheless, since the cognition of the qualifier is a cause for the cognition of the qualified, one must simply state that prior to the presentation of such a cow-individual qualified by cowness, the cognition of the qualifying cowness has already arisen.

Since the power of the qualifier is established by the meaning [of the qualified] when there is the power of the qualified, the power exists even with respect to "cowness" (*gotva*). In that regard, it is undisputed that the power which resides in the individual qualified by cowness is indeed delimited by cowness (*gotvāvacchinna*). But as for the power with respect to cowness itself, is that power delimited or undelimited? If it is delimited, then "cowness-ness" (*gotvatva*) must be stated as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*).

Since there is a rule that the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) must be included within the denotable itself, if "cowness-ness" (*gotvatva*) were also delimited, it would lead to an infinite regress by requiring yet another delimitor. To avoid this, one must accept that the primary denotative power (*śakti*) resides in "cowness" (*go-tva*) as being undelimited (*niravacchinna*). In this way, when a cognition of cowness arises prior to the cognition of an individual cow, because that [cognition of cowness] lacks any qualifying mode (*niṣprakāraka*), it is undelimited and constitutes indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*); thus, the existence of undelimited cognition is logically consistent.

If "cowness" (*gotva*) were also possessed of qualifiers, then indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) would simply vanish. Thus, just as "cowness" is partless (*akhaṇḍa*), meaning it is not constituted by any delimiting property (*avacchedaka-dharma*), so too is "substratumness" (*āśrayatva*) partless and not constituted by any delimiting property; this is the intended meaning. The establishment of substratumness should be understood through the inclusive cognition "water, water" and by its being the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "water," just like "waterness" (*jalatva*).

In the examples, he demonstrates the application of the definition of "objecthood" (*karmatva*) in the phrase "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*). By the expression "because it is the locus of softening" (*viklittyāśrayatvāt*), it is stated that objecthood consists in being the locus of the fruit of the action denoted by the root—which is distinct from the locus of that same action—while being brought about by the operation expressed by the root as residing in the agent. Indicating that the Naiyāyikas' acceptance of the root *kṛ* (to do/make) as having only "effort" (*yatna*) as its meaning is incorrect, he says: "he makes a pot" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*). This is because "origination" (*utpatti*) is the meaning of the verbal root.

However, the point here is that the meaning [of the root] is not merely "producing" (*utpādana*), because it has been established that the root *kṛ* has the sense of "origination" (*utpatti*) after first refuting its having the sense of "exertion" (*yatna*). Anticipating the objection that in verbal roots whose meanings involve objects—such as *jñā* (to know) and *iṣ* (to desire)—the status of the object (*karmatva*) would be untenable because there is no exertion (*yatna*) such as knowledge or desire, he says: "In the case of *jānāti*," etc. Regarding "the destruction of the veil" (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*): the meaning of the root *jñā* is an activity conducive to the destruction of the veil.

The meaning of the statement "one knows the jar" (*ghaṭaṃ jānāti*) is that the jar possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*) because it is the locus of the result, which consists in the destruction of the veil produced by the action. Furthermore, the activity conducive to the destruction of the veil is precisely the mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) taking on the form of the jar and so forth. As it has been said: "The intellect (*buddhi*) and the reflection of consciousness residing therein (*cidābhāsa*)—these two pervade the jar. Therein, ignorance (*ajñāna*) is destroyed by the intellect, while the jar shines forth by means of the reflection. The meaning of this is that the destruction of ignorance through the mental modification constitutes the "destruction of the veil."

[Objection: Granted that when a jar exists, it is possible for it to be the locus of the destruction of the veil produced by a mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*); however, since this is impossible when a jar is destroyed or not yet arisen, how can it be its object? To this, he says: "past and future," etc. "Even in the case of the imperceptible" means: just as in the case of the perceptible, so too in the case of the imperceptible. "Of that which is produced by cognition"—that is, produced by a mental modification—"of that"—namely, of the destruction of the veil—"because of its necessity"—meaning, because it must necessarily be admitted.

He demonstrates the reasoning for accepting that the destruction of the veil (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*) is the locus [of the cognition] even in the case of a pot that is out of sight, by saying "otherwise" (*anyathā*). This refers to the non-acceptance of the destruction of the veil in the case of a pot that has already perished and so forth. The meaning is as follows: "Just as before" (*yathā pūrvam*); since the pot existed previously, the mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*) at that time could indeed produce the destruction of the veil; however, because the pot does not exist now, it is impossible for the present mental modification to produce the destruction of the veil. Consequently, the linguistic usage "I know the pot just as before" would not occur.

In this context, *yathāpūrvam* is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of not deviating from the meaning of the prior term. It is an adverbial modifier of the verb "to know" (*jānāti*). *Yathāpūrvam* means "not deviating from what was known previously. The meaning is that there would be no such knowledge as that in which there is no deviation from prior knowledge.

The meaning is this: in the state when a jar exists, because the destruction (i.e., the removal) of that veil or covering in the form of ignorance residing in the existing jar has been effected by the mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*) of that moment, a clearly manifest cognition of the jar arises; likewise, in the state when a jar does not exist, because the destruction of the veil residing in the non-existent jar has not been effected by the mental modification of that moment, and because the veil still persists, a clearly manifest cognition of the jar does not arise.

Because there is a transcendence of prior knowledge, the expression "I know [the jar] as before" would not occur. However, it is established by experience that just as a very clear cognition arises regarding an existing jar, so too does a very clear cognition arise regarding a non-existing jar. To account for such an experience, one must necessarily admit that there is a destruction of the veil even with respect to a non-existing jar; the meaning is that the destruction of the veil is the cause of a very clear cognition.

The sense is that otherwise, just as in the case of an existing jar, there would not be a clearly manifest cognition of a non-existing jar. Now, one might object: how can the status of being the locus for the removal of an obscuration apply to a jar that has been destroyed or one yet to come, since its locus is non-existent? For it is only when something exists that such a status can be rightly asserted. To this, he says: "And the status of being the locus for the past and so forth. [This is] "as for the Naiyāyikas."

The meaning is as follows: Just as the Naiyāyikas, in accordance with experience, have accepted that past objects such as jars possess the status of being the locus of knowledge by virtue of being its objects, so too do we accept, in accordance with experience, that past jars possess the status of being the locus of the removal of concealment (āvaraṇabhaṅga) by virtue of being its objects. Now, one might object: even if past jars exist as objects, there is disagreement regarding their being the locus of knowledge by virtue of being its objects; therefore, the example is inconsistent. To this, he says: "In the theory of the pre-existence of the effect" (satkāryavāda).

According to the Vedic scripture, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," every collection of effects, such as a jar and the like, existed previously in its cause in a subtle form. Although the conventional usage of "the jar is produced" and "the jar is destroyed" is observed, nevertheless, the meaning of "produced" is that it has become manifest through the operation of the staff, the wheel, and so forth; and the meaning of "destroyed" is that it has become unmanifest.

The pot, however, exists even prior to its manifestation in the form of clay; likewise, even after its destruction, the pot exists in the clay in an unmanifested form. For it is not possible for that which is non-existent to come into being, nor for that which exists to be destroyed; just as oil is not seen in sand even with a thousand efforts.

The meaning is as follows: the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of an effect is simply its existence in a subtle form within the cause; because it exists in a subtle form within the cause, just as in the case of the statement "the jar is born," the jar's status as an agent (*kāraka*) and its agency (*kartṛtva*) are logically established, so too is its status as the locus of the fruit consisting in the removal of the veil (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*). The sense is that the doctrine which holds that the effect is always existent—that is, always already present and never non-existent—is the *satkāryavāda* (the theory that the effect pre-exists).

[Objection: But if the effect exists at all times, the linguistic usages "it does not exist" and "it perishes" would be untenable. To this, he says: "by admitting concealment" (*tirobhāvābhyupagamāt*). The meaning is that when concealment is produced by the causal complex that brings about concealment, that very state of concealment is the non-existence and the perishing of entities. [The phrase] "in which the sequence has been obtained" means when such concealment has occurred. The meaning is that the usage "it perishes" is based on the presentness inherent in the arising of concealment.

By the phrase "having attained its sequence" (*labdhakrama*), its nature as an activity (*vyāpāra*) is indicated. By the phrase "is perceived" (*pratīyate*), perception is stated to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). "Disappearance" (*tirobhāva*) means abiding in a subtle form within the cause; thus, even when a jar has disappeared, because it continues to abide in a subtle form within its cause, there is no logical inconsistency in its being the substratum for the removal of obscuration (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*). This is the intended meaning.

In order to clarify the extracted meaning of the definition characterized by "the state of being the object of the verbal root" (*niruktakarmatva*), he raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). Regarding the example "Caitra [goes to] Caitra": the definition of the object (*karman*) has been stated as "that which is the substratum of the result produced by the operation conveyed by the verbal root under discussion. In the sentence "Caitra goes to the village," the meaning of the root *gam* is an operation conducive to conjunction (*saṃyoga*); and that [operation], consisting of the placing of the foot, resides in the agent (*kartṛ*), Caitra.

And thus, just as a village receives the designation of "object" (*karman*) because it is the locus of the result—namely, conjunction—which is produced by the activity consisting of the placement of the foot included within the verbal root *gam*, so too, since conjunction resides in two places and such a conjunction exists in Caitra as well, Caitra would also incur the status of an object because he is the locus of the result produced by the activity included within the relevant verbal root; consequently, the usage "Caitra goes to Caitra" (*caitraścaitraṃ gacchati*) would result.

The meaning is that since the referent Caitra is characterized by both agency and objecthood, the single word "Caitra" would consequently have to terminate in both the nominative case and the accusative case.

The point is this: just as in the sentence "Caitra goes from Prayāga to Kāśī," the result produced by the action consisting of the placement of the foot—which is denoted by the verbal root *gam* (to go)—is conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and that [conjunction] resides in Kāśī; likewise, since disjunction (*vibhāga*) is also a result produced by such an action, one might argue that because Prayāga is the substratum of the result in the form of disjunction, it too would incur the status of an object (*karman*). Consequently, the usage "He goes to Prayāga" (*prayāgaṃ gacchati*) would follow as a logical consequence. He refutes this objection with the word "no."

In this regard, he refutes the first objection with the words "just as a village," and so forth. Just as a village is the locus of the result—namely, conjunction—which is produced by the operation that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root *gam* (to go), so too Caitra, although he is the agent and thus the locus of such a result in the form of conjunction, nevertheless, since both the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "object" (*karman*) would apply to Caitra by virtue of his being the locus of the operation and the locus of the result produced by it, the designation of "agent" takes precedence over the designation of "object" due to its higher status in the rules of application. Consequently, the usage "Caitra goes to Caitra" (*caitraścaitram*) does not result.

This is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Even if the technical designation *karman* (object) is set aside, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) would still be unavoidable on the basis of the actual state of being an object, defined as being the locus of the result produced by the action. To this, he says: "In the production of the accusative. The meaning is that the accusative arises only when the designation *karman* is present; it does not arise merely by taking the status of being the locus of the result. He states the refutation [of the opponent's view] regarding the acceptance of the locus of the result as the cause for the production of the accusative: "Otherwise," etc. In the expression *gamayati*, the meaning of the root *gam* is an operation conducive to conjunction with a location in front.

The meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is an operation conducive to an operation of that kind [the primary action]. In that context, Caitra receives the designation of agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of being the locus of the operation denoted by the causative suffix. Gokula receives the designation of object (*karman*) by virtue of being the locus of the result produced by the operation denoted by the verbal root *gam* (to go). Kṛṣṇa, however, receives the designation of object by virtue of being the locus of the result produced by the operation denoted by the meaning of the causative suffix. Thus, in the sentence "Caitra causes Gokula to lead Kṛṣṇa" (*gamayati gokulaṃ kṛṣṇaṃ caitraḥ*), the accusative case ending occurs after the word *kṛṣṇa* just as it does after the word *gokula*. [Similarly] regarding *pācayati* (he causes to cook): The meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is an operation conducive to an operation of that kind [the primary action]. In that context, Caitra receives the designation of agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of being the locus of the operation denoted by the causative suffix. The wood (*kāṣṭha*) receives the designation of object (*karman*) by virtue of being the locus of the result produced by the operation denoted by the verbal root *pac* (to cook). Kṛṣṇa, however, receives the designation of object by virtue of being the locus of the result produced by the operation denoted by the meaning of the causative suffix. Thus, in the sentence "Caitra causes the wood to cook Kṛṣṇa" (*pācayati kāṣṭhaṃ kṛṣṇaṃ caitraḥ*), the accusative case ending occurs after the word *kṛṣṇa* just as it does after the word *kāṣṭha*. This is because the status of being an object is determined by the result produced by the operation denoted by the meaning of the causative suffix. Therefore, the rule "that which is intended by the agent to be reached by the operation is called the object" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*) applies here as well. Consequently, the accusative case ending occurs after the word *kṛṣṇa* just as it does after the word *kāṣṭha*. The meaning of the root *pac* (to cook) is an operation conducive to softening (*viklitti*). The meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) following it is an operation conducive to such an operation. In that context, Caitra receives the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) because he is the locus of the operation expressed by the causative suffix. Rice (*taṇḍula*) receives the designation of "object" (*karman*) because it is the locus of the result, which consists of softening, produced by the operation expressed by the verbal root *pac*.

Although Kṛṣṇa, as the substratum of the operation denoted by the root *pac*, would acquire the designation of "object" (*karman*) because he is the substratum of the result produced by the operation denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the rule governing the object-designation must—if it is to apply at all—apply only to that which is the substratum of the result produced by the operation denoted by the *ṇic* suffix when it is derived from a verbal root included in the list beginning with *gati-buddhi*. This restriction is established by the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasāna-artha-śabdakarma-akarmaka-āṇi-kartṛ-kasya ca*. Consequently, since the causative form of *pac* in the present instance is derived from the root *pac*, [the designation of object does not apply].

Because it does not have as its root a verbal base (dhātu) whose meaning is "motion" (*gati*) and so forth, *kṛṣṇa* does not receive the technical designation of "object" (*karman*), but rather the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) alone; consequently, the third case ending occurs. Thus, the construction *pācayati taṇḍulaṃ kṛṣṇena caitraḥ* ("Caitra causes Kṛṣṇa to cook the rice") is established.

This being the case, if it were admitted that the occurrence of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) arises simply by taking the fact of being the substratum of a result produced by an action—even in the absence of the technical designation "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*)—then an undesirable consequence would follow: just as from the word *kṛṣṇa* in the sentence *gamayati gokulaṃ kṛṣṇam*, the accusative would also arise from the word *kṛṣṇa* when used with verbs such as *pācayati* (e.g., *pācayati kṛṣṇam*). Therefore, one must necessarily accept that the designation "object" itself is the cause for the occurrence of the accusative, and not merely the fact of being the substratum of a result produced by an action in reality.

[The opponent] says: "But surely, in the case of *caitraścaitram*, since the word *caitra* denoting the agent would be the locus of the result produced by the action, a second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would result; this is not what I am saying. Rather, my point is that because *caitra* is the locus of the operation and the locus of the result produced by that operation, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) would result in the form: 'the present going has Caitra as its agent and Caitra as its object'. To this he replies, "Not so," stating: "For those who have such linguistic proficiency (*tathā vyutpannānām*)."

The meaning is that for those who possess the apprehension of linguistic competency (*śaktigraha*)—namely, that the sentence "Caitra goes" possesses the capacity to generate a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) of the form "the going has Caitra as its agent and Caitra as its object"—such a verbal cognition is indeed desired and not undesired. The underlying point is that, in general, the presentation of the substratum (*āśraya*) is the cause of a verbal cognition in which the fruit of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvarthaphala*) is the qualificand.

The sense is that, likewise, it is inconsistent to claim that such a verbal cognition would undesirably result from the sentence "Caitra goes. Since one does not experience the cognition "the going has Caitra as its agent and Caitra as its object" from the sentence "Caitra goes," it is improper to argue that this is merely an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*); therefore, he says, "Or let it be stated. This means: let it be admitted. [Regarding the phrase] "by way of the relation of qualifierhood" (*prakāratā-sambandhena*).

The intended meaning is that, in order to produce a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) where the fruit of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha-phala*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), one must accept the following causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*): the cause is the presentation of a substratum (*āśraya*) qualified by the property of not being the locus of the root-meaning's operation (*vyāpāra*). Here, it should be understood that the effect is the verbal cognition having the fruit of the root-meaning as its qualificand, and the cause is the presentation of a substratum qualified by the property of not being the locus of the root-meaning's operation.

The application of the definition in the sentence *caitro grāmaṃ gacchati* ("Caitra goes to the village") is as follows: the meaning of the verbal root *gam* is an activity conducive to conjunction with a region in front; and here, the "activity" consists of the successive placing of the feet forward. The "region in front" is the village. According to the established tenet of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), the verbal cognition has the activity as its primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*); thus, the aforementioned activity is [the primary object]. Caitra is construed with the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix *laṭ*, by way of identity (*abheda*). The village is construed with the fruit of the action—conjunction with a location—which is the meaning of the verbal root *gam*, by way of the relation of "residing in" (*niṣṭhatva*).

The connection of the result, which consists of such contact, with the operation occurs through the relation of being conducive (*anukūlatā*). Thus, it should be understood that the village, as the locus of the result denoted by the verbal root, possesses the status of a qualifier (*prakāratā*), while the result denoted by the root residing therein possesses the status of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*).

In the case of a verbal cognition whose qualificandum is the conjunction with a location in front—which is the fruit of the root-meaning—the cause for generating that verbal cognition is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) of the locus of the fruit (the substratum qualified by non-identity with the locus of the root-meaning's operation), which possesses a relation of being the qualifier as determined by the qualificandum-ness residing in the fruit of the root-meaning. Since such a presentation pertains only to the village, the resulting cognition is "the going has Caitra as its agent and the village as its object," and not otherwise.

Regarding the phrase "having Caitra as its object": since Caitra, although he is the locus of the result of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*), is not the locus of the verbal root's activity (*vyāpāra*), there is no presentation of him as the locus of the result qualified by not being the locus of the verbal root's activity; therefore, the cognition "the going has Caitra as its object" does not arise. Rather, the cognition "the going has Caitra as its agent and the village as its object" is established by universal experience—this is the intended meaning. Thus, with the thought that there is no fault [in this view], he says: "In the present case, of Caitra," and so forth.

In response to the second objection—that in the sentence "He goes from Prayāga to Kāśī," it would follow that he "goes to Prayāga"—the author says, "But the status of Prayāga as an object," and so on, while refuting that objection. The phrase "even though it might be possible" means that even the possibility of Prayāga having the status of an object (*karmatva*) does not exist. As for the expression "because it has already been stated": in the section defining the object (*karman*), where it is said that "the status of being an object consists in being the locus of the result produced by the action," and since "action" (*kriyā*) is nothing other than the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), what is meant is "being the locus of the result produced by the action which is the meaning of the verbal root."

And thus, since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is a qualifier of the action (*kriyā*), by the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the meaning of the verbal root is also obtained as a qualifier of the result (*phala*). Consequently, the definition of the object (*karman*) is established as follows: "being the locus of the result of that verbal root's meaning, while being produced by the action of that same verbal root's meaning. It has been stated that in the sentence *prayāgāt kāśīṃ gacchati* ("He goes from Prayāga to Kāśī"), the meaning of the root *gam* is an activity conducive to conjunction with a space in front.

The meaning of a verbal root (*dhātu*) consists of two things: the result in the form of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the activity conducive to that result. In this regard, although it can be said that disjunction (*vibhāga*)—just like conjunction—is a result because it is produced by the activity consisting of the placement of the foot located in Caitra, nevertheless, disjunction is not denoted by the verbal root *gam* (to go) in the same way that conjunction is denoted by it; rather, it arises as an inseparable concomitant (*nāntarīyakatayā*) of the act of going.

Furthermore, although Prayāga is the locus of the result—namely, separation—which is produced by the operation denoted by the verbal root *gam*, there is not even a suspicion that it possesses the status of an object (*karman*). This is because separation is not denoted by the verbal root *gam*, and thus Prayāga lacks the quality of being the locus of a result of the operation denoted by *gam* that is itself denoted by *gam*. It should be understood that the statement denying the possibility of Prayāga being an object is intended on the grounds that separation is not the meaning of the verbal root *gam*.

In another manner, he restates the view of the Naiyāyikas, who seek to remove the defects pointed out in the two previously mentioned positions, beginning with the words "The Naiyāyikas, however," and so forth. "To ward off the first defect" means: to avoid the defect consisting in the undesirable consequence that in the sentence *caitro gacchati* ("Caitra goes"), one would have to use the construction *caitraścaitraṃ gacchati* ("Caitra goes to Caitra"). "Inherence in another" (*parasamavetatva*) means: existence, by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), in that which is other than—that is, different from—the referent of the base of the accusative case, namely the agent such as Caitra.

The meaning is that they "accept" (upādadate)—that is, they take it upon themselves—that this is the denotation of the second case (accusative). And thus, the sense is established that "the denotation of the second case is that which possesses a fruit produced by an action inhering in another [agent]" (parasamavetakriyājanyaphalaśālī). Even so, he says "the second defect" because the removal of the second defect does not occur; the meaning is that there is the second defect consisting in the contingency of Prayāga being treated as the object (karmatā) in the sentence "He goes from Prayāga to Kāśī" (prayāgāt kāśīṃ gacchati). [This refers to] "the state of being the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root" (dhātvarthatāvacchedakatvam).

The meaning is that they adopt a qualification with respect to the fruit (*phala*). Consequently, the intended definition results in this: "An object (*karman*) is that which possesses a fruit delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthatāvacchedaka*), which is produced by an action residing in another (*parasamaveta-kriyājanya*). Furthermore, the status of being delimited by the meaning of the verbal root with respect to the fruit consists in its being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatāpannatva*) as determined by a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in what is denoted by the verbal root, provided that it is itself denoted by the verbal root. [This applies] to the action which is the meaning of the verbal root.

In this context, the second-case suffix (dvitīyā) conveys the qualifier "inherence in another" (*parasamavetatva*), which is construed with the action denoted by the verbal root that is co-occurrent with the result-producing [action]. The meaning is as follows: an object (*karman*) is that which possesses a result produced by the operation—the action denoted by the verbal root—which exists through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) in someone other than the referent of the base of the second-case suffix, such as a village (*grāma*) and so forth; for instance, Caitra and the like. Thus, although the conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is the result of the action denoted by the root *gam*, is equally resident in both the village and Caitra, it is the conjunction with the village [that is the result].

With respect to the village, which is the referent of the second case (dvitīyā-prakṛti), Caitra—who is "other" than that—is the locus of the action produced by the operation residing therein; thus, because the village possesses the fruit produced by an action inherent in another, it receives the designation of "object" (karman) and takes the second case. However, in the case of Caitra's conjunction [expressed as] *caitram*, since Caitra—who is the agent—is not "other" than Caitra, who is the referent of the second case-prakṛti, he lacks the quality of possessing a fruit produced by an action inherent in another (because he possesses a fruit produced by an action inherent in himself); therefore, Caitra does not receive the designation of "object."

The meaning is that there is no possibility of the erroneous usage "Caitra [is] Caitra" because of the non-occurrence of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*). Likewise, regarding "the relation between cause and effect": in order to produce a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) where the mode (*prakāra*) is "residing in another" (*parasamavetatva*), which is denoted by the second case ending, it is accepted that the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) of the action denoted by the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Thus, a distinct causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is posited. By this, the claim that the qualifier "residing in another" is construed with the action denoted by the verbal root through the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*) is justified; such is the intended meaning.

"And 'remoteness' (*paratvam*)": the meaning is that it is the remoteness which constitutes the factor of "residing in another" (*parasamavetatva*), which is expressed by the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*). By virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), what is grasped as "remoteness" is [the action's] being further removed from the primary object denoted by the base of the second case-ending. Consequently, in examples such as "Caitra cooks rice" (*caitrastaṇḍulaṃ pacati*), the status of the rice as the object (*karmatva*) is established; he clarifies the nature of the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) that arises therefrom with the words "rice-ness" (*taṇḍulānyeti*).

With respect to the second [type of object], which is other than the rice (*taṇḍula*) that constitutes the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), there is an agent such as Caitra; the action (*vyāpāra*) existing in him by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*) produces a result in the form of softening (*viklitti*). Because the rice is the substratum (*āśraya*) of that result—which is characterized by being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) co-located (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the state of being denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu-vācyatva*)—it receives the designation of "object" (*karman*).

However, in the case of "caitraścaitram" (Caitra [goes] to Caitra), such an expression is not possible because the activity conducive to the conjunction residing in Caitra—the referent of the second-case base—is not resident in anything other than Caitra. Thus, the demonstration of the form of the verbal cognition is as follows: "inherent in the rice-grain," and so forth.

The meaning of this, in brief, is as follows: the softening (*viklitti*) residing in the rice and denoted by the verbal root; the activity (*vyāpāra*) residing in Caitra—who is distinct from the rice—which is conducive to such softening; and the volitional effort (*kṛti*) conducive to such an activity; and finally, Caitra, who possesses such an effort. This verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is to be understood according to the Nyāya school's doctrine, because the present exposition is an introduction to that very system. This is the intended sense.

The established doctrine [of the Naiyāyikas] is that verbal cognition has the subject ending in the nominative case as its primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*), that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an operation conducive to a result, and that the meaning of the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is effort (*kṛti*). He states "not so" because this Naiyāyika position is untenable due to being burdened by complexity (*gaurava*). [He refers to the complexity] such as "residing in another" (*parasamavetatva*) and so forth.

The point is that it is not reasonable to postulate that "residing in another" (*parasamavetatva*)—which is not touched by the words of the Sūtra and is therefore merely imagined by one's own fancy—is the denotation of the second case-ending, because such a postulation involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and other flaws, which are quite evident. Now, one might object: "Even if 'residing in another' is cumbersome, since the refutation of the objection cannot be achieved without positing it as the denotation of the second case, such complexity does not constitute a fault. To this, he says: "Why would there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? [He then adds: "Of the second case... and so forth.

The meaning is that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) consisting in the undesirable consequence (*prayogāpatti*) of using the expression "Caitra [goes] to Caitra. Regarding the first [alternative], the point is that even if one assumes that being inherent in another (*parasamavetatva*) is the denotation of the accusative case, although the undesirable consequence of the usage "Caitra [goes] to Caitra" does not occur, the over-extension in the form of the accusative case applying elsewhere remains as it was. He demonstrates that very same over-extension elsewhere with the example "He causes Kṛṣṇa to cook" (*pācayati kṛṣṇam*). The meaning is that instead of the form "by Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇena*), there would be the occurrence of the accusative case "Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇam*).

In this context, Kṛṣṇa is the *prayojya* (the one to be prompted), and the cowherd (*gopa*) is the *prayojaka* (the prompter). Thus, the meaning is as follows: relative to Kṛṣṇa, who is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) of the accusative case, there is the cowherd who stands subsequent [in the sentence]; the result produced by the operation inherent in that [cowherd], which is expressed by the verbal root with the causative suffix (*ṇij*), and which consists of an operation conducive to softening (*viklitti*)—serving as a qualifier of the operation denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇij*)—is such that the status of being an object (*karmatva*), defined as possessing such a result, exists in Kṛṣṇa, the *prayojya*. Consequently, the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) would arise that the word "Kṛṣṇa" should take the accusative case ending.

Consequently, it must be accepted that when the second case-affix (*dvitīyā*) is introduced, the sole cause is the technical designation "object" (*karman*), and not the possession of the aforementioned result. However, if it is argued that in constructions such as *pācayati* ("he causes to cook"), the designation "object" does not apply to the possessor of the aforementioned result due to the restriction in the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārtha...*, then since the occurrence of the second case-affix can be prevented by that very [restriction], there is no need for the conceptualization that "residing in another" (*parasamavetatva*) is the denotation of the second case-affix; this is the underlying point.

In the example "gokulaṃ kṛṣṇam" (Kṛṣṇa [goes to] Gokula), just as the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs after the word *kṛṣṇa* because Kṛṣṇa—the object (*prayojya*)—possesses the fruit produced by the operation of its own meaning (*nijartha-vyāpāra*) residing in the agent (*prayojaka*), so too should the second case ending occur as "kṛṣṇam" in constructions such as "pācayati" (he causes to cook). This is the sense that should be understood. Now, one might object: the cause for the application of the second case ending is precisely the status of being an object (*karmatva*), defined as possessing a fruit delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthatāvacchedaka-phala*) which is produced by an operation inherent in another (*parasamaveta-vyāpāra-janya*), and not the technical designation "object" (*karma-saṃjñā*).

In the sentence *pācayati kṛṣṇena gopaḥ* ("The cowherd causes Kṛṣṇa to cook"), although the status of being an object (*karmatva*)—defined as possessing the result delimited by the meaning of the verbal root, which is produced by an operation inherent in a cowherd other than Kṛṣṇa (the base meaning of the second case)—exists in the prompted agent Kṛṣṇa, [the rule] *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇāmaṇikartā sa ṇau* (Pāṇini 1.4.52) requires that the intended expression of this aforementioned objecthood be applied only to causative forms (*ṇijanta*) derived from roots belonging to the class of roots beginning with *gati* and *buddhi* mentioned in that sūtra, and not to causative forms like *pācayati* derived from roots other than those beginning with *gati*. This is because [the rule] teaches [this restriction].

In the case of "the cowherd causes the black [cow] to cook" (*pācayati kṛṣṇaṃ gopaḥ*), there would be the undesirable consequence of a second-case ending (*dvitīyāpattiḥ*), because a case-ending arises precisely when one intends to express [grammatical relations] such as being the object (*karmatva*). Therefore, he says: "The rice cooks by itself" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacyate svayameva*). The meaning is that there would be the consequence of a second-case ending in the case of a reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*). Demonstrating an example for this, he says: "He cooks the rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*).

The meaning is as follows: just as the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs after the word *taṇḍula* (rice) because the rice possesses the fruit—namely, the state of being softened (*viklitti*), which is the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) produced by an operation (*vyāpāra*) inherent in Caitra who is distinct from the rice (the primary sense of the second case)—since the operation conducive to softening is the meaning of the root *pac*, and both the fruit and the operation are denoted by the root *pac*. This is the intended sense.

The meaning is as follows: in the case of the expression *taṇḍulaḥ pacyate svayameva* ("the rice cooks by itself"), the rice, acting as the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*), possesses the result—namely, softening (*viklitti*)—which is delimited by the meaning of the verbal root and is produced by the operation consisting of conjunction inherent in the fire that is distinct from the rice (the referent of the base of the second-case suffix). Consequently, because it possesses the status of an object (*karman*), there would arise the undesirable consequence of the usage *taṇḍulaṃ pacyate svayameva*. Thus, in this context, the meaning intended for the verbal root *pac* is conjunction with fire conducive to softening.

The intention is that both softening (*viklitti*) and contact with fire (*agni-saṃyoga*) are intended to be expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*). Thus he says: "favorable to softening, [the rice-grains]... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because of being the locus of the meaning of the root": the meaning is "because of being the locus of the result in the form of softening, which is produced by the meaning of the root in the form of contact with fire. Therefore, it must be accepted that the sole cause for the arising of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā-vibhakti*) is the technical designation "object" (*karman*), and not the state of possessing a result as previously described—namely, "residing in another" (*parasamaveta*) and so forth.

The intention is as follows: when it is accepted that the introduction of case-endings (*vibhakti*) is the cause for the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as "object" (*karman*) and so forth, then in the example *taṇḍulaḥ pacyate svayameva* ("the rice cooks by itself"), although the designation "object" would apply to the rice—which is both the object and the agent—this is sublated by the subsequent designation "agent. Consequently, there is no possibility of a second case ending; rather, only the first case ending occurs, and thus there is no fault whatsoever. It should be understood that this objection is raised on the basis of assuming that "contact with fire" (*agni-saṃyoga*) is intended as the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

However, it should be understood that this objection does not apply if it is asserted that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) consists either in the activity residing solely in the rice-grain—which is the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*)—and which is conducive to softening, or in the result alone. If it is argued: "Even if the fault consisting in the undesirable consequence of the usage *caitraścaitram* (‘Caitra [cooks] Caitra’) is thus avoided, there still arises the undesirable consequence of a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) from the sentence *caitro gacchati* (‘Caitra goes’) in the form: ‘the going has Caitra as its agent and Caitra as its object’," he replies: "There would also be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of verbal cognition. [He adds: "In the very manner already stated."

The meaning is that [the objection] is refuted by the very manner already stated—such as "let it be said that there is another causal relation for those who are proficient," and so forth. Furthermore, even if it is accepted that the accusative case expresses "subsistence in another" (*parasamavetatva*), that "otherness" (*paratva*) must have the referent of the accusative base as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and not any other; and "subsistence in another" must connect only with the action denoted by the verbal root (*dhātvartha-kriyā*), and not with the result (*phala*). Thus, in order to secure these two restrictive rules, one would have to postulate various such distinct causal relations.

The sense is that because an excess of respect [for the opponent] is unavoidable, the view of the Logicians (*tārkika*) is entirely improper. He states the division of the object (*karman*) as taught in the *Vākyapadīya* with the words "And this," etc. The meaning is: the object consists of that which serves as the locus of the result produced by the operation denoted by the verbal root (*dhātvartha-vyāpāra*). "Sevenfold" means consisting of seven types. He demonstrates those very seven types with the words beginning "That which is to be produced" (*nirvartya*), etc. The syntactical connection is: "That object which is most desired (*īpsitatama*) is considered to be threefold—namely, that which is to be produced (*nirvartya*), that which is to be modified (*vikārya*), and that which is to be reached (*prāpya*). "But the other" means: distinct from that which is most desired.

"Fourfold" means of four kinds. He demonstrates this very fourfold nature by the words "by indifference," etc. The meaning is: that which is to be reached—that is, the locus of the fruit produced by an action—when there is an absence of being desired (*īpsitatva*) and an absence of being detested (*dveṣyatva*), is the first kind. That which is undesired (*anīpsita*) or detested is the second. That which is not designated by other technical names—that is, not intended to be expressed by designations such as *apādāna* (ablative) and so forth, and which is the object (*karma*) prescribed by the rule *akathitaṃ ca*—is the third kind. "Preceded by another" [refers to the fourth].

When there is the application of another technical designation (saṃjñā), that which is designated as "object" (karman) occurs; for example, in the case of *krūram abhikrudhyati* ("he is angry at the cruel one"), the designation of "recipient" (saṃpradāna) would otherwise apply by the rule *krudhadruherṣyāsūyārthānāṃ yaṃ prati kopaḥ*, but it is instead designated as "object" by the rule *krudhadruhor upasṛṣṭayoḥ*. This means it is the fourth [type of object]. Here, the intention is merely to demonstrate the fourfold nature [of objects], and not to follow the sequence of the first, second, and so on. He states the definition of the three types of objects beginning with the "to-be-produced" (*nirvartya*): "that which is non-existent" (*yadasat*).

In the view of the Naiyāyikas, the production of an effect such as a jar occurs as something previously non-existent; according to that school, this is the definition of an object to be produced (*nirvartya-karman*). According to the Sāṃkhya school, he says "or existent" (*sad vā*). For in their view, the manifestation of an effect such as a jar—which is already existent—occurs through its birth. [He adds] "without cutting off the primordial nature" (*prakṛtyaccheda*).

Among the two types of objects to be modified (*vikārya-karma*), one is that which has reached—meaning attained—destruction or annihilation, such as wood and the like, which are of the nature of a material cause (*prakṛti*); here the suffix *kta* is used in the active sense from the root *bhū* meaning "to reach. However, another arises through the production of a different quality or a different form; this is the second type of object to be modified. He states the definition of the object to be reached (*prāpya-karma*) as "that which is characterized by the action... (*kriyākṛta*).

The meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is action (*vyāpāra*). That which is to be reached (*prāpya-karman*) is that object where a specific change produced by that action is not perceived either through direct perception or through inference; this is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). He states the examples in order: "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*). The first is the *nirvartya* (that which is brought into being). The Naiyāyikas maintain the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*), while the Sāṃkhyas maintain the theory of the existent effect (*satkāryavāda*). However, for the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), it is precisely the theory of the existent effect as accepted by the Sāṃkhyas that is intended. [Examples of the other two types are: "wood becomes ash" (*kāṣṭhaṃ bhasma*) and "gold becomes an earring" (*suvarṇaṃ kuṇḍalam*).

In this context, the meaning of the root *kṛ* is an operation conducive to production, preceded by an operation conducive to transformation. For this very reason, the status of being an object (*karman*) is successfully maintained for each of the two pairs—namely, wood and ash, and gold and earring—based on the cognition: "transforming the wood, he produces ash."

In the first case, "the wood becomes ashes," the modification (*vikāra*) consists in the destruction of the substrate, the wood; in the latter case, "gold becomes an earring," the modification consists in a specific form. Thus, in both instances, there is the status of an object as a modification (*vikārya-karmatā*). The third [type of object] means "that which is to be reached" (*prāpya*). Here, in the case of a jar, no distinction produced by action is perceived either through perception or inference. In the case of an object to be brought into being (*nirvartya*), the distinction consists in the acquisition of its own nature; in the case of an object of modification (*vikārya*) as well, it sometimes consists in the acquisition of its own nature, and sometimes in the production of a different quality.

By means of inference (*anumāna*), for example: "The son experiences happiness. For here, there is an inference of happiness based on the brightening of his face. "He touches the grass," or "He is going to the village," and so forth—this is neutral (*udāsīna*). But "He eats poison"—this is hateful (*dveṣya*). In both cases, the designation of "object" (*karman*) applies by the rule "and that which is likewise engaged" (*tathā yuktam ca*).
