"Milk the cow" (*gāṃ dogdhi*): the meaning is that the cow receives the designation of "object" by the rule "that which is not otherwise mentioned" (*akathitam ca*), because the status of being the "point of departure" (*apādāna*) residing in the cow is not intended to be expressed. "He is angry with the cruel man" (*krūram abhikrudhyati*).

In this context, although the designation of "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*) would have applied by the rule *krudhadruheṣya*, that is set aside; because the designation of "object" (*karman*) is prescribed by the rule *krudhadruhoḥ* [Pāṇini 1.4.37], the meaning is that the object must be preceded by something else. Likewise, in examples such as *vaikuṇṭham adhyāste*, one should understand that Vaikuṇṭha possesses the status of an object preceded by its location.

He explains the third meaning as it follows in sequence with the words "of the third case" (*tṛtīyāyāḥ*). This means "of the agentive third case" (*kartṛtṛtīyāyāḥ*). "The substratum" (*āśraya*) means merely the substratum itself. It will be stated later that for the instrumental third case (*karaṇatṛtīyā*), however, both the substratum and its operation (*vyāpāra*) are denoted. He states the proof for the fact that the agentive third case has the substratum as its meaning with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*), etc., according to the maxim: "A cognition whose qualifier has not been grasped does not arise regarding the qualified object," [referring here] to that which resides in the independent entity.

Because independence (*svātantrya*) is present in the intellect due to its being prominently manifested, he says "and independence. Anticipating the objection that if independence—defined as not being dependent on another—is taken as the basis, then in cases such as *caitreṇa pācayati maitram* ("He causes Maitra to cook by means of Caitra"), Caitra would not attain the status of agent because he is dependent on the instigator (*prayojaka*), he states the intended meaning: "of the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvartha*). This means "as presented by the verbal root."

If it were stated merely that [the object] is "the substratum of the meaning of the verbal root" (dhātvarthāśrayatva), there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to the object (karman), because the object is also the substratum of the fruit (phala) which is the meaning of the root; therefore, the term "operation" (vyāpāra) is included. If it were stated merely that [the agent] is "the substratum of an operation," there would be over-extension to the instrument (karaṇa), because the instrument is the substratum of an operation induced by an operation residing in the agent; therefore, the phrase "meaning of the verbal root" is included. If anything whatsoever that is the substratum of an operation denoted by a verbal root were considered the agent, then even in the sentence "He cooks in a pot with firewood" (kāṣṭhaiḥ sthālyāṃ pacati), the firewood and other such factors would also have the status of agent, even when used in conjunction with the root *pac*.

In expressions such as "the wood burns" (*kāṣṭhaṃ jvalati*) or "the pot shines" (*sthālī prakāśate*), the wood and so forth are [considered agents] because they are the substrata of whatever activity is denoted by the verbal root. Furthermore, since any arbitrary activity denoted by a root would not serve to distinguish [the specific agent], only the activity denoted by the root in its current context (*prakṛtadhātu*) should be taken. Consequently, because the wood and so forth lack the status of being the substratum for the activity of blowing and so on denoted by the root *pac* (to cook) in its current context, there is no occurrence of their being designated as the agent (*kartṛ*) when used in syntactic coordination with the root *pac*. Moreover, even among the activities denoted by the root in its current context, only that which has become the primary one (*pradhānībhūta*) should be taken.

Therefore, since the root *nī* (to lead) denotes not merely an action conducive to conjunction, but an action conducive to an action that is itself conducive to conjunction, the goat (*ajā*) does not possess the status of an agent (*kartṛ*) in the sentence "Caitra leads the goat to the village" (*caitro grāmam ajāṃ nayati*). Here, the second action is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and it resides in Caitra. The first action, however, is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the second action, and it is precisely this [first action] that resides in the goat; thus, it should be understood that the goat does not have the status of an agent. Nor should it be argued that the goat’s status as an agent is precluded by the technical designation of "object" (*karman*), for that would result in the goat being deprived of its agency altogether.

Regarding the technical designation (saṃjñā) of "object" (*karman*) defined as "that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamam*), since it finds its scope in examples such as *caitraḥ taṇḍulam pacati* ("Caitra cooks rice"), it lacks both the status of an exception (*apavāda*) and the quality of being subsequent (*paratva*). On the contrary, due to its subsequent position, the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) itself would actually be the sublater. To provide the proof for the fact that the word *svatantra* has the meaning [of independence] as explained, he says: *dhātunokta*. The syntactical connection is: "The status of being an agent is always intended for a factor of action (*kāraka*) whose action is expressed by the verbal root."

The meaning is that since the *Vākyapadīya* states that "the agent (*kartṛ*) is that *kāraka* which is the action (*kriyā*), consisting of an operation (*vyāpāra*), that culminates in [a result] as expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*)," it follows that agency (*kartṛtva*) consists precisely in being the substratum of the operation that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root.

But surely, if such autonomy (svātantrya) is adopted as the basis [for agency], then in cases such as *sthālyāṃ pacati* ("he cooks in the pot"), the pot and so forth would also incur the status of an agent (*kartṛ*), because they are the substratum of the activity consisting of holding and so on, which is denoted by the verbal root *pac*; for the activity consisting of holding the rice-grains and so on—which is conducive to their softening—is intended to be the meaning of the root *pac*. To this, he says: "For this very reason, when... For this very reason—namely, precisely because of the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the pot and so forth in the aforementioned example.

Nor should it be said that the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) is sublated by the designations of "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth because they are without scope (*niravakāśa*). For the reason is this: since the designation of "locus" also applies within the domain of the designation of "agent," and since that [designation of locus] too would be without scope, there would result the undesirable consequence of these two being synonymous (*paryāyatā*). He states—from "yo yadā... up to "...sthālī pacatītyādi saṃgacchate"—that the usage "the fire cooks" (*agniḥ pacati*) and so forth is consistent precisely because of the acceptance that whenever something is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the activity denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), it is then the agent. Thus, the usage "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*) and so forth is also consistent.

One might object: "If it is accepted that when an operation residing in something is expressed by a verbal root, that thing is the agent, then—since the relationship of both agency and objectivity can occur for even a single entity depending on the speaker's intention—would this not contradict the statement made by the venerable Patañjali in the section [of the Mahābhāṣya] beginning with 'kartṛkarmavyapadeśācca,' where he asserts through his *Nyāsa* that the simultaneous connection of a single entity with both agency and objectivity is improper due to its contradiction? With this in mind, he raises the objection starting with "nanvevam" and so forth.

The point is this: having enjoined meditation with the words "he should perform the sacrifice" (*kratuṃ kurvīta*), the text states "consisting of mind, having breath for its body" (*manomayaḥ prāṇaśarīraḥ*) as the object of that injunction of meditation. In that regard, one might suspect that because the connection with mind, breath, and so forth is possible directly in the case of the individual self (*jīvātman*), the individual self is here indicated as the object of meditation by the terms "consisting of mind" and so on. Anticipating this objection, [the Sūtra] considers that if the one expressed by the terms "consisting of mind" and so on were indeed the individual self, then in the subsequent portion of the passage—namely, "departing from here, I shall attain him"—[it would have to be so].

The designation of both agent and object applied to the single individual soul (jīva)—who is denoted by terms such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya)—is contradictory, because he is simultaneously the object of attainment and the agent of attainment. This is because the meaning of the passage is: "from here—from this body—having departed, having gone forth, that is, having abandoned this body—I shall attain, I shall reach, this very one—the individual self under discussion who is denoted by terms such as 'consisting of mind'. Thus, the sense is established.

In this context, by the word *etam* ("this"), the previously mentioned mind-made (*manomaya*) individual self (*jīvātman*) is indicated as the object of attainment; and by the person [denoted by] the periphrastic future form *abhisaṃbhavitāsmi* ("I shall attain"), the embodied worshipper (*śārīra upāsakaḥ*) is designated as the agent of attainment. [The form *abhisaṃbhavitāsmi* is derived from] the root *bhū* with the prefix *sam-upa*, meaning "to attain," which is conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); here, by grammatical exception (*vyatyaya*), the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is used in place of the periphrastic future (*luṭ*).

Alternatively, according to the view of certain authorities that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs only by virtue of the concomitant application of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), it should be understood that in the absence of the *ṇic*, the active voice (*parasmaipada*) applies as a general rule, except in cases of specific irregularity. Regarding this, Śaṅkara’s commentary states: "And when another interpretation is available, it is not proper for a single entity to be designated simultaneously as both agent and object."

By stating "this being the case, when there is a distinction [of states]," it is indicated that the postulation of a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*)—as in the expression "one kills oneself by means of oneself"—is an untenable resort and thus not logical. In that context, although it is possible for a single entity to have two designations at different times, it is not proper for one entity to have two designations simultaneously. With the intention that the perception of the effects of two designations at once in the present scriptural passage would be contradictory, he provides the resolution: "It is said," and so forth. "In this way" means: if one accepts both agency and objecthood for a single entity.

"Of the one consisting of mind" (manomayasya) means "of that which is denoted by the word *manomaya*. "In the state of being a living soul" (jīvatve) means "in the state of being distinct from Brahman. "The remainder of the sentence" (vākyaśeṣa) means "the remainder of the sentence beginning with 'departing from here' (*etamitaḥ pretya*)," and so forth. "Of him" (tasya) means "of the individual self (jīvātman) denoted by the word *manomaya*. Thus should the explanation of the words found in the root text be understood. He states the manner of the resolution: "Of the living soul alone," and so forth.

When it is established by such passages as "consisting of mind, having breath for its body" that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the object of meditation, then its status as the one who attains [the goal] must also be predicated of that same soul. This is because the word "this" (*etam*) in the phrase "him" refers back to the subject previously introduced. The term "of him" (*tasya*) means "of the individual self. The agency is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) in the finite verb "I shall attain" (*abhisaṃbhavitāsmi*), since, according to the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve ca*, the suffix *luṭ* (the future tense marker) is prescribed in the sense of the agent.

In that case, it is not logical—and indeed impossible—for a single entity to simultaneously possess both the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "object" (*karman*). This is because, according to the rule *ā kaḍārād ekā saṃjñā*, the designation "agent," being subsequent [in the sequence of rules], subverts the designation "object. Consequently, the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) in the word *etam* would not be applicable.

Now, if it were argued that in the phrase "I shall manifest" (*abhisaṃbhavitāsmi*), the periphrastic future suffix (*luṭ*) does not denote a pure agent (*kartṛ*), but rather a reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*)—just as in the previous sentence, that which was indicated as the object (*karman*) becomes the agent; for example, in the sentence "He cooks the rice," the rice is designated as the object, yet in the sentence "The rice cooks by itself," it functions as the agent—if this is said, he replies "no," because it would entail the application of the *yaṅ* affix and other such anomalies.

[Objection: But surely, even if the *luṭ* [suffix] has both object and agent as its referent (*karmakartṛtva*), there is no occurrence of *yaK* because the *tās-* [of the periphrastic future] lacks the status of being a *sārvadhātuka*. To this he says: "beginning with *yaK*" (*yagādi*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the *ciṇvadbhāva*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), and so forth is intended. Thus, the sense is that through the *ciṇvadbhāva*, the augment *vṛddhi* and the middle voice would result. "By way of contradiction between words" (*śabdavirodhadvārā*) means: by way of the contradiction consisting in the impossibility of two designations and their respective operations occurring simultaneously for a single thing. "That" refers to the contradiction in the form of the impossibility of two designations for one thing at once. "The cause of distinction" (*bhedahetu*).

The meaning is that [the suffix -maya] serves as the cause for the distinction between the object of worship and the worshiper, namely between the Supreme Self (paramātman) and the individual self (jīvātman). Thus, it is established that by terms such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya), the Supreme Self alone is indicated, and not the individual self; therefore, there is no contradiction with the previously mentioned determination by the venerable Vyāsa—this is the intended sense.

[Objection: If this is so, then the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) would also, like the third case-ending denoting the instrument (*karaṇa*), result in expressing a substratum (*āśraya*) qualified by an operation (*vyāpāra*), rather than expressing the substratum alone. To this, he says: "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*). This means: when agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being the substratum of the operation expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*). [The phrase] "of the factor of operation" (*vyāpārāṃśasya*) means: of the factor of operation which is a constituent of the definition of agency. [The phrase] "because it is obtainable from the verbal root" (*dhātulabhyatvāt*) means: because it is conveyed by the verbal root. [The phrase] "the substratum alone" (*āśrayamātram*)— [Note: The provided text ends abruptly.]

The sense is that this follows the logical principle (*nyāya*) that the meaning of a word must be something not obtainable through any other means. By the word "only" (*mātra*), the exclusion of the operation (*vyāpāra*) is intended. He restates the definition of agency (*kartṛtva*) as propounded by the Mīmāṃsakas in order to refute it: "the state of being the impeller of the entire set of causal factors" (*kārakacakraprayoktṛtva*). This means the state of being the initiator of the collection of causal factors capable of entering into connection with the action denoted by the verbal root under discussion. Furthermore, he restates the definition of agency accepted by the Naiyāyikas—out of consideration for its greater parsimony (*lāghava*) compared to the aforementioned view—as "the state of being the impeller of the entire set of causal factors."

The meaning is: "the state of being the initiator of a collection of factors (kārakas) that are capable of being connected with the action inherent in the verbal root in question. Furthermore, in accordance with parsimony even over the aforementioned definition, he restates the agency (kartṛtva) as accepted by the Naiyāyikas: "or, it is the state of being the locus of effort" (*kṛtyāśrayatva*). The meaning is: "agency is the state of being the locus of effort conducive to the operation that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root in question. And this state of being a locus is to be understood through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).

Therefore, although the pot possesses the state of being a locus (*āśrayatva*) for the effort conducive to cooking by way of the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*), there is no unwarranted consequence (*āpatti*) such as "the pot cooks" or "it is cooked by the pot. He states that both these types of agency (*kartṛtva*) are afflicted by the fault of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) with the words "non-pervasive. The point is that in cases such as "the staff acts" (*daṇḍaḥ karoti*) or "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*), since the staff and so forth are insentient, they lack the status of being an instigator (*prayoktṛ*) of the entire set of causal factors (*kāraka-cakra*), and thus, due to the absence of being a locus of effort, they would not possess agency. He describes the classification of the agent with the words "And this... (*ayaṃ ca*).

The meaning is that the "agent" (kartṛ) is mentioned as having the sense of the third case (instrumental). And "distinction" (vibhāga) refers to a description made by way of properties that are pervaded by agency. He demonstrates the threefold nature [of the agent] with the words beginning with "pure" (śuddha). The meaning is that an agent distinct from the causal agent (hetukartṛ) and the reflexive agent (karmakartṛ) is the "pure" agent. An agent who is the substratum of the operation signified by the causative suffix (ṇij) is the "instigating agent" (prayojakakartṛ).

The "agent-as-object" (*karmakartṛ*), however, is that which, while being the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal root that serves as the base for the causative suffix (*ṇic*), is also the substratum of the result produced by the activity expressed by the meaning of the *ṇic*; this is the sense of "the instigating agent" (*prayojyakartṛ*). That is to say, one who is designated as the "agent" (*kartṛ*) in the non-causative state becomes designated as the "object" (*karman*) in the causative state is what is meant by "agent-as-object. The intention here is that the definition of "agent-as-object" is not intended to be merely the state of being the substratum of an activity that resides solely in the substratum of the result.

He states examples for the agents (*kartṛ*) beginning with the *śuddha* (pure), in sequence: *mayā hariḥ*, *kāryate*, and *gamayati kṛṣṇam*. He demonstrates the verbal cognitions (*śābdabodha*) corresponding to those examples in that very order: "the operation having a locus non-different from me," "the operation having a locus non-different from Hari," and "the operation consisting of going whose object is Gokula. These should be understood as their respective verbal cognitions in this sequence; in the first example, [it is expressed] by the word *mayā*.

In the first example, Hari is the pure (*śuddha*) agent because he possesses an activity that is non-co-referential with both the causative agency and the objecthood. In the second example, from the causative form of the root *kṛ*, there is the present indicative (*laṭ*) in the passive sense (*yak*); here, Hari is the causative agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*). In the third example, since Kṛṣṇa—who is the agent in the non-causative (*aṇ*) form—is designated as the object (*karman*) in the causative (*ṇic*) form by the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārtha-śabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇikartā sa ṇau*, Kṛṣṇa is a "patient-agent" (*karmakartṛ*).

And thus, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*). Since the technical designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) is sublated by the designation of "object" (*karman-saṃjñā*), there is no deficiency whatsoever, because even in the absence of that [technical] designation, the actual status of being an agent—in the form of being the substratum of the activity conveyed by the verbal root in question—is present. Regarding the phrase "conducive to service": "service" (*sevā*) refers to such acts as massaging the feet or the like, or else it means affection (*prīti*). According to the view of the moderns (*navīna*), however, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) should be understood as: "service having Hari as its object, produced by an activity whose substratum is non-different from me," and so forth.

For they accept that when there is a co-utterance with the causal factor *karman*, the resulting verbal cognition has the fruit (*phala*) as its primary qualificand. Likewise, in the case of "kāryate hariṇā" (it is caused to be done by Hari), the understanding to be derived is: "an act of production brought about by an operation whose locus is non-different from Hari."

He states that the locus qualified by the operation is the denotation of the instrumental third case (*karaṇatṛtīyā*), saying: "But [as for] the instrumental third case... Now, one might object: there is no evidence that both the locus and the operation are denotable by the instrumental third case, since the technical designation *karaṇa* (instrument) is prescribed only for that which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*). To this he replies: "For instance... For the instrument is indeed the most effective means; therein, the sense of the suffix *-tama* is excellence (*prakarṣa*). And that [excellence] consists in possessing an operation that produces the result without any intervention.

And such excellence (prakarṣa) is to be understood as being in relation to other *kārakas*, but not in relation to other *karaṇas*. This is because the suffix *-tamap*, prescribed after the word *sādhaka* which denotes a *kāraka* in general, conveys excellence specifically delimited by the category of *kāraka*. Furthermore, excellence in relation to one *karaṇa* cannot exist in another *karaṇa*. Therefore, there is no logical inconsistency in such usage as "he goes by means of speed (*rayena*), by means of a lamp (*dīpikayā*), along the path (*pathā*)."

For here, no excellence whatsoever is perceived in the lamp relative to the chariot, or in the chariot relative to the lamp. "Such an operation" means: the sense is that the instrument (*karaṇa*) is precisely that cause which is characterized by an operation that immediately precedes the production of the result. Thus, the intention is that since the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) cannot denote the instrument when it refers to the substratum of the operation, the sūtra *sādhakatamaṃ* [Pāṇini 1.4.42] alone is the authority for its definition.

And thus, it should be understood that in the root text [of the *Vākyapadīya*], the word "substratum" (*āśraya*) in the phrase "the substratum, the limit, and the object" is also an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the operation (*vyāpāra*). To support this point, he cites the consensus of the *Vākyapadīya*, beginning with "And it has been said. Regarding the term "action" (*kriyā*): here, the word "action" refers to the result (*phala*). Since the result—the meaning of the verbal root—is perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), its treatment as "action" is clear from the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* (Pāṇini 3.1.87). He explains the purpose of the phrase "is intended to be expressed" (*vivakṣyate*) with the words "In reality," etc.

That state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is, in reality, indefinable—meaning it is impossible to specify—because it resides in a particular entity. He states the reason for this with the words "for not" (*na hi*). For indeed, because that state of being an instrument does not reside solely in a particular entity—that is, it is not restricted to a specific thing alone—is the meaning. He provides the reason for its not being restricted to a particular entity alone with the word "pot" (*sthālyā*). The meaning is that even a pot, which is the object of the determination of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*), may assume the state of being an instrument according to the speaker's intention.

Although, according to the manner stated above, it is possible for all [factors] to function as instruments (*karaṇa*), there is no intention to express the instrumentality of all of them simultaneously; thus, the undesirable consequence of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) does not arise everywhere. He states "due to the absence of that" (*tadabhāvāt*) because, precisely due to the lack of an intention to express the instrumentality of all [factors] simultaneously, there is scope for the second (*dvitīyā*) and seventh (*saptamī*) case endings and so forth. "Due to the absence of the intention to express instrumentality" is the meaning. "At once" (*sakṛt*) means "simultaneously" (*yugapat*).

The point is that since there is no intention to express the simultaneous instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of multiple factors such as the rice and the pot, the accusative and other case-endings occur for the rice and so forth in the sentence "he cooks rice in a pot" (*taṇḍulaṃ sthālyāṃ pacati*). Now, one might object: if all factors are accepted as instruments based on speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), would this not contradict the section [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*] stating, "The agent [is established] because the meaning of the scripture is thus rendered purposeful" (*kartā śāstrārthavattvāt*)? To this he says: "And it is not so."

Having raised the doubt as to whether the soul (*jīva*) is the agent or rather the intellect (*buddhi*), it was stated by the sūtra "The soul alone is the agent, because otherwise the scriptures would be purposeless" (*kartā śāstrārthavattvāt*) that the soul alone is the agent and that agency does not belong to the intellect. To further strengthen this point, another reason was stated: "Because of the reversal of capacities" (*śaktiviparyayāt*).

The meaning of this is as follows: if the intellect (*buddhi*) alone, which is denoted by the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), were the agent, then there would be a contradiction with the instrumental case used for the term "consciousness" in the scriptural passage, "by the consciousness of these vital breaths" (*tadeṣāṃ prāṇānāṃ vijñānena*). That is to say, the intellect's capacity as an instrument would be lost, and it would instead incur the capacity of being an agent. This is the sense.

Furthermore, since in all instances such as "I go" or "I drink," activity is observed to be preceded by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), one must admit that the object of the notion of "I" is the intellect (buddhi) alone, which is endowed with the capacity for agency. Consequently, if it were argued that some other instrument must be postulated for that agent intellect, then the claim that the individual soul (jīva) alone is the agent and not the intellect—based on the resulting contradiction of capacities—would be untenable. Thus, that [previous] position would not be consistent.

Since the reversal of the power [of words] according to the speaker's intention is established by the scriptures, there is no contradiction, and thus it does not constitute a fault. Therefore, if it is argued that it is not appropriate to maintain that all things possess instrumentality based on intention, we reply: "In that case, for these... [tadeṣām iti].

The meaning is as follows: "of the vital breaths" means of the sense organs; "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to their power of apprehension. By [identifying them with] consciousness—that is, with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) denoted by the term *manas*—there would follow the loss of the status of instrument (*karaṇatva*) which has been established for them, and the acquisition of an unestablished status as agent (*kartṛtva*). Thus, the purport is that it would result in the abandonment of what is established and the introduction of what is not established. It does not mean, however, that the status of instrument is not intended for all of them.

The sense is that there is no contradiction whatsoever when that which is established as an instrument (*karaṇa*) in one scriptural passage is intended as an agent (*kartṛ*) in another, because it is only the simultaneous intention of both agency and instrumentality that is contradictory. This is the underlying thought. For this very reason, he says: "In reality, however" (*vastutastu*). Regarding the phrase "merely a secondary mention" (*anvācayamātram*): "this" refers to the objection consisting of the contingency of a reversal of powers; the meaning is that this is merely incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*), not the primary point.

The intention is that the primary purpose [of this section] is precisely the refutation of the intellect (*buddhi*) as the agent. He clarifies this very point with the words, "And just as the carpenter... [and so on]. Regarding the phrase "in the Bhāṣya itself": having raised the doubt—after the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) has been established by the previously mentioned reasons such as the meaningfulness of the scriptures (*śāstrārthavattva*)—as to whether that agency is innate or adventitious (*aupādhika*), [it is argued that] if agency were innate, there would be no liberation.

Because agency (*kartṛtva*) is of the nature of suffering (*duḥkha*); for if agency were the very essence of the Self, then—just as heat cannot be separated from fire—an agent could never be disjoined from its agency. As for the illustration that agency is of the nature of suffering: just as a carpenter with an axe and other tools in his hand becomes miserable, but becomes happy when divested of them, so too the Self, being an agent dependent upon instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*), becomes miserable; but when independent of those, being a non-agent, it becomes happy. Thus it is.

By means of the illustration, it is quite clear that the self's agency is caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Thus, the intent of the reversal of capacity (*śakti-viparyaya*) is solely the refutation of the intellect's (*buddhi*) agency, and not the abandonment of the intellect's status as an instrument (*karaṇa*); the sense is that the reversal of capacity is merely incidental.

He states the meaning of the locative case with the words "of the locative as well. Now, one might object: since the locative is prescribed for the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), how can its meaning be the substratum (*āśraya*)? To this he says: "And that. The meaning is: "and that which is designated as the locus. One might further object: even by that much, the status of being a substratum (*ādhāra*)—not the status of being a substratum (*āśraya*)—is obtained as the meaning of the locative from the rule *ādhāro 'dhikaraṇam* (Pāṇini 1.4.45). To this he says: "And that nature. The meaning is: "and the nature of being a substratum. [This refers to] the status of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*).

The meaning is that there is no evidence for *ādhāratva* (the state of being a substratum) being something distinct from *āśrayatva* (the state of being a locus). Thus, the intention is that there is only a difference in name, not in the actual entity. Now, one might object: "From the meaning of the Sūtra, it is understood that the meaning of the locative case is the locus of the action residing in the agent or the object, and not the mere locus. To this, he says: "In that regard, the factor of the locus (*āśrayāṃśa*). The meaning is that between the action and its locus, since the action is already obtained by the verbal root itself, the factor of the locus alone—which cannot be obtained through any other means—is the meaning expressed by the locative case.

"Reality" (tattvam) means that the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) is the delimiting factor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). And it has already been stated previously that this [substratum] is of the nature of an indivisible power (*akhaṇḍa-śakti*). Now, one might raise the objection: "By the rule *ādhāro’dhikaraṇam* (Pāṇini 1.4.45), the technical designation 'locus' (*adhikaraṇa-saṃjñā*) is prescribed on the basis of mere substratum-hood; would this not then apply to the object (*karman*), the agent (*kartṛ*), and the instrument (*karaṇa*)? To this, he says "na ca" and so forth. "Object-agent," etc.

The meaning is as follows: "of the action" (karman) refers to that which is the substratum of the fruit; "of the agent" (kartṛ) refers to that which is the substratum of the activity conducive to the fruit; and "of the instrument" (karaṇa) refers to that which is the substratum of the activity immediately preceding the accomplishment of the action in the form of the fruit. Regarding the phrase "the designation 'substratum'": the meaning is that the designation prescribed for a substratum is the designation "locus" (adhikaraṇa). The intended sense is that if the designation "substratum" were not explicitly enjoined, an inconsistency would arise according to the literal reading [of the rule]. Nor should it be argued that the designation "locus" itself is enjoined for the substratum by this sūtra.

Since the locus (*ādhāra*) has been mentioned first, it is the object to be designated (*uddeśya*), while that which is mentioned later is the designation (*saṃjñā*). Therefore, the intention is to assign the technical name "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) specifically to the locus, and not conversely. This point is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule defining the term *vṛddhi*. He provides the resolution with the words "It would indeed be so," etc. The meaning is this: although the designation "locus" would apply to the substrata of the results and so forth, nevertheless, the designation "locus" is superseded by the designations "object" (*karman*) and the rest.

If the designation *adhikaraṇa* (locus) were to apply everywhere simply because something is situated upon a substratum, then the designations such as *karman* (object) and so forth would have no scope; therefore, because they belong to the domain beginning with *ā kaḍārāt*, the designation *adhikaraṇa* is not applied here, as it is superseded by the designations *karman* and others which are without scope [for that term]. This is the meaning.

Now, if the designation *adhikaraṇa* (locus) is sublated by designations such as *karman* (object), then what scope remains for the designation *adhikaraṇa*? Nor should it be said that its scope consists of that which is indirectly the locus of action; for when the direct locus of action is possible, it is improper to adopt that which is indirectly the locus of action. To this, he says: "Having introduced [the topic] with the heading ‘in a kāraka’...”, etc., meaning “of the locative case prescribed [by Pāṇini 2.3.36]”.

The meaning is: "of that locative case which is prescribed for what is designated as *adhikaraṇa* (locus) under the governing rule concerning *kārakas*. "Only the substratum of the action" means "only that which is the direct substratum of the action. By the use of the particle *eva* ("only"), there is the exclusion of the mat and so forth, which have Caitra or others as their substratum. Thus, the intention is that such a designation of *adhikaraṇa* would apply only to the agent or the object [when they are the direct substratum], but not to the mat and so forth which have Caitra or others as their substratum.

Since the technical designations "agent" (kartṛ) and "object" (karman) are prescribed for the substrata of the acts of "direct realization" (sākṣātkriyā), the intention is that by the logic of remainder (pariśeṣanyāya), the substratum of the action [of motion] is understood through its connection with the substratum of the act of direct realization. With this intent, he provides the answer: "Even so, here... [and] "...by way of the agent and the object. Such a meaning is obtained precisely from the force of the sūtra itself. For instance, in the rule *ādhāro 'dhikaraṇam* ("the substratum is the locus"), the governing term *kārake* ("in the context of a kāraka") is transformed into the nominative case; and that [term] serves as a qualifier of the substratum (*ādhāra*).

It is understood that "the locus (ādhāra) is the kāraka termed adhikaraṇa. Furthermore, a kāraka is that which produces an action, based on the etymological derivation: "it performs" (karoti), meaning "it generates an action" (kriyāṃ janayati). Thus, when there arises the expectancy "of what is the locus?", it is understood—by virtue of its immediate proximity—to be "of the action."

Action (*kriyā*) consists of the operation and the result of the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*). In that context, since the substrata of action are already occupied by the designations "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "object" (*karman*) through the two subsequent [rules], this present rule finds no scope; therefore, its purpose is to provide the designation "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) for the substratum of the action that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root, by way of the agent and the object. "Being the substratum of that" means being the substratum of the action consisting of the operation and the result residing in the agent and the object. "It certainly exists," etc.

It should be understood that since the status of being the locus (*āśraya*) of an action exists through a traditional succession (*paramparayā*), usages such as *sthālyāṃ pacati* ("he cooks in a pot") and *kaṭe śete* ("he sleeps on a mat"), which employ the locative case for the locus (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*), are justified. He shows the agreement of Hari with the meaning of the aforementioned sūtra, stating: "And it has been said... [referring to the verse] "...separated by the agent and the object. In common worldly usage, the locus pertains to substances, qualities, and actions; however, in this grammatical system, because it falls under the section on *kārakas*, it pertains exclusively to action.

The technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "object" (*karman*), which consist of the substrata of the action—the direct result of the operation that is the meaning of the verbal root—are set aside [by the designation "locus"]. Therefore, it was stated [in the rule] "that which is separated from them" (*tadvyavahitām*). Although time is the direct substratum of the action, nevertheless, within the governing heading on "factors of action" (*kāraka-adhikāra*), there is no application of the comparative suffix *-tama*; this has been established by the inclusion of that suffix [in the rule *sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam*]. For instance, "the factor of action" (*kāraka*) and "the accomplisher" (*sādhaka*) are not different in meaning; that is to say, they are synonymous.

And thus, since [the status of a *kāraka*] is already established by the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "kāraka" itself, the fact that the term "sādhaka" (instrument) is mentioned again must be understood as signifying "the most effective instrument" (*sādhakatama*). Therefore, by this seemingly redundant inclusion of the superlative suffix *-tama*, it is indicated that in the governing heading for *kārakas*, excellence (*prakarpa*) is not to be understood through the inherent power of the word alone. Consequently, in examples such as "a crocodile in the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) and "the family of the Gargas at the well" (*kūpe gargakulam*), the designation of "locus" (*adhikaraṇa-saṃjñā*) is successfully established for the Ganges and the like.

Otherwise, since the status of being a locus (*ādhāra*) would already be established by the force of the great technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*) "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*)—which is etymologically meaningful (*anvartha*) in the rule *ādhāro'dhikaraṇam*—the inclusion of the term "locus" (*ādhāra*) once again would imply, by its own power, that only that locus which pervades all parts (*sarvāvayavavyāpti*) should bear the designation of "locus. Consequently, in examples such as "oil in sesame seeds" (*tileṣu tailam*) or "clarified butter in curds" (*dadhani sarpiḥ*), only the sesame seeds and the like would receive the designation of "locus," and not the Ganges or similar [indirect] loci. Thus, in the present context, it is established that even an indirect support of the action (*kriyādhāra*) is included.

Although "separated" (*vyavahitām*) was already stated, the further mention of "not directly" (*asākṣāt*) is intended to indicate—following common worldly usage—that even the connection [of the locus] occurs only through a mediated succession (*paramparayā*). Regarding the phrase "benefiting in the accomplishment of the action": Helārāja explains that in examples such as "he sits on a mat" (*kaṭe āste*) or "he cooks in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ pacati*), the agent and the object do not themselves accomplish the action; rather, the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the support of the action. The meaning is that by benefiting that [action], it benefits the action situated therein. In other words, it brings about the primary action through its own inherent action of supporting and so forth.

Although in examples such as *taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice"), the rice and other objects possess the status of being the locus (*āśraya*) of the action by way of the object (*karman*) which is the fruit of the verbal root's meaning, nevertheless, there is no fault; for this is overridden by the subsequent technical designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*), since the rice possesses the status of being the locus of the fruit produced by the operation (*vyāpāra*). Others, however, maintain that the locus-factor (*adhikaraṇakāraka*) is construed only with the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, because in cases such as *kaṭe śete* ("he sleeps on a mat"), the cognition arises in the form: "the sleeping, whose agent is Caitra, has the mat as its locus. Thus, its connection to the action occurs precisely through that [agent].

The understanding of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of case-factors (*kāraka*) with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) also occurs through such a traditional sequence by the force of this very treatise. For this very reason, there is compounding (*samāsa*) in cases such as *akṣaśauṇḍa* ("skilled at dice"). For this same reason, no doubt regarding a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) was raised in that regard in the Bhāṣya. Thus, Kaiyaṭa and others—who claim that semantic competency exists by way of an internalized action (*antarbhūtakriyā*)—are indeed to be questioned; for in examples such as *akṣaśauṇḍaḥ* ("skilled at dice") and *akṣapravīṇaḥ* ("expert at dice"), there is no experience of cognition occurring through the inclusion of an intermediate action, as there is in the case of *dadhyodana* ("curd-rice") and the like. Rather, they say that the cognition experienced is simply "one who possesses expertise regarding dice."

He states that the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is threefold by saying "and this. "Threefold" means consisting of three types. A "type" (*prakāra*) is a particular (*viśeṣa*) that differentiates a general category (*sāmānya*). He clarifies this very point with the words beginning "aupāśleṣika. The meaning is: *aupāśleṣika* is a locus produced by contact (*upaśleṣa*), such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other relations. *Vaiṣayika* is [a locus] produced by the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*). *Abhivyāpaka* is [a locus] produced by the pervasion of the entire whole (*avayavin*). He gives examples for these in order: "He sleeps on a mat" (*kaṭe śete*).

The word "Devadatta" is understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Here, with respect to the action of lying down residing in the agent who is directly Devadatta himself, the mat possesses the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) because it serves as its substratum through Devadatta, by virtue of the relationship of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). This is an example of a proximate locus (*upaśleṣikādhikaraṇa*) mediated by the agent. The understanding is that there is an operation conducive to lying down whose locus is non-different from the mat through a mediated sequence (*paramparayā*). Similarly, in the expression "he dwells with the teacher" (*gurau vasati*), the locus is also proximate, being mediated by the agent.

The term *aupaśleṣika* (proximate) is derived from the etymology: *upa* meaning "nearby," *śleṣaḥ* meaning "contact" or "connection," and that which is produced by this is *aupaśleṣika*. The resulting cognition is: "an operation conducive to cooking whose locus is, through a traditional lineage, non-different from the teacher. An example of a proximate locus (*aupaśleṣikādhikaraṇa*) mediated by an object (*karman*) should be understood as "he cooks in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ pacati*), and so forth. Here, the pot possesses the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) because it serves as a substratum through the rice, having established a relationship of conjunction with the act of cooking residing directly in the rice, which is the object.

The understanding should be inferred as follows: "the operation conducive to that softening which, through a series, has its locus in a substrate not distinct from the pot. He provides an example of the objective (vaiṣayika) locus: "there is a desire for liberation" (*mokṣecchāsti*). A locus distinct from the contact-based (*aupaśleṣika*) and the pervasive (*abhivyāpaka*) is the objective locus. Here, with respect to the action of existence (*sattā*) residing in the desire—which is the direct agent—the status of being a locus belongs to liberation because it serves as the substratum of desire by virtue of the relationship of objecthood (*viṣayatā*).

The understanding [of the locative case] is either an operation conducive to existence (*sattā*) whose object is non-different from liberation (*mokṣa*) through a traditional succession, or it is the existence residing in the desire for liberation. He provides an example of a pervasive substratum (*abhivyāpakam adhikaraṇam*): "oil in sesame seeds" (*tileṣu tailam*). Here, with respect to the action of existence belonging directly to the agent in the form of oil, the sesame seeds possess the status of a substratum because they are the locus of existence by means of the oil, having prioritized their total pervasion (*kṛtsnavyāpti*). The understanding is that there is an operation conducive to the existence residing in the oil, which has as its locus something non-different from the sesame seeds through a traditional succession.

He states the meaning of the ablative case as "non-prescription" (*avidhi*). He provides the authority for the ablative having the sense of a limit (*avadhi*) by stating, "the ablative is used in the sense of the *apādāna*. Now, one might ask: even if the *sūtra* establishes that the *apādāna* has the sense of the ablative, how is it established that the limit (*avadhi*) has the sense of the ablative? To this he replies: "And that" (*tac ca*). The meaning is: "and that [which is the *apādāna*]."

Apāya is the operation that produces separation; when such an operation exists, that which is fixed, stable, and serves as the limit (avadhi) between the two substrata of the separation produced by that operation—due to proximity—is called the *apādāna*. When a separation arises from the movement of one of two conjoined objects, that which is not the locus of such movement—that is, by implication, that which is not the locus of the operation producing the separation—is the stable entity intended here as the limit. Thus, that which serves as the limit receives the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *apādāna*.

The meaning is that the fifth case (*pañcamī*) signifies the limit (*avadhi*), because the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) is prescribed for the limit by the rule: "In the event of a definite departure from the object of the sutra... He demonstrates the agreement of Hari (Patañjali) regarding this point with the words "And it has been said. [He quotes the passage] beginning with "That which is indifferent during departure" and ending with "separately, separately. He explains the meaning of this passage by Hari with the words "In departure. Departure (*apāya*) means separation (*viśleṣa*), that is to say, division. With the intention that the word "departure" here refers indirectly (*lakṣaṇayā*) to the action that causes departure, he says: "in the action which is the cause of separation."

By the word "indifferent" (*udāsīnam*), the meaning of the term *dhruva* (fixed) is stated. He explains that indifference is the state of not being a substratum for action by saying "not a substratum" (*anāśraya*). By proximity, the meaning is: not being a substratum for the action that causes the separation arising from the verbal root under discussion. And that indifferent thing—whether moving or stationary—is called "fixed" (*dhruva*) regardless of how it exists. Now, one might object: if that which is defined as indifferent is stationary, then let it be called fixed; but if it is moving, how can it be called fixed? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "because of the absence of absorption in that" (*atadāveśāt*).

The meaning is: because it is not entered by any action that causes separation. Thus, in common worldly usage, a stable object devoid of any activity such as vibration is called "fixed" (dhruva). However, in this treatise, the sense is that what is called "fixed" is that which is devoid of even the slightest action that serves as a cause for separation.

Since separation resides in two things, between the two bases of separation, that which is not the locus of the action producing the separation is called the *apādāna*. With the intention that the definition thus implies that the designated entity (the *saṃjñin*)—which is by implication the locus of separation—is not the locus of such an action, he says: "And so it is. This means: when, by the rule *apāye dhruvam*, one intends to express the state of being devoid of the action that produces separation.

If the qualification beginning with *viśleṣa* (separation) and ending with *satī* (existing) were not stated, then there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the technical term *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) to Caitra, who is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the sentence "Caitra goes from Prayāga to Kāśī. This is because the verb *gam* denotes an action that produces separation, and since separation resides in two locations (*dviṣṭha*), it exists equally in Caitra as it does in Prayāga. Consequently, the technical term *apādāna* would override the term *kartṛ*.

The point is that the term *kartṛ-saṃjñā* (the designation of "agent") finds its scope in cases such as *caitraḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("Caitra cooks rice"). However, when the qualifying condition in the second part [of the definition] is stated, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Caitra, because although he is the locus of separation (*viśleṣa*), he is not the locus of the action that produces that separation; this is the intended meaning. Now, if the substantive "being the locus of separation" were not stated, then in the very example mentioned previously, there would be an over-extension to Kāśī as the object (*karman*), since like Prayāga, Kāśī is also not the locus of the action that produces the separation.

However, when the qualificand is specified, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to Kāśī, because, like Prayāga, it lacks the status of being the locus of separation. Thus, both the qualifier and the qualificand have been included in order to exclude over-extension in both cases—namely, the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). This should be noted: in verbs such as *gacchati*, *yāti*, *iyarti*, and *atati*, although each respective root denotes an action that produces separation, separation itself is not denoted by those respective roots.

For this very reason, although such a separation is produced by the operation expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*), it lacks the status of being a "result" (*phala*). This is because the status of being a result consists in being the object of a presentation produced by that root, while simultaneously being produced by the operation expressed by that same root. Where separation is not expressed by the verbal root, the locus of such separation possesses the status of an "ablative" (*apādāna*). For example, in sentences such as *vṛkṣāt parṇaṃ patati* ("The leaf falls from the tree"), the meaning of the root *pat* is an operation conducive to conjunction that produces separation.

In that case, although conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is denoted by the verbal root, disjunction (*vibhāga*) is not; therefore, the tree, which is the locus of such disjunction, possesses the status of an *apādāna* (ablative). However, where disjunction is denoted by the verbal root, because disjunction is the result (*phala*), the designation of *karma* (object) applies to the locus of such disjunction by virtue of its higher rank, thereby overriding the designation of *apādāna*. Thus, in the example "the bird leaves the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ tyajati khagaḥ*), the meaning of the root *tyaj* is an operation conducive to disjunction.

In this context, since separation (*vibhāga*) is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), it constitutes the "result" (*phala*); therefore, the tree, which is the locus of such separation, receives the designation of "object" (*karman*) alone, and not the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*), because the separation is expressed by the verbal root. In the view of the moderns (*navīna*), even in the aforementioned verbal roots, separation is likewise denoted by the root. For this very reason, they state that the status of being a "limit" (*avadhitva*) consists in being the locus of the separation that is the meaning of the relevant verbal root, while not being the locus of the activity that produces that separation as expressed by the relevant verbal root.

In such cases as "he comes from the village" (*grāmād āyāti*) or "he departs from the village" (*grāmād vibhajate*), although separation (*vibhāga*) is the result when used in connection with a verbal root whose meaning is an action coreferential with that separation, the locus of such separation is designated as the *apādāna* (ablative). However, in cases such as "he abandons the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ tyajati*), where the verbal root signifies an action that is not coreferential with the separation, the locus of the separation is designated as the *karman* (object). This is the established rule.

And thus, in cases such as "he goes from Prayāga to Kāśī," even though separation (*vibhāga*) is the meaning of the verbal root, Prayāga—the locus of such a separation—is not the *karman* (object), because it is understood that the separation is co-locative with the activity (*vyāpāra*). It should be understood that only the locus of a separation that is non-co-locative with the activity is a *karman*. He states an example to exclude [cases] by the phrase "the leaf falls from the tree," which serves to exclude the application of the truth-condition (*satyanta*) in the definition of the *apādāna* (ablative).

In this context, the meaning of the verbal root *pat* (to fall) is an activity conducive to a conjunction produced by disjunction. Here, the activity residing in the leaf which is conducive to conjunction is the generator of the disjunction between the tree and the leaf; and since disjunction, like conjunction, is dual-locatable (*dviṣṭha*), it resides in both the tree and the leaf.

This being the case, if it were merely stated that "the status of an *apādāna* consists in being the locus of separation," then the designation *apādāna* would undesirably apply to the leaf as well, just as it does to the tree, since both are loci of separation. To prevent this, the qualification "provided that [it is not itself the agent]" (*satyantam*) has been stated. Consequently, although the leaf is indeed the locus of separation, its exclusion from the designation *apādāna* is established because it is the locus of the activity that produces the separation.

One might object: "Since the over-extension [of the definition] to a leaf is already avoided by the mere condition that it be the locus of disjunction while not being the locus of the action denoted by the verb in question, what is the purpose of including the qualifier 'cause of disjunction' as a modifier of the action? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "from a running horse. Here too, the meaning of the verbal root *pat* (to fall) is exactly as before.

The activity conducive to conjunction that resides in the person mounted on the horse is the generator of the disjunction between the horse and the person; thus, although the horse is the substratum of that disjunction, because of the qualification "running," it is characterized by the action of running denoted by the verb in question. Consequently, since the horse is not non-substratum of the action denoted by the verb in question, it would not possess the status of an *apādāna* (ablative point). Therefore, the term "cause of separation" (*viśleṣahetu*) is provided as a qualification of the action.

The meaning is this: although the horse is connected with the action of running denoted by the root *ṛ* (to run), the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) still applies because it is not the substratum of the action conducive to conjunction denoted by the root *pat* (to fall)—the cause of separation—since that action of separation resides solely in the person mounted on the horse. By this, it is clarified that even though the horse is moving, for the person who falls from the horse, that very horse remains fixed (*dhruva*) relative to him as he falls.

In the sentence "The leaf falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt parṇaṃ patati*), the understanding to be conveyed is: "An operation conducive to conjunction, residing in the leaf, which generates a disjunction having the tree as its limit. When it is said, "He falls from the horse" (*aśvāt patati*), there might arise the doubt that the horse's status as an *apādāna* (ablative point) occurs only at a time when it is not the locus of any other action; therefore, the qualifier "running" (*dhāvataḥ*) is employed to remove that doubt. The understanding follows the pattern: "An operation conducive to conjunction, residing in the rider, which generates a disjunction having the horse as its limit."

One might object: "In the case of the expression 'he falls from the horse as it falls from the wall,' since the word 'falling' (patataḥ) functions as a qualifier, one perceives that the horse is the locus of an action that produces disjunction; therefore, the horse should not be considered the *apādāna* (ablative point of departure). Anticipating this objection, he says: "from which horse" (*yasmādaśvāt*). The meaning is: although that horse from which he falls is indeed the locus of some action that produces a spatial separation, it remains *dhruva* (fixed/stable) for him who is falling, insofar as it is not the locus of the action that produces the [relevant] disjunction. This is the intended sense: in this usage, two actions that produce disjunction are present.

In that case, one [action] produces a disjunction having the wall as its limit, and it resides in the horse; the second, however, produces a disjunction having the horse as its limit, and it resides in the man. Thus, due to the difference in substrata, disjunction is also twofold: the disjunction between the wall and the horse, which has the wall as its limit and resides in the horse; and the second is the disjunction between the horse and the rider, which has the horse as its limit and resides in the rider.

This being the case, regarding the statement "that which is not the substratum of the action causing disjunction," there arises a doubt that the status of *apādāna* (ablative) is untenable for one's own self in the aforementioned instance because of the inclusion of "disjunction" in a general sense. However, if "disjunction" is understood in its specific sense—as "not being the substratum of the action that produces that very disjunction whose limit (avadhi) resides in that [entity]"—then the aforementioned untenability does not arise.

In the expression "he falls from the horse as it falls from the wall," the horse possesses the status of the limit (*avadhi*) for the disjunction residing in both the horse and its rider; since such a disjunction—produced by an action residing solely in the rider—is not present in the horse itself, the horse does not serve as the substratum (*āśraya*) of that disjunction-producing action, and thus its status as the *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) is logically established.

Although the horse possesses the status of being the locus of the action that causes its separation from the wall-horse, nevertheless, that action does not cause the separation of the horse from its rider; thus, with the intention that the horse's non-locus-status regarding the action causing that [specific] separation remains unassailable, he says: "the action which is the cause of separation from that," and so on, ending with "is to be qualified."

The intention is as follows: since the meaning of the word *tat* (that) is dependent upon the meaning of the word *yat* (which), the specific instance of separation (*viśleṣa*)—established by the two words *yat* and *tat*—must be introduced into the definition of the "limit" (*avadhi*) as "that which is the terminus of a separation while not being the substratum of the action that causes that separation. Thus, the point is that it is not contradictory for a horse to be the non-substratum of the action that produces the separation residing in the rider. In this way, the state of being fixed (*dhruvatva*) is established even for a wall and so forth; thus he says: "of that too."

The meaning is as follows: when this horse falls, the wall and other such objects certainly remain [in their place] during that fall of the horse. This is because the action residing solely in the horse—which causes the disjunction (viśleṣa) based on both the wall and the horse—is not present in the wall; consequently, the wall and so forth are not the substratum of that action which would cause the disjunction between the wall and the horse.

One might object: "Even so, in a case where two [ram]s, being conjoined, simultaneously produce a separation through the action of moving backward, there would be no status as an *apādāna* (ablative) for each of them—expressed as 'the two rams move away from each other'—because the separation is one and the same, and thus each individual ram possesses the action that produces that very separation, meaning there is no lack of being the substratum of the action producing that separation. To refute this doubt, he says: "Both... and "...the action of the other ram. Here, the doubt is addressed by the portion of the verse beginning with "both" and ending with "in the separation."

The meaning of that [compound] is as follows: "ubhayakarmaka" means both [meṣau], i.e., the two rams; their action is the activity related to them. Alternatively, it means the action of both, i.e., of the two rams. It is a *vyadhikaraṇa* (non-co-referential) *bahuvrīhi* compound, where the word "separation" (*vibhāga*) is the external referent (*nyapadārtha*), and such an action exists as its generator. Or else, the word "ubhaya" refers by implication (*lakṣaṇayā*) to that which resides in both; thus, it is a *samānādhikaraṇa* (co-referential) *bahuvrīhi*: "that which has an action—i.e., an activity—residing in both. The rest is as before.

The meaning is: "in a disjunction produced by an action residing in both [entities]. However, in some printed editions, the reading "ubhayakarmaje" (produced by the action of both) is seen in the lower portion; that appears to be easily understood. Although, in a disjunction produced by an action residing in both, both rams are indeed the substrata of the actions that cause the separation—this being the ellipsis—it would follow that they could not possess the status of an *apādāna* (ablative point). The refutation of this objection is provided by the portion of the verse beginning with "pravibhakte tu," which states that there is no distinction [between the two cases].

Regarding the term "pravibhaktau" (when divided): this means that when the two actions producing separation, which reside in those respective goats, are established as distinct due to the difference between the specific goats serving as their substrates—such that the action producing separation residing in one goat is not the same action residing in the other goat, and the action residing in the other goat is not the action residing in the first goat—they remain so established, and not otherwise. Regarding the word "tatra": [it refers to that state].

The meaning is: "where one ram remains motionless and another ram moves away from that ram. This very point is clarified by the verse beginning with "the action of the other ram" (*meṣāntarakriyā*), as he says: "just as [from] the motionless [ram]. This is an example from a situation where disjunction is produced by the action of only one of the two. [The phrase] "from the motionless ram" [is used].

Just as in a situation where one ram, which is not the substratum of the action producing the disjunction, moves away from another ram that is the substratum of such an action, the first ram is considered fixed (dhruva) with respect to the action of the second ram because it is not the substratum of that action; likewise, in a situation where a disjunction is produced by actions residing in both [ramms], although the disjunction is one, a distinction in the action is postulated based on the specific property of belonging to each respective ram. Thus, with respect to the action residing in one ram, the other ram is considered fixed.

Furthermore, it is easily established that for a single ram, there is the state of being the locus of action (kriyā) and the state of being fixed (dhruvatva) by taking up the action residing in the other [ram]. In a case where the disjunction is produced by an action residing in one of the two, it is possible for the property of "not being the substratum of the action producing that separation" to belong to the other; thus, as in the expression "the ram moves away from the ram," even in a case where the separation is produced by actions residing in both, one may—by means of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the property of "residing in each respective ram"—postulate a difference in the actions based on the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth, which serve as limiting adjuncts that create a distinction [between the self], as in the case of "the self moves itself."

The sense is that since it is possible for one of the two [rams] to be the non-substratum of the action that causes separation from the other, the statement "the two rams move away from each other" is justified. However, the moderns (navīnāḥ) say: "The status of being an *apādāna* consists in being the substratum of the disjunction produced by the operation denoted by the verb in question; and this is intended only with respect to those two things denoted by the word 'paraspara' (each other). But as for the two things denoted by the word 'meṣa' (ram), because they are the substrata of the action, their status as *kartṛ* (agent) is intended, not their status as the substratum of disjunction. This is because the intention [of the speaker] follows the actual usage."

And thus, by means of the passage beginning with "tadviśleṣa" and ending with "tatkriyāyām apādānatvam," he demonstrates the nature of the definition of the *apādāna* (ablative) as it has been established. Among these, the meaning of the portion ending with "satī" is quite clear. Regarding "tajjanaka": since the word "tat" (that) refers to "viśleṣa" (separation), the meaning is "the generator of that [separation]. Regarding "tatkriyānāśraya": here, because the word "tat" refers to a specific action qualified by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of residing in that particular ram, the meaning is "not being the substratum of that specific action. Regarding "tatkriyāyām": [this refers to the action of separation].

Here too, the term "that" (*tat*) refers to a specific action; the sense is that it is established that [the tree] is the *apādāna* (ablative point) with respect to that specific action. And the inclusion of the phrase "specific action" is for the sake of establishing the status of the *apādāna* in such cases as "two rams move away from each other. Now, one might object: where the separation is produced solely by an action residing in the tree, the expression "the cloth falls from the tree" would not be possible, because the tree lacks the status of being the locus of that action which produces the separation between the tree and the cloth. To this, he says: "And here, 'action'... [and so forth].

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvartha*): it refers specifically to that which is expressed by the verbal root under discussion, such as *patati* ("he falls"), and not to mere motion (*spanda*) alone. By taking "mere motion," there arises the doubt that since motion exists in the tree, the tree could not logically function as the *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure). However, when the "meaning of the verbal root" is taken, the status of the tree as *apādāna* is established because the tree is not the locus of the action conducive to the conjunction that produces the separation denoted by the root *pat* in the expression *patati*. The word "by that" (*tena*) means: by the inclusion of the action conveyed by the verbal root under discussion. Regarding the example *sagacchate*: *Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "sagacchata iti". Based on the context of the preceding grammatical analysis, this likely introduces an example where the agent of the action is not the substratum of the action conducive to the separation.*

The meaning of the root *pat* (to fall) is an action conducive to a conjunction that produces a disjunction. Thus, the action produced by the root *pat* in this context—which generates the disjunction between the tree and the cloth—resides in the cloth and not in the tree. Consequently, since the tree is not the substratum of the action producing the disjunction denoted by the root in question, its status as an *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) is logically consistent; this is the meaning.

If it is objected that, since in this case the separation of the tree from the cloth is produced by an action residing in the cloth and not by an action residing in the tree, the qualification "possessing a separation born of the action of the tree" is inconsistent with respect to the cloth—this is not so. By the movement of the tree, such an action is produced in the cloth that, having separated from the tree, causes that cloth to fall downward.

If, however, the action of motion had not arisen in the tree, then the action producing disjunction would not have arisen in the cloth, and consequently the cloth would not have fallen downward; thus, with the intention that the action of motion residing in the tree is the cause of the cloth's falling through this causal chain, the qualifier "possessing disjunction produced by the action of the tree" was stated. Now, considering the complexity [of the definition] if the aforementioned *apādāna* were the meaning of the fifth case (*pañcamī*), he says: "In fact," and "only this much."

The meaning is that [the *apādāna*] is characterized by such qualifiers as: "being the locus of separation (*viśleṣa*) while not being the locus of that action which produces the separation. Regarding the phrase "to be expressed by the fifth case (*pañcamī*"): the meaning is that it is not the delimitor of what is to be expressed by the fifth case. That which is to be expressed by the fifth case is the *apādāna*; and that, while being the locus of separation, is not the locus of the action that produces that separation. However, the delimitor of what is to be expressed is *apādānatva* (the state of being an *apādāna*), and that is characterized by the aforementioned qualifiers, beginning with "being the locus of separation" and ending with "not being the locus of the action."

And thus, the meaning of the *Nirukta* is that the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative) is not what is directly expressed (*vācya*) by the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*), but rather that [status] is the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of what is expressed by it. It should be understood that this mode of expression—that the status of being an *apādāna* is not directly expressed by the fifth case-ending—is indeed logical, since we observe that even a delimitor of what is expressed can itself be expressed. By the word "mere" (*mātra*) in the phrase "merely a definition" (*lakṣaṇamātram*), the status of being a delimitor of what is expressed is excluded.

Now, if it is not the case that the specific entity expressed by the ablative case is "that which is the locus of separation and is the substratum of the action that produces separation," then, in response to the inquiry "What, then, is expressed by the ablative? it is accepted that only that which is the locus of separation is expressed by the ablative.

Furthermore, if "being the locus of separation" alone is intended by the term *apādāna* (ablative), then in the sentence "Devadatta comes from the village," since the root *ā-yā* signifies an activity conducive to a conjunction with a subsequent location preceded by a disjunction, and since disjunction—like conjunction—is inherent in both [loci], the disjunction produced by the action denoted by the verbal root *ā-yā* exists not only in the village but also in Devadatta. Consequently, just as the village possesses the status of an *apādāna*, Devadatta would also incur that same status.

If it is argued that this would lead to the undesirable usage "He comes from Devadatta from the village," we say no. In the sentence "Caitra goes to the village," since the result—consisting of conjunction with a subsequent location produced by the operation denoted by the root *gam* (to go)—resides both in the village and in Caitra, Caitra would likewise possess the status of an object (*karman*), just like the village. Anticipating this objection—that Caitra would incur the designation of "object" because he is the locus of the result produced by the operation, while simultaneously being the locus of the operation itself—we respond as follows: [The definition of an object applies only when the result resides in something other than the agent. Since the result produced by the operation resides in the village and not in Caitra, Caitra does not incur the designation of "object. Furthermore, [the definition of an agent applies] because he is the locus of the operation. Thus, there is no conflict between the two designations. Therefore, the undesirable usage "Caitra goes to Caitra" does not arise. Consequently, the rule for the designation of "object" is established as follows: "That which is distinct from the agent and is the locus of the result produced by the operation denoted by the verbal root is called the object (*karman*). This is the intended meaning.

The designation *kartṛ* (agent) would apply; however, because it is subsequent [to the designation *karman*] according to the rule *ā kaḍārāt*, the designation *kartṛ* subordinates the designation *karman*, and thus the undesirable result of "Caitra [is the object] of Caitra" (*caitraścaitram*) does not arise—this is how the objection has been resolved.

By that same logic, in the present case as well, Devadatta would attain the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) by virtue of being the locus of the separation produced by the operation denoted by the root in question; yet he would also attain the designation of *kartṛ* (agent) by virtue of being the locus of the operation denoted by the root in question. Since the designation of *kartṛ* takes precedence and thus sublates the designation of *apādāna*, the undesirable consequence—such as "grāmād devadattāt" (from the village, from Devadatta)—would not arise. Because such a resolution can be stated, the [notion of] the ablative case-meaning is not included in the scope of what is expressed [by the verbal suffix], due to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*).

It appears that the inclusion of the component "not being the locus of those rays which produce disjunction" must be postulated—this is the sense of "it appears" (pratibhāti) and "it is pleasing" (rocate). Having reflected on all this, he says: "In the manner stated for the meaning of the second case," and so forth, ending with "it appears. He raises an objection: "And even so... The meaning is: [the objection is raised] in order to prevent undesirable usages such as "Devadatta from Devadatta" and the like. [The example given is: "He moves away from the tree" (vṛkṣāt spandate).

The intention of the objector is as follows: since it is understood from the sentence that "the [bird] has moved slightly away from—that is, become slightly separated from—the tree," the tree possesses the status of being the locus of the disjunction produced by that [action], while not being the locus of the operation denoted by the verbal root *spand* (to move) which constitutes the primary action; thus, the tree would incur the undesired consequence (*āpatti*) of being an *apādāna* (ablative). This undesirable consequence applies even under the view that the meaning expressed by the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) is a qualified entity consisting of "being the locus of disjunction while not being the locus of that action which produces it. He dispels this aforementioned consequence by accepting it as desired, stating: "Because it is accepted" (*iṣṭatvāt*).

The meaning is as follows: since the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative point) is desired for that which is the locus of the disjunction produced by the operation denoted by the root *cal* (to move), as in "he moved from his seat" (*āsanāccalitaḥ*) or "he moved from the kingdom" (*rājyāccalitaḥ*), there is no obstacle to accepting the status of *apādāna* for that which is the locus of the disjunction produced by the operation denoted by the root *spand* (to quiver), which has the same meaning; therefore, it is accepted.
