The intention of the one who offers the criticism in the form of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that "he moves from the tree" (*vṫkṣāt spandate*) would be as follows: Since we observe such usages as "he has moved from his seat" (*āsanāccalitaḥ*), there is an understanding of a separation (*vibhāga*) produced by an operation denoted by the root *cal* (to move), and because separation depends upon a limit (*avadhi*), the substratum of such a separation is indeed the *apādāna* (ablative) in those cases. However, since the root *spand* (to quiver/move slightly) signifies mere motion and does not convey separation, there is no status as a limit; therefore, the usage "he moves from the tree" is not appropriate, but rather "he moves on the tree" (*vṛkṣe spandate*).

Others, however, hold that when used in conjunction with a transitive root (*sakarmaka-dhātu*), the status of *apādāna* belongs to the locus of the disjunction produced by the operation denoted by such a root—as in "He goes from Prayāga to Kāśī" (*prayāgāt kāśīṃ gacchati*). But since the root *spand* (to vibrate) is intransitive, they maintain that when it is used in conjunction [with another verb], it is not appropriate for the locus of the disjunction produced by the operation denoted by such a root to have the status of *apādāna*. With this intention, he states the passage beginning with "pañcamījanyopasthiteḥ" and ending with "hetutvam."

The meaning is as follows: since it is accepted that there is a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) such that the presence of an operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by a transitive root (*sakarmakadhātu*)—by virtue of being the cause of the disjunction that constitutes the referent of the *apādāna*—is the cause for that cognition which has the *apādānatva* (the state of being an ablative) as its qualifier and is produced by a fifth case suffix (*pañcamī*), then in the expression "it moves from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt spandate*), because the root *spand* (to move) presents an operation that does not produce disjunction and is therefore intransitive (*akarmaka*), there can be no cognition of *apādānatva* when it is used in co-occurrence with it; thus, the expression "it moves from the tree" is considered improper.

He states that this method of resolution is merely a semblance of a resolution (*samādhānābhāsa*), saying: "it is a semblance of a resolution. If the aforementioned causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) were accepted in order to prevent the cognition of the *apādāna* (ablative) case in the expression "it moves from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt spandate*), then in the case of "he has moved from the kingdom" (*rājyāccalitaḥ*) as well, there would be no cognition of the *apādāna* even when co-occurring with that [verb], because the root *cal-* (to move), which denotes an activity that produces separation, is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Consequently, the usage "he has moved from the kingdom" and similar constructions would be untenable. However, if [the relationship is established] in the case of "he has moved from his seat" (*āsanāccalitaḥ*)...

The sense is as follows: if, for the sake of accounting for such usages as these, one intends—on the strength of experience—that there is a cognition of the status of an *apādāna* (ablative source) whenever a verb denoting motion (*calad-dhātu*) is used in proximity [to another], then, since a cognition of the status of an *apādāna* would be unavoidable whenever a verb denoting motion (*spanda-dhātu*) is used in proximity to a word denoting that object (*dartha*), the usage *vṛkṣāt spandate* ("it moves from the tree") would be unavoidable; thus, the proposed solution in the form of a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is merely a semblance of a solution. The phrase "is rejected" (*apāsta*) means that even such a semblance of a solution is rejected.

The intention is as follows: if one accepts the aforementioned causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) [that the cause of separation is the *apādāna*] in order to exclude the usage "the tree trembles" (*vṛkṣāt spandate*), then the usage "he has moved from the kingdom" (*rājyāc calitaḥ*)—which is desired by the learned (*śiṣṭa*)—would be untenable; therefore, such a causal relationship cannot be accepted. Consequently, one must allow for the desired outcome even in the case of the usage "the tree trembles. He raises an objection with the words "And even so... (*na caivam api*). The meaning is: even if the usage "the tree trembles" is accounted for by making the state of being the locus of disjunction (*vibhāgaśrayatva*) the trigger for the technical designation *apādāna*. [In response, he gives the example: "he leaves the tree" (*vṛkṣāt tyajati*).

Here, the bird is the agent (*kartṛ*). Regarding the objection that "the [use of the ablative] *vṛkṣāt* in 'he leaves from the tree' (*vṛkṣāt tyajati*) would be unavoidable": if it is argued that since the tree possesses the status of being the locus of separation while not being the locus of the activity that produces that separation, the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) applies, and thus the usage *vṛkṣāt tyajati* is unavoidable—[we reply]: no. Because the meaning of the root *tyaj* is "an activity conducive to separation," and because separation is the "result" (*phala*) as it constitutes the meaning of the verbal root, the tree is the locus of the result produced by the activity. Consequently, the designation of "object" (*karman*) applies by virtue of its superior strength; this stronger designation sublates the designation of "ablative. Thus, since the ablative case is impossible, only the accusative case occurs.

One might raise the objection: "Since the designation *apādāna* is sublated by the designation *karman*, the designation *apādāna* does not exist [therein]; thus, even though the fifth case (*pañcamī*) lacks grammatical correctness, there arises the undesirable consequence that such usage—produced under the delusion that the *apādāna* designation applies—would still convey the status of being an *apādāna*. He refutes this doubt with the words beginning "from delusion" (*bhramāt*). The phrase "absence of cognition" (*bodhābhāva*) means the absence of the cognition of the status of being an *apādāna*. The phrase "established by experience" (*anubhavasiddha*) means established by the means of valid cognition consisting of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) in the form of experience. The phrase "generated by the fifth case" (*pañcamījanyā*)... [is used].

The causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) should be understood as follows: when the understanding of *apādānatva* (the status of being a point of departure) produced by the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is intended to be the effect (*bhāvya*), then the presentation of an operation that causes separation—produced by a verbal root other than roots such as *tyaj-* (to abandon)—is the cause. In other words, the understanding of *apādānatva* produced by the fifth case is the effect, and the cognition produced by a verbal root other than roots such as *tyaj-* is the cause. By the phrase "roots such as *tyaj-*," the verbal root *pat-* found in the usage of the Bhāṣya, namely "narakaṃ patitaḥ" (he has fallen into hell), is to be included.

For in that case, it is clear that the meaning of the verbal root *pat* (to fall) is an operation conducive to separation (*vibhāga*). By the inclusion of the word "yadi" (if) in the phrase "yadi bodhābhāvaḥ" (if there is an absence of cognition), it is understood that the cognition of [the status of] the *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) is indeed intended there. Thus, the sense is that the aforementioned causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is irrelevant.

Now, one might object that since the root *dyut* (to shine) signifies illumination in the expression "it flashes from the cloud" (*balāhakād vidyotate*), just as in "the sun shines" (*savitā prakāśate*), there is no perception of separation (*vibhāga*) from the cloud; therefore, its status as an ablative (*apādāna*) is untenable. To this, he says: "The word 'having emerged' (*niḥsṛtya*) must be supplied. The sense is that by taking the root *dyut* to mean "flashing preceded by emergence," and thereby accepting the status of the ablative as defined by the action of emerging, the use of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is justified.

In this context, the "supply" (adhyāhāra) is simply the occurrence of the verbal root *vidyot* preceded by the prefix *niḥsṛ*; the meaning is "having emerged from the cloud, it flashes. As stated by Kaiyaṭa: "A 'cloud' (*balāhaka*) is an aggregate of smoke, light, water, and wind; because one intends to express the distinction between the lightning—which is light as a constituent part—and the cloud which consists of such an aggregate, the cloud functions as the point of departure (*avadhi*)."

He dispels the objection—namely, that in the statement "form is distinct from taste," since there is no emission in the form of an activity conducive to disjunction-preceded conjunction within the form itself, it is impossible for "from taste" to function as the *apādāna* (ablative point of departure)—by means of the words beginning with "conceptually constructed" (*buddhiparikalpita*).

The sense is this: since a real conjunction or disjunction between the two qualities, color and taste, is impossible, one must accept their conjunction and disjunction as being conceptually constructed by the intellect (*buddhiparikalpita*). Having thus accepted such a disjunction as the basis [of the relation], the ablative case in "rasāt" (from taste) is justified by relying on that disjunction as the limit (*avadhi*). Considering that this status of being an *apādāna* (ablative point of departure) is merely figurative (*gauṇa*) because it is conceptually constructed, he says: "pṛthagvinā... (Pāṇini 2.3.32). By this sūtra, it should be understood that the ablative case in "rasāt" is employed when used in connection with the meaning of the word "pṛthak" (separate).

The meaning is that color (rūpa) is qualified by a distinctness (pṛthaktva) whose counter-correlative is taste (rasa). And "this" means "taking up" (ādāna). He states that it is threefold due to the difference in sub-classifications of the status of being an ablative (apādānatva), beginning with "nirdiṣṭaviṣayam" and so forth. The meaning is: that whose object (viṣaya)—the entity defining the separation—is "indicated" (nirdiṣṭa), i.e., made known through its own power (śakti). With the intention that here the word "object" refers to the motion (gati) residing in the cause (nimitta) which defines the separation, he says "where [it is] directly" (yatra sākṣāt). This means: even without the mental supply (adhyāhāra) of an action that produces the separation.

"By the verbal root (*dhātu*)" means by a well-known verbal root such as *patati* (falls) or *gacchati* (goes), which signifies an operation that produces separation (*vibhāga*). "Motion" (*gati*) means an action that generates separation. "Is indicated" (*nirdiśyate*) means it is presented; the sense is that the *apādāna* (ablative case-relation) therein is one whose locus is specified, and this constitutes the definition of a "specified-locus" (*nirdiṣṭaviṣaya*) [ablative]. He provides an example of the specified-locus: "as in, 'He falls from the horse' (*aśvāt patati*)."

He defines "having an appropriated object" (*upāttaviṣaya*): "appropriated" means accepted by means of a secondary characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, and not by its own inherent power (*śakti*); "object" refers to that which determines the separation (*vibhāga*). Relying on this meaning of the compound, he says: "wherein there is another verbal root. The meaning of another verbal root, such as "emerging" (*niḥsaraṇa*), which determines the separation, serves as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) or qualifier for the root's own meaning; when a verbal root expresses such a meaning, that [separation] has an "appropriated object," and thus it is called the *apādāna* (ablative) case. He provides an example of this: "as in *balāhakāt*" (from the cloud).

Just as in the case of "the sun shines" (*savitā prakāśate*), since no separation [of light] is perceived from the root *vidyotate* when it has the sense of "shining," one accepts that the function of *vidyotate* is, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), shining preceded by the emergence of the meaning of another verbal root; thus he says, "having emergence as its subordinate part," and so on. The understanding is: "The shining performed by lightning at a time subsequent to the emergence which has the cloud as its limit. He defines [the term] "action requiring [another action]" (*apekṣitakriyam*) with the words "requiring," and so on.

"Apekṣitā" means "expected," which signifies that there is an action—specifically an action producing separation—that is required. "The last" (antya) means that action whose requirement is expected. Since expectancy arises when an implied action is not explicitly stated, the questioner, keeping the perceptible act of coming in mind, asks, "From where do you come? The respondent likewise answers, "From Pāṭaliputra."

With the intention that both sentences here—in the form of question and answer—require a verb to be supplied, he says: "having supplied the action of 'coming' as the sense. Thus, the meaning is that in the interrogative sentence "From where have you come? the word "come" (*āgata*) is to be understood, and likewise in the answer-sentence "From Pāṭaliputra," the phrase "I have come" (*āgato 'ham*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

The meaning of the interrogative sentence is: "Being what, do you possess the activity of coming which produces a separation relative to a certain location? And the meaning of the responsive sentence should be understood as: "I possess the activity of coming which produces a separation relative to Pāṭaliputra. By this, it is indicated that even the action of "going" (gamana) and "being gone over" (gamyamāna) serves as the motivator for case-endings (*kāraka-vibhakti*).

Now he states the meaning of the dative case: "the intended recipient" (*uddeśya*). Regarding "the meaning of the dative": the meaning is that it is the meaning of the dative used in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). He provides the proof for the fact that the intended recipient is the meaning of the dative used in the sense of the recipient by saying: "For instance" (*tathā hi*). One might object: although the status of the recipient as the meaning of the dative is established by the rule *caturthī saṃpradāne* ("the dative is used for the recipient"), the status of the intended recipient as the meaning of the dative is not thereby established. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that" (*tac ca*). The meaning is: "and that [which is the recipient]."

The syntactical connection is: "that which one aims at by means of the object" (karmaṇā yam abhipraiti), according to the Sūtra; thus, [the word] "intended recipient" (uddeśya) is the predicate. He states a qualification that establishes the status of the recipient as being the intended recipient, beginning with "by means of the object" (karmaṇā) and ending with "having this meaning" (ityarthakāt). "By means of the object" means "by means of that which has become an instrument" (karaṇabhūtena). This instrumentality is relative to the act of connecting. The meaning is: that person whom the agent aims at—that is, desires to connect with, or intends—by means of a substance such as a cow, which is designated as the "object" (karman); that person is the recipient (saṃpradāna).

In this context, "object" (*karman*) should be understood in its technical sense as that which is most desired by the agent, and so forth. Therefore, the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient) is prescribed for the goal of an intransitive action—that which the action aims at. Thus, the meaning is that the *saṃpradāna* is that which is intended as the goal for the sake of establishing a connection with the "object"—defined here as the substratum of the result produced by the operation (*vyāpāra*) presented by some verbal root. Consequently, the intention is that the dative case signifies the goal. This very point is expressed by the phrase "this indeed."

The meaning is that being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) itself is what is called "being the subordinate" (*śeṣitva*) or "being the principal" (*aṅgitva*). Regarding the phrase "having that as its intended object": that which has "that"—namely, the recipient—as its intended object is a thing, such as a cow, which has become the object of a desire directed toward such [a recipient]; that is said to be "subordinate" (*śeṣa*). "In the former system" (*pūrvatantra*) means in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*, specifically in the sūtra: "The subordinate is so because it exists for the sake of another" (*śeṣaḥ parārthatvāt*). And "existing for the sake of another" (*parārthatva*) consists in being pervaded by an activity that proceeds with the aim of another.

The primary or principal action (*para-pradhāna*), or alternatively, the supreme fruit (*para-utkṛṣṭa-phala*) such as heaven; the state of being pervaded by the human effort (*kṛti*) of a person engaged in that [action] for the sake of that [fruit]—meaning the state of being related to it by way of being a causal factor (*kāraka*). For example, it is well known that the *prayāja*, *anuyāja*, threshing (*avaghāta*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and so forth, are pervaded by the effort of a person engaged for the sake of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*); thus, they possess the status of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*).

However, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to the *darśa* sacrifice and others, because they lack the quality of being pervaded by the human effort initiated with the *prayāja* offerings as their objective; the meaning is that no person ever initiates an action solely for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings. "It has been defined" means that this and so forth have been described. By this, the status of being the principal (*śeṣitva*) in the case of the Brahmin and the status of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) in the case of the cow have been demonstrated. "For this very reason" means precisely because the status of being the principal is the motivator for the primary ritual act (*pradhānakarma*). "Like the throwing away (*prāsana*)" refers to the section in the *Jaiminīya* [Mīmāṃsā-sūtra]. "When the Soma has been purchased" [refers to the context].

Following the purchase of the Soma, there arises a doubt as to whether the handing over of the staff (*daṇḍa*) to the Maitrāvaruṇa priest is a disposal act (*pratipattikarma*) or a purposeful act (*arthakarma*). Having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it is a disposal act—on the grounds that "he throws the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit" [is a disposal] and because the staff is employed for the consecration (*dīkṣā*) in the statement "he consecrates with the staff"—[the siddhāntin replies]: because the dative case is heard in the phrase "to the Maitrāvaruṇa," and because the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) consists in being the objective of an action, and because the state of being an objective...

The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is thus consistent: because the status of being the primary object (*pradhānatva*) is co-extensive with the status of being the intended recipient (*uddeśyatva*), it is understood that the Maitrāvaruṇa priest possesses primacy characterized by being the recipient; therefore, the giving of the staff is a primary act (*pradhānakarma*) for the sake of a purposeful result (*arthakarma*), and not a disposal act (*pratipattikarma*). A disposal act (*pratipattikarma*) is the casting of a substance that has been used or is scattered into a prescribed location.

However, that which assists the primary action independently is called both a *pradhānakarma* (primary object) and an *arthakarma* (purposeful action); this is the distinction between an *arthakarma* and an *pratipattikarma* (disposal action). Now, one might object: "In a case where the root *dā* (to give) has an operation consisting of a desire conducive to washing, since the washerman is the locus of the result—namely, the washing—produced by such an operation consisting of a desire, he is an *object* (*karman*). Furthermore, because he is intended (*abhipreyamāṇa*) by the object, namely the cloth, the washerman would have the status of a *recipient* (*saṃpradāna*), and thus one would have to say 'he gives the cloth to the washerman' (*rajakāya vastraṃ dadāti*). Anticipating this objection, [the author] accepts it as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

He refutes [the objection] with the words "to the washerman," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "even this": its connection is with what follows, namely, that "this is indeed desired by him. He states that the usage in the *Bhāṣya* is the authority for the desirability of such constructions as "to the washerman" (*rajakāya*) and so on, by citing the example "the teacher Khaḍika. This refers to a teacher of children. As for the expression "a slap for the pupil" (*śiṣyāya capeṭām*): a *capeṭā* is an open palm; in the Prākṛta language, it is called *cāpaṭa*.

In this context, since the root *dā* signifies an operation conducive to a specific type of contact (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*), if one were to accept the designation of "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*) only when it is joined with the primary verbal root *dā* (meaning "to give"), then the example from the Bhāṣya, "He gives a slap to the pupil" (*śiṣyāya capeṭāṃ dadāti*), would be untenable. Nor should it be argued that here the root *dā* is used figuratively (*bhākta*), as in the expression "The boy is a lion," where the word "lion" is applied to the boy.

The statement made by the author of the Vārttika—"the term 'action' (*kriyā*) must be included [in the definition of *saṃpradāna*]"—in order to justify the dative case in the example *patye śete* (she lies down for her husband), was refuted by the authors of the Bhāṣya on the grounds that the designation *saṃpradāna* is not to be understood as being based on its literal meaning (*anvartha*). This was because they relied on the interpretation of the Sūtra that "the *saṃpradāna* is an object intended to be connected with an action that results from an operation (*vyāpāra*) presented by some verbal root (*dhātu*)," thereby rejecting the view that the designation *saṃpradāna* is etymologically descriptive. Thus, regarding the aforementioned usage...

And because the primary sense is accepted for such usages as *rajakāya* (for the washerman), the statement "one should not give instruction (*mati*) to a Śūdra" is likewise consistent for this very reason. In that context, the root *dā* (to give) has the meaning of "informing," and the word *mati* refers to the Vedas and so forth which produce that [instruction]. The meaning understood is: "One should not perform an act of informing which has a Śūdra as its recipient and the Vedas or similar texts as its object, [the Vedas] being the producers of knowledge. He describes the view of the Vṛttikāras, who consider the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient) to be etymologically significant, with the words: "The Vṛttikāras, however..."

The term *dāna* (giving) is so called because "it is properly given" (*samyak pradīyate*). Thus, the intended meaning is that the sense of the verbal root *dā* (to give) is an activity conducive to the cessation of one's own ownership and the subsequent arising of another's ownership. Consequently, they maintain that in expressions such as *rajakāya vastraṃ dadāti* ("he gives a garment to the washerman"), since the aforementioned meaning of the root *dā* is absent, the genitive case alone is used to express a general relationship, as in *rajakasya vastraṃ dadāti* ("he gives the garment of the washerman"). In the case of *viprāya gāṃ dadāti* ("he gives a cow to the Brahmin"), the Brahmin is the intended recipient (*uddeśya*) of the act of giving, for the purpose of establishing a connection with the cow, which has become the object (*karman*) of the act of giving.

The relationship between the cow and the Brahmin is that of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*). Thus, the understanding is: an activity conducive to the production of another's ownership, which has the Brahmin as its objective (*uddeśya*) and the cow as its object (*karman*). In the expression "he tells news to Maitra," Maitra is the objective of the act of telling for the sake of establishing a connection with the news, which has become the object of the act of telling. The relationship between Maitra and the news is that of knower and known (*jñātṛjñeyabhāva*). Thus, the understanding is: an act of telling which has Maitra as its non-different recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and the news as its object.

He analyzes that [definition] with the words "and this" (*idaṃ ca*). The meaning is: "and the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) which is mentioned by the rule *karmaṇā yam abhipraiti*. This connects with the phrase "it is of three kinds. Furthermore, "analysis" (*vibhāga*) refers to a statement made by way of subordinate properties (*avāntaradharma*) within the category of being a recipient. Regarding the phrase "because of non-rejection" (*anirākaraṇāt*), [he explains] "a factor of relinquishment" (*tyāgāṅgam*). "Relinquishment" (*tyāga*) means giving; its "factor" (*aṅga*) means its qualifier. The meaning is: "being a factor of relinquishment" consists in being perceived as a qualifier of the relinquishment that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root used in co-utterance (*samabhivyāhṛtadhātvartha*). [The phrase] "desired by the object" (*karmaṇepsitam*)...

The meaning is: that which is intended to be connected with the object (karma) consisting of the locus of the result produced by the abandonment [of ownership] expressed by the verbal root used in conjunction [with the verb *dā*]. And thus, that kāraka which is intended to be connected with the act of giving as a constituent part of that abandonment is the recipient; for it does not reject the agent. Furthermore, it attains the status of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) through the instigation of the agent and by granting its consent. In this regard, he demonstrates the recipient characterized by non-rejection with the example: "to Sūrya."

In this context, the meaning of the root *dā* (to give) is "renunciation," which consists of the desire for the cessation of one's own ownership and the desire for the arising of another's ownership. Here, Sūrya is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) because he does not refuse the giver of the *arghya* by saying, "The *arghya* should not be given. He neither requests nor consents; thus, the absence of both requesting and consenting in Sūrya is intended to indicate that he is not occupied with those [mental states]. Consequently, the sense is that "non-refusal" consists in being devoid of any activity conducive to either engagement or withdrawal.

He shows that the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) can be caused by instigation (*preraṇā*) with the example "to the Brahmin" (*viprāya*). Here, the meaning is that one gives because one has been prompted by the Brahmin [with the thought], "Give to me. And instigation is an activity conducive to making known that [the act of] giving, which resides in the agent, is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). He states that the recipient can also be caused by permission (*anumati*) with the example "to the teacher" (*upādhyāyāya*). Here, the sense is that the teacher neither requests nor refuses the gift of a cow, but rather simply permits the gift of the cow as it is being given.

And *anumati* (consent) is the activity conducive to the acceptance of the meaning expressed by another—such as "I wish to give this cow to you"—in the form of uttering words such as "Let it be given; I shall accept it. That is to say, it is the activity conducive to the acceptance of the result, namely the ownership (*svasvatva*) residing in the cow and so forth, in the form of uttering words such as "So be it" (*tathā*). Others, however, define the state of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) as the state of being the object of a desire characterized by being the determiner of the result residing in the object of the action of the respective verbal root.

The meaning is that [the object] is the state of being the objective of a desire by virtue of its being the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of that fruit which resides in the object and constitutes the meaning of the verbal root. They say that since the Brahmin is the objective of a desire through the relation of being the determiner of that fruit residing in the object—such as a cow—which consists in the cessation of one's own ownership followed by the production of another's ownership, he receives the designation of *saṃpradāna* (recipient). He now explains the cognition of the syntactic connection between the base-meaning of the second case and so forth and the meaning of the case-ending, starting with the words "In all these cases."

In expressions such as *hariṃ bhajati* ("he worships Hari"), regarding the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*): the meaning of the base functions as a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix through the relation of identity (*abheda*). In that context, the referent of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*), which is the locus (*āśraya*), is construed with the result (*phala*) through the relation of being located therein (*ādheyatā*). The syntactic connection is as follows: "The softening (*viklitti*) is that which possesses a location (*ādheyatā*) defined by a substratum-ness (*ādhāratā*) residing in that locus which is non-different from the rice-grains."

The understanding of the syntactic relation (*anvayabodha*) should be inferred in such a manner as: "the act of giving having the cow as its object and the Brahmin as its non-differentiated recipient," or "the falling residing in the leaf having the tree as its non-differentiated limit. The substratum (*āśraya*), which is the meaning of the instrumental case in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), is construed with the operation (*vyāpāra*) expressed by the instrumental suffix. The resulting understanding of the syntactic relation is: "the operation is that which possesses the location-ness (*ādheyatā*) defined by the substratum-ness residing in that which is non-different from the arrow. Now, an objection is raised: the construction of the substratum—the meaning of the accusative case—with the fruit of the verbal root's meaning via the relation of location-ness (*ādheyatā-sambandha*) is not possible.

If it is argued that this is not so because it is unestablished (avyutpanna) that a word-meaning such as "hare" (hari), which is non-different from [the agent], can be construed with the meaning of a verbal root (dhātvartha) through a relation of difference, we say no. For the rule of linguistic competency (vyutpatti) is simply that there is no mutual construing between the meaning of a nominal stem and the meaning of a verbal root without mediating the meaning of a case-ending (vibhaktyartha). In the present case, since the construing occurs by way of the meaning of a case-ending, there is no obstacle to such a construction.

Now, one might object that an identity relation between the meanings of a base and its suffix is not possible, because case-endings (*vibhakti*) denote only properties such as "object-ness" (*karmatva*) and so forth. To this he says: "In the view that case-endings denote only properties. It is appropriate to hold that case-endings denote only properties such as "object-ness" due to parsimony (*lāghava*). The word "only" (*mātra*) serves to exclude the substratum (*dharmin*). [The objection continues: "Regarding 'in the object' (*karmaṇi*)," for it would result in a violation of the natural sense of rules such as *karmaṇi dvitīyā* ("the second case ending is used in the sense of the object").

The meaning is as follows: in common worldly usage, words such as *karman* (object) and others are understood to refer to the substratum (*dharmin*), because they possess a denotative power (*śakti*) directed toward that which is qualified by "object-ness" (*karmatva*) and so forth; therefore, in the technical treatise (*śāstra*) as well, it is necessary for them to refer to the substratum. Otherwise, the author would have stated simply "the second case ending [is used] when there is object-ness" (*karmatve dvitīyā*) and so on, rather than saying "in the object" (*karmaṇi*), "in the instrument" (*karaṇe*), and so forth. Thus, the sense is that if words like *karman* were to denote properties such as "object-ness," there would be a violation of the natural intent (*svarasa*) of the Sūtra.

Is it not the case that the meaning of rules such as *karmaṇi dvitīyā* ("the second [case-ending] is used when the object is to be expressed") is not intended to be "when the object is to be denoted," but rather "when the object is to be understood"? And the maintenance of such a meaning occurs through the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). Thus, there is no risk of violating the natural intent of the Sūtra.

Nor should it be argued that even when the meaning of the suffix is *āśrayatva* (substratumness) and the base-meaning such as "Hari" is construed with it, the resulting cognition is merely "the substratumness residing in Hari," and not "Hari is the possessor of substratumness"—for how then could the accusative case serve as the basis for the negation of its status as an object? This is because, while the base-meaning such as "Hari" is being construed with *āśrayatva*, there can arise a subsequent mental cognition (*pārṣṭhika-mānasa-bodha*) in the form "Hari is the substratum."

Just as from the sentence "Devadatta is a friend of the king," once the state of being a king's friend is understood in Devadatta through the scope of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśakti*), the state of being a friend is the meaning [of the compound]. Wishing to dispel this doubt, he says: "In the case of *kṛt* suffixes, *taddhita* suffixes, and so forth. This refers to *kṛt* suffixes such as in "the rice is cooked" (*pakvastandulaḥ*), and to *taddhita* suffixes such as in "a horse that is capable" (*śakto'śvaḥ*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), suffixes such as the present participle *śānac*—as in "the rice being cooked" (*pacyamānastandulaḥ*)—are to be included. This is because it is observed to be so.

The meaning is that in instances of etymological derivation (*nirukta*), it is observed that suffixes such as *kṛt* which denote an action (*karman*) actually denote the substratum (*dharmin*). Thus, just as the suffixes *kta* and others prescribed by rules such as "of those two alone" (*tayoreva*) denote the substratum, it is logical that in rules such as "the second case ending is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) as well, they should likewise denote the substratum; this is the intended sense.

[Objection: But surely, for your view as well, there is the consequence of violating the natural intent (*svarasa*) of the sūtra "karmaṇi dvitīyā" (Pāṇini 2.3.2) and others—which teach the expressive power (*śakti*) [of case endings] with respect to the object—since you must assume that their expressive power pertains only to the substratum (*āśraya*), because the result (*phala*) is already obtainable from the verbal root (*dhātu*). If it is argued that this assumption regarding the mere substratum is made in accordance with parsimony (*lāghava*), then it is exactly the same in my view as well, since parsimony leads me to assume that power resides in the property (*dharma*) itself. To this, he says: "having the meaning of the second case ending, etc. [and gives the example] "prāptodakaḥ" [and mentions] "in being denoters of the substratum."

In the case of the expression *prāptodakaḥ* ("one who has reached water"), there is the compound meaning "the object of reaching (*prāpti*) whose agent is water. To account for the experience-based cognition that takes the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between this compound meaning and the word *grāma* ("village") as its object, it is necessary that the second case suffix (*dvitīyā*) possesses a denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the object (*karman*). Otherwise, since even a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose meaning is the referent of the second case would result in denoting "objectness" (*karmatva*), coreferentiality would be untenable. He states, "The [meanings] such as object, etc., belong to the case-suffixes" (*supāṃ karmādayo ’rthāḥ*), showing that the *Mahābhāṣya* is also an authority for the view that words such as "object" denote the substratum (*dharmin*) itself.

If the property of being an object (*karmatva*) and so forth were intended as the meaning of the second and subsequent case-endings (*sup*) by way of being their denotation (*vācya*), then one would have simply said, "the meanings of the *sup*-endings are also [such properties] as being an object. Since it has not been stated thus, the implication is that the denotability of properties such as being an object by the second and other case-endings is unauthoritative, as it is not accepted by the three sages (*munitraya*).

Now, one might argue: even if it follows that there must be *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in words such as *karman* in the rule "the second case-affix occurs after a word denoting the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to hold that the second case-affixes and so on denote only the property (*dharma*). Let it be, then, that even a *bahuvrīhi* compound denotes only the property, and its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) may be established through *lakṣaṇā*. To this, he says: "This is the direction [of the argument]" (*iti dig iti*). The meaning of this "direction" is as follows: if this were the case, then the fact that primary suffixes (*taddhita*) such as *-tavya* denote the substratum (*dharmin*) would not be established.

If it is argued that in expressions such as "the rice is to be cooked" (*paktavyās taṇḍulāḥ*), the words [denoting the object] must signify the substratum (dharmin) because of the experience of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the rice and so forth—this is not so; for such coreferentiality is established through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone. If it is further argued that the understanding of mere objecthood (*karmatva*) from "to be cooked" and similar forms contradicts experience, the point is that this [contradiction] is equally present in cases such as "water has been reached" (*prāptodaka*).

Now, it may be argued that the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) and others do not denote the substratum (*āśraya*), because the substratum is already obtained from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which constitutes the base, just as the fruit and the operation are obtained from the verbal root. Rather, they denote merely the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva-mātra*), since this is not obtainable through any other means. Furthermore, because there is non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the possessor of the property (*dharmin*), the designation "object" (*karman*) and so forth is not untenable. For this very reason, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the second case-ending and others express the power (*śakti*) of objecthood and so forth, the capacity of a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *prāptodaka* ("to whom water has arrived") to convey the possessor of the property is successfully maintained.

Since power (*śakti*) alone, when it has attained non-difference from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), is what is expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*), and since the substratum (*āśraya*) is understood precisely from forms such as *pacati*, *paktā*, and *pakva*—which are derived from verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and primary nominal suffixes (*kṛt*) etc.—and furthermore, because of the conventional usage [of Pāṇini's rule] "when a pronoun is used as an adjunct in grammatical coreferentiality" (*yuṣmad-upapade samānādhikaraṇe*), it is logical that the substratum possesses its own power; with this intention, he says "of the substratum also," and so forth. The meaning is that since the substratum is obtained by the base itself (*prakṛti*), it is not expressed by the case-ending. "Not by the case-ending" means not expressed by case-endings such as the accusative (*dvitīyā*) and others.

Now, if "substratum-ness" (āśrayatva) is what is to be denoted, one must accept that "substratum-ness-ness" (āśrayatātva) is the delimitor of the denotative capacity (śakyatāvacchedaka); and in that case, there would be prolixity (gaurava), because it consists in being resident in all substrata while not residing in anything other than those substrata. To this he says: "That itself" (tad eva). The meaning is "substratum-ness itself. By the word "itself" (eva), the exclusion of "substratum-ness-ness" is intended. Anticipating the objection—namely, how something that resides in that [substratum] can be the delimitor of the denotative capacity residing in that very thing—he says: "By way of identity" (tādātmyena).

The point is this: even though identity (*tādātmya*) does not necessarily determine the occurrence [of a relation], it is still possible for there to be relatedness (*saṃbandhitva*) by means of it; thus, since the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) is related to itself through identity, there is no inconsistency in its being the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of denotability residing in itself. Regarding the phrase "the operation (*vyāpāra*) also": here, the word "also" (*api*) includes the substratum (*āśraya*). Regarding the phrase "mere division (*vibhāga-mātra*)," the word "mere" (*mātra*) excludes the state of being a substratum. By the phrase "mere status as the object of reference (*uddeśyatva-mātra*)," the word "mere" excludes the state of being a substratum. "Therefore" (*ata eva*): [refers to the preceding arguments].

The meaning is: precisely because it has been demonstrated that the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) and others denote powers such as objecthood (*karmatva*). Regarding the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*: for in this context, in usages such as "one threshes rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), "bring the cow" (*gāmānaya*), and "one should sacrifice an animal" (*paśumālabheta*), the referent of words like "rice" (*vrīhi*) is the individual (*vyakti*). Why? Because the individual is capable of being connected with actions such as threshing.

For a generic form (*ākṛti*) is not capable of being driven away, brought, or sacrificed; therefore, the individual (*vyakti*) is the word-meaning. Having thus presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the author replies]: "Indeed, individuals are infinite, because it is impossible to determine the exact number of cows existing in various places throughout the past and the future. Furthermore, a word for 'cow' learned in relation to a white individual would deviate from its own meaning when applied to a black individual. Therefore, due to these two reasons—infinity and deviation—it is not possible for the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) to reside in the individual."

However, since the *Bhāṣya* states that for one who holds substance (*dravya*) to be the word-meaning, form (*ākṛti*) is not non-word-meaning, the denotable object must be understood as qualified. In this regard, according to the principles that "a cognition does not arise with respect to a qualificand unless its qualifier has been apprehended" and "denotation does not reach the qualificand because its capacity is exhausted by the qualifier," it is appropriate that the word-meaning is the form itself. If the actions such as threshing (*avahanti*) were not applicable to the form, then the individual (*vyakti*) would have to be indicated there as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, in such cases as "one should pile the Śyenacit," it is observed that the generic form (ākṛti) alone is connected to the action by way of being the correlate of similarity. Therefore, thinking that the established conclusion—that the generic form is the word-meaning—is not contradicted, he says: "Or rather, it is the power (śakti) itself. This means that for all six case-inflections, the meaning is indeed the power of the objecthood (karmatva) and so forth.

Having thus explained the meaning of the case-terminations denoting the *kārakas*, he now explains the meaning of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) by way of a relevant transition in the verse: "The relation" (*saṃbandha*). [He states: "The sixth case is for the remainder" (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*). The meaning is this: the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to a relation—such as that of owner and owned—which is distinct from the meanings of the *kāraka* case-terminations and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); since the sixth case is prescribed there, its meaning is "relation. In this regard, there is a misconception that, just as in the opinion of some others the other case-terminations denote the substratum (*dharmin*), so too does this one.

To refute that [position], he says in the *Sāra*: "Merely a relation" (*saṃbandhamātra*). By the word "merely," there is an exclusion of the related entities (*saṃbandhin*). And that relation is expressed sometimes in the form of the general property of "relation-ness" (*saṃbandhatva*), as in "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*) and so forth; but sometimes it is expressed in a specific form, as in "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the sixth case [denoting] a kāraka": the meaning of the sixth case prescribed by rules such as *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* is the power (*śakti*) of being that particular *kāraka*. As for the statement "power is the *kāraka*": [this is the view].

The meaning is as follows: here, in the rule for the seventh and fifth case endings (*saptamī-pañcamyau*), the word *kāraka* refers to the powers (*śakti*) such as agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth, and not to the agents (*kartr*) themselves, according to the commentary. Since the "middle" (*madhya*) depends upon two limits, namely the preceding and the following, the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is "the middle between two *kārakas*. The term *kālādhvanoḥ* ("of time and distance") is understood from the previous rule. Thus, the sense of the rule is that the seventh and fifth case endings occur after words denoting time or distance situated between two such powers. For example: "Having eaten today, he will eat in two days (*dvyahe*) or after two days (*dvyahāt*)."

The agency defined by the act of eating on this day is one thing, and the agency defined by the act of eating occurring on the second day thereafter is another; this time [the intervening period] lies between these two powers of agency (*kartṛtva-śakti*). Furthermore, if the word *kāraka* here were intended to mean the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, then—since the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed when there is identity of the agent—and because the agent in the form of Devadatta is one, the usage of the intermediate [period] would be impossible, and thus the seventh and fifth case endings would not occur.

The meaning is that [this] is seen in the Bhāṣya, stating: "But the capacity for agency (kartṛtva-śakti) is indeed differentiated by the difference in the acts of eating due to the difference in location and time. The meaning of the locative and ablative case endings is "occurring at the immediately subsequent time. The state of having the present-day object as its locus (adhikaraṇa) is construed with the act of eating; and that act of eating, which is expressed by the suffix -ktvā and thus construed [with the preceding], is construed with the [subsequent] act of eating through two relations: being posterior in time to itself, and having the same agent (samāna-kartṛka). The meaning of the case ending in question is also construed in that very same place.

The meaning is as follows: this refers to that act of eating which occurs on a day subsequent to the day of the aforementioned eating, shares the same agent as that eating, and takes place on the second day immediately following that day. In the sentence "Standing here, one might pierce the target at a distance of a *krośa*," the meaning of the case-ending is the state of being located in the immediate vicinity. This connects with the fact that the entity expressed by the word "here" (*iha*) has its locus in this very place.

In such a state, [the relation] resides in the substratum of the meaning of the *kṛt*-suffix; that [relation] resides in the agent who is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*); and that [agent] resides in the act of piercing (*vyadhana*). In that very act, there is the status of having as its object a target situated in a location immediately following the *krośa*. Thus, it should be understood that the cognition is: "piercing, which is the object of possibility, has as its agent the one who is the agent of the act of staying located in this place, and has as its object a target situated in a location immediately following the *krośa* immediately after this place."

Having thus described the meanings of the well-distinguished case-endings (*vibhakti*), he explains the comprehension of the sentence-meaning—which consists of all the *kārakas* together with their mutual relations—in accordance with that, beginning with the words "In this way" (*evaṃ ca*). The meaning is: "given that it has been established, according to the method stated, that the accusative and other cases denote the substrata (*dharmin*) such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). Regarding the phrase "of Devadatta" (*devadattasya*) and so forth: in the expression "of Devadatta," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes the relation of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*). The cow (*gauḥ*) is connected to Devadatta by means of the aforementioned relation. "The cow" (*gauḥ*) is the object (*karman*). "To the Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇāya*) is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). "From the house" (*gehāt*) is the point of departure (*apādāna*).

"In the Gaṅgā" is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); "with the hand" is the instrument (*karaṇa*); "by me" is the agent factor (*kartṛ-kāraka*); "is given" is the verbal form in the passive sense (*karman*). Having synthesized all of this, he indicates the comprehension of the sentence-meaning with the passage beginning "related to Devadatta" and ending with "the operation residing in me. He explains the word *yathāyatham* found in the verse as "in the manner stated," noting that *yathāyatham* is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) meaning "according to its own respective [factors]."

Whichever case-ending is capable of conveying a particular meaning, that meaning should be understood as belonging to that case-ending. This was stated previously in the *Sāra*: "The referent (*āśraya*) is the meaning of the second, third, and seventh [cases]," and so forth. Regarding the word "here" (*atra*): it means when the case-endings (*sup*) denote the substratum (*dharmī*) such as the object (*karman*). Regarding the phrase "in the state of being the object-sphere" (*viṣayatāyām*): [it refers to the capacity of the case-ending to signify the relation of being the locus].

Regarding the statement "one knows the pot" (*ghaṭaṃ jānāti*), from the experience of understanding that this means "knowledge having the pot as its object," the ancient Naiyāyikas claim that in such cases the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā-vibhakti*) has the sense of "objectness" (*viṣayatā*) as its secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇā*). To these, [the author] replies with the words "supāṃ karmeti" (Pāṇini 2.3.2). He clarifies this point with the passage beginning "This is the intention" (*ayaṃ bhāvaḥ*). The meanings of the nominal suffixes (*sup*) include "object" (*karman*) and so forth, as well as "number" (*saṃkhyā*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "object and so forth," other factors of action (*kāraka*) such as the "instrument" (*karaṇa*) are included.

By the word "also" (*api*), the powers (*śakti*) such as "object-ness" (*karmatva*) and so forth—spoken of in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *saptamīpañcamyau*—"are included," according to which [the view] that power is the grammatical factor (*kāraka*). Likewise, regarding the phrase "of the *tiṅ*s": the meaning is that for those *tiṅ*s as well, the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and number (*saṃkhyā*) are the meanings. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): the meaning is "among the *sup*s and the *tiṅ*s. Regarding the word "restriction" (*niyama*): restriction is indeed of two kinds—restriction of the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*) and restriction of the meaning (*arthaniyama*). Among these, restriction of the suffix is also of two kinds: that which depends on [suffixes] in general, and that which depends on the specific meaning of the stem (*prakṛta*).

In this context, there is a restriction on the suffixes (*pratyayaniyama*) of the form: "The first case (*prathamā*) occurs only for the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*)," and "The second case (*dvitīyā*) occurs only for the object (*karman*). This is because of the statement of the learned: "A restriction applies to that which is other than where the word *eva* (only) is placed. Thus, the result is the exclusion of the first case when it is other than the meaning of the nominal stem, and the exclusion of the second case when it is other than the meaning of the object; for "restriction" (*niyama*) means "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*). Alternatively, there is a restriction on the meanings (*arthaniyama*): "The second case occurs only for the object," and "The first case occurs only for the meaning of the nominal stem."

This is because of the previously stated reasoning regarding the particle *eva*. In the case of the object (*karman*), the phrase "not another" results in the exclusion of the connection between other [suffixes] and the meaning of the object. Among the two types of restrictive rules (*niyama*) concerning expectancy, if one adopts a general restrictive rule for suffixes—namely, that if the first case-suffix occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then it refers only to the meaning of the stem itself when devoid of suitability for the object and so forth, and not to an addition such as objecthood (*karmatva*) which is co-located with the meaning of the stem—then, in the case of the meaning of an indeclinable (*avyaya*), [the first case-suffix applies].

Since indeclinables lack gender, number, and case-role (*kāraka*), and since they lack suitability for [the functions of] object (*karman*) and so forth, a case-ending (*vibhakti*) would not apply to them; therefore, he says "restriction" (*niyama*). The meaning is that the restriction of meaning is well-known.

In this regard, if a case-ending is introduced after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is capable of expressing an object (*karman*) or other such meanings, then when it expresses the object, it must be the accusative (*dvitīyā*); and if a case-ending is introduced after a nominal stem whose meaning is devoid of the object and the like, yet is capable of expressing those meanings, then it must be the nominative (*prathamā*). Thus, under the view that the rule pertains to the meaning (*arthaniyama*), there is a restriction such that the accusative alone occurs for the object and the nominative alone occurs for the meaning of the nominal stem itself. For by this restriction, the exclusion of other case-endings is achieved only where the possibility of meanings such as the object exists; it is on the basis of this proximity (*pratyāsatti*) that the phrase "capable of expressing the object and so forth" is obtained.

And thus, case endings are established even from indeclinables (avyaya) whose meanings are devoid of objects such as the "object" (karman) and so forth. If a case ending is to be applied based on that which is capable of possessing an object and so forth, then the form of the rule is established as: "the first case is to be used for such-and-such a meaning, and the second case for such-and-such a meaning. Consequently, since indeclinables lack the capacity to possess objects and so forth, they do not enter into the scope of this restrictive rule; and because the rule does not apply, all seven case endings occur after an indeclinable by virtue of the general rule. This is the intended meaning.

Thus, even under the view that the suffixes are restricted [by their meanings], he says—"The restriction applies to the base meanings"—in order to establish the case endings from indeclinables (*avyaya*). This means that the restriction concerns the meanings of the bases; that is to say, the restriction on the suffixes is relative to the meanings of the bases. Under this view, if a second case ending occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) capable of expressing an object (*karman*) and so forth, it occurs only when there is an object, and not when there is a cause (*kāraṇa*) and so forth. Similarly, the first case ending occurs only upon the meaning of the nominal stem itself when that stem is devoid of such [object] relations, and not when an object or other relation is present.

The form of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) is this: "From a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) capable of expressing a determinate meaning, the singular number and so forth [take] the singular case-ending and so forth, but not the dual and so forth. Even in this view, since indeclinables (*avyaya*) do not enter into the form of the restrictive rule, when the restriction does not apply, the case-endings (*svādi*) arise from the nominal stem according to the general rule; thus, all seven case-endings are established for indeclinables. However, under the view that the restriction applies to the suffixes with respect to the general category, no case-ending would be obtained from an indeclinable; therefore, that [case-ending] must be established by the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) of the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*.

Although it is impossible to say that [the case endings] denote only the object and not anything else—since they denote both number and object—or that they denote only the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and not anything else, nevertheless, one can say: "only when there is an object, and not in its absence," and "only when there is the meaning of the nominal stem, and not in its absence. The phrase "in its absence" means: in the presence of other meanings co-located with the absence of objecthood, such as the instrumental (*karaṇa*), etc.; or in the presence of other meanings co-located with the absence of the meaning of the nominal stem, such as the agent (*kartṛ*), etc.

Nor should it be argued that because no other meaning is established that is co-referential with the absence of the nominal stem's meaning, there is no established object to be excluded by the restrictive rule; for the result of that exclusion is simply this: that the nominative case occurs only when the nominal stem has its own meaning, and not when it is devoid of meaning. Furthermore, it is not the case that meanings devoid of substance are unestablished, since there exist indeclinables (*nipāta*) devoid of meaning used for the purpose of filling out a verse-line, such as *ca*, *vai*, *tu*, *hi*, and so forth.

This is because those [words] lack the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), which consists of the form that serves as the cause for the occurrence of its own referent (*svārtha*) and substance (*dravya*), along with their substratum. Nor should it be argued that the exclusion of case-endings (*vibhakti*) from meaningless items is indeed intended; for in the example "dhārmiko 'si vai tvā sukhaṃ prāpnoti," the very purpose of the rule "sapūrvāyāḥ prathamāyā vibhāṣā" is the application of the *tvā* substitute, and thus the exclusion of case-endings from meaningless items is not desired.

However, given the existence of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*, there is no fault in the form of the non-application of the first case (*prathamā*) after meaningless particles (*anarthaka-nipāta*). And thus, from the present verse and its Vārttika, as well as the Bhāṣya located therein, it is established that the locus (*dharmī*), such as the object (*karman*), is the expressed meaning (*vācyatā*), and likewise, the restriction of the meanings such as the object is obtained.

And thus, with the intention that the Naiyāyikas’ acceptance of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) for the sense of "object" (*viṣayatva*) and so forth in the case of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is improper because it contradicts the aforementioned Bhāṣya and Vārttika, he says: "In either case, it is contrary to the established rule. In this regard, if one accepts *lakṣaṇā* for the second case in the sense of "object-ness," the contradiction with the grammatical rule—"the second case is used only in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇy eva dvitīyā*)—is evident. Furthermore, it should be understood that even under the view that the rule concerns the meaning (*arthaniyamapakṣa*), there is a contradiction with the rule—"the sixth case is used only for the remainder" (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhy eva*)—because "object-ness" (*viṣayatā*) is a type of "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

And thus, since characteristics such as being contrary to a restrictive rule (*niyama*) are not the causes for [the application of] ungrammatical forms, and because the aforementioned nature of "objectness" (*karmatva*) is absent in the case of "objecthood" (*viṣayatā*), the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) is not prescribed there by the grammatical treatise. Consequently, even when the second case is uttered with the intention of denoting "objecthood," the prohibition—"one should not speak untruth"—does indeed apply to the ritual act of speaking, such as false speech. Furthermore, the acceptance of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) on the strength of one's own experience is not a cause for the occurrence of a case-ending; therefore, he says: "For this very reason."

The meaning is: because there is an absence of any ground for *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is being applied. Regarding the term "usage" (*vyavahāra*): it means the usage of the ancient Naiyāyikas that one should not employ *lakṣaṇā* in respect to a case-ending. The underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) behind such usage is this: that a case-ending prescribed by the grammatical treatise for a specific meaning does not apply when the word has a metaphorical meaning.

And thus, the sense is that the statement of the modern Naiyāyikas—that there is not only a contradiction with grammar but also a contradiction with the established doctrines of their own ancient and traditional Naiyāyika predecessors—is indeed to be disregarded. "Dig" (the direction) [indicates that this is merely a brief indication].

As for the meaning of *div* [as "object"]: since in expressions such as *ghaṭaṃ jānāti* ("he knows the pot"), the operation conducive to the attainment of the status of being an object can be the very meaning of the verbal root *jñā*, it is possible to justify the usage by treating it as a primary (*mukhya*) object alone. Consequently, if one were to arbitrarily accept a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) there, the instruction regarding the meaning of the case-ending would result in futility; therefore, accepting a metaphorical indication in that context is utterly improper. || 24 ||

Thus ends the determination of the meanings of case-endings in the *Śāṅkarī*, a commentary on the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*. In this commentary on the *Bhūṣaṇa* composed by Śaṅkara, the son of Raṅgabhaṭṭa, the determination of the meanings of case-endings is complete. (3)
Now follows the determination of the meaning of names.

Having defined the meanings of all nominal stems (*nāman*), verbal roots (*mūladhātu*), and the meanings of suffixes (*tiṅ*) derived from them, as well as the meanings of case-endings (*sub*) in connection with those, the author now defines the meanings of nominal stems (*nāmārtha*) by way of the appropriate occasion (*avasara-saṃgati*). Thus he says: "The meanings of nominal stems" (*nāmārthān*). This means the meanings of nominal bases (*prātipadikārtha*). Regarding the meanings of nominal stems, they are said to be "one, two, three," and so forth. To prevent the suspicion that words such as *eka* (one) might refer to unintended meanings due to their common usage, he states the specific meanings intended in this context, beginning with "one is a genus" (*ekaṃ jātiḥ*).

In this context, by the term *jāti* (genus), what is intended is the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) residing in each respective object, and not *jāti* in the technical sense of being inherent in many while possessing unity and eternity. Furthermore, uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*) consists in existing in that particular object while not existing in anything other than it. Consequently, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) even in the case of *ākāśatva*, *abhāvatva*, and so forth, despite their lacking the status of *jāti* as defined by inherence in many. In the technical treatises, it is precisely this unique property residing in each respective object that is designated by the term *svārtha* (its own meaning).

And this very [universal] is said to be the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) [of the word]. As for the proof that the universal (*jāti*) is the denotatum of a word, one should consider the *vārttika* located in the sūtra "When denoting a genus" (*jātyākhyāyām*), which states: "The inclusion of *aṇ* among its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) is not a general rule (*aparibhāṣyam*), because it is established by the inclusion of the form (*ākṛtigrahaṇāt*)," as well as the *bhāṣya* on the *sarūpa-sūtra*, which says: "Vājapyāyana [holds that the word denotes] the form (*ākṛti*). Furthermore, this theory of the expressive power residing in the universal (*jātiśaktivāda*) is favored by the Mīmāṃsakas; for they maintain that the expressive power of words resides in the universal due to parsimony (*lāghava*).

The sense is that because the universal (*jāti*) is one, its denotative power (*śakti*) is also one, which results in parsimony (*lāghava*). Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the determination of the power of words occurs only with respect to individuals (*vyakti*), as established by linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*)—the crown jewel among the means of grasping power—how can the power be established as residing in the universal? To this, the answer is: because there would be complexity (*gaurava*) if the power were located in individuals due to their infinity.

Because individual cows of the past, future, and present are infinite, it is impossible for them all to exist at one time; consequently, it is impossible to grasp the expressive power (*śakti*) with respect to so many individuals. Furthermore, to postulate a distinct expressive power for each individual basis would involve excessive complexity (*gaurava*). If it is argued that, in order to avoid this complexity of expressive power, the power should be postulated in only a single individual, we say no. For, due to the absence of expressive power in other individuals, there would be no cognition of those other individuals. Therefore, the expressive power is determined to reside in the genus (*jāti*) alone.

[Objection: But in that case, how is there syntactic connection (*anvaya*) in instances such as "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*) or "Pound the rice" (*vrīhīn avahanti*), given that bringing and pounding are impossible with respect to a universal (*jāti*)? [Reply: In those cases, the connection is established by means of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), wherein [the word] indicates its own substratum (*svāśraya*). Thus, since it is possible for the individual (*vyakti*) to appear everywhere through *lakṣaṇā* via the relation of being its own substratum, the postulation of a primary denotative power (*śakti*) in that regard is indeed fruitless; so they say. According to this view, he demonstrates the reason why the universal possesses the denotative power, stating: "By parsimony" (*lāghavena*).

The meaning is that since the power [of a word] directed toward a single object is also possible as one due to the unity of the genus (*jāti*), it is more appropriate for that [genus] alone to be the denotable meaning (*vācya*) on account of parsimony (*lāghava*). Regarding the phrase "due to complexity" (*gauravāt*): although it is appropriate for the power of a word to reside in the individual (*vyakti*) because the primary means of grasping that power—namely, the practical usage of leading, bringing, and so forth—is most directly applicable to the individual, nevertheless, because individuals are infinite, it is impossible for them all to be present at once; thus, since it is impossible to grasp the power with respect to all individuals, if the power were grasped with respect to only one individual...

The point is that since it would follow that another individual not within the scope of the word's expressive power (śakti) could not appear in the verbal cognition (śābdabodha), and since it would be cumbersome to postulate a separate power for every individual—resulting in an infinity of powers—it is not appropriate to postulate the word's power as residing in the individual.

[Objection: Surely, in the theory that the universal (*jāti*) is the denotation, since the universal is the denoted object, one must accept that properties such as *gotvatva* (cowness-ness) residing in such a universal possess the status of being the delimitors of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*). Consequently, it would necessarily follow that this [delimitor, namely *gotvatva*]—which consists in subsisting in all cows while not subsisting in anything other than cows through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*)—is itself the denoted object, because the status of being a delimitor of denotability consists in being a qualifier (*prakāra*) within a portion of the denoted object. Thus, there is a contrary complexity (*gaurava*). [Reply: This is not so.

Just as that which is non-definable (alakṣya) can nonetheless serve as a delimitor of definability (lakṣyatāvacchedakatva), so too it is possible for that which is inexpressible (aśakya) to serve as a delimitor of expressibility (śakyatāvacchedakatva); for there is no evidence that the delimitor of expressibility must necessarily itself be expressible. Others, however, maintain that just as in the view that the word has the individual as its denotation (vyaktiśaktimate), the power (śakti) resides in the aspect of cowness (gotva) and so forth, and that the status of being a delimitor of expressibility (śakyatāvacchedakatā) is "undelimited" (niravacchinna)—meaning it is not constituted by another property serving as a qualifier—so too in the view that the word has the universal as its denotation (jātiśaktimate), that power is undelimited and not constituted by another property serving as a qualifier.

The point is this: just as in the case of "this is a jar" and so forth, although the cognition of the jar is delimited (i.e., composed of another property, namely the jar-ness, which serves as its qualifier) by virtue of having jar-ness as its mode (*prakāra*), the cognition of jar-ness itself is undelimited because it is not composed of yet another property serving as its qualifier, namely "jar-ness-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*); likewise, since the cognition of the universal "cow-ness" is undelimited because it is not composed of another property such as "cow-ness-ness," there is no complexity (*gaurava*).

Now, one might object: "Even though individuals are infinite, since each individual is a single entity, there is only one power (śakti). Thus, since there is no difference between the position that the power resides in the universal (jāti) and the position that it resides in the individual (vyakti), why is there such partiality for the theory that the power resides in the universal? [The answer is: Because in the position that the power resides in a single individual, there would be no inclusion of all individuals within such a power.

[Objection: Even on the view that the word’s power (śakti) resides in the universal (jāti), although the universal is presented by that power, since there is no power with respect to the individual (vyakti), not even a single individual would be presented; how, then, can there be an inclusion of all individuals? Nor should it be said that, on that view, the presentation of the individual need not occur at all, because the presentation of the individual is necessary for its connection with actions such as "bringing" (ānayana). [Response: This is true; however, the inclusion of all individuals is possible through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).

And thus, since those who maintain that the word’s power resides in the universal (jāti) include all individuals by means of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) in other individuals through the assumption of the power residing in a single individual, the assumption of a plurality of functions is identical in both the theory of the power of the universal and the theory of the power of the individual. With the intention of showing that there is likewise no parsimony (lāghava) even in the theory of the power of the universal, he says: "Nor [is there parsimony] regarding the individuals either. "Lack of a decisive criterion" (vinigamanāviraha) means the absence of any reasoning that would determine one of the two alternatives.

Establishing the argument that consists of parsimony (*lāghava*)—which favors the view that the word's power resides in the genus (*jāti*)—the author first demonstrates the complexity (*gaurava*) of the view that the power resides in the individual (*vyakti*), beginning with the words "For thus" (*evaṃ hi*). Regarding the phrase "in the case of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward another individual": the word "being accepted" (*svīkriyamāṇāyām*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. And the acceptance of such a secondary indication is necessary because the cognition of another individual would otherwise be inexplicable. Regarding the term "inhering in itself" (*svasamaveta*): the meaning is "the state of being the locus of that genus which inheres in itself."

Here, by the word "itself" (sva), there is intended the yellow individual cow as the substratum of the [genus] power; the genus "cowness" (gotvajāti) is inherent in that—that is, it exists in it through the relation of inherence (samavāya); and since the state of being its substratum also belongs to the white cow, the definition is thus consistent. Even in the view that the power resides in the genus (jātiśaktipakṣa), the acceptance of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) with respect to the individual is necessary because otherwise the connection with actions such as "bringing" would be inexplicable; this is what he states with the words "But by the genus... and "the state of being the substratum."

The meaning is "having itself as its substratum. Its own [nature] is "cowness" (*gotva*); having that as its substratum exists in all individual cows—this is the application of the definition (*lakṣaṇasamanvaya*). Consequently, in the view that the universal (*jāti*) is the denotable object, there is primary denotation (*śakti*) toward the universal and secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the individual; whereas in the view that the individual is the denotable object, there is primary denotation toward the individual and secondary indication toward another individual. Thus, although it is necessary to accept the operation of secondary indication accompanied by primary denotation in order to account for the inclusion of all individuals in both views, in the view where the universal possesses the power of denotation, the indication is proximate, whereas in the view where the individual possesses the power...

The definition [of secondary signification] as "remoteness" (viprakṛṣṭā lakṣaṇā) entails parsimony in the case of the universal (jāti) theory, whereas in the case of the individual (vyakti) theory, prolixity (gaurava) indeed exists. For instance, secondary signification is a relation with that which is directly denoted by the word itself. Here, "itself" refers to the word "cow"; its "directly denoted" object is the universal "cowness" (gotvajāti); and the relation to that universal exists directly in all individual cows. Thus, in the theory of the word's power residing in the universal, the relation with the directly denoted is proximate.

In the view that the word’s power resides in the individual (vyakti), however—the word "cow" itself is the *sva* (the word), and its own object (*svaśakya*) is a yellow cow; since there is no direct relation between that [yellow cow] and another individual, the relation with other individuals must be stated as being mediated by the cowness (*gotva*) inherent in that [first] individual.

And thus, [in the theory of the denotative power residing in the individual (vyakti-śakti-vāda)], there is the yellow cow-individual, the "cowness" (gotva) inhering in it—that is, existing therein by way of the relation of inherence—and the relation of that [cowness] to all other cow-individuals such as the white one; since the relation of one individual to another individual is remote, there is the complexity (gaurava) consisting in the remoteness of the relation to the denotable object in the theory of the power residing in the individual. But in the theory of the power residing in the genus (jāti-śakti-vāda), that is not the case; rather, there is the simplicity (lāghava) characterized by proximity to the denotable object—this is the intended meaning.

And thus, as stated, simplicity (*lāghava*) serves as the decisive criterion (*vinigamaka*); therefore, there is no lack of a decisive factor—this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "Since we accept that the word-potency (*śakti*) resides in all individual instances (*vyakti*) as qualified by their respective universals (*jāti*), such as 'cowness' (*gotva*), there is no burden of infinite potencies resulting from the infinity of individuals. With this intention, he says: "Furthermore, in the case of the denotation of the qualified (*viśiṣṭavācyatva*). "In this way" means: when the potency for the qualified is accepted. "Not unperceived" refers to the principle: "A cognition does not apprehend the qualified without having first apprehended the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)."

Since the cognition of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is the cause of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*), such a cognition whose qualifiers have not been apprehended cannot have as its object a substantive qualified by those qualifiers. By employing two negative particles (*nañ*) in the phrase "not un-apprehended" (*nāgṛhītā*), it is indicated that the cognition of the qualifier must necessarily precede. Thus, prior to the cognition of the substantive, the cognition of the qualifier is indispensable. Once the cognition of the qualifier has arisen, the causal capacity [of the qualifier] is exhausted by that alone and does not reach the substantive.
