As it has been said: "The denotation [of a word] cannot reach the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), as its power is exhausted by the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Thus, since the theory of the denotation of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa-śakti-vāda*) is beset by the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*), it ultimately results in the position of the denotation of the universal alone (*jāti-śakti-pakṣa*). Therefore, the sense is that it is logical that the universal alone is the denoted meaning, on account of its parsimony (*lāghava*) and its being the necessary basis (*upajīvyatva*). Now, one might object: "If it is accepted that the universal alone is the denoted meaning, then the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*) would not arise from it. Nor should it be argued that this is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*), as in the case of the statement "Devadatta is fat," where [the fact of his] eating at night is implied.

Because the individual (vyakti) is not present [in the cognition] through the primary function (vṛtti), it would be impossible for the objecthood (karmatva) and so forth to be construed with it in expressions such as "one should give a cow" (gāṃ dadyāt). This is because of the linguistic rule (vyutpatti) that suffixes convey their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base (prakṛti). Furthermore, the construction of other word-meanings could not occur in the individual, since such construction occurs only with that which is the qualificand (viśeṣya) in the apprehension of the function. Otherwise, upon hearing the sentence "bring the jar," there would be the undesirable consequence of the construction of bringing and so forth even with the ether (ākāśa), which is present [in the cognition] by way of inherence (samavāya). Therefore, he says: "But the cognition of the individual is [by means of] indication (lakṣaṇā). By "indication," [he means:]...

The understanding of the individual (vyakti) through indication (lakṣaṇā) by means of the relation of "having itself as its locus" (svāśrayatva-sambandha) is easily obtained. Thus, the meaning is that since the individual is presented by the function [of indication], the application of case-meanings and so forth to the individual is indeed possible.

If it is objected: "Since metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) depends upon the recognition of the impossibility of the connection between the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) and so forth, in the case of the expression 'there is a cow' (*gaurasti*), because there is no recognition of the impossibility of the connection for the sense 'there is cowness' (*gotvamasti*), it would follow that there is no cognition of an individual cow qualified by cowness"—[we reply: the phrase "by way of metaphorical indication" means "by way of conventional metaphorical indication" (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*). The point is that since conventional metaphorical indication is not distinct from primary denotation (*śakti*), it does not depend on the recognition of the impossibility of the connection and so forth. With this very intention, he says: "This is the direction [of the argument]" (*iti dig*).

Raising objections against the theory that the word denotes the universal (*jāti*) and stating the proof for the theory that it denotes the individual (*vyakti*), he explains that a single word refers to the individual, beginning with "Or else" (*yadvā*). "Only the individual" (*kevalavyaktireva*): by the particle *eva*, the universal is excluded. Since the exclusion of the universal is already established by the word *kevala* itself, the particle *eva* is for the sake of clarity. He states the reason why the word "one" (*eka*) refers to the individual alone, beginning with "In the view that there is only the individual" (*kevalavyaktipakṣe*).

However, according to the view that the word-meaning is an individual qualified by its genus (*jāti*), in order to produce a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) where that genus is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and its substratum is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the cause must be the apprehension of the expressive power (*śaktigraha*) whose qualificandumness is delimited by that genus. Consequently, in rules such as *asya cvau* and *erac*, since it would be possible for the letters 'a', 'i', and so on, to denote the eighteen individuals—such as the eighteen forms of 'a'—which are the substrata of the respective genera of "a-ness" (*atva*) and so forth, the explicit mention of the term *aṇ* in the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* would be redundant. This redundancy is equally clear even under the theory that the expressive power resides in the genus alone.

However, the sense is that since the inclusion of the term *aṇ* is necessary for the sake of establishing the apprehension of eighteen individual instances such as *akāra* and so on under the theory that the word-potency resides solely in the individual (*kevalavyaktiśaktipakṣa*), it is inferred that Pāṇini had this very theory of sole potency in the individual in mind. Thus, the intention is that even the theory of sole potency in the individual is approved by both the scripture and its author.

Likewise, under the view that the word's power resides solely in the genus (*jāti*), or under the view that its power resides in the individual qualified by the genus (*jātiviśiṣṭavyakti*), it would not be necessary to compose the *ekaśeṣa* sūtra; for even with a single word, it is possible to denote multiple individuals subsumed under that same genus. However, under the view that the word's power resides solely in the individual (*kevalavyakti*), since a single word denotes only a single individual, it is necessary to employ words such as "two" (*dvi*) and so forth to convey two or more individuals. Therefore, in that case, the *ekaśeṣa* sūtra must be composed for the purpose of establishing the presence of one [individual] to the exclusion of the others.

By the composition of the *ekaśeṣa* sūtra, it is understood that the sage Pāṇini held the view that the word's expressive power resides solely in the individual (*kevalavyaktiśaktipakṣa*) in his mind. Thus, the meaning is that the view of the expressive power residing solely in the individual is also approved by the *sarūpa* sūtra. The phrase "by the inclusion of the term *aṇ*" is to be construed with "by its composition," as well as with "of the *ekaśeṣa*. And the meaning is "by the composition of the *sarūpa* sūtra. "Of that too" means "of the view that the expressive power resides solely in the individual as well. [This is] because it is established by the treatise (*śāstra*).

The meaning is: "because it is supported by the authoritative treatises (*śāstra*). Having thus stated that the treatise is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the position that the word has power only toward the individual (*vyakti*), he states [the following] while also adducing reasoning as a means of valid cognition for that [position]: "And this is reasonable" (*yuktaṃ caitat*). The meaning is: "This is also consistent with reason. He demonstrates that very reasoning with the words: "by means of linguistic usage" (*vyavahāreṇa*). The meaning is: because, immediately after hearing the instigating statement "Bring the jar," one determines that the grasp of power resides only in the individual, based on the linguistic usage consisting of the act of bringing the jar performed by Caitra, who is the person being instigated.

[Objection: "Surely, because individuals are infinite, there would result an infinity of powers (śakti). If it is argued that this fault does not arise because the power resides in only a certain individual—[we reply: if it is admitted that another individual which is the object of the power also appears in the verbal cognition, then it would follow that even a horse could appear from the word 'cow'. Furthermore, there would be a collapse of the causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) which is the cause of verbal cognition—namely, that the grasp of the power regarding a particular object is the cause of the verbal cognition regarding that same object. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of the delimitor of the relatedness" (*saṃbandhitāvacchedakasya*).

The "related" (*saṃbandhī*) is that which is the substratum of a relation; and "relation" (*saṃbandha*) here means *śakti* (power/potency). The meaning is: "the substratum of power. That very [substratum] is called the "denotable" (*śakya*). "In that" means in the denotable; "of its delimitor" means of the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). The construction is: "of that which consists of a universal" (*jāteḥ*), meaning of that which has the form of a universal. And thus, because it is precisely the delimitor of denotability that is intended as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), there is a neuter designation.

The sense is that if "of the delimitor of denotability" (*śakyatāvacchedakasya*) is intended as a qualifier, then because a qualifier takes on the gender of the qualified (*viśeṣya*), one would have to say "of the female delimitor of denotability" (*śakyatāvacchedakāyāḥ*). Regarding the phrase "due to the unity of the universal" (*jāteraikyāt*): since there exists only a single power (*śakti*) delimited by a single property across individuals unified by a universal, there is no complexity (*gaurava*). The essential point is that due to the unity of the delimitor of denotability, there is unity of the power. He raises an objection with "But it is not so" (*na caivam*).

Thus, regarding the fact that "potness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth are the delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*): the phrase "because they are delimiters of denotability" means that since being a delimiter of denotability consists in being a delimiter of the objective determination (*viśeṣyatāvacchedakatva*) residing in a part of the denotable while itself being denotable, it follows necessarily that potness and the like must also be denotable; this is the intended meaning. "That alone must be denotable" implies that the position that the individual alone is denotable is utterly untenable. Regarding the phrase "even though [it] is not a cause": [this refers to the fact that even if it is not a cause for the production of a cognition].

Just as, when the causality of a staff with respect to a jar is apprehended through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), one accepts that "staffness" (*daṇḍatva*)—though itself not the cause due to being otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*)—is the delimitor of that causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*); and just as one accepts that "bankness" (*tīratva*) is the delimitor of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) even though it is not itself the indicated meaning because it lacks connection with the flowing current; so too, there is no obstacle to accepting that "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and the like, though they are themselves not the denotable meaning (*aśakya*), are the delimiters of such denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), provided they possess the status of being denotable.

The point is that there is no evidence for accepting the rule that "that which has become a qualifier (viśeṣaṇatā) determined by a qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) resting on a portion of the denotable meaning (śakyārtha) possesses the status of being a delimitor of denotability (śakyatāvacchedakatva). Regarding this stated point, he cites the statement of Bhaṭṭa found in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* as supporting proof—namely, "And it has been said," and "Even though there is infinity," etc.

The meaning of the verse is as follows: although individual instances such as jars (*ghaṭa*)—which are intended to be denotable—are manifold and thus impossible to delimit individually, one takes as a *upalakṣaṇa* (an indirect indicator) a single property such as the inclusive genus (*jāti*), which, despite being itself incapable of being denoted, serves to distinguish those that are capable of being so denoted; having accepted this [property] as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), the word—consisting of "cow" and so forth—possesses an easily graspable relation, namely, a relation of denotability residing in the individual cows and the like, and it will not fail to convey an individual instance that was not the object of the initial apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*).

The nature of a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), such as a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, is this: having rendered all its own substrates objects of the apprehension of linguistic capacity (*śaktigraha*), it itself remains neither an object of the apprehension of linguistic capacity nor an object of cognition. The sense is that, because the capacity is determined with respect to all individuals through the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*) of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so on.

[Objection: "But even in the theory that the genus (*jāti*) is the denotative power (*śakti*), the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*) is necessary for the purpose of connecting [the word] with actions such as giving; and even in the theory that the individual is the denotative power, the recourse to the genus as a secondary qualifier (*upalakṣaṇa*)—for the sake of being the delimiting factor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*)—is also necessary. Therefore, having considered these two aforementioned positions, the theory of the denotative power residing in the qualified (*viśiṣṭa-śakti-vāda*) alone is logical. To this, he says: "In reality, however" (*vastutastu*). "[For one for whom] the form (*ākṛti*) is the word-meaning" (*ākṛtipadārthakasya*): this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one for whom the form is the word-meaning. "From the *Bhāṣya*" (*iti bhāṣyāt*): this is the *Bhāṣya* located in the *Sarūpa-sūtra*.

"Or the qualified is the denotation. This means that things such as cows, qualified by their genus (*jāti*), are the denotations of words such as "cow. However, others [hold that] for one who maintains that the form (*ākṛti*) is the word-meaning, the substance (*dravya*) is not not the word-meaning; nor, for one who maintains that the substance is the word-meaning, is the form not the word-meaning. Both are the word-meaning for both [theories]. For someone, one [element] is primary and the other is secondary. Thus, in the *Bhāṣya* on the theory that the substance is the word-meaning, because it is stated that the form is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is the cognition of many individuals unified by that genus through a single word alone.

It is indicated that, because of this possibility, even in that view, the *ekaśeṣa* (the grammatical rule for retaining only one of identical words) need not be commenced. Furthermore, it is indicated that in the theory where the universal (*jāti*) is the denoted meaning, the individual (*vyakti*) serves as the delimiting factor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), whereas in the theory where the individual is the denoted meaning, the universal serves as the delimiting factor of denotability. Thus they say. However, it is the individual such as a cow, qualified by the universal, alone that is the denoted meaning, and not the universal qualified by the cow. This is because the aforementioned position is untenable, as there is no experience of the cognition of the universal "cowness" (*gotvajāti*) as qualified by the cow upon hearing words such as "cow."

[Objection: "But surely, if the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is the word-meaning, the term 'one' (*eka*) would be contradictory; therefore, he says: 'And of this [term] 'one'... The word 'and' (*ca*) has the sense of 'but' (*tu*). The phrase 'of this [term] 'one'' means 'of the word *eka*'. The word 'this' (*ayam*) means 'that which is about to be stated'. The phrase 'and in the cognition of the power' (*śaktijñāne ca*)—the intention is as follows: the apprehension of the power (*śaktigraha*) regarding a particular object is the cause for the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) regarding that same object. For example, it is attested by experience that a verbal cognition regarding a jar arises only when there is an apprehension of the power regarding the jar."

The meaning is that only when there is knowledge of the word-potency (*śakti*)—in the form "the word 'pot' conveys an object possessing pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvavad-artha*)—does a cognition regarding a pot arise from the word 'pot' in the sentence "Bring the pot. Here, the knowledge of potency is the cause (*kāraṇa*), and the cognition of the individual object is the effect (*kārya*). In this context, that property (*dharma*) qualified by which the knowledge of potency serves as the cause of cognition is the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*).

Furthermore, in the cognition qualified by "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva), the cause is precisely the knowledge of the word's denotative power (śaktijñāna) having "pot-ness" as its object; thus, the meaning is that the delimitor of such causality (kāraṇatāvacchedaka) is the universal (jāti) such as "pot-ness. Regarding the objects of the power: the word, the meaning, and the cognition are the objects of the power. The word is the "denoter" (vācaka) because it possesses the status of being the generator (janakatā) relative to the producedness residing in the cognition. The meaning is the object of the power by virtue of being the object of the cognition produced by the word; that [meaning] is the "denoted" (vācya).

And thus, regarding the object of that causality of cognition which resides in the knowledge of *śakti*, the meaning is as follows: the universal (*jāti*) such as "cowness" (*gotva*) alone is the delimitor of the objective relation residing in the individual (e.g., a cow) that serves as the object of the word-generated cognition through the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā-sambandha*). Since that [universal] is one and the same, it is intended that the referent of a noun is one; this is to be construed with the statement that the individual cow, which is the object of *śakti*—defined as being cognizable through the relation of objecthood—is delimited by the objective relation residing in it, namely the universal "cowness," and that [universal] is indeed one.

The intention behind the phrase "one [universal]" (*ekam*) is that the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) should be understood by including only one universal (*sāmānya*). The sense is that the universal alone is the delimiting factor of such causality (*tādṛśakāraṇatāvacchedaka*). Thus, in a cognition such as "this is a cow," the causality resides in the knowledge of the power residing in the genus "cowness" (*gotvajāti*) and so forth, because of parsimony (*lāghava*); it does not reside in the knowledge of the power residing in an individual qualified by the genus "cowness," because of prolixity (*gaurava*). This is the point.

And thus, the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the causality for cognition residing in the knowledge of power (*śakti-jñāna-niṣṭha-bodha-kāraṇatā*), which is the defining characteristic of such causality, is precisely the universal (*sāmānya*) such as "cowness" (*gotva*). This is the truth. The apprehension of power (*śakti-graha*)—in the form "this meaning is to be understood from this word," which has the word as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the meaning as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), or in the form "this word should cause this meaning to be understood," which has the meaning as the qualifier and the word as the qualificand—occurs only with respect to individual entities (*vyakti*) such as cows, as delimited by universals such as "cowness."

At the time of grasping the word-potency (*śaktigraha*), there occurs the manifestation of all individuals as subsumed under that genus (*tajjātyanugatīkṛta*). For this very reason, at the time of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) as well, there occurs the manifestation of all individuals as subsumed under that genus. The causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) should be understood according to the manner stated above. Now, an objection is raised: "If the cognition of potency is in the form 'the cow is denotable by the word *go*,' then just as there arises a cognition having the individual cow as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and the property of cowness (*gotva*) as its qualifier (*prakāra*), so too there would arise a cognition having the property of cowness (*gotvatva*) as its qualifier and the property of cowness (*gotva*) itself as its qualificandum. To this, he says: "And just as... (*yathā ca*).

Regarding the causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) such that, for the production of a cognition of a jar qualified by "jar-ness" (ghaṭatva), the cause is a knowledge of the power (śaktijñāna) whose object is merely "jar-ness" and which lacks "the nature of jar-ness" (ghaṭatvatva) as its qualifier—that is, one devoid of the qualifier "the nature of jar-ness"—this has been summarized in the *Bhūṣaṇa*; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. This is what is intended by the phrase "having accepted," etc., meaning having accepted the denotability (vācyatva) of the qualified entity (viśiṣṭa), as stated in the passage beginning with "In reality, however" (*vastutastu*). [The phrase] "dvikamiti" means...

A collection of two [is formed] by the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃjñāsaṃghasūtrādhyayaneṣu* (Pāṇini 5.1.58), with the suffix *kan*. "Genus and individual" (*jātivyaktī*) means having entered into a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified; the meaning of a noun is either an individual qualified by a genus, or a genus qualified by an individual. Although, for one who holds that the form (*ākṛti*) is the referent of a word, the substance (*dravya*) is not the referent, and for one who holds that the substance is the referent, the form is not the referent.

Although the *Bhāṣya* statement, "the meaning of the word for both [the universal and the individual] is both," establishes that the universal and the individual, when taken separately, constitute the meaning of the word, nevertheless, the intention is that by the subsequent *Bhāṣya* statement, "for someone, one thing is subordinate and another is primary," it is determined that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides only in the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*). "From the prima facie view" (*pūrvapakṣāt*) means from the position that there is a single word-meaning. "As before" (*pūrvavat*) [refers to the previous discussion].

This must be resolved by accepting the meaning that, through the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā-sambandha*), a single universal alone is the delimitor of the causal efficacy residing in the knowledge of the word’s power (*śaktijñāna*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction: under the view that [the denotation] is one, only one thing would be the meaning of the noun; whereas under the view that it is two, both things would be the meaning of the noun. It should be understood that while in the previous case the contradiction was resolved by taking the qualified entity as the word-meaning, here it is resolved by taking both [the qualifier and the qualified] as the word-meaning.

One might object: "Is it not the case that gender (*liṅga*), such as femininity and so forth, is a worldly property consisting of a specific configuration of parts characterized by definitions such as 'a woman possesses breasts and hair'? Because it is not universal, it is not useful for the formal procedures (*prakriyā*) of this treatise; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of *natva* (the substitution of *n* for *t*) in forms like *dārān*, and because such a gender is entirely absent in insentient things, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of the suffix *ṭāp* in words like *khaṭvā*. Therefore, following the method of the *Bhāṣya*, he first states that gender is also the meaning of a nominal stem, saying: "The triad" (*trikam*). A "triad" (*trikam*) is a collection (*samūha*) of three; [the suffix *-ka*] is added as before.

Clarifying the meaning of the word *trika*, he says: "jāti-vyakti," and so forth. Because there are three genders (*liṅga*), he characterizes their specific distinctions—namely, the neuter and the others—according to the view of the Bhāṣya: "sattva-rajas-tamas. "The state of equilibrium" means that the persistence of the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* and the rest, in a condition devoid of deficiency or excess, is precisely what constitutes the neuter gender. "Excess" means the increase of *sattva* and the others; that itself is the masculine gender. "Deficiency" means decrease, that is to say, their diminution.

The meaning is that its nature is femininity. Now, an objection may be raised: since contradictory properties such as increase and decrease cannot coexist in a single object like a riverbank, the forms *taṭaḥ* (masculine), *taṭī* (feminine), and *taṭam* (neuter) would be untenable. Furthermore, since increase and the like are impossible in the Supreme Brahman, which transcends all modifications, the linguistic usage associated with masculinity and neuter gender—such as "the Self is Brahman"—would also be untenable. To this, he says: "residing in those respective words. This means it resides in words distinguished by various grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), such as genus, quality, action, and name.

The gender of a word resides in the word itself, as established by the usage of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in expressions such as "the word is masculine," and by the authority of rules in the grammatical treatise such as "after *āṅ*, *nā* is substituted [for *śas*] except in the feminine; *na* is substituted for *śas* after that [word] when it is masculine; [and] *su* and *am* are elided after a neuter [noun]," as stated in the Bhāṣya.

The point is this: if gender were inherent in the object (*arthaniṣṭhatva*) by way of having the nature of accumulation (*upacaya*) and so forth, then in cases such as *taṭas* (m.), *taṭī* (f.), and *taṭam* (n.), the grammatical operations conditioned by the three genders would be impossible, because mutually contradictory states such as accumulation cannot coexist in a single word. Furthermore, the expression *ātmā brahma* (the Self is Brahman) would also be untenable. Therefore, it is said that "it is denotable by the word [itself]"; the meaning is that the gender inherent in the word itself is what is expressed by it.

The word "Kṛṣṇa," "Śrī," "Jñāna," and so forth, possesses gender—such as masculinity and the like—which resides in that [object]; thus, there is a coordination (samanvaya) in that the gender residing in the object is denotable by words such as "Kṛṣṇa. Now, even under the view that gender resides in the word as stated in the Bhāṣya, the problem remains: it is impossible for multiple mutually contradictory genders to coexist within a single word. To this, he says: "Taking up that very same contradictory [quality]" (*tameva viruddha*). Words differ by taking up contradictory attributes in the form of femininity, masculinity, and so on.

Since mutually contradictory properties such as femininity and masculinity cannot coexist in a single entity, a difference in words arises from the difference in their properties (*dharma*). Just as the phonemes *a* and others are distinguished by shortness, length, acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and so forth, likewise words such as *taṭa* with identical sequences [of phonemes] are distinct. Thus, the masculine word *taṭa* is one thing and the feminine word *taṭa* is another; therefore, due to this difference in words, there is no occasion for the aforementioned objection.

Regarding this mark (liṅga), it is established in the *Śabdakaustubha* that the authority for determining whether certain words possess one, two, or even all three marks lies in the *Liṅgānuśāsana*. Now, if these states such as increase (*upacaya*) and so forth constitute the gender-mark, then because these states are mutually contradictory, they cannot coexist in a single word; on what basis, then, is the conventional usage of certain words as having multiple genders? To this, he says: "In the case of some words having multiple genders... [and so forth].

Even though the gender (liṅga) such as masculinity—which consists of accumulation and so forth—is contradictory [in different instances], the conventional usage of "possessing multiple genders" can be maintained either by superimposing non-difference upon words because they share the same phonetic sequence (*samānānupūrvīkatva*), or by treating them as a collective representation (*tantra*) of those [instances]. Thus, it should be understood that in words like *taṭa* which have the same phonetic sequence, there are three genders; in words like *chāgā*, there are two; and in words like *padārtha*, there is only one. And so it is said: "In this way..."

The meaning is: when the conventional gender (*pāribhāṣika-liṅga*), which consists of accumulation (*upacaya*) and so forth and resides solely in the word, serves as the cause for the linguistic usage of "female," "male," and so on. In the case of the words *padārtha*, *vyakti*, and *vastu*, there are respectively masculinity, femininity, and neuter-ness; thus, regarding every object, there arises a linguistic usage consisting of the simultaneous employment of those specific words—*padārtha* and so forth—which denote masculinity and the rest, in the form: "this is the object (*padārtha*)," "this is the individual (*vyakti*)," or "this is the thing (*vastu*). For example: *taṭaḥ* (masculine), *taṭī* (feminine).

Even though the worldly gender (liṅga) found in expressions such as "a woman possessing breasts and hair" does not exist [in the case of a river], it is nonetheless possible for words like *taṭa* ("bank"), which are differentiated by mutually contradictory technical genders, to undergo grammatical operations conditioned by their respective genders, such as masculinity.

If, however, even the technical gender (*pāribhāṣika-liṅga*) mentioned in the Bhāṣya as being "the mark of the worldly" (*laukika-liṅga*) were to reside in the object itself, then, since in a female individual there exists only femininity (*strītva*), which consists of diminution (*apacaya*), there would be no usage of the words *padārtha* and *vastu* in the sense of "this is the referent" (*ayam padārthaḥ*) or "this is the thing" (*idam vastu*) with respect to her; for in a woman, masculinity (*puṃstva*) and neuterness (*napuṃsakatva*) are absent.

Thus, since in a male (puṃs) only masculinity consisting of accumulation (upacaya) exists, there would be no linguistic usage by means of the terms "individual" (vyakti) or "entity" (vastu)—such as "this is an individual" or "this is an entity"—because femininity and neuterness are absent in a male. Since states such as accumulation and so forth are mutually contradictory, it is impossible for them to coexist in a single object; therefore, an object must exist in accordance with only one particular state. Consequently, it is established by reasoning that only a single gender can belong to a given object.

Furthermore, because it is utterly impossible for two or three genders to coexist in a single object, if gender were inherent in the word, then since an object would be entirely devoid of gender, there would be no obstacle to its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as *padārtha* (object), *vyakti* (individual), and so forth—which denote merely masculinity, femininity, and the like. Consequently, common usage such as "this is the object" or "this is the individual" would be perfectly consistent everywhere. Nor [is there any problem] even if gender resides in the word, for although the gender mentioned in the Bhāṣya is mutually contradictory...

It must be stated that such doubts certainly arise—for instance, that it is impossible for gender (*liṅga*) to coexist within a single word, or that it is impossible for a word to be designated as having two or more genders—and so forth. However, this has already been answered. Furthermore, it is not appropriate to rely here upon worldly gender (*laukikaliṅga*) as residing in the object; for that would be contradicted in the case of insentient things like *kaṭu* (pungent), which would result in the non-application of suffixes such as *ṭāp*. As for worldly gender, it is traditionally defined as: "A woman is known by her breasts and hair; a man by his body hair."

Regarding the statement, "That which is the interval between these two, in its absence, is the neuter," here, because the word *keśa* (hair) denotes the Lord (*bhagavat*), the state of being the Lord constitutes "femininity"; whereas in the expression "a hairy man" (*lomaśaḥ puruṣaḥ*), because the word *loman* (hair) denotes the phallus (*śiśna*), the possession of the phallus constitutes "masculinity. The state of being a neuter consists in merely possessing those respective forms. And this [definition] is grounded solely in the object itself.

In that regard, when possible, the denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as "man" (*pumān*) resides only in that which possesses scriptural masculinity qualified by worldly masculinity through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and not in mere worldly [sex] nor in mere scriptural [sex].

Although it would have been appropriate to assign the technical designation "light" (*laghu*) as in the case of *ṭi*, *ghu*, and so on, the designation "heavy" (*guru*) is instead applied in cases such as "masculine" (*pumān*) and "feminine" (*strī*). Thus, even if the designations "masculine" and so forth—like the designation "number" (*saṃkhyā*)—serve the purpose of including a broader range of referents, one must explain that in instances such as *dārān* (wives), the substitution of *na* for *ta* occurs by taking only the purely grammatical (*śāstrīya*) masculinity, since the worldly (*laukika*) masculinity is absent in the conventional meaning.

The point is that since the denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as "male" (*pumān*) is accepted only with respect to scriptural masculinity qualified by worldly masculinity, there is a deficiency when a sacrifice is performed with a female animal in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*); for in that case, the word conveys only scriptural masculinity qualified by worldly masculinity. More will be said on this later. Similarly, it should be understood that words such as "maiden" (*kumārī*) are also denotative of scriptural femininity qualified by worldly femininity.

Now, if it is argued that since the aforementioned technical gender (*liṅga*), which resides solely in the word, is the cause for the conventional usage of "female," "male," and so forth, then—inasmuch as that [gender] exists even in the word *paśu* (beast) which denotes a female—the contingency would arise that one could perform a sacrifice with a female beast in the injunction "one should sacrifice with a beast" (*paśunā yajeta*). This is because the gender expressed by the word *paśu*, like the gender expressed by words such as *padārtha* (category), is common to both female and male, and thus lacks the power to determine a specific referent. To this, he says: "And that gender... The meaning is that gender resides solely in the word.

"By way of delimiting the object" means that it determines even the qualifier of the object by being itself a qualifier of the object. When both a female animal and a male animal are presented upon hearing the word *paśu* (animal), there arises the inquiry: "With what kind of animal should the sacrifice be performed—is it with a female animal or a male animal? In response to this, the masculinity residing in the word *paśu* [functions as a qualifier] through the relation of "being denotable by its own locus" (*svāśrayavācyatva*). Here, "itself" (*sva*) is masculinity; its "locus" (*svāśraya*) is the word *paśu*; and "denotability by that" (*tadvācyatva*) resides in the male individual.

Since, through such a relationship, the word *paśu* (animal) presents the meaning "four-footed creature" as a qualifier, there is an indirect connection with a male animal characterized by biological masculinity and possessing worldly masculinity—namely, that "one should sacrifice with a male animal"—and since it is precisely such a male animal that is enjoined, there is no possibility of performing the sacrifice with a female animal.

The meaning is as follows: because of the usage "not with a female animal" (*na strīvihitena paśunā*), the word *paśu* (animal) is understood to have the masculine gender; and since the masculine word *paśu* denotes only a male individual, it is established by the science of grammatical gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) that a word denotes a specific object only as qualified by a specific gender. Thus, gender serves to determine the specific object by excluding female individuals. Having this in mind, it was stated in the root-text: "the gender expressed by words such as 'animal' [is] masculinity"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

It must be understood that because [the rule] "there is no [slaughter] in the case of a female animal" exists, the injunction "with an animal" (paśunā) does not employ goats and the like as components of the sacrifice—that is, it does not cause them to be taken up. Now, one might object: the technical (pāribhāṣika) masculinity denoted by the word "animal" (paśu) indeed exists even in a female animal, through the relation of being denoted by its own substratum, just as it exists in a male animal.

And thus, since it is impossible to maintain the rule that the masculine word *paśu* denotes only an animal qualified by worldly masculinity—and because, consequently, the exclusion of female animals is impossible and the gender cannot determine a specific meaning—the flaw that a female animal could also perform the sacrifice remains exactly as it was; this is what is raised in the objection: "Nor [is there a restriction] regarding the individual and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of eternal neuter-ness, masculinity, the words *vastu* (entity) and *padārtha* (category), and others.

Just as the word *vyakti*—ending in the suffix *ktin*, which is prescribed for the feminine (*striyām ktin*)—is invariably feminine, and since every object such as a jar or a cloth is denotable by the word *vyakti*, the femininity conveyed by that word extends to all objects through the relation of being denoted by its own substratum; and for this very reason, that [femininity] does not exclude those objects—likewise, the masculinity conveyed by words such as *paśu* (animal) also extends to female animals through a mediated relation consisting of being denoted by its own substratum.

It is indeed possible. "Commonality" (*sādhāraṇyam*) means the state of occurring in both female and male [animals]. And thus, even the masculinity denoted by the word *paśu* (animal) would not serve to exclude the female animal; for the sense is that only that which resides exclusively in a male animal excludes the female animal, whereas that which is common to both female and male does not.

He offers a rebuttal with the words "of the word *vyakti*," based on the following intention: since the word *vyakti*, which ends in the suffix *ktin*, is eternally feminine, its denoted gender—femininity—is common to all objects such as males and neuters through the relation of being expressed by its own substratum; however, there is no evidence that the word *paśu* is eternally masculine, and thus the masculinity denoted by it is not common to both females and males. [The phrase] "because it is seen in the Veda" [is used].

The intention is that because one observes usages such as *paśvā* and so forth, the word *paśu* occurs even in the feminine gender. In the masculine gender, the failure to obtain the stated form is evident due to the application of the *nā* substitute [for the case-ending]. Likewise, due to the application of the *guṇa* substitution by the rule *gher ṅiti*, the form *paśve* would also be unestablished. Thus, since the feminine form of the word *paśu* is also seen in the Veda, the intention is that this word does not denote an individual (*vyakti*) and so forth, nor is it common to both genders.

Consequently, the word *paśu* denoting a male animal as qualified by worldly masculinity is distinct [from the word *paśu* denoting a female], and the word *paśu* denoting a male animal as qualified by worldly masculinity is also distinct [from the word *paśu* denoting a neuter]. In this context, because of the statement "not in the feminine" (*astriyām*), since the suffix *nā* does not apply to the feminine, and because the suffix *nā* is observed in the form *paśunā*, this word *paśu*—being taken as masculine—denotes only that which is qualified by scriptural masculinity, namely, worldly masculinity. That is to say, the masculine word *paśu* is the designator of only a male animal according to worldly usage.

The intention is as follows: since the animal is prescribed as possessing both worldly masculinity (*laukikapuṃstva*) and scriptural masculinity (*śāstrīyapuṃstva*), and because the scriptural gender of masculinity exists in the female animal through the relation of being denotable by its own substratum via a chain of succession—due to the superimposition of non-difference upon words based on their identical sequence—it does not follow that a female animal could perform the sacrifice, for it lacks the scriptural masculinity qualified by worldly masculinity.

Furthermore, if the operation triggered by gender were governed solely by the scriptural gender, regardless of the worldly gender, then the prohibition "not in the case of a feminine" (*na striyām*) would apply even to a male animal, because the gender residing in the word *paśu* (which denotes a female) exists in a male animal as well through the relation of being denoted by its own substratum. Consequently, the absence of the suffix *nābh* in the form *paśunā* would not be difficult to obtain. For this reason too, it must be stated that the operation triggered by gender is governed by the scriptural gender as qualified by the worldly gender.

And thus, since the prohibition "not for a feminine" (*astriyām*) applies only to that which possesses both a worldly femininity (*laukika-strītvaviśiṣṭa-śāstrīya-strītvavatī*), the form *paśu* is established because the [feminine] substitute does not apply to the word *paśu* when it denotes a female animal. However, in the case of a male animal, although the technical femininity (*śāstrīya-strītvam*) exists, the prohibition "not for a feminine" does not apply because the technical femininity qualified by worldly femininity is absent; consequently, the masculine substitute does apply to the word *paśu* when it denotes a male animal. The point is that the masculine gender is determined by the specific mention of the form *paśunā*.

It should be understood that the meaning of the statement "that which is expressed by the word *paśu* (animal) does not exist in a female animal" is that the scriptural masculinity (*śāstrīyapuṃstva*), as qualified by worldly masculinity (*laukikapuṃstva*), does not exist in a female animal. However, if the term were intended to refer solely to scriptural masculinity, its inconsistency would be evident. He demonstrates the consensus of the Mīmāṃsakas regarding the point that, because the negative particle (*nañ*) is heard in the expression *paśunā*, the word *paśu* refers only to an animal possessing scriptural masculinity as qualified by worldly masculinity—this is indicated by the phrase "In the Mīmāṃsā."

In the first pāda of the fourth chapter, under the sūtra *tathā ca liṅgam* (4.1.17), it is argued that the masculine gender (*puṃliṅga*) in the word *paśu* (animal/sacrificial beast) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). Why? Because one might object: "The masculine gender is seen applied to the word *vṛkṣa* (tree) even though the referent 'tree' is devoid of gender; likewise, the feminine gender is seen applied to the word *makṣikā* (fly) even when referring to a male individual. Having raised this doubt, [the author] replies: Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), which are established as not otherwise possible (*ananyathāsiddha*), just as the class-property (*jāti*) of "being an animal" or its singularity is the meaning of the word in the usage of elders, why should the gender (*liṅga*) not also be the meaning of the word?

It may be so; however, the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the words *vṛkṣa* and *makṣikā* is established solely by the force of usage by those who are learned (*abhiyukta*). Therefore, it is concluded that just as singularity is intended to be expressed, so too is the masculine gender. Consequently, it is determined that only a male animal is to be sacrificed, and that it must be one alone—neither a female animal nor two.

Even if masculinity (*pumbhāva*) is intended [as the meaning of the suffix], if the application were to occur regardless of worldly gender (*laukikaliṅga*), then—since purely scriptural masculinity would be common to both males and females—the exclusion of female individuals would not take place, and thus the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) would be undermined. However, if the application occurs with the assistance of worldly gender, then scriptural masculinity qualified by worldly masculinity does not exist in a female animal; consequently, there is no logical inconsistency in the exclusion of female animals.

With the intention that the same should be understood in the present case as well, he says: "Because singularity and masculinity are intended [to be significant] in the injunction ‘one should sacrifice with an animal’ (paśunā yajeta)," and so on, ending with "because it has been established. Now, it was argued that there is no evidence for the word *paśu* being invariably masculine; however, that is inconsistent. For the fact that words ending in the suffix *-up* are invariably masculine is determined by the grammatical treatise (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*) itself. Furthermore, it is stated in the Vedabhāṣya regarding the form *paśvā*: "In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the rule allowing the optional application [of the feminine suffix] in the case of *jas* and other endings applies, and thus there is an absence of the *nāb* substitution in *paśvā*."

And thus, since the masculinity denoted by the word *paśu* (animal) is a gender (*liṅga*) conveyed by words such as *vyakti* (individual), it is common to both female and male; therefore, because it is impossible for it to exclude the female individual, [the author] prevents the contingency of including female animals by another means, stating: "In reality, however" (*vastutastu*). He says: "Even in the *Vedabhāṣya*" (*vedabhāṣye’pi*), because if the word *paśu* were invariably masculine, the usage *paśvā* and so forth would be untenable. [He further states: "Not the absence of an absence" (*nābhāvābhāvaḥ*).

And thus, the point is that even though the word *paśu* is eternally masculine (*nityapuṃliṅga*), there is no logical inconsistency in such usages as *paśvā* (instrumental singular). "Because of the determination of its eternal masculinity"—the point is that, since masculinity is common [to both genders], it is impossible for it to exclude female individuals. Therefore, although by the aforementioned reasoning it is impossible for [masculinity] to be the differentiator of female individuals, he explains another reasoning that does differentiate them: "Or rather, the goat (*chāga*) is the mantra... and so on.

Or rather, it is a goat, because of the wording of the mantra; for in the injunction "one should sacrifice the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma," it has been determined that by the word "animal" (paśu) only a goat is to be understood, and not a horse or other animals, on account of the mantra phrase "of the omentum of the goat."

In this context, because the specific animal "goat" (*chāga*) is heard [in the text], the goat alone is taken, disregarding horses and other animals; just as that is so, since the genitive form ending in *sya*—namely *chāgasya*—is not possible for a female goat (*chāgī*), the male goat characterized by worldly masculinity is taken, and not the female goat; thus the determination of masculinity is made. The point is that the word *chāga* lacks an inherent gender (*nityaliṅgatva*) like a word denoting a universal class (*jāti*). The meaning is that in the present case as well, masculinity must be determined for that very same reason.

By the use of the particle *eva* in the phrase "by logic alone" (*nyāyenaiva*), it is indicated that there is no possibility for the masculine gender expressed by the word *paśu* to exclude the feminine gender; the intention is that the word *paśu*, like words such as *padārtha*, possesses a permanent (inherent) gender. Now, let it be granted that this is the case in the instance cited above; however, since the gender residing in pronouns is common to both sentient and insentient beings, as well as to females and males, the *adhvaryu*-priest's injunction (*praiṣa*) "Bring fire for him" (*prāsmā agniṃ bharata*) would apply even to a female sheep (*meṣī*) dedicated to Sarasvatī. Nor is this a desirable consequence.

In the section concerning the characteristics of *ūha* (modification), it is stated that "because of the specification of the gender, the *sārasvatī* [offering] is not included among those of common procedure, due to its femininity"; this implies that even though the animals are subject to the same ritual procedure, the mantra is not applied there because of the masculine gender specification. Nor should it be argued that since it is taught that "the neuter is used for the general," the neuter form *asmai* should be applicable to both the ram and the ewe; for by the subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) in the phrase "may his mother follow him, may his father follow him," the masculine gender is determined.

If it is argued that the form *enad* would result [in the case of a neuter pronoun used as a subsequent reference] due to the Vārttika stating "in the case of a neuter subsequent reference (*anvādeśe*), *enad* should be prescribed," it is replied: since the word *asmai*, *enam*, and so forth, causes the recollection of the animals as qualified by masculinity and so on—just as they cause the recollection of things qualified by the nature of a goat and so on—there is no possibility for the application of *enad* to a neuter [subsequent reference]. This detailed discussion should be consulted in the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*. With this intention, he says: "It has been explained at length in the *Bhūṣaṇa*. The meaning is that [the denotation of a nominal stem] consists of a triad: its own meaning (svārtha), substance (dravya), and gender (liṅga), accompanied by number (saṃkhyā) such as oneness and so forth. A "tetrad" (catuṣka) is a collection of four; a "pentad" (pañcaka) means a collection of five. The meaning is that [the denotation of a word] consists of a tetrad: its own meaning, substance, gender, and number, accompanied by the grammatical relations (kārakas) such as the agent (kartṛ) and so forth. He raises an objection in order to establish that gender, number, and kāraka are indeed the meanings of a noun (nāman), beginning with "But surely... (nanu).

The phrase "by means of positive and negative concomitance" (anvayavyatirekābhyām) means by means of the presence and absence of cognition; that is, because the feminine gender is cognized from words such as *ajā* and *aśvā* when used in conjunction with suffixes like *ṭāp*, whereas it is not cognized when those suffixes are absent. Similarly, regarding number and case-role (*kāraka*), since unity and objecthood are understood upon hearing the singular accusative ending in *ghaṭam*, but these two are not understood when that ending is not heard, it follows that it is appropriate for the triad beginning with gender to have the suffix as their denotative meaning. This is the intended sense. The phrase "from that very [suffix]" (*tata eva*) means "from the suffix alone."

He says, "True," meaning that while it is true that when the presence of gender (*liṅga*) and so forth occurs, their status as the meaning of the suffix is determined—and thus it is not proper to rely on them being the meaning of the nominal stem (*nāman*)—there is indeed a reason supporting their status as the meaning of the nominal stem just as there is a reason supporting their status as the meaning of the suffix. He states this with the words "devoid of a suffix" (*pratyayavarjita*), as in the example: "He sees the curd" (*dadhi paśyati*).

According to the grammatical rule *svamornapuṃsakāt*, for grammarians there is knowledge of the suffix *am*, which is the second-case singular ending derived from a neuter base. For others, however, since the suffix *am* is not heard, there is no knowledge of the suffix. Even in the absence of knowledge of the suffix, the fact that the cognition "the act of seeing has as its object that which is qualified by both neuter gender and singularity" arises from that sentence is established by experience; thus, it is proven that the triad of gender and so forth constitutes the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).

Otherwise, there would be a clear contradiction with experience. By the phrase "in 'paśyati' and so forth," the expression "the king goes to the enemy" and others are included. Furthermore, since it is observed that in the grammatical treatise (śāstra) gender is taught as belonging specifically to the base (prakṛti), it is more appropriate that gender is the meaning of the nominal stem (nāmārtha); thus he says: "of the instruction on gender. "For this very reason" means: because the reasoning applies equally in both cases—whether gender and the rest are denoted by the suffix (pratyaya) or denoted by the base (prakṛti). "There is no insistence" means...

The meaning is that one should not maintain such a dogmatic insistence as to whether it is more appropriate for the gender and so forth to be denoted by the suffix (*pratyaya*) or more appropriate for them to be denoted by the stem (*prakṛti*). Although there are arguments for both positions, he states, "because denotative capacity [in the suffix] is more logical," because of the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*). The sense is that while it would involve excessive complexity (*gaurava*) to assume denotative capacity for an infinite number of stems, it is more parsimonious to assume denotative capacity for the relatively few suffixes, such as *ṭāp* and the *svādi* group.

Now, one might object: since the cognition of femininity from words such as *vāk* and *śarad*—even without feminine suffixes like *ṭāp* and others—is established by the experience of all people, there is a deviation in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), namely, the presence of the effect (the cognition of gender) even in the absence of the cause (the feminine suffix). Furthermore, according to the maxim that "the meaning of the base and the suffix [are understood together]," gender would result in being the predominant meaning of the suffix. Therefore, gender must indeed be the meaning of the noun-base (*nāmārtha*). As for number and case-role (*kāraka*), however, whether they are the meaning of the noun-base or the meaning of the suffix, he says: "they are either indicators (*dyotikā*) or expressers (*vācikā*)."

The point is that in the *Vākyapadīya*, Hari describes two positions regarding number and grammatical relation (*kāraka*): on the view that case-endings (*vibhakti*) indicate duality and so forth, number and relation are the meaning of the nominal base (*nāman*); whereas on the view that they denote these, number and relation are the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). However, some maintain that even number and relation are exclusively the meaning of the nominal base.

Nor should it be argued that it is more appropriate to assume, based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that the case-endings (*vibhakti*) alone are the denoters of those [number, gender, and so forth]; for in examples such as *dadhi paśya* ("look at the curd") and *madhu ānaya* ("bring the honey"), there is a deviation from negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), since number and grammatical function (*saṃkhyā-kāraka*) are cognized even in the absence of a case-ending. Therefore, they say that the position that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) is the fivefold [set] is superior, because it is established by universal experience that from a nominal stem there arises a cognition whose qualifier (*prakāra*) consists of genus, gender, number, and grammatical function, and whose qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is the substance (*dravya*).

The phrase "in many places" expresses the intended meaning of using the term *śāstra* (treatise) in a general sense—that these [views] are presented in the treatise even without being explicitly specified in each respective sūtra. The point is that the use of the term *śāstra* in a general sense indicates that these positions are discussed in various places throughout the foundational texts, such as the Bhāṣya, in connection with their respective sūtras. The phrase "as the primary [subject]" implies that all these views were indeed set forth by the author of the Bhāṣya within the context of the *sarūpa-sūtra*.

In the phrase "in the *sarūpa-sūtra* etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) should be understood as including Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the *anabhihita-sūtra* and the *tatra upapadaṃ saptamīstham* rule. Here, it should be noted that five positions regarding the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) have been set forth in various places in the treatise: [the stem expresses] one, two, three, four, or five meanings.

Among these, the position that "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) consists of one [factor]" has been set aside here because it is accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas alone, and because it is untenable due to the fact that a universal (*jāti*) devoid of a substratum is never experienced in cognition. Thus, there are five positions: that the meaning of the nominal stem consists of two starting from the beginning, three starting from the beginning, four starting from the beginning, four excluding number (*saṃkhyā*), and five starting from the beginning.

In this regard, it is stated according to the Bhāṣya which view necessitates the *anabhihita* sūtra and which renders it superfluous: In the view that "the first two" (number and case-role) constitute the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), both number and case-role are the meaning of the case-ending. In the view that "the first four" constitute the meaning of the case-ending, only the case-role is the meaning of the case-ending. In the view that "the four excluding number" constitute the meaning of the case-ending, only number is the meaning of the case-ending.

In the view that there are five meanings [of case endings], since number and grammatical relation (*kāraka*) do not constitute the meaning of the suffix itself, in that view they are merely indicated (*dyotya*) by the suffix. And it is precisely because they are indicated that the *Mahābhāṣya*—in the passage stating "the meanings of the *sup*-suffixes are [grammatical relations] such as the object (*karman*), and likewise number is the meaning of the *tiṅ*-suffixes"—uses the conventional expression "meaning of the suffix" (*vibhaktyarthatva*) for them. Thus, among the three positions—the first being the group of two, the second the group of three, and the third the group of four excluding number—number becomes the meaning of the suffix in all cases.

Thus, in the three alternative views—namely, that the *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is the meaning of the case-ending from the very beginning, or that it is the meaning of the case-ending along with the number, or that it is the meaning of the case-ending alone—the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of rules such as *svaujas*, *karmaṇi dvitīyā*, and *dvyekayoḥ* is established. This is as follows: in the rule *svaujas*, there are two words, namely *prātipadikāt* and *am*; in *karmaṇi*, there are also two words, namely *karmaṇi* and *dvitīyā*; and likewise, in *dvyekayoḥ*, there are two words, namely *dvyekayoḥ* and *dvivacanaikavacane*.

In this way, six words are produced; therein, since the ablative case (*pañcamī*) denoting a *kāraka* is generally not possible according to grammatical treatises (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*), the ablative characterized by connection with direction (*dig-yoga-lakṣaṇa-pañcamī*) is to be understood. The meaning of the ablative is "limit" (*avadhi*). Thus, the word ending in the ablative, namely *prātipadikāt*, is construed with the suffix *am* which is to be prescribed as the limit; the meaning is that the suffix *am* occurs when it possesses posteriority relative to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as its limit.

The word *karmāṇi* (in the locative case) connects with the word *dvyekayoḥ* through the relation of residing-in (*niṣṭhatva-sambandha*), meaning "when there is duality or singularity residing in the object. Furthermore, the word *dvyekayoḥ* connects with the suffix *am* through the relation of denotation (*vācakatva-sambandha*), meaning "the suffix *am* denotes singularity. Finally, the words *dvitīyā* and *dvivacanaikavacane* connect with *am* itself through the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*), meaning that *am* is non-different from the second case ending, the dual number, and the singular number.

And thus the meaning of the major sentence (mahāvākyārtha) is: "The suffix *am* occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) to express the singularity residing in the object. This is the sentence-meaning according to the three positions regarding the meaning of the number-inflection (*saṃkhyāvibhakti*). In this case, within the cognition arising from the rule (*sūtra*), the number (*saṃkhyā*) is predominant. However, according to the three positions regarding the meaning of the case-inflection (*kārakavibhakti*), it is as follows: since there is a rule that number must always appear as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the phrase "in the case of two or one" (*dvye-kayoḥ*) is construed with "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) by means of the relation of being contained therein (*ādheyatā-sambandha*). The meaning is: "that which is the object when there is singularity."

In the expression "on the tree, on the branch" (*vṛkṣe śākhāyām*), the locative case (*saptamī*) is used because one intends to express that the substratum (*ādheya*) is itself the locus (*ādhāra*). Thus, the meaning of the sentence is this: after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), when there is an object qualified by singularity, the singular accusative case-ending (*dvitīyaikavacana*) occurs, signifying an object qualified by singularity. On this view, in the cognition produced by the Sūtra, the object (*karman*) and so forth are primary.

In the view that "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five factors," the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is as follows: when the singularity residing in the object denoted by that [nominal stem] is to be indicated, the singular accusative suffix *am* occurs after the nominal stem. This is one interpretation. Alternatively: when the object qualified by the singularity residing in its own meaning is to be indicated after a nominal stem, the singular accusative suffix *am* occurs. In the first of these sentence-meanings, because of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the phrase "singularity residing in the object," number (*saṃkhyā*) holds primacy in the cognition produced by the rule.

In the second view, however, since the understanding arising from the sūtra follows the construction "in an object qualified by oneness," the primacy belongs to the object (*karman*) and so forth. Furthermore, in the position that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of the five factors (number, gender, substance, case-role, and the suffix-meaning), it has already been stated previously that number and the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) are meanings of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) solely as things indicated (*dyotya*).

This being the case, if the rule *anabhihite* were not formulated, then in the example *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat was made"), although the mere object (*karman*) is expressed by the suffix *-kta*, its singularity would remain unexpressed. Consequently, even when the singularity residing in the object is to be indicated, the application of the singular accusative case ending (*am*) would be unavoidable under the first interpretation of the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), which holds that this consists of five factors. Therefore, the governing heading (*adhikāra*) *anabhihita* is necessary for the purpose of qualifying subordinate objects and so forth.

Thus, when the singularity residing in the unexpressed object (*anabhihitakarma*) is to be indicated, the suffix *am* [the accusative case-ending] applies; since the object has already been expressed by the *kta* suffix, the suffix *am* would consequently apply in the example "the mat is made" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ*). This is the meaning. And so, the sense is that if the view is held that number is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), then the governing rule concerning the "unexpressed" (*anabhihitādhikāra*) is necessary. Furthermore, it should be understood that even under the views where the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) consists of two, three, or four factors—including number as something distinct from the stem-meaning—the rule regarding the "unexpressed" is indispensable, because number is considered the meaning of the case-ending.

In the view that "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) consists of five [factors]," however, because the object (*karman*) qualified by singularity is the second sentence-meaning, the object (*karman*) and so forth are primary within the cognition produced by the sūtra. Consequently, by the maxim *uktārthānām aprayogaḥ* ("there is no employment of those whose meaning has already been expressed"), the accusative case would not apply in examples such as *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat was made"). Since this result is already established, the governing heading *anabhihite* ("when not [already] expressed") is unnecessary. Thus, the sense is that under the alternative view that "the kāraka is the meaning of the case-ending," the rule *anabhihita-sūtra* is redundant.

Thus, even under the views that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) consists of two, three, or four factors starting from the first, it should be understood that the rule *anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1) would be rendered useless, because the *kāraka* (case-role) is already expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*). || 25 ||

In response to the objection that it is improper to establish that a word is the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) because one does not experience the manifestation of the word "pot" and so forth in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by sentences such as "bring the pot," he says: "The word, for its part... This means "the word also. "It manifests" means that the word itself manifests in the verbal cognition, just like its own object, the substance, and so on. To provide proof for this point, he cites the statement of Hari: "There is no [cognition]... etc.

In the experience of learned people in the world, there is no such cognition consisting of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) wherein the manifestation of the word-form as a qualifier does not occur; this is the meaning. For every cognition, being of the nature of verbal comprehension, appears and is perceived as invariably permeated and eternally connected with "word"—that is, with the word-form as its qualifier—according to the reasoning of the venerable Haribhadra, who possesses the experience of cognitions regarding all the principles of the various scriptures. This is the intended sense.

Even in cases where there is perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*), the manifestation of the word (*śabdabhāna*) is indeed present as something superimposed (*āropita*) due to the identity (*tādātmya*) between the word and its object; this is what is indicated by the use of the particle *iva* in the phrase "as if" (*anukalpitam iva*). The meaning is that the manifestation of the word in cognitions such as perception is logically established through the identity of the word and its object. Furthermore, this identity between the word and its object cannot be denied, as it is established by experience in accordance with linguistic usages such as "he hears the object" (*arthaṃ śṛṇoti*) and "he speaks the object" (*arthaṃ vadati*).

For it is not possible for an object possessing a shell-like neck and other features to hear or speak; the meaning is that this is never at all possible. Rather, it is only the word denoting that object which can be heard or uttered. Therefore, expressions such as "he hears the object" are logically untenable. However, if one accepts the identity (*tādātmya*) between the word and its object, then such usage is justified because the understanding arises from hearing the word that has attained identity with that object.

Thus, since the hearing and articulation of the meaning would otherwise be inexplicable, the identity (*tādātmya*) of the word and its meaning must be accepted even by one who does not wish to assert it. For this very reason, the use of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is consistent in such cases as those where the capacity [of words] is grasped through Vedic revelation and traditional law (*śruti-smṛti*), for example: "The single-syllabled Brahman is *om*," "The name *Rāma* consists of two syllables," "The breaking of the pride of the wielder of the Pināka bow [is achieved by the name Rāma]," and "Vṛddhi is *ā*, *ai*, and *au*."

As for the objection that if there were identity (*tādātmya*) between word and meaning, the utterance of the word "fire" would result in burning the mouth, and so forth—that has been refuted in the *Mañjarī*. For identity consists of both difference and non-difference, being defined as the state of being perceived as non-distinct while remaining distinct from the other. In this view, the distinction between word and meaning is real, whereas their non-distinction is merely superimposed (*āropita*). Precisely because of this real distinction, it is impossible for the utterance of the word "fire" to cause a burning sensation in the mouth; nor is such a consequence possible due to the superimposed non-distinction.

For indeed, in the world, an effect of fire such as burning is not observed to arise from *guñjā* seeds characterized by the superimposed property of being fire; the meaning is that it is certainly not so observed. Therefore, the point is that even if one accepts the identity (*tādātmya*) between the object and the word, the aforementioned defect does not follow. Now, one might ask: "Let it be that the word appears [in cognition] in this way, but how can the word be the denoted object (*nāmārthatva*)? To this, he says: "Recite 'Viṣṇu'."

If, in this context, the word "Viṣṇu" were not present [in consciousness] just as its own meaning, the substance, and the gender are present, then—since it would be impossible to utter the meaning—the understanding of the sentence-meaning "utter Viṣṇu" would be untenable. Therefore, from a word, there arises the presence (upasthiti) of its own expressive word as well, just like its meaning. And this presence pertains only to that word which possesses the same sequence of phonemes as was uttered, and not to synonyms such as "Nārāyaṇa" and the like.

And thus, when the word *viṣṇu* is present, because its meaning is construed with it through the relation of denotation (*vācakatā-sambandha*), there arises the understanding of the sense: "Utter the word *viṣṇu*, which denotes the object having the form of the four-armed one. The point is that the word itself is also the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Regarding the phrase "by means of indication" (*lakṣaṇayā*), the meaning is: by means of a relation consisting of the connection between [the word] itself and its own denoted meaning (*sva-śakya-sambandha*).

If it is argued that the word *viṣṇu* is itself (*svam*), its own denotable meaning (*svaśakya*) is the form of Lakṣmī’s husband, and the relation to that [meaning] exists in the word *viṣṇu* by way of being its denotation; thus, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the relation of being the denoter of its own denoted meaning, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is established—this is not so. For even by that much, the status of the word as the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārthatva*) [or rather, its being denoted by the nominal stem] is not proven. Furthermore, secondary indication is of two kinds: that which has a specific motive (*prayojanavatī*) and that which is conventional (*nirūḍhā*).

If it is argued that it possesses a purpose—just as in the case of "a hamlet on the Ganges," where the purpose is the cognition of coolness, purity, and so forth regarding the hamlet—then a purpose for the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) here must be stated. If it is argued that it is a conventionalized (*nirūḍha*) usage because no such purpose is observed, he replies: "Because it is not distinct from primary denotation" (*śaktyanatirekāt*). The meaning is that conventionalized secondary function is not something separate from primary denotation.

Just as the understanding that "this word has this power (śakti) with respect to this meaning" arises by virtue of grasping an beginningless intention (tātparya), so too established metaphorical indication (nirūḍhalakṣaṇā) is dependent upon the grasping of an beginningless intention; this is the meaning. And just as the beginningless intention for the word *viṣṇu* is well-known to refer to the Lord of Lakṣmī, the same applies to the word *viṣṇu* [in other contexts] as well; thus, the point is that resorting to established metaphorical indication is indeed nothing other than resorting to primary denotative power (śakti). Furthermore, he states that metaphorical indication is not possible in all cases: "Pronounce *ja-ba-ḍa-da-śa*."

Because a collection [of letters] lacks the capacity to denote anything whatsoever, and because—despite each individual letter possessing a denotative meaning according to the authority of the *Ekākṣarakośa* and other lexicons—there is no cognition of that meaning from a collection such as "jabagaḍadaśa," the collection lacks a denotative meaning due to the absence of a graspable denotation; consequently, even indication (*lakṣaṇā*), which consists of a relationship with the denoted meaning, is impossible there.

The point is this: where even the primary meaning (śakyārtha) is not grasped, there the possibility of indication (lakṣaṇā)—which consists in a relation to that primary meaning—is cast far away; therefore, one must admit that a word possesses a power (śakti) with respect to its own form as well, just as it does with respect to its own meaning, substance, and so forth. For if the word itself were presented [to consciousness] just like its meaning, then such a collection [of sounds] would be the primary meaning of such a word, and consequently, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning in the command "jabagaḍadaśam uccāraya" (pronounce jabagaḍadaśa) would be untenable.

Now, one might object: "Even if the secondary function (lakṣaṇā) is not known because its primary meanings are unknown, let there still be comprehension of the sentence-meaning, since the secondary function—in the form of denoting the respective primary meanings of the individual parts 'ja-ba-ga-i'-ti'—actually exists. To this, he says: "of that which is unknown."

In the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), although the word *gaṅgā* actually exists, if its relation to its own denotation—the flowing river—is not known, it fails to produce the cognition of the indicated meaning, namely the bank; therefore, it is necessary that only a known function (*vṛtti*) serves as the cause for the presentation of the meaning. Thus, the point is that in the present case, because the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not apprehended, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning does not arise. Now, if one insists that the comprehension of the sentence-meaning should occur in the aforementioned instance by virtue of a knowledge of the function having arisen at some time or other, he says: "Speak the word *gāvi*. Here, *gāvi* is a certain meaningless word belonging to the colloquial dialect (*bhāṣā*).

Even in the case of imitations of sounds such as "gāvi," since the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of such imitative words is accepted by everyone, there would be no comprehension of meaning—according to the Naiyāyikas—if there were no denotative power (*śakti*) in the imitations, because the object of denotation (*śakya*) could not be grasped; furthermore, since the relation of denotatum and denoter (*lakṣaṇā*), which consists in the connection with the object of denotation, would also not be grasped, there would be no comprehension of meaning. Moreover, due to the absence of "meaningfulness" (*arthavattva*)—defined as the capacity to produce the comprehension of meaning through a linguistic function (*vṛtti*)—the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) would not occur, and its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) would likewise not exist. Therefore, imitations possess denotative power with respect to the sound itself.

With the intention that [the word] must be accepted [as a name], he states that even a word—consisting of the sixfold [categories] together with the five previously mentioned [factors] such as its own meaning (svārtha) and substance (dravya)—is in some cases the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). He indicates the specific instance where "in some cases" was stated by saying: "yadi... śabdo 'pi. Because it was said "yadi... śabdo 'pi bhedena," the meaning of "kvacit" (in some cases) refers to the context of imitation (*anukaraṇa*). That imitation is of two kinds: of the unmanifest (*avyakta*) and of the manifest (*vyakta*). "Of the unmanifest" means of sound (*dhvani*).

"Of the manifest" means "of the phoneme. *Paṭat* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a certain sound produced by the falling of fruit; that is the first [type]. In that case, the object of imitation consists of sound (*dhvani*), whereas the imitation itself consists of phonemes (*varṇa*); such is the difference between the two. The second [type] occurs in expressions such as "He said 'cow' (*gaur*)," where the word *iti* is employed to indicate a reversal of the meaning of the word.

In this regard, there is a distinction between the original (*anukārya*) and the imitation (*anukaraṇa*): the former has as its referent categories such as meaning, substance, and so forth, whereas the latter has as its referent the word itself, even though both possess identical sequential order (*ānupūrvī*). Furthermore, the nature of being an imitation (*anukaraṇatva*) consists in being the object of an utterance whose sole intention is the word-form itself.
