For this very reason, in cases such as *agner ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.33), there is no status of being an imitation; because the word appears as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it lacks the property of having the word-form alone as its intended meaning.

Just as from the word *go* (cow) within the sentence "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), there is the presentation (*upasthiti*) of its own fivefold meaning, so too the presentation of the word's own form (*śabdasvarūpa*) is established by experience. This is likewise the case in instances of imitation (*anukaraṇa*). Thus, it has been stated that in some cases the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) consists of all six categories. In that context, the imitator (*anukaraṇa*) is designated as the "presenting" element, while the thing imitated (*anukārya*) is the "presented" element. If, however, a distinction between these two is intended, then the meaning of the imitator becomes the very form of the word being imitated.

That being the case, if the expressive power (*śakti*) of the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) toward the object that is the nature of the word being imitated (*anukārya-śabda-svarūpa*) is not accepted, then it would follow that an object which is not the content of a word-generated mental presentation (*padajanyopasthiti*) could not appear in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). For this reason, in order to establish that the object is indeed the content of a word-generated presentation—which is necessary to account for its appearance in verbal cognition—it must be admitted that the imitation possesses expressive power toward the object that is the nature of the word being imitated.

The point is that otherwise, since an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is not connected with its object—which consists of the actual form of the word being imitated—it would lack the capacity to produce the cognition of that [object] through a linguistic function (*vṛtti*); consequently, the actual form of the word being imitated would not appear in the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). For this very reason, because an imitation possesses "meaningfulness" (*arthavattva*)—defined as the capacity to generate a cognition of meaning through a linguistic function—it receives the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), which triggers the addition of case-endings (*sub*) and so forth; thus, the usage "He says 'gaur' (*gaur ity ayam āha*)" and its grammatical correctness are established.

If, however, the difference between the two is not intended to be expressed, but rather their non-difference alone is intended, then—since the relationship of signifier and signified (vācyavācakabhāva) depends upon difference and that relationship is impossible where there is non-difference—the nature of the word as the object of imitation would not appear in verbal cognition, because it would lack the status of being an object of the mental presentation (upasthiti) produced by the word. To this, it is replied: just as even when a jar is present, if the eye is not accompanied by light, then the perception of the jar does not arise despite the presence of the jar.

Thus, by the force of experience, the causality of the object (*viṣaya*) with respect to perception (*pratyakṣa*) is established. And so, just as a jar is the cause of the perception of a jar, sound (*śabda*) is the cause of the auditory perception (*śrāvaṇapratyakṣa*); therefore, since the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the imitator as non-different from the imitated—which consists in its own perception by the sense of hearing—is produced solely by the word (*pada*), such a word-generated presentation being taken into account, the appearance of the imitated in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) certainly occurs, and thus there is nothing lacking.

Although the *Vākyapadīya* states that "there is no such cognition [of a word] that disregards its status as an object," and thus in all cases—such as the verbal cognition arising from "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*)—the word "jar" and so forth appear in the cognition, nevertheless, in the case of imitation (*anukaraṇa*), one clearly observes a difference in the use of words based on whether the case-endings (*sub*) are produced or not, depending on the presence or absence of distinction (between the imitated and the imitator). Consequently, since the word's own form (*svarūpa*) is understood just like its own meaning, it has been stated in some places that even in the case of imitation, the "meaning of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārtha*) is sixfold.

[The opponent] objects: "But surely, since both positions—whether [the word] consists of difference or non-difference—require the acceptance of a function of the word even in its sixth aspect (the phoneme), just as in the five aspects beginning with 'one's own meaning' (*svārtha*) for the sake of presenting the object to be imitated (*anukārya*), it is improper for the root text to state that this requirement is necessary only in the case of the position of difference. With this intention, he reveals the intent of the root text, starting with "This is the sense" (*ayaṃ bhāvaḥ*). [He states: "There is a difference between the object to be imitated and the imitation."

The sense is that when one intends to express the difference between the two, in cases such as *paṭat* (the imitation of the sound "paṭa"), the difference between the original (*anukārya*) and the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is established through their connection with contradictory properties, namely, consisting of sound (*dhvani-mayatva*) versus consisting of phonemes (*varṇa-mayatva*). However, in cases such as *gaurityayamāha* ("He said 'cow'"), their difference is established by the two contradictory properties of having meaning as its object (*artha-padārthakatva*) versus having the word itself as its object (*śabda-padārthakatva*). [Regarding the phrase] "because the word is not present," this refers to the absence of denotative power (*śakti*), and so forth.

And thus, the meaning is that in the absence of *śakti* (denotative power), it is impossible for the object of imitation (*anukārya*) to be the object of a presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a word. "For the sake of its establishment" means for the sake of establishing its status as the object of a presentation generated by a word; otherwise, it would not be an object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), because only the presentation of a word-meaning generated by a word through a *vṛtti* (linguistic relation) is the cause of verbal cognition. "*Śakti*" refers to the nature of the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*). "*Upeyā*" means it must certainly be accepted.

The sense is that otherwise, an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) that is unrelated [to its object] would be incapable of bringing the object of imitation (*anukārya*) to mind. He states "in non-difference" (*abhede*) to show that when there is no difference between the object of imitation and the imitation, the status of being an object of verbal cognition occurs even without an additional power (*atirikta-śakti*). The word "intended" (*vivakṣita*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "In that view" (*tatpakṣe*) means in the view of the non-difference between the object of imitation and the imitation. "Because the object is a cause in perception" (*pratyakṣe viṣayasya hetutvāt*).

The meaning is as follows: even when the eye is assisted by light, if a jar were not present, the perception of the jar would not arise; however, since it does arise when that [jar] is present, by the force of experience, the jar is the cause of its own visual perception. Similarly, in the auditory perception of sound, the sound itself is the cause. Regarding the phrase "having the form of its own perception": this means having the nature of a direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the imitative sound (*anukaraṇa-śabda*) which is non-different from the object being imitated (*anukārya*), through the sense organ of hearing. This constitutes the presence (*upasthiti*).

The point is that such a mental presence (*upasthiti*) is produced solely by a word, because auditory perception of a word occurs only when the word exists. Regarding the phrase "being the object of verbal cognition" (*śābdabodhaviṣayatā*): the point is that the status of the original (*anukārya*) as an object of verbal cognition is established by taking the word-form of the imitation (*anukaraṇa*), which is non-different from the original, as a word-produced presence in the form of auditory perception.

In this regard, the following should be understood: according to the view of non-difference (*abheda-pakṣa*), just as the word itself appears in verbal cognition by taking up the word-generated mental presentation (*padajanyopasthiti*) in the form of one's own perception, so too—in cases such as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*)—the words "jar" and so forth must necessarily appear by taking up their own word-generated mental presentations in the form of one's own perception through the auditory organ. Thus, it is established that every verbal cognition has the word as its object.

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *svaṃ rūpam*: "Or rather not; for the comprehension of an object is preceded by the word; therefore, there is the exclusion of the object. "Or rather not" means that the sūtra *svaṃ rūpam* need not be stated. What is the reason? Because the comprehension of an object is preceded by the word—of the phrase "preceded by the word," the meaning is "preceded by the knowledge of the word. "Comprehension of an object" means the cognition of the object.

For it is only a word that has been apprehended which possesses the capacity to convey meaning, and not one that conveys meaning by its mere existence like the eye and other sense organs. Therefore, when one person says "The cow is to be led" (*gaur āneyā*) with the intention of saying "The white cow is to be led" (*gaur āneyā*), and the other, having not heard it correctly, asks "What did you say?", and the former replies "I said 'cow' (*gauḥ*)," the latter proceeds to act precisely because of the understanding of the meaning derived from that [word].

Having thus stated the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—that the existence of the cognition of the object follows from the existence of the cognition of the word—he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "And for this reason [the meaning] is preceded by the word; for even when a person is called by name, if that name has not been perceived by him, he then asks: 'What did you say? By this, the negative concomitance in the form of the absence of the cognition of the object upon the absence of the cognition of the word is stated. And thus, according to the aforementioned *Bhāṣya*, both the word and its meaning are manifested through the word. In the phrase "for it is preceded by the word" (*śabdapūrvako hi*), the particle *hi* signifies well-known fact (*prasiddhi*).

The meaning is that it is well-known in the world that a listener’s comprehension of an object is preceded by the cognition of the word. And here, in grammar, the possibility of an operation applies to the word, not to the object; therefore, there is an exclusion of the object. If it is argued that this statement regarding the exclusion of the object is incorrect—since experience establishes that both the word and its object are manifested from the word—it is replied as follows:

Because the operation (*kārya*) is impossible with respect to the meaning (*artha*), the meaning is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); because the operation is possible with respect to the word (*śabda*), the word is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Thus, the sense is that the operation must be performed upon a word that possesses meaning, by virtue of the meaning. For this very thing is what is called the "exclusion" (*nivṛtti*) of the meaning: namely, its relinquishment of the status of being the qualificand. Nor should it be argued that if a word were to appear in every cognition, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of all synonyms appearing as well, due to a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*).

There is no fault here because the word that has been uttered alone appears, due to its being the cause in the form of being perceived first by virtue of its suitability for the cognition of the meaning. Thus, it should be understood that in the *Udyota*, the meaning of the statement "therefore there is the exclusion of the meaning" is explained as "the exclusion of other words expressive of that meaning. However, in common worldly usage, where a word cannot fulfill its function—namely, the connection with the meanings of other words—it serves as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the meaning serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); thus, the operation must be performed upon the meaning presented by the word.

For example, when it is said, "The bee is blue," the quality of blueness does not apply to the word; for blueness is impossible in the word "bee. Rather, it applies to the six-legged insect which is denoted by the word "bee," because it is only there that such a quality is possible. And in cases where an operation is impossible with respect to the meaning, the meaning serves as the qualifier and the word as the qualificand; therefore, the operation must be performed upon the word that expresses that meaning.

For example, in the case of the command "pronounce Viṣṇu," since it is impossible for the act of pronunciation to be connected with the referent of the word *viṣṇu*—namely, the four-armed deity—it must be understood that the connection with the co-occurring action occurs with the word *viṣṇu* itself, which denotes that referent. Now, if one were to accept that whatever is the object of a presentation (upasthiti) generated by a word in a general sense appears in verbal cognition (śābdabodha), then it would follow that space (*ākāśa*), which is the object of a presentation generated by the word "pot" through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), would also become an object of the verbal cognition produced by a sentence such as "the pot exists. Therefore, he says: "to avoid over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*).

"For the sake of exclusion" (*vāraṇāya*) means for the sake of removing the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) consisting of the aforementioned undesirable consequence. "Only the presentation of the word" (*padopasthitireva*) means only the presentation of the word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*). However, it is stated as "the presentation of the word" because of the possibility of [confusion with] the sound that is being imitated (*anukārya-śabda*). And that presentation of the word-meaning, by virtue of the qualification "produced by a linguistic function" (*vṛttijanyā*), implies that it must be produced by the knowledge of a linguistic function (*vṛttijñānajanya*).

The meaning is as follows: likewise, although the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) between space and the word "pot" is present, because it is not presented by the word "pot" through its own function (*vṛtti*), it does not appear in the cognition produced by a sentence such as "the pot exists. Similarly, in cases such as "He says 'go' (*gavity ayam āha*)," even if the imitation (*anukaraṇa*)—which is non-different from the original (*anukārya*)—is presented by the word under the view of non-difference, the original cannot be the object of verbal cognition because it is not presented by the word through its own function; this is the intended sense. [This applies] to that which possesses a function by way of being its substratum (*āśrayatayā*).

In the view that the object of imitation (*anukārya*) and the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) are non-different, the object of imitation possesses a function (*vṛtti*) consisting of denotative power (*vācakatā*), because it denotes some meaning. Since that function is defined by its relation to a meaning, it exists in the object of imitation through the relation of substratum-ness (*āśrayatā-sambandha*). Thus, because the object of imitation possesses such a function, there is no logical inconsistency in its being the object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*); for it is accepted that a meaning possessing a function appears in verbal cognition through the relation of substratum-ness. This is the intended sense.

Now, if it were the case that only "possession of occurrence" (*vṛttimattva*)—by way of the relation of substratumhood (*āśrayatā*)—is the regulator for being the object of verbal cognition, then an object possessing occurrence by way of the relation of relatumhood (*nirūpakatā*) would not appear in verbal cognition. Therefore, he says: "either relatumhood or substratumhood. The appearance in verbal cognition of an object possessing occurrence is accepted by way of either the relation of relatumhood or the relation of substratumhood. The point is that there is no insistence that the object possessing occurrence must be related by one and the same relation alone.

The object is the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of the function (*vṛtti*) consisting of power (*śakti*), and in that case, there is the property of being a determiner (*nirūpakatā*); the word, however, is the locus (*āśraya*), and in that case, there is the property of being a locus (*āśrayatā*). Thus, the object possesses the function consisting of power through the relation of being a determiner; and the word possesses such a function through the relation of being a locus.

Even though common people experience the manifestation of only the object qualified by its conch-shell neck and other features—which possesses a linguistic function (vṛtti) as the relatum—in the comprehension of the sentence-meaning in cases such as "bring the jar," nevertheless, based on the strength of the experience of the most eminent scholar Bhartṛhari, the author of the *Vākyapadīya*, who stated that "there is no cognition in the world that disregards the status of being an object," it is accepted that the word which possesses the function also manifests in the comprehension as the substratum. With this intention, he said: "by way of either one of the two relations."

For this very reason, in the case of "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), the process of verbal comprehension—which consists of the presentation of all factors—is consistent with the understanding that the act of bringing has as its object a cow qualified by cowness (*gotva*), femaleness (*strītva*), and singularity (*ekatva*), and which is denoted by the word "cow. Thus, in the case of an imitation (*anukaraṇa*), even though the imitated word (*anukārya*) appears within the sound [of the imitation] under both the views of difference and non-difference, according to the view of difference, the power (*śakti*) of the imitation resides in the imitated word.

And since that capacity (śakti) resides in the imitated form (anukārya) by way of the relation of "determiningness" (nirūpakatā), while it resides in the imitation (anukaraṇa) by way of the relation of "substratum-ness" (āśrayatā), the imitation is designated as a nominal stem (prātipadika) because it conveys the meaning which is the determiner of the capacity-based function (vṛtti). Furthermore, because the imitated word possesses the function by way of the relation of determiningness, its appearance in verbal cognition (śābdabodha) is established. The meaning of the *arthavat* sūtra is that a word which conveys an object that is the determiner of a function receives the designation of a nominal stem.

The term *saṃjñā* refers to that which conveys meaning through its function (*vṛtti*). For this very reason, in the view that the original (*anukārya*) and the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) are non-different, a function—which is synonymous with the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*)—is impossible because it is rooted in difference. Consequently, since it is impossible to attribute "possessing a function" (*vṛttimattva*) to the original and the imitation, the imitation lacks "meaningfulness" (*arthavattva*) in the form of conveying meaning through a function; thus, it does not receive the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). And because there is no subsequent derivation of case-endings (*sub*), there is an absence of the designation of a word (*pada*).

In the example *gavityayamāha*, because the letter *v* is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*), the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya* does not occur. Furthermore, precisely because it lacks the technical designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*), an inflectional ending (*vibhakti*) is not added here, as would be the case in the rule *bhuvo vuk* (where *bhū* is treated as a stem). Thus, in *bhū sattāyām*, no case-ending has been applied.

If it is objected that, on the view of non-difference (*abheda-pakṣa*), since the imitated (*anukārya*) and the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) lack the possession of a linguistic function (*vṛttimattva*), the imitated object would not appear in verbal cognition—given that the possession of a linguistic function is the regulating factor for the appearance of a word in verbal cognition—it is replied as follows: On the view of non-difference, because the imitated possesses the denotation of some meaning, there exists a linguistic function between the word and its meaning. In that case, the meaning is the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of the function, while the imitated word is the substratum (*āśraya*).

And thus, the object (*artha*) possesses its occurrence (*vṛtti*) through the relation of being the qualifier (*nirūpakatā*), whereas the imitated word (*anukārya-śabda*) possesses its occurrence through the relation of being the locus (*āśrayatā*). In that case, because the imitation (*anukaraṇa*), which has attained non-difference from the imitated (*anukārya*), also possesses occurrence through the relation of being the locus, the imitated object manifests in verbal cognition (*śābda-bhāna*). However, the imitation does not receive the technical designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*), because it lacks "meaningfulness" (*arthavattva*) in the form of conveying meaning through its own occurrence (*vṛtti*).

Nor should it be argued that because the original (*anukārya*) possesses meaningfulness (*arthavattva*)—consisting in its capacity to convey meaning through its own function—the imitation (*anukaraṇa*), having attained non-difference from that original, would also unavoidably possess such meaningfulness and thus acquire the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). The point is this: even under the view of non-difference, although the original may express some meaning, the imitation lacks the capacity to express that meaning; for it is established by experience that the meaning of the original is not understood from the imitation.

Regarding the non-difference (*abheda*) view, the proof for the existence of some meaning for the *anukārya* (the original to be imitated) is precisely the citation of its meaning, such as "the root *bhū* [is used] in the sense of existence" (*bhūsattāyām*). For who understands there that the meaning of existence belongs to the imitation itself? Rather, the universal experience is that it belongs to the root *bhū* which is the *anukārya*. In the difference (*bheda*) view, however, no meaning whatsoever is cognized from the imitation; rather, through the function (*vṛtti*) of expressive power (*śakti*), the cognition of the object consisting of the form of the word that is the *anukārya* arises from the imitation.

In this regard, it should be understood that because the *anukārya* (the original form being imitated) possesses occurrence (*vṛtti*) by way of the relation of "being the object of determination" (*nirūpakatā-sambandha*), it appears in verbal cognition (*śābda-bhāna*). As for the *anukaraṇa* (the imitation), however, its designation as a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) is established because it conveys an object that possesses such occurrence, namely the nature of the word-form of the *anukārya*.

Now, one might ask: how can the *anukaraṇa* be the locus of occurrence? If it is argued that the *anukaraṇa* is the locus of occurrence as determined by the *anukārya*, we reply: since the relation between the object of determination (*nirūpya*) and the determiner (*nirūpaka*) is rooted in difference, it is impossible when there is non-difference between the *anukārya* and the *anukaraṇa*; therefore, it cannot be said that the *anukaraṇa* is the locus of occurrence as determined by the *anukārya*.

Nor should it be argued that, under the view of non-difference (*abheda*), the very same basis for the function (*vṛttyāśrayatā*) which exists in the original object (*anukārya*)—namely, its being the locus of a function determined by specific objects such as individual cows (*govyaktyādi*) because it denotes those respective meanings—also exists in the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) which has attained non-difference from that original object. This is because there is no experience whatsoever of the cognition of the original object’s meaning, such as an individual cow, from the imitation; therefore, it is impossible to assert that the basis for the function determined by such meanings exists even in the imitation that has attained non-difference from the original object. Hence, he says: "The relation belongs to both" (*saṃbandhasyobhaya*).

A relation has two relata, and these two are the determiners of the relation; furthermore, the relation is determined by the pair of relata. Therefore, a relation is said to be distinct from its relata and to reside in both (dviṣṭha). Regarding the relation between the word "jar" and its referent, the two relata that determine it are the word "jar" and its referent. It is well known in the world that a relation is everywhere determined by both [relata], and nowhere is a relation seen to be determined by only one.

The relationship between word and meaning is of the nature of the indicator (bodhaka) and the indicated (bodhya). By this, it is indicated that this very relationship is *śakti* (power/potency). Among these, the power in the form of being an indicator resides in the word, while the power in the form of being the indicated resides in both the word and its meaning. Thus, both the word and its meaning are substrata of the function (*vṛtti*).

And thus, just as the meaning of a word appears in verbal cognition because it is the substratum of the function consisting of being the object of cognition (*bodhyatā*), so too the appearance of the word itself in verbal cognition would be possible because it is the substratum of the function consisting of being the signifier (*bodhakatā*). In this manner, the appearance of the word in every instance of verbal cognition is to be established.

In the case of imitation (*anukaraṇa*), according to the view that there is non-difference [between the imitator and the imitated], the object of imitation—such as a specific cow (*govyakti*)—is the locus of a linguistic function (*vṛtti*) relative to its respective meaning. Consequently, the imitator, having attained non-difference from that [object], must also be accepted as being the locus of such a function. This must be admitted precisely on the strength of the experience of the manifestation of the word in the form of the object of imitation when verbal cognition arises. Thus, since the imitator is also the locus of a linguistic function, there exists a word-presentation (*padopasthiti*) produced by that function; therefore, the objection that the manifestation of the object of imitation in verbal cognition is untenable is refuted. This is the underlying sense.

However, in the view that there is a difference [between the imitator and the imitated], the status of being the locus of a function (*vṛtti*) as determined by each respective object such as the individual cow (*govyakti*) belongs only to the imitated and not to the imitator; thus, the sense is that for the purpose of bringing the imitated to mind through the imitator, it is necessary to postulate a separate power (*śakti*) in that [imitator]. And in this way, because a word brings its own form to mind, the coexistence of both "being the object to be presented" and "being the presenter" within the word is established. Now, one might object: according to the method described above, it is impossible to say that the imitator is the locus of a function.

Because it is not experienced that the cognition of specific objects such as individual cows arises from imitation; and thus, since imitation lacks the status of being a locus of the power (*śakti*)—defined as the capacity to denote (*bodhakatā*)—which is characterized by the state of being denotable (*bodhyatā*) residing in objects such as individuals, it is impossible for imitation to be a locus of a linguistic function (*vṛtti*). If this is argued, it is replied: The power of denotation is well-established in the word, whereas the power of being denotable resides in the object, such as the individual cow. In that regard, because imitation is itself a word, the power of denotation certainly exists in it.

Furthermore, since the state of being the object of cognition (bodhyatā) as determined by the denotative power (bodhakatā) residing in an imitative word (*anukaraṇa-śabda*) is well-known to apply to things such as individual cows (*govyaktyādi*), it is postulated that this [denotative power] resides in the imitative word itself, because there would otherwise be a contradiction regarding those objects. That is to say, the state of being the locus of the relation consisting of the state of being the object of cognition as determined by the denotative power residing in itself belongs to the word itself. Consequently, since the imitative word is also a locus of the function (*vṛtti*), the mental presence of the word-meaning produced by the word exists; thus, others maintain that there is no logical inconsistency in the manifestation of the word within verbal cognition (*śābda*).

The sense is that, in this way, the coexistence of the state of being the object of cognition (*bodhyatā*) and the state of being the cognizer (*bodhakatā*) in a single locus is postulated. This co-location of the state of being the object of cognition and the state of being the cognizer is not merely an invention of my own imagination; rather, it is also the consensus of the authors of the treatises. He clarifies this by means of the authority of Hari’s statement with the words "And it has been said. *Grāhyatva* is the state of being the object of cognition (*bodhyatva*); *grāhakatva* is the state of being the cognizer (*bodhakatva*). "Of light" means of lamps and the like. "These" refers to the two powers consisting of the state of being the object of cognition and the state of being the cognizer.

All words possess the two powers previously mentioned; however, they exist separately—that is, they are established independently—this is the sense. By this, it is demonstrated that these two powers are not invariably concomitant. The meaning is as follows: it is undisputed that the conjunction of light, such as from a lamp, is the cause for the visual perception of a substance like a jar; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of visual perception of jars and the like occurring even in darkness.

And likewise, just as the conjunction of light with a jar or similar object produces perception not only of the jar but of itself as well, so too, when an object is present, the two powers inherent in the light of a lamp or other source are established by common experience in the world. In the same way, a word, aided by the power residing in it which has the object as its domain, produces the perception of both the object and its own nature.

And just as, in the absence of an object, that very same conjunction with light produces perception only of itself and not of a jar or other things; so too, when there is no intentionality (*tātparya*) toward an external object but there is intentionality toward the word, that very same word produces perception only of itself through such a function residing in itself alone. This very point is obtained from the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "one's own form" (*svarūpam*); therefore, he cites another verse which serves as an authoritative proof for that meaning: "disregarding the status of being an object."

The meaning is not made known by words without disregarding the self's status as an object of cognition and without [the self] attaining that status; rather, the meaning is made known by words only after the self's status as an object of cognition has been established. The underlying idea is that a word produces the cognition of its meaning only when it itself is known.

When an object such as a jar is present, the state of being an apprehended object (grāhyatā) as defined by the state of being an apprehending agent (grāhakatā) residing in light is established through perception in the jar and so forth. However, when the object such as a jar is not present, because the state of being an apprehended object defined by the state of being an apprehending agent residing in light is sublated in the jar due to the absence of the object, that [apprehension] turns back from it; then, by the logic of "rebound" (pratyāghātanyāya), when it culminates in itself alone, it follows that the very self is the locus of the state of being an apprehended object defined by the state of being an apprehending agent residing in itself. Thus, there is the perception of light alone.

It occurs as follows: in the case of imitation (anukaraṇa), according to the view that there is non-difference [between the imitated and the imitation], the denotability residing in the word of imitation—which is defined by the denotedness [in the object]—is obstructed because there is no intention (*tātparya*) regarding the meaning such as "cow" (*go*) and so forth; thus, having turned back from that, it returns to the word of imitation itself, and consequently, only the phonetic form of the word becomes directly perceived. And thus, the intended meaning is that the fact that denotedness—defined by denotability residing in the word—has the word as its substratum is accepted by the authors of the grammatical treatises. || 26 ||

"By way of a digression" (prasaṅgāt) means: by way of the occasion for an investigation into the fact that a word is the meaning of a noun. "The proof of non-difference" (abhede sādhakam) means: that which establishes the non-difference between the object imitated (anukārya) and the imitation (anukaraṇa). "He says 'go'—therefore [the example] 'he says go'" (āha—brūte—ata eva gavityāheti): the explanation of the phrase "for this very reason" (ata eva) is "he says go," and so forth. "They are not distinct" (na bhidyante) means: they are not intended to be expressed as being different from the object imitated.

The sense is that, since imitative words (*anukaraṇaśabda*) thus lack meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), the very desire to express non-difference from the object being imitated (*anukārya*) is the cause [of their grammatical correctness]. Regarding the phrase "in the absence of such application" (*ityādyapravṛttau*): the sense is that there is an absence of meaningfulness in the form of generating a comprehension of meaning through a linguistic function (*vṛtti*). Regarding the statement "it is established as correct" (*sādhutvamityupapadyate*): the sense is that, since there is an absence of incorrectness (*asādhutva*) according to the method to be explained, its correctness (*sādhutva*)—based on factors such as being employed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*)—remains uncontradicted. Now, one might ask: even in the absence of non-difference, why is its correctness not [established]? In response to this doubt, he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*).

The meaning is that difference alone is accepted. Regarding the terms *pratyayaḥ* (suffix) and *paraśca* (and subsequent): since the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used in the rule for suffixes, the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) "from that [which is indicated by the fifth case], the subsequent [element is affected]" (*tasmādityuttarasya*) applies; thus, once the status of the suffix as being subsequent to the base (*prakṛti*) is established, the rule *paraśca* serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that only a base followed by a suffix should be employed. It is with this very intention that it is recited: "A base should not be used alone, nor should a suffix be used alone."

The condition (*pratyaya*) is to be applied. Thus, it should be understood that according to the view that restrictive rules (*niyama-śāstra*) function by way of prohibition (*niṣedha-mukhena*), the transgression of the prohibition is explicit; whereas, according to the *bhāṣya*’s established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that they function by way of injunction (*vidhi-mukhena*), there is a transgression of an implied prohibition (*ārthika-niṣedha*).

The sense is that under the view of non-difference (*abheda-pakṣa*), because there is an absence of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) according to the method stated, there is an absence of "stemhood" (*prakṛtitva*)—defined as being occupied by the delimiting condition of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) in the rule for the prescription of suffixes. Consequently, the prohibition "not alone" (*na kevalā*) applies to that which is fit to be the limit for the prescription of a suffix; and since the prohibition "one should not employ what is not a word" (*apadaṃ na prayuñjīta*) applies only to that which is fit to be a word but lacks the status of a word, neither of the two prohibitions arises. It should be understood that even though [the item] generates the cognition of meaning through its function (*vṛtti*) under the view of non-difference, it does not possess the status of a nominal stem because it lacks the generation of the cognition of meaning that is the object of the relation of denotative power (*śakti*). || 27 ||

Thus ends the determination of the meaning of nouns in the *Sāra*, a commentary on the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, composed by Śaṅkara, the son of Raṅgabhaṭṭa; this was the exposition of the meanings of nouns within the *Sāra* commentary. (4)
Now follows the determination of the expressive power of compounds (*samāsa*).

Regarding the term "compounds" (*samāsān*): the state of being a compound (*samāsatva*) consists in possessing the designation "compound" through a relationship established by the convention set by the sages such as Pāṇini, the authors of the grammatical treatise. In short, a compound is that aggregate in which two words are compounded with one another. In the word *samāsa*, the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*) according to the rule *halaśca*. He analyzes [the term]: the meaning of the verbal root *bhaj* preceded by the prefix *vi-* is the act of stating by way of presenting a subordinate property (*avāntaradharma*).

And thus, by way of specifying a sub-class of compounds (*samāsatvāvāntaradharma*), he states: "of *sup*s with *sup*s," "with *tiṅ*s," and "with a noun (*nāman*). He says "two words" (*padadvaya*); by the word "also" (*api*), compounds consisting of three or more words are included. Therefore, there is no failure to include compounds such as *dvyahnajātaḥ*, *citrājaradguḥ*, and *hotṛpotṛneṣṭodgatāraḥ*. Accordingly, being composed of multiple *sub*-inflected bases is a sub-class of the property of being a compound. He provides an example of a compound composed of multiple *sub*-inflected bases, beginning with "king’s man" (*rājapuruṣa*). [He also mentions] "of *sup*s with *tiṅ*s."

This explanation begins with "the preceding word ends in a *sup*-suffix," and so forth. Thus, the intermediate property (*avāntaradharma*) consists in being composed of preceding and succeeding words that are respectively *sub*-ending and *tiṅ*-ending. In this manner, the intermediate property should be inferred by oneself in subsequent cases as well. An example is *paryabhūṣat* and *anuvyacalat*. Regarding the rule "after a word denoting motion that has an acute accent" (*gatimatodāttavatā*), this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), as it also includes the separation of the *yoga* (rule) by the word *saha*. An example is found in the *Ṛgveda Saṃhitā*: *devo devān kratunā paryabhūṣat*.

There is a simultaneous compound of *anvi-* with *vyacalat* and of *vī-* with *acalat*. Since a compound occurs in both cases by means of the rule-splitting (*yogavibhāga*) "with *saha*," the substitution of *yaṇ* and the accentuation of the compound are established because of the prohibition against Śākala’s version by the rule "not in a compound" (*na samāse*). Others, however, hold that since the singular number is intended there in the rule for *su*, the compound occurs first with *vi-* and afterwards with *anu-*. In that case, even though the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs due to the prohibition of Śākala, the final acute accent does not apply, because of the suppression (*nighāta*) of the finite verb by the rule "a finite verb [is unaccented] after another finite verb."

Regarding *anorgatiḥ gatāviti nighātaḥ*: they say that because of the substitution of *ve* for *vi* by the rule *udāttasvaritayorityaṭaḥ svaritatvam*, the *aṭ* [augment] becomes svarita. An example of the rule *supāṃ nāmnā* is *kumbhakāraḥ*. In the ungrammatical (alaukika) analytical sentence *kumbha-as, kāra-a*, there is a compound by the rule *upapadamatiṅ*. And by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) *gatikārakopapadānām*, this occurs prior to the derivation of the case-suffix (*su*) from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) *kāra*. The meaning of "prior to the derivation of the suffix" (*subutpatteḥ prāk*) here should be understood as "prior to the derivation of the suffix in the final member" (*uttarapade*).

Regarding the phrase "otherwise" (*anyathā*): it should be understood that even in the case of the prior member (*pūrvapada*), the meaning of "prior to the arising of the *su*-suffix" applies to the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) as well. Otherwise, if the compound were to apply only prior to the arising of the *su*-suffix in the prior member, then in the word *carmakrītī*, the prior member *carmaṇi* would lack the status of a *pada* due to the absence of a case-ending; consequently, the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) would not occur. Thus, the intermediate property (*avāntaradharma*) is the state of having a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as its sole subsequent member, while the prior member is one to which a *su*-suffix has been added.

The explanation of *supāṃ dhātunā* is: "the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is merely a verbal root (*dhātumātra*). The intermediate property (*avāntaradharma*) consists in being composed of a verbal root as the subsequent member, qualified by having a *sub*-ending word as the prior member (*pūrvapada*). *kaṭaprūḥ*: [one who] moves toward a mat. From the root *pruṅ* in the sense of "moving," the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). *āyatastūḥ*: one who praises at length; the meaning is "he praises for a long time. As before, *kvip* is applied in the sense of the agent. In both cases, the vowel of the root is lengthened by the rule *kvibvacipracchiśridruśrupruṣṭvāṃ dīrgho’samprasāraṇaṃ ca*. [This is stated] "from the Vārttika."

The compound is formed by means of a *nipātana* (irregular derivation) mentioned in the *vārttika* on the rule *anyebhyo’pi dṛśyate*. According to the *bhāṣya*: where the whole (*samudāya*) is explicitly stated and the parts (*avayava*) are inferred from it, that is a *nipātana*; whereas where the parts are explicitly stated and the whole is inferred from them, that is a formal rule (*vidhi*). The sense is that because the suffix *kvip* removes the entire [stem], only the verbal root remains as the final member (*uttarapada*) due to its elision (*lopa*). Regarding the expression *tiṅāṃ tiṅā*, the meaning is that both words are themselves *tiṅ*-ending forms.

The intermediate property consists in being composed of two finite verbs (tiṅanta) that function as the preceding and following members [of the compound]. "Pibatā" means "pibata-khādata," which refers to that action in which it is continuously stated: "Drink! Eat! The meaning should be understood in the same way for "pacatabhṛjjata" as well. Regarding the term "ākhyāta": the meaning is that when the continuity or uninterruptedness of an action is to be conveyed, a finite verb is compounded with another finite verb. Regarding the phrase "from the *antargaṇa-sūtra*": the ellipsis to be supplied is "this compound occurs."

The explanation of the rule *tiṅāṃ subantena* is "the first member (*pūrvapada*) ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*)" and so forth. The intermediate property (*avāntaradharma*) consists in being composed of a subsequent member ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*) qualified by having a preceding member that ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). Regarding *jahistamba*: one who says repeatedly "strike the pillar" (*stambaṃ jahi*) is called *jahistamba*. The meaning of the compound is the agent of striking the pillar. Regarding *jahikarmaṇā*: [it refers to the object of the act of striking].

The word *jahīti* is a verbal form (*tiṅanta*). It is compounded with a nominal form (*subanta*) expressing the object, provided that repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is understood and the compound denotes the agent (*kartṛ*). This is the meaning. The phrase "from the *gaṇasūtra* included within the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-group" means that it is a compound. The phrase "explained in the Bhāṣya" refers to its derivation there.

In this regard, one might ask: "Since the word *sup* (a nominal suffix) will imply the sense of 'together'—just as in the rule *vṛddho yūnā*—" what is the purpose of including the word *saha* ('together')? To this question, it is replied: "The technical designation of *samāsa* (compound) must apply only to those two things that are co-existent (*sahabhūta*), and not to each individually. Having stated this, it is further explained by means of the maxim of the "completion of the sentence in the whole" (*samudāye vākyaparisamāpti-nyāya*), as in the case of the "punishment of the Gargas," that the designation of *samāsa* applies only to the two co-existent elements and not to each one separately. Consequently, since the desired result is already established in this way, the inclusion of the word *saha* is understood to be for the purpose of indicating its connection with the following rule.

The "yoga" here refers to the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*; a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) is performed so that it may serve as a direct auxiliary (*aṅga*) to it. [The first part is: "With *saha*," a *sup*-ending word is compounded; with what? With a "competent" (*samartha*) word—as in *paryabhūṣat* and *anuvyacalat*. Then: "with a *sup*-ending word," a *sup*-ending word is compounded with another *sup*-ending word. This is both an *adhikāra* (governing heading) and a *lakṣaṇa* (definitional rule). Since it has been stated, "this will be the defining rule for that compound for which no other defining rule exists," the sense is that this sixfold compound is established by the *yogavibhāga* of the rule beginning with *saha*. || 28 ||

"Tadbhedam" means "the distinction of compounds. Having explained [this] by way of derivation, [he speaks of] the "division," which is fourfold—namely, consisting of *avyayībhāva*, *tatpuruṣa*, *bahuvrīhi*, and *dvandva*. Regarding the phrase "by means of 'under-extension' (*avyāpti*) and so forth": under-extension (*avyāpti*) is the failure of a definition to apply to even one part of the objects to be defined (*lakṣya*). For example, if "possessing a blue color" were made the definition of a cow, there would be under-extension with respect to a yellow cow, because the blue color is absent therein. Over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is the property of applying to the objects to be defined while also applying to what is not an object to be defined.

For example, if "having horns" (*śṛṅgitva*) is made the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of a cow, then even though "having horns" exists in the cow—which is the object to be defined (*lakṣya*)—there is the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because "having horns" also exists in buffaloes and the like. "Non-occurrence in any instance of the object to be defined" (*lakṣyamātrāvṛttitva*) is the fault of impossibility (*asaṃbhava*). For example, if "possessing a single hoof" (*ekaśaphavattva*) is made the definition of a cow, then because all individual cows possess two hooves, "possessing a single hoof" does not exist in any [cow] at all. The phrase "of that definition" (*tallakṣaṇasya*) means "of the definition of compounds such as the *avyayībhāva*."

And the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is a property (*dharma*) free from the three defects of under-extension (*avyāpti*), over-extension (*ativyāpti*), and impossibility (*asaṃbhava*). For this very reason, the learned state that such words alone should be included in a definition—words by which these defects of under-extension and so forth do not manifest. Regarding the term "generality" (*prāyikatva*): that which occurs mostly (*prāyeṇa bhavam*) is "general" (*prāyika*); its state is "generality" (*tattvam*). It means a general statement (*prāyovāda*). That is to say, the classification and the formulation of the definition are made with the intention of referring to the majority of cases.

The sense is that although it is observed in many instances, because it is not observed in some, the division stated by the ancients and the definition provided are merely general (prāyika) and not universal (sārvatrika). This is what he says:

The compound (*samāsa*), however, is of four kinds; that is, it has four modes. The suffix *dhā* is prescribed in the sense of "mode" (*prakāra*). A "mode" is defined as a specific property that differentiates a general category. He demonstrates these very modes with the words beginning "avyayībhāva," etc. The meaning is: due to the difference in the properties that serve as the delimiters of the divisions. The word "this" refers to the fourfold division just mentioned. The phrase "it is a common statement" means it is generally applicable (*prāyika*). He provides the reason for the general applicability of the division stated by the ancient authorities with the words beginning "bhūtapūrva."

"Because they are not included" means that these compounds lack the designations such as *avyayībhāva* and so forth. In this regard, the compound in *bhūtapūrva* is formed by the rule *sup supā*; the compound in *āyatastūḥ* is due to the irregularity (*nipātana*) mentioned in the Vārttika *kvibvacipracchi...*; and the compound in *vāgarthāvivā* is based on the rule "there is a compound with *iva*. Since these are prescribed by sūtras falling under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of compounds, it is impossible to maintain the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*) that they are excluded from the fourfold division of compounds.

With the intention that even the doctrine stating "the *avyayībhāva* is that in which the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha*) is predominant," etc., is merely general (*prāyika*), he says: "The definition beginning with 'etc. is also general. The phrase "in which the meaning of the prior member is predominant" means that the meaning of the prior member is the primary element therein. Thus, the intended sense is that the *avyayībhāva* is that which generates a cognition in which the primary objecthood (*mukhya-viśeṣyatā*) resides in the meaning of the prior member.

Therefore, even in cases such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), although there is the generation of a cognition whose primary qualificandum-ness (*mukhya-viśeṣyatā*) resides in the king and is determined by a mode-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in "kingship" (the suffix *tva*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] there. This is because the primary qualificandum-ness belonging to the cognition produced by the compound *rājapuruṣa* does not reside in the king himself. The same should be understood for subsequent examples as well. In the case of the avyayībhāva compound *upakumbham*, since it generates a cognition where the meaning of the prior member is the primary qualificandum—namely, "in the vicinity of the jar"—the definition is fully applicable.

"Having the meaning of the second member as predominant" means that a *tatpuruṣa* compound is that which generates a cognition whose primary qualificandum (mukhya-viśeṣyatā) resides in the object denoted by the second member, as determined by a modehood (prakāratā) residing in the object denoted by the first member. Consequently, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the word *kumbha* in the expression *upakumbham*, even though that word generates a cognition whose primary qualificandum resides in the jar (*kumbha*), as determined by a modehood residing in "jar-ness" (*kumbhatva*). This is because the word *kumbha* lacks the primary qualificandumhood belonging to the cognition produced by the compound *upakumbham*. [Regarding the phrase] "the meanings of both members":

The meaning is that [the compound] has multiple word-meanings as its primary referent (*pradhāna*). By this, there is no failure to include compounds composed of three, four, or more words. Regarding the term *anyapadārtha*: it means a word-meaning distinct from the word-meanings that constitute the compound.

In the case of *rāmakṛṣṇau* ("Rāma and Kṛṣṇa"), the application of the definition should be understood as occurring appropriately because Rāma and Kṛṣṇa—characterized by their association—are perceived as the primary objects (*viśeṣya*) of the preceding and following words respectively; and in the case of *citraguḥ* ("one who has brindled cows"), it occurs because the cowherd, who is the referent of the compound (*anyapadārtha*) consisting of the owner of cows not identical with the brindled ones, is perceived as the primary object. He states the reason for the merely conventional nature of these definitions with the verse beginning "unmattagaṅgam" ("the mad Gaṅgā"). Regarding the phrase "paraspara... (mutually...).

"Because of mutual deviation"—the meaning is that the delimitors of the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka*) and the delimitors of the defined (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) subsist in that which possesses the mutual absence of each other. The point is that although the authors of the treatises use the term "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*) specifically for over-extension (*ativyāpti*), here both under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension are intended as defects. He demonstrates this very deviation with the words "For instance" (*tathāhi*). "Unmattagaṅgam" is an *avyayībhāva* compound. And its status as an *avyayībhāva* consists in being a compound where the meaning of the first member is predominant.

In short, [the definition] means: the capacity to generate a cognition in which the primary qualificand-ness (mukhyaviśeṣyatā) resides in the meaning of the prior member (pūrvapadārtha), as determined by a mode-ness (prakāratā) residing in the meaning of the subsequent member (uttarapadārtha) due to proximity. Here, the definition (lakṣaṇa) is: "that which generates a cognition in which the primary qualificand-ness resides in the meaning of the prior member. The definiendum (lakṣya), however, is the *avyayībhāva* compound. The delimiting property of the definition (lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka) is: "the capacity to generate a cognition in which the primary qualificand-ness resides in the meaning of the prior member. The delimiting property of the definiendum (lakṣyatāvacchedaka), however, is: "the state of being an *avyayībhāva*."

In the case of *unmattagaṅgām*, since a distinct referent (*anyapadārtha*)—namely, a specific location—is perceived as the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*) with respect to the Gaṅgā who is non-different from the madwoman (*unmattābhinnagaṅgā*), the status of being an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāvatva*) exists in that which lacks the predominance of the prior member (i.e., that which is qualified by the absence of the delimiting property of the definition). Consequently, there is an over-extension (*avyāpti*) of the definition of *avyayībhāva* stated by the ancients, namely that it "does not subsist in a part of the thing to be defined. Similarly, the definition of *bahuvrīhi* is: "A *bahuvrīhi* is that in which the other member's meaning is predominant."

The meaning is as follows: in the case of *unmattagaṅgām*, even though there is predominance of the external referent (*anyapadārthaprādhānya*), it lacks the status of being a *bahuvrīhi*; thus, while the delimiting characteristic of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*)—namely, the status of being a *bahuvrīhi*—is absent, the delimiting characteristic of the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka*)—namely, the predominance of the external referent—is present. Consequently, there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of *bahuvrīhi* stated by the ancients, which consists in its application to what is not the intended object (*alakṣyavṛttitva*). He provides the authority for the predominance of the external referent in the case of *unmattagaṅgam*: "And [in the sense] of an external referent, when it is a name (*saṃjñāyām*)."

The phrase "due to the compound" (*samāsāt*) is the reason for the predominance of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*). Regarding the term *sūpa*: in an *avyayībhāva* compound, there is an apprehension of the meaning "a trace related to soup. Since this [apprehension] occurs in a case where there is no status as a *tatpuruṣa*, yet there exists the capacity to generate a cognition whose primary qualificandum-residency (*mukhya-viśeṣyatā*) resides in the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*), there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of *tatpuruṣa* stated by the ancients, which consists in its occurrence in non-examples (*alakṣyavṛttitva*). Likewise, since there is an absence of the capacity to generate a cognition whose primary qualificandum-residency resides in the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapada*), there is a non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) consisting in its non-occurrence in even a portion of the examples (*lakṣyaikadeśāvṛttitva*).

The meaning is that there is an under-extension (*avyāpti*) of the definition of *avyayībhāva* stated by the ancient authorities. Now, one might object: what is the proof for the status of *sūpapratī* as an *avyayībhāva*? Furthermore, since in the rule prescribing the formation of *avyayībhāva* compounds the indeclinable (*avyaya*) is mentioned first, how can there be a final placement (*paranipāta*) of the indeclinable here? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "From the compound [formed] with *su* and *prati* in the sense of 'mere' (*mātrārtha*). This means: because the compound is prescribed by a rule situated within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) on *avyayībhāva*. [He then says: "The meaning of the prior member," etc.

Since there is the cognition of the meaning "half related to *pippalī*," and because there exists the capacity to generate a cognition in which the primary objecthood (*mukhyaviśeṣyatā*) resides in the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*), the definition of *avyayībhāva* stated by the ancients—consisting in not occurring in that which lacks the status of *avyayībhāva*—suffers from the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Likewise, since there is an absence of predominance of the meaning of the second member (*uttarapada*), the definition of *tatpuruṣa* stated by the ancients—consisting in not occurring in even a portion of the intended instances (*lakṣyaikadeśa*)—suffers from the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*).

In the same way, it should be understood that in examples such as *pūrvakāya* (the front part of the body) and others, because the predominance of the meaning of the first member exists according to the method of etymological derivation (*nirukti*), there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of an *avyayībhāva* compound and under-extension (*avyāpti*) of the definition of a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Regarding the phrase "dvitrāḥ" (two or three) as a *bahuvrīhi*: the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is "two or three. The *bahuvrīhi* is formed by the rule "śeṣo bahuvrīhiḥ" (the remainder is *bahuvrīhi*) in conjunction with the rule "saṃkhyā-avyaya-asanna... read within that governing section. The suffix *ḍac* is applied as a compound-final affix (*samāsānta*) by the rule "bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye ḍac."

Regarding the term *dvitrāḥ*: because it produces a cognition in which the primary qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) resides in either of the two meanings of the constituent members, it lacks the status of a *dvandva* compound (as defined by the absence of such a relation). Consequently, the definition of *dvandva* stated by the ancients suffers from the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), since it applies to what is not the intended object (*alakṣyavṛttitva*). Furthermore, because it does not produce a cognition in which the primary qualificandhood resides in the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*), the definition of *bahuvrīhi* suffers from the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*), as it does not apply to even a portion of its intended objects. As for *śaśakuśa*: the term *dvandva* is used here in the sense of conjunction (*cārthe dvandvaḥ*), whereas [in the previous example] it was used in the sense of collective aggregation (*samāhāre dvandvaḥ*).

The compound *śaśakuśapalāśānāṃ samāhāraḥ* (the collection of hare, kuśa-grass, and palāśa-tree) generates a cognition whose primary focus (*mukhyaviśeṣyatā*) resides in the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) consisting of the aggregate (*samāhāra*). Consequently, there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of *bahuvrīhi* stated by the ancients—defined as that which functions upon what is not its own [constituent] referent—and there is an under-extension (*avyāpti*) of the definition of *dvandva*, because it lacks the capacity to generate a cognition whose focus resides in both constituent referents.

In this context, in accordance with the opening phrase "śaśakuśapalāśam," it should be understood that the term "non-pervasion of *dvandva*" means non-pervasion of the *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective compound). Others, however, maintain that by the general mention of the word "*dvandva*," it is indicated that even in an *itaretara-yoga-dvandva* (copulative compound) such as "dhavakhadirau" (the *dhava* and *khadira* trees), there is the impossibility of generating a cognition where both members are the qualificands (*viśeṣya*).

The intended meaning of this is as follows: upon careful consideration of the Bhāṣya on the rule *cārthe dvandvaḥ*, it is established that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, just as the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant, so too in a *itaretarayoga* [dvandva], the collection of the meanings of the words (*cārthasamūha*) alone is predominant. In this regard, however, there is this distinction: in an *itaretarayoga*, the meaning of the compound is a collection in which the distinctions between the individual members are manifest; whereas in a *samāhāra-dvandva*, it is a collection in which the distinctions between the individual members are not manifest.

The state of having manifested distinctions among its constituent parts (*udbhūtāvayavabhedatva*) consists in the superimposition of the number residing in those parts; conversely, when there is no such superimposition of the number residing in the parts, it is the state of having unmanifested distinctions among its constituent parts (*anudbhūtāvayavabhedatva*). This very same state has been designated elsewhere as "the concealment of the distinctions among constituent parts" (*tirohitāvayavabhedatva*). Thus, since in both cases the aggregate alone is predominant, one should understand that according to this view, the definition of *dvandva* stated by the ancients is impossible, while their definition of *bahuvrīhi* suffers from over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the *dvandva*.

Having thus refuted the definitions of *avyayībhāva* and other compounds as stated by earlier authors—such as "that in which the meaning of the prior member is predominant"—the author states their definitions according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) in the passage beginning with "In the established doctrine, however" (*siddhānte tu*). The term "under the heading of *avyayībhāva*" (*avyayībhāvādhikāra*) means that a compound is an *avyayībhāva* if it is a compound prescribed by a rule recited within the section governing *avyayībhāva*. Similarly, a compound is a *tatpuruṣa* if it is a compound prescribed by a rule recited within the section governing *tatpuruṣa*. This same principle should be understood for the subsequent categories as well.

The delimiting factor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), however, is the status of being an *avyayībhāva* compound and so forth. As for compounds such as *bhūtapūrva* ("formerly been"), since they do not fall under the delimiting factors of the definiendum, there is no harm in their not being included. "Impossibility" (*asaṃbhava*) means: non-occurrence in any of the instances of the definiendum. It is the absence of the application of a definition to any single instance among the individual cows that constitute the definiendum. For example, the possession of a single hoof in a cow.

This is because, among individual cows, since the state of having two hooves is present, the state of having one hoof is non-existent anywhere. In this way, he demonstrates the impossibility—namely, that the definitions of *avyayībhāva* compounds and so forth, such as "that in which the meaning of the first member is predominant"—apply only to specific instances (*lakṣyamātrāvṛttitva*). He does so with the words "because of what has occurred before" (*bhūtapūrvyāt*) and so on. That which existed previously is "what has occurred before" (*bhūtapūrva*). The state of being what has occurred before is "bhūtapūrvya. The suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*).

The property of generating a cognition in which the meaning of the first member is the qualificand (viśeṣyaka), which occurs at a time prior to the formation of the compound (i.e., in the popular analytical statement *kumbhasya samīpam*), does not constitute the defining characteristic of an *avyayībhāva* compound.

In the view that a compound functions by abandoning its own meaning (*jahatsvārthāvṛttipakṣa*), the constituent words of the compound would be as devoid of meaning as the individual phonemes that constitute a meaningful word; consequently, since the preceding and following words lack semantic content, it would be impossible to claim that the avyayībhāva compound *upakumbham* generates a cognition characterized by a qualificand-ness residing in the meaning of the first member, which is itself determined by a qualifier-ness residing in the meaning of the second member. He clarifies this very point through an illustration: "residing in a line-drawn cow (*rekhāgavaya*) and so forth."

The "line-drawn gavaya" (rekhāgavaya) refers to a beast resembling a cow but lacking the dewlap on its neck; the meaning is that it is a gavaya depicted in a painting. Since the horns, tail, and so forth residing in such a [depicted] thing do not belong to a conscious animal, they cannot constitute the definition of a conscious animal. Only that which invariably exists within the object to be defined (lakṣya) can serve as its definition.

For example, when the definition of a cow is formulated as "having horns while possessing a dewlap," it is well known that only when the dewlap and horns actually exist in a real individual cow can that cow be recognized through that definition; otherwise, it cannot. For this very reason, having a single hoof does not constitute a definition of a cow, because it is absent in cows. Furthermore, it is perfectly clear that the tail and other features residing in a variegated gavaya do not belong to a real cow.

Furthermore, if one were to think that a tail and so forth depicted in a painting must necessarily be dependent upon a living being, then it would follow that when a leg is severed from a painted elephant, the leg of the actual living being would also be severed. Moreover, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to undergo the expiatory rite (prāyaścitta) prescribed for killing a cow upon the killing of a painted cow.

Therefore, because the tail and so forth belonging to an insentient animal made of clay or similar materials lack the status of being an animal belonging to a living being, they do not constitute the definition of a real animal. Just as this is the case, likewise, for those who consider the effect to be the word, since the function (*vṛtti*) is accomplished from the sentence itself, the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) which exists prior to that function—standing in the place of a "line-drawn gavaya" (*rekhāgavaya*)—does not produce a cognition in which the primary qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) resides in the meaning of the first member as found in such a sentence; consequently, that [cognition] does not exist in the *avyayībhāva* compound, which occupies the position of a real animal.

The meaning of the term *bhāva* (the state of being) is that it constitutes the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). In this very same way, the property of generating a cognition whose qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) resides in the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) cannot possibly be the definition of a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Likewise, it should be inferred that even in the cases that follow, the property of generating such-and-such a cognition does not constitute the definition of such-and-such a compound, because that property does not reside within those respective compounds. The underlying intention is that, by accepting a distinct expressive power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*), the individual members [of the compound] are devoid of meaning, just like the phonemes [of a word].

He says, "But the capacity to produce understanding" (*bodhakatā tu*), because the property of being a producer of such-and-such an understanding does not reside in each respective compound, and thus it lacks the status of a definition for each respective compound; nevertheless, it remains the case that they cause the understanding of those respective compounds. The phrase "in exactly that manner" (*tadvad eva*) means "just like a line-drawn cow" (*rekhā-gavaya*) and so forth.

Just as, for example, although the tail and other features belonging to living beings and animals do not exist in the non-sentient drawings of gavayas and the like, such drawings nevertheless cause the recollection of the tails and so forth found in actual living beings and animals due to their similarity, and thereby convey the knowledge of those living beings and animals; likewise, although the predominance of the meanings of the preceding words and so forth—which exists in the constituent analytical sentences (*vigraha-vākya*) prior to the formation of a compound—does not exist within the compound itself (*vṛtti*), it nevertheless causes the recollection of the specific meanings residing in the compound due to their similarity, and thereby conveys the knowledge of that *avyayībhāva* and other types of compounds through that medium.

This is the intended meaning. For this very reason, it is stated in the *kārikā* that "even that"—meaning even the general rule (*utsarga*) mentioned by the ancient authorities—"has been maintained," that is, accepted. || 29 ||

Now, one might object: "Even if, under the *jahatsvārthavṛtti* (abandoning its own meaning) view, it is difficult to maintain that compounds such as *avyayībhāva* produce a cognition whose primary qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) resides in the meaning of the first member and so forth, it is easy to maintain this under the *ajahatsvārthavṛtti* (not abandoning its own meaning) view. With this intention, he says "Now... and so on. "Due to the predominance of the meaning of the first member, etc. means: the capacity to produce a cognition whose primary qualificandum resides in the meaning of the first member, the meaning of the second member, the meaning of another word, or the meanings of both members. "In the compound"—that is, in *avyayībhāva* and the like. "Easy to maintain" means: [it is easily established].

The meaning is that it can be easily stated. Thus, the intention is that the definitions stated by the ancients are not impossible to maintain. Regarding the rule "the prescription of words depends on semantic competency" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*): therein, semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) is of two kinds—characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) and characterized by unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). Between these two, that which is the mutual connection of words whose meanings are individually complete, arising from the force of expectancy and so forth, is called semantic competency characterized by expectancy.

This is because of the etymological derivation *vyapekṣā* as "mutual expectation" (*viśiṣṭā apekṣā*), and because of the derivation *samartha* as "capable of connection" (*saṃbandhārtha*). And this occurs only in sentences such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*). In that case, each individual word is construed with whatever other word is proximate to it and semantically compatible. Thus, there arise [constructions] such as "the king's man and the horse," "the man of the king and of Devadatta," and "the man of the angry king."

The capacity (*sāmarthya*) characterized by "becoming one in meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), however, consists in the fact that words—which during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*) are grasped individually as possessing their own respective meanings—possess, through the power of the aggregate (*samudāya-śakti*), the capacity to convey a single, qualified meaning. This is based on the etymological derivations: "that which has a connected meaning is *samartha*," and "that which has a combined meaning is *samartha*. Here, "connection" (*saṅgati*) and "combination" (*saṃsarga*) refer precisely to becoming one (*ekībhāva*), just as in the expression "the ghee and oil have become mixed," it is understood that they have become one.

Or, as in the case of "mixed fire," it is understood from the Bhāṣya that [the term] means "become one. And this capacity exists only in a *vṛtti* (compound) such as "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*). For this very reason, in the expression "the king’s man who is wealthy" (*ṛddhasya rājapuruṣaḥ*), the qualification "wealthy" does not apply to the king, who is the possessor of the man; for the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) constitutes a single word-meaning (*ekapadārtha*), whereas the king is merely a part of that word-meaning. This is what was stated by the phrase "in various ways" (*anekadhā*).

"Ekārthībhāvaḥ sāmarthyam adhikāraḥ" (the state of having a single meaning is the capacity [sāmarthya] and the governing rule [adhikāra]), "vyapekṣā sāmarthyam adhikāraḥ" (mutual expectancy is the capacity and the governing rule), and "dvividhaṃ sāmarthyam adhikāraḥ" (capacity is of two kinds and it is the governing rule)—these are the three positions. Thus, when the *samartha* sūtra functions as a paribhāṣā, there are six possible positions arising from these three sets of alternatives, such as "ekārthībhāvaḥ sāmarthyam paribhāṣā ca" (the state of having a single meaning is the capacity and it is a paribhāṣā). Therefore, the meaning of the phrase "in many ways" (*anekadhā*) is "in six ways" (*ṣaḍdhā*). Regarding the term *jahatsvārthā*: [it refers to the view that in a compound, the constituent members abandon their own individual meanings].

In this regard, it results that *ekārthībhāva* (the state of having a single meaning) consists precisely in the abandonment of one's own [original] meaning (*jahatsvārthatva*), while *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy) consists precisely in the non-abandonment of one's own meaning (*ajahatsvārthatva*). In the view of *ekārthībhāva*, since the presentation of the qualified meaning is possible through the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*) alone, the constituent parts do not present their own meanings, as that would be redundant (*vaiyarthyāt*). Since mutual expectancy—in the form of a requirement for reciprocal connection—is impossible without the non-abandonment of one's own meaning, the sense is that in the view of *vyapekṣā*, the constituent parts indeed present their own meanings. This is what is meant by "the stated arrangement."

The meaning is that there is a systematic rule (vyavasthā) such as "an avyayībhāva compound is one in which the meaning of the first member is predominant. Regarding the phrase "it is not impossible": this is because such [predominance] is possible in cases like *upakumbham* and other avyayībhāva compounds. The meaning is that this impossibility just mentioned does not occur in the way that defects such as under-extension (*avyāpti*) or over-extension (*ativyāpti*) occur in examples like *sūpapratī*. Having reflected thus, he says: "that which abandons its own meaning" (*jahatsvārthā*) and "that which does not abandon its own meaning" (*ajahatsvārthā*). [In the former case,] words abandon their own meanings.

The word *jahīti* is a present participle (*śatṛnta*) derived from the root *hā*, and not a finite verb (*laḍanta*). The intention is that, according to the rule *saptamīviśeṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 2.1.40), because of the mention of the locative case (*saptamī*), a *bahuvrīhi* compound may sometimes occur even between words that do not share the same grammatical subject (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Others maintain that it is also possible for the compound to have coreferential members (*samānādhikaraṇa*), such as *jahatsvārtha*, which means "that whose meaning abandons its own constituent words" (*jahati svāni... yaṃ sa jahatsvaḥ; tādṛśo 'rtho yasyāṃ sā*). Thus, in the *vṛtti*, the words [of the compound] are devoid of meaning (*ānarthakya*).

The point is this: if one does not accept the meaninglessness of the words constituting a functional unit (vṛtti), then there would likewise be no meaninglessness for the phonemes constituting a meaningful word (śakta). Now, although the phonemes constituting a meaningful word might be considered meaningless because they do not convey a meaning on their own anywhere, it might be argued that since words such as "rāja" convey meaning within a sentence, and since a compound (samāsa) generates the understanding of a meaning observed in the sentence, meaninglessness is impossible. With this in mind, he says, "This is the point," and so forth. [He concludes with] "by the very power of the compound."

The meaning is "by the power of the whole alone. By the particle *eva* ("alone"), the power of the individual parts (*avayava-śakti*) is excluded. The power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*) is as follows: it consists of the cognition that a word such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man") has the power to denote a person who possesses a relation with a king, and so forth. And this [power] is indeed necessary; otherwise, since the relation would not be denotable by the words constituting the complex formation (*vṛtti*), its appearance in the resulting cognition would be inexplicable.
