Nor should it be argued that because the relation in the analytical expression "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) necessarily appears as a relation (*saṃsargatayā*) when the two words are separate, it is appropriate for it to appear as a relation even in the compound (*vṛtti*), and thus there is no inconsistency in the compound and the analytical sentence having the same meaning. For in the cognition produced by a sentence, it is impossible for the relation to appear as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*). Consequently, even in the case of "the king's man," the presentation of the qualified object occurs solely through the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*) aided by the powers of its constituent parts (*avayavaśakti*).

In the case of a *vṛtti* (compound), however, the presentation of the qualified meaning occurs solely through the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*), because the constituent words are devoid of meaning [in that context]. Furthermore, the sense is that in cases such as "he wishes to hear the *Rathantara*," since the meanings of the constituents are not perceived, the power of the whole is absolutely necessary. More will be said on this later. Regarding the phrase "qualified by the king" (*rājaviśiṣṭa*): the meaning is "a person qualified by a king" through a relation such as ownership (*svāmitva*). "When there is the possibility of its appearing" (*bhānasaṃbhave*) means "when it is possible for it to be manifested. "The capacity to convey that" (*tadbodhakatvam*) refers to the capacity to convey that [qualified object].

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that the capacity of the two words constituting the compound to convey meanings such as "king" (*rājan*) and so forth need not be postulated. The underlying intention is that this is because there would be no purpose [for such a postulation] and because it would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of repetitive cognition (*bodhāvṛtti*). Now, one might object: "There is no risk of repetitive cognition due to the maxim that 'when there is a convergence (*saṃbheda*), one of the two is redundant'. The nature of this maxim is as follows: *saṃbheda* means "conjunction" (*saṃgama*). This is according to the *Amarakośa*, which states: "*saṃbhedaḥ* is the confluence of rivers (*sindhusaṃgama*)."

Regarding the confluence of the two rivers, the Kṛṣṇā and the Veṇṇā, there is the "uselessness" (vaiyarthyam) or redundancy of one of them, namely the river Veṇṇā; for, since the Veṇṇā is subsumed within the Kṛṣṇā, its purpose is fulfilled by the Kṛṣṇā alone, rendering it devoid of utility. For this very reason, after the confluence, the river is designated only by the name Kṛṣṇā, and not by the name Veṇṇā. Thus, the sense is that it is well known in the world that the confluence—the act of merging—is redundant because one of the two lacks a distinct purpose.

In the same way, when two denoters, two indicators, or a denoter and an indicator—whether as a base and a suffix, or both as a base and a suffix—are combined in a single instance, one of them becomes redundant; the meaning is that the denotative function of one must not be intended.

For this very reason, in the expression *dvāv apūpau*, since the meaning of duality is already expressed by the word *dvi* (two), the dual suffix in *apūpau* functions as a restatement (*anuvādaka*). Alternatively, since the dual suffix expresses the meaning of duality, the word *dvau* itself functions as a restatement. Consequently, there is no risk of understanding the meaning "four cakes" through the recurrence of the number two—as in *dvau dvau*—according to the maxim that "what is stated twice is well-stated" (*dvirbaddhaṃ subaddham*), for it is a worldly convention to employ words whose meaning has already been expressed in order to reinforce that meaning. This is the intended sense.

There is yet another possible meaning for the principle of etymology stated by the words "by means of combination" (*saṃbhedena*) and so forth: when there is a combination (*saṃbheda*), the redundancy of either one does not occur; rather, both are utilized, as in the case of the word *dviputra* ("having two sons"), where the word *dvi* presents a collection of two in which the distinction between the parts is not manifested.

Regarding the word "two" (*dvau*) here, however, the intended meaning is that the aggregate, by virtue of its inherent nature, is conveyed by the dual number as having its constituent parts manifested as distinct; thus, because there is a specific distinction [in the case of the aggregate], nothing is redundant. Furthermore, raising the objection that even if the individual parts convey the meaning in the present context, since they are merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*), there is no risk of repetitive cognition (*bodhāvṛtti*), and therefore nothing is contradictory, he says: "O Bull... (*vṛṣabha*).

By means of the principle of etymology (*nirukta-nyāya*), it is argued that it is more appropriate to assume the meaninglessness of the constituent parts within a compound; this is clarified by the example of the words *vṛṣa* and *yāva*. The underlying point is as follows: although the word *vṛṣa* has the same meaning as the word *vṛṣabha*, the word *vṛṣa* contained within the word *vṛṣabha* does not convey that specific meaning; likewise, although the word *yāva* has the same meaning as the word *yāvaka*, the word *yāva* contained within the word *yāvaka* does not [convey that meaning].

That [the word] possesses the capacity to convey that meaning is established by experience. And thus, in order to account for such an experience, one must necessarily accept the following rule: that the specific sequence of letters (*ānupūrvī*), which does not enter into the definition of the delimitors of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*), is itself the delimitor of expressive power.

The point is this: if it were admitted that the word *yāva*—which is a constituent of the word *yāvaka*—possesses meaning (*arthavattva*), then one would have to accept that the phonetic sequence *yāva* (beginning with *ya* and ending with *a*) is the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) residing in the word *yāvaka*. This would result in a violation of the previously stated rule and thus contradict experience. Consequently, the intended meaning is that the word *yāva* pertains to a different sentence altogether and is entirely distinct from the word *yāvaka*.

Thus, if one accepts that the constituent parts of a compound such as *rājapuruṣa* possess meaning, then the sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*) in the form "rājapuruṣa" which serves as the delimitor of the expressive power residing in the whole would require that the sequences of phonemes "rāja" and "puruṣa" themselves be accepted as the delimiters of that expressive power. However, this is untenable because it contradicts the aforementioned rule; this is the intended sense.

And thus, the underlying intention is: how is it possible for the constituent words of a compound (vṛtti) to convey meaning? Now, one might object: while words such as *yāva* and *yāvaka* are synonyms—such that even if the word *yāva* within the term *yāvaka* lacks the capacity to convey meaning—there is no evidence whatsoever to suggest that the constituent words like *rāja-* in a compound such as *rājapuruṣa* are devoid of meaning, given that the two words *rāja-* and *puruṣa-* do not have identical meanings.

The rule is that only in cases where words have synonymous meanings such as *vṛṣa* and *vṛṣabha*, it is the phonetic sequence (*ānupūrvī*)—which is not included within the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)—that serves as the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). Therefore, there is no fault in the present case.

Furthermore, considering that in words like *paṅkaja* (lotus), which possess both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) meanings, the sequence of the parts enters into the sequence of the whole—which serves as the determinant of the word's denotative power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*)—the previously stated rule becomes impossible; thus, the author states the objection regarding the parts of a compound conveying their own individual meanings within the commentary: "Otherwise, by the word *rāja*" (*anyathā rājapadena*). "Otherwise" means: if the parts of a compound were to convey their own respective meanings.

The meaning is as follows: just as in the sentence "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the word "king" presents the king independently (that is, without being syntactically connected to anything else), so too in the compound, because the word "king" presents the king independently, there would be the possibility of connecting the qualifier "prosperous" (*ṛddhasya*) to the king—resulting in the undesirable form "the prosperous king's man" (*ṛddhasya rājapuruṣaḥ*), just like "the man of the prosperous king" (*ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*).

But in the case of *jahatsvārthatva* (the theory that the component words abandon their own meanings), since the meaning of "king" (*rājan*) and so forth is presented merely as a qualifier of the person, it constitutes only a portion of the word-meaning; therefore, there is no fault because there is no connection with the qualifier. And thus, the intention is that in a *vṛtti* (compound), the members are not presented independently—this is what is meant by "meaninglessness" (*nairarthakya*), but it does not mean they are entirely meaningless like individual phonemes (*varṇa*). This is shown by the term *ajahat*, which is a *bahuvrīhi* compound consisting of words in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇa-pada*), analyzed as: "that [compound] in which [the members] do not abandon (*na jahati*) their own meaning (*svārtham*)."

"Non-abandoning its own [meaning]" (*ajahatsva*) refers to that which does not abandon its own [meaning]; "having non-abandoning its own meaning as its object" (*ajahatsvārtha*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing within it another *samānādhikaraṇa* (co-referential) *bahuvrīhi*, to be understood as before. Now, one might raise the objection: "If the cognition of a person qualified by a king and so forth can occur through the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*) alone, then—according to the reasoning stated previously—it is impossible for the individual parts to bring their own meanings to mind. Thus, the position that [the compound] 'does not abandon its own meaning' (*ajahatsvārthatva*) is devoid of logical foundation. To dispel this doubt, he says: "The intention is this... and "It is not something additional... (*nātirikteti*).

The meaning is that [the relation] is "additional" (atirikta) in comparison to the powers of the already established parts (avayava). The sense is that there is no evidence—specifically, the *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise-unaccountability) of the postulator—for such a [separate] postulation. [Objection: But surely the very cognition of the relation between the king and so forth is what postulates the additional power. Nor should it be argued that it is not contradictory for a relation to appear as a *saṃsarga* (relational content) even if it is not [previously] presented [as a distinct entity]. For the connection of the meanings of two nouns (*nāmartha*) by way of a relation of difference (*bhedasaṃbandha*) is contrary to linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Having this in mind, he says: "Precisely from the already established words 'king' and so forth."

"Of the postulation of a [separate] power for the whole" means: of the postulation of a power belonging to the aggregate. "Because it is refuted by the principle of complexity" (gaurava) means: because the postulation of a power in the aggregate is rejected on the grounds of complexity, since the cognition [of meaning] is already accomplished by the powers of the individual components which have necessarily been established.

The meaning is as follows: since the grammatical rule "the non-difference relation between the meanings of two nouns" (*nāmārthayor abhedānvayaḥ*) is restricted to cases other than compounds (*samāsa*), the application of the relation of difference (*bheda-sambandha*) is justified; thus, even the cognition of relations such as owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) as a mode of connection (*saṃsarga-vidhayā*) is not untenable. Now, one might object that by adding the qualifier "other than those included in a compound" (*vṛttighaṭaketaratva*) to the rule "between the meanings of two nouns," and thereby interpreting it to mean "non-difference relation between the meanings of two nouns other than those included in a compound," there is excessive complexity (*gaurava*). To this, he replies: "Even the abandonment of an established power [of expression]. (That is, such complexity is acceptable when it avoids abandoning what has already been established.)

The meaning is that there is an abandonment of the power residing in each individual word, which was previously established prior to the formation of the compound (*vṛtti*). Regarding the term "unauthoritative" (*aprāmāṇika*): it is improper to postulate that a single and the same word possesses meaningfulness prior to the *vṛtti* and lacks meaningfulness after the *vṛtti*, based on the distinction between non-compounded and compounded states; for in cases such as *sapta-ṛṣīṇām*, one must instead accept the meaningfulness of the constituent words within the *vṛtti* precisely in order to establish the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-substitution) and other rules triggered by their status as word-final (*padāntatva*).

The sense is that this is because of consistency (*sāmañjasyāt*). Now, an objection: even if the meanings such as "king" and so forth are presented through the powers residing in each individual word, if one does not admit a power for the qualified [meaning], then—since there would be no presentation of the qualified object in the form of "a person qualified by a king" due to the connection with ownership and the like—that object could not be the content of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). To this, he says: "And thus... (*tathā ca*). Regarding the phrase "expectancy and so forth" (*ākāṅkṣādīti*): by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), compatibility (*yogyatā*) and proximity (*saṃnidhi*) are included. Expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is of the nature of the thought, upon the knowledge of the meaning of one word, "What is the object to be connected with this? regarding the other word's meaning.

*Yogyatā* (semantic competency) is the possession of properties that necessitate mutual connection. *Saṃnidhi* (proximity), however, is the non-intervention of words that are not conducive to the cognition of a connection with the relevant [words]. Regarding the phrase "by means of established denotative power (*klṛptaśaktyā*)": the point is that once the individual word-meanings such as "king" and so forth have been presented, a cognition of a qualified object—such as "a person qualified by a king"—is possible through mutual connection via the relation of owner and owned, driven by factors such as expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Therefore, a separate denotative power for the qualified [whole] is not necessary. This very [point is expressed by the words] "this alone," etc.

The meaning is that since the cognition of the qualified object is accomplished by the very powers of the individual parts (*avayava*), there is an absence of the postulation of a power for the whole (*samudāya*). Regarding the phrase "as another view" (*matāntaratvena*): thus, the *Bhāṣya* on the *Sūtra* on semantic competency (*samartha*) states, "Some [hold that] semantic competency is mutual expectancy (*parasparavyapekṣā*). Even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *citragu*, where the referent of the other word (*anyapadārtha*) is the denotation of the whole, the cow—conjoined with "variegated" (*citra*)—is connected to it through the relation of ownership; thus, mutual expectancy is possible even there.

Even in the case of a *dvandva* compound, when the meaning of the whole is a collection (*samūha*), there is indeed the possibility of *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy) because the meanings of the constituent words are connected through the relation of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*). In the case of *avyayībhāva*, *tatpuruṣa*, and other compounds, however, *vyapekṣā* is quite evident. As for the proof that the "other referent" (*anyapadārtha*) and so forth constitute the denotation of the whole compound, it is the very sūtras themselves: *anekam anyapadārthe* and *cārthe dvandvaḥ*.

It should be understood that precisely because of the absence of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), there is no compound formation for words such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king’s man) or *puruṣo devadattasya* (the man of Devadatta). To ward off the undesirable consequence that might arise under this view, he says: "And not here... [referring to the phrase] "...the undesirable consequence of the connection with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇānvayāpatti*). It should be understood that in examples such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king’s man) or *puruṣo devadattasya* (the man of Devadatta), there is no compound formation for the words *rājapuruṣa* and so forth. To ward off the undesirable consequence that might arise under this view, he says: "And not here... [referring to the phrase] "...the undesirable consequence of the connection with a qualifier."

In the sentence "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), because the king is presented independently, the qualifier "wealthy" (*ṛddhasya*) can apply to him; likewise, the qualifier "wealthy" would also apply to the meaning of the word *rāja-* as a constituent of the compound *rājapuruṣa*. The point is that the meaning of the word *rāja-* possesses independence, which serves as the cause for the application of a qualifier. [The phrase] "from the Vārttika" refers to this Vārttika on the Bhāṣya.

The meaning is that the Vārttika teaches that a compound is not valid when there is a connection with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Their intention is that, rather than postulating a separate power (*śakti*) for compounds and so forth, it is simpler to merely formulate the specific rule (*vacana*). "Of those who hold this view" means of the ancient grammarians who maintain, in the sūtra *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*, that capacity (*sāmarthya*) consists solely of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). "The settled rule" (*vyavasthā*).

The meaning is that, in the view of *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy), because the meanings of both the preceding and following members exist [independently], there is a systematic arrangement such as "the compound is dominated by the meaning of the first member" (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*). Thus, it is said to be "easy to establish. Even though defects such as under-extension (*avyāpti*) exist, it is not impossible (*asaṃbhavinī*), because it is not a locus for the defect of impossibility (*asaṃbhava*). Furthermore, this position is necessary; for if, in the *samartha-sūtra*, only the capacity consisting of *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning) were accepted, then the rule regarding "behaving like the final member" (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) would not be included, since *ekārthībhāva* is impossible in that case.

Nor should it be argued that the non-inclusion [of the vocative] as being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) is simply not desired; for if that were the case, the author would have placed the *samartha* rule immediately after the sūtra "subāmantrite parāṅgavat."

Furthermore, just as in passages such as *kiṃ te divo duhitarmartabhojanam*, where by virtue of the treatment of *divaḥ* as if it were the subsequent member of a compound (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), the eighth-lecture (*aṣṭamika*) enclitic accent (*nighāta*) applies, so too in the case of *ṛtena mitrāvaruṇāvṛdhāvṛtaspṛśā*, there would result for *ṛtena* the acute accent on the first syllable of the vocative (*āmantritādyudāttatva*) according to the sixth lecture (*ṣāṣṭhika*), because the enclitic accent of the eighth lecture does not apply due to the absence of being preceded by a word (*padātparatva*) and because it stands at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pādādisthatva*).

However, under the view that semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) consists in mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), once the *samartha-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding semantic competency) has taken effect, there is no aforementioned defect; for the word *ṛtena* connects only with the action of pervasion (*vyāpti-kriyā*) denoted by the form *āśāthe*—which has the sense of *ānaśāthe*—and thus lacks mutual expectancy with the word *mitrāvaruṇau*. This is clearly understood from the Vedabhāṣya and other such works.

Having thus explained the two types of *vṛtti*, he explains the distinction between the *vṛttis* by way of a relevant connection (*prasaṅga*), namely that what has been recalled cannot be neglected: "These, moreover... The meaning is as follows: *vṛtteḥ* refers to the *vṛtti* consisting of compounds and so forth; *bhedaṃ* means the distinction motivated by meanings such as difference (*bheda*) or relation (*saṃsarga*). "Both types of *vṛtti*" means both types of *vṛtti* characterized as *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning their own meaning) and *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning their own meaning). "In three ways" means that because there exist three kinds of denotable objects—namely, difference, relation, and both—the two *vṛttis* are likewise of three kinds.

Since the word "difference" (bheda) is observed to be used even in the sense of "particularity" (viśeṣa), he shows the intended meaning by stating: "Difference is mutual non-existence" (bhedo 'nyonyābhāvaḥ). Although difference and relation are co-extensive—since difference is invariably concomitant with relation, and relation is invariably concomitant with difference—nevertheless, when difference is the expressed meaning, then relation is to be inferred; and when relation is the expressed meaning, then difference is to be inferred.

In the Bhāṣya it is stated that "capacity" (sāmarthya) consists of either difference (bheda) or relation (saṃsarga). In this context, the meaning of "difference" is the capacity to bring about the presentation of an object possessing difference; and the meaning of "relation" is the capacity to bring about the presentation of an object possessing relation. Regarding the term "possessing difference" (bhedavat), the formation of the word occurs by incorporating the sense of the particle *eva* (only), as in the case of *tapodhana* ("one whose wealth is austerity," i.e., one for whom austerity alone is wealth). Thus, the meaning is "that in which difference alone exists"—this is what is meant by "possessing difference. The same should be understood regarding the statement "relation is the capacity."

Furthermore, if difference (*bheda*) and connection (*saṃsarga*) were not present in the complex formation (*vṛtti*), then there would be no semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) at all; for semantic capacity consists essentially of difference and connection. Precisely because of the existence of this semantic capacity in the form of difference and connection, expressions such as *rājñaḥ puruṣo 'śvaśca* ("the king's man and the horse") or *rājñaḥ puruṣo bhāryāyāśca* ("the king's man and [the wife's]") do not result in *rājapuruṣo 'śvaśca* or *rājapuruṣo bhāryāyāśca*. Therefore, one must necessarily maintain that the meaning consisting of difference and connection alone is presented by the complex formation.

It should be understood that it is established in this way that the very capacity to convey a meaning characterized by both distinction (*bheda*) and connection (*saṃsarga*) constitutes the power of *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning). Furthermore, distinction and connection are presented through the function (*vṛtti*) either separately or together. The intended meaning is based on the description of three positions in the *Bhāṣya*: that the power (*sāmarthya*) consists of distinction, connection, or both. "And likewise" means: when distinction is included within the denotable content (*vācya*).

In examples such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), he demonstrates the mode of cognition [involved] by stating "distinct from what does not belong to the king. "What does not belong to the king" (*arājakīya*) means that which is related to someone other than the king; "distinct from that" (*tadbhinna*) is the meaning. The meaning of *rājapuruṣa* is: a person who has a different owner than the king, possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) resides in that [other owner]. In other words, it means "not related to anyone other than the king. The point is that in the case of *rājapuruṣa*, the absence of ownership (*svatva*)—as characterized by the state of being owned (*svāmitā*) residing in someone other than the king—is understood.

An illustration for the sake of the instruction of beginners: King Devadatta; his servant is Viṣṇumitra. Caitra is different from the king; his servant is Maitra. With respect to such a Maitra, Viṣṇumitra is different; thus, the meaning is that there is a difference residing in such a Maitra, having [Maitra] as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*). In other words, the relation of Caitra—who is different from the king—does not exist in Viṣṇumitra.

In this world, suppose a man named Vaiśākha, having mistaken a man named Jyeṣṭha—who is not a royal official (i.e., distinct from those related to the king)—for such an official, proceeds to revile the king. In the meantime, a man named Āṣāḍha says to Vaiśākha, "This man named Jyeṣṭha is a royal official. Upon hearing this, Vaiśākha desists from reviling the king. By this much, the meaning—that the term "royal official" implies one who is distinct from a non-royal person—is clearly understood.

The meaning is that the complex term *rājapuruṣa* has a primary denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to that which is distinct from the relation-holder who is different from the king. Here, this should be understood: just as in the case of Viṣṇumitra, who is the "king’s man," the relation of Caitra—who is distinct from the king—is excluded, so too in the case of a king named Devadatta, the relation of Maitra—who is distinct from Viṣṇumitra (who is not distinct from the "king’s man")—is excluded; thus, the difference consists in the form of mutual non-exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*).

King Devadatta understands that Viṣṇumitra alone possesses the relation of ownership (*svatā*) as determined by the lordship (*svāmitā*) residing in himself, and not in anyone else distinct from his royal servant, Maitra; likewise, the royal servant Viṣṇumitra also understands that the relation of lordship as determined by the ownership residing in himself exists only in King Devadatta, and not in anyone else, such as Caitra. Thus, because of this mutual exclusion on both sides, mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is evident.

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "When 'the king's' is said here, everything that belongs to him is implicated; [the word] 'man' excludes [him] from other masters, and 'man' also [excludes the king] from his other possessions. The sense is that, in this way, difference (*bheda*) must necessarily be included within what is expressed. Otherwise, he states the subverting argument: "if this were not expressible," meaning if difference were not included within the expressed meaning. [For example: "The king’s man is handsome."

Just as the application of the qualifier "handsome" occurs in the person who is the possessor of the function (the servant), so too would there be an application of the qualifier "Devadatta's. This is because, just as the cognition arises that "the person whose master is the king is handsome," so too would the cognitions arise that "the person related to the king is related to Devadatta," or "the person whose master is the king is also the master of Devadatta. Consequently, the construction *rājapuruṣo devadattasya ca* ("the king’s man and [the man] of Devadatta") would result; such is the meaning.

Devadatta is a certain citizen here who has been banished by the king. One might object: "Is it not the case that, according to the Vārttika stating 'there is no connection with a qualifier for a compound' (*vṛttasya vā viśeṣaṇayogo na*), the connection of a qualifier is prohibited for that which constitutes a compound? How then can there be the application of the qualifier 'handsome' (*sundara*) to the person who is part of the compound? If this is asked, the answer is no. The prohibition of the connection with a qualifier applies only to that which is non-primary (*apradhāna*) within the compound, but not to that which is primary (*pradhāna*). For the meaning of that rule is that the connection with a qualifier certainly does occur for the primary element.

For this very reason, in the expression "a man who is a hero like a tiger," although the quality of being a qualifier as determined by the primary term (*puruṣa*) exists in the referent of the word *śūra*, the formation of a compound under the rule "that which is compared with tigers, etc. (*upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ*) would otherwise occur; therefore, the phrase "when the common property is not employed" (*sāmānyāprayoge*) is purposeful for the sake of prohibiting that. Thus, because the bravery—which is the common attribute shared by the standard of comparison and the object of comparison—is employed here, no compound is formed.

Otherwise, because there would be a prohibition against the connection of a qualifier with that which constitutes a member of a compound, the formation of the compound itself would be impossible whenever a qualifier is present; thus, the statement "provided there is no employment of a general term" (*sāmānyāprayoge*), which is intended to prohibit such compounds, would be rendered useless. And so, this very statement "provided there is no employment of a general term" indicates that even for the principal element within a compound, there can be a connection with a qualifier of a different class from those qualifiers already expressed [by other words]; this is the underlying sense.

[Objection: But if the distinction (bheda) is included within the denotation [of the compound], then since the usage "the king's man of Devadatta" (rājapuruṣo devadattasya ca) would result, how is this avoided? To this he says: "Because of its contradiction with that" (tadvirodhāt). The meaning understood from the word *rājapuruṣa* is "one who is not related to anyone other than the king. Since a relation of ownership (*svatva*) characterized by anyone other than the king is thereby negated in the man, and because the relation of Devadatta—who is other than the king—to the man is opposed to the negation of a relation with anyone other than the king, the usage "the king's man of Devadatta" does not result; such is the intended sense.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that the exclusion of such expressions as *rājapuruṣo devadattasya* ('the king’s servant belongs to Devadatta') is easily accomplished simply from the literal understanding of the word as 'one who has a relation with the king' (i.e., one whose relation is determined by the king)? For there arises an implicit cognition that he does not have a relation with anyone other than the king, since a relation determined by the king is incompatible with a relation determined by someone other than the king. Thus, even if difference (*bheda*) is not included within the denoted meaning (*vācya*), there is no harm. [Reply: You are mistaken.

The meaning is as follows: since there is no sublation (bādhaka) regarding a person who is related to someone other than the king, and because a relation with the king is also possible, and because such is observed in common experience, there is no contradiction between the relation with the king and the relation with one other than the king; thus, even though the relation with one other than the king is implied (ārthikī), the cognition "he is not related to anyone other than the king" does not necessarily arise. To introduce the view that only the relation (saṃsarga) is denoted and not the exclusion (bheda), he prepares the introductory stage (bhūmikā) by saying: "one who possesses a relation with the king."

The meaning is: "possessing a relation of ownership designated by the king. Regarding the phrase "verbal manifestation" (*śābdaṃ bhānam*): such a cognition first arises from the word; however, the cognition of difference—namely, "distinct from that which does not belong to the king" or "not related to one distinct from the king"—arises later by virtue of the indicators of intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). With the intention that the relation itself is the denoted meaning because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*) due to its being the first to appear, he says: "the relation" (*saṃsarga*).

The point is this: since difference (*bheda*) depends on factors that apprehend the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*), it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*); therefore, it is not directly denoted (*vācya*), but rather its meaning is implied (*ārthika*). However, when a person related to the king is required for some specific task, then in the expression *rājapuruṣa*, the relation (*saṃsarga*) is what is denoted. Now, he provides the introductory transition (*pātanikā*) to show the view that both [difference and relation] are denoted, stating: "due to the absence of a decisive criterion" (*vinigamanāviraha*).

The meaning is that there is an absence of any authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to determine, between these two, whether it is indeed difference (*bheda*) that is denoted, or rather, it is indeed relation (*saṃsarga*) that is denoted. Regarding the phrase "even in the case of one who has no owner": this means even in the case of one who is not related to a king, nor related to anyone other than a king—that is, even in the case of an independent person entirely devoid of a relationship with an owner. Regarding the phrase "and the consequence of the usage [occurring]": this means that even in the absence of a relationship with an owner, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the usage "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*). This undesirable consequence applies to the view that difference alone is what is denoted.

For according to that view, the meaning of "rājapuruṣaḥ" (the king's man) is "one who is distinct from those not belonging to the king"—that is to say, one who does not possess a relationship with anyone other than the king; in other words, one who lacks a relationship as defined by anyone other than the king.

In that regard, the absence of a relation with the king is possible for a person devoid of a relation with the master just as it is for a person who has a relation with the king; thus, the meaning is that the usage "king’s man" (*rājapuruṣa*) would result even for one who lacks a master, since such a relation is possible even for a person devoid of a master. Having reflected on this in his mind, he says: "or both. This means difference (*bheda*) and relation (*saṃsarga*). And so it is said: "tathā ca" (and likewise).

The meaning is: "given that both are denotable. In the Bhāṣya it is stated that "difference and connection constitute the semantic capacity" (*sāmarthya*); the intention of this is as follows: because difference and connection are co-extensive (*samaniyata*), and because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish either one side exclusively, both must be denotable. Thus, according to the Vṛtti, by the proximity of the word *rāja-* (king), the individual person (*puruṣavyakti*) who possesses the relation to the king and lacks the relation to another master is presented by the word *puruṣa-* itself.

Therefore, there is no relation between the king and his own interior, because the referent of the word "king" is absent therein. Nor is there a relation between the man and his own interior, because the man has already grasped the relation with the king; this is the intended meaning. With this intention, he says: "[the man] is distinct from what does not belong to the king and possesses a relation with the king. The intended meaning is that the collective expression "king's man" (rājapuruṣa) has its denotative power (*śakti*) residing in one who possesses a relation with the king, as qualified by the property of being distinct from what does not belong to the king.

Thus, even though there is the existence of being ownerless and being distinct from the king (or distinct from the relation to the king), since there is an absence of the relation to the king, the undesirable consequence of the usage "rājapuruṣa" (the king’s man) does not arise; this is the intended meaning, and therefore there is no defect whatsoever. || 30 ||

"Of the theory of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāvāda*)" means: of that which has been described as having the nature of functioning with its own meaning ungenerated. "The arguments" refers to the arguments to be stated later, consisting of the heaviness of reasoning—namely, the assumption of meaninglessness for the words *rāja-* and *puruṣa-* within the compound *rājapuruṣa*, just as the words *vṛṣa-* and *yāva-* within the words *vṛṣabha* and *yāvaka* are assumed to be meaningless. "In the Bhāṣya" means: in the Bhāṣya passage beginning with, "There is no prohibition of the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* after a non-case-inflected word ending in *na*. "Because of being contradictory" means: [because it contradicts the established doctrine].

The meaning is: "because of contradiction with the *Nirukta*, logic (*yukti*), and the *Bhāṣya*. Regarding the phrase "rooted in that": the meaning is "rooted in the theory of syntactic dependence (*vyapekṣāvāda*). The intention is that in the theory of syntactic dependence, both the preceding and following members of a compound possess semantic value. Regarding the word "untenable" (*ayukta*): the intention is that since the theory of syntactic dependence is untenable due to its contradiction with logic and the *Bhāṣya*, the general rule (*utsarga*) dependent upon it—namely, that [a compound] is "predominant in the sense of the first member" (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*), and so forth—is also untenable.

He says "But what... because even an improper general rule (*utsarga*) can convey the meaning of a compound through a traditional succession, like a line-drawn gavaya (*rekhā-gavaya*). Regarding "like a line-drawn gavaya": just as one understands the tail and other limbs of a living animal by means of the tail and other limbs situated on a line-drawn gavaya, and thus understands the animal possessing such limbs—thereby conveying the actual animal through a traditional succession—in the same way, there is an understanding of the power residing in a compound formation (*vṛtti*) such as a *samāsa* by means of the general rule that "the first member is predominant" and so forth; and by that [understanding],...

Thinking that the meaning of a compound and other types of *vṛtti* is understood through a sequence [of meanings], and thus the general rule (*utsarga*) brings about the cognition of a qualified meaning, he provides a resolution: "In a compound, indeed, it is distinct... He says, "...of many properties of *vṛtti*," in order to avoid the charge of deficiency. He states, "The term 'compound' refers to *vṛtti* in general," meaning *vṛtti* such as those ending in *kṛt*-suffixes and so on. The intention is that the word *mātra* signifies "entirety. Because they are the substrata of a *vṛtti* consisting of a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) that generates a single presentation (*ekopasthiti*), the term "vṛtti" is applied to *kṛdanta* forms and the like.

Regarding the term *padavidhi*: "vidhi" means that which is prescribed (*vidhīyate*); the suffix *kvip* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, it means "an operation" (*kārya*). The compound "the prescription of words" (*padānāṃ vidhiḥ*) is formed with a genitive case ending according to the rule for the residual category (*śeṣalakṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Its meaning is "pertaining to words. Consequently, the sense is: "that operation which is prescribed for words that already exist. He explains the term *samarthapada* as "in the analytical sentence" (*vigrahavākye*). An "analytical sentence" (*vigraha*) is so called because by it the meaning of the compound is specifically grasped or known (*viśeṣeṇa gṛhyate jñāyate*). And since it is both such [a word] and a sentence, it is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).

Just as in the case of the compound *rājapuruṣaḥ*, the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) expressing its meaning is *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*; the word *rājapuruṣa* is capable of denoting that which is the meaning of this [sentence], because it is from this [sentence] that the cognition of it arises. The sense is that since a sentence that makes known the meaning of a derivative form (*vṛtti*) is precisely what constitutes an analytical statement (*vigraha*), the compound and so forth are capable of denoting that meaning. That [meaning] is "a person qualified by a king. The meaning is that such a compound and so forth is "capable" (*samartha*).

The meaning of "samartha" (capable) is "being competent," which implies being correct (*sādhu*). Regarding the phrase "from the acquisition [of the meaning] from the Bhāṣya": for there it is stated that *sāmarthya* (capacity/semantic integration) is the unification of meanings (*aikārthībhāva*) of words that originally have separate meanings; it is said that in the sentence "the king's servant" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the meanings are separate, whereas in the compound they become unified. In that context, since capacity cannot be established even by a hundred statements if it is non-existent, the sense is obtained that the correctness (*sādhutva*) of that which is "samartha"—that is, characterized by capacity—is what is being prescribed. [The term] "having the word as its locus" (*padoddeśyakā*)...

Regarding the statement "the prescription of words" (*padānāṃ vidhiḥ*), this meaning—being the object of subsequent cognition—is intended by a compound formed with a genitive of general relation (*saṃbandhasāmānya-ṣaṣṭhī*). However, the compound is not formed with that [genitive] which denotes a relation consisting of the state of being the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*). This is because such a relation is established by experience as appearing solely as a relational connection (*saṃsarga*), and thus it is unfit for a compound; furthermore, there is no alternative way [to account for it], and since it lacks the status of being the meaning of the genitive in cases such as *nīlo ghaṭaḥ* ("a blue pot"), where the blue color is the subject and the pot is the predicate, the genitive is excluded.

As for the claim that in the case of compounds (*samāsa*) the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) is not perceived at all—that is incorrect. It should be understood that in cases such as "The priests with red turbans perform the ritual" (*lohitoṣṇīṣā ṛtvijaḥ pracaranti*), a subsequent cognition arises—through an analysis of what is already established and what is not—which takes the turbans and so forth as the subject and the redness and so forth as the predicate; this is established by universal experience. Thus, [the relationship] exists indeed in all five types of word-derivations (*vṛtti*). Here, by the term "word" (*pada*), that which possesses meaning (*arthavat*) is intended, and not merely that which ends in a *su*-affix. Therefore, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of *ekaśeṣa* or in forms ending in *kṛt*-suffixes and the like.

If the term *pada* is understood as denoting that which ends in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*), then in compounds such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* and in secondary derivative forms (*taddhita*) such as *augagavaḥ*, the status of being a "rule conditioned by a word" (*padavidhi*) is self-evident. Furthermore, even for primary derivatives (*kṛt*) whose occurrence is triggered by a co-occurring word (*upapada*), such as in the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*, they possess the status of *padavidhi* through a mediated sequence.

Since *kyac* and other affixes are prescribed after words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*) among the verbal roots ending in *san*, *na*, etc., they are *pada-vidhi*s (rules applying to finished words) within the domain of *sub-dhātus*. Furthermore, because the rule for *ekaśeṣa* is prescribed by the continued application of the phrase "in a *dvandva*," its status as a *pada-vidhi* must be maintained in some manner. In the rule *kṛt-taddhita-*, the term *kṛt* refers to a word ending in a *kṛt*-affix, and the term *taddhita* refers to that which contains such an affix; thus, there is no failure to include forms such as *bahupaṭuḥ* and *sarvakaḥ*.

Due to the application of the maxim regarding semantic competency (*samartha-paribhāṣā*) to primary derivatives (*kṛt*) and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), the suffix *aṇ* is not applied in the case of "he makes a cloth" (*paṭaṃ karoti*) or "bring the jar" (*kumbham ānaya*), because these are not [derived from] a word denoting an agent; nor is a secondary derivative applied in the case of "the offspring of a wealthy cowherd" (*ṛddhasyopagor apatyam*). According to the Bhāṣya—"semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) is the unification of meanings that were previously distinct"—it follows that for words observed in common usage, which denote meanings that are the objects of separate cognitions produced by their respective words, the generation of a single cognition through a single power directed toward a qualified object-constellation is what constitutes "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*).

The term *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning) is an indication by means of the suffix *cv-* intended to convey that the "oneness of meaning" of the constituent words of a compound is figurative (*gauṇa*). Just as the usage of existence regarding words is figurative because words themselves are non-existent, so too should it be understood that the usage of their being "one in meaning" is likewise figurative. The phrase ending with "of words observed in common usage" is included to exclude the integration of meaning from words that end in case-endings (*vibhakti*).

Just as the meaning of a case-ending is understood through that very case-ending and not by any other word, so too, because a case-ending is never observed in common usage to have an object of presentation distinct from itself, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to words ending in case-endings. Since suffixes in forms such as *aupagava* are never observed in common usage to have an object of presentation distinct from themselves, the phrase "generated by any [particular] word" serves as a qualification for the presentation.

In cases such as "Upagu has an offspring" (*upagoḥ apatyam asti*), where the meaning of the word *apatya* (offspring) is [already] present, there is no failure to include it, because it is observed in common usage to be an object of a separate presentation (*pṛthag-upasthiti*) generated by the word *apatya*. The phrase "having meanings that are objects of a separate presentation generated by some word" (*yatkiṃcit-padajanya-pṛthag-upasthiti-viṣayārthakāḥ*) means: a "separate presentation" is a presentation [of an item] as being unconnected with other meanings; those words whose meanings are the objects of such a presentation are "those having meanings that are objects of a separate presentation generated by some word. The state of being such is "that-ness" (*tattvam*). By virtue of having such meanings, these are words observed in common usage.

The meaning is that there is the production of a single presentation by means of a single power directed toward a qualified object. For example, in the sentence "the king's man," from the word *rājan* (king) there arises a presentation of the referent of the word *rājan* as unconnected with the referent of the word *puruṣa* (man), and from the word *puruṣa* there arises a presentation of the referent of the word *puruṣa* as unconnected with the referent of the word *rājan*. Since these two words, *rājan* and *puruṣa*, are observed in common usage to have meanings that are objects of separate presentations, [in the compound] they possess a single power directed toward a man qualified by a king, [expressing] a man qualified by a king.

Thus, the definition is the state of generating a single unified presentation (*upasthiti*) of such a form. The compound *rājapuruṣa* possesses a primary denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to a person qualified by a king. In a sentence (*vākya*), after the meanings have been presented separately, there occurs a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) by virtue of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors; however, in a derivative formation (*vṛtti*) such as a compound, the meaning is presented as already mutually connected—this is the intended sense. Furthermore, this capacity (*sāmarthya*) consisting of "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) exists only in a derivative formation; therefore, it is necessary in all five types of formations, including those ending in *kṛt*-suffixes, *taddhita*-suffixes, and so forth.

In that regard, in compounds such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man") and in specific forms ending in secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) such as *aupagava* ("son of Upagu"), the status of being a "function" (*vṛttitva*) is quite evident, because they possess the capacity to denote the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), which consists in generating a single unified mental presentation (*ekopasthiti*).

In cases such as "one who studies grammar is a *vaiyākaraṇa*" (*vyākaraṇam adhīte vaiyākaraṇaḥ*) or "one who cooks is a *pācakaḥ*" (*pacati iti pācakaḥ*), since it is accepted that the verbal suffix—which conveys the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) or the primary derivative (*kṛt*)—generates a cognition in which the agent is the qualificand, there is no impairment of its capacity to express the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigraha-vākya*); thus, even in those instances, the status of being a *vṛtti* (compound/derivative formation) certainly exists. However, in the case of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one of identical forms), there is no status of being a *vṛtti*, because there is a lack of evidence for it; specifically, due to the impossibility of the aforementioned "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), it lacks the capacity to present its own meaning as connected with the meaning of another word.

In this regard, it should be understood that the *Śekhara* states that the meaning consisting of those respective collections (the lotus-parts) appears through its own function (*svavṛtti*) alone. Now, one might object: since the word *paṅkaja* is also a compound with an upapada, a specific unitary power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) is not accepted there either according to the previously mentioned reasoning; therefore, its inclusion as an example is inconsistent. To address this, the author explains the root text differently: "of those who accept a specific power" (*viśiṣṭaśakyasvīkartṝṇām*). This refers to [the view] beginning with "in the case of a *vṛtti*" etc., which should be understood as referring to the Naiyāyikas and others who maintain the theory of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāvādinaḥ*). [The phrase] "proving the existence of power" (*śaktisādhakam*)...

The sense is that this [argument] serves precisely to establish the existence of a specific power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*), by way of demonstrating the defects in the theory of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) according to the method to be explained hereafter. In the view of the proponents of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣāvādins*), who do not accept a specific power in a compound (*vṛtti*), when the meanings of the words are presented in cases such as "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*) through the established powers of the constituent parts like the word "king," a cognition of the qualified meaning arises due to mutual expectancy and so forth; likewise, since the presentation of the qualified meaning could also occur from the word *paṅkaja* (lotus), the conventional power (*rūḍhi*) would be abolished.

The meaning is "it would result [in that]. If it is argued, "Let there be the destruction of conventional usage; indeed, that is desired," he says "no"—"even for the agent of the production of mud. This means: even for that which is intended by way of the form of being the agent of the production of mud. He establishes the destruction of conventional usage with the words "only from the etymological derivation" (*yogāt*). The meaning is: "by that alone," namely, by the etymological derivation, which is the power of the individual word-roots (*avayavaśakti*).

In that regard, due to the diversity of linguistic derivation—that is, by virtue of a distinct capacity for signifying meaning—the object of the noun *paṅka* (mud) is construed with the sense of the verbal root *jan* (to arise) through the relation of being the locus (*adhikaraṇatā*) that characterizes the action. Furthermore, such an arising is construed with the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix *ḍa*, through the relation of being its substratum (*āśrayatā*). Thus, when the understanding "the substratum of an arising whose locus is mud" is established, the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) [of the word *paṅkaja*] would not be proven due to its lack of necessity; the point is that such a collective power would thereby be eliminated.

One might raise the objection that even though a lotus (*padma*) can be the object of cognition by virtue of being the locus of its production in mud, a collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) in the form of *ekārthībhāva* must still be postulated for the sake of cognizing it specifically as a "lotus" (i.e., by the form of *padmatva*). Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words beginning "na ca padmatvarūpeṇa," etc. [The phrase] "upasthitayaḥ" means...

The point is that without a knowledge of the expressive power (*śakti*) residing in that which is delimited by *padmatva* (lotus-ness), it is impossible for a lotus to be presented in the form of *padmatva*; for a cognition of the expressive power delimited by a particular property (*taddharma*) is the cause of a presentation where that property serves as the qualifier (*prakāra*). This is because, without a knowledge of the expressive power in the form "the word 'ghaṭa' is expressive of that which is delimited by *ghaṭatva*," no cognition arises from the word 'ghaṭa' in which *ghaṭa* is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and *ghaṭatva* is the qualifier.

He states a counter-argument (*pratibandī*), saying "even in the case of words such as *citragu*," [meaning] that if you postulate a collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) for the sake of understanding a specific form, then the same must be postulated elsewhere as well. The meaning is this: although the cognition of the owner of cows is possible through the word *citragu* by means of the etymological derivation (*yoga*)—"one to whom variegated cows belong"—in the general form of being related to variegated cows, it would follow that one must postulate a collective power even for words like *citragu* in order to cognize the specific form of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), namely the owner, as a possessor (*svāmitva*).

If it is argued: "Let there be no assumption of a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) in words such as *citrāṅga* (having variegated limbs); rather, let the master be presented there as the possessor through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the whole or through the indication of the final member [of the compound]," the author replies with the words "by indication alone," etc., stating that this can be easily asserted even in the case of the word *paṅkaja*. The meaning is that even in the word *paṅkaja*, the presentation of the lotus as a lotus (*padmatva*) can be asserted through the indication of the whole or through the indication of the suffix *-ja*.

And thus, the meaning is that the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) would not be established. He states "in this way" (*evam*) to indicate that the word *paṅkaja* is an illustration for other words as well that possess both etymological and conventional meanings (*yoga-rūḍha*). Regarding the term *rathakāra*, the phrase "the collective power would not be established" is to be supplied and connected by ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*). Now, one might object: "Let there be no collective power here; the understanding is experienced precisely through [the word] being the agent of the production of a chariot. Anticipating this doubt, he says "and thus" (*tathā ca*). [He cites the example: "In the rainy season, the *rathakāra* [should perform the Agnicayana]."

By this Vedic text, the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) for a chariot-maker (rathakāra) during the rainy season is prescribed. Here, the word *rathakāra* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring to a specific caste distinct from the three [twice-born] classes. As it has been stated: "A chariot-maker is born from a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother; a Māhiṣya is one produced from a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother; and a Karaṇī is one produced from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother. And with respect to this specific caste, the term *rathakāra* does not function according to its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "one who makes a chariot" (*rathaṃ karoti*).

Because the term "chariot-maker" (*rathakāra*) is observed to be applied even to one who does not actually construct a chariot, but belongs to that same class; thus, this word *rathakāra* is conventionally established (*ruḍha*) for a specific caste, being synonymous with *saudhanvana*. In the Vedic text, "In the rainy season, the chariot-maker [should perform the sacrifice]," it is precisely this specific caste that is understood by the word *rathakāra*, and not just anyone—a Brahmin or other—who constructs a chariot based on its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). This is because conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) takes precedence over etymological derivation (*yoga*), as it is more immediately present and thus more intrinsic (*antaraṅga*).

[Objection: But surely, by following the etymological meaning of the components [of the word], the term *rathakāra* should refer here only to a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), such as a Brahmin and so on. That being the case, since his consecration (*ādhāna*) is already established, there would be the economy of effort consisting merely in enjoining the rainy season as the occasion for the act of making a chariot. However, if the conventional meaning were accepted, then because he is distinct from the three castes, his consecration would not be established and would thus have to be enjoined, and furthermore, the study of the Veda required for it would have to be postulated—this would result in complexity (*gaurava*). [Reply: No, that is not so.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the meaning derived from etymological derivation (*yogartha*) arises only after one has reflected upon the roots, suffixes, their respective meanings, and their syntactic connection within the constituent parts of the derivative word; whereas the conventional meaning (*rūḍhyartha*) arises immediately upon hearing such a word, without any consideration of roots, suffixes, and so forth. Thus, because conventional meaning is stronger than etymological meaning, [the opponent] argued accordingly. However, all of this is contradicted by the case of the word *rathakāra*, which can be explained through its well-established etymological power alone without resorting to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or other means. With this intention, [the author] says: "Without metaphorical indication, by means of the established etymology... and so on, ending with "...it would be improper."

Now, it might be argued that figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) cannot be asserted at all in the case of the word *paṅkaja* (lotus). For instance, if the indication were in the whole (*samudāya*), then since there is no primary denotative power (*śakti*) in the whole, its primary meaning would not exist; and because the relation to the primary meaning—which constitutes indication—is thus impossible, indication itself would be utterly difficult to discern there. If, on the other hand, the indication were in the suffix *-ḍa*, then the meaning of the stem (*prakṛti*) could not be construed with it. Thus, in the absence of any scope for indication, one must simply admit, as a last resort, a primary denotative power in the whole.

In cases such as *rājapuruṣa* (king’s man), however, since the comprehension of the qualified meaning can be accomplished through the individual meanings of each constituent part alone, it is indeed inappropriate to postulate a power (*śakti*) for the whole. Furthermore, the objection regarding the contradiction with the *Rathakārādhikaraṇa* is difficult to maintain.

Based on the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the mantras beginning with "O Saudhanvanas, O Ṛbhus, you who possess divine vision; O Lord of Vows of the gods, I establish you with the vow of the Ṛbhus," it is understood that the qualification belongs specifically to the *rathakāra* (chariot-maker)—who is a member of a mixed caste (*anuloma-jāti*) synonymous with the *saudhanvana*—since a specific kind of installation is prescribed there for that conventional meaning. Furthermore, the postulation of a new [Vedic] knowledge (*apūrva-vidyā*) is not a defect, as a complexity resulting from the final outcome (*phalamukha-gaurava*) does not constitute a flaw.

In a collective expression such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), there is no evidence whatsoever that establishes such a [unitary] power (*śakti*) by virtue of which the meaning of the individual components would have to be abandoned; therefore, he says "another proof" (*sādhakāntaram*). This means that there is another proof for the abandonment of the meanings of the individual components. Regarding the phrase "of the properties of a compound" (*vṛttidharmāṇām*): the "properties of a compound" are those mentioned in the Bhāṣya, such as the non-connection with the gender and number of the qualifiers, and so forth.

In the compound *rājapuruṣa*, there is an absence of the qualification "of a wealthy king" (*ṛddhasya*) regarding the king; in *mṛgakṣīram* and similar cases, there is no perception of femininity in the word *mṛga* and so forth; and in the constituent word *rāja-* within the compound, there is no perception of a specific number, whether it be "of a king" (*rājñaḥ*) or "of kings" (*rājñām*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one should include cases such as *rājñaḥ puruṣo'śvaśca* (the king's man and horse), where the use of the conjunction *ca* is absent in the compound *rājapuruṣo'śvaśca*.

In order to establish such properties as [the meaning of] *vṛtti* (function/occurrence) through the formulation of various corresponding statements in each respective case, there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*); therefore, a collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) must be admitted. The point is that accepting a collective power is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) than the requirement of composing numerous individual statements. To clarify this very point, he says: "This is the sense" (*ayaṃ bhāvaḥ*). "[There would be] the connection with qualifiers and so forth. (*syād viśeṣaṇādyanvayaḥ*)—this refers to the objection raised by the opponent.

The point is that, if a specific capacity [of the compound] were not admitted, there would be a usage such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) just as there is the usage "the man of the wealthy king" (*ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*). He states the reason for the connection with the qualifier by saying "by the word 'king'. Regarding the term "independently": in a sentence, once the referents of "king" and so forth have been presented by the words "king" and so forth, they subsequently connect with one another through the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors; thus, the respective meanings are presented by the words "king" and so forth in their own independence.

And likewise, when the king is construed with the person (*puruṣa*), then the qualifier "prosperous" (*ṛddha*) is construed with the king, because at that time the king is present independently. The point is that in the process of effecting the construction of a qualifier, the cause for the desired construction of a qualifier is the state of being known as not being a qualifier of anything else. For this alone is independence: namely, being known as not being a qualifier of anything else.

The phrase "by way of not being a qualifier of another" means "by way of not having attained the status of being a qualifier as defined by another. For this very reason, in cases such as "the jar is eternal," since jar-ness and the like are known to have attained the status of being a qualifier as defined by another [namely, eternity], the referent of the word "eternal" does not undergo syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with them.

And just as in a sentence, at the time of forming the connection with the king and so forth, because [the king] is known as not having attained the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) relative to anything else, the connection with the qualifier "wealthy" (*ṛddhasya*) indeed occurs there; likewise, even in the compound *rājapuruṣa*, since the king would have the connection with the qualifier "wealthy," the undesirable usage *ṛddhasya rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king's man of the wealthy [man]") would result.

This is the sense: according to the view that does not admit a distinct power (*śakti*) for the compound, just as in a sentence, in the compound as well, there exists a presentation (*upasthiti*) characterized by independence (*svātantrya*), consisting in the fact that the king is known as not having attained the status of being a qualifier relative to anything else.

However, if one postulates a power (śakti) residing in the composite whole (samudāya), then the understanding of word-meanings arising from the occurrence [of that whole] necessarily has as its object a qualified entity in which the members stand in a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified. Consequently, the king’s own referent is presented by the word "king" only as having attained the status of a qualifier relative to the man; thus, because the king lacks independent presentation, there can be no syntactic connection with qualifiers such as "wealthy" (*ṛddhasya*) and so forth—this is the intended meaning. In this way, unlike the case of "the king's man and the horse," one does not say "the king-man and the horse."

Because that which is known as a qualifier in one instance cannot be a qualifier again in another; thus, unlike the expression "the king's man and the wife," the expression "the king’s man and the wife" [of the same king] does not occur. This is because the man is presented precisely through his qualification by the king, and it is unestablished by linguistic convention (*avyutpanna*) that a further qualifier can relate to a qualificand already known as qualified by one of its own kind. However, the expression "the king’s man is handsome" (*rājapuruṣaḥ sundaraḥ*) certainly occurs, as there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*).

In this context, the intention is that the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the person, as determined by the eightfold beauty (*sundarī*), is simply "personhood" (*puruṣatva*) and not even the relation to the king. Therefore, the essential point is that a compound (*vṛtti*) certainly occurs even when the principal member (*pradhāna*) possesses a qualifier. Regarding the phrase "to prevent the restriction of compounds": if a compound were to occur only when there is semantic expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) as its capacity (*sāmarthya*), then, since the use of a sentence would necessarily be the default state, a compound that is initiated [only] when that expectancy exists would invariably exclude the sentence.

Therefore, in order to establish that [the compound] can optionally set aside that [other rule], the rule *vibhāṣā* would have to be formulated. However, under the view of *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning), since the compound is established in the absence of *ekārthībhāva*, and the sentence is established in the case of *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy), the governing heading *vibhāṣā* need not be formulated; the point is that because their domains are distinct, there is no possibility of the sentence being sublated by the compound. He raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*), etc., anticipating the thought that [the rule] has indeed already been formulated.

And thus, according to the statement "of those with qualifiers" (*saviśeṣaṇānām*), there is no connection of a qualifier with the king who is a constituent of the compound *rājapuruṣa*; nor is there the aforementioned defect that the sentence is permanently replaced by the compound. This is the intent of the objection. Regarding the view of those who accept *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning), he states that the rule *vibhāṣā* is established by reasoning, beginning with the words "when there is a desire to express mutual expectancy" (*vyapekṣāvivakṣāyām*). He further states that the rule beginning with "of those with qualifiers" (*saviśeṣaṇa*) is likewise established by reasoning, beginning with the words "in the case of a specific power" (*viśiṣṭaśaktau*).

The point is that since the meaning of "king" (rāja) and so forth is presented as already connected with another meaning [the minister], it constitutes only a part of the word-meaning (*padārthaikadeśatva*). Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility of connection": for in a compound (*vṛtti*), a subordinate term (*upasarjana*) expresses its own meaning as already connected with the meaning of another; yet, when it itself requires a qualifier, it possesses primacy (*prādhānya*). How, then, could primacy and subordinacy exist simultaneously? The meaning is that because of the contradiction between being primary and subordinate at once, the rule stating "when accompanied by a qualifier" (*saviśeṣaṇa*) is established by reason alone.

"From this very reason" means: because the state of having a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is accepted by the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*). "The refutation also" means: the refutation consisting in the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of having to formulate a collection of rules such as "the prohibition of the substitution of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* and of the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*) [does not apply] when there are various case-relations (*nānākāraka*). || 31 ||

He himself states the collection of faults resulting from the non-acceptance of *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning), as explained by the *Bhāṣya*, Kaiyaṭa, and others, beginning with the words "tathā" (so too). In expressions such as *dhavakhadirau* (the dhava and khadira trees) up to *saptaparṇa*, there is a sequential syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of these nine [words] with nine [concepts], starting with mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) and ending with distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). Thus, the meaning is that the meanings such as "concomitance" (*sāhitya*) and so forth, which are perceived in *dhavakhadirau* and similar cases, would have to be explicitly stated by the word itself.

In that regard, concerning a *dvandva* compound such as *dhava-khadirau*, the rule "a *dvandva* [is formed] in the sense of 'and' (*cārthe*)" implies that multiple *subanta* items occur in the sense of "and," and that this [aggregate] receives the designation *dvandva*. Thus, one must accept a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) and perform the prescription of the meaning; this constitutes complexity (*gaurava*).

Likewise, by the rule "nirādayaḥ krāntādyarthe," a compound consisting of a word beginning with *nir* and ending in the fifth case (ablative) occurs in the sense of "having gone beyond" (*krānta*) and so forth, and it receives the designation of a compound (*samāsa*). Thus, the teaching of the meaning must be formulated by means of distinct sentences, which is cumbersome. Furthermore, for cases such as *gaura-ratha* and others, one would have to postulate separate rules to prescribe those specific meanings, which is likewise cumbersome.

In this regard, in the case of *goratha*, the meaning is "a chariot yoked with oxen," which is a sense of conjunction (*yuktārtha*); in *ghṛtaghaṭa*, the meaning is "a jar filled with ghee," which is a sense of being full (*pūrṇārtha*); in *guḍadhānā*, the meaning is "parched grains mixed with molasses," which is a sense of mixture (*miśrārtha*); in *keśacūḍa*, the meaning is "one whose crest consists of a mass of hair," which is a sense of aggregation (*saṃghātārtha*); in *suvarṇālaṃkāra*, the meaning is "an ornament that is a modification of gold," which is a sense of transformation (*vikārārtha*); in *dvidaśā*, the meaning is "ten repeated twice" (twenty), whereby there is an elision of the suffix *suc*; [and] *saptaparṇa*.

In this context, the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is understood from the phrase "that which has seven leaves each" (*sapta sapta parṇāni yasya*). Thus, if one does not accept *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning) within a compound, there would be the flaw of unnecessary complexity resulting from the formulation of numerous unprecedented rules, such as "for those with qualifiers" (*saviśeṣaṇānām*) and "in a compound, elision must be stated" (*vṛttau ca lopo vaktavyaḥ*). With this intention, he says: "for the purpose of prohibiting [the use of] *ca* and so forth. [The phrase] "from *ca*" [is explained as follows].

Just as the use of the particle *ca* occurs in a sentence such as "the *dhava* and the *khadira* tree," so too its use would follow in a compound (*vṛtti*) such as *dhavakhadirau*; therefore, its elision must be prescribed. However, according to the view that the compound expresses a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), since a single meaning characterized as a collective whole emerges, the distinction [between the individual members] ceases. Consequently, because the expressed object—the conjunction (*samuccaya*) based on that distinction—is absent, the indicator (*dyotaka*) of that conjunction is also absent; thus, the use of *ca* does not occur. This is the intended meaning.

Moreover, this possession of a specific power (*viśiṣṭa-śaktimatva*) by the *vṛtti* (compound) is indeed established by common worldly usage (*loka-siddha*), because there is no prescription of meaning in the technical treatise (*śāstra*) [itself], and because it is not observed in cases such as *acatura*. In the case of *dhava-khadira*, the compound has a specific power with respect to a specific meaning in the form of a collection of *dhava* and *khadira* trees; and since that power is established by common usage, the rule *cārthe dvandvaḥ* and so forth merely prescribes the designation "dvandva" after having restated the *vṛtti* in the sense of "ca. Thus, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in the view of *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning).

In the theory of expectancy (*vyapekṣāvāda*), it has already been stated previously that there is the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) due to sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*), since even the qualified meaning would have to be prescribed. This should likewise be understood for subsequent cases such as *niṣkauśāmbi* and so forth. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*) following "the word *ca* and others," he provides examples such as *ghanaśyāma*. Regarding the phrase "of *iva* and others": because of the connection with the rule "there is elision here" (*atra lopaḥ*), the meaning is that elision must be stated. Regarding the phrase "and of those mentioned before": the meaning is that in cases such as *niṣkauśāmbi*, the elision of words such as *krānta* (in *niṣkrānta*) must be stated.

The cognition of the qualified object (*viśiṣṭārthabodha*) is: "one who possesses a blackness similar to the blackness found in a cloud. Likewise, when the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one whose gait is like that of a swan," the cognition of the qualified object—provided that the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is accepted—is: "one who is the agent of a gait similar to the gait performed by a swan. Thus, the point is that since the meaning of the particle *iva* is included within the meaning of the composite whole, its non-usage is already established. He says, "another objection," because these objections will be refuted later; [he refers to it as] "the destruction of many linguistic usages" (*bahuvyutpattibhañjana*).

He clarifies the refutation itself with the words "In this regard, the intention is as follows," and so on. The meaning is that the cognition of ownership and the like is established by experience; for from the analytical sentence *citrā gāvo yasya* ("one whose cows are variegated"), there arises a cognition in which the referent of the word *go* (cow) is the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*), namely, "one whose cows are variegated. However, from the compound (*samāsa*), there arises a cognition in which the relation to the variegated cows is the qualifier and the referent of the other word (*anyapadārtha*)—the owner of the variegated cows—is the primary qualificand. Thus, the cognition of ownership and so forth is established by experience.

One might object: "In the compound *citraguḥ*, through the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there would be the cognition of the intended meaning, namely the owner of the brindled cow. To this, he raises the doubt with the words "not so" (*na ca*). He provides the resolution with the words "because that is impossible" (*tad-asambhavāt*). This means: because it is impossible to obtain the intended meaning through indication.

The point is this: although in the case of *citragu* (the "owner of brindled cows") it might be possible to somehow obtain the sense of ownership and so forth through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), in cases such as *prāptodaka* ("to whom water has come"), it is impossible to obtain the intended meaning through indication; therefore, the derivation is not universally maintained by means of indication, and thus resorting to indication in *citragu* is improper. From the sentence *prāptam udakaṃ yam*, the understanding is that "water is the agent of the attainment whose object is [the person]"; whereas from the compound, the understanding is that "the village is the object of the attainment whose agent is water."

In that case, if from the very beginning there were a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of "water" in the word *udaka*, then because water would be only one part of the referent (*padārtha*), the agent who has attained the referent already attained could not be connected to it; therefore, he says: "non-different from the agent of attainment. Since the root *āp* preceded by *pra* has the sense of "going," the suffix *kta* denotes the agent; thus, the meaning is "the agent of the action of attaining. And the meaning is that the agent, which is the referent of the suffix *kta*, is connected to "water" through non-difference. [This applies] even in the case of secondary signification.
