However, since it is accepted that the connection of kārakas with the action occurs only by way of the meaning of the case-ending (vibhakti), the meaning of the phrase *śubhreṇa* is: "the action which characterizes the instrumentality residing in that instrument which is non-different from the referent of the word *śubhra*. It should be understood that precisely because the meaning of the case-ending serves as an intermediary, there is no violation of the rule stating that the direct, distinct connection between the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is unestablished.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that if there were no mutual connection between the qualifier and the qualified in the phrase "with white rice," then there would be no delimitation between the referent of the word "white" and the referent of the word "rice"; consequently, even under the injunction "one should worship Śiva with white rice," it would follow that one could worship Śiva with black rice or with any other white substance whatsoever.

In both words denoting the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), the instrument (*karaṇa*) understood from the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) connects independently with the act of worship; thus, after the distinct cognitions "one should worship with the white [substance]" and "one should worship with rice," a mental connection between the two as qualifier and qualified is admitted. This very [connection] is called *pārṣṇika* or *pārṣṭhika* (posterior) connection.

Therefore, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), that which is white is indeed rice, and that which is rice is indeed white; thus, because there is no fault—since the understanding is that the worship has Śiva as its object and rice inseparable from white as its instrument through mutual delimitation (*pariccheda*)—this is the intended meaning. "Delimitation" means the determination of an object in its specific form.

For this very reason, in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, regarding the scriptural injunction "He purchases Soma with a reddish-brown, yellow-eyed, one-year-old [cow]," the three words beginning with "with the reddish-brown" (*aruṇayā*)—each expressing an instrument (*karaṇa*) denoted by the third case—are construed independently within the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of purchasing. Thus, one should effect the Soma by means of a purchase that is itself accomplished by those productive operations which have "reddish-brownness" as their instrument, "yellow-eyed-ness" as their instrument, and "one-year-old-ness" as their instrument.

It should be understood that the Mīmāṃsakas accept that the subsequent (pārṣṭhika) cognition of non-difference—namely, that "I shall buy [the cow] from you," based on the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra, and that the cow qualified by redness (*āruṇya*) is the very same one endowed with yellow eyes, and that very same one qualified by being one-year-old—is consistent due to the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). And so it is said: "And likewise" (*tathā ca*); this means that since the presence (*upasthiti*) produced by the case-ending following the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) must necessarily be a cause as a qualifier for the cognition whose object is the meaning of the nominal stem. "Because of the impossibility of syntactic connection" (*anvayāsaṃbhavāt*).

The meaning is that in a compound (*samāsa*), because there is no case-ending (*vibhakti*), the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the meanings of the prior and subsequent members—such as "king" and "servant" in *rājapuruṣa*—is possible. Regarding the phrase "of the aggregate" (*samudāyasya*): it means of the aggregate in the form of a compound such as *rājapuruṣa*. Regarding "power" (*śakti*): the meaning is that a power in the form of the signifier-signified relationship (*vācyavācakabhāva*) must necessarily be admitted with respect to the referent, such as the "servant," as qualified by the relation to the "king" and so forth. He states "furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*) to show that in every compound, without the acceptance of a specific power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*), the intended meaning cannot be established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound such as *rājapuruṣa*, there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the first member due to its primacy. Having raised the alternative as to whether this [indication] pertains to the related object (*saṃbandhin*) or to the relation (*saṃbandha*), he refutes the first position by stating "because it contradicts the [author's own] commentary. According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the compound *rājapuruṣa* has its primary denotative power (*śakti*) upon the person who is related to the king through the relation of ownership; thus, the cognition arises that the person possesses ownership as defined by the lordship residing in the king—that is, a cognition produced by a relation of difference in the form of the master-servant relationship.

The cognition "the man of the king" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) arises from the sentence "the man of the king is exactly such [as previously described]," because this sentence is an analysis (*vivaraṇa*) of the compound *rājapuruṣa*. An analysis is the explanation of the meaning of a word by means of other words having the same meaning; that is to say, it is the state of being an analytical sentence (*vigrahavākyatva*).

And the state of being an *vigraha* (analytic expansion) belongs to a sentence that has the same meaning as the compound, or to a sentence that causes the understanding of the meaning of the compound. This being the case, if one maintains that in examples such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("king's man"), there is a cognition of non-difference—namely, "a man non-different from [one] possessing a relation to the king"—arising precisely through the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *rājan* with respect to its relatum, then such a cognition cannot be due to secondary signification; for it would contradict the cognition produced by the explanatory sentence (*vivaraṇavākya*), which takes the form: "the substratum [of the relation] has the relation to the king as its qualifier" (*rājasaṃbandhaprakārakāśrayatvasaṃsargavān*). Thus, there is no secondary signification.

[Objection: Is it not correct? However, the point is that one must admit that the expressive power (*śakti*) of the compound *rājapuruṣa* resides precisely in the person related to the king through the relation of ownership (*svatva-saṃsarga*). [Reply: But surely, having the same meaning as the constituent members (*samāsa-samānārthakatva*) does not mean that the compound produces a cognition in which there is a particular qualificandum and a particular qualifier by means of a particular relation; rather, it means producing a cognition in which there is that same qualificandum and that same qualifier by means of that same relation.

If that were the case, then expressions such as *vyākaraṇam adhīte* (he studies grammar) and *pacati* (he cooks) would fail to be analyzed as derivative (*taddhita*) and primary (*kṛt*) suffixal formations like *vaiyākaraṇaḥ* (grammarian) and *pācakaḥ* (cook), because they would not possess the capacity to generate a cognition whose object is the meaning that is the object of a compound-generated cognition. Rather, [the definition of a compound] is the capacity to generate a cognition whose object is the meaning that is the object of a compound-generated cognition; and this is indeed absent in the present case, because the expression *rājñaḥ puruṣasya* (of the king’s man) generates a cognition whose object is the relation between the king and the man, which is the object of a compound-generated cognition. Therefore, he says: "Otherwise... (*anyathā*).

The meaning is: provided that the nature of the analytical statement (*vigraha*) consists solely in generating a cognition of the object that is the referent of the cognition produced by the compound. In other words, there is an absence of identity of meaning with the compound. "Therefore" means: from the explanatory sentence in the form of an analysis. It is established by experience that the power (*śakti*) of the compound is determined precisely through such analysis. And that experience is only consistent when there is a rule of identity of meaning between the analysis and the word being analyzed.

The point is that if one were to accept that even something not synonymous can function as a *vivaraṇa* (explanatory paraphrase), then the rule that a *vivaraṇa* must be synonymous with the term being explained would be violated; consequently, the determination of the meaning of a word based on the testimony of experts (*abhiyuktokta*) through such *vivaraṇas* would become impossible. Thus, the conclusion that the suffix *ākhyāta* denotes "effort" (*yatna*) because it is paraphrased by the verb *karoti*, which denotes "fruit" (*phala*), and so forth, would be undermined. Alternatively, the point is that the well-established empirical fact—that a syntactic analysis (*vigrahavākya*), such as "the king's man," serves to determine the meaning conveyed by the resulting compound—would be destroyed.

He rejects the final alternative—that there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in relation to the word *rāja*—on the grounds that it would lead to an undesirable consequence (*bodhaprasaṅgāt*). The meaning is as follows: if there were indication in relation to the connection, then the connection with the king, which is indicated by the word *rāja*, being the referent of a noun (*nāmārtha*), would be construed with the person (*puruṣa*) only through identity (*abheda*), and not through the relation of substratumhood (*āśrayatā*) such that "the person is the locus of the king's connection. Consequently, the cognition would result in "the person is non-different from the connection with the king" through identity alone, and not through a relation of difference. This is the intended sense.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that for the cognition of non-difference between a name and its referent, the requirement of identical case-endings (*samānavibhaktikatva*) is the regulating factor? Since that is absent here, how can it be claimed that there arises the cognition 'the person whose nature is the relation with the king'? To this, he says: "viruddhavibhakti... and so forth.

The point is this: since there is a deviation in cases such as *dadhīti dadhi* (where the word *dadhi* follows [the particle] *iti* and lacks a case-ending) and *secanakṛdvārī* (where both members lack case-endings), it is impossible for "having the same case-ending" (*samānavibhaktikatva*) to be the cause for the cognition of non-difference (*abheda*) between the meanings of two nouns. Therefore, one must accept that "the absence of contradictory case-endings" (*viruddhavibhaktirāhitya*) alone is the cause for the cognition of non-difference.

The phrase "of the two meanings of nominal stems" (*prātipadikārthayoḥ*) is stated in order to exclude the relation of identity (*abheda*) between the meaning of a verbal root and the meaning of a nominal stem—which possess conflicting case-endings—in examples such as *stokaṃ pacati* ("he cooks slightly"). Consequently, for the production of a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) where the meaning of a nominal stem is the qualifier (*prakāra*) related by the relation of identity (*abheda-saṃsarga*), the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a name that lacks a conflicting case-ending, acting as the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā-sambandhena*). Since such causality exists in the case of the meaning of the subsequent member of a compound like *rājapuruṣaḥ* (e.g., the person, *puruṣa*), the relation of identity would be unavoidable.

The intended meaning [of the objection] is as follows: One might argue that the causal relation stated—namely, that for the cognition of non-difference where the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is the qualifier, the cause is the presentation produced by two nominal stems lacking contradictory case-endings—is also untenable. For in the expression *caitrasya sutasya dhanam* ("the wealth of Caitra’s son"), since the words *caitra* and *suta*, which denote the qualifier and the qualified respectively, are followed by the same case-ending (the genitive), they lack contradictory case-endings; consequently, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of an unwanted cognition of non-difference between Caitra and his son. To this, we say: no.

The phrase "having a conflicting case-ending" (*viruddhavibhakti*) means having a case-ending with a conflicting meaning, that is to say, a case-ending with a distinct meaning. Thus, the intended sense is that the absence of case-endings with distinct meanings is the governing factor (*tantrya-niyāmaka*) for the cognition of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*). However, in the expression *caitrasya sutasya dhanam* ("the wealth of Caitra’s son"), the two case-endings do not have the same meaning; rather, they have distinct meanings, because the meaning of one is "being produced" (*janyatva*) while the meaning of the other is "ownership" (*svatva*). Therefore, there is no undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-difference between Caitra and his son.

This is the intended meaning. It should be understood that although both genitive endings in the expression "the king's man's wealth" (rājñaḥ puruṣasya dhanam) denote ownership, there is no fault because those two instances of ownership are distinct due to the difference in their respective relata (nirūpaka).

Alternatively, the meaning of the expression *viruddhavibhakti* (having different case-endings) is exactly as it is heard [in the literal sense]. In order to exclude the relation of identity (*abhedānvaya*) in cases such as *rājñaḥ puruṣasya dhanam* ("the wealth of the king's servant"), one must accept the aforementioned causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) for the cognition of the relation between the meanings of two nominal stems (*prātipadika*), without including the meaning of the case-ending. For example, in the case of *ṛddhasya rājñaḥ* ("of the wealthy king"), there is a relation between the meanings of the words *ṛddha* and *rājan* without including the meaning of the genitive ending in *ṛddhasya*. Or likewise, in compounds such as *rājapuruṣa*, [the relation is understood] precisely without including the meaning of the case-ending.

With the intention that the relation between the meanings of the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) is established precisely there, and that the previously mentioned linguistic capacity (*vyutpatti*) consisting of the nature of cause and effect must be accepted in that very context, he says "it has been explained," and so forth. "For this very reason" means: for the very reason that one accepts a specific power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) which is the cause for the absence of separate presentation (*pṛthag-upasthiti*) in a compound (*samāsa*).

The meaning is as follows: when two things stand in the relation of qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*), such that there is a person who possesses a qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a mode-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in the king, this resulting specific object (*viśiṣṭārtha*) is said to have "power" (*śakti*) [in the word], which is called "power for the qualified" (*viśiṣṭaśakti*). Regarding the phrase "of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer": by the sentence "The first consumption belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer," the act of consuming qualified by "firstness" is enjoined with reference to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer, namely, the Hotṛ priest.

[Objection: "Surely, since the eating of the remnants of the oblation by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is already established by the scriptural injunction, let only the priority [of that eating] be enjoined for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), rather than enjoining a qualified action (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), which involves complexity (*gaurava*). To this, he replies with the passage beginning "bhakṣam uddiśya" and ending with "na yuktam. He states the reason for its being improper in the passage beginning with "ekaprasaratā... and so forth.

The term *ekaprasaratā* refers to the state of two meanings having a single flow (*ekaprasara*)—that is, an entry into a single grammatical operation (*ekavṛtti*). The meaning is that a breach of this [state] would occur; for if that were the case, because the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) would be obstructed, the compound *prathamabhakṣaḥ* would not be possible.

For the constituent words of a compound, acting together through a single function (*vṛtti*), express one specific, unified meaning; therefore, in accordance with the speaker's intention regarding that single meaning, it must be understood as either the subject (*uddeśyatva*) or the predicate (*vidheyatva*). For example, in "The *dhava* and *khadira* trees are beautiful" (*dhavakhadirau sundarau*) or "These two trees are the *dhava* and *khadira*" (*imau vṛkṣau dhavakhadirau*). However, it is not appropriate to grasp the status of subject for some part of that [unified] meaning and the status of predicate for another part.

Where there is a separate presentation of the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) by means of two distinct words, there such a connection [of the former with the latter] occurs. However, in a compound (*samāsa*), because of the force of "single-meaningness" (*ekārthībhāva*), there is no separate presentation from the word; and since it has been stated by the authors of the *Laghu-mañjūṣā* that when there is no separate presentation, there can be no connection in the form of a subject-predicate relationship.

Furthermore, if in the phrase *prathamabhakṣaḥ* (the first eating), priority (*prāthamya*) were intended to be predicated with respect to the referent of the word *bhakṣa* (eating) contained within the compound, then those two words expressing that [priority] could not possibly enter into a single compound formation. However, since a compound has already been formed in the sentence *vaṣaṭkartuḥ prathamabhakṣaḥ*, it must be understood that—in accordance with that [compound]—it is the qualified meaning as a whole that is intended to be the predicate here, according to the constraints of the linguistic expression. This is how it should be understood.

For this very thing is what is called the "frustration of the single semantic thrust" (*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*), namely, the frustration of the capacity consisting in the generation of a single qualified cognition. It is stated in the Mīmāṃsā that when there is a connection by way of the relationship between the subject and the predicate (*uddeśya-vidheyabhāva*), separate cognitions are the cause [of such a connection], and thus, in the case of such a connection, that capacity is frustrated. He says "in the third [chapter]"—the meaning is: in the tenth topic (*adhikaraṇa*) of the fifth section (*pāda*) of the third chapter, in the sūtra: "And one should consume [the soma] because of the *vaṣaṭ* call."

It has been stated that precisely for fear of violating the principle of *ekaprasaratā* (the unity of a single expressive thrust), it is not appropriate in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the *citrayā*" (*citrayā yajeta*) to enjoin the quality of variegation (*citratva*) by means of the single word *citrayā* while simultaneously referring to the feminine agent (*strī-kāraka*). To explain: *vṛtti* (the function of a word) is the relationship between a word and its meaning, taking the form of either *śakti* (denotative power) or *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function). In the present case, the word *citrayā* possesses a denotative power (*śakti*) directed toward an object qualified by two properties: variegation and femininity. Thus, both variegation and femininity enter into this single *vṛtti*, which consists of such a denotative power.

In this case, there would be a breakdown [of the grammatical rule] if "variegatedness" (*citratvam*) were enjoined here by way of restating the feminine agent. For it is necessary that the denotative power (*śakti*) of the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) arise separately. Here, however, because both femininity and variegatedness enter into a single denotative power, the relationship of subject and predicate between them is not possible; such is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "with three parts" (*tryaṅgaiḥ*): it is heard in the context of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*)—namely, "one sacrifices to Sviṣṭakṛt with three parts."

In this context, since the sacrifice of eleven limbs is prescribed by such injunctions as "he cuts off from the heart first," and since the principle of "the modification follows the model" (prakṛtivadvikṛtiḥ) applies, it would follow that the sacrifice should be performed with all eleven limbs; it is for this reason that the following sentence is commenced.

Having raised the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument that, for the sake of parsimony, a threefoldness is enjoined there by reference to the constituent parts (aṅga), and not another constituent part qualified by threefoldness because that would involve the complexity of a qualified injunction—the meaning [of the siddhāntin] is as follows: if, here in the phrase "tryaṅgaiḥ," threefoldness were to be enjoined with reference to the meaning of the word "aṅga" contained within the compound, then those two words expressing that [meaning] could not even find a place in a single compound; this implies that the unity of semantic flow (ekaprasaratā) would be destroyed.

Since the compound *tryaṅgaiḥ* has indeed already been formed, it is understood according to that [compound] that, by the very nature of the word (*śabdamaryādā*), it is precisely another member characterized by the number three that is the object of the injunction (*vidheya*). In that case, since the meaning qualified by the attribute is not obtained from any other source, the result is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) alone. However, when some part of that [qualified object] is already obtained from elsewhere, the qualified injunction results in its application to the unobtained portion, according to the maxim of "distinguishing between what is obtained and what is not obtained" (*prāptāprāptaviveka-nyāya*); this is a separate matter.

Just as in compound words such as *rājapuruṣa* (king’s man), the understanding of the word-meaning arises by virtue of a collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) rooted in expectancy, and this pertains to two things that stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), so too is the apprehension of that specific power (*viśiṣṭaśaktigraha*) as follows: "The compound word *rājapuruṣa*, etc., has its power [denotative function] with respect to a person who possesses a connection to a king. In that case, by the maxim of "distinguishing between what is already obtained and what is not yet obtained" (*prāptāprāptavivekanyāya*), that specific power culminates in the aspect of the relation as well as in the aspects of the qualifier and so forth.

The meaning is that, as stated in the *Mañjūṣā*, the cognition [of the parts] occurs through the very powers of the constituent parts already established for [words like] "king" (*rājan*) and so on; however, according to the internal logic of the word (*śabdamaryādā*), a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) must be accepted in such cases. Thus, in the present instance, a qualified injunction in the form of an injunction for another limb qualified by the number three is accepted. And those other limbs have been shown by the author of the *Kalpasūtra*: "The right shoulder, the left hip, and the third, the rectum—these are for the *Sviṣṭakṛt*."

Therefore, it has been stated that the Sviṣṭakṛt offering should be made with the three portions remaining from the sacrifice; he indicates that point [in the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra] by saying "and in the tenth. This means that in the third section of the seventh pāda of the tenth adhyāya, this was established as the final conclusion (*siddhāntita*) in the sūtra beginning with "from the sacrificial remains—by the three portions, etc.

Furthermore, this is consistent with the theory of qualified denotation (*viśiṣṭa-śakti-pakṣa*), because, just as both the jar and the jar-ness are presented from the word "jar," the eating qualified by primacy and the portions qualified by the number three are presented through that very qualified denotation; thus, their connection in the form of subject and predicate within the sentence-meaning would otherwise be impossible.

The intended meaning is as follows: if the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) were not admitted, then even in a compound, there would be a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) based on the relationship between the subject and the predicate (*uddeśya-vidheya-bhāva*), as in the sentences "the first [portion] is to be eaten" or "with three parts," which would clearly contradict the established conclusions (*adhikaraṇa*) of the Mīmāṃsā school. He states that the commencement of the *aruṇā* section is justified precisely because the acceptance of a qualified power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) in compounds is necessary: "And it is consistent with the *aruṇā* [section], otherwise..."

The point is that if one does not accept a distinct power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) in a compound, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself would be impossible, and consequently, the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the "red" quality) would become untenable. To explain: in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in proximity to the act of purchase: "He buys Soma with a red, yellow-eyed, one-year-old cow."

Regarding this, there arises a doubt: is the word *aruṇayā* connected with the act of purchase (*kraya*), or is it connected through syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) with all the substances mentioned in the context, such as the cups (*graha*) and the bowls (*camasa*)? In this regard, the word *aruṇā* denotes a specific color, which is a quality (*guṇa*). Furthermore, its status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) for the action of purchasing is contradicted when applied to a specific color, because a color is incorporeal (*amūrta*).

Having separated [the term *aruṇayā*] from this sentence, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is advanced that—by means of the third-case hearing (*tṛtīyā-śruti*)—the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) is enjoined by restating the substances belonging to the context, such that one should effect the substance which is the means for the *apūrva* of the Jyotiṣṭoma by means of the quality of redness. In response to this, [the established view is stated]: the cognition of compatibility (*yogyatā*) is not a cause for verbal comprehension; rather, it is merely the case that the certainty of incompatibility acts as an obstacle to comprehension. Furthermore, compatibility consists in possessing the properties that serve as the basis for mutual syntactic connection (*parasparānvaya*), as in the case of "sprinkle with milk" (*payasā siñcati*).

In the case of "he sprinkles with water," the definition is satisfied because the property of being water (*jalatva*), which is the cause for the connection with the act of sprinkling, exists in the water; likewise, the property of being the act of sprinkling (*sekatva*), which is the cause for the connection with the instrument of water, exists in the action of sprinkling. However, in the expression "he sprinkles with fire" (*vahninā siñcati*), there is no verbal comprehension because of the certainty of semantic inappropriateness (*ayogyatāniścaya*), since the property of being a liquid substance (*dravadravyatva*), which is the cause for the connection with the act of sprinkling, does not exist in fire.

And in the present case, since there is a rule that factors of action (*kāraka*) must connect only with the action, and because the absence of a certainty regarding semantic incompatibility exists, the connection of "redness" (*āruṇya*) with the act of purchasing is established; however, its subsequent connection with the substance is a secondary matter, so there is no fear of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This is how the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) has been established. In this regard, it is not possible for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) to be stated [as it was previously].

Even if one does not accept a distinct power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) in a compound, since the words *piṅgākṣī* (tawny-eyed) and *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old) would have "tawny-ness," "eye-ness," "oneness," and "year-ness" as their denotable meanings, these too—being immaterial—could not possibly function as instruments for the act of buying. Consequently, the instrument for the act of buying could not be obtained from this sentence; thus, there is no possibility of even suspecting a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) regarding the quality of "redness" (*āruṇya*).

Furthermore, since there is no basis for suspecting a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) when the prescription of substances indicated by all three [words] is possible—and because the designation of substances through figurative indication (*lākṣaṇika*) is equally applicable to all three, namely the two *bahuvrīhi* compounds and the word "red" (*aruṇa*)—there is no determining factor (*vinigamaka*) to establish that the two *bahuvrīhis* alone prescribe the substance while the word "red" does not. Moreover, it is impossible for [the redness] to be included in the context (*prakaraṇa*) through a syntactical split.

For instance, even in the case of a *prakaraṇa* (context), a connection with actions is impossible because [the word] is formless (*amūrta*), and a connection with substances is also impossible because it is not a *kāraka* (participant in an action). Therefore, since the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is untenable, and to avoid the consequence of nullifying the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, he says—with the intention that a specific power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) in a compound is necessary—"It has been explained at length in the *Bhūṣaṇa*. This means it has been summarized in detail in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*. Let the details suffice.

The contradiction with the Jaimini-sūtras on the part of the followers of Jaimini (the Mīmāṃsakas) is utterly improper; therefore, they must necessarily accept the theory of the specific power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) in a compound. This is the meaning; enough with further elaboration. || 34 ||

Indeed, one might object that having established the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) with respect to the Mīmāṃsakas and others, the statement "the verbal suffixes, secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), and kṛt suffixes," etc., would be inconsistent with the preceding text. To dispel this doubt and demonstrate its consistency, he says, beginning with "rājapuruṣa" and so on. Regarding the phrase "and he is a king": here, although the word *rāja* is part of the analytical sentence (*vigraha-vākya*), it refers specifically to the one related to the king; thus, the intention is that the analytical sentence’s identity of meaning with the compound remains intact. This is precisely the analysis (*vigraha*).

By the use of the particle *eva*, the analysis "the king’s man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*)—where the king is already established—is excluded. Now, one might argue: "Even if the analysis is with a word ending in the genitive case, the word *rāja-* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean 'one related to the king,' while the genitive case itself signifies non-difference (*abheda*); thus, the status of having the same meaning as the compound is indeed maintained. This is not correct. For in the analytical statement (*vigraha*), non-difference—which is not specified by the relation to the king—is manifested primarily as the meaning of the genitive case, whereas in the compound, it is not manifested in that way.

Furthermore, there is no evidence that the genitive case has the sense of non-difference (*abheda*). If it is argued that the genitive is used for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) and thus there is no loss of its having the same meaning as the compound, that too is not correct; for since the genitive is prescribed only in the sense of a relation (*saṃbandha*), its use for the sake of mere grammatical correctness is untenable. By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "this belongs to the cow" (*gavāmayam eva*), the well-known analytical statement (*vigraha*) "one whose cows are variegated" (*citrā gāvo yasya*) is excluded. He states the reason for using the analysis "this [wealth] of variegated cows" (*citrāṇāṃ gavām ayam*) by saying "because they have the same meaning" (*samānārthatva*).

From the compound *citraguḥ*, there arises a cognition in which the owner of cows (*gosvāmī*)—who is non-different from the variegated ones (*citrābhinna*)—is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and the variegated cows (*citrago*) are the qualifier (*prakāra*). Since such a cognition, having that very qualifier and qualificand, arises from the aforementioned analytical statement (*vigraha*), it is more appropriate to have the analytical statement *citragavām ayam* (this belongs to the variegated cows) as the expansion of the compound, because a compound and its analytical statement must possess identical meanings. This is because of the rule that the analytical statement and that which is being analyzed must have identical meanings; otherwise, the determination of the expressive power (*śakti*) would not be possible from the analytical statement. This is the intended meaning.

One might object: "Since the technical designation *bahuvrīhi* is prescribed for a compound consisting of multiple words ending in the nominative case when they denote something other than their own primary referents (*anyapadārtha*), it follows that in the absence of such a designation, the sentence composed of those nominative-ending words must necessarily remain as the analytical expansion (*vigraha*). Therefore, it is more appropriate for such a sentence to serve as the *vigraha*, rather than one composed of words ending in the genitive case. Anticipating this objection, the author provides the following resolution, beginning with the words "Even though" (*yadyapi*). [The phrase] "is obtained from the *sūtra*" refers to the following rule: Pāṇini 2.2.24: *anekam anyapadārthe* (When multiple words ending in the nominative case denote something other than their own primary referents, they form a *bahuvrīhi* compound). This rule establishes that the *bahuvrīhi* designation applies specifically to the state of being a compound. Consequently, a sentence that is not a compound cannot be designated as a *bahuvrīhi*. Since the *vigraha* is intended to reveal the meaning of the compound, it is necessary for it to possess the same structural characteristics as the compound itself; thus, the *vigraha* must consist of words ending in the genitive case. This is further supported by the fact that the *samāsānta* suffixes (such as *ac*) and accentual rules apply only to compounds, not to mere sentences. Therefore, the *vigraha* of a *bahuvrīhi* is properly expressed through a sentence containing genitive endings.

The meaning of the *Bhāṣya* statement "the remainder from the triplet" (*trikataḥ śeṣaḥ*) is that the "remainder" refers to that triplet for which a specific compound has not been stated; and such a triplet is precisely *su*, *au*, and *jas*. The phrase "ending in the nominative" means consisting of words ending in the nominative case. Regarding the word "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*), since compounding is optional, it means in the case of its absence. "The sentence" (*vākyam*) means a sentence such as "he whose cows are brindled" (*citrā gāvo yasya*).

Although the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and the absence of compounding (*samāsābhāva*) would make the sentence "the king’s man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) unavoidable, nevertheless, it is utterly impossible for such a sentence to function as an *anvaya-vigraha* (analytic expansion). He states this with the words "because of having different meanings" (*bhinnārthatvāt*). The meaning is that the sense of such a sentence differs from the sense of the compound (*samāsārtha*).

From the compound *rājapuruṣaḥ*, there arises a cognition characterized by the relation of identity (*abheda-saṃsarga*) having the king as its qualifier; from the sentence *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*, there arises a cognition characterized by the relation of substratum (*āśrayatva-saṃsarga*) having the king’s connection as its qualifier; from the compound *citraguḥ*, there arises a cognition in the form "the owner of brindled cows," which has the meaning of the constituent members as qualifiers and the meaning of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) as the qualificand; and from the sentence *citrā gāvo yasya*, there arises a cognition in the form "he whose cows are brindled," which has the meaning of the external referent as the qualifier and the meaning of the constituent members as the qualificand.

The point is that because the meanings of a sentence (*vākya*) and a compound (*samāsa*) differ from one another due to the production of distinct cognitions, "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) and "one whose cows are variegated" (*citrā gāvo yasya*) cannot function as the *vigraha* (analytic expansion) for their respective compounds. Likewise, in cases such as "one to whom water has come" (*prāptodakaḥ*), the phrase "by whom water was obtained" (*prāptam udakaṃ yam*) does not serve as the *vigraha*; rather, it is only the aforementioned [compound] itself that is the *vigraha*.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that only phrases such as "he is a king and a man" (*rājā cāsau puruṣaśca*), "this belongs to variegated cows" (*citrāṇāṃ gavām ayam*), or "this is of the water that has been obtained" (*prāptasyodakasyāyam*) constitute the analytical expansion (*vigraha*), because the compound possesses the same meaning as its constituent parts. They refute them incidentally with the words: "the verb [is the expansion] of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) and the primary derivative (*kṛt*). Thus, for a secondary derivative such as the suffix *ṭhak* prescribed in rules like "one who plays with that" (*tena dīvyati*), and for a primary derivative such as the suffix *aṇ* prescribed in "the suffix *aṇ* after an object" (*karmaṇyaṇ*), there exists a verbal form—a finite verb (*tiṅanta*)—which serves as the explanatory expansion and conveys the same meaning.

However, the meaning is that a reversal of the relationship between qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*) is observed between words ending in *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffixes and those ending in *tiṅ*. He demonstrates this very reversal with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*), etc. Regarding "dice-player" (*ākṣika*): by the rule *tena dīvyati*, the suffix *ṭhak* is added to the word *akṣa* to denote the agent of the act of playing. Regarding "potter" (*kumbhakāra*): by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*, when a direct object (*karman*) is the governing word (*upapada*), the suffix *aṇ* is added to the root *kṛ* to denote the agent. In the case of "dice-player," the understanding is that he is the substratum (*āśraya*) of an activity whose instrument (*karaṇa*) is the dice.

In the case of "he plays with dice" (*akṣair dīvyati*), where [the compound] is its analysis (*vigraha*), the understanding is that there is a productive urge (*bhāvanā*) conducive to playing, which has the dice as its instrument. In the case of "pot-maker" (*kumbhakāra*), the understanding is that there is a substratum of activity conducive to the production of a pot. And in the case of its analysis, "he makes a pot" (*kumbhaṃ karoti*), the understanding is likewise that there is a productive urge conducive to the production of a pot. He states the reason why the meaning of the analysis and the meaning of the term being analyzed differ: "in the case of a *kṛt* suffix," and so forth.

The meaning is that the "primacy"—that is, the status of being the primary qualificand—belongs to the factors denoted by those [words], such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, because of the rule that "the meanings of the base and the suffix [are related as qualifier and qualified]. And regarding the phrase "in the verb" (*ākhyāte ca*): the meaning is that in the verbal form ending in *tiṅ*, the "primacy"—that is, the status of being the primary qualificand—belongs to the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), because of the statement of Yāska: "The verb has the action as its primary element" (*bhāvapradhānam ākhyātam*). Regarding the phrase "even for the Mīmāṃsaka": the ellipsis is that he also accepts this reversal of the relationship between the qualificand and the qualifier. [This] does not contradict the nature of being an explanation (*vivaraṇatva*).

The point is this: just as it is accepted that a sentence which demonstrates the meaning of a *taddhita* or a *kṛt* suffix remains a "definition" (*vivaraṇa*) even if the roles of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) are reversed, so too it is possible for the sentence "one who has variegated cows" (*citrā gāvo yasya*) to function as a definition. Thus, the intended meaning is that "being a vigraha" consists solely in generating a cognition whose object is identical to the cognition generated by the compound (*vṛtti*), and not in generating a cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is identical to the cognition generated by the compound.

Furthermore, there is no obstacle to such analyses as "he whose cows are variegated" (*citrā gāvo yasya*) being the *vigraha* (etymological analysis). Moreover, regarding the analysis "this belongs to the variegated cows" (*citrāṇāṃ gavām ayam*), it would contradict the words of the Sage [Pāṇini] such as: "The *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*)," "A word other than one ending in the first case is compounded with a word expressing the agent or object," "The *bahuvrīhi* occurs in the sense of a case-ending other than the first," "The *bahuvrīhi* is the remainder (*śeṣa*)," and "The 'remainder' refers to that which is excluded from the three kārakas. Nor can it be argued that there is no contradiction with the aforementioned words of the Sage because only words ending in the first case are introduced into the *alaukika-vākya* (pre-compositional sentence), for [the analysis in question does not conform to this].

That which is non-worldly (*alaukika*)—namely, the entry of items ending in case-suffixes—is appropriate only for those very same items ending in case-suffixes once they have become established (*pariniṣṭhita*), because it is more fitting for them to enter [into the formation] when there is the possibility of conveying a worldly meaning; however, this does not apply to items ending in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). For it is improper to abandon what is present and instead imagine a worldly analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) composed of words that are not present. Even in cases like "one to whom there are variegated cows" (*citrā gāvo yasya*) imagined for the purpose of demonstrating the meaning of the compound, the understanding is precisely "related to variegated cows" (*citragosambandhī*), due to the reversal of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified.

The elders demonstrate that the term *citragu* ("one who has brindled cows") is used specifically to indicate a transposition [of the relationship], such that he for whom there are brindled cows is called *citragu*. In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra defining *sarvanāman*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is also shown as "those of which 'all' (*sarva*) is the first. Kaiyaṭa notes that because pronouns (*sarvanāman*) generally refer to the principal element, the expression *sa citraguḥ* indicates the predominance of the owner. For this very reason, they show the analysis of *māsajāta* ("born after a month") as "he for whom a month has passed since birth" (*māso jātasya yasya saḥ*).

In the sentence "citragavo yasya" (he whose cows are variegated), the understanding is that the one who possesses the connection with variegated cows is what is denoted by the word *citragu*. In cases such as "pacatīti pācakaḥ" (one who cooks is a cook), the understanding is that the word *pācaka* has the same meaning as the expression "pacati". Furthermore, from the analysis "pacati pākaṃ karoti" (he cooks, i.e., he performs the act of cooking), the understanding is that the word *pacati* denotes the action of cooking performed by a single agent; the same applies elsewhere. Thus, the author of the Mañjūṣā states that the identity of meaning between the derivative form (*vṛtti*) and its analytical expansion (*vigraha*) is perfectly clear. 35.

He prepares the preliminary argument (*bhūmikā*) for the sake of not undermining the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the *Niṣādasthapati* section, beginning with "But let it be so" and ending with "there would be no establishment. "Power" (*śakti*) means that in every compound there is a power residing in the qualified whole (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*). "Likewise, the analysis (*vigraha*)" means that the analysis in the form of "one whose cows are variegated" (*citrā gāvo yasya*) may also exist. "Because there is no difference in possessing power" means...

The meaning is that because there is no distinction—and thus equality—between "possessing power" (*śaktimattva*) and "possessing specific power" (*viśiṣṭaśaktimattva*), which both consist in the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), it would follow that the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* and the *karmadhāraya* compounds are equivalent. Regarding the phrase "the established conclusion" (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*): the established conclusion reached in that context was that, since the *karmadhāraya* is simpler than the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*, the word *niṣādasthapati* is a *karmadhāraya*; [if the above were true], that conclusion would not be consistent. Anticipating this objection, he says: "when the verbal cognition has reached its final form."

"And this is the verbal cognition that culminates. This means the verbal cognition that culminates—that is, which is established by the limits of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśakti*)—is the verbal cognition arising from the specific power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) of the compound (*samāsa*). Therefore, "this is not remote from that": that which is not remote from the compound is the proximate moment; the meaning is the moment immediately preceding the application of the technical designation "compound," which serves as the locus for the use of the ordinary procedural sentence (*laukikaprakriyāvākya*).

The meaning is that the relationship between the *antaraṅga* (internal) and *bahiraṅga* (external), which is established by taking into account the state of the application of a sentence involving an *alaukika-prakriyā-vākya* (unmanifested intermediate process) based on such a moment (*kṣaṇa*), is easily explained even in the case of a compound (*samāsa*). Thus, the sense is that there is no possibility of contradiction with the *Niṣādasthapati-adhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the "chief of the Niṣādas") due to the consideration of the *antaraṅga-bahiraṅga* relationship residing in the meaning of the *alaukika-prakriyā-vākya*, in accordance with the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*). Elucidating this very point, he says: "This is the sense," and so forth, ending with "the word *niṣādasthapati*."

The meaning is that this is found in the Vedic scripture (śruti) stating, "One should cause the Niṣāda-sthapati to sacrifice by means of this [rite]. "In the view of the power of the compound" means the established position (siddhānta) that the compound *niṣādasthapati* has a power (*śakti*) toward a qualified meaning consisting of *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meanings). "In the form of a Niṣāda" means a *karmadhāraya* compound whose sense is "a sthapati who is non-different from a Niṣāda. "And of the Niṣādas" means a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound whose sense is "a sthapati related to the Niṣādas. "Owned by a Niṣāda" [is the meaning].

The meaning is that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the referent of the external word (*anyapadārtha*) is "one for whom the *sthapati* (chief) is a *niṣāda*. The intention is that the word *sthapati* is a synonym for "master" (*svāmin*). Thus, the compound *niṣādasthapati* is multivalent (*nānārthaka*) because it possesses the denotative power (*śakti*) in all three aforementioned senses; for it is accepted that when there is an intended meaning (*tātparya*), a cognition arises of both one who is related to a *niṣāda* and one whose master is a *niṣāda*, and therefore its denotative power in those cases is also necessary. This is what is meant by "in the multivalent [sense]."

The meaning is: "when there is the presentation of multiple meanings through functions such as *śakti* (denotative power) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "from the speaker's intention" (*tātparyāt*): its meaning is that when a word like *hari*, which denotes multiple objects, is used, there arises a comprehension—that is, a certainty—of a specific [meaning] due to the speaker's intention, in accordance with the speaker's intended purpose. The phrase "by means of logic" (*nyāyena*) implies the completion of the sentence with: "when a doubt has arisen as to where the intention lies."

In the word *niṣādasthapati*, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is "extrinsic" (*bahiraṅga*) because it generates a cognition whose object is a meaning distinct from the perceived meaning of the sentence formed by its constituent parts, whereas the *tatpuruṣa* compound generates a cognition whose object is solely the perceived meaning of the sentence formed by its constituent parts.

In the case of *svaṃ niṣādasthapatiḥ*, it is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound. Regarding the two constituent words therein, the sentence formed by those two words—namely, "the chief (sthapati) of the Niṣādas" (*niṣādānāṃ sthapatiḥ*)—yields a meaning perceived as "a chief related to the Niṣādas. Because the tatpuruṣa generates a cognition whose object is precisely that meaning, it is more *antaraṅga* (proximate/internal) than the bahuvrīhi compound.

However, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, there is a sentence composed of its constituent members, such as "citrā gāvaḥ" (the cows are brindled). The meaning observed therein is "the cows are non-different from the brindled ones. Compared to that, the *anyapadārtha* (meaning of another word), which takes the form of the owner, is something additional. Since the *bahuvrīhi* generates the cognition of that much meaning, it is more complex (*bahiraṅga*) than the *tatpuruṣa*. Because the *tatpuruṣa* lacks the capacity to generate a meaning beyond the meanings of the words constituting the compound itself, it possesses simplicity (*lāghava*) relative to the *bahuvrīhi*.

The point is that, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, there is greater complexity (*gaurava*) compared to a *tatpuruṣa* because it generates the cognition of a referent distinct from the referents of the words constituting the compound. In the same way, it should be understood that a *karmadhāraya* is simpler than a genitive *tatpuruṣa*.

The meaning is as follows: because the meanings of the constituent words in a *karmadhāraya* compound are construed through identity (*abheda*), it generates a cognition whose object is a single referent; thus, compared to a *tatpuruṣa*, the *karmadhāraya* possesses parsimony (*lāghava*). In a genitive *tatpuruṣa* (*ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*), however, because the meanings of the constituent words are construed through difference (*bheda*), it generates a cognition whose objects are two distinct referents; thus, it possesses complexity (*gaurava*) relative to the *karmadhāraya*. Regarding the phrase "in that assumption" (*tatkalpanāyām*): the ellipsis (*śeṣa*) is to be supplied as "when the assumption of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) for the word *niṣādasthapati* has arisen."

It refers precisely to the meaning already present [in the mind]. According to the maxim that "when grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, it is improper to resort to non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*"), one assumes and determines that the intended meaning (the *tātparya*) conforms to the economy (*lāghava*) resulting from the immediate mental presence (*upasthiti*) of the *sthapati* who is a *niṣāda*, rather than a *sthapati* related to a *niṣāda*.

The summarized meaning is as follows: since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which consists in the generation of a cognition of a single object through non-differential connection, is possible, it is contrary to reason to have grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), which consists in the generation of a cognition of connection through a relation of difference. This is because, in a *karmadhāraya* compound, there is brevity (*lāghava*) due to the two words expressing only a single referent through non-differential connection; whereas in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there is prolixity (*gaurava*) due to the two words expressing two distinct referents separately through differential connection.

Now, one might object: "In the Mīmāṃsaka view, since there is no denotative power (*śakti*) in a compound, how can the term *niṣādasthapati* have multiple meanings? To this he says: "Even for others. This means even for those such as the Naiyāyikas who maintain the theory of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). "When there is an intention" means when there is an intention toward the sense of a genitive tatpuruṣa or other such compounds. "Just as in the case of 'Let him bring in the sticks'"—this is the illustration.

In this regard, just as in the case of the word *yaṣṭidhara* (staff-bearer), even though there is no impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) with the primary meanings of "staff" and "bearer," a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) is nevertheless applied to the staff-bearer due to the impossibility of the intended meaning (*tātparyānupapatti*), so too—in the case of the term *niṣādasthapati*—even though there is no impossibility of syntactic connection, a secondary signification toward the sense of a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound and the like is unavoidable due to the impossibility of the intended meaning. This is the sense. Consequently, although the word has multiple possible referents, the intended meaning is determined to be that of a *karmadhāraya* compound in accordance with whatever degree of parsimony (*lāghava*) occurs in the presentation of a particular meaning; such is the purport. || 36 ||

Thus ends the determination of the power of compounds (*samāsa-śakti-nirṇaya*) in the *Śāṅkarī*, a commentary on the *Śrī-Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, composed by Śaṅkara, the son of Raṅgabhaṭṭa; herein concludes the determination of power regarding compounds in the *Sārīya* exposition. (5)
The Essence of the Adornment of Grammar (Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra)
(Therein, the second part) || Now follows the determination of power (śakti).

Establishing the capacity (*śakti*) in each word by way of a relevant transition (*prasaṅga*), he prepares the ground with the words "on account of the occasion regarding capacity" (*śaktiprasaṅgāt*). The meaning is: because that which has been brought to mind on the occasion of defining the capacity of compounds cannot be neglected. "Of that" means "of the capacity. Capacity is the relation between a word and its referent.

The Naiyāyikas [hold that] this [power] consists either in a desire of God having the meaning as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*), in the form "this meaning is to be understood from this word," or in a desire of God having the word as its qualificandum, in the form "let this word convey this meaning. They designate this very thing as the "divine convention" (*īśvarīya-saṅketa*). Modern Naiyāyikas state that power is either the desire of God, or his knowledge, or his volition. To refute them, [the author] first demonstrates their nature [by stating]: "of the sense organs, with respect to their own objects..."

The meaning of this is as follows: just as the eyes and other sense organs possess an innate capacity (*yogyatā*)—consisting in their possessing a property that delimits their status as producers—for generating cognitions of objects such as color-form, independent of human effort; likewise, the innate relationship itself is the capacity for words regarding their meanings, being the property that delimits their status as producers of the cognition of those meanings. He states this with respect to each term, beginning with "of the sense organs"—meaning the eyes and so forth—and by the word "visual" (*cākṣuṣa*), he intends to include all direct perceptions such as gustatory perception and the like.

Regarding the statement "fitness is beginningless" (*anādir yogyatā*), the meaning to be understood is that its beginning does not exist; that very [fitness] is "power" (*śakti*). This means that power is precisely the nature of being the cause of cognition. However, others maintain that it is impossible for the relationship in the form of "power"—which is postulated because the production of a cognition regarding an object by a word unconnected to that object would otherwise be inexplicable—to consist in the capacity to produce cognition, as this would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

Furthermore, relationhood consists in being a determiner of a qualified cognition while being distinct from its relata and residing in both [relata]. For only that which, like the conjunction between a jar and the ground, subsists in both relata is a relation; desire or causality, however, do not possess the nature of a relation because they reside only in one term and lack residence in both.

One might object: "Since there is the desire, 'This meaning is to be understood from this word,' both the word and its meaning are perceived as objects of that desire—just like the understanding itself—how can it be said that the desire does not reside in both? If this is raised, we reply: No. For in that case, neither the word nor the word-meaning is the object of the desire; rather, it is the understanding (*bodha*) itself that is such [an object]. Thus, it is the objective relation (*viṣayatā*) residing in the understanding alone that determines the locus of the desire, and not the objective relation residing in the word and its meaning which are the objects of the understanding.

This is because there is no cognition [of the form] "this word or this object possesses desire. The intention is that since it is possible for cognition itself to be the direct locus of desire through the relation of objective content (*viṣayatā*), there is no evidence for accepting that the word and its meaning are the loci of desire through an indirect relation. [Objection: But surely, since the meaning—just like the word—is a cause of verbal cognition, both possess the capacity to generate cognition; therefore, like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), its status as a relation is unavoidable. [Reply: No.

Just as it is established by experience that although both the staff and the wheel are generators of a jar, there is no mutual relationship between them, so too, although both the word and its meaning are generators of cognition, a mutual relationship between them is difficult to establish.

Furthermore, only that which determines a qualified cognition (viśiṣṭapratīti) possesses the nature of a relation. For example, in the case of "the pot on the floor," conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is a relation because it determines the qualified cognition that "the floor is the locus of the conjunction as determined by the pot. Similarly, since desire (*icchā*) and the state of being a producer (*janakatva*) lack the capacity to determine a qualified cognition, they cannot possibly be relations. Therefore, they assert that the relation between a word and its meaning is indeed something other than these, namely *śakti* (potency), which is synonymous with the "relation of the signified and the signifier" (*vācyavācakabhāva*).

The Naiyāyika objects: "But surely not [that the power is the beginningless capacity to cause cognition]. The meaning is that it is impossible for a beginningless capacity to cause cognition to be the *śakti* (power). He states the reason why that [beginningless capacity] cannot be the power: "Because of modern... This means, for example, names such as Caitra or Maitra which have been designated by a father or others in the present day. "Due to the absence of that" means because the capacity to cause cognition qualified by beginninglessness does not exist [in such cases].

"Because of its absence" means because the causality of a cognition characterized by beginninglessness is non-existent. Although the causality of a cognition is experienced in the case of a contemporary convention (*saṃketa*), nevertheless, since such causality of cognition lacks beginninglessness due to being finite (*sādi*), one must understand that there is an absence of the qualified [property] resulting from the absence of the qualifier. Consequently, the intended meaning is that verbal cognition would not arise from a contemporary convention. To the objection that there is no evidence for the absence of beginninglessness in a modern [convention], he says: "Otherwise. This refers to the opposite of what was stated.

The meaning is that [the cause] exists in the modern [word], despite its beginninglessness. Regarding "convention made by the father and others": if the causality characterized by beginninglessness were present in the modern [word], then even at a time when one lacks knowledge of the convention established by the father and others, verbal comprehension would result from it. However, according to our established doctrine, this does not occur because of the absence of knowledge of the convention; such is the sense. Regarding "indirect (lākṣaṇika)":...

Even in the case of a word like "Gaṅgā," which functions through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there would be the consequence of having to postulate a cause for producing a cognition characterized by beginninglessness; thus, since the cognition of the riverbank and so forth could occur even without indication, there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition of denotation]. Therefore, it must be stated that the knowledge of convention (*saṃketa*) is also a cause for cognition. This is because it is necessary; the meaning is that it must necessarily be required, since cognition does not arise without the knowledge of convention. "That alone" means that it must be accepted that convention itself is the denotative power (*śakti*).

This also serves to refute the view that [convention] is the beginningless cause of cognition. Thus Gadādharabhaṭṭācārya states in his *Śaktivāda*: "Convention (*saṃketa*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*) are the word-functions (*padavṛtti*) with respect to a meaning. The meaning of the locative case in "with respect to a meaning" (*arthe*) is "being determined by" (*nirūpitatva*). Consequently, the distinction is as follows: the function residing in words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), which is determined by the object [the jar], is convention; the function residing in words such as "Ganges" (*gaṅgā*), which is determined by an object such as the riverbank (*tīra*), is indication.

Although it should have been stated that "function (vṛtti) consists of primary denotation (śakti) and indication (lakṣaṇā)," the term "convention" (saṃketa) is used in place of "primary denotation" for the purpose of including conventions established by fathers and others. The Naiyāyikas maintain precisely this: function is the relationship between a word and its meaning that is conducive to the presentation of the object suitable for verbal cognition, and it is either primary denotation or indication.

Although there exists even a divine will (*īśvarecchā*) in the form "let the cognition of the bank arise from the word *gaṅgā*," which would entail that the cognition of the bank occurs through primary denotation (*śakti*) itself, nevertheless, because there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) stating "the bank is the denoted meaning (*vācya*) of the word *gaṅgā*," the word *gaṅgā* has only secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the sense of the bank. This is because one can infer the absence of a specific divine will in the form "let the cognition of the bank arise from the word *gaṅgā*"; whereas, with respect to the object consisting of the flow of water, there is primary denotation. This is the traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*). [The phrase] "in the case of a father or others who have adopted [the child]" refers to this.

In this regard, because there is no convention (*saṃketa*) established by the Blessed One (God) such that "let the object of the cognition produced by the word 'Caitra' arise," the convention is one made by a father or others; whereas in the case of [the word] "cow" and so forth, the convention is that of the Blessed One. Thus, the intention is that *śakti* (denotative power) is merely convention, and not a convention qualified by the attribute of being "belonging to God. Having raised the alternative—whether this convention is the cause [of comprehension] in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), in a general sense (*sāmānyataḥ*), or in a specific form (*viśeṣarūpeṇa*)—he refutes them, saying: "It is said... [and] "it is not the cause in its own nature."

The meaning is that a cause existing as a convention by virtue of its own nature (*svarūpasan*) is not [the cause]. He states the reason for this: "from one whose power has not been grasped" (*agṛhītaśaktikāt*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; the word refers to something other than its constituent parts. The meaning is: "even from a word whose convention has not been grasped. "Because of the consequence of cognition" (*bodhaprasaṅgāt*) means: because the convention, which is the cause of that [cognition], exists there by virtue of its own nature. The point is that it is established by experience that verbal cognition does not arise without the knowledge of convention. "Known in a general way" (*sāmānyataḥ jñātaḥ*).

The meaning is that a cause [of verbal cognition] is not something made an object of knowledge by any form whatsoever. [For example,] by means of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth; for if that were the case, just as in the case of objects such as jars and cloths, there would be the undesirable consequence of verbal cognition arising from words like "jar" even when one has knowledge of the convention [in general]. The point is that it is established by experience that verbal cognition arises only when there is knowledge of the convention in the specific form: "The word 'jar' has a convention with respect to an object possessing a conch-shaped neck and so forth. [This is stated] by way of its being a convention (*saṃketatvena*).

The meaning is that even in its specific form—as being a convention established by God (*īśvarīyasaṃketa*)—the knowledge of such a convention is not the cause [of verbal cognition]. Regarding the phrase "even in the case of words such as 'cow' (*gavādi*)": even there, for those who do not possess the knowledge of it as a convention established by God, verbal cognition arises simply through the apprehension of the capacity (*śakti*) to produce the understanding of the respective meanings; therefore, the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between the knowledge of the convention and verbal cognition is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Deviation, in this context, refers to the breakdown of the causal relationship.

In this regard, in the first case, although the convention—which serves as the cause—exists in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), there is a deviation from positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*) because the effect, which is verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), is absent. In the latter case, even in the absence of the cause, which is the knowledge of the convention, the effect, which is verbal cognition, is produced; thus, a deviation from negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) is to be observed. To demonstrate those who are devoid of the knowledge of the convention—specifically by way of the Lord’s convention—he says: "of the worldly people, the Mīmāṃsakas, and so forth. This means: both the worldly people and the Mīmāṃsakas, etc.

By the term "worldly" (*laukika*), the common folk and the Mīmāṃsakas who deny the existence of a Lord (*nirīśvaravādin*) are to be understood here. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), Buddhists and others are to be included, who likewise assert the non-existence of a Lord. Now, one might object: even if it is impossible for them to know [the relationship] as a divine convention (*īśvarīya-saṃketa*), it is certainly possible for them to know it simply as a convention (*saṃketa*). To this, he replies: "by the cognition of those respective meanings. The meaning is: only for those who possess the knowledge that a word such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) produces a cognition of an object characterized by a broad base, a belly, and so forth.

By the word *eva* (only/itself), there is the exclusion of a cognition whose qualifier (*prakāra*) is "the state of being a convention" (*saṃketatva*). Thus, even in the absence of knowledge that [the word] possesses the state of being a convention, since verbal comprehension arises by virtue of the apprehension that it generates an understanding of the aforementioned meaning, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*); therefore, even the knowledge of the convention as having the state of being a convention is not the cause. Rather, the point is that the power (*śakti*) of a word consists solely in its being a generator of the understanding of the meaning.

One might object: "Even if the knowledge of convention cannot be the cause of verbal cognition because the understanding of an object such as a 'jar' arises for common folk and others who lack knowledge of conventions—merely from the knowledge of the causal capacity [of the word] in the form 'the word 'jar' produces the cognition of the object jar'—nevertheless, since there is no deviation, the knowledge of convention can indeed be the cause of verbal cognition by virtue of being the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) of the capacity to produce cognition. Thus he raises the objection with the words "na cārthadhī... and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: "the capacity to produce the cognition of an object" means the capacity to produce the understanding of an object; and that [capacity] is the fitness (*yogyatā*) for producing the cognition of an object. Furthermore, fitness consists in possessing a property (*dharma*) that delimits that [capacity], and since this property has already been established, it is simply the convention (*saṃketa*) of God and so forth, because postulating something not yet established would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Thus, regarding words such as "pot," that which is the capacity to produce the cognition of an object is delimited by the convention; therefore, the knowledge of the convention, by virtue of being that delimitor, indeed becomes the cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).

"That knowledge" refers to the knowledge of the convention (*saṃketa*). "Likewise" means it is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). The sense is that since the capacity to produce the cognition of an object arises only through the cooperation of the knowledge of the convention, there is no deviation from the knowledge of the convention [in its being the cause of verbal cognition]. He states that this is not tenable with the words "even then. This means even when the causality is posited by way of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the capacity to produce the cognition of an object. [He says] "by parsimony" (*lāghavena*).

Since it is appropriate that causality consists in being the producer of the cognition of an object (*arthadhījanakatātva*), there is parsimony (*lāghava*) because the property of "being the delimitant of the producer of the cognition of an object" need not be included within the scope of the delimitant of the causal capacity itself. The essence of this is as follows: when considering whether the word alone is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), and if so, in what form its causality resides, it is apprehended through parsimony simply as "the producer of the cognition of an object. Consequently, pursuing the matter all the way to "being the delimitant of the producer of the cognition of an object" is cumbersome.

Since it is cumbersome to assume that the cognition "this word possesses the delimiting property of being a generator of the cognition of an object" is the cause of verbal comprehension, whereas it is simpler to assume that the cognition "this word has the capacity to produce the cognition of an object" is the cause, it follows that the view favored by the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas)—that the very capacity to signify is *śakti*—is established.

The meaning is as follows: "This word possesses the property that delimits its capacity to produce a cognition of an object" means that the word "pot" (ghaṭa) and so forth is the locus of that property which delimits the capacity to produce a cognition of an object such as a pot—namely, the convention (saṃketa). The general statement "this word" serves to introduce the specific sentence "the word 'pot' conveys the meaning of a pot," according to the maxim that "a generality does not exist without particulars."

In this context, the convention (*saṃketa*), which consists of the property that delimits the capacity to produce a cognition through the relation of substratehood (*āśrayatā-sambandha*), is the qualifier (*prakāra*) in words such as "pot. Since both the delimitorhood (*avacchedakatā*) and the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) reside in that convention, which is of the nature of such a property, there is complexity (*gaurava*) if one were to hold that the cognition "this word possesses the property that delimits the capacity to produce a cognition of the object" is the cause [of verbal understanding] by virtue of being a cognition whose qualifierhood resides in the convention delimited by the delimitorhood of the capacity to produce a cognition of objects such as pots. Therefore, this...

Regarding the cognition "this word possesses the capacity to produce a cognition of its object": the word "pot" (ghaṭa) is the locus of the capacity to produce a cognition of the object "pot"; here, the capacity to produce a cognition of the object "pot" is the qualifier (*prakāra*) in the word "pot" by virtue of the relation of locus-ness (*āśrayatā*); the delimiting property of the qualifier (*prakāratāvacchedaka*) is the nature of being a capacity to produce a cognition; and since the qualifier-ness is delimited by the nature of being a capacity to produce a cognition, this [cognition]—by virtue of being a cognition whose qualifier-ness is delimited by the nature of being a capacity to produce a cognition of the object "pot"—[serves as the basis for the subsequent inferential cognition].

The postulation that [the word] is the cause of verbal cognition is appropriate due to parsimony (*lāghava*). This should be understood as follows: just as the cognition "this is a jar" (*ayaṃ ghaṭaḥ*) is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), because in this cognition both the jar and jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) appear; and since jar-ness is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the jar is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), this becomes a cognition having jar-ness as its mode (*prakāra*); in the same way, the cognition "this word generates the understanding of an object" is a cognition having the property of being a generator of the understanding of an object as its mode.

Just as the cognition "the staff possesses the property that delimits its being the cause of a jar" is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*)—because in this cognition the staff appears as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the property that delimits its being the cause of a jar appears as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), whereby it becomes a cognition having the property that delimits its being the cause of a jar as its qualifier (*prakāra*)—in the same way, the cognition "this word possesses the property that delimits its being the generator of the understanding of an object" is a cognition having the property that delimits its being the generator of the understanding of an object as its qualifier.

He raises the objection of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the cognition whose qualifier is "the capacity to produce the understanding of an object" by stating: "Nor [is there deviation] in the case of a modern convention," and so forth. In the case of a modern convention, such as that concerning Caitra, Maitra, and others, since the understanding of the meaning arises from the knowledge of the convention—namely, the knowledge that "the word 'Caitra' has a convention applied to that specific individual"—there is a deviation of this knowledge of the capacity to produce the understanding of the meaning. The remainder of the sense is that there is a negative deviation (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), because the effect exists even in the absence of the cause.

The particle *eva* (only) serves to exclude the knowledge that a word generates the understanding of a meaning; the sense is that [understanding occurs] from the mere knowledge of the convention (*saṃketa*), even without the knowledge that it generates the understanding of a meaning. He says "not [an instance of] deviation" (*vyabhicāra*) with the words "even there" (*tatrāpi*). This means: even in such cases where the understanding of the meaning arises from the mere knowledge of the convention. [The convention is expressed as]: "This word [denotes] this meaning."

The meaning is as follows: the convention (*saṃketa*) is precisely that desire which has as its qualifier the capacity to produce a cognition whose qualificandum is this word and whose object is this meaning. When such a convention, in the form of that desire, is known, it follows by implication that there arises a knowledge of the fact that this word possesses the capacity to produce a cognition of this meaning. Consequently, since the cause of understanding—namely, the capacity to generate a cognition of the meaning—is present in the word, neither positive nor negative deviation (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) is possible.

According to the view of the Naiyāyikas, since a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) having the nominative case-ending as its primary qualificand is accepted, the cognition "May this word convey this meaning"—namely, that the word 'cow' and so forth is the locus of the capacity to generate a cognition whose object is the cow and so forth—possesses the property of being a cognition characterized by the capacity to generate a cognition of the object. Consequently, because the property of being a cognition characterized by the capacity to generate a cognition of the object remains intact in the word 'cow' and so forth, there is no positive deviation (vyatireka-vyabhicāra)—that is to say, no occurrence of an effect in the absence of its cause.

"By means of immersion" (avagāhena) means by taking as an object the capacity of the word to generate a cognition of the meaning within such a desire-cognition (*icchājñāna*).
