According to the rule that in a desire-cognition possessing an object, whatever possesses the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) relative to that desire also possesses that same status in the cognition of that desire, in the present case, "the capacity to generate a cognition having this word as its qualificand and this meaning as its object" is the qualifier in the desire; therefore, in the cognition of such a desire, it is precisely "the capacity to generate a cognition having this word as its qualificand and this meaning as its object" [that is the qualifier].

In short, there is no lack of concomitance (*avyabhicāra*) because the cognition of the word as having the property of generating a comprehension of the meaning—where that [meaning] is the qualifier—is intact. One might object: "The causality of the cognition of the word's capacity to generate a comprehension of the meaning must be accepted as being such that it does not become a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) relative to anything else. To this he replies with the words "not independently" (*na ca svātantryeṇa*), which means: "as not becoming a qualifier relative to a qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in something else."

In the present context, since the capacity to produce a cognition (*bodhajanakatva*) is a qualifier of the desire (*icchā*), and the knowledge of that capacity to produce a cognition is itself a qualifier of the desire, the knowledge of the denotative power (*bodhakatājñāna*) is not independent; this is the intended meaning. "Otherwise" means: even in the case of dependence consisting in being a qualifier, if the knowledge of denotative power were a cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). "This is not the producer of that cognition": the underlying idea is as follows—due to an error, a certain person named Caitra has acquired the cognition of an individual cloth (*paṭavyakti*) from the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*).

Now, even for one who knows that the word "jar" does not produce the cognition of a cloth-entity precisely because it is non-erroneous regarding its own object, and who thus recognizes the absence of the word "jar's" expressive power (*śakti*) with respect to a cloth-entity—since Caitra has understood the object in the form of a cloth from the word "jar"—there would arise the possibility of Maitra, who possesses such a [false] apprehension, cognizing the object in the form of a cloth from the word "jar. This is because the apprehension that "the word 'jar' has expressive power with respect to the object in the form of a cloth" could still occur.

In the case of the expression "this is not that which produces the cognition of the object," since the capacity to produce a cognition of an object exists as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) within the absence denoted by the negative particle (*nañ*), [the word would otherwise produce such a cognition]. Therefore, in order to prevent the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a cloth-entity might be cognized from the word "pot," it must necessarily be stated that the knowledge of the capacity to produce a cognition of an object *independently* (i.e., as a primary qualifier) is the cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). In the present instance, although there exists a knowledge that produces a cognition [of the pot] as a qualifier within the absence denoted by the negative particle, because it has not attained the status of a primary qualifier, the knowledge of its capacity to produce a cognition [as a primary qualifier] is absent; thus, no cognition of an object in the form of a cloth arises from the word "pot."

If it is argued that, likewise, in the case of a modern convention, although there exists the knowledge of the capacity to produce a cognition as a qualifier in the desire [of the speaker] regarding Caitra and others, there is no knowledge of the capacity to produce a cognition independently; thus, due to the absence of the qualifier, there is an absence of the qualified [cause], and consequently, the knowledge of the capacity to produce a cognition—which is the cause of verbal comprehension—exhibits a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a modern convention, [the author] says "no" to this: "for one who holds the apprehension that 'this is not the producer of that cognition.'"

The phrase "the word 'jar' does not produce the cognition of a cloth" means for one who possesses such knowledge and is non-deluded; that is to say, for a person who has ascertained the absence of the capacity to produce the cognition of a cloth in the word "jar. "By sublation" (bādheneti) means by the absence of the knowledge that the word "jar" produces the cognition of a cloth. "Grasping another [property] in the word" (pade paragraham iti) means even for one who knows that the cognition "the word 'jar' possesses the capacity to produce the cognition of a cloth" belongs to a deluded person other than oneself. "Because of the impossibility of grasping that" (tad‌grahāsaṃbhavād iti).

The meaning is that the cognition of the word "pot" (ghaṭapada) as being a generator of the cognition of a "cloth" (paṭadhījanakatva) never arises [in such a person]. For an unerring person who possesses the certain knowledge that the word "pot" lacks the property of generating the cognition of a cloth—even if the cognition of an erring person that the word "pot" does possess the property of generating the cognition of a cloth exists in some way (as the counter-positive of its absence)—how could the cognition "the word 'pot' possesses the property of generating the cognition of a cloth" ever arise in that unerring person?

The meaning is that [the word] would not arise at all. This is because, in every causal operation, the absence of an obstructer must necessarily be admitted as a cause; thus, in the case of the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*), there exists a powerful obstructer in the form of a certain cognition—namely, the knowledge that the word "jar" lacks the capacity to produce the cognition of a cloth (*paṭa*). Consequently, since a non-deluded person lacks the knowledge that the word "jar" produces the cognition of a cloth, it follows that the cognition of an individual cloth cannot arise from the word "jar. Otherwise... [as follows].

The meaning is that even when there is a certainty regarding the absence of the capacity to produce the cognition of a cloth in the word "pot"—which is the opposite of what was stated—one nevertheless accepts the cognition of the capacity to produce the cognition of a cloth in that word "pot. A cognition that has a qualifier (prakāra) where that qualifier is absent is an erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*) or a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*); such an erroneous cognition arose for Caitra in the form "this is silver," which has "silverness" as its qualifier, with respect to a mother-of-pearl shell that lacks silverness.

And that erroneous cognition of Caitra—namely, "this mother-of-pearl, which lacks silverness, has been grasped by him in the form of silver"—is known by Maitra. Therefore, Maitra is one who knows Caitra’s error; yet he is himself entirely non-erroneous, because there is a sublation-determination (*bādhaniścaya*) regarding the presence of silverness as a qualifier in the object standing before him, in the form "this is not silver."

The point is this: if, on the grounds that Caitra possesses the cognition of this [object] as silver, Maitra—who possesses a cognition having "silverness" as its qualifier and a particular object as its qualificandum—is also accepted as the locus of error because he likewise possesses such a cognition, then it would follow that even the knower of the error would be subject to error. Therefore, one must understand that in the case of a sublation such as "this is not silver," a cognition having "silverness" as its qualifier—namely, "this is silver"—does not arise at all.

He states the apprehender of the capacity (*śakti*), which consists in the power to generate the cognition of an object, with the words "And this... The *sāmarthya* (capacity) existing in a word, which consists in its being established as beginningless (*anādisiddha*) as the generator of the cognition of an object, is apprehended through the knowledge of the convention (*saṃketa*) made by a father or others. The instruction that "the word 'jar' denotes an object characterized by a conch-shaped neck and so forth" is the convention. By the phrase "by a father and so forth," a trustworthy person (*āpta*) is to be understood. Thus, it is clear that there is no verbal comprehension prior to the knowledge of the convention.

One might object: "In cases such as 'There is a hamlet on the Gaṅgā,' even though the word *gaṅgā* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*), since it generates the cognition of the bank as its meaning, it possesses the status of being a cause of cognition from time immemorial, which is the cause of verbal comprehension; therefore, it would follow that the word *gaṅgā* is actually denotative (*śakta*) of the bank. To ward off this consequence—the undesirable result that figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would be abolished—the author says: "Nor [is there such a consequence]. The meaning is: the consequence of the abolition of figurative indication is not a defect, but rather an ornament, precisely because it is desired.

He states the reason for accepting the abolition of [the primary] definition (lakṣaṇoccheda): "Because of commonality" (sādhāraṇyāt). The meaning is that just as linguistic usage—the crown jewel among the graspers of word-potency (śaktigrahaka)—exists with respect to the primary denotation (śakya), so too does it exist with respect to the indicated sense (lakṣya), such as the riverbank. Thus, linguistic usage, which is the foremost means of apprehending potency, is present in the same manner for both the primary denotation and the indicated sense.

Just as there is usage by elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) consisting of the employment of the word "Gaṅgā" for the specific object that is a flow of water, so too, since the employment of the word "Gaṅgā" is observed in the usage of elders for the object that is the bank of the Gaṅgā, and because the employment of the word "Gaṅgā" is identical in both the denoted (*śakya*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*), let there be the primary power (*śakti*) of the word "Gaṅgā" with respect to the bank—which is the indicated object—just as it exists with respect to the flow of water, which is the denoted object.

Let there be the annihilation of the [specific] denotative capacity (*lakṣaṇoccheda*); there is no loss whatsoever, because the view that "all words denote all objects" is accepted by the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), as stated in the *Bhāṣya*. By this, the objection that "there is no denotative power (*śakti*) of the word 'Gaṅgā' and the like toward the riverbank and so forth, due to the absence of a lexicon or other means of grasping denotative power (*śaktigraha*)" is refuted; the sense is that the usage (*vyavahāra*), which is the crest-jewel among the graspers of denotative power, exists in that case as well.

The distinction between the primary meaning (*mukhya*) and the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) is established by way of being well-known (*prasiddhi*) or not well-known (*aprasiddhi*). Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is simply a power (*śakti*) that is not well-known. Just as the specific power of words such as *gaṅgā* is grasped in a specific form regarding the current (*pravāha*) and so forth through usage and other means, in the same way, prior to the reflection upon the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) and so forth with respect to the bank (*tīra*) and the like, the power is not grasped in a specific form; thus, because it is not well-known, it is designated as "indication"—this is the intended meaning.

Is it not the case that the Bhāṣya statement, "all [words] denote all meanings," is from the perspective of a yogin, since for such yogins alone is there the possibility of knowing all those words and their meanings in their specific forms?

However, for people like us, since there is an absence of knowledge of all words and their meanings in their specific forms, and since knowledge of them in a general form is useless for understanding, it is improper—viewed from our perspective—to say that the word *gaṅgā* has a primary denotative power (*śakti*) toward a meaning such as a riverbank. Therefore, a distinct function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) must indeed be admitted in the word *gaṅgā* for the sake of the cognition of the bank and other such meanings. Furthermore, the usage of the word *gaṅgā* in the sense of the bank by elders is justified as the means of apprehending that indication. For this very reason, it is said: "The bank, the shore, and the riverbank."

With the intention that the word *gaṅgā* is not recited in the middle of the synonyms for "bank" (*tīra*) in the *Kośa*, he says: "And what [if]... regarding "the presentation produced by perception and so forth. It is observed in the world that for a person who has not grasped the word-potency—such as one who has not grasped the potency of the word *ghaṭa* (pot) to mean an object possessing a conch-like neck and so on—even though he perceives a pot with his eyes, no verbal cognition arises from the sentence "Bring the pot"; however, for one who has grasped the potency, it does arise. Thus [it is].

It is established that the presentation of an object (*arthopasthiti*) arising from the contact of the sense-organ with its object (*cakṣuḥ-saṃnikarṣa*) and so forth does not serve as a cause (*aṅga*) for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). This is stated [in the text] as "because it is not a constituent part of verbal cognition" (*śābdabodhānaṅgatvāt*). Even when there is a perceptual presentation of an object such as a jar due to the contact of the sense-organ with the object, no understanding of the meaning arises from the verbal expression "jar" for a person who has not grasped the word's expressive power (*śakti*). Therefore, the meaning is that the presentation of an object produced by perception and other means is not a constituent part (*anaṅga*), that is, not a cause (*akāraṇatva*), of verbal cognition.

And thus, it is impossible to state a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) such that "the presentation of an object (*arthopasthiti*) produced by any means whatsoever" is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). This is because there is a deviation from the positive concomitance (*anvayavyabhicāra*): even when the cause is present, the effect may not arise. Rather, the meaning is that one must accept that the cause of verbal cognition is specifically the presentation of an object produced by the knowledge of *śakti* (denotative power) and the presentation of an object produced by the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function). Regarding the term "complexity" (*gaurava*): it refers to the complexity resulting from the postulation of two distinct causal relationships according to the manner described above.

"Syāt" means "it would follow. "Of us" (asmākam) refers to us grammarians who maintain that the word *gaṅgā* possesses denotative power (*śakti*) not only in the primary sense—the flowing water—but also in the indicated sense—the bank, because usage (*vyavahāra*), which is the crest-jewel among the graspers of denotative power, applies equally to both the denoted and the indicated; thus, for us, there is simplicity (*lāghavam*) in this view.

The meaning is that there is parsimony (*lāghava*) because one single causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) can be postulated: since the word-potency (*padaśakti*) exists in both the primary sense (*śakyārtha*) and the indicated sense (*lakṣyārtha*), the presentation of the object (*arthopasthiti*) produced by the knowledge of that potency is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). [Objection: But just as it is a universal practice among all people that a particular flow of water is the denotation (*vācya*) of the word "Ganges," it is not a universal practice that the bank (*tīra*) is the denotation of the word "Ganges"; therefore, it is improper to postulate a word-potency for the word "Ganges" with respect to the bank.

And thus, since another mode of operation called *lakṣaṇā* (indication) must necessarily be accepted, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*), because the complexity established by reasoning is not a defect. Regarding the phrase "deviation in each case," the intention is as follows: just as a staff delimited by the property of being a staff (*daṇḍatva*) is the cause for an effect delimited by the property of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*), so too, with respect to verbal cognition delimited by the property of being verbal cognition, both the presentation of the meaning generated by *śakti* (primary denotation) and the presentation of the meaning generated by *lakṣaṇā* are the causes, according to the logic of the staff, the wheel, and so forth.

Similarly, the causality of a jar is established in the collection of causes such as the wheel, the potter’s cloth, and so forth, but not in each individual cause like the wheel; for it is established by universal experience that the effect—the jar—is not produced from the wheel alone in the absence of the staff, nor from the staff alone in the absence of the wheel. Likewise, the meaning is that the causality of verbal cognition (śābdabodha) regarding both the denotable (śakya) and the indicated (lakṣya) objects resides in the two aforementioned types of mental presence (upasthiti), but not in each individual type of presence.

And thus, just as the staff, the wheel, and so forth are required as causes for the production of a mere jar, so too are the aforementioned two types of mental presence required as causes for verbal cognition in general (i.e., both primary and secondary [metaphorical] verbal cognitions).

In that regard, regarding the function [of *lakṣaṇā*], although there is the presence of a presentation of the meaning produced by *lakṣaṇā* in cases such as "mustard oil" (*sārṣapaṃ tailam*), there is no presentation of the meaning produced by *śakti*. Likewise, in cases such as "he bathes in the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ snāti*), although there is the presence of a presentation of the meaning produced by *śakti*, there is no presentation of the meaning produced by *lakṣaṇā*. Thus, because the effect is produced even in the absence of the cause, there is a mutual reciprocal deviation (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) between the two presentations. He explains this very deviation with the words: "even without the presentation produced by *śakti*," and so forth.

The meaning is that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*): although there exists an apprehension of the jar produced by the knowledge of its primary power (*śakti*) in the case of "Bring the jar," there is no apprehension of it produced by the knowledge of its secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*); likewise, although there exists an apprehension of the bank produced by the knowledge of its secondary signification in the case of "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā," there is no apprehension of it produced by the knowledge of its primary power. To avoid this deviation, he raises an objection: "And not [by] 'immediately subsequent-ness' (*avyavahitottaratva*)."

The intention is as follows: the respective mental representations—namely, the representation of an object generated by word-power (*śakti*) and the representation of an object generated by indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—are the cause, and verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is the effect. Verbal comprehension exists as the effect; and by virtue of its relation to such an effect, that verbal comprehension possesses those respective representations. When the inquiry arises as to what constitutes the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of this effectness and by what relation it [subsists], he says: "by the relation of immediate succession" (*avyavahitottaratva*).

The meaning is that in a verbal cognition (*śabdabodha*), there exists the property of occurring at a time immediately following the respective mental presentation (*upasthiti*); thus, the state of possessing such a presentation, which is co-locative (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the property of occurring at that subsequent time, is the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*). The point is that a verbal cognition which arises without any interval immediately after the mental presentation of an object produced by a specific word-meaning relation (*vṛtti*) is precisely the effect of that respective presentation.

In this matter, for the benefit of beginners, here is the essence of the point: since only that which invariably precedes an effect can be its cause, every effect indeed exists at a time subsequent to its cause. Thus, in the present context, the effect in the form of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) necessarily occurs at a later time relative to the cause, which is the mental presentation of the meaning produced by the respective word-meanings. In this regard, the term "subsequent" (*uttarakālabhava*) is qualified by the addition of the attribute "immediacy" (*avyavahitatva*) with respect to that later time.

And thus, a verbal cognition in which there exists the property of occurring at such a subsequent time—namely, a time immediately following its causes—is the effect of the mental presentation (arthopasthiti) of the meanings produced by their respective word-potencies (vṛtti).

In this regard, the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) concerning the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) arises immediately after the mental presentation (*arthopasthiti*) produced by denotative power (*śakti*), and likewise, the verbal cognition concerning the secondary meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) arises immediately after the mental presentation produced by indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, that verbal cognition which occurs at the time immediately following the mental presentation produced by denotative power is itself the effect of the presentation produced by denotative power; similarly, that [verbal cognition] which occurs at the time immediately following the mental presentation produced by indication...

That verbal cognition (śābdabodha) is the effect produced by a presentation (upasthiti) generated through secondary signification (lakṣaṇā). That is to say, it follows that there is a distinct causal relationship: the presentation generated by primary denotation (śakti) is the cause for a verbal cognition whose object is the primary meaning (śakyārtha), and the presentation generated by secondary signification is the cause for a verbal cognition whose object is the secondary meaning (lakṣyārtha).

Furthermore, the delimiting factor of causality (kāraṇatāvacchedaka) is "the state of being a presentation generated by primary denotation" in the case of a verbal cognition concerning the primary meaning, whereas it is "the state of being a presentation generated by secondary signification" in the case of a verbal cognition concerning the secondary meaning.

The meaning resulting from the phrase "immediately following" (*avyavahitottara*) and so forth is as follows: with respect to a verbal cognition occurring immediately after an apprehension (*upasthiti*) produced by a knowledge of the primary power (*śakti*) residing in a given word, that apprehension produced by the knowledge of the primary power residing in that word is the cause; likewise, with respect to a verbal cognition occurring immediately after an apprehension produced by a knowledge of the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) residing in a given word, that apprehension produced by the knowledge of the secondary function residing in that word is the cause.

The meaning of this is as follows: the cause for the production of a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) occurring immediately after an apprehension (*upasthiti*)—which itself is produced by the knowledge of a primary denotative power (*śakti*) residing in the word "Ganges" and directed toward that which is delimited by "stream-ness" (*pravāhatva*)—is that very apprehension produced by the knowledge of the power residing in the word "Ganges. Furthermore, [the cause] is the apprehension produced by the knowledge of a secondary indicative power (*lakṣaṇā*) residing in the word "Ganges," which is directed toward that which is delimited by "bank-ness" (*tīratva*) as related to the stream that is the primary denotation of the word "Ganges."

And it is also held that the mental presentation (upasthiti) produced by the knowledge of the secondary function (lakṣaṇā) residing in the word "Gaṅgā" is the cause for producing a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) that occurs at a time immediately following such a mental presentation.

Furthermore, in the case of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the sequence is as follows: first, there is the presentation of the primary meaning (*pravāha*) produced by the cognition of the word's power (*śakti*); immediately after that, there is the presentation of the meaning "bank" (*tīra*) produced by the cognition of the metaphorical indication—which consists in the relation to the primary meaning—and following that, the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). Thus, because the presentation of the meaning "bank" produced by the cognition of the metaphorical indication intervenes between the presentation of the meaning produced by the power and the verbal comprehension, even though the verbal comprehension occurs subsequent to the presentation of the meaning produced by the power, [the former is not considered its immediate cause].

Because there is no absence of immediate succession [between the two], the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) whose object is the meaning "bank" cannot be the effect of the mental presentation (upasthiti) of the meaning produced by primary denotation (śakti); rather, it is the effect of the mental presentation of the meaning produced by secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) alone, since that arises immediately after the mental presentation of the meaning "bank" through secondary indication. Therefore, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) here.

In the case of "He bathes in the Gaṅgā," since the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) concerning the denoted meaning (the stream) arises immediately after the presentation of that meaning produced by the primary power (śakti), such a verbal cognition regarding the denoted meaning is the effect of the presentation of the meaning produced by the primary power alone, and not of the presentation of the meaning produced by secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). This is because indication does not apply there, and thus the presentation of the indicated meaning is entirely impossible. And so, the point is that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) even in that case. To this, he says "no" with the words: "because of the infinite [number of] causes and effects."

Regarding the principle that "the mental presentation (upasthiti) produced by word-power (śakti) is the cause for the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) whose object is the denotable meaning," the term "presentation produced by word-power" does not refer to the general category of such presentations in its capacity as a general property (*sāmānya*). If it were so, then because a general property is incorporeal (*amūrta*), it would be impossible to state that it occurs immediately prior to the verbal cognition. Rather, it refers to specific individual instances (*vyakti*) of the presentation produced by word-power.

The meaning is that, likewise, because the mental representations (*upasthiti*) are infinite, there would result an infinity of causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) due to their various distinctions. He states "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*) because the same logic applies. Just as it was argued that there is a deviation in negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyabhicāra*)—since the effect in the form of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) arises through one mental representation of a word-meaning even in the absence of another mental representation of a word-meaning, given that the causal relation exists between the two types of mental representations of word-meanings in the process of verbal comprehension—so too, with respect to the effect in the form of the mental representation of a word-meaning...

It must be stated that the knowledge of both [the object and its] capacity (śakti) is the cause; thus, even in the absence of one individual cause, there is no deviation in negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyabhicāra), because the effect—the production of the cognition—is still brought about by the other cause.

The meaning is as follows: if, however, in order to avoid over-extension (*vyabhicāra*), one posits a distinct causal relationship such that the knowledge of *śakti* (denotative power) is the cause for the mental presentation of a word-meaning produced by *śakti*, and the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā* (indicative power) is the cause for the mental presentation of a word-meaning produced by *lakṣaṇā*, then the complexity resulting from the postulation of these two separate causal relationships is to be understood as before.

An objection is raised: "Is it not the case that since a word such as *gaṅgā* has a denotative power (*śakti*) not only for the flow of water but also for the bank and so forth, the causal relation for every verbal cognition is of a single uniform type—namely, that the cause is the presentation [of the object] produced by denotative power—and thus there is simplicity? Even in that case, there remains the complexity resulting from the postulation of multiple causal relations. This is expressed in the phrase: "And this is not the word... (na cedam padam).

According to the principle that "there is no universal without particulars," this general statement—namely, "the word 'pot' denotes the object whose form is a pot"—is intended to convey the essential nature of specific statements such as "the word 'pot' denotes the object whose form is a pot. Even when one posits a single causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) in the form "the cognition of the word's capacity (that the word 'pot' denotes the object whose form is a pot) is the cause for the cognition of the object whose form is a pot," [this still holds] "due to the difference between the word and its meaning. This means: due to the difference between the word and its meaning—that is, by way of the difference of words and the difference of meanings.

"The assumption of numerous cause-and-effect relations involves complexity (gaurava). This is the underlying idea: just as, even when the object is identical—as in the case of the cognition of a jar (*ghaṭa*)—one assumes numerous cause-and-effect relations based on the difference between words such as *kalaśa* and others (all denoting the same object), so too, even when the word is identical, one must assume them based on the difference in objects. For instance, regarding the cognition of a jar, the knowledge of the linguistic capacity (*śakti*) that 'the word *ghaṭa* denotes the object in the form of a jar' is the cause; likewise, regarding the cognition of a cloth (*paṭa*), [the word *ghaṭa* would otherwise have to be the cause]."

The implication is that since it is necessary to postulate numerous cause-and-effect relationships—such as the knowledge of a word's power (*śakti*) being the cause for the cognition of the meaning of a cloth-form—the Vaiyākaraṇa who asserts that the presentation of word-meanings occurs everywhere (in cases of both primary and secondary meanings) through *śakti* alone, also incurs an equal degree of complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from the postulation of many such relationships. [This concludes the discussion on] "the deviation of another's position."

Regarding the apprehension of a cloth (*paṭa*), the knowledge of the word-potency (*śakti*)—namely, "the word *pada* denotes the object that is the form of a cloth" and "the word *ghaṭa* denotes the object that is the form of a cloth"—is the cause; thus, two forms of knowledge of potency are established as the causes for the apprehension of a cloth.

In this context, the meaning is as follows: there is a mutual deviation from the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), because even without the knowledge of the word-potency in the form "the word *paṭa* denotes the object that is cloth," the cognition of the cloth arises from the knowledge of the word-potency in the form "the word *ghaṭa* denotes the object that is cloth"; likewise, even without the knowledge of the word-potency in the form "the word *ghaṭa* denotes the object that is cloth," the cognition of the cloth arises from the knowledge of the word-potency in the form "the word *pada* denotes the object that is cloth. Thus, the effect is produced even in the absence of the [specific] cause.

To exclude this deviation, if it is said that among the two types of knowledge of expressive power (śakti) which serve as causes—namely, "the word *paṭa* conveys the meaning 'cloth'" and "the word *ghaṭa* conveys the meaning 'cloth'*"—only that presentation of an object (*arthopasthiti*) which arises immediately and without mediation following a particular knowledge of expressive power is called the effect of that particular knowledge of expressive power; for example, the [cognition] arising immediately after the knowledge of expressive power in the form "the word *paṭa* conveys the object which is cloth. *(Note: This appears to be a typographical error in the source text, as the word *ghaṭa* does not convey the meaning 'cloth'.)*

Since [the cognition of the word-meaning] arises through the intervention of the presentation of the cloth-meaning, the presentation of the cloth-meaning that arises without such intervention becomes the effect of the knowledge of the word-potency (*śaktijñāna*) in the form: "The word 'cloth' denotes the meaning of a cloth. This is the point: the presentation of the cloth-meaning is the effect, and the knowledge of potency in its two-fold form is the cause. Furthermore, the delimitor of the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) is not merely "being the presentation of the cloth-meaning," but rather "being the presentation of the cloth-meaning" as qualified by the relation of immediate succession to the word.

The meaning is that the property of being the presentation of the object "cloth" qualified by immediate succession is accepted as the delimiting factor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*). The point is that the element of "immediacy" is included in order to eliminate deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

And thus, since the mental presentation of the object "cloth" arising from the word "paṭa" occurs immediately after the knowledge of the word-potency in the form "the word *paṭa* denotes the object that is cloth," it follows that the knowledge of potency in the form "the word *paṭa* denotes the object that is cloth" is the cause of the presentation of the object "cloth" produced by the well-known potency; in this way, one causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) is established.

Furthermore, the mental representation of the object "cloth" (*paṭa*) that arises following the knowledge of the word-potential (*śaktijñāna*) in the form "the word 'pot' denotes the object that is cloth" does not arise without an interval; rather, it arises only with an interval. Thus, this mental representation of the object "cloth," which arises with an interval, is not the effect of the knowledge of potential in the form "the word 'cloth' denotes the object that is cloth," but is instead the effect of the knowledge of potential in the form "the word 'pot' denotes the object that is cloth."

Thus, the second causal relation is established: with respect to the presentation of the object "cloth" produced by a power that is not [previously] known, the knowledge of power (śaktijñāna) in the form "the word 'ghaṭa' denotes the object that is cloth" is the cause. Consequently, although there is no mutual deviation (vyabhicāra) due to the postulation of these distinct causal relations, the complexity (gaurava) resulting from the postulation of multiple causal relations becomes exceedingly great.

If it is asked: "Since the single word 'ghaṭa' possesses the expressive power (*śakti*) for both meanings in the form of the word 'ghaṭa', what is the reason for the disparity that the presentation of a jar occurs without mediation, whereas the presentation of a cloth occurs with mediation? It is replied: the expressive power of a specific word for a specific meaning is determined through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), which consists in the employment of that specific word for that specific meaning.

Just as, through observing the use of the word "Ganges" (*gaṅgā*) for a particular stream in the linguistic usage of elders, the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word "Ganges" is known to reside in that particular stream; likewise, through observing the use of the word "Ganges" even for the meaning of a riverbank in expressions such as "a hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), it is known that the word "Ganges" possesses denotative power with respect to the riverbank as well. Among these, because the word "Ganges" is observed to be used predominantly for the meaning of the stream, the denotative power of the word "Ganges" residing in that particular stream is known as the "well-known" (*prasiddhā*) power.

In cases such as "there is a hamlet on the bank of the Gaṅgā," since the word *gaṅgā* is observed to be used only occasionally for the bank, the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *gaṅgā* toward the bank would remain unestablished; thus, its inclusion in the lexicon [as denoting the bank] would be inconsistent. Furthermore, in a case where the primary power is not established, the word *gaṅgā*—which primarily signifies the current—is understood to have the power to denote the bank only if the speaker’s specific intention (*tātparya*) is that, for some reason, the word *gaṅgā* should convey the sense of the bank; otherwise, it is not so grasped.

In the case under consideration, because the word "ghaṭa" (pot) is observed to be used predominantly for an object possessing a conch-shaped neck and so forth, its denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to such an object is well-known; however, since the word "ghaṭa" is observed to be used for the object "cloth" only occasionally, its denotative power with respect to the object "cloth" remains unknown.

Thus, between these two—the presentation of the cloth (*paṭa*) and the knowledge of the linguistic capacity (*śakti*)—the presentation of the object "cloth" arising from the knowledge of capacity in the form "the word *ghaṭa* denotes the object 'cloth'" occurs only through an intervention by the knowledge of the speaker's intention (*vaktṛtātparya*). Therefore, it should be understood that this presentation is the effect of the second knowledge of capacity alone, not of the first.

Furthermore, the meaning is that because the indicated (lakṣya) objects are manifold, one must postulate a multiplicity of causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) in the following manner: for a verbal cognition whose object is delimited by "stream-ness" (*pravāhatva*) arising from a word such as *gaṅgā*, the cause is the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by the knowledge of the expressive power (*śakti*) residing in the word *gaṅgā* as delimited by "stream-ness"; and for a verbal cognition whose object is delimited by "bank-ness" (*tīratva*), the cause is the mental presence produced by the knowledge of the expressive power residing in the word *gaṅgā* as delimited by "bank-ness," and so forth. Thus, due to the plurality of indicated meanings, there arises a necessity to assume a plurality of causal relations.

The sense is that, against the Grammarian who asserts that there is only a single causal relationship—namely, that the mental presentation (upasthiti) produced by primary denotation (*śakti*) is the cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*)—the proponent of the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) has demonstrated the "complexity" (*gaurava*) resulting from the postulation of multiple causal relationships.

Now, one might object: "Even if there is complexity in my view—which does not accept the function of indication (lakṣaṇā)—nevertheless, in my view there are two causal relations, whereas in your view, which accepts the function of indication, there are three causal relations; thus, the position that accepts indication is more complex than mine. To demonstrate this, the Grammarian says: "In accordance with the error regarding power (śakti)."

Furthermore, when someone has the misconception that the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) possesses a denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the object "cloth," then—since it is universally admitted that the cloth is presented from the word "pot"—it becomes necessary to include both the expressive words such as "pot" and "cloth," as well as the expressed objects such as the cloth, within the knowledge of the power that serves as the cause for the presentation of the cloth. This is because one would have to state: "The word 'cloth' is the signifier of the object in the form of cloth; the word 'pot' is the signifier of the object in the form of cloth. Thus, there must be a distinction based on each specific word such as "pot" or "cloth," and a distinction based on each specific meaning such as "pot" or "cloth."

Furthermore, the burden resulting from the postulation of an infinite causal relationship between [the primary] meanings and their causes applies equally to you who accept the operation of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) as I do; however, for you, there is an additional burden compared to me, arising from the postulation of a causal relationship between the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā* and the cognition of the meaning "bank" in the case of the word *gaṅgā*—specifically, that the word *gaṅgā* indicates the bank through *lakṣaṇā*.

For me, however, it is unnecessary to postulate such a causal relationship between the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā* and its effect, because both error and *lakṣaṇā* are subsumed under the causal relationship between the knowledge of an unestablished power (*śakti*) and its effect.

And thus, for me, there are only two causal relations (kāryakāraṇabhāva) connected to the two powers—well-known and unknown. For you, however, let there indeed be a well-known causal relation such that "the word *paṭa* is the signifier of the object in the form of cloth" with respect to the presentation of cloth; yet, in order to account for the presentation of cloth arising from the word *ghaṭa* during a state of error regarding power (*śaktibhrama*), a causal relation of the form "the word *ghaṭa* is the signifier of the object in the form of cloth" with respect to the presentation of cloth is also necessary. Moreover...

The sense is that there are three types of causal relations (kāryakāraṇabhāva): namely, the causal relation between the knowledge of the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) and the recollection of the secondary meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), the causal relation between the knowledge of the secondary meaning and the recollection of the object on the bank (*tīra*), and the causal relation between the knowledge of the definition of indication (*lakṣaṇājñāna*)—in the form "the word 'Ganges' indicates the object in the form of the bank with respect to the recollection of the bank as its secondary meaning"—and the resulting cognition. Thus, there are three such causal relations.

Just as in the view of the Grammarians—who do not accept *lakṣaṇā*—the causal relation is one alone, such that the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is the presentation [of meaning] generated by *śakti*, and the cause of the presentation of the word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*) is the knowledge of *śakti*; so too, in my own view which does accept *lakṣaṇā*, the causal relation is likewise one alone. Thus he says: "Now, that which is generated by a *vṛtti*," and so forth.

The general assumption is that the presentation of word-meanings (padārthopasthiti) produced by a *vṛtti* is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), and the knowledge of the *vṛtti* is the cause of the presentation of word-meanings; thus, as one who accepts *lakṣaṇā*, I maintain only a single causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). By the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "as the mere presentation" (*upasthititvenaiva*), the distinct status of being a cause of verbal cognition—specifically as a presentation produced by the knowledge of *śakti* or as a presentation produced by the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā*—is excluded.

If it is argued that even for me, who accepts the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the causal relationship is exactly the same [as yours], and thus there is no additional complexity (*gaurava*), the author says "if this is so, [we reply] no" in order to refute it: "because [the function] is other than *śakti* (denotative power) and *lakṣaṇā*. The underlying point is this: since the property of being produced by a function delimited by the state of being either *śakti* or *lakṣaṇā* exists in both the presentation of an object generated by *śakti* and the presentation of an object generated by *lakṣaṇā*, your intention is that there is indeed only one single causal relationship.

Regarding the phrase "the subsequent apprehension of the word-meaning produced by the *vṛtti*," one must state that *vṛttitva* (the nature of being a *vṛtti*) is the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the causal capacity residing in that *vṛtti*, which is the cause of the apprehension of the word-meaning that serves as the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). However, when one seeks to know the essential nature of what this *vṛttitva* is, it must be stated that *vṛttitva* is either the state of being either *śakti* (primary denotation) or *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication); or else, it is the state of being that relationship between a word and its meaning which is conducive to and productive of that apprehension of the meaning which is the cause of verbal cognition.

However, he states "due to complexity" (*gauravāt*) because there is complexity in accepting that such a state-of-being-a-constituent (*tādṛśavṛttitva*) serves as the delimiting condition of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*). This is the meaning: the sense of "one-or-the-other-ness" (*anyataratva*) is "the being different from what is different from both. For example, a jar or a cloth is "one-or-the-other" of a jar and a cloth.

That which is distinct from both the jar and the cloth—such as a stone—is "distinctness from that. This [distinctness] resides either in the jar or in the cloth; thus, it is a distinction differentiated by the difference between the counter-correlatives (pratiyogin), namely, the jar-counter-correlative and the cloth-counter-correlative. The counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) residing in the stone is delimited by such a pair of distinctions. A jar or a cloth possesses a distinction having such counter-correlativity. Similarly, in the case of the power (śakti), "the state of being either power or definition" refers to the distinctness from a stone, etc., which is distinct from both power and definition; this [distinctness] resides in the power.

The meaning is as follows: because it exists in *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) as well, the property of being a "mode of operation" (*vṛttitva*)—which is non-different from that which is delimited by two absences whose counter-correlates are, respectively, *śakti* (primary denotation) and *lakṣaṇā*, or else that which is described by the passage ending with "the relation of being the cause of verbal cognition," etc.—is more cumbersome in its formal structure than *śaktitva* (the nature of primary denotation).

The point is this: since the aforementioned two-fold *vṛtti* (linguistic function) is more cumbersome than the nature of *śakti* (denotative power), which we intend to be the capacity to generate verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), it is more appropriate to state the causal relationship as follows: "the presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) produced by *vṛtti* is not the cause of verbal cognition."

Having thus stated the defect characterized by prolixity (*gaurava*) regarding the two previously mentioned types of function (*vṛtti*), he states another defect concerning the second nature of function described as "that which is conducive to the presentation of the word-meaning which is the cause of verbal cognition" (*śābdabodha-hetu-padārthopasthity-anukūla*): "Because there is no knowledge of the function [of the word] that presents the word-meaning, which is the delimiting factor for being the cause of verbal cognition."

Having stated the causal relationship in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) such that "the presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) is the cause with respect to verbal cognition, and the knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛttijñāna*) is the cause with respect to the presentation of word-meanings," it is further established that even regarding the presentation of word-meanings—which is itself a cause of verbal cognition—there exists a causal relationship; thus, it is proven that in verbal cognition, it is not merely the presentation of word-meanings that is the cause, but rather the presentation of word-meanings produced by the knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛttijñāna*).

And thus, the causality for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) resides in the presentation of the word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*) produced by the knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛttijñāna*). The delimitant (*avacchedaka*) of such causality is the presentation of the word-meaning produced by the knowledge of the linguistic function. This very thing is the delimitant of the causality for verbal cognition. In the compound *padārthopasthitivṛtteḥ*, the term *vṛtti* is a qualifier of the delimitant of the causality for verbal cognition, analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi*: "that in which the linguistic function (*vṛtti*)—meaning the presence (*sthiti*)—resides within the presentation of the word-meaning. Because the *bahuvrīhi* has been previously used in the masculine, the masculine form is applied here.

And likewise, "in the absence of knowledge" (ajñāne) means when there is a non-existence of knowledge regarding that which delimits the causality of the presentation of word-meanings—namely, the property of being a presentation of word-meanings produced by a knowledge of the *vṛtti* (the denotative relation). "Because of impossibility" (asaṃbhavāt): this is the sense: the "delimitor of causality" (*hetutāvacchedaka*) is the delimitor of the causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*).

"That property by which a cause is qualified is the delimitor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*). For example, with respect to a jar, a staff is a cause only when it is qualified by the property of "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*); therefore, staff-ness is the delimitor of causality. According to this rule, knowledge of the delimited (*avacchedya*) is not possible without knowledge of the delimitor (*avacchedaka*).

In the context under discussion, the definition of "vṛttitva" (the state of being a vṛtti) is the nature of that relation between a word and its object which generates the cognition of that object conducive to the presentation of the word-meaning; thus, the causal relationship between the presentation of the word-meaning and the vṛtti is specified. In that regard, it must be stated that the delimitor (avacchedaka) of the causality residing in the vṛtti is "vṛttitva" itself.

However, since the state of being a denotative function (*niruktavṛttitva*) is more cumbersome than the state of being a primary power (*śaktitva*), and because it is a maxim that "when a simpler property is possible, there is no [recourse to] a cumbersome one"—meaning that when it is possible to posit a simpler property as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), one should not posit a cumbersome property as the delimiting factor—for this very reason, in the inference "that which possesses a knowable fire (prameyavahnimān) [exists] because of smoke," one disregards the cumbersome property of "knowable fire-ness" (*prameyavanhitva*) as the delimiting factor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), and instead [adopts] that which is co-extensive with knowable fire-ness...

Since it is accepted that *kevala-vahnitva* (the mere nature of fire) alone is the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) due to its simplicity, then by the rule [that a property must be delimited], a delimitor in the form of "non-occurrence" (*avṛttitva*) is unestablished because it is not a delimitor. Consequently, because the delimitant of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) is unknown, the causality residing in occurrence (*vṛtti*) is difficult to grasp, for the knowledge of causality is dependent upon the knowledge of the delimitant of causality.

And thus, since occurrence is not known as a cause, it is impossible to state that "occurrence is the cause"; therefore, there is an ignorance of the causal relation between the presentation of the object (*padārthopasthiti*) and occurrence.

And it is precisely due to the ignorance of this causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) regarding the knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛtti*) that there is an ignorance of the delimitor of the causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), which consists in the condition of being an object-representation (*padārthopasthiti*) produced by the knowledge of the linguistic function. This is because, with respect to the knowledge of the sentence-meaning, the knowledge of the meanings of all the words constituting the sentence is the cause; and thus, [the absence of such knowledge] is necessitated by the absence of the knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛttijñāna*) which constitutes its own [sentence's] parts.

There is an absence of the cognition that serves as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the causal efficacy (*kāraṇatā*) for verbal comprehension—namely, the state of being an object-representation (*padārthopasthiti*) produced by the knowledge of word-meaning relations (*vṛttijñāna*). Due to this absence of the cognition that delimits such causal efficacy, there is also an absence of the cognition of the causal efficacy residing in the object-representation with respect to verbal comprehension—which [efficacy] is delimited by and dependent upon the cognition of its delimitant. Consequently, since it is impossible to assert that "object-representation is the cause of verbal comprehension," the mutual relationship of cause and effect between verbal comprehension and the object-representation produced by the knowledge of word-meaning relations cannot be established.

The sense is that because the presence of the word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*) produced by the knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛtti-jñāna*) is the cause and verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is the effect, there is an absence of knowledge [of these] all the more so due to their being difficult to state. Here, the two genitives in *śābdabodhakasya* and *hetuvṛtteḥ* are in apposition. Thus, when there is the inquiry—"What is the delimitant (*avacchedaka*) of that causality, which is the status of being a cause of verbal cognition, residing in the presence of the word-meaning?"—he says: "the presence of the word-meaning" (*padārthopasthiti*).

The meaning is: "in the absence of the knowledge of that function (vṛtti) which serves as the cause for the presentation of the word-meaning. In this regard, although the causality of verbal cognition resides—by way of the relation of pervasion (paryāpti)—in the presentation of the word-meaning produced by the knowledge of the function, nevertheless, it also resides by way of the relation of substratum (āśrayatā) in the function itself, which constitutes a part of that [causal complex].

The sense is as follows: just as the causality of a jar (ghaṭakāraṇatā) exists in the collection of causes such as the staff, wheel, and cloth by way of the relation of "sufficiency" (paryāpti), yet it is said that "the causality of the jar resides in the staff" because it also exists in the staff alone by way of the relation of "substratum-ness" (āśrayatā); similarly [in the present case]. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "ignorance of such a function," the genitive case is used in the sense of a relation; thus, it appears correct to me that the meaning is: "that function which, being related to the delimitor of the causehood (hetutāvacchedaka)—meaning, having entered the scope of the delimitor of the causehood of verbal cognition—is the cause of the presentation of the word-meaning."

Alternatively, considering that according to the maxim "a cognition of a qualified object does not arise without the apprehension of its qualifier," the knowledge of the qualifier is a cause for the cognition of the qualified; and since it is impossible to have a cognition of a function (vṛtti) as qualified [by its locus] without first knowing the locus-ness (vṛttitva) of that function, the nature of locus-ness is demonstrated by the second definition, beginning with "śābdabodhe" and ending with "padapadārthayoḥ sambandhatvam."

In that context, since the definition of *vṛtti* (the relation between word and meaning) is provided as "that which, upon the presentation of the word-meaning, is the cause of verbal cognition," it follows that one must necessarily know that the presentation of the word-meaning possesses the status of being a cause of verbal cognition. Therefore, the meaning is that *vṛtti* is the nature of that relationship between the word and its meaning which is conducive to—that is, which generates—a presentation of the word-meaning characterized by being a cause of verbal cognition.

And thus, since the knowledge of the relation between word and meaning—consisting in its being a *vṛtti* (linguistic function)—is the cause for the knowledge of the causal relationship between verbal cognition and the presentation of the meaning, and since the knowledge of that causal relationship between verbal cognition and the presentation of the meaning is the cause for the knowledge of the relation between word and meaning as a *vṛtti*, there arises a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Consequently, because the knowledge of the *vṛtti* is impossible, the knowledge of the *vṛtti* as qualified by that [relation] is also impossible; therefore, the presentation of the meaning produced by the knowledge of the *vṛtti* cannot serve as the cause for verbal cognition.

The meaning to be understood is that the causal relationship between the apprehension of word-meanings and verbal cognition—as constituted by the mental state [of the listener]—cannot be easily stated in this manner.

Now, one might object: "Even in the view that accepts *lakṣaṇā* (indication), the causality for the presentation of the word-meaning does not exist as distinct [factors], such that the knowledge of *śakti* (denotative power) is the cause for the presentation of the word-meaning, while the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā* is [separately] the cause; rather, the causality for the presentation of the word-meaning exists in a single form, namely, solely as the knowledge of *śakti*. To this, he raises the following doubt: "Now, even for me... The meaning is: "Just as for you who do not accept *lakṣaṇā*, so too for me who do accept it."

In this context, "it is held" (*mata*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. "Precisely as the cognition of *śakti*" (*śaktijñānatvenaiva*) means: not merely as the cognition of *śakti*, but rather [not] as the cognition of *lakṣaṇā* (indication). "As a cause" (*hetutā*) means: as a cause with respect to verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), and as a cause with respect to the presentation of the word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*) conducive to that [comprehension]. Thus, even in the systems of the Naiyāyikas and others, the presentation produced by *śakti* is the cause for verbal comprehension, and the cognition of *śakti* is the cause for the presentation of the word-meaning; the sense is that there is only one respective causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) for each.

Now, one might object: "In the view that 'indication (lakṣaṇā) is the presentation of the unexpressed based on the expressed,' indication does not consist of expressive power (śakti). This is because the presentation of the meaning 'bank' and so forth is possible from the very thing that is the actual expressed meaning of the word 'Ganges' and so forth, namely the flowing stream; furthermore, the knowledge of expressive power has no utility toward the presentation of the meaning 'bank' and so forth. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The relation with the expressed" (*śakyasaṃbandha*).

The "capable" (śakyasya) refers to the meaning presented by the expressive power; "relation" (saṃbandhaḥ) is the relation to that which is related to it. Indication (lakṣaṇā) is that function of a word denoting a primary meaning whereby it operates upon a non-primary meaning. For a word to convey its meaning, there are two operations: the primary and the non-primary. Among these, the direct relation between a word and its meaning is the primary operation, which is called "power" (śakti) or "denotation" (abhidhā).

However, where the primary meaning is untenable due to syntactic connection (*anvaya*) and so forth, a non-primary function is apprehended; that very function is called *lakṣaṇā* (indication). The meaning is that *lakṣaṇā* is the relationship between a word and its [non-primary] meaning, established through a succession of possible [primary] meanings.

For example, in the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) of the word *gaṅgā* is a particular flow of water; however, there is an incompatibility regarding the connection of the primary meaning of the word *ghoṣa*—namely, a cowherd settlement—with that [flow], for a direct relationship between a hamlet and a flow of water is not possible. If it were so, it would follow that the hamlet itself would be carried away by the current.

However, a direct relationship with the bank is apprehended for the primary meaning, which consists of the flow; therefore, the meaning is that the very relationship between the flow and the bank is the function of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) for the purpose of conveying the bank as the meaning of the word *gaṅgā*. Here, because the term "capable" (*śakya*) means "presented by what is capable," the capacity (*śakti*) enters [the definition] as a qualifier.

Thus, the intention is that the cause for the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā* is precisely the form "the bank related to the flow, which is the denotable object (*śakya*) of the word *gaṅgā*," and not a form such as "the bank related to the flow."

And thus, since power (*śakti*) enters as a qualifier within *lakṣaṇā*—which consists of a relation possible for the word itself—even in the case of *lakṣaṇā*, the knowledge of power is the cause of the presentation of the word-meaning through a mediated sequence; and in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), the presentation of the word-meaning produced by power is the cause. Therefore, the causal relation exists precisely as "power-ness" (*śaktitvena*). To the objection that this is not to be trusted, he says: "If it be so, [we reply] no. Regarding "knowledge of power": the meaning is that there is a causal relation between the presentation of the word-meaning and the knowledge of power.

Regarding the phrase "having the same object-domain" (*samānaviṣayatvasya*): its meaning is that the knowledge of the word-potency (*śaktijñāna*) residing in a word, as determined by a specific meaning, is the cause for the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) of that meaning. For instance, the knowledge of the potency residing in the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*), as determined by the meaning "the form of a pot," is the cause for the mental presentation of the meaning "the form of a pot. This is the intended sense.

In this context, since the word "pot" (ghaṭa) has its expressive power (śakti) with respect to the object qualified by potness (ghaṭatva), and because there exists a grasp of that expressive power as having the object qualified by potness as its content, the presentation of the word-meaning (padārthopasthiti) is also accepted as having precisely that [object qualified by potness] as its content, according to the principle of proximity (pratyāsaktinyāya). Thus, the established doctrine is that the presentation of the word-meaning possesses the same form as the grasp of the expressive power, insofar as the grasp of the expressive power has a certain object as its content, the presentation of the word-meaning likewise has that very object as its content.

The point is this: if the apprehension of the word’s denotative power (*śaktigraha*) has as its object a jar qualified by "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), then the resulting mental presentation (*upasthiti*) must likewise have as its object a jar qualified by "jar-ness," and not a bank qualified by "bank-ness" (*tīratva*). Similarly, if the presentation has as its object a jar qualified by "jar-ness," then the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) must also have as its object a jar qualified by "jar-ness" alone, and not anything else. This is because, in the root text, the mention of "the apprehension of the denotative power and the presentation of the word-meaning" is intended to indicate, by way of illustration, the "apprehension of the denotative power and the verbal cognition. Otherwise... [the rest of the sentence follows].

Regarding the opposite of what was stated: the meaning is that in the causal relationship between the knowledge of a word's power (*śakti*) and the mental presentation of the object (*padārthopasthiti*), one does not accept the requirement of having the same object (*samānaviṣayakatva*). By the phrase "one who has not grasped the relation," the absence of the cognitive function known as *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is indicated. Furthermore, it is indicated that when the relation between the Ganges and its bank is grasped, the presentation of the bank is indeed desired from the knowledge that "the current is the primary denotation (*śakya*) of the word 'Ganges'."

Even for a person who has not grasped the relationship between the current of water and its banks, yet has grasped the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word "Ganges" with respect to a particular flow of water, there would arise the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of understanding the bank from the word "Ganges," because that [power] exists. This means: because the knowledge of the power (*śaktijñāna*), which is the cause for the presentation of the word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*), exists. The underlying point is that there is no rule requiring the knowledge of the power and the presentation of the word-meaning to have the same object (*samānaviṣayatva*).

It is logical that a person who possesses knowledge of Devadatta’s relation with Caitra—since Devadatta is Caitra’s father—but lacks any knowledge whatsoever of the relation between Maitra and Caitra, should remember Caitra upon seeing Devadatta; for he has grasped the relation between Devadatta and Caitra, and it is through the recollection of Caitra [that this occurs]. However, by way of remembering Caitra...

One could not, under any circumstances, recollect Maitra as being related to that [Caitra], because the relation of Caitra with Maitra, while existing together with Maitra, has not been apprehended by him at all.

Similarly, suppose a person knows the relationship that exists between the word "Ganges" and its flow, but does not know the actual relationship that exists between the flow and the bank. This person, possessing both knowledge and ignorance, would upon hearing the word "Ganges," remember the flow which is related to it; however, through the remembrance of the flow, he would not remember the bank which is related to it, because he is unaware of the relationship between the bank and the flow.

The meaning is: "because it has not been apprehended in any way whatsoever. However, the point is this: if one accepts the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) merely as "the cognition of word-meaning is caused by the knowledge of the word's expressive power (*śaktijñāna*)," without including the condition of having a "common object" (*samānaviṣayakatva*), then since the knowledge of the expressive power exists here [in the case of *gaṅgā*], the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of cognizing the bank from the word *gaṅgā*—just as one cognizes the current—would be difficult to avoid. But if the causal relationship is accepted by including the commonality of objects such that "the cognition of word-meaning is caused by a knowledge of the expressive power having a common object," then this fault does not arise.

Since the apprehension of the word *gaṅgā*’s denotative power (*śakti*) has as its object the meaning qualified by "being a stream," it is logical that the cognition of the word-meaning must likewise have as its object the meaning qualified by "being a stream. Consequently, because the knowledge of the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*)—in the form "the bank is related to the denotatum of the word *gaṅgā*"—has as its object the meaning qualified by "bank-ness" (*tīratva*), the resulting cognition of the meaning qualified by "bank-ness," even if it somehow involves the denotative power, lacks the same objective domain (*samānaviṣayakatva*) as the apprehension of the power; therefore, [the bank] is not [cognized] from the knowledge of the power in the same way that the stream is.

The meaning is as follows: the cognition of the word-meaning is the cognition of the bank; however, the knowledge of the word’s expressive power (*śaktijñāna*) has as its object a thing qualified by being a "flow" (*pravāhatva*), whereas the cognition of the word-meaning has as its object a thing qualified by being a "bank" (*tīratva*). Since the knowledge of the expressive power and the mental presence of the word-meaning thus have different objects, it is impossible for the knowledge of the expressive power to bring about the mental presence of the bank.

In a case where the relationship between the word *gaṅgā* and the current has been grasped, but the relationship between the current and the bank has not been grasped, there is no cognition of the bank due to the absence of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) caused by the ignorance of that relationship; rather, only the current is cognized. According to our view, however, there is indeed no indication at all. It should be understood that since the word *gaṅgā* possesses a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for the bank as well as for the current, both the current and the bank are presented through that very power (*śakti*) by the word *gaṅgā* itself.

He states another objection with the words "api ca" (furthermore). "Smarataḥ" means that one remembers both the sentence "Bring the jar" and the individual elephant by way of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*). A collective apprehension is a cognition characterized by multiple primary object-nesses (*mukhya-viśeṣyatā*) as determined by multiple modes (*prakāratā*). Here, the word "ālambana" is synonymous with "viṣaya" (object); thus, it means "one who possesses a cognition consisting of a memory whose objects form a collection. The point is that although the memory has both the sentence and the elephant as its objects, it is nonetheless a single, unitary cognition.

"Of one possessing a memory with a collective objective" (*samūhālambana-smaraṇavat*). Here, it should be understood that the memory has as its object both the jar produced by the word "jar" and the elephant-driver produced by the word "elephant," according to the principle that "the cognition of one related thing [evokes] the other. Thus, the memory has both the jar and the elephant-driver as its objects. "From words such as 'jar'" (*ghaṭādi-padebhyaḥ*): this means from the words "jar" and so forth that constitute the sentence "Bring the jar," which is the object of the memory. "From the elephant" (*gajāt*): this means from the individual elephant that is the object of the memory. "Of the jar, etc. (*ghaṭādeḥ*): [this refers to the relation between the word and its meaning].

The pot and the act of bringing are presented through the knowledge of the word-potency residing in the words [denoting them], whereas the elephant-driver is presented through the relation of the controlled and the controller (*niyāmya-niyāmaka-bhāva*), and not from the knowledge of word-potency. Nevertheless, since there exists the quality of being produced by word-potency within a single cognition consisting of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*)—which is the nature of the presentation of word-meanings—there would result the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that the elephant-driver, like the pot and the act of bringing, would also be the object of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).

To avoid this defect, one must state the causal relationship as follows: for the production of a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) regarding a particular object, the cause is the mental presentation (upasthiti) of that object which is generated by a linguistic function (vṛtti) directed toward that specific part [of the meaning].

Just as in the case under discussion, when the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) regarding a jar is to be produced, there exists an apprehension (upasthiti) of the jar brought about by a linguistic convention (vṛtti) directed toward the jar; however, when the verbal cognition regarding the elephant-driver (hastipaka) is to be produced, there is no such apprehension of the elephant-driver brought about by a convention directed toward the elephant-driver. Rather, by the principle of the cognition of one related member (ekasaṃbandhijñāna), the elephant-driver residing in the elephant appears through the relation of the regulated and the regulator (niyāmyaniyāmaka-bhāva) from the individual elephant that is the object of memory; therefore, this is not the case in the present instance.

The sense is that the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) belongs to the mahout, just as in the case of bringing a jar. Alternatively, in the present context, although the condition of being produced by the knowledge of the *vṛtti* (the denotative function) exists in the presentation of word-meanings—which consists of a collective cognition (*samūhālambana-jñāna*)—and although it also exists in the presentation of the mahout, the presentation of the jar is delimited by the objecthood of the jar (*ghaṭaviṣayatvāvacchinna*), whereas the presentation of the mahout is not delimited by the objecthood of the mahout (*hastipakaviṣayatvāvacchinna*), but rather is delimited by the relation of residing in the elephant (*gajaniṣṭhatvasambandhāvacchinna*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that the elephant-driver (*hastipaka*) is not the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) by way of being the object (*viṣayatā*) in respect to the generative capacity residing in the *vṛtti*-cognition; for, since there is no cognition of the elephant-driver as the substantive (*dharmin*) in the *vṛtti*-cognition—just as there is no such cognition of the jar—the aforementioned erroneous comprehension does not arise. The phrase "because of the existence of being produced by the *vṛtti*" means "because of the existence of being produced by the cognition of the expressive power (*śakti*). It should be noted that although one ought to say "being produced by the expressive power" (*śaktijanyatva*) here, the use of the term "being produced by the *vṛtti*" (*vṛttijanyatva*) is intended to demonstrate the flaw even in the position that the cause is the "representation (*upasthiti*) produced by the *vṛtti*."

The sense is that, in this way, the rule follows that the knowledge of the word's power (*śaktijñāna*), the mental presentation of the word-meaning (*padārthopasthiti*), and the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) must necessarily have the same object. Regarding the phrase "and thus": in order to prevent the verbal cognition of the elephant-driver from arising from a cause consisting of a mental presentation of the word-meaning that takes both the jar and the elephant-driver as its collective object (*samūhālambana*), it is established that for a verbal cognition to occur with respect to a particular object, the cause must be a mental presentation generated by a linguistic function (*vṛtti*) directed toward that specific part [of the meaning]. (In other words, even for the portion referring to the elephant-driver, only a presentation generated by a linguistic function serves as the cause.)

The meaning is: "and because the acceptance of the relation of cause and effect is necessary. [The objection is: "Causality is impossible. Since the knowledge of *śakti* (primary denotative power) is the cause for the presentation of a word-meaning, and since *śakti* enters into *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication), in cases of *lakṣaṇā* such as "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the presentation of the bank occurs from the very knowledge of the *śakti* of the word "Gaṅgā," just like the presentation of the current; thus, the knowledge of *śakti* alone is the cause even for the presentation of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*). Therefore, [the objection continues] regarding *lakṣaṇā* as well...

The meaning is that the previously stated view—that the cause [of verbal cognition] is the knowledge of the *vṛtti* (the denotative function) as a capacity—is not tenable. This is the underlying idea: in a case where there is a simultaneous presentation (*samūhālambana*) of both a jar and an elephant-driver, just as there is a cognition of the jar, a cognition of the elephant-driver would also necessarily follow. To prevent this, it must necessarily be asserted that for a verbal cognition regarding a particular object, the cause is the presentation produced by the knowledge of the *vṛtti* regarding that very object.

The meaning of this is as follows: with respect to the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) concerning a jar, the knowledge of the *vṛtti* (the relation between word and meaning) that "the word 'jar' has the power (*śakti*) to denote the object in the form of a jar"—and the resulting mental presentation (*arthopasthiti*) of the object "jar" produced by such knowledge of the *vṛtti*—is the cause for the verbal cognition concerning a jar in sentences such as "Bring the jar."

In the case of a collective mental presentation (*samūhālambana*) consisting of the objects "pot," "elephant," and "elephant-driver," while there exists, with respect to the pot-portion, a presentation produced by a word-based cognition (*vṛttijñāna*) having the pot as its object, there is no such presentation produced by a word-based cognition having the elephant-driver as its object—namely, one based on the cognition that the word "elephant-driver" has the power (*śakti*) to denote the driver of an elephant—because the elephant-driver is not presented from the word. Rather, [the cognition of the driver arises] from the individual elephant, which is the object of memory, [and from which his driver is inferred].

The mere recollection arises in this way; and thus, since in the cognition of the mental modification (vṛtti) there is no appearance of the elephant-driver through the relation of objectivity (viṣayatā-sambandha), as there is of the jar, there is no cognition of the elephant-driver in the same manner as there is of the jar.
