Similarly, although the word *gaṅgā* has the capacity for the specific current (*pravāha*) when that current is presented [to consciousness], and thus there exists the property of being produced by a knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛtti*) residing in the word *gaṅgā*—by way of the relation of objectivity (*viṣayatā*)—with respect to the presentation of the bank (*tīra*), there is nevertheless no such property of being produced by a knowledge of the linguistic function residing in the word *gaṅgā* with respect to the bank as its object. Therefore, even though the presentation of the bank possesses the property of being produced by a knowledge of the linguistic function residing in the word *gaṅgā* insofar as it is related to the current (which is the denoted object of the word *gaṅgā*), it does not [qualify as a primary meaning] because it lacks the property of being produced by a knowledge of the linguistic function residing in the word *gaṅgā* which has the bank itself as its object.

The presentation of the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) occurs through the knowledge of the capacity (śakti). Otherwise, it would be improper for there to be a knowledge of the function (vṛtti) regarding the current (pravāha), while the presentation pertains to the bank (tīra); for the principle is that the presentation must have the same object as the knowledge of the function. This is the intended sense.

For us, who maintain that there is only *śakti* (primary denotative power), the word has *śakti* alone as its function toward every meaning, whether it be the primary (*mukhya*) or the indicated (*lakṣya*). Thus, the word "Gaṅgā" possesses *śakti* even with respect to the bank; consequently, the knowledge of the *vṛtti* (word-meaning relation) regarding the bank results in a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) whose object is precisely the bank, and so there is no fault. By this [phrase]—meaning: because it is impossible for the knowledge of the two types of *vṛtti*, namely *śakti* and *lakṣaṇā*, to be a cause in a single uniform manner.

This means that, due to the refutation—namely, the undesirable consequence of a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) arising for the elephant-driver at the aforementioned place—it is impossible for the knowledge of *śakti* (denotative power) to be the cause not only for the presentation of the denoted meaning (*śakyārtha*), but also for the presentation of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*). "Caused by *śakti*" (*śaktiprayojyaiva*) means that "being caused" (*prayojyatva*) refers to being produced either directly or indirectly, whereas "being produced" (*janyatva*) should be understood as being produced only directly.

And likewise, in cases of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) such as "a cowherd settlement on the Ganges," since indication—consisting of a relation to its own primary denotation—is produced by the knowledge of that primary power (*śakti*), the representation (*upasthiti*) of the bank as the object of indication is necessarily brought about by the knowledge of the primary power (indirectly). Therefore, according to the theory of indication (*lakṣaṇāvāda*), there is no need to postulate a separate causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) for that case; rather, the cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is the representation produced by the primary power, and [the cause] for the representation of the word-meaning is...

The meaning is as follows: the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is of only one kind, namely that "the cognition of capacity (*śaktijñāna*) is the cause"; it is not the case, as some claim, that there is a separate causal relation between the cognition of capacity and the cognition of indication (*lakṣaṇājñāna*). Thus, what has been asserted—that even for me, who accepts indication, there is such a distinct causal relation—is refuted and should be understood as rejected. He states the reason for this refutation in the words "of that which is not over-extended" (*anatiprasaktasya*), etc.; the meaning is that it is impossible to state a state of being employed (*prayojyatva*) that is free from the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

The point is this: for a person who possesses the knowledge of the word-potential (*śakti*) such that "the word 'pot' (ghaṭa) has its potentiality directed toward that which possesses a conch-like neck and so forth," when the meaning of the object "conch-like neck" is presented by the word "pot," and when space (*ākāśa*), which is related to itself [as its locus] by way of that pot, is also presented, it would follow that such space too would become an object of the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by the word "pot."

The meaning is that even when such a [conceptual] space (ākāśa) is presented, there exists the state of being prompted by the knowledge of the word-potency residing in the word "pot" (i.e., its being indirectly produced by the knowledge of the word-potency residing in the word "pot"). Therefore, it is difficult to define "being prompted by potency" in a way that is free from over-extension; thus he says this in the *Bhūṣaṇa*. The meaning is that this has been explained in detail in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*. || 37 ||

He provides the introduction to the root [of his argument] with his own refined view, stating "nanu" (but surely), etc. "Evam" means: if the capacity to produce cognition (*bodhajanakatva*) alone constitutes *śakti* (linguistic potency). "Bhāṣāditaḥ" means: from worldly words consisting of corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), such as *gāvi*, *goṇī*, *gotā*, and so forth. "Bodhadarśanāt" means: because the cognition of an individual cow possessing a dewlap and other characteristics is established by experience (*anubhava*) in the world through words such as *gāvī*. Regarding that, he says "tatrāpīti" (even there...).

The meaning is: "even in the case of words such as *gāvī* and others, which consist of corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*). The phrase "it would have to be" means that the acceptance of a power (*śakti*) consisting in the capacity to produce comprehension would necessarily be required. However, according to the view that "the power is the will of God" (*īśvarecchā*), although a will such as "let comprehension of a jar arise from the word *gagarī*" must be admitted because comprehension does indeed arise from the word *gagarī*, no relation to the word *gagarī* is postulated within that will; this is because there is an absence of lexicons (*kośa*) or other evidence to support such a relation. Thus, it is not [the case] in the corrupt form.

The sense is that there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of postulating a denotative power (*śakti*). He says "And if so" (*tathā ca*) in response to the objection that one might accept the postulation of a denotative power even for non-Sanskrit words such as *gagarī*, which are corrupt forms of speech; the meaning is that words like *gavī* and others would also attain the status of being grammatically correct (*sādhutva*). He states the reason for the attainment of correctness for these vernacular words with the words "of the state of possessing denotative power itself" (*śaktatvasyaiva*). "In the section on Grammar" (*vyākaraṇādhikaraṇe*) means: in the Jaimini-sūtra, *tatra tattvamabhiyogaviśeṣāt syāt* (JS 1.3.9.27).

In this regard, after stating the rule—based on two statements that set forth merit and defect, namely, "A single word, correctly understood and properly employed, becomes a cow of plenty in the heavenly world" and "Therefore, a Brahmin should not speak like a barbarian nor use corrupt speech; for he who uses corrupt speech is indeed a barbarian"—that one should employ only correct words (*sādhūni*) and not corrupt ones (*apaśabdāḥ*), it was further stated: "Only *go* and *agrya* are correct, but *gāvī* and so forth are not."

Words such as *gāvaḥ* and others are called "refined" (*saṃskṛta*) because they have been refined by the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*), whereas words such as *gāvī* and others are not so; thus they are called colloquial words (*bhāṣā-śabda*). In this regard, although linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*)—the crown jewel for grasping the primary signification—is equal in both Sanskrit and the vernaculars, the expressive power (*śakti*) is postulated only in Sanskrit, because it is uniform across all regions and established by the science of grammar.

Since spoken languages (bhāṣā) differ according to their respective regions and because they would result in being synonyms for Sanskrit, expressive power (śakti) is not postulated in them. Nor should it be said that there would be no comprehension from corrupt forms (apabhraṃśa); for in this very kārikā, the manner in which corrupt forms convey meaning will be demonstrated. And thus, since words such as "go" (cow) possess expressive power and since it has been stated that words such as "go" are correct (sādhavaḥ), the conclusion is that correctness (sādhutva) is nothing other than the possession of expressive power—this is the intended sense. [The phrase] "of two kinds" (dvidhā) [is explained as follows].

He resolves the doubt that even corrupt words (*apabhraṃśas*) might possess correctness (*sādhutā*) by means of two methods. Among these, one method is the non-acceptance of the direct denotative capacity (*sākṣād-bodhakatva*) of corrupt words; the other is the admission of their denotative capacity (*vācakatva*), which results in the acceptance of what is otherwise undesirable. It should be understood that the first method follows the view of the Naiyāyikas and others, while the second is his own view; thus he says: "The incorrect [word] [is known] through inference" (*asādhuranumānena*). Regarding the term *asādhuh*: it refers to a word in the form of a corrupt language, such as *gāvī*, *gagarī*, and so forth. Regarding the phrase *anumānena*: [it means] "through inference."

The meaning is: "having inferred the correct word. "Denotative" means "indicative"; that is to say, it is accepted by some—namely, the Naiyāyikas and others. The point is that from an incorrect word there is a recollection of the correct word, and from the recollected correct word the understanding of the meaning arises; thus, the incorrect word conveys the meaning through this indirect succession.

And thus, just as writing has utility only for the recollection of words and not for being the direct denoter of objects such as cows, so too corrupt (asādhu) speech has utility only for the recollection of correct (sādhu) words and not for being the direct denoter of objects such as cows; this is the sense that corrupt forms lack correctness (*sādhutva*). Regarding the phrase "utility only for the recollection of correct words," the intention is that corrupt forms do not possess direct denotative power because they lack correctness, and because the cognition of their incorrectness acts as an obstacle [to communication].

The meaning is that, consequently, it results that correctness (*sādhutva*) consists precisely in being a direct denoter (*vācaka*). Regarding this point, he cites the consensus of Hari (Patañjali), saying "For it has been said," etc. "Those" refers to corrupt words (*apabhraṣṭaśabda*). "In the production of cognition" means they are the causes for the comprehension of meanings such as "cow" and so forth. He states another perspective: "Identity" (*tādātmya*). For the identity between word and meaning resides precisely in the correct word; because one accepts the identity of a meaning with that very word which denotes that meaning.

Although identity with the meaning is not possible for corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) because they lack denotative power, nevertheless, the meaning is said to be identical with the corrupt form through a mediated sequence: namely, by virtue of its identity with the correct word (*sādhu-śabda*), which has itself attained identity with the meaning. The phrase "as if having accepted" (*upagamyeva*) means "as if having grasped. The particle "as if" (*iva*) is used to indicate that the apprehension of identity between the corrupt form and the correct word is erroneous; by this, their lack of denotative power is implied.

This is because it is admitted that the corrupt form possesses identity with the meaning-expressing [correct] word. The underlying idea is this: when the word *go* is intended to be uttered, if due to a deficiency in the vocal organs one utters *gāvī*, then—since this is in reality the word *go* itself—the corrupt words such as *gāvī*, appearing through their identity with the correct word (*sādhuśabda*), become the manifesters of the object in the form of a cow and so forth. He states the justification for the absence of direct denotative power in corrupt forms (apabhraṃśas) with the words "not by the learned" (*na śiṣṭaiḥ*).

The learned have compiled synonyms for correct words (*sādhavaḥ*) in lexicons (*nighaṇṭu*), dictionaries (*kośa*), and so forth, such as "māheyī, saurabheyī, gauḥ, usrā, mātā, śṛṅgiṇī," and others. Since those corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśāḥ*) are not included by the learned in such collections of synonym groups within lexicons and the like, the meaning is that corrupt forms are not directly expressive. He clarifies the very point already stated in the verse beginning with "te sādhuṣu... with the words "baṃbaṃbe... and so on.

When a child being instructed in the utterance of words speaks indistinctly, saying "baṃbaṃba," at that time—for those who know it, meaning those who know the correct word—when that indistinct sound brings the distinct correct word to mind (the word "smṛte" being understood), a determination, meaning a certainty regarding the object, occurs. The sense is that because an incorrect word has the correct word as its source, the correct word is remembered through similarity.

In this context, the reading *baṃ baṃ be* alone is appropriate, and not *ambāmbā*; the intention is that the latter (*ambāmbā*) lacks grammatical correctness. He explains the second verse, beginning with *na śiṣṭaiḥ*, as follows: "Thus, in the case of what is correct" (*evaṃ sādhau*). The word "thus" (*evam*) refers to this.

The meaning is as follows: when an incorrect word such as *gāvī* is employed in place of a correct word (*sādhū*) like *go*, that apabhraṃśa—the incorrect word—is used; by means of this incorrect word, some well-known meaning is expressed—that is, communicated—preceded by the [recollection of] the correct word. According to the maxim "what is said twice is well-secured," he raises an objection (*nanu*) in order to strengthen the very point previously stated.

The question is: what is the proof that Apabhraṃśa words lack the capacity to directly denote their respective meanings? To provide the reason for the statement that there is no such proof, he says: "because it postulates a [linguistic] power," and so forth. In cases such as "Bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), the fact that elders employ the word *ghaṭa* to convey an object possessing a conch-shaped neck and other features leads one to understand that the word *ghaṭa* has a denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to that object.

Thus, the meaning is that the usage of elders—specifically, the employment of the word *ghaṭa* with respect to an object characterized by a conch-shaped neck—is precisely what postulates the power of the word *ghaṭa* to denote the property of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*).

This very usage of elders that establishes expressive power (*śakti*) is observed in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) just as it is observed in correct words (*sādhuśabda*). Since the usage of elders that establishes expressive power is identical for both correct and incorrect words, just as correct words directly denote their respective meanings, so too do corrupt forms such as *gāvī* and others directly [denote them].

[The meaning is that] words such as *go* (cow) would be the denoters of their respective objects; thus, the point is that there is no evidence for the absence of direct denotative power in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśas*). He accepts this by saying, "True" (*satyam*), thereby indicating his agreement with its truth.

It is observed that words found in languages such as Mahārāṣṭrī differ according to the specific regions—namely, the differences between regions such as Mahārāṣṭra, Northern India, and Draviḍa. For example, the word *ghāgara* is used by the people of Mahārāṣṭra in the sense of a jar (*ghaṭa*), whereas the people of Northern India use the word *gagarī* for that very same object.

Furthermore, since those [words] are divided by difference of region and are thus manifold and infinite, the postulation of a denotative power (*śakti*) for each of those infinite words would result in an infinity of powers; consequently, there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, denotative power is not postulated for words existing in the vernaculars (*bhāṣā*). The implication is that corrupt words (*asādhu-śabda*) do not possess direct denotative capacity. One might object: "Complexity that is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not a fault," to which he replies: "Nor [is it a fault] in the case of synonyms... etc.

The point is this: just as "Viṣṇu," "Nārāyaṇa," "Kṛṣṇa," and so forth are all various synonyms denoting a single object, and the expressive power (*vācakatā-śakti*)—defined with respect to that single object—is postulated in the multiple words such as "Viṣṇu" and others without considering it a burden (*gaurava*), so too let the expressive power defined with respect to the single object "pot" reside in the numerous vernacular words such as *ghaṭa*, *rūpa*, *ekārtha*, *nirūpita*, *avācakatā*, and *śakti*.

Nor is there any [need for] complexity, because it would not follow that one must postulate a single expressive power (*śakti*) determined by a single meaning even for synonyms such as *Viṣṇu* and others. Therefore, with the intention that it is improper to postulate an expressive power for vernacular words like *gagarī*—even though they are distinct—just as one does for synonyms like *Viṣṇu*, it was stated: "the equality of synonyms. Thus, if it is argued that vernacular words such as *gagarī* are also direct denoters (*sākṣādvācaka*), just like the synonymous words for *Viṣṇu* and so on, [the answer is: no.

Just as a justification for postulating a primary denotative power (*śakti*) is found in the case of many synonyms such as Viṣṇu and others, there is no such justification for postulating a primary denotative power in the case of many words belonging to the colloquial languages (*bhāṣā*); therefore, a primary denotative power is not postulated for words situated in the colloquial languages. To clarify this very point, he demonstrates the disparity between the example and the subject of the illustration with the words beginning "teṣām" (of those).

Regarding those synonyms of Viṣṇu and others—such as Nārāyaṇa and so forth—in all regions from the Himalayas to the Setubandha, among the princes of Vihāra, Uttarāpatha, Hindusthāna, Mālava, Madra, Mahārāṣṭra, Karṇāṭaka, Drāviḍa, and all such respective lands, because they are one—that is to say, because they possess an identical form and belong to a single class—and due to the absence of any deciding factor [to the contrary], just as the word "Viṣṇu" conveys that same meaning in all regions, so too do the words "Nārāyaṇa" and others convey that very same meaning in all regions.

It is well known that [words] convey their meanings. For this very reason, among synonyms such as Viṣṇu and others, one might suppose that expressive power (*śakti*) belongs to only one of them and not to the others; however, since there is no decisive evidence for this and because synonyms like Viṣṇu and others possess an identical form in all regions, it is postulated that the denotative power resides in all these synonyms as being determined by a single referent.

The point is this: if there were a difference in form (bhinnarūpatā), then the denotative power (śakti) would be established only for that synonym which is well-known everywhere, and not for others. However, since synonyms such as Viṣṇu and the like possess a uniform form across all regions, there is an absence of a determining factor (vinigamanāviraha). And because of this absence of a determining factor, even if one were to postulate a separate denotative power for each synonym, the resulting complexity (gaurava) does not constitute a logical fault.

The meaning is as follows: since the capacity [of words] is established for each individual synonym such as "Viṣṇu" and others through the linguistic usage of elders (vṛddha-vyavahāra) throughout all regions—which is the means of grasping that capacity—it follows that the very uniformity of these synonyms like "Viṣṇu" and so forth serves as the proof for the assumption of an infinity of capacities. The construction is that corrupt forms (apabhraṃśas) do not possess such uniformity.

Since words existing in languages such as Apabhraṃśa—exemplified by *gagari* and others—are differentiated according to region and thus lack uniformity, the word *gagari* expresses the meaning of "pot" in one region, whereas the word *vāgara* does not express the meaning of "pot" in that same region; and the word *ghāgara* denotes the object "pot" in another region, while the word *gagari* does not convey that meaning in that region.

The point is this: since words existing in various spoken dialects (*bhāṣā*) differ according to region and thus lack a single uniform form, there is an absence of the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) across all regions—which is the means for grasping word-potency (*śakti*)—as there is in the case of correct words (*sādhuśabda*). Consequently, it is established that there is no potency in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), and because it would be utterly improper to postulate a potency that contradicts this, potency is not postulated for them. The meaning is: if they possessed a single uniform form, then potency would exist in corrupt forms just as it does in correct words. "Otherwise" [refers to the following].

"In the case of the opposite of what was stated" means that even though there is a lack of uniformity among corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśas*), one would have to postulate a denotative power (*śakti*) for them. "As synonyms" (*paryāyatayā*): since corrupt forms would possess denotative power just as correct forms (*sādhu*) do, they would have to be enumerated in lexicons and similar works as synonyms of correct forms—just as correct forms are so enumerated—and thus the same requirement would apply to corrupt forms. "And if this were so" (*evañcet*): meaning, if corrupt forms lacked direct denotative capacity. "The view" (*matam*): [refers to the following].

It should be understood that the view held by the Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others—that *sādhutva* (correctness) is simply the capacity [to convey meaning]—is based precisely on the statement from the *Vākyapadīya*: "They [infer] correctness through inference," and so forth. The word "now" (*idānīm*) means: immediately after the presentation of the views of the Mīmāṃsakas and others regarding the fact that Apabhraṃśa words are not directly expressive (*avācaka*). The phrase "his own view" (*svamatam*) means: the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*). The expression "no difference in expressiveness" (*vācakatvāviśeṣa*) [refers to the fact that both correct and corrupt forms are equally capable of conveying meaning].

Anticipating the objection that since the capacity of corrupt words (*apabhraṃśa*) to convey meaning has been established through the agreement of Harirāja, the Grammarians’ postulation of a primary denotative power (*śakti*) in them is merely a stubborn prejudice, the author—intending to show that according to the method stated by the Naiyāyikas and others, the communicative capacity of corrupt words is difficult to maintain—states: "The sense is this," and "In the case of incapacity."

The meaning is this: if expressive power (*śakti*), in the form of the capacity to convey meaning, were not postulated for corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), then no understanding of meaning would arise from them; yet it is established by the experience of everyone that such understanding does indeed arise. He raises an objection—“Not so” (*na ca*)—suggesting that the capacity of corrupt forms to convey meaning might exist through some other means even without postulating such a power. [He answers with] “Because of the recollection of the correct word” (*sādhusmaraṇāt*).

The sense is that since corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) have correct words (*sādhuśabda*) as their source, a correct word is remembered through its similarity to those corrupt forms; and from the remembered correct word, the understanding of the meaning arises. Thus, the capacity to convey meaning in corrupt forms is indirect, not direct, because they lack inherent expressive power (*śakti*). If this is argued, he says "not so" with the words "tānaviduṣām" (of those who do not know them). This means: of those who do not know the correct words by virtue of their being the conveyors of those respective meanings.

He states the reason for the common people's lack of knowledge of correct words (*sādhu-śabda*) with the phrase "of the common people" (*pāmarāṇām*). This means those who are unacquainted with Sanskrit. The sense is that "common people" refers to those who are proficient only in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*). With the word "from understanding" (*bodhāt*), the meaning is: from the understanding of objects such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) derived from corrupt forms such as *gagarī*. And with the phrase "and because of their lack of understanding of the correct word," the meaning is: since they are proficient only in corrupt forms, they lack knowledge of the correct word in its capacity to convey those respective meanings; therefore, it is absolutely impossible for the common people to derive an understanding of objects such as "cow" (*go*) from correct words.

And thus, since it is experienced in the world that even for those who lack knowledge of correct words (*sādhu-śabda*), the comprehension of meanings such as "cow" (*gāva*) arises from corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) such as *gāvī*, it is logical that corrupt forms are direct denoters (*vācaka*); the intention [of the author] is that the claim that they convey meaning only indirectly through the inference of correct words is not tenable.

One might raise the objection: "Could understanding from corrupt forms (apabhraṃśas) be possible by assuming that the expressive power residing in correct words—which is defined by meanings such as 'cow'—actually exists in those corrupt forms due to an error? To this, he says: "Nor [is it] from an error regarding the power. Having deliberated whether the intended error regarding the power in a corrupt form refers to the power of being a signifier (*bodhakatva*) or to the power consisting of the Will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*), he states that the first case is not tenable: "Of the signifier-ness" (*bodhakatvasya*). This means: of the capacity to produce the cognition of a particular meaning in a corrupt form. He adds: "By way of non-sublation" (*abādheneti*).

The meaning is that because there is no certainty regarding a subverting cognition (bādhajñāna) in the form "this [corrupt word] does not convey that meaning," the capacity to produce comprehension is unrefuted in corrupt words (apabhraṃśa). Regarding the phrase "because its apprehension is not erroneous": the meaning is that it is impossible for the apprehension of the capacity to produce comprehension in a corrupt word to be an error.

The meaning is as follows: just as, after the cognition of a snake in a rope, one approaches and through close inspection gains a subsequent sublating cognition (*bādhajñāna*) that "this is not a snake, but a rope," whereby the erroneous nature of the previously arisen cognition of the snake is inferred; likewise, since there is no sublation by any subsequent cognition regarding the knowledge of the object in the form of a jar arising from the word *gagarī*, it is impossible to infer that the grasp of the expressive power (*bodhakatva*) in the corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*) is erroneous.

The sense is that, by assuming the erroneous nature of a cognition, the very sublation (*bādha*) of the object of such a cognition serves as the cause [of its falsity]. Regarding the second alternative, he says: "By the will of God" (*īśvarecchā*). "Having pure existence (*sanmātra*) as its object": here, according to the lexicon which states, "the word *mātra* [is used] in the sense of totality (*kārtsnya*) and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*)," the word *mātra* signifies "entirety. Furthermore, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "the jar exists" (*ghaṭaḥ san*) and "the cloth exists" (*paṭaḥ san*), existence (*sattva*) is understood to pervade all things, both sentient and insentient; thus, existence is also perceived in words.

The meaning is that [the word] is the power in the form of God’s will, which has as its object all words, both corrupt (*apabhraṃśa*) and non-corrupt (*anapabhraṃśa*). Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of sublation": just as there exists a divine will directed toward non-corrupt words, such as "Let the object possessing a conch-shaped neck and so forth become the object of the cognition produced by the word *ghaṭa*," likewise there also exists a divine will directed toward corrupt words, such as "Let the object in the form of a jar become the object of the cognition produced by the word *gagarī*."

Because acceptance [of linguistic usage] is necessary, there is no sublation of the power—which consists of the will of God—even in the case of corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*). Otherwise, it would not be possible for the will of God to have all words as its object; this is the meaning. Since the cognition of specific meanings from corrupt linguistic sounds such as *gagarī*, *gāvī*, and so forth is established by the universal experience of both the learned (*śiṣṭa*) and the unlearned (*aśiṣṭa*), there is no sublation even in the case of corrupt forms due to the will of God. Thus, even in the view that the power is the will of God, it cannot be maintained that the knowledge of that power is an error (*bhrama*).

The intention is that when a cognition is erroneous, the sublation of its object (*viṣayabādha*) alone is the determining factor; and in the present case, such sublation of the object does not exist. With the view that it is in every way impossible for the power (*śakti*) itself to be erroneous in its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), he states the nature of the power: "the specific word and word-meaning," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: this general statement—“Let this word convey this meaning,” which indicates the power (*śakti*) of a word as determined by its meaning—is not intended to be understood as a mere generality (*sāmānya*) devoid of particulars; rather, it serves as an indicator for specific statements (individual propositions) such as, “Let the word ‘jar’ convey the object jar,” or “Let the word ‘cloth’ convey the object cloth,” and so forth, either by way of specifying each instance (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*) or through its own essential nature (*pratipadoktasvarūpeṇa*).

Furthermore, it must be stated that *śakti* (denotative power) consists of a desire characterized by a specific word and a specific meaning—for instance, a desire whose objective-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) resides in the object "pot" and is determined by a mode-ness (*prakāratā*) consisting in being the object of a cognition produced by the word "ghaṭa. In the present case, the *śakti* to be asserted is precisely a desire whose mode-ness consists in being the object of a cognition produced by the word "gagarī" and whose objective-ness resides in the pot. If such a [desire] exists, then there can be no error regarding *śakti*; if it does not exist, then even less can an error regarding *śakti* be established.

The point is that in some cases, it is the very cognition of something well-known as being devoid of its own [actual] object that constitutes error; for example, when there is a cognition having "silverness" as its qualifier with respect to a mother-of-pearl—which lacks silverness—regarding a "silverness" that is well-known in the case of real silver, it is precisely that cognition which is designated by the term "error."

Although, in accordance with statements that convey power (*śakti*) by way of a general orientation—such as "let this word convey this meaning"—there might arise the possibility of error regarding power as it consists of words and word-meanings in a general form, such as the thought: "the word *paṭa* (cloth) has power over a jar," or "the word *ghaṭa* (jar) has power over what is not cloth."

Nevertheless, the sense is that it is all the more impossible to claim the erroneous nature of a power (śakti) defined by specific words and word-meanings—such as "the word *ghaṭa* has power with respect to a jar" and "the word *paṭa* has power with respect to a cloth"—in accordance with statements that communicate such powers through the form of nominal bases (*prātipadika*). This is because such powers are apprehended through "pointing with the finger" (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*).

Furthermore, as for the "error regarding power" (*śaktibhrama*) mentioned earlier in this very section by the passage beginning with "in accordance with the error regarding power," that should be construed in accordance with a statement that makes known power in a general form, such as "may this word convey this meaning," because it is precisely at that time that the possibility of an error regarding power arises. It should not, however, be construed in accordance with a statement that makes known power in a specific form, such as "the word 'jar' has power with respect to a jar," because even the possibility of an error regarding power does not exist at that time. This is how it should be understood.

Even in the view accepted by the Grammarians—that Apabhraṃśas possess direct denotative power—he cites the support of the *Vākyapadīya*, saying "And it has been said. The meaning is that even words in the form of Apabhraṃśa languages are *śakta*—that is, they are indeed direct denoters (*sākṣād-vācakāḥ*) and not [denoters] through the mediation of the recollection of the correct [Sanskrit] word. Regarding the phrase "in the case of defects" (*viguṇeṣu*): according to the maxim that "a cognition of the qualified does not arise unless the qualifier has been grasped," the defect residing in the speaker—which is prominent here—is to be understood as a deficiency of the sense organ (*indriyāsāmarthya*), specifically in the form of a dullness of the tongue (*jihvājāḍyādi*).

Thus, corrupted forms (*apabhraṃśa*) arise due to defects such as the dullness of the speaker's tongue; when the speakers—the three types of utterers—are defective, meaning possessed of defects such as the dullness of the tongue, then those forms which have attained renown—that is, reached fame—among certain meanings through tradition (where "tradition" [*pāramparya*] means "succession," with the suffix *pyañ* added in the sense of the base itself according to the rule *caturvarṇādi*), for those corrupted forms, the correct word (*sādhu-śabda*) is non-expressive, meaning it does not convey the meaning.

Now, it might be argued that it is incorrect to say that a correct word (*sādhur*) is non-expressive, because it is universally accepted that the correct words also possess the capacity to express the same meaning for which corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśāḥ*) are employed; therefore, it must be explained as follows: the correct word, being the source (*prakṛti*) of the corrupt forms, is not directly expressive in that context, but rather—since corrupt forms have correct words as their source—it is through the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "these are indeed those [same words]," despite some modification of their phonetic properties, that they are understood as having attained identity with the correct form, being delimited by their respective sequences of sounds (*ānupūrvī*).

"Only the unrefined [people] are directly called Ācakas. "Divine speech" means the speech of the gods, consisting of the Sanskrit language. "Due to incapacity" means due to the inability to pronounce Sanskrit words caused by defects such as a dullness of the tongue. "By speakers" means by those who speak; the ellipsis is that it was made "intermingled," meaning its original sequence was disrupted. "By those who perceive impermanence" means by the Naiyāyikas, who argue that all words are impermanent and that the *sphoṭa* does not exist at all.

In this work titled *Vādaiśaktivicāra*, there arises a misconception (*buddhiviparyaya*)—namely, the erroneous view that only the correct forms (*sādhavaḥ*) are the words of speakers (*vācakāḥ*), whereas corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśāḥ*) are not; such is the meaning of the term "misconception" (*vaiparītyam*). This is the essential point: speech in the form of an apabhraṃśa, even when its phonetic sequence (*ānupūrvī*) is disrupted due to defects in the vocal organs and other factors of the speakers, does not differ from the specific, pure [Sanskrit] word. Even with some transposition of phonemes, by applying principles such as "that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]," it remains indeed of divine nature, i.e., of the form of Sanskrit (*saṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, because Apabhraṃśas have Saṃskṛta as their source, they are non-different from their source and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti*) due to identity, based on the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is that very same [word]. Thus, since the capacity to directly denote meaning (*vācakatva*) is possible for Apabhraṃśas themselves, the Naiyāyikas—having postulated a distinction between Saṃskṛta and Apabhraṃśa—maintain that only Saṃskṛta is the expressive medium (*vācikā*), and not speech in the form of Apabhraṃśa; this is what has been stated.

Now, with the intention that even words consisting of *apabhraṃśa* (corrupt) forms are indeed expressive—since there is a lack of evidence for the claim that only *saṃskṛta* (refined) forms are expressive—he says "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*). The phrase "due to the absence of a decisive criterion" (*vinigamanāvirahāt*) means due to the absence of any proof that determines one side [of the alternative] exclusively.

Just as the refined (saṃskṛtā) speech is uniform across all regions from the Himalayas to Rāmeśvara, such that this refined word "gauḥ" (cow) is employed in the Mahārāṣṭra country exactly with that same sequence of phonemes and that same meaning by those proficient in Sanskrit, and likewise in countries such as Saurāṣṭra and Mālava; so too is the case with corrupt (apabhraṃśa) forms of speech such as "gagarī," which, although lacking uniformity across all regions, [is used] in each respective region.

It is of one and the same form—that is, of an identical form—just as, for example, in regions suitable for the circulation of Mahārāṣṭrī, the word *gagarī* is seen everywhere to be employed in the sense of "water-jar" (*ghāgara*). Although the word *gagarī* is not seen in regions such as those of the Yavanas where the transfer of meaning is unsuitable, nevertheless, since it is seen in all regions other than those of the Yavanas and so forth, even speech in the form of an *apabhraṃśa* remains of one and the same form in every region.

And thus, in the expression "in all places" (*sarvadeśe*), the word "all" (*sarva*) refers to the intended [specific] places, and not to every place without exception (*sākalyena*). For if that were the case, since Sanskrit does not exist in regions consisting of Yavanas, Hūṇas, and so forth, it would follow that even this [Sanskrit] would fail to possess a uniform nature across all places without exception.

The point is this: since there is no difference in the fact that both types of speech—the refined (saṃskṛta) and the corrupt (apabhraṃśa)—possess the same form across many regions, there is a lack of any authoritative means of proof to determine one side over the other as to whether it is only the refined speech that is expressive and not the corrupt form. Regarding the phrase "even in the vernacular" (bhāṣāyām api), the meaning is "even in that which is of the nature of corrupt speech. Regarding the word "capacity" (śakti), the meaning is that one must necessarily admit a capacity—also known as the relationship between the signifier and the signified—in corrupt forms just as one does in refined ones.

Since languages differ according to their regional variations and thus possess diverse forms, it is not reasonable to postulate a [single] expressive power (*śakti*) for them, as this would entail unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). With this intention, he raises an objection with the words "And not... (*na ca*). "Of those"—meaning of the languages. "The defect" (*doṣa*) means that the very multiplicity of languages is the defect; that is, it acts as an obstacle to postulating expressive power in languages. The underlying sense is that expressive power is not postulated for languages of diverse forms due to the resulting complexity. He states that this is not correct with the passage beginning "Like Sanskrit" (*saṃskṛtavat*) and ending with "because of its remaining in that state" (*tādavasthyāt*).

Regarding the phrase "like Sanskrit": just as the Sanskrit language—such as *go* and so forth—is uniform in all regions suitable for its dissemination, such as Mahārāṣṭra and others, because it is entirely absent in regions like Yavana and so on, it is necessary to restrict the meaning of the word "all" [in the context of] "all regions suitable for dissemination. Thus, just as the Sanskrit language exists in a uniform form across the intended regions, so too the Apabhraṃśa language exists in a uniform form alone within the intended regions of Uttara Hindustāna.

Since in the regions of Northern India the word *gagarī* alone is the apabhraṃśa for the meaning "water-jar" (*ghaṭī*), and not forms such as *ghāgara*; likewise, in the Mahārāṣṭra region, the apabhraṃśa *ghaḍā* is used for the masculine gendered meaning "jar," *ghāgara* for the meaning "water-jar" (*ghaṭī*), and *kalaśī* for the meaning "pitcher" (*kalaśī*), but *gagarī* is not the apabhraṃśa there.

Furthermore, just as the Sanskrit language is uniform in form across all intended regions, so too each Apabhraṃśa form of speech is uniform in its own respective region; such being the case, the point remains that there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) to establish that the Sanskrit word alone is expressive and not the Apabhraṃśa word. This is the sense. [The phrase] "by way of unity everywhere" refers to this.

The meaning is: "in a uniform manner" regarding those [sounds] suitable for circulation in Mahārāṣṭra. He states another proof for the denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) of Apabhraṃśa words with the words "Furthermore" (*kiṃca*). Regarding the term "delimiting factor" (*avacchedikā*): a word is that which possesses denotative power (*śakta*); the denotative power resides in the word; and "denotative power" means the capacity to produce the cognition of a meaning. That which delimits this [capacity] is the sequence of phonemes residing in words such as *ghaṭa*, namely: the phoneme 'a' following 'gh', followed by 'a', followed by 'ṭ', followed by 'a'. The meaning is that this sequence of phonemes is the delimiting factor of the capacity to produce the cognition of the meaning.

Just as that [denotative capacity] exists as distinct and distinct in synonyms such as *ghaṭaḥ*, *kumbhaḥ*, and *kalaśaḥ*, so too does the sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*) which delimits the denotative capacity exist as distinct and distinct even in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) such as *ghāgara* and *gagarī*; what, then, is the distinction between the correct word and the corrupt form?

The point is this: just as various successions (anupūrvīs) residing in synonyms such as *Viṣṇu*, *Nārāyaṇa*, and *Kṛṣṇa* are accepted as delimiters of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*), so too should those residing in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) be accepted as delimiters of expressive power, since there is no difference between them. Thus, the intended meaning is that just as Sanskrit words are direct denoters of specific meanings, so too are corrupt words direct denoters; it is not proper to maintain a distinction between them.

With this intention, he concludes: "And thus, like the refined [Sanskrit] words," and so forth. Now, one might object: "If vernacular words are also expressive, just like refined words, then vernacular terms such as *gagarī*, *gāvī*, and others should be enumerated in lexicons and similar works as synonyms for refined terms, just as *āpaḥ*, *strī*, *bhūmni*, *vār*, *vāri*, *salilam*, *kamalam*, and *jalam* are. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not as synonyms. He states the reason why corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśas*) are not enumerated in lexicons and the like: "Only of the correct [words]," and so forth.

By the word *eva* (only/alone), there is the exclusion of *asādhūnām*—that is, corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*). The meaning is that words characterized by the property of correctness (*sādhutva*) are enumerated in lexicons (*kośa*) and such sources, but not merely those characterized by the property of being expressive (*vācakatā*). "Because of the statement of a classification" means because they are presented through a classification in this manner: "Indra, Marutvān, Maghavān, Biḍaujas, Pākasāsana," and so forth.

"Now, if correctness (*sādhutva*)—as enumerated in the *Kośa* and other works—is the determinant [of wordhood], then it might be argued that the correctness of corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) could also be easily asserted. This is the sense of the objection introduced by "nanu" (now, if...). "In this way" (*evam*) means: if even corrupt forms possess expressive power (*śaktatva*). "Their correctness would follow" refers to the corrupt forms. The underlying point is that in the section on Grammar (*Vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa*, Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.9), correctness has been stated to consist precisely in possessing expressive power. "The restriction" (*niyama*)... [refers to the rule].

In the *Paspaśāhnika* of the *Mahābhāṣya*, it is stated: "Since the comprehension of meaning is the same whether by means of correct words (*śabda*) or corrupt words (*apaśabda*), the restriction regarding merit (*dharma*) is established by the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*). In this context, "sameness" (*samānatva*) should be understood as being without the prior recollection of another word [of the same form].

Just as it is established by experience that from a refined word such as *go* (cow), the comprehension of meaning arises immediately without the recollection of another word, so too from an apabhraṃśa (corrupt) form, the comprehension of meaning arises immediately without the recollection of another word. Thus, it should be understood that the understanding of meaning arising from both refined and corrupt forms is identical insofar as it lacks the necessity of being preceded by the recollection of another word.

Furthermore, if corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) were not direct denoters like Sanskrit, but instead conveyed meaning only by first recalling another word [in the correct form], then the qualification of "equality" given regarding the comprehension of meaning through the medium of both Sanskrit and corrupt forms would be inconsistent—it would be without a subject matter. Therefore, it must be admitted that corrupt forms, just like Sanskrit, are indeed direct denoters.

Since Apabhraṃśa words possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), they can also function as suggestors (*vyañjaka*). This is clearly consistent with the examples of language provided by the authors of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: "O Mother, you have indeed established that there are no household supplies today. So tell me, what is to be done? The day will not remain like this. The Sanskrit equivalent of the aforementioned Prakrit verse is: *mātargṛhopakaraṇamadya khalu nāstīti sādhitaṃ tvayā | tadbhaṇa kiṃ karaṇīyamevameva na vāsaraḥ sthātī* || [Thus ends the section.]

Here, it is implied: "Grant permission for me to go outside the house. [Objection: If the comprehension of meaning occurs equally through both correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*), what is the purpose of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*)? To this, he says: "By the treatise, there is a restriction regarding *dharma*. The meaning is that by means of the knowledge of the division between base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*)—such as "this is its base" and "this is its suffix"—the treatise establishes the restriction that only words such as *go* (cow) produce merit when employed, and not words such as *gagarī*, *gāvī*, and so forth. Thus, it is said: "in the production of merit."

"A single word, correctly understood, well-employed, and in accordance with the scriptures, becomes a cow of plenty (kāmadhuk) in the heavenly world"—this statement from the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ" establishes the injunction that one should speak with correct words (*sādhu*) for the sake of generating merit; the meaning is that the employment of correct words produces merit. The sense is that through an injunction, the desired result is made known regarding what is to be performed. Regarding the phrase "for the generation of sin": this refers to the prohibition "not with incorrect words" (*nāsādhubhiḥ*), meaning that the employment of incorrect words (*asādhu*) is taught as a generator of sin.

The sense is that by means of a prohibition, there arises the cognition of the undesirability of that which is prohibited. And thus, he states what follows from this: "the possession of the property that delimits the status of being a generator. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it means "in the case of correct words" (*sādhuśabdeṣu*). Regarding "genus" (*jāti*): it refers to a specific genus established by the scriptural authority of the verse beginning "A single word... (*ekaḥ śabda-*), which has the meaning: "well-known"—that is, known as correct; "possessed of grammatical rules"—that is, intended [to be used] according to the path of exposition laid down in the grammatical treatises; and "well-employed"—meaning employed according to the path prescribed in the *Śikṣā* and other such works. This is a specific genus (*jātiviśeṣaḥ*).

The meaning is that it is the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the capacity to produce merit (*puṇyajanakatā*). And that is a specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*); it should be understood as being cognizable by one who possesses the thorough study of the scriptures, just like the true nature of gems (*ratnatattva*). Furthermore, it is stated in the *Laghumañjūṣā* that "correctness" (*sādhutva*) is a specific universal residing in words qualified by their meanings, which is manifested by grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and serves as the delimitor of the capacity to produce merit. If it is argued that this [universal] cannot be a universal because it would be mixed (*saṃkara*) with [the universals of] the phoneme *ka* and so forth, the point is that let it be a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). And "that which makes it known" [refers to grammar].

The meaning is that it is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) and the inferential mark (*anumāpaka*) of that genus which serves as the delimiting factor for the production of merit. Regarding the phrase "from the lexicon, etc.": by the word "etc. following "lexicon," there is the inclusion of usage by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), the statements of authoritative persons (*āpta-vākya*), and so forth. The phrase beginning with "from grammar, etc. is intended to include analogy (*upamāna*). The lexicon and the rest are mentioned first because they directly apprehend the expressive power (*śakti*) of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and because the apprehension of that power occurs for the most part precisely from the lexicon and other such sources. "In this very way" [refers to the same process].

The meaning is that grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is acquired only by those specific words when they are qualified by their respective specific meanings. Regarding the phrase "not producing a result in the case of a Brāhmaṇa": in the injunction "A king should sacrifice with the Rājasūya," the word *rāja* (king) denotes a Kṣatriya by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Since a Brāhmaṇa lacks the entitlement (*adhikāra*) for the Rājasūya, just as there is an absence of result-producing capacity when the Rājasūya is performed by a Brāhmaṇa, so too there is no grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) in employing words such as *go* (cow) in reference to a horse; for words such as *go* possess grammatical correctness only when used in their own [specific] meanings, such as a cow.

The intended meaning is that correctness (*sādhutva*) is accepted as consisting in the capacity to produce merit (*puṇya*). For this very reason, it is consistent to say that the word *aśva* with a dental *ś* is correct when it denotes a horse, whereas the word *aśva* with a palatal *ś* is correct when it denotes a poor man. Now, one might object: since words such as *Caitra* and *Maitra*, which denote modern individuals, are not derived by the grammatical treatises (*śāstra*) on the basis of those modern individuals as their referents, they would lack correctness in reference to those modern individuals. To this, he says: "modern Devadatta," etc.

The meaning is that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of even modern names such as Devadatta and others should be understood, because it has been established by the commentary beginning with the words, "One should give a name consisting of two or four syllables, having a lineage of three ancestors. He states the conclusion: "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*). This means: whatever word has been [demonstrated] by grammar to be applicable to a particular meaning.

The point is that names such as *kūcī* and *mañcī* (or *dhoṇḍopanta*, *koṇḍopanta*), which are formed in accordance with the local dialects of various regions, are not grammatically correct (*sādhavaḥ*) because they have not been derived according to the rules of the treatise (*śāstra*). He states the correctness of secondary (*gauṇa*) words with the words "of the secondary": in expressions such as "the boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*), the meaning is that words like "lion" have come into use—i.e., have become applicable—to a person due to their connection with qualities such as bravery and ferocity. The suffix *aṇ* is applied here according to the rule *tata āgataḥ*. [This applies] to a quality (*guṇe*), such as the property of being a cow (*gotva*) and so forth.

"Because of being taught" means because of being taught through the superimposition of "cowness" (gotva) due to the connection with qualities such as horns found in cows. "By taking that [quality] into account" means by taking those respective properties into account—that is, by the superimposition of the property that serves as the delimitor of applicability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). "It is indeed correct" means that words such as "lion," which are applied to a young boy through the superimposition of qualities such as bravery found in a lion, are indeed correct. The cause for this superimposition is the possession of qualities such as cruelty and bravery.

The point is that in expressions such as "the boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*), the boy and so forth appear in the form of "lion-ness" (*siṃhatva*) and so on. It should be understood that even in cases such as "the hamlet is on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the bank and so forth appear in the form of "Ganges-ness," which is the delimitor of the denotative power (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Regarding the phrase "but those [words] which are non-primary and indicative" (*ādhanikalākṣaṇikānām tu*): the meaning is that such indicative words—which are employed through some relation other than the form that delimits their primary denotative power, and whose intended referent is not the primary object—are indeed ungrammatical (*asādhutva*).

Some, however, interpret the present text by taking it as referring to words such as "white" (*śukla*) that denote qualities (*guṇa*). For instance: "Because of the derivation regarding the quality. This means: because of the derivation [of the word] with respect to the quality—such as white, blue, and so on—which is its own power; and because of the derivation [established] by the rule "there is elision of the *matup* suffix after words denoting qualities" (*guṇavacanebhyo matupo luk*) and by the lexicon stating "words like 'white' are masculine when denoting a quality" (*guṇe śuklādayaḥ puṃsi*), it should be understood that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of secondary words (*gauṇa*)—that is, words like "white" which refer to the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) when employed by way of their primary meaning—is established. Thus, for them, [the example] "The lion protects me... [is explained].

It should be understood that this would result in the failure to include [words] such as these. "For this very reason" means: because there is a rule that words used with any arbitrary connection according to one's own whim—regarding any object whatsoever that does not fall within the intended scope of the treatise—are necessarily incorrect (*asādhutva*). "The meaning is 'give to the Brāhmaṇa'"—here, because the Brāhmaṇa, who is connected with the object of the act of giving, possesses the status of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) is employed.

The meaning is that "giving" (dāna) refers to any act involving material objects whose recipient is a Brāhmaṇa, as prescribed by rule. Here, the meaning of the dative case is "recipient" (saṃpradāna). As for the phrase "even by indication" (lakṣaṇayāpi), the intended sense is this: indication (lakṣaṇā) is indeed a relation [of the word] with its own power (śakti).

The meaning of the second case (dvitīyā) is that which is related to its own [verb] and is capable of being its object (*karman*). Since such a relation exists in a Brāhmaṇa who bears the designation of "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*), one might argue that by taking the sense of "recipient" for the second case through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the usage *brāhmaṇaṃ dehi* ("give to the Brāhmaṇa") would be valid even as a figurative expression for *brāhmaṇāya dehi*. However, the point is that this usage is ungrammatical even as a figurative expression, because such a type of secondary indication is not sanctioned by the grammatical treatises (*śāstra*). This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, if the use of one case-ending (*vibhakti*) in the sense of another through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) were accepted by the scriptures, then the grammatical rules prescribing the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and others for the purpose of denoting the object (*karman*) would be entirely redundant; for it would be possible to convey the meaning of the object through the sixth case and so forth by means of such indication. Since, however, the rules prescribing the sixth case and others for the purpose of denoting the object are indeed formulated, it is understood from this very fact that such a form of indication does not fall within the intended scope of the scriptures.

The rules prescribing the sixth case (genitive) and others for the sake of the object—such as *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*, *gatyarthakarmaṇi*, and so forth—are intended to show that modern etymologists who fall outside the scope of the intent of the grammatical treatises (*śāstra*) produce only what is ungrammatical (*asādhu*). This is the underlying meaning. || 38 ||

"Excessive power" (*atiriktaśakti*) means a power that is distinct from a particular volition (*icchāviśeṣa*). And that [power] consists either in the capacity to produce cognition (*bodhajanakatā*) or in the form of a distinct category (*padārthāntara*). Regarding "the means of apprehending [it]," he states the means for knowing the power: "In the case of a word denoting a relation, [the power resides] in the relation."

This is its meaning: just as there exists in the eyes and other sense organs an innate capacity—consisting in the possession of a property that delimits their power to produce cognitions of objects such as color-form—which does not depend on human effort for the production of such cognitions, so too in the case of words, there exists an innate relation characterized by identity with the object, which is itself the capacity—that is, the property that delimits their power to produce the cognition of their respective meanings.

In the case of a term denoting a related entity (*saṃbandhiśabda*), fitness (*yogyatā*) consists precisely in the relationship between the word and its object characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), which is the determiner of the cognition of that fitness; and that [fitness] is innate (*svābhāvikī*). The meaning is that this very [fitness] is *śakti* (the expressive power). Now, if this is so, one might ask: "What is the use of convention (*saṃketa*)? To this he says: "from convention" (*samayāt*). The meaning is that this very innate fitness is known through the traditional usage of elders (*pāramparika-vṛddha-vyavahāra*). He provides an illustration for this: "like mother, son," and so forth.

This relationship of producer and produced between this word and its son is not established by convention, because it is the demonstration of that which is already established in reality. Just as the relationship of producer and produced between mother and son is already established and ascertained through the linguistic usage of authoritative instruction and so forth, in the same way, the relationship between word and meaning, though already existing, is determined through the usage of elders.

The point is this: for those who are unacquainted with lexicons, grammatical treatises (*vyākaraṇa*), and so forth, the knowledge of the expressive power (*śakti*) of words arises from the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), wherein specific words are employed to convey specific meanings. Regarding the phrase "the relation (*saṃbandha*) is the object": in the linguistic usage "this belongs to that," the relation is the object—that is, the object of cognition. Regarding "fitness (*yogyatā*)," in the linguistic usage "this is fit for that," fitness is the object; the meaning is that it is the object of cognition.

"Since this is so, therefore from that convention—the capacity in the form of denotative power (bodhakatā) which consists in fitness for linguistic usage and the like—there arises cognition (saṃvit), meaning knowledge; such is the meaning stated in the Darpaṇa commentary. That very point has been written by me. He states the utility of demonstrating the meanings of the words 'fitness for relation' (saṃbandhayogyatā) and 'word' (śabda) in the present context with the words 'the word "jar"' (ghaṭapadam). Here, 'fit' (yogya) means the object in the form of a jar is fit—that is, it is fit for generating a cognition having that [jar] as its object. 'Related to this' (etatsaṃbandhī) means related to the jar."

That is the capacity (*śakti*). And thus, the initial apprehension of capacity arises from the aforementioned linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*); and since the apprehension of the capacity of words such as "relation" (*saṃbandha*) and so forth is required therein, the purpose of that [usage] has been demonstrated—this is the intended meaning (*tātparya*). || 39 ||

Thus ends the determination of the nature of *śakti* (power) in the *Śāṅkarī*, a commentary on the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, composed by Śaṅkara, the son of Raṅgabhaṭṭa; this concludes the exposition of the nature of *śakti* within the detailed explanation of the *Sāra*. (6)
Now follows the determination of the meaning of the negative particle (nañ).

Since it has been stated that "it is a *nañ*-compound," one might suspect that the meaning of the *nañ*-compound is being expressed by this [term]; in order to dispel that doubt, he says: "the meaning of *nañ*. By stating that "superimposedness (*āropitatva*) is what is illuminated by *nañ*," he shows that it is indeed the meaning of *nañ* itself that is being demonstrated, and not the meaning of the *nañ*-compound. He says: "and in the *nañ*-compound, of the other [word]. Regarding "in the *nañ*-compound": this refers to that which is prescribed by Pāṇini’s sūtra beginning with "nañ. He states the meaning of the "other word" as: "of the subsequent word-meaning. [He adds: "because of its predominance."

The meaning is that because the subsequent word-meaning possesses the status of being the qualificandum (viśeṣyatva) as determined by the modehood (prakāratā) residing in the prior word-meaning, the designation of "pronominal" (sarvanāman) is established for words ending in *sarva* and others in cases such as *atasmai* and *asarve*.

This is the sense: in expressions such as *ghaṭaḥ paṭo na* ("the cloth is not a pot") and *ghaṭo nāsti* ("the pot does not exist"), since it is established by universal experience that there is a cognition of negation—namely, that the cloth possesses the absence of identity with the pot, or that existence has the absence whose counter-positive is the pot as its agent—it is necessary that the negative particle (*nañ*) has the meaning of non-existence (*abhāva*). Thus, it is possible to set aside [the traditional rules regarding] the predominance of the subsequent word-meaning and so forth.

If it is objected: "In expressions such as 'the cloth is not a jar' (*ghaṭaḥ paṭo na*) or 'the jar does not exist' (*ghaṭo nāsti*), there is the experience of a cognition where the absence is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), namely, 'the absence of identity with the jar residing in the cloth' or 'the absence of existence having the jar as its agent. Since this is experienced, the same would apply to cases like 'not-all' (*asarva*). Furthermore, in cases like 'absence of all' (*sarvābhāva*), because there is a cognition where the absence is the qualificand, the primary status would belong to the meaning of the preceding word (*pūrvapadārtha-prādhānya*). How, then, can the primary status of the meaning of the subsequent word (*uttarapadārtha-prādhānya*) and so forth be easily established? [Response: It is precisely for the sake of establishing the primary status of the meaning of the subsequent word and so forth that [the compound] is said to have a superimposed meaning (*āropitārthakatva*).

He states that something must be accepted regarding the negative particle (*nañ*): "The state of being superimposed (*āropitatva*) is what is indicated by *nañ*. He explains "for this very reason" as meaning: precisely because of the justification for the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārthaprādhānya*), and so forth. "The state of being superimposed" means the superimposed status of Brāhmaṇahood and the like; the meaning is that the negative particle within the word *abrāhmaṇa* indicates that the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "Brāhmaṇa" and so on is superimposed. Now, one might ask: if the negative particle has the sense of non-existence (*abhāva*), how could there be an inconsistency regarding the predominance of the subsequent member? To this he says: "This is the point."

In the case of *asarva* and so forth, when the meaning is "that which possesses superimposed universality" (*āropitasarvatvavān*), the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) is established because the referent of the word *sarva* functions as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). The phrase "otherwise" (*anyathā*) refers to the opposite of what has been stated. This means: when, in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the negative particle (*nañ*) signifies difference (*bhedārthaka*), and when there is an absence of predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha-prādhānya*) due to the predominance of the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha-prādhānya*).

Just as in the case of *atisarva*—where, in the sense of "one who has transcended all," a compound is formed by the Vārttika rule *atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā*, and because the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the word *sarva* becomes a subordinate element (*upasarjana*). Consequently, due to the prohibition "those that have become subordinate elements (*upasarjana*) in a name (*saṃjñā*) are not [treated as] *sarvādi*," it lacks the status of being a *sarvādi* and thus does not receive the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*)—so too here, when the negative particle *nañ* has the sense of difference (*bheda*), in the case of *abrāhmaṇa*, [it refers to] one who is different from a Brāhmaṇa.

Thus, in the sense of "different from all" (*sarvabhinna*), because the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha*) is primary and the word *sarva* is subordinate (*upasarjana*), it would not receive the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). Consequently, usages such as *asarve*, *asarvasmai*, and so forth, would be untenable; the point is that what is presented as the object of cognition [in a compound] is subordinate by virtue of being a qualifier of another. Now, one might object: since in expressions like *asarva* we accept the understanding that "all" (*sarva*) is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the difference, the primacy of the word *sarva*'s meaning can be maintained. To this, he says: "The pot does not exist" (*ghaṭo nāsti*).

The meaning is that [the cognition] "the absence of the jar is the locus of existence" or "the absence of the existence whose agent is the jar" arises precisely through the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) of that absence, as this is established by experience. Now, one might object: "In this way, you are denying the cognition 'not a jar'—namely, 'different from a jar'—which is common to all people. Anticipating this, he says: "And according to our view," etc. "That," etc.

In expressions such as "the pot is not the cloth," the meaning is that there is a cognition whose object is difference, specifically "the cloth is different from the pot. Regarding the term *ārtha*: it is called *ārtha* because it has arisen from the sense (*artha*); it is synonymous with *ārthika*, as previously explained. Since the cognition "it is different from the pot" is established by implication through the superimposition of "potness" upon that which is actually different from the pot, its existence is not denied. Regarding the term *mānasa*: it means produced by the mind (*manas*), and not produced by words (*śabda*).

In this regard, the notion that [the absence] is produced by words is merely an error, because it is actually prompted by words; such is the intended meaning. In cases such as "the jar does not exist," where there is a cognition having the absence (the meaning of the non-composite *nañ*) as its qualificandum, the cause is the presentation generated by the verbal root occurring in syntactic proximity with the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*); thus, a fixed rule of causal relation has been established.

Precisely because of the rule of the causal relationship established by etymology (*nirukta-kāryakāraṇabhāva-niyama*), in the expressions "you are not" (*tvaṃ nāsi*) and "I am not" (*ahaṃ nāsmi*), there is an absence of existence whose agent is you, and an absence of existence whose agent is me; thus, since the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad* denote the grammatical participant (*kāraka*) that is not directly expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), their coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established, which accounts for the distribution of the second and first persons. Furthermore, the distribution of numbers is established in cases such as "two pots do not exist" (*ghaṭau na staḥ*) and "pots do not exist" (*ghaṭā na santi*).

However, if one were to accept the meaning that "existence" (sattā) has you as its counter-correlate and me as its counter-correlate, then because there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the second person pronoun (*yuṣmad*) and the first person pronoun (*asmad*) with the verb ending (*tiṅ*), that [usage] would not occur. Rather, since non-existence is coreferential with the verb ending, the first person alone would occur in all cases; thus, the lack of a fixed rule (*avyavasthā*) is quite evident.

In the expression *ahaṃ nāsmi* ("I am not"), the suffix *-laṭ* denotes the agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, since the agent—which is the *kāraka* expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*)—is the denotation of the word *asmat*, the referent of *asmat* (the "I") is non-different from the agent who is the referent of the first-person singular pronoun *mām*. Consequently, there is a lack of existence (*sattā*) residing in that agent; in this way, because the referent of *asmat* is construed with the agent—the meaning of the suffix—through identity, there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the suffix. In this very same manner, coreferentiality with the suffix is to be understood everywhere.

One might ask: "What is the loss if the term *asarva* lacks the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*)? To this he says: "And so" (*tathā ca*). If it is accepted that "difference has everything as its counter-correlate," then because the word *sarva* would be a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), it would fall outside the group beginning with *sarva*; consequently, since the condition of ending in *sarva* etc. would be absent, *asarva* would lack the status of a pronoun. Thus, the substitution of *smāy* and so forth would not occur, and forms such as *asarvasmāt* would not be established. Regarding the phrase "and here" (*atra ca*): it means in the view that the state of being superimposed (*āropitatva*) is what is expressed by the negative particle (*nañ*).

Regarding the phrase "being the object of superimposition" (*āropaviṣayatva*): its connection with the referent of the subsequent word, such as "Brāhmaṇa," occurs through the relation of difference (*bhedasaṃbandha*). Furthermore, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the superimposition is understood as having the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) as its qualifier. Thus, from the expression "non-Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇa*), the cognition arises that "there is a Brāhmaṇa who is the object of superimposition. And in the presence of the negative particle (*nañ*), the term "non-Brāhmaṇa" denotes precisely a Kṣatriya or the like who possesses a superimposed Brāhmaṇahood; this is the meaning.

Alternatively, the meaning of "being the object of superimposition" (*āropaviṣayatva*) is "having as its cause of application the object of superimposition. Furthermore, in the expression "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the state of being the object of superimposition appears both as a qualifier (*prakāra*) and as a relation (*saṃsarga*), just like the genitive case-meaning consisting of the owner-owned relationship. From expressions such as "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), there arises the cognition: "one who possesses Brahminhood that is superimposed. Since the state of possessing Brahminhood qualified by superimposition exists only in one who is different from a Brahmin, the word "non-Brahmin" is not applied to an actual Brahmin.

With the intention that, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is simply superimposition (*āropa*) and not the state of being the object of superimposition (*āropaviṣayatva*) due to its complexity (*gaurava*), he says: "mere superimposition" (*āropamātram*). This superimposition is the meaning [of *nañ*], whether it is indicated (*dyotya*) or expressed (*vācya*). He further states that this [superimposition] functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the meaning of the subsequent word (*uttarapadārtha*) by means of the relation of being the object (*viṣayatā-sambandha*), saying: "the relation is the state of being the object" (*viṣayatvaṃ saṃsargaḥ*). Since the state of being the object is obtained through the very condition of the relation itself, and according to the maxim "that which is not obtainable otherwise is the word-meaning," mere superimposition is the meaning of the negative particle.

Just as by the statement "But the *tiṅ*s are remembered [to denote] the locus," although the *tiṅ*s are said to express both the locus of the result and the locus of the operation, it is stated that the meaning of the *tiṅ* is merely the locus, because the result and the operation are obtainable from the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself—this being in accordance with the maxim that "the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained otherwise"—such is the intended sense here.

Even under the view that the negation (*nañ*) expresses superimposition (*āropa*), since the object of superimposition is a qualifier of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha*) by way of the relation of "objectness" (*viṣayatā-sambandha*), the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member in a *nañ*-tatpuruṣa compound is to be understood as being maintained through the sense: "a Brāhmaṇa who is the object of superimposition. However, according to the opinion of the Bhāṣya, the negation (*nañ*) serves to indicate the intention (*tātparya*) of the co-occurring words such as "Brāhmaṇa" when they denote a superimposed ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*); thus, the status of being "suggested" (*dyotyatva*)—consisting in the role of indicating intention—is accepted for the superimposition that is the meaning of the negation.

The meaning is that the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as an indicator of the speaker’s intention (*tātparyagrāhaka*) regarding the sense of "that which makes known [an object] by way of a superimposed ground for application" (*āropita-pravṛttinimitta*). This refers to those words such as *brāhmaṇa* and so forth that are co-uttered with the negative particle itself—namely, those occurring in usages like *abrāhmaṇaḥ*, *asaḥ*, or *asarvaḥ*—and it indicates that the negative particle conveys an object qualified by the superimposed property of being a *brāhmaṇa* (or non-existence, or non-universality), which serves as the ground for the application of those terms.

Alternatively, it may be analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "that in which a superimposed ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) resides. Thus, the meaning to be understood is that the two negatives (*nañ*) serve to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) regarding the cognition of having a superimposed ground for application. It should be noted, however, that if the superimposition itself were denoted by the negative particle, then the connection of the superimposition with the primary referent of the word "Brāhmaṇa"—which possesses non-superimposed Brāhmaṇahood—would be difficult to establish due to contradiction.

Now, one might object: "Even if it is accepted that the negative particle (*nañ*) expresses the meaning of superimposition (*āropa*), there is no harm; for since superimposition can function as a qualifier of the meaning of the subsequent word through the relation of objective content (*viṣayatā-saṃsarga*), it has been stated that the predominance of the subsequent word's meaning can be maintained in a *nañ-tatpuruṣa* compound.
