To this, he says: "The mention of its being 'suggested' (*dyotyatva-ukti*)."

In accordance with the established tenet of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇasiddhānta*) that particles (*nipāta*) are merely indicative (*dyotaka*), it has been stated that "superimposition" (*āropitatva*) is what is indicated by the negative particle (*nañ*); however, one should understand that there is no harm whatsoever in accepting its denotative function (*vācakatva*) in the present context. As for the Naiyāyika position that prefixes (*prādayaḥ*) are indicative while particles beginning with *ca* (*cādayaḥ*) are denotative, the author of the root-text himself will later demonstrate that this is untenable due to the absence of any justification for such a disparity. In reality, however, it is more logical that superimposition is indeed indicated by the negative particle; for those who follow the *Bhāṣya* state that if it were denoted (*vācyatva*), the very fault [of infinite regress] has already been mentioned. (40)

To introduce an alternative position, he prepares the ground with the statement: "The pot does not exist. Since the cognition "the absence of existence whose agent is the pot" is common to all people, it is not established by the experience of anyone that the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of superimposition (*āropa*). Furthermore, the claim that the negative particle within compounds such as *asadbrāhmaṇa* (a non-Brahmin) has the sense of superimposition contradicts experience and denies the meaning of absence (*abhāva*) which is established by the experience of everyone; therefore, he says: "Or let its meaning be absence."

Since it is a general rule that pronouns refer to the principal element [in a compound], just as in the rule *krayyas tadarthe* (P. 5.1.97), the word *tat* refers back to the act of buying (*krayaṇa*)—which serves as a qualifier of the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*)—so too here, with the intention that the word *tat* in the phrase *tadartha* refers back to the negative particle (*nañ*) which is present as a qualifier in the expression *nañdyotya*, he says: "Its meaning (*tadarthaḥ*) means the meaning of *nañ*. He adds the word "meaning" (*artha*).

In the present context, the word "artha" (meaning) refers to the meaning that is the object of the cognition produced by the negative particle (*nañ*). By this, the inclusion of both being indicated (*dyotyatva*) and being denoted (*vācyatva*) is established; the intention is not that it refers to the meaning denoted by a word (*śabdavācyārtha*), as is the case elsewhere. Regarding the phrase "of the Bhāṣya": this means "of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with 'nivṛttapadārthakaḥ'. He states the meaning of such a Bhāṣya passage as: "that whose word-meaning has ceased (*nivṛttaḥ padārtho yasya*). [The suffix] *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).

The word *nivṛtta* has the meaning "cessation" (*nivartana*) when the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *vṛt* by the rule *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ*. Cessation is non-existence (*abhāva*). Thus, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) whose referent is this [cessation] is non-existence. This is what he states with the words "having non-existence as its meaning. The phrase "according to that intention" means according to the purport of the Bhāṣya, which holds that the negative particle has non-existence as its meaning.

He restates Kaiyaṭa’s statement with the words "As for... (*yattu*) and so forth, pointing out that Kaiyaṭa’s alternative explanation of the Bhāṣya passage "nivṛttapadārthakaḥ" contradicts the intended meaning of the Bhāṣya. The phrase *nivṛttapadārthakaḥ* means "that in which the word-meaning has ceased. Here, the referent of the compound (the *anyapadārtha*) is the Kṣatriya and others. In such individuals as the Kṣatriya, the word-meaning consisting of Brāhmaṇahood has ceased; that is, it does not exist in reality. The sense is that since Kṣatriyas and others have Brāhmaṇahood only superimposed through similarity and the like, they do not constitute the primary denotation of the negative particle (*nañ*).

The sense is that, because of parsimony (*lāghava*) and common worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*), it is logical to accept that negation (*nañ*) denotes only non-existence (*abhāva*) with respect to superimposition (*āropa*). "Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means in the opposite of what was stated; that is to say, disregarding worldly consensus and so forth, to accept that a Kṣatriya or similar person—in whom Brāhmaṇahood has been superimposed (i.e., one in whom Brāhmaṇahood is falsely attributed)—is the denotation of the negative particle. In the phrase "of such a person and so forth" (*sādṛśasyādeḥ*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes qualities such as "insignificance" (*alpatva*) which will be cited later in the text.

The meaning is that since similarity and other such qualities are also perceived in expressions like "abrāhmaṇa" (non-Brahmin), the negative particle (*nañ*) would consequently have to be expressive of those as well. Having cited the rule beginning with "tatsādṛśyamabhāvaśca" (similarity to that, non-existence, etc.), he states "abrāhmaṇam" and so forth to provide examples in their respective order. The meaning of [the example] "brāhmaṇasadṛśaḥ" (one similar to a Brahmin) is its referent. The meaning of "apāpam" (sinless) is the absolute absence of sin. The meaning of "anaśvaḥ" (non-horse) is "other than a horse. The distinction is that in the case of "abrāhmaṇa," there is a cognition of difference as a constituent of the similarity, rather than a cognition of mere difference alone.

Since similarity consists in possessing many of the properties belonging to that [object] while being different from it, it should be understood that "otherness" (*anyatva*) is a constituent factor of similarity. In the expression "a girl with a small belly" (*anudarā kanyā*), the understanding is "one with a small belly. In the expression "they are non-animals" (*apaśavo vā*), the meaning is "animals that are not praiseworthy. In the expression "non-dharma" (*adharma*), what is perceived is a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) opposed to dharma, and not merely something different from it. This is the implied meaning (*ārthika-artha*): in all cases, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is simply absence (*abhāva*).

Likewise, following the cognition "a Brāhmaṇa is the counter-positive of an absence," there arises a mental cognition of similarity and so forth. When the word *abrāhmaṇa* is employed to convey a Brāhmaṇa as the counter-positive of an absence, it is for the purpose of conveying a Kṣatriya or others by way of their similarity [to a Brāhmaṇa]; it is in this manner that there is a mental cognition of similarity.

In the expression "a girl with a small belly" (*anudarā kanyā*), since the absolute non-existence of a belly is entirely impossible, the term results in the sense of "small. In the case of "asura," since the meaning of "gods" (*surāṇām*) can be understood from the word *sura* itself, the word *asura* is employed to indicate the counter-positive of that absence; thus, by way of opposition, it refers to those who are hostile to the gods, such as the Daityas. In this manner, the cognition of opposition is mental. This same principle should be inferred in other cases as well.

The point is this: by this method, the intention is that similarity and so forth possess an implied meaning (*ārthika-arthatva*), and thus the statement of the learned authorities—“the state of being similar to that,” and so on—is made; it is not intended to mean that [negation] is directly denotable (*vācyatva*) by the negative particle (*nañ*). Now, one might raise the objection: "If the absence, which is the meaning of *nañ*, were to connect as a qualifier with something distinct from its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), there would be a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*), and consequently, compounds such as *abrāhmaṇa* would be impossible. Desiring to dispel this doubt, he says: "In the counter-positive," and so forth.

The absence, which is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), possesses a qualifierhood (*viśeṣaṇatva*) determined by a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Thus, in expressions such as "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), the cognition is that the Brahmin is qualified by an absence related through the relation of counter-correlativity delimited by Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇatva*). This [cognition] is thus derived from the meaning. In the case of "the cloth is not a jar" (*aghaṭaḥ paṭaḥ*), the cognition is that the jar is the counter-correlate of a difference residing in the cloth. Since *nañ* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*), there is no contradiction in the cloth, which is the referent of a nominal stem, being construed with the meaning of *nañ* through the relation of locusness (*ādheyatā*).

When it is said, "by one who brings what is not a jar," the bringing of a jar does not occur, because of the functional capacity of the negative particle (*nañ*). The sense is that, following the verbal cognition, it is only possible to bring that which possesses an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is the jar. He states the result of the *nañ*-compound being dominated by the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada-pradhāna*) with the words "And thus," etc. The connection is as follows: the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*), the restriction to the singular number, its status as a *tatpuruṣa* compound, and the regulation of person, number, and so forth—these four [properties] of the first-case-inflected words become established. Regarding "the designation of a pronoun":

Regarding the term *asarve*: here, since the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is non-existence (*abhāva*), and because this non-existence has the referent of the word *sarva* as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) acting as a qualifier, there arises the cognition that "all [things] are qualified by the absence [of being all]. Consequently, because the referent of the word *sarva* is primary, it belongs to the class beginning with *sarva* (*sarvādi*); thus, by the rule of extension to what ends in such a word (*tadantavidhi*), its designation as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is established. Regarding the term *anekam*: this is precisely the primary purpose for the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārthaprādhānya*). Thus, the Bhāṣya states: "This very case is included under the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member."

"What is it? "It is 'many' (aneka). "What is included here? "'Singular' (ekavacana). The meaning is that 'one' (eka) is the counter-positive of non-existence; thus, by virtue of the predominance of the sense of the final member [of the compound], the use of the singular number in the word *aneka* is justified. In the same way, the singular number is established in the expression *sevyate 'nekayā* ("she is served by many"). Otherwise, since that which is different from one is "many," there would have to be only the dual or plural numbers, and not the singular—this is the intended sense.

In this way, it should be understood that Pāṇini’s very rule [Pāṇ. 2.2.24], *anekaṃ ca*, is the authority for the fact that the meaning of the suffix *ñ* (i.e., plurality) functions as a qualifier of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha*). By the rule *svaujasam* (Pāṇ. 4.1.2), having prescribed the singular, dual, and plural case-endings after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the dual alone remains for the meaning "two"; thus, by implication, the singular and plural are excluded there. Similarly, for the meaning "many," the plural alone remains, and consequently, the singular and dual are excluded there. It is in this manner that [the rule operates].

The author of the *Sāra* has stated that the rule regarding the singular number is established by accepting the restrictive force of [Pāṇini’s rules] such as "dvyekayoḥ" (2.4.1). In the case of *abrāhmaṇa*, the meaning is "a Brāhmaṇa characterized by the absence [of Brāhmaṇahood]" through the relation of counter-correlativity delimited by Brāhmaṇahood; thus, because the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is predominant, the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is established as a *tatpuruṣa*. This is what is meant by the statement "it is a *tatpuruṣa*. The intention is that, provided it is possible, the predominance of the meaning of the final member—even if it is merely common—is appropriate for a *tatpuruṣa*.

[The objection is: "You are not. [The reply is: Since the referent of *yuṣmad* (the second person pronoun) is the counter-positive of non-existence (*abhāvapratiyogī*), the referent of *yuṣmad* is primary. Consequently, because the agent—the meaning of the present tense suffix (*laṭ*)—is construed as non-different from the referent of *yuṣmad* through the relation of identity (*abhedānvaya*), there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the referent of *yuṣmad* and the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Thus, by the rule *yuṣmadyupapade*, the middle voice (*madhyamapuruṣa*) is justified. Similarly, in the case of *na ahaṃ bhavāmi* ("I am not"), the first person (*uttama*) is established by the rule *asmadyuttamaḥ*.

Likewise, the grammatical distinction between the dual and plural numbers—such as "you two are not" (*ayuvām bhavathaḥ*) and "you [plural] are not" (*ayūyam bhavathaḥ*)—is also rendered possible. He states "otherwise" (*anyathā*) because, if one were to accept that the primary meaning of the first member of the compound is an absence whose counter-correlate is the meaning of the subsequent member, then the distinction of person (*puruṣa*) and so forth would not be possible. The meaning is: "when the absence, which is the sense of the negative particle (*nañ*), has predominance as determined by the meaning of the subsequent member. The phrase "like this" (*itibad*) refers to this very point.

Just as in the case of "your non-existence" (*tvad-abhāvaḥ*) and "my non-existence" (*mad-abhāvaḥ*), because there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the second-person pronoun *yuṣmad* and the first-person pronoun *asmad*, the middle and first persons do not occur; rather, since there is coreferentiality with the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) through the negation whose counter-correlate is the meaning of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the first person alone occurs by the rule "in the remainder [of cases], the first person. Similarly, in the cases "you are not" (*atvam bhavasi*) and "I am not" (*anahaṃ bhavāmi*), if one accepts that the meanings of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) determined by the negation (*nañ-artha*), then one must accept the predominance of the prior member of the compound.

Thus, [the verb] would necessarily be in the first person alone. Similarly, dual and plural forms such as *ayuvāṃ bhavathaḥ* (you two are) and *ayūyaṃ bhavatha* (you all are) would also not occur, because the agent (*kartṛ*)—which is the referent of the second person—is singular. Regarding the phrase "in the aspect of non-existence" (*abhāvāṃśe*): the meaning is that there is a non-existence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is the referents of the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Consequently, the meaning is that this occurs when there is a substratum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) in the aspect of non-existence, which is itself determined by a qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in the referents of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. The phrase "because [the agent] is not present in finite verbs" (*tiṅṣu asattvāt*) means...

The meaning is that because the primary absence [of the agent] denotes a *kāraka* expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), it stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [absence]; therefore, the referent of *yuṣmad*, which is a qualifier of that [absence], lacks coreferentiality with the verbal suffixes. Regarding the term "person" (*puruṣa*): it means the "middle" and other persons as designated for the triad beginning with *ti* (i.e., *tip*, *tas*, *jhi*). He establishes the systematic arrangement of "persons" and so forth according to his own view, stating: "In our view... The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "but" (*tu*).

Regarding the statement "you are not" (*atvaṃ bhavasi*) and so forth, since the existence [of the action] has as its locus that which is non-different from the referent of *yuṣmad*—which is the counter-correlative of the absence—the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the referents of *yuṣmad* and so on with the meaning of the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) exists; therefore, the determination of person (*puruṣavyavasthā*) is not untenable. Now, one might object: if the meaning of the subsequent member of the compound is predominant, then in the case of "bring a non-jar" (*aghaṭam ānaya*), since the state of being the counter-correlative of an absence resides in the jar, it would follow that even the bringing of a jar occurs after the cognition of that [absence]. To this, he says: "or the qualificand" (*viśeṣyo vā*). Because the status of being a qualificand requires the expectancy for the status of being a qualifier, he says: "the counter-correlative" (*pratiyoginī*).

The meaning is "the counter-positive," which consists of the referent of the second member of the compound. The sense of the locative case is "being determined by" (*nirūpitatva*). Thus, the meaning is that the negative particle (*nañ*) signifies an absence (*abhāva*) which possesses a subjecthood (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a qualifierhood (*viśeṣaṇatā*) residing in the counter-positive, which consists of the referent of the second member of the compound.

And likewise, in the case of "abrāhmaṇaḥ" (non-Brahmin), since he is a Kṣatriya, the absence that is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of "Brahmin"—namely, the absence of Brahminhood residing in the object denoted by the final member of the compound due to proximity—is possible only in the Kṣatriya and others; thus, the meaning of "abrāhmaṇa" is a Kṣatriya or similar person. The cognition is: "one who possesses that [absence], namely, a Kṣatriya. Now, one might raise the objection: "In this way, forms such as *asaḥ* (not all) and *asarve* (not all) would be unestablished. Anticipating this, he says: "The point is this," and "even though it is figurative (*gauṇatve’pi*)."

The meaning is: even though the referent of each respective word contained within a *nañ*-compound is subordinate (*upasarjana*) by virtue of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) determined by a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the absence that is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). "On account of an indicator" (*jñāpakāt*) means: on account of the indicator consisting in the mention of "non-compounds with *nañ*" (*anañ-samāsa*). He establishes this very status as an indicator with the words beginning "asaḥ śivaḥ" (He is not Śiva). By the rule *etattadoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.132), the elision of the final *s* of the forms *eta-* and *tad-*—which are designated as pronouns (*sarvanāman*)—is prescribed when followed by a consonant (*hal*).

The meaning is as follows: if, in a negative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*), the meaning of the prior member were predominant, then *etad* and *tad*—being subordinate members (*upasarjana*) within that compound—would fall outside the group beginning with *sarva*. Consequently, they would lack the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and the elision of the case-ending (*sulopa*) would not apply. Thus, the mention of "non-negative compound" (*anañ-samāsa*) would be redundant; this redundancy serves to indicate that even when subordinate in a negative compound, words beginning with *sarva* still possess the status of a pronoun. One might object: "Even if they are subordinate, since the words *etad* and *tad* exist in forms such as *aneṣo dadāti* and *asaḥ śivaḥ*, the elision of the case-ending would still apply there. Therefore, the mention of 'non-negative compound' is necessary to prevent that. To this, the following is said: [the rule applies] only when the word ending in the genitive case is used in the sense of a possessor (*svasvāmibhāva*). Since in the examples *aneṣo dadāti* and *asaḥ śivaḥ*, the genitive case is not employed in the sense of possession, the elision does not occur. Furthermore, the mention of "non-negative compound" is indeed necessary for the sake of the subsequent sūtra (*na bahuvrīhau*); otherwise, in a form like *anekaḥ* (where *na* is a negative particle), the elision would undesirably apply because *eka* is a word beginning with *sarva*. Thus, the mention of "non-negative compound" is required to exclude cases where *na* functions as a negative particle. However, in the present context, it is mentioned specifically to indicate that the status of being a pronoun applies even when these words are subordinate in a negative compound. This is the intended meaning.

Nor should it be argued that the mention of "non-compound" (*anañsamāsa*) is redundant because, since the suffix *su* denotes the number inherent in the meaning of the words *etad* and *tad*, and since the meaning of *nañ* is the absence [of the positive], when the former meaning is predominant, the *su* would not denote the number inherent in the meaning of *etad* and *tad*—and thus the elision of *su* would not apply. This is because there is no evidence for the genitive case in the rule *etattadoḥ* to signify such a relationship [as "inherence in the meaning"].

Since it is appropriate that the meaning be "there is elision of the *s* of this *etattad-* when it is immediately followed [by a case-ending]," one must supply the subsequent word (*anantara-pada*) as in the example *gapoṣṭak*. Thus, since the mention of "non-compound" (*anañ-samāsa*) serves its intended purpose, how can it function as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? To this, he says: "of *ak-*."

The intended meaning is that, by means of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of those accompanied by *akac*, it is appropriate to understand *etad* and *tad* only as those termed "pronouns" (*sarvanāman*) which are eligible for *akac*; for it is established that, just like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*viprayoga*) also serves as a cause for the comprehension of a specific distinction, as seen in examples such as *aśaṅkhavaktraḥ* ("one who does not have a conch-shell face") and *harir* ("the lion"). And so forth (*tathā ca*): this means that when *etad* and *tad* are understood only as those termed "pronouns" through the exclusion of those [forms] ending in *ak*, [the following applies].

The point is this: in examples such as *asaḥ śivaḥ* ("non-Śiva"), since the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), i.e., absence, functions as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the word *as-* becomes a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Consequently, because it falls outside the group of words beginning with *sarva*, it lacks the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and thus the elision of the case-ending (*sulopa*) would not apply anyway; therefore, the inclusion of the phrase "not in a compound with *nañ*" (*anañsamāsa*) is redundant and serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned principle. Furthermore, it should be understood that even if one were to accept the mere mention of the word *tat* (in the rule), the elision of the case-ending according to *halṅyābbhyaḥ* would be unavoidable in cases like *atitat*, because the quality of being a pronoun (*atva*) is absent in a subordinate member; thus, the inclusion of "not in a compound with *nañ*" remains useless.

"An indicator (*jñāpaka*)" means that even though a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) has the meaning of the prior member as its primary sense, it serves as an indicator for the application of grammatical operations conditioned by the primacy of the meaning of the subsequent member. The intention is that by this, the determination of person and number is also established in cases such as *atvaṃ bhavasi* (you are not you) and *ayuvāṃ bhavathaḥ* (you two are not you two). "Due to conformity with the qualified object (*viśeṣya-anurodhāt*)" means that the word *su*, which is carried over from the rule *sub-āmantrite...* (Pāṇini 2.1.2), is the qualified object and is necessarily in the singular; therefore, the intention is that the singular number is employed in the qualifier *anaika* (not one) in conformity with that [qualified object].

One might raise the following objection: "If a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is predominant in the sense of its first member, then *anekam* means 'different from one' (*eka-bhinna*). Since that which is different from one possesses plurality (*anekatva*), let either the dual or the plural be employed after the word *aneka*. Furthermore, in accordance with that, let the dual or plural be used for the subsequent term *su* (the suffix), just as in the rule *nandigrahipacādibhyaḥ*, where the term *dhātoḥ* (from roots) is modified into *dhātubhyaḥ* (from roots [plural]) while remaining in force. Anticipating this, he says: "Moreover, from the word *aneka*..."

If it were stated that "two *sub*-ending words" (*aneka subante*), then a *bahuvrīhi* compound could not be formed from many *sub*-ending words; for by the rule *anekam anyapadārthe*, which prescribes *bahuvrīhi* for exactly two *sub*-ending words when they refer to another word's meaning (*anyapadārtha*), a *bahuvrīhi* would be restricted to only two such words.

Now, regarding the rule "then [there is composition] when there are many [words] in the sense of another word" (*anekam anyapadārthe*), since the plural number is employed, it would follow that only many inflected words (*subanta*) existing in the sense of another word are compounded; consequently, a *bahuvrīhi* would not occur between two inflected words. However, since a *bahuvrīhi* is desired for both two and many inflected words, the singular number is used as a generic term (*jātyaikavacana*) to include both cases. Having prescribed the dual for duality and the plural for plurality, the rule "the singular" (*ekavacanam*) prescribes the singular number in a general sense.

Pāṇini established that the default singular number used to denote such a count is [actually] plural; likewise, in the phrase *sevyate 'nekayā* ("she is served by many"), the poet employed the singular number after the word *anekā* (many) in order to convey the connection of "service" with each individual woman among those women presented by the word *anekā*, in accordance with the gender of the substantive (*yoṣā*). However, the singular was not employed by taking the predominance of the meaning of the second member of the compound as the basis.

The meaning is that, according to the position favored by the Bhāṣya—wherein the absence (the meaning of the negative particle *nañ*) possesses the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) as determined by its being a qualifier residing in the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha*)—the predominance of the subsequent member's meaning is impossible. In this context, the word *yoṣā* refers to a collection of women and is therefore singular; thus, the argument that one must accept the predominance of the subsequent member's meaning in a *nañ*-compound in order to conform to usages such as "she is served by many" is refuted.

The intention [of the author] is that the fact of the word ending in the singular number (*ekavacanāntatva*) in *anekayā* and so forth has been established otherwise. "For this very reason" means: precisely because of the predominance of the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārthaprādhānya*) in a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*). Regarding the phrase "many fall from the ocean": the term *sūpapādam* means "capable of being easily established. It is derived from the root *pad* with the prefix *upa-pa*, followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), and the suffix *khal* in the sense of the object (*karman*). When there is predominance of the meaning of the prior member, the meaning is "that which is different from one" (*ekabhinnam*). Since that which is different from one is "many" (*aneka*), the plural number in *anekaiḥ* is easily established. This is the meaning.

The point is this: if the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) were predominant, the use of the plural ending for the word *aneka* here would be untenable; since the meaning of the single word constituting the final member would be predominant, there would have to be only the singular ending, because it is appropriate that the case-suffix (*sup*) following the compound expresses the number belonging to the principal referent of the members being compounded.

[Objection: But if, on account of conforming to the qualified (*viśeṣya*), the singular number is justified in cases such as *aneka* (not one), then in the case of *avarṣāḥ* (non-summer) and *ahemantaḥ* (non-winter) as well, the ending in the singular would follow by conforming to the qualified term, namely "winter" (*hemanta*). [Response: This is not so; for it has been stated in the Bhāṣya itself that "the gender and number of adjectives depend upon their substratum. Thus, since it is accepted that in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the gender and number sometimes belong to the subsequent member (*anuyogin*) and sometimes to the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), there is no fault—this is the sense.

An objection is raised: "In the rule *etattadoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.102), the mention of the term *anañ-samāsa* (non-negative compound) was stated by the author of the Sāra to be an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that even when the meaning of the prior member is predominant and the meaning of the subsequent member is subordinate in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) still applies. Thus, although forms such as *asaḥ* are established, one might object that in cases like *atvaṃ bhavasi*, the determination of person (*puruṣa-vyavasthā*) would be untenable. Anticipating this, he provides the following resolution: "In *atvaṃ bhavasi* etc. [The word *tvam*] refers metonymically (*lakṣaṇā*) to something other than the actual *yuṣmad*; the negative particle (*nañ*) serves merely to indicate the intended sense (*tātparya-grāhaka*) for such a metonymical reference.

"Indicative power" (*dyotakatva*) consists precisely in being a conveyer of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). That is to say, when used in conjunction with the negative particle *nañ*, the word "you" (*yuṣmad*) functions with respect to that which is different from "you. By the phrase "atvaṃ bhavasi" and so forth, one should understand "anahaṃ bhavāmi" (I am not you). "And likewise" means: and when the negative particle is indicative. "By the meaning of 'you' as distinct" means by the meaning of the word "you" in the form of something other than "you. "Because of coreferentiality with the verbal suffix" (*tiṅ*) [is the reason].

Because the referent of the word *yuṣmat* (you) is construed non-differently with the agent denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), and because [the suffix] denotes a grammatical participant (*kāraka*) expressed by a verbal suffix, there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Consequently, from the verbal cognition that "the activity of becoming resides in that agent which is the referent of the suffix and is non-different from what is non-different from you," the determination of person (*puruṣavyavasthā*) is established. However, there is no insistence that the referents of the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* must be the primary [referents]. The verbal meaning is: "The activity of becoming is such that its substratum—the locus—is of the nature of the agent denoted by the suffix and is non-different from that referent of *yuṣmad* which consists in being non-different from you. In this same way, the verbal cognition in the case of "I am not" (*nāhaṃ bhavāmi*) is to be inferred.

In the *Śākari*, it was previously stated that if one accepts the view that—even when the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha*) is predominant in a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*)—the grammatical operations triggered by the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha*) still take effect, then the mention of "negative compound" (*nañsamāsagrahaṇa*) serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicative mark); thus, the determination of person (*puruṣavyavasthā*) is established even without resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). However, it should be understood that the author of the *Sāra* has established the determination of person through a different method according to the aforementioned reasoning, with the intention that the mention of "not a negative compound" (*anañsamāsagrahaṇa*) serves as the *jñāpaka* specifically for the technical designation of pronouns (*sarvanāmasaṃjñā*).

He explains the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the negative particle (*nañ*) which has the sense of a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) with the words beginning with "evam" (thus). Regarding the phrase "having a substratum non-different from you": since the referent of the word *yuṣmat* (you) is connected by way of non-difference with the agent, which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the meaning is the absence of that efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—that is, the operation (*vyāpāra*) conducive to softening—which has a substratum non-different from the referent of *yuṣmat*. Operation (*vyāpāra*), efficient force (*bhāvanā*), production (*utpādanā*), and action (*kriyā*) are synonyms for operation; such is the intended meaning.

Synonymy (*paryāyatva*) consists in having distinct determinants of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) while the determinant of the capacity [to denote] (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) remains one and the same—as in the case of "that which has a substratum non-different from a jar. The meaning is: that which has a substratum (*āśraya*) non-different from a jar—that is, having the form of a jar—is its existence (*astitva*), i.e., the action of being (*astikriyā*); the negation of that is what is intended. The phrase "of the non-compounded *nañ*" means the *nañ* whose scope is a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). However, this is not tenable according to the literal reading, because [the negation] would only connect with the action (*kriyā*). Therefore, [the author says] "no."

The authority for this is found in the commentary on the sixteenth kārikā, "saṃbodhanāntaṃ kṛtvorthāḥ," where the passage beginning with "it is not logical" was already stated; that should be consulted there. Here, the mention of "action" (kriyā) is also an indication of "quality" (guṇa). For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the *nañ* sūtra: "Having first applied [the negation] to the action and the quality, it subsequently effects their cessation. The meaning of this is: having enjoined [the action or quality], there is a prohibition of it.

Therefore, even when there is a cognition of the absence of a quality (*guṇābhāva*), it is understood as a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation). An example of a quality is: "Not one thing is dear to us" (*na naḥ, ekaṃ priyam*). Here, "naḥ" is in the genitive plural. For in this case, by the negation of "one dear thing," the cognition of "many dear things" arises. Here, "oneness" (*ekatva*) is a quality in the form of a number, and its negation is [the subject]. By the very force of the negation—"not one thing is dear to us"—there arises the cognition of an object endowed with another number.

And likewise, even in the definition of *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation)—namely, "that in which the negative particle (*nañ*) occurs together with a verb"—the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) should be understood as an indicator for "quality" (*guṇa*). As for the phrase "and that": it means "and the absence (*abhāva*) which is the meaning of *nañ*. It is denotable (*śakya*) by way of its specific forms, namely absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) are included.

Having in mind the objection that—due to parsimony—the denotative power (*śakti*) of the negative particle (*nañ*) should be postulated as residing only in the universal form consisting of "the nature of being an absence" which pervades all absences, and not in specific forms such as "the nature of absolute absence" (*atyantābhāvatva*) due to their complexity, he says: "because there is cognition [of it] in those respective forms. This means that the cognition [of the negative particle] in its respective specific forms, such as "the nature of absolute absence," is established by experience (*anubhava*).

The meaning is as follows: just as from the word *pacati* ("he cooks"), the operation (*vyāpāra*) is understood specifically in its particular forms such as blowing or heating from below, and not in a general form such as "conduciveness" (*anukūlatva*) or "operation-ness" (*vyāpāratva*), so it is here. In the *Paramalaghumañjūṣā*, however, it is stated that for the non-compounded negative particle (*nañ*), the meanings are absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). Absolute non-existence is the absence of a relation other than identity (*tādātmya*); mutual non-existence is the absence of the relation of identity, which is to say, difference (*bheda*).
But for the compounded negative particle, it is said that its meaning is simply non-existence (*abhāva*). (41)

Thus ends the determination of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) within the *Sāṃkarya* section of the commentary on the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, composed by Śaṅkara, the son of Raṅgabhaṭṭa; the determination of the meaning of the negative particle in the exposition of the *Sāra* is complete. (7)
Now begins the determination of the meanings of particles (nipāta).

In the course of defining the meaning of the particle *nañ*, while determining the meanings of all other particles as well, [the author] sets forth the following argument to indicate that the Naiyāyika position—that *pra* and so on are indicators (*dyotaka*) while *ca* and so on are denoters (*vācaka*)—is untenable: "The *pra*s and so on are indicators," and so forth. This means they possess the capacity characterized by being indicators. And being an indicator generally consists in being that which suggests the capacity residing in the word with which it is co-uttered; for there is no reason for such a distinction.

The meaning is that there is no evidence for making such a distinction as that *upasargas* (prepositions) possess denotative power (*dyotakatva*) while *cādis* (conjunctions) possess expressive power (*vācakatva*). Furthermore, since both *prādis* and *cādis* function as *nipātas*, it is more parsimonious (*lāghavena*) to assume that *cādis* also possess denotative power, just like *prādis*. Bearing such an intention in mind, he establishes the denotative nature of *nipātas*, stating: "By which [reason] *prādis* and so forth are denotative..."

By the same reason that particles such as *pra* and others are accepted as being indicative (*dyotaka*), one must likewise accept that particles such as *ca* and others are also indicative. Clarifying that very reason for which *pra* and others are indicative, [the author] says: "The point is this. Regarding the example "he follows after God" (*īśvaramanubhavati*) and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes examples such as "he conquers excellently" (*prajayati*). In the phrase "following after, etc. (*anubhavādi*), the word "etc. (*ādi*) comprises "excelling in victory" (*prakṛṣṭajaya*) and the like.

Regarding the meaning such as "experience" (*anubhava*) that is perceived in expressions like *anubhavati*, is that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) contained within such usage? No, he says—because it would lead to an absurdity (*āpatti*). If that experience and so forth were the denotation (*śakya*) of the root, then even in cases such as *bhavati* when devoid of a prefix (*upasarga*), the meaning of experience and so on would be perceived; yet it is not so perceived. Therefore, the meaning is that this is certainly not the denotative meaning of the root.

Anticipating the objection that "let that [meaning] be expressed by the prefix (upasarga) through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)," he refutes it with the words "not the meaning of the prefix. The phrase "tathā sati" means: "if the meanings such as 'experiencing' (anubhava), which are perceived in cases like *anubhavati*, were to be expressed by the prefix. The phrase "because of the consequence of non-connection" (*ananvayāpatteḥ*) [is explained as follows].

Regarding the statement "he experiences" (*anubhavati*), in the universally established cognition that the meaning of the suffix *laṭ* (present tense) is an activity conducive to experience whose agent is present in time, the object of the experience would not be construed with the agent of the *laṭ* because, since the prefix (*upasarga*) expresses the sense of "experience," that sense is not expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*). He states the reason for this: "of suffixes" (*pratyayānām*). This is because of the rule that suffixes denote their own meanings as conjoined with the meaning of their own base (*prakṛti*).

The meaning is that, in the present context, since the object consisting of the experience (*anubhava*) is not denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), it is impossible for there to be a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) such as "the operation conducive to experience whose agent is the meaning of the *tiṅ* suffix. Now, one might argue that the following rule should be postulated: "Suffixes convey their own meaning as connected with either the meaning of their own base (*prakṛti*) or with the meaning of another element co-occurring with it"; and thus, in the case of "he experiences" (*anubhavati*).

With the intention that there is no fault in the present case—since the verbal suffix *tiṅ* denotes an agent who possesses an activity associated with an object consisting of an experience expressed by a prefix co-occurring with the root *bhū* (which is the base of the *tiṅ*-suffix), and this is logically consistent with the construction "the activity conducive to experience [is] the agent denoted by the *tiṅ*-meaning"—he states another objection regarding "he follows" (*anugacchati*) and so forth.

The point is this: since the root *an* is employed here as being intended to denote an object in the form of experience (*anubhava*), and in accordance with that, even the verbal root *gam*, which denotes a specific activity conducive to conjunction, must be accepted as expressing activity in general; consequently, there would arise the undesirable consequence of the cognition of an "experience" as the meaning, namely: "an activity conducive to experience whose agent is the meaning of the *tiṅ*-suffix."

In reality, however, since the specific activity (vyāpāra) is already occupied by the conjunction with a northern region (uttaradeśa-saṃyoga), it is impossible for the meaning of "experience" (anubhava)—which is denoted by the prefix *anu*—to be construed with it; thus, there can be no cognition of the meaning "experience. This is the sense in which the claim that the root *gam* denotes "activity in general" is lacking in authoritative justification.

Therefore, regarding the grammatical derivation (vyutpatti) such as "the meaning of the base [is connected] with the meanings of the suffixes," one must understand that the previously stated objection remains valid: because it is cumbersome and lacks authoritative support to include the phrase "co-occurring with that" (*tatsamabhivyāhṛta*), the meaning of the verbal root (*anubhava*)—being expressible by the prefix *anu* and not by the verbal root itself—could not be construed with the agent, which is the meaning of the personal ending (*tiṅ*). Consequently, the rule "between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root" (*nāmārtha-dhātvarthayoḥ*) need not be restricted to cases other than particles (*nipāta*), as its scope is already limited by this very consideration. This is the intended sense.

If it is argued that [the meaning] is expressed by that verbal root as qualified by the prefix, he says "no" to that as well: "not a qualified object. The reason is "due to complexity" (*gauravāt*); the meaning is that because the qualified [object] possesses a dual nature, there would be complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating the delimiting condition of expressive power (*vācakatva-kalpana*) for the sequence of the qualified form.

If it is argued that in the case of *prajayati*, victory (*jaya*) is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), while excellence (*prakarṣa*) is denoted by the prefix (*upasarga*), and thus there is no complexity regarding the delimitors of semantic capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka-gaurava*), we reply: excellence, being the meaning of a noun (*nāmartha*), could not be construed with victory, which is the meaning of the verbal root; for there is a grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root do not directly connect through a relation of difference (*bheda*). If one were to introduce the qualification "other than a particle" (*nipātātirikta*) within the term "meaning of a noun," there would be both complexity and a lack of authoritative evidence—this is the intended sense. Concluding, he says: "And so... (*tathā ca*).

The meaning is: "and because, according to the method of etymological derivation (*nirukti*), it is impossible for either the verbal root (*dhātu*) or the prefix (*upasarga*) to denote the experience. He states his own established position: "of the root alone" (*dhātoḥ eva*). This means "of that very root belonging to the *bhū* class and so forth. By the word "alone" (*eva*), the prefix is excluded. [Objection: But how can there be a cognition of the meaning of experience without a linguistic function (*vṛtti*)? To this he says: "let there be indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for that which denotes 'existence' and so forth. The phrase ending in the genitive case, "of existence" (*vidyamānatva*), etc., is a qualifying attribute of the root that contains a reason.

Since the verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes meanings such as "existence," because in expressions like *ghaṭo bhavati* ("the pot comes into being") there is the cognition of meanings such as existence, it is therefore possible for the verbal root alone to possess indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the form of a relation to its primary meaning (*śakya-sambandha*). The meaning is that indication in the form of a relation to the primary meaning is not possible for a prefix (*upasarga*), because a prefix is never used in isolation and thus lacks the capacity to denote any meaning whatsoever. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "existence etc.," the meaning of "origination" (*utpatti*) is included. He states the purpose of employing a prefix with the words "But the prefix... (*upasargastu*).

The meaning is that when one accepts a figurative (lakṣaṇā) function of the verbal root (*dhātu*) in such a sense, [the prefix] serves as the indicator of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). And "intentionality" (*tātparyatva*) consists in being uttered with the desire: "May there arise in the hearer an understanding of a figurative meaning in the form of experience (*anubhava*), etc., based on the verbal root. Now, if this is the case, the status of prefixes as indicators of intention is obtained, but not their status as illuminators (*dyotaka*); thus, the traditional doctrine of their being "illuminators" would not be consistent. To this, he says: "And so, it is precisely the indication of intention," and so forth.

He states "And that" (*tacceti*), because such suggestiveness (*dyotakatva*) exists even in particles (*nipāta*) like *ca* and others which you accept as denoters (*vācaka*). Since no meaning is established by a mere proposition (*pratijñā*) alone, he demonstrates this by applying the stated point to particles such as *ca*, beginning with "Like Caitra" (*caitramiva*). In the co-occurrence with the word *iva*, the word *caitra* refers to one similar to Caitra through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); the word *iva*, however, serves to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) for the word *caitra* to have secondary indication in the sense of "one similar to Caitra."

The meaning is that one perceives [the object] as qualified by a similarity characterized by Caitra. Thus, pointing out that the disparity created by the Naiyāyikas—namely, that while *pra* and other particles are indicators (*dyotaka*), *ca* and others cannot be indicators for the same reason—is unjustified, he says: "because it is easy to state" (*suvacatvāt*). This means that it is easily possible to assert the following: the word *caitra* indicates (*lakṣya*) an object qualified by similarity, while the word *iva* serves to capture the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). He states another argument regarding that status as an indicator: "they are both worshipped" (*upāsyete*).

The understanding is that [the meaning of the root] is an activity conducive to meditation (*upāsanā*) which is based on the object denoted by the suffix *laṭ* (present tense) as non-different from Hari and Hara. Here, one must consider three alternatives regarding the nature of the meaning "meditation" as it is perceived: is it denotable by the prefix (*upasarga*) alone, is it denotable by the verbal root (*dhātu*) qualified by the prefix, or is it denotable by the verbal root alone? Regarding the first alternative, he says "tathā sati" (if that were so), meaning: if the meaning in the form of meditation were denotable by the prefix. He then says "svārtha... and so forth.

The meaning of "having an object" (*sakarmakatva*) is this: one's own root-meaning (*sva-dhātuḥ*), which is the result expressed by that [root], has a distinct locus from the operation (*vyāpāra*) which expresses that [result]; the state of expressing such an operation is "having an object. Thus, since the root *ās* lacks the expression of a result in the form of "worship," it lacks "having an object," and therefore the *L*-suffix would not occur in the sense of the object; it is not the second [alternative]. He says "due to complexity" (*gauravāt*): the meaning is that there is complexity in assuming that the specific sequential order (*viśiṣṭānupūrvī*) is the delimiting factor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) when the meaning is expressed by the root as qualified by a prefix (*upasarga*).

Furthermore, because that which is qualified [by a prefix] is not included in the *bhvādi* class, it would fail to receive the designation of "root" (*dhātu*). If you argue that its inclusion [in the list] must be postulated, it should be understood that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and other such operations for the qualified form.

If, however, you accept the third alternative—that the meaning consisting of "reverential attendance" (*upāsana*) is denotable by the root alone—then, in the presence of the prefix *upa*, the meaning perceived as "reverential attendance" is actually indicated by the root *ās*; thus, the status of being a "suggestor" (*dyotaka*) is established for the prefix *upa*, on the grounds that its function is assumed to be that of making the intended meaning clear (*tātparyagrāhakatva*). This is the underlying sense.

One might object: "Even though the verbal root lacks a direct object, let there be a suffix denoting the abstract state (bhāve lakāraḥ) in the word *upāsyate*. With this intention, he says: "In the word *dṛśya*, the word 'object' (*karmaṇi*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. If the suffix were in the sense of the abstract state, the usage "*hariharāv upāsyete*" (Hari and Hara are both worshipped) would not be possible. Therefore, the meaning is that for the sake of establishing such usage, it must necessarily be accepted—according to the method explained—that the root *ās* preceded by the prefix *upa* possesses a direct object. || 42 ||

"Indicating that [meaning]" (*tat-dyotakatvam*). "Even in the case of *ca* and so forth" (*cādiṣv api*) means: even in the case of *ca* and other particles which, according to the Naiyāyika school, are considered to be expressive (*vācaka*). He says they are "equal"—that is, identical—by stating: "likewise in another instance, a particle. Regarding "in another instance": he states "such as *sākṣāt*" (*sākṣād iti*), meaning that even in the case of a particle other than those beginning with *pra*, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is seen to denote the object (*karman*). The meaning is: an operation conducive to perception, characterized by being the object of a cognition produced by the senses. "It is adorned" (*alaṃkriyate*) refers to a specific operation conducive to beauty. "*Ūrī*" refers to an operation conducive to acceptance (*svīkṛti*).

"Even here" means even in the examples mentioned, such as "is directly perceived" (*sākṣātkriyate*). "That respective object" means the object of perception and so forth. "In the object" (*karmaṇi*) means the substratum of the result consisting of direct perception and so on. "That respective meaning" means the capacity to convey an activity conducive to perception and so forth. The sense is that when there is the co-occurrence of the root with the particles *sākṣāt* and others, the meaning that is understood there belongs to the verbal root by way of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). He states the result of this: "by the suffixes" (*lakāra*).

The meaning is that the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is established in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, the intention is that it is logical for particles (*nipāta*) such as *upa-* and others to function as indicators (*dyotaka*), just like prefixes (*upasarga*). However, if it is maintained that when a particle is used in conjunction with a verbal root, the power (*śakti*) of the root resides in the meaning being cognized—since roots have multiple meanings—and the particle merely brings to light (*unnāyaka*) the power inherent in the word with which it is co-occurrent; and if "bringing to light" means "awakening the power" (*śaktyudbodhakatva*), and this very "awakening of the power" is what constitutes being an indicator (*dyotakatva*), then [the following applies]:

It should be understood that the phrase "denoting those respective meanings" is correct exactly as it is heard [in the text]. He raises an objection—that the assumption of transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) for the root *kṛ* in the sense of "direct realization" (*sākṣātkāra*) and so forth is redundant—with the words "even though. The sense is that transitivity certainly exists, because the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is observed in the accusative case in examples such as "the pot is being made" (*ghaṭaḥ kriyate*). The meaning of the phrase "in these senses" is that there would be no transitivity in the sense of direct realization and the like.

He says "otherwise" (*anyathā*) because the fact that the root *kṛ* is transitive in one sense is irrelevant when one relies on its being transitive in another sense. The meaning is: if the root *kṛ* is established as transitive in some sense, then by relying on that, one may accept its transitivity even in another sense—as in the expression "the wind transforms" (*vāyur vikurute*).

Since the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is observed to be transitive in the expression "he makes a pot" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), one understands from the sentence "the air undergoes a transformation" (*vāyur vikāram āpadyate*) that the air alone is the substratum of both the transformation and the operation conducive to it; consequently, even in the case of an intransitive verb, it would result in being transitive. In that case, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) prescribed by the rule *akarmakācca* would not occur. Furthermore, the suffix in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve lakāraḥ*) in the expression "it is transformed by the air" (*vāyunā vikriyate*) would not be possible.

Furthermore, since direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) and the like do not constitute the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the teacher and others could not have the status of an object (*karman*); for the status of an object belongs only to that which is the locus of the fruit of the verbal root’s meaning—this is the sense. Consequently, because the status of being transitive (*sakarmakatva*) would otherwise be untenable, one must accept either a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for the root *kṛñ* in the sense of direct realization and so forth; such is the intention. He restates the view of the Naiyāyikas with the words "Now," etc., [and] "of those two which are equal to perception."

Here, by virtue of the locative case [in the definition], the *kośa* (lexicon) serves as the indicator of the primary denotative power (*śakti*), stating that "the word *sākṣāt* is the denotator of both 'perception' (*pratyakṣa*) and 'equality' (*tulya*). For this very reason, the well-known convention that only denotative words are listed in a lexicon is consistent. Although no lexicon is seen that indicates the primary denotative power of the term *nipāta* in the sense of "worship" (*upāsana*), nevertheless, based on the statement in the *Nirukta*—"they are called *nipātas* because they fall (*nipatanti*) upon various meanings"—it is inferred that *nipāta* also denotes the sense of worship. The phrase "conducive to that" [refers to this].

The meaning is that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is precisely the activity conducive to [the result], such as meditation or direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). The intention is that the result (*phala*), however, is indeed the meaning of the particle (*nipāta*). Thus, in examples such as "the teacher is directly realized" (*guruḥ sākṣātkriyate*), the cognition is as follows: "the activity conducive to the production of a direct realization, which resides in a locus non-different from the teacher, by means of the relation of objectness (*viṣayatā-sambandha*)," and so forth. Now, one might object: if the verbal root does not denote the result, then according to the previously stated principle—that a root is transitive when its own meaning is a result residing in a different locus (*svārthaphalavyadhikaraṇa*)—it would not be transitive. To this, he says: "its own [meaning] and the particle connected with it," etc.

The term *sva-dhātuḥ* refers to the verbal root itself, as well as the particles (*nipāta*) associated with it. The meaning is that "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*) consists in the denotation of an operation (*vyāpāra*) that has a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) from the result (*phala*), which constitutes the meaning of either one of these two [the root or the particle]. Regarding the phrase "when not joined": just as particles such as *pra-* and others are seen to be indicators (*dyotaka*), so too are particles such as *ca-* and others; this is the illustrative point derived from the example.

In the statement, "In the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta), the Guru is worshipped; in the case of the illustrated (dārṣṭāntika), Śiva is directly realized," worship (upāsanā) and direct realization (sākṣātkāra) are expressed by the indeclinables (nipāta), while the mere activity conducive to them is expressed by the verbal roots (dhātu). Since the roots *ās* and *kṛ* express an activity that has as its locus something other than the result—which consists of worship and direct realization and is the meaning of the indeclinable co-occurring with those roots—they are transitive (sakarmaka).

The point is that in both cases, even without the particle having a merely indicative (*dyotaka*) function, the status of the teacher and so forth as the object (*karman*) is established by their being the substratum of the result—namely, the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) which constitutes the meaning of the act of worship (*upāsanā*). Therefore, the two examples are not inconsistent. This [argument] is not a proof; that is to say, it does not prove either that the suffix (*lakāra*) denotes the teacher and so forth as the object of the act of worship in instances such as *guruḥ upāsyate*, nor does it prove that the verbal root expresses a qualified meaning or that particles are merely indicative.

If this is argued, he says "no" to that, [stating]: "between the meaning of a noun (*nāmārtha*) and the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*). This is because of the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root through a relation of direct difference (*sākṣādbheda-sambandha*). In the case at hand, there would not even be a connection of the meaning of the noun—consisting of the fruit such as *upāsanā* (meditation)—with the activity denoted by the verbal root through a relation of difference consisting of "conduciveness" (*anukūlatā*); how much less, then, could there be the denotation of the teacher (*guru*) and so forth as the object (*karman*) of the action by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*), etc.? As for the lexicon entry beginning with "directly (*sākṣāt*) means equal to perception (*pratyakṣa*)," etc., [it refers to something else].

The sense is that [the term] "upapanna" (appropriate) is employed for the sake of illumination. Otherwise—that is, if one were to accept a direct, distinct relation between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root—the following would occur: in the expression *taṇḍulaḥ pacati* ("The rice cooks"), the word *taṇḍula* takes the nominative case (*prathamā*) because, by not intending to express the status of being an object (*karmatva*), it intends to express merely the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Such a usage would be entirely incorrect in the sense of *taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("He cooks the rice"). In this case, the noun-meaning, *taṇḍula*, would have to relate to the verbal-root-meaning, the action of cooking, through a relation of difference—namely, through the relation of being an object (*karmatā*).

The point is that since it is possible for "objectness" (*karmatva*) to appear as a relational qualifier (*saṃsarga*), even in the absence of the accusative case-ending—which is the indicator of the relation of objectness—an unintended cognition would result, namely: "an operation conducive to softening (of rice) which has rice as its object. This is because such a cognition from the aforementioned sentence contradicts actual experience.

In the derivation [of the term *nāmapada*] as "the meaning of a name and the meaning of a verbal root," if one were to include the qualification "names are those other than particles (*nipāta*"), then there would be no contingency regarding the impossibility of the connection between the meaning of a particle and the meaning of a verbal root; therefore, he says: "Furthermore... (*kiṃ ca*). "Just as" (*itivaditi*): the meaning is that just as in the case of the words "excellence" (*prakarṣa*) and "certainty" (*niścaya*), because they denote their respective meanings, the connection with qualifiers such as "abundance" (*bhūyastva*) occurs therein, so it is here. "It might also be thus" (*ityapi syāditi*).

If prefixes (*prādi*) were to denote meanings such as "intensity" (*prakarpa*), then because [the quality of] "abundance" (*bhūyastva*) and so forth would be construed with them, expressions such as *bhūyān pretya* (having died more abundantly) would also be used; however, this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*) that the meaning of the prefix would become the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). The point is that from such usage, such a meaning is not perceived. "In our view" means in the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), who maintain that prefixes are merely indicators (*dyotaka*). "There is no such connection" means there is no connection with qualifiers such as "abundance."

"Because [prefixes] such as *pra* lack meaning"—that is to say, they lack denotative power (*vācakatva*). Therefore, the sense is that the indicative function (*dyotakatā*) of prefixes such as *pra* is established. "Another proof" means another argument regarding this matter, namely, that prefixes and particles have only an indicative function. "A beautiful conjunction."

Since the word *samuccaya* (conjunction) expresses the meaning of conjunction, just as the qualifier "beautiful" (*śobhana*) applies there [to the object], so too, if particles were denotative, the application of "beautiful" would result for the meaning presented by the particle. Consequently, the usage *śobhanaśca* ("and beautiful") would occur, and the meaning presented by the noun would be perceived as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). The phrase "because it can be resolved in the same way" means that this undesirable consequence can be resolved by the same reason—that is, by the reason of being meaningless (*nirarthakatva*).

Just as when a verbal root is used in conjunction with prefixes such as *pra*, there is a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the meaning understood therein, while the prefixes themselves are merely indicators (*dyotaka*); likewise, when a verbal root is used in conjunction with particles such as *ca*, there is a secondary figurative indication of the meaning understood therein, while the particles *ca* and so forth are merely indicators. Thus, since the particles *ca* and others are devoid of independent meaning (*anarthaka*), the meaning is that there can be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with qualifiers such as "beautiful" (*śobhana*) in those cases.

Furthermore, the demonstration that in the expression “*śobhanaḥ samuccayaḥ*” (a beautiful conjunction), just as the meaning denoted by the word *samuccaya* appears as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), so too in the expression “*śobhanaśca*” (and beautiful) there would follow the appearance [of the conjunction] as the substantive, is indeed improper. The point is that since particles such as *ca* are devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*), the connection of qualifiers such as “beautiful” cannot occur there at all; how then could there be a status of being a substantive as defined by a qualifier? Consequently, the intended sense is that there is no possibility of such usage as “*bhūyān pra*” or “*śobhanaśca*.”

Indeed, it is accepted that the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is such that, for the production of a cognition having the meaning of a noun as its qualifier (*nāmārthaprakāraka*) through a relation of identity (*abhedasaṃbandha*), the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a word other than a particle (*nipāta*). Here, the cognition having the meaning of a noun as its qualifier is the effect; and the cause of that is the mental presentation produced by a word other than a particle.

It is logical that in the cases of "bhūyān prakarṣaḥ" (greater excellence) and "śobhanaḥ samuccayaḥ" (beautiful collection), because there is a mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by words distinct from particles (*nipāta*), there arises a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in which the meanings of the nouns such as "beautiful" (*śobhana*) function as qualifiers through identity, based on the comprehension of the meaning: "excellence qualified by abundance" and "collection identical with the beautiful. Thus, the resulting understanding is that excellence is non-different from its greater degree, and the collection is non-different from the beautiful. This is the correct view.

In the case of [the words] *bhūyān* and *pra*, as well as *śobhanaḥ*, since there is only the presence of the mental representation (*upasthiti*) produced by the particles themselves, the absence of a cause means that no verbal cognition having the meaning of a noun as its qualifier arises through identity; therefore, even though particles possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), there is no defect whatsoever. To this he says: "Moreover" (*api ca*). Regarding "denotative power": the meaning is the acceptance of the denotative power of particles. Regarding "impossibility": in the example *ghaṭaśca* ("a pot and"), the meaning of the word *ghaṭa* is "that which possesses a neck like a conch-shell," while the meaning of *ca* is conjunction (*samuccaya*).

For a conjunction that is non-different from the pot cannot have a relation of identity (*abheda-anvaya*) with these two [the jar and the cloth]; rather, the conjunction must be related to them as having the jar as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogika*), which implies a relation of difference (*bheda-anvaya*). However, such a relation is difficult to establish, because of the grammatical rule that there is a relation of identity between the meanings of nouns that possess the same case-ending.

The meaning is that, because the cognition of a relation between two nominal meanings through difference requires the presence of a word possessing a case-ending that is incompatible with the case-ending following the first word, such a condition being absent in the present case, a relation of difference between the nominal meanings is impossible. Consequently, the implication is that sentences such as "the pot is" (*ghaṭaś cet*) would have to be the source [of such usage]. "Otherwise" means: the acceptance of a relation of difference between nominal meanings even without a sixth-case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth. For example: "The king, the man" (*rājā puruṣaḥ*).

The meaning is that even from two words with the same case-ending, there would result a cognition of a distinct relation, such as "the man is related to the king. In the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), since particles (*nipāta*) are indicators (*dyotaka*), when a particle is co-uttered with a nominal stem, that very stem conveys its own meaning as qualified by the meaning of the particle. Thus, because they are presented by a single word (*ekapada*), there is no [independent] syntactic connection (*anvaya*); for this reason alone, there is no fault in the form of a distinct connection in cases such as "and a pot" (*ghaṭaśca*).

The point is that in expressions such as *ghaṭaśca* ("pot and"), the word *ghaṭa* alone conveys the meaning consisting of the pot together with the conjunction (*samuccaya*). In the *Sāra*, the statement "without the genitive case and so forth" is intended to indicate that when the genitive and other cases are present, there is indeed a relation of difference between the meanings of the nouns as well, mediated by the meaning of those cases. For this very reason, in the expression *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), the cognition of a relation of difference in the form of the owner-possessed relationship—as in "the man is the possessor characterized by ownership residing in the king"—is logically consistent.

By the phrase "the sixth [case], direction," and so forth, the inclusion of the second case and others having that same meaning is intended. Now, one might object: "In that case, just as one says 'the collection of the pot' (*ghaṭasya samuccayaḥ*), one should also say 'and the pot' (*ghaṭasya ca*). To this he replies with the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). If particles were denotative (*vācaka*), then there would be a relation through difference between the meanings of two nouns bearing different case-endings, as in "the collection of the *dhava* and the *khadira* trees"; in such a case, one would have to say "of the *dhava*" and "of the *khadira*" (*dhavasya ca, khadirasya ca*), because otherwise the connection would be impossible. However, the meaning is not "the *dhava* and the *khadira*" (*dhavaśca khadiraśca*).

In the sentence "The jar and the cloth exist" (*ghaṭaḥ paṭaścāsti*), the jar is construed with the action of existence (*astikriyā*). For this very reason, the nominative case is used there due to its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the finite verb (*tiṅ*). The cognition is: "The jar exists, and the cloth possesses conjunction (*samuccaya*). When there is an expectancy for the correlate (*pratiyogi*) of the conjunction, because of proximity, the jar functions as that correlate; however, in the case of the cloth, the conjunction (the meaning of *ca*) is construed as distinct [from the cloth], and not as "the conjunction of the cloth. Even if particles (*nipāta*) were denotative (*vācaka*), how could the genitive case in "of the *dhava* and of the *khadira*" (*dhavasya ca khadirasya ca*) be introduced? The grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) "between the meanings of two nouns" (*nāmārthayoḥ*) applies to cases other than particles.

Therefore, the connection of the aggregate (samuccaya) with the cloth through the relation of the object of application (anuyogitā) is not untenable; this has been established in the Mañjūṣā. || 43 ||

He raises an objection with "nanu" (but surely). Regarding the phrase "understanding of connection through difference": in order to prevent the understanding of a connection through difference—such as "the man belongs to the king"—from the expression "rājā puruṣaḥ" (the king [is] the man), a causal relationship has been postulated wherein the cause for the understanding of a connection through difference between the meanings of two nominal stems is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a word possessing a case-ending that is incompatible with the case-ending following the first word. By adopting the view that this relationship holds only in cases other than those involving particles (*nipāta*), one concludes that just as in the expression "the conjunction of *dhava* and *khadira*," it must be expressed as "of the *dhava* and of the *khadira*" (*dhavasya ca khadirasya ca*).

Anticipating the objection that the fault previously stated—namely, that [the word] would not denote both *dhava* and *khadira*—is thereby avoided, he says: "The word-meaning connects with a similar [word]. Regarding the term "similar," he uses "with a similar" (*sadṛśena*) instead of "with a similar one" (*sadṛśāt*) in order to dispel the misconception that it refers to a case-ending (*āvantam*), as in the example *vācā niśā*. He further specifies "with a coordinate [term]" (*samānādhikaraṇena*) because, otherwise, since even words with different case-endings possess some degree of similarity—such as being nominal stems (*prātipadika*)—it would follow that non-differential connection (*abhedānvaya*) could occur even with such [words].

The meaning is: "by means of an object whose presentation is produced by words lacking different case-endings. The intention is that similarity is intended by virtue of being the object of a presentation produced by words possessing identical case-endings. "Anvayati" (is connected) means it is connected through identity (*abheda*). "Asamānādhikaraṇa" (non-co-referential) means by means of an object whose presentation is produced by words possessing contradictory case-endings. "Kadā ca" (and when) means "at no time whatsoever. "Na" (not) means it is not connected through identity.

The meaning is: "precisely because of the previously stated rule, namely, that [the relation holds] between the referents of two nouns that possess the same case-ending. Furthermore, having the same case-ending means having a case-ending that is of the same class as the case-ending of its own base (*prakṛti*). And this "sameness of class" is to be understood by means of the properties of being first-case, second-case, and so forth, which serve as the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) for the classification of case-endings.

The word *nīla* expresses its own qualifier; the case-ending (*vibhakti*) derived from it is the second case (*dvitīyā*), namely *-am*; a case-ending of the same class as that is the very same *-am* case-ending; and since the state of possessing such a case-ending exists in *ghaṭam*, which ends in the second case, there is a "samānavibhaktikatva" (identity of case-ending) between the words *nīla* and *ghaṭa* in the expression *nīlaṃ ghaṭaṃ paśya*. Thus, the definition is consistent.

The meaning of the principle "the word-meaning connects with a similar [meaning]" (*padārthaḥ sadṛśānveti*) is as follows: an object presented by a word ending in a particular type of case-suffix connects only through identity (*abheda*) with an object presented by another word ending in a case-suffix of that same type. The meaning of the phrase "and never through division" (*vibhāgena kadā ca na*) is that it never connects through identity with an object presented by a word ending in a case-suffix of a different type.

Now, if particles (*nipāta*) are denotative, then the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) stated regarding the comprehension of the relation between two word-meanings (*prātipadikārtha*) through difference would have to be restricted to cases other than particles. With this in mind—that is, with the intention that since the meaning of "and" (*ca*), namely conjunction (*samuccaya*), and so forth, is the meaning of a particle, the relation of one word-meaning with another distinct word-meaning through difference is not untenable—he says: "This is the meaning."

In the case of "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), in order to prevent the understanding of a relation of identity (*abheda-anvaya*), one must necessarily accept the rule that there is a relation of identity between the referents of two words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists in being expressive of a single referent while lacking a case-ending that is incompatible with the case-ending following the first word. In the expression "the wealth of the king’s son" (*rājñaḥ sutasya dhanam*), although the words *rāja* and *suta* lack incompatible case-endings, there is no relation of identity between them.

Because in one case the genitive denotes the state of being produced (*janyatva*) and in the other it denotes ownership (*svatva*), there is an absence of denoting a single identical referent. Consequently, in the expression *ghaṭaś ca* ("and the pot"), it is impossible to state that the meaning presented by the nominal stem *ghaṭa* is construed with the meaning [of the particle] through a relation of difference, such as "a conjunction having the pot as its counter-correlative."

If, however, one were to insert the condition "other than a particle" (*nipātātirikta*) within the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that constitutes the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), then the meaning would be that there is a relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the meanings of those nominal stems which are other than particles. If it is argued that by thus inserting "other than a particle," there is no obstacle to a relation of difference (*bheda-anvaya*) in cases involving particles such as "and" (*ca*) in the example *ghaṭaśca* ("a jar and [something else]"), the proponent—intending to show that there is no evidence for such an insertion and that it would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*)—says: "The restriction to what is other than a particle," and so forth.

One might object: "In the case of *ghaṭaśca* ('pot and'), the very impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) through distinction would serve as the proof for the inclusion of the condition 'other than a particle' (*nipātātirikta*).
