To this he says: "And [the charge of] complexity" (*gauravaṃ ca*). If it is argued that complexity established by evidence is not a fault, he replies: "For us" (*asmākam*). This means: for us Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), who maintain that particles are indicators (*dyotaka*). He says "because they are indicators" (*dyotakatvāt*). Since there is no actual syntactic connection at all when particles are accepted as indicators, the charge of "impossibility of syntactic connection" is cast far away.

The meaning is that when used in conjunction with particles (*nipāta*), the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) itself, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), conveys the conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so forth of the meaning of the particle as qualified by the meaning of the nominal stem; thus, the particles like *ca* function as indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). [The opponent's claim that] "there is no connection at all" is refuted.

The meaning is that when a particle (*nipāta*) is used in co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*), the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself conveys the meaning of the particle (such as "and" or "or") as qualified by its own primary meaning; since the collection and so forth of the particle's meaning are already obtained through the co-uttered nominal stem, there is no separate presentation [of those meanings], and thus no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) at all. The point is that a relation takes the form of a connection (*anvaya*) only between two things that have been presented separately. [The author concludes: "This is not a fault."

The meaning is that there is no fault here—namely, the fault of the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) through distinction as in "the jar" (*ghaṭaśca*), which would result in the fault stated [earlier] that it ought to be "of the jar and of the *khadira* tree" (*ghaṭasya ca khadirasya ca*). This is because the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) of the particle *ca* has as its object the meanings of the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) presented separately. In the present case, both in "the jar" (*ghaṭaśca*) and in "of the jar and of the *khadira* tree" (*ghaṭasya ca khadirasya ca*), the conjunction of the jar is presented by the word "jar" itself, and the conjunction of the *khadira* tree is presented by the word "*khadira*" itself. It is for this very reason that [it is so].

The meaning is that this is precisely because there is no inclusion of the phrase "other than a particle" (*nipātātiriktetyasyāniveśāt*) in the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) for understanding the non-difference relation (*abhedānvaya*) between the meanings of two nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Regarding the statement "it is metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*) with respect to its counter-correlate (*tatpratiyogike*)," the meaning of the word *ghaṭa* (pot) is that which possesses a conch-shaped neck and so forth. The meaning of the negative particle *nañ* in the expression "is not" (*nāsti*) is absence (*abhāva*). Since one experiences a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in the form "an absence whose counter-correlate is a pot," through the relation of difference (*bheda*), it is intended that the pot is related to the meaning of the negative particle—namely, absence—by way of the relation of difference, characterized by having a counter-correlativity delimited by potness (*ghaṭatvāvacchinna-pratiyogitākatva*). However, that [intended relation] is difficult to obtain.

This is because of the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is construed as non-different (*abheda*) [from its case-meaning]. Therefore, for the Naiyāyikas, the word *ghaṭa* is taken to have a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "that which has a jar as its counter-positive" (*ghaṭapratiyogika*). Consequently, the non-different construal (*abheda-anvaya*) between the word *ghaṭa* and the meaning of the negative particle *nañ* is established.

If, however, the qualification "other than a particle" (*nipātātirikta*) were introduced into the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) governing the cognition of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*), then here—in the case of the connection between the meanings of the nominal stems *ghaṭa* and *nañ*, which are presented by the nominal stem and the particle respectively—there would be no obstacle to their being related through the relation of difference (*bheda-sambandha*) consisting in the state of being a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitākatva*). Consequently, the recourse to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would be entirely futile. Thus, the meaning is that even the Naiyāyikas accept that the qualification "other than a particle" is not included in the aforementioned linguistic rule. || 44 ||

Anticipating the objection that—rather than postulating a denotative power (*vācakatva-śakti*) for the meanings of conjunction and so forth in numerous words such as "pot" and "cloth" when co-occurring with particles like *ca* (and), it is more appropriate to postulate such a power for the very few particles themselves due to parsimony (*lāghava*)—the author says: "Moreover" (*api ca*). Regarding the phrase "in poetry and so forth": this refers to Raghuvaṃśa, Canto 4, Verse 66, specifically the line "with arrows [like] goads" (*śarair ustraiḥ*). The first half of the verse is: "From there he set out toward the northern quarter, like the sun."

"Anvaya would not occur" means that one must accept that particles (*nipāta*) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*). The logical inconsistency of this [position] will become clear immediately below. "Another proof" refers to the fact that particles function as indicators (*dyotaka*); this is the ellipsis to be supplied. "With arrows like camels, [he struck] the Northerners"—here, "resembling camels" is an adjective qualifying the arrows, while "resembling water" is an adjective qualifying the Northerners. "This is the meaning" means that this is the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). "And this" means the aforementioned verbal cognition of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*).

The meaning is as follows: the verbal cognition described is justified because the particle *iva* functions like a prefix (*upasarga*) as an indicator (*dyotaka*), whereby the word *usra* refers to things similar to the dawn (*usra-sadṛśa*), and thus the third case ending is consistent as an adjective qualifying the arrows in the sense of "with arrows similar to the dawn. Furthermore, the word *rasa* refers to those similar to nectar (*rasa-sadṛśa*), and thus the second case ending is consistent as an adjective qualifying the Northerners (*udīcya*) in the sense of "Northerners who are like nectar. "Otherwise" means that if one does not accept the indicative function (*dyotakatva*) of particles and instead assumes they possess denotative power (*vācakatva*).

Regarding the phrase "contradiction with grammatical derivation" (*vyutpattivirodha*): the meaning is that in the word *uṣreḥ*, the third-case suffix cannot denote the instrument (*karaṇa*) as connected with the meaning of its own base (*prakṛti*), namely the word *usra*, because of the rule that suffixes denote the meaning of their bases (*prakṛtyartha...*). He clarifies this very point with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). As for the statement "and *usra* is not the instrument here": although the third case was employed in *usraih* to express the instrument, the referent of the word *usra* is not the instrument in this context—the action of rescuing the king from the northern region (*udagdeśīya-rāja-uddharaṇa-kriyā*).

Because, unlike the word *usra* (cow), there is no absence of its functioning as a qualifier of the instrument (*karaṇa*) when it is construed with a similar object; rather, the similar object expressed by the particle *iva* is the instrument. Thus it is said: "even though the similar object denoted by *iva* is the instrument..."

The meaning is that even though it is possible for that which is similar [to the sun] to function as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in relation to the act of drawing out (*uddharaṇa*), by virtue of being non-different from the sun and thus serving as a qualifier of the arrow; nevertheless, the meaning is that the instrumentality of that—namely, the instrumentality residing in the object similar to the sun—cannot be conveyed by this instrumental case suffix (*tṛtīyā-pratyaya*) following the word *usra*. He states the reason for this: "because it is not the meaning of the base" (*aprakṛtyarthatvāt*). This means that the object similar to the sun, which is the meaning of the particle *iva*, is not the meaning of the word *usra*, which serves as the base (*prakṛti*) for the instrumental case suffix.

The point is that in the same way, it is not possible to convey the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) for the word *sadṛśa* (similar) when it follows the word *usra* (ox), because of the rule that suffixes denote the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), and so forth. Having raised the objection that the third case ending might occur after the word *iva* because the status of being an instrument is possible—since that which is similar to the meaning of *iva* functions as a qualifier of the arrow (*śara*) which has become the instrument through non-difference from it—the author says: "of the word *iva*" (*ivaśabdasya*). Regarding the phrase "by virtue of having non-existence as its meaning" (*asattvārthakatayā*): *sattva* means substance (*dravya*), and that [substance] is what is connected with gender, number, and grammatical function (*kāraka*).

That which is different from that [substance] is non-substance (*asattva*). And what is non-substance does not connect with gender, number, or case-role (*kāraka*). Thus, the meaning is: "by virtue of having as its referent that which does not connect with gender, number, or case-role. The point is that by the rule *cādayo’sattve*, particles (*nipāta*) such as *ca* and others, which have non-substantial referents, are assigned the technical designation of *nipāta*; therefore, particles possess the nature of having a non-substantial referent, characterized by their lack of connection with gender, number, and case-role. [The phrase] "because of the impossibility of the third case" [is used].

The meaning is that since the sense of "likeness" (*sadṛśarūpa*)—which is presented [in the mind] as not being connected with a *kāraka* (participant in an action)—cannot be construed with a *kāraka*, it is impossible for the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), which signifies instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), to occur after the word *iva*. Consequently, due to the absence of the third case-ending after the word *iva*, the instrumentality of the "similar thing" would not be obtained; and because the object denoted by the word *uṣṭra* lacks instrumentality, the third case-ending following the word *uṣṭra* would be both meaningless and grammatically incorrect (*asādhutva*).

One might object: "Since the inclusion of *sup* in the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ* indicates that all case-endings (*sarvavibhakti*) are applicable after an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and since the word *iva* has the sense of similarity (*sadṛśadharmin*), when the third case ending produced from it is elided because it denotes an existent entity (*sattvārthaka*), one would understand the instrumentality of that which is similar to the sense of 'like' (*ivārtha*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "Or, when possible" (*saṃbhave vā*). [He adds: "Because of the consequence of its being heard" (*śravaṇaprasaṅgāt*).

The meaning is as follows: when the object denoted by the word *iva*—namely, similarity (*sādṛśya*)—is construed with the act of lifting (*uddharaṇa-kriyā*) as its instrumental factor (*karaṇa-kāraka*), it is impossible to claim that such a word *iva* has the sense of non-existence (*asattva*), which consists in its not being construed with a case-role (*kāraka*). Consequently, the designation of "particle" (*nipāta-saṃjñā*), which was established based on its having the sense of non-existence, would be revoked. Due to this revocation, the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ* would not apply; thus, because the elision (*luk*) would not occur, the third-case ending following the word *iva* would result in being heard [in the utterance]. The word *vā* is used in the sense of indifference (*anāsthā*).

The word "eva" (only) indicates the impossibility of the occurrence of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) when there is no substance (*asattva*). The sense is that, by the very nature of the power of words (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvya*), even that which is presented by the word "iva" (like) possesses the nature of a non-substance (*asattvarūpatva*), just like the operation (*vyāpāra*) presented by the verbal root. Furthermore, because the rule "avyayād āpsupaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.82) ordains the elision (*luk*) of case-endings after indeclinables, the instrumental case-ending that arises is meaningless; thus, it is impossible to demonstrate through it the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) residing in the object of comparison. He states another objection: "and because of the consequence of a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*)."

The meaning is that since the object *uṣṭra* lacks the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) as defined by the action of pulling out (*uddharaṇa*), there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasañja*) of the third-case suffix (*tṛtīyā*)—which signifies the instrument—not being connected to it. Regarding the phrase "and the hearing of case-endings" (*supāṃ ca śravaṇam*), he states that the word "and" (*ca*) is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakrama*), explaining it as "the hearing of case-endings and [so forth]. Now, even if the word *iva* denotes a substantive (*sattva*), one might object that because it is listed among the indeclinables (*avyaya*), there would be no occurrence of the hearing of case-endings; therefore, the word "and" (*ca*) is included in the root text, and he shows what is intended to be included by it: "by the word 'and' following the word *uṣṭra*, etc."

"Is included" (*samuccīyate*) means that the non-connection with the third [case-ending] is subsumed; this shows what is to be subsumed by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in such expressions as "like speech and meaning" (*vāgarthāviva*). Regarding the phrase "because of the absence of being the object of the act of salutation" (*vandikarmatvābhāvāt*): since there is no connection with the word "like" (*iva*) in the sense of [the two being] joined together—as there is in the case of "speech and meaning"—there is no connection for those two [words] in the act of salutation. Consequently, the accusative case-ending following them would not have a connection there [as denoting the object].

Furthermore, because the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is sublated by the fact that there can be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the word and its meaning through non-difference (*abheda*) with the action (*karman*) specified by the act of salutation (*vandikriyā*), [the following holds]. Even though the objecthood of that which resembles the meaning of "as" (*iva*)—namely, Pārvatī and Parameśvara—is established through a connection of non-difference with the action, the dative case-suffix (*dvitīyā*) following the word *vāgartha* cannot possibly convey the connection of objecthood to the meaning of "as," because the meaning of "as" is not the referent of the word *vāgartha*, which serves as the base (*prakṛti*) for that dative suffix.

This is because the meaning of *iva* cannot be the referent of the second case (*dvitīyā*), given the rule that suffixes convey their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Regarding the word "having taken" (*saṃgṛhya*): the meaning is that the non-connection of the second case following [the word *vāgartha*] with the referent of the word *vāgartha* is included, as well as the impossibility of such a second case conveying the objecthood (*karmatva*) residing in the meaning of *iva*.

In our view, however, since the compound *vāgarthapada* refers to words and meanings that resemble [the actual] word and meaning, and since the particle *iva* serves to indicate that resemblance, there is an identification between the word and its meaning. Thus, by way of qualifying Pārvatī and Parameśvara, the act of salutation is performed; the status of being the object (*karmatva*), as previously described, is perfectly consistent.

Likewise, in the expression *usrair*, since the word *usra* itself has the sense of "resembling a bull" (*usrasadṛśa*), there is no grammatical inconsistency regarding the instrumental case; for that which resembles a bull functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) relative to the act of drawing out (*uddharaṇa*), by virtue of being a qualifier of the arrows through non-difference (*abheda*). This is so provided that particles (*nipāta*) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*). In this view, the meaning of the word *iva* is "similarity. Here, the bulls (*usra*) are the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the arrows (*śara*) are the object of comparison (*upameya*). The established rule is that the standard of comparison is understood as a qualifier and the object of comparison as the qualificand.

In that context, since the arrows of the object of comparison (*upameya*) function as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the act of extraction, the third case ending—which denotes the instrumental factor—is applied to them. As for the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), however, because of the rule "the case ending is indeed the same for both the standard of comparison and the object of comparison," and because it is appropriate for the case ending following the object of comparison to be of the same class, the third case alone is used; and this [third case] has non-difference (*abheda*) as its meaning. With this intention, he says: "The case ending of the qualifier has non-difference as its meaning."

In expressions such as "see the blue lotus" (*nīlaṃ kamalaṃ paśya*), the cognition is that of an act of seeing whose object is a lotus non-different from blue; thus, because there is a relation of non-difference (*abheda*) between the blue and the lotus, the meaning of the case-ending of the qualifier is non-difference, and not the state of being an object (*karmatva*). Consequently, the second case-ending in the word *vāgarthau* and the third case-ending in the word *usrair* signify non-difference, rather than signifying the state of being an object or the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*). Therefore, the point is that there is no lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) for the second or third case-endings used as qualifiers.

Or, it may serve merely for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). This means that, according to the *Bhāṣya* statement "one should not employ what is not a word" (*apadaṃ na prayuñjīta*), the case-ending of the qualifier serves only to produce the grammatical correctness of the word. Furthermore, it is proper to employ a case-ending of the same class as the one following the word denoting the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), because of the rule that "a single [case] ending [should follow]. However, if a case-ending contrary to the one residing in the qualificand were employed, there would be no syntactic connection (*abhedānvaya*) between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*).

Because the absence of incompatible case-endings (*viruddhavibhaktirāhitya*) is the determining factor for the cognition of non-difference (*abhedānvayabodha*), it is for this very reason that in such instances as "The face is delightful like the moon," there arises a cognition of the non-difference between the moon and the face—the object of comparison and the subject of comparison—namely, "The face, which is the delighter, is non-different from the moon, which is the standard of comparison. Thus, [the figure] is indeed *ananvaya* (non-connection).

And when the case-ending of the qualifier has non-difference as its meaning, or serves merely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutvamātra*), even then, since the particle *iva* is not denotative, there is simply no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) for the qualifier-case-ending; this is the meaning. He clarifies this very lack of connection with the words beginning "of those similar to cows" (*usrasadṛśaśarāṇām*). This is a three-word *dvandva* compound consisting of *usra*, *sadṛśa*, and *śara*. The meaning is "of the three word-meanings beginning with *usra*. "In a state of grammatical coreferentiality" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) means: because they possess a mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by words that lack conflicting case-endings.

If it is asked: "In the phrase *nanu jñairusrairiva*, even though the words *usra* and *śara* possess the same case-ending and thus are not constrained by conflicting case-endings, how can the word *kathīrava* have the same case-ending as the words *usra* and *śara*?"—then listen: the meaning of the word *iva* is "similarity" (*sadṛśa*). Because this [meaning] is construed non-differently (*abhedena*) with the arrows that function as the instrument (*karaṇa*), it takes the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) due to its being an instrument.

It should not be argued that if the word *eva* signifies "having a similar property" (*sadṛśadharmyartha*), then because it would possess the nature of a substantive (*sattvārthaka*), its status as a non-substantive (*asattvarūpatā*) would be destroyed; consequently, since it would no longer be a particle (*nipāta*), the elision of case-endings would not apply, resulting in the undesirable consequence of hearing the third-case ending following it. This is because even if it were a substantive, particles such as *iva* and others are listed among the "vowels and so forth" (*svarādi*), and thus their status as indeclinables (*avyaya*) allows for the elision of case-endings to be easily established, rendering the objection untenable.

For this very reason, in the *Dīdhiti*, regarding the statement "there is fragrance only in earth" (*pṛthivyāmeva gandhaḥ*), it is stated that the word *eva*—which conveys the sense that "there is fragrance in earth, but not elsewhere"—possesses the same case-ending as the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) with which it is co-occurrent; furthermore, it is noted that even its hearing [is possible] because it is not elided by *luk*. This is consistent. Thus, the point is that since the arrows are similar to the sun, their having the same case-ending ensures they are not constrained by conflicting case-endings. [The phrase] "because of the impossibility of connection through difference" [means]: [Note: The provided text contains a fragmentary commentary on grammatical logic (*vaiyākaraṇa-nyāya*) concerning the function of the particle *eva* and the conditions for semantic connection (*anvaya*). The core argument establishes that when *eva* is used to restrict a term's scope (e.g., *pṛthivyām eva gandhaḥ*), it must share the same case-suffix as the nominal stem it qualifies. This allows for a syntactic relationship where the restriction applies to the specific locus while excluding others, thereby resolving potential conflicts in case-suffixes.]

The meaning is that there would be no connection of the object "cow" (*usrapadārtha*) with the similarity—which is a part of the similar object—by way of the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā-sambandha*); nor would there be a connection of the similar object with the arrows by way of the relation of being the locus of similarity residing in itself (*svaniṣṭha-sādṛśya-anuyogitva-sambandha*). This is because of the rule that two nominal stem meanings (*prātipadikārtha*), when devoid of conflicting case-endings, can only be connected through identity (*abheda*). Anticipating the objection—"If it is impossible to state the connection here through difference (*bheda*), then let it be through identity (*abheda*) alone"—he says: "It is not [possible] even through identity, because of contradiction (*bādhāt*)."

In this context, even a relation through non-difference (*abheda*) cannot be asserted; the meaning is that a relation of non-difference is impossible because it is contradicted (*bādha*). He demonstrates this very contradiction with the words "not indeed [as] non-different from a cow" (*na hy usrābhinnetyādi*). If the referent of the word *usra* (cow) were related by non-difference to the sense of "similar," then there would be a contradiction regarding the non-difference of that which is similar to and non-different from a cow within the referent of the word *śara* (reed).

The principle that "that which is non-different from what is non-different from something else is itself non-different from that thing" [is invoked here]: clay is non-different from the two potsherds, and the jar is non-different from those two potsherds; therefore, the jar's non-difference from the clay must be asserted, just as one says the jar is non-different from the clay. However, in this case, it would have to be said that the jar is non-different from the cow—since the cow is non-different from the bull, the bull is non-different from the similar [bull], and the similar bull is non-different from the arrow; thus, the jar would have to be non-different from such an arrow, just as it is non-different from the clay. But that is not possible.

Just as it can be said that "the jar is non-different from the clay" because the persistence of the clay in the jar is experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it cannot be said that "the reed (*śara*) is non-different from the ox (*usrā*)," because the persistence of the nature of an ox in the reed is not experienced. How could there be non-difference in the reed of such a similarity that exists as non-difference from the ox? The meaning is: not at all. Thus, the application of non-difference to the reed—which is similar to what is non-different from the ox—is sublated (*bādhita*).

If, however, one first establishes the connection of the "similar" with the arrow through non-difference, and then establishes the connection of the "bull" with that "arrow non-different from the similar," even then, because the connection with "bull-ness" is not observed, the non-difference of the bull from the arrow is indeed sublated. Thus, the sense is that even by way of non-difference, such a connection is not possible.

If it is asked: "In the Siddhānta, regarding the expression 'with arrows resembling camels' (*uṣṭrasadṛśaiḥ śaraiḥ*), how can there be a relation of identity (*abhedānvaya*) between the two similar things?"—the answer is as follows: In the presence of the word *iva*, the word *uṣṭra* itself signifies the meaning "one who resembles a camel. Thus, because they are presented by a single word, there is no mutual relation at all between the camel and that which resembles a camel. Consequently, there is no obstacle to the part of that [compound]—namely, the "resembling" element, which serves as the qualificand—entering into a relation of identity with the "arrows."

If one insists on a relation there [in the case of *go-sadṛśa*] similar to the relation of the principal element—the person (*puruṣa*), which is a constituent part of the referent of the compound *rājapuruṣa*—to the action of bringing in the expression "bring the king's man" (*rājapuruṣam ānaya*), then the relation between the cow (*usra*) and that which resembles the cow would be one of difference, expressed as "qualified by a similarity defined by the cow. Thus, there is no obstacle to the non-difference relation (*abhedānvaya*) between the two words *usra* and *sadṛśa*, even though they possess the same case-ending.

In the phrase "like word and meaning" (*vāgarthāvivā*), the compound *vāgarthapada* itself signifies that which is similar to word and meaning; this [similarity] is then construed as non-difference with the object, namely Pārvatī and Parameśvara. Furthermore, since similarity is what is immediately present, it should be understood here as being "joined together" (*saṃpṛktatva*). And "being joined together" means "being eternally connected. Thus, the meaning is: "Just as word and meaning are eternally connected, so too are Pārvatī and Parameśvara eternally connected."

And thus, the understanding is that the act of salutation has as its object Pārvatī and Parameśvara, who are non-different from each other and resemble speech and meaning that are eternally connected. In the phrase "with arrows like spears" (*śarairustraiḥ*) as well, the similarity consists in their being the means for the act of uprooting. Just as a spear is the means for the act of extracting sap, so too are the arrows the means for the act of uprooting the king. Therefore, the understanding to be known is that the uprooting of the king is accomplished by means of arrows which are non-different from spears that serve as the instruments of uprooting. (45)

He raises an objection with "nanu" (but surely). "In your view" means: in your view as one who maintains that particles (*nipāta*) possess indicative power (*dyotakatva*); that is to say, in the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*). "The consequence of the definition being over-extensive (*avyāpti*)" means: the definition of a *tatpuruṣa* compound—that it is one where the meaning of the final member is predominant—would result in a lack of application to the specific case of a *nañ-tatpuruṣa*, which is but a portion of the class of *tatpuruṣas*. He states the reason for this: "because there is an absence of predominance of the meaning of the final member."

The meaning is as follows: since predominance (*prādhānya*) is determined by its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), if the preceding word *nañ* were meaningless, then—due to the absence of a qualifier that determines predominance—it would be impossible for the meaning of the subsequent word to possess predominance. Regarding the phrase "of the prefix" (*upasargasya*): the meaning is "of a mere particle" (*nipāta-mātra*). The intention is that the mention of "prefix" (*upasarga*) serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all particles. A "prefix" (*upa*) is so called because it stands near (*samīpastha*) and indicates—that is, makes known (*lakṣyate jñāyate*)—its own related object; thus, it is an "indicator" (*upalakṣaṇa*).

The meaning is that the word *upasarga* (prefix), by virtue of its own function as a particle (*nipāta*), indicates itself and its own related [verb] as well as the following vowel (*ac*). Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of meaningfulness" (*arthavattvābhāvena*): the meaning is that there is an absence of meaningfulness because it functions as an indicator (*dyotaka*). The intention is that, according to the *arthavat-sūtra*, "meaningfulness" consists in the capacity to convey a meaning through either direct denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

And thus, with the intention that because it is meaningless, the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would not exist, and consequently the case-endings such as *su* and others would not arise after a particle (*nipāta*), he says: "and in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). In a negative compound such as *abrāhmaṇa*, there is primacy—meaning predominance or the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)—belonging to the other member, namely the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). That which exists [as primacy] should be understood as being relative only to what is indicated by the negative particle—that is, relative to the meaning indicated by *nañ*.

The meaning is as follows: by taking up only the indicated sense (*dyotya-artha*), the particle possesses meaningfulness; because it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the case-suffix (*sub*) is produced from it. Regarding the phrase "the indicated sense": the predominance of the sense of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārthaprādhānya*) consists in its having attained the status of a qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) residing in the sense of the prior member. By the term "sense of the prior member," all three types of senses—the expressed (*vācya*), the indicated (*lakṣya*), and the indicated (*dyotya*)—are included; thus, there is no loss of the predominance of the sense of the subsequent member. This is the intended meaning. The phrase "because of meaningfulness" (*arthavattvāt*) [is used].

Since it is accepted that *dyotakatā* (indicative function) is also a type of *vṛtti* (linguistic operation), just like *śakti* (denotative power) and *lakṣaṇā* (indication), it is possible to maintain that even an indicator (*dyotaka*) possesses *arthavattva* (meaningfulness) by means of that *vṛtti*. Consequently, there is no impossibility regarding its designation as a *prātipadika* (nominal stem). Thus, the intended meaning is that what is sought to be maintained in the *arthavat-sūtra* is meaningfulness in the form of "conveying a meaning through any one of the *vṛttis*: denotation, indication, or indicative function."

[Objection: But surely, even if a particle (*nipāta*) which is merely indicative (*dyotaka*) were to receive the technical designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), no case-ending (*sub*) could arise from it because it lacks meaning pertaining to substance (*asattvārthakatva*), and thus lacks number, objecthood (*karman*), and so forth. Nor can this undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) be accepted, for it would lead to the non-occurrence of rules such as *jaśtva* and *rutva* in examples like *udgacchati uccaiḥ*. Therefore, he says: "In reality... [The case-ending arises] by virtue of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

In the view that [particles] are merely indicators (*dyotaka*), particles (*nipāta*) lack meaning; consequently, they do not receive the designation of *prātipadika*. Furthermore, since indeclinables (*avyaya*) such as *svara* lack number, object, and so forth, the suffixes (*sup*) would not arise after them. Thus, the rule prescribing their elision (*luk*) would be purposeless; its very existence indicates that suffixes do arise after indeclinables—this is the underlying point. Accordingly, even if the definition of "meaningful" (*arthavat*) in the *arthavat-sūtra* includes the capacity to convey meaning through either direct denotation (*śakti*) or secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there is no deficiency whatsoever.

Now, one might object: since words such as *svar* (heaven) and others, though denoting non-substances (*asattvavacana*), are seen to be connected with case-relations such as the object (*karman*)—as in "he causes the benediction to be recited" (*svasti vācayati*), "he sacrifices in the morning" (*prātaryajate*), "he sees heaven" (*svaḥ paśyati*), and "he has fallen from heaven" (*svaḥ patitaḥ*)—it would be necessary to state that the case-suffixes (*sup*) prescribed for those meanings apply even after indeclinables (*avyaya*). Consequently, the rule [Pāṇini 2.4.82] would lack the status of a *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence). To this, he says: "of an indeclinable that is devoid of meaning" (*nipātasyānarthakasya*).

In the view that [particles] possess the function of *dyotakatā* (indicative indication), there is no inconsistency regarding the derivation of case endings (*sub*) from them, because the current Vārttika establishes their status as nominal stems (*prātipadika*). In reality, however, since particles convey meaning through the function of *dyotakatā*, they possess meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), and thus their status as nominal stems is established. For this very reason, the Vārttika—which contains the phrase "anarthaka-pada" (meaningless word)—is consistent. The underlying sense is that if all particles were indeed meaningless, then the qualifier "anarthakasya" (of the meaningless) would be non-excluding (*avyāvartaka*) with respect to particles.

For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa’s statement that "the term 'meaningless' (anarthaka) is used for the purpose of indicating that this [rule] applies even to those particles such as *tu*, *hi*, *ca*, *sma*, *ha*, *vai*, and so forth, for which there is no meaning to be expressed," is consistent.

And since particles (*nipāta*) possess meaningfulness only by taking on the indicated meaning (*dyotya-artha*), their status as nominal stems (*prātipadika*) is established by the very rule [P. 1.2.46]; thus, the Vārttika beginning with "of a particle" (*nipātasya*) is rejected. However, raising the objection—how then is the status of a nominal stem maintained in cases such as *hi*, *ca*, and *smā*?—he says: "The kṛt, taddhita, and compound [stems]," and so forth. He concludes the statement regarding the meaningfulness of particles with the words: "Therefore, it is logical," and so forth.

Regarding the indicative nature (*dyotakatva*) of particles (*nipātas*), he states the consensus of the authors of the *Mīmāṃsā-vārttika* on the section concerning "form" (*ākṛti*; Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.35) with the words "And it has been said. The phrase "of four kinds" means consisting of nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*). The phrase "in a word" means in the form of that which ends in a nominal suffix (*subanta*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). The determination of the meaning is made for the two-fold [word], namely the two types distinguished as noun and verb. He states the reason why the determination of meaning applies specifically to nouns and verbs: "because of the arising of doubt."

The meaning [of a word] is either the name (nāman), or the genus (jāti), or the individual (vyakti), or the individual qualified by the genus; as for the meaning of a verbal root (dhātu), is it mere activity (vyāpāra), or mere result (phala), or activity conducive to the result? Because such doubts arise, the two [categories of words, namely prepositions and particles,] are now being defined—this is the sense. He states the reason why their meanings are not [already] defined: "of those two" (tayoh). This means that prepositions (upasarga) and particles (nipāta) do not possess the capacity to generate the cognition of meaning through either direct denotation (śakti) or indication (lakṣaṇā).

By stating the absence of the operation of either denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the author suggests that these two [prefixes and particles] convey meaning by way of being indicators (*dyotaka*); with this intention, he says: "which indicate the meaning of which. "Those two" refers to prefixes and particles; "the meaning of which" means they are the generators of the apprehension of the function (*vṛtti*) whose object is the specific meaning of either a noun (*nāman*) or a verb (*ākhyāta*). The sense is: that word consisting of a noun or a verb, which is the denoter (*vācaka*), is now being examined. By the phrase "by the prefix," it is established that prefixes are indeed indicators only. "The other" refers to...

The meaning is that [the word] is qualified by a form distinct from the form as it has been specified. For example, in the case of the root *hṛ*, the specified form is "taking" (*haraṇa*); the meaning "striking" (*āghāta*), which is a form distinct from that, becomes perceived as something other [than mere taking] due to the power of the prefix (*upasarga*) in expressions such as *prahāra* ("a blow"). Similarly, the meaning of the root *ji* is victory (*jaya*) qualified by the nature of victory; however, in the expression *prajayati* ("he conquers completely"), because it is qualified by the excellence of victory (*prakṛṣṭajayatva*), something other [than simple victory] is perceived.

Now, one might object that by this statement of Hari (Patañjali), it is only the prefix (*upasarga*) that is said to possess denotative power (*dyotakatva*), and not the particles (*nipāta*). To this he says: "It is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the particle. The meaning is that, by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it refers to that which is designated as a particle. Regarding the phrase "of another word": the meaning is that it should be understood as an indicator. The sense is this: just as by the force of co-occurrence with a prefix, a different meaning of the verbal root is perceived, so too by the force of co-occurrence with a particle—in the case of "the face is like the moon" (*candra iva mukham*)—a different meaning, namely the form of something similar to the moon, is perceived for the other word, "moon" (*candra*). || 46 ||

Now, in order to establish that particles (*nipāta*) possess denotative power, he says: "But surely... (*nanu*). Regarding the phrase "by means of positive and negative concomitance" (*anvayavyatirekābhyām*): the meaning is that since in expressions such as *candra iva mukham* ("the face is like the moon"), when words designated as particles—such as *iva*—are present, there is a cognition of meanings such as similarity, whereas in the absence of *iva* and other such particles, there is no cognition of such meanings, it is logical that particles possess denotative power just like words such as *ghaṭa* ("pot"). [Objection: But if particles possess denotative power, there would be the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from the postulation of a linguistic capacity (*śakti*) for them; to this he replies: "Because they are signifiers" (*bodhakatā*).

The meaning is: because there is no sublation (*bādha*) of that power which consists in being a cause of cognition (*bodhakatā*). By the inclusion of the term "being a cause of cognition," the sublation of powers consisting of the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) and so forth is indicated. Thus, the meaning is that the very capacity to convey a particular meaning is what constitutes being expressive (*vācakatva*); therefore, just as with words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), particles (*nipāta*) possess expressiveness alone. Now, one might object: when a particle such as *iva* is used in co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with another word, that word presents its own meaning as qualified by the meaning manifested (*dyotya*) by the *iva*, whereas when it is not so used, it is observed to present only its own meaning; this is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

For instance, in the expression "the face is like the moon" (*candra iva mukham*), when the word *iva* is present, there is the cognition of the moon as qualified by similarity; whereas in the absence of the word *iva*, as in "the moon is the face" (*candro mukham*), there is no cognition of the moon as so qualified. Thus, since positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are useful for establishing that particles (*nipāta*) are indicators (*dyotaka*), they do not serve as proofs for their being denoters (*vācaka*). Therefore, he says: "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). [He explains] "in the manner stated": in the case of *pra-jayati*, the "excellent victory" (*prakṛṣṭa-jaya*) that is perceived is not denoted by the prefix (*upasarga*).

If that were the case, since it would not be the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), it could not be construed with the meaning of the suffix (*ākhyāta*); for there is a rule that suffixes convey their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the verbal root. Nor can it be the meaning of the root alone; for if that were so, then even without a prefix (*upasarga*), one would perceive the excellence of victory (and the like) in cases such as *jayati*, just as one perceives other meanings [in the presence of a prefix]. Nor can it be denoted by the root as qualified by the prefix; for if that were so, since the qualified entity would possess both forms, it would be cumbersome to postulate a denotative power (*śakti*) for both.

Therefore, since the root itself, whose capacity for denoting victory is already established, brings about the notion of "intense victory" through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), the prefix *pra-* does not have "intensity" as its meaning according to the maxim that "the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained otherwise. This is because, in the manner described, the prefix is utilized merely to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) regarding the root’s indication of such a meaning. As for the example "he cooks" (*pacati*): when "he cooks" is uttered, the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) qualified by the agent that is perceived is not directly expressed by the verbal root.

If that were the case, then even in instances such as *pacanam*, *paktiḥ*, and *pākaḥ*, there would result the undesirable consequence of the cognition of the agent’s qualification within the *bhāvanā*. Nor is [the *bhāvanā*] the meaning of the *tiṅ*-suffix; for if that were so, in the absence of a *tiṅ*-suffix—as in *paktvā* and *paktum*—there would result the non-cognition of the *bhāvanā*. Nor is it denoted by the *tiṅ*-suffix as qualified by the verbal root (*dhātu*); because postulating denotative power in a qualified entity involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, since the *bhāvanā* qualified by the agent can be presented through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) from the verbal root itself, the function of the *tiṅ*-suffix and so forth must simply be to indicate the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) regarding such a secondary indication.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "tiṅ-ādeḥ," the inclusion of *kṛt*, *san*, and so forth is intended. Having in mind a lack of conviction regarding the indicative nature (*dyotakatva*) of particles (*nipāta*) in this manner, he states another position—that particles possess denotative power (*vācakatva*)—with the words "the denotative power of particles. [This occurs] when there is positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); that is, when those two exist.

The point is this: if the denotative capacity of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and the like for meanings such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—namely, that when there is the employment of verbal suffixes there is the cognition of the meanings of agent, object, etc., and when there is an absence of the employment of verbal suffixes there is an absence of the cognition of the meanings of agent, etc.—then, by means of those same positive and negative concomitances, let particles (*nipāta*) also possess the denotative capacity for their respective meanings, just as the verbal suffixes do. The Mīmāṃsakas, however, maintain that these particles are indeed denotative (*vācaka*), not merely indicative (*dyotaka*).

For this is what they have stated in the *Samuccaya-adhikaraṇa*: "Since conjunction (*samuccaya*) is not perceived from the word 'tree' alone, whereas it is understood upon hearing the word 'and' (*ca*), the word 'and' itself is the denoter of that [conjunction], not a mere indicator (*dyotaka*). Furthermore, if it were an indicator, one would have to postulate a denotative power (*śakti*) for the other words in that context, and a power of indication for the word 'and'; thus there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). For this very reason, the statement in both systems of Mīmāṃsā that the negative particle (*nañ*) possesses a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is consistent.

The meaning is this: if particles (*nipāta*) were denotative (*vācaka*), the negative particle (*nañ*) would possess a primary denoted meaning (*śakyārtha*); consequently, since a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—consisting of a relationship with that denoted meaning—is possible, the aforementioned statement from the two Mīmāṃsā works would be consistent. However, if particles were merely indicative (*dyotaka*), there would be no denoted meaning for them; thus, because a secondary indication—which is constituted by a relationship with a denoted meaning—would be impossible, that statement would not be consistent. This position of the Mīmāṃsakas is untenable.

For, according to the maxim that "the meaning of a word is indeed not obtainable through any other means," since meanings such as conjunction (*samuccaya*) are understood from another word through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone, it is impossible to postulate a further denotative power (*śakti*) for that [word]. For this very reason, when the bank is presented through indication alone, no further denotative power is postulated for the word *gaṅgā* with respect to it. Otherwise, one would have to postulate a denotative power even for words such as *gaṅgā* with respect to the bank and so forth.

When used in conjunction with particles such as *ca*, words like "tree" convey a qualified meaning; when not so used, other words do not convey that qualified meaning. Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), these particles function merely as indicators of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya-grāhaka*). Consequently, since their role is established otherwise, these two facts do not prove that particles possess denotative power (*vācakatva*). Nor should it be argued that if they were denotative, there would be a dual assumption of power: a power of denotation in other words regarding the meaning indicated by the particle, and a power of indication (*dyotakatā*) in the particle itself (such as *ca*).

With the intention that other words accept figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) while particles (*nipāta*) serve to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*), he says "But not... The meaning is this: it is not correct to claim that the view of others—the Mīmāṃsakas—which is established in the section on conjunction (*samuccaya-adhikaraṇa*) and consists merely of [particles] being denoters (*vācaka*), is our own view. Rather, some are denoters and some are indicators (*dyotaka*). As it is stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "It is a denoter of particulars because they are possible, or else it is an indicator. And so it is.

The meaning is: "if particles (nipāta) were denotative. Regarding the phrase "in a domain other than [that of] particles": the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) other than a particle—these two do not have a relation of difference (*bheda-sambandha*) as their mode of connection; that is to say, such a connection is not established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).

For this very reason, in the sentence *odanaḥ pacati* ("The rice cooks"), the meaning of the nominal stem other than a particle—namely, *odana* (rice)—does not connect with the meaning of the verbal root, *pāka* (cooking), by way of the relation of objecthood (*karmatā*). Consequently, no cognition arises from it in the form "the cooking has rice as its object" (*odana-karmakaḥ pākaḥ*).

The point is this: because the rule is formulated as "other than a particle" (*nipātātirikteti*), the syntactic connection between the meaning of a particle and the meaning of a verbal root through a relation of difference is not unestablished. Thus, in the case of *prajayati*, the excellence (*prakarpa*), which is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consisting of the particle *pra*, is construed with the meaning of the root *ji* (victory) by way of the relation of substratum (*āśrayatā-sambandha*). Consequently, the cognition of "excellent victory" is logically justified. [Regarding the term] *samānādhikaraṇa* ("having a common locus"):

The rule that "there is a relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the meanings of two nominal stems (*prātipadika*) having the same case-ending" is also restricted; its meaning is that it applies to cases other than those involving particles (*nipāta*). That is to say, there is a relation of non-difference between the meanings of two nouns (*nāman*) having the same case-ending, provided they are other than particles. For this very reason, in the sentence *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's servant"), there is no cognition of a relation of non-difference between the meanings of the two nominal stems *rājan* and *puruṣa*, because the words *rājan* and *puruṣa* do not possess the same case-ending.

It should be understood that "having the same case-ending" (samānavibhaktikatva) means "having case-endings with the same meaning. Consequently, in the expression *rājñaḥ sutasya dhanam* ("the wealth of the king's son"), there is no syntactic connection between the king and the son by way of identity (*abhedena*). This is because the two genitive case-endings have different meanings—one signifying "being produced from" (*janyatva*) in one instance and the other signifying "ownership" (*svatva*) in the other—and thus they lack the quality of having the same meaning.

In cases such as "the pot and [the cloth]" (*ghaṭaś ca*), however, although the nominal stems *ghaṭa* and *ca* possess identical case-endings, since the conjunction (*samuccaya*) is the meaning of the particle (*nipāta*), there indeed occurs an application (*anvaya*) between the pot and the conjunction by way of a relation consisting of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*), namely: "the conjunction whose counter-correlate is the pot."

Even though [states such as] experience (*anubhava*) and direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) are denotable by particles (*nipāta*), in order to establish that a verbal root (*dhātu*) possesses an object (*sakarmaka*), it must be stated that "having an object" consists in expressing an operation (*vyāpāra*) that has a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) from the result (*phala*) which is the meaning of either the root itself or the particle associated with it. "The root itself" (*sva*) refers to the verbal root, and "associated with it" refers to the particle joined with it; the meaning is: the state of expressing an operation whose locus is distinct from that result which constitutes the meaning of either one of those two.

In expressions such as *anubhūyate*, the particle *anu* and others are connected with the verbal root (*dhātu*). The result (*phala*) that constitutes the meaning of that [root]—such as direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), experience (*anubhava*), and so forth—is located in the teacher, Śiva, or another [agent]. Since the verbal root denotes an activity (*vyāpāra*) residing in a different locus, such as Devadatta, its status as a transitive verb (*sakarmaka*) remains intact; thus, in expressions such as *sākṣātkriyate*, the formation of the *lakāra* (verbal suffixes) and so forth in the passive voice is established.

In the case of the word *pratiṣṭhate*, since the prefix *pra-* does not denote "initial motion," one must adopt the following grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) in order to establish its connection with the meaning of the verb: "suffixes convey their own meaning as connected with either the meaning of the verbal root co-occurring with the base, or the meaning of the particle [prefix] co-occurring with the base."

In the case of the expression *tena pratiṣṭhate*, the understanding that "the initial departure resides in the agent"—arising from the connection of the meaning of the particle (which is coreferential with the verbal base) with the agent expressed by the suffix *te*—is established by experience and can be accounted for. Thus, one must accept the following causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*): for a verbal cognition whose qualificand is the meaning of a noun and which is related [to it] through the relation of difference (*bhedasaṃbandha*), the cause is the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by either a suffix or a particle.

For this very reason, in the case of *rājā puruṣaḥ* ("The king is a man"), there does not arise a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in which the meaning of the noun "king" (*rāja*) is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the relation of difference (*bheda*) is the connective relation (*saṃsarga*), such that [the cognition would be] "the man possesses the relation of ownership as determined by the king. This is because the relation of difference is not presented (*anupasthiti*) by the suffix following the word *rāja*. However, in the case of *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("The man of the king"), there does arise a cognition in which the meaning of the noun is the qualifier and the relation of difference is the connective relation; for the relation of difference is present through the presentation generated by the genitive suffix (*ṣaṣṭhī*) following the word *rāja*.

In the case of "ghaṭaśca" (pot and), because the pot is construed with the conjunction through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*), there arises a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in which the pot—the referent of the noun—is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and difference (*bheda*) is the relation (*saṃsarga*), namely: "the conjunction has the pot as its counter-correlate. This is because the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the conjunction is produced by the particle (*nipāta*), and it is accepted that the presentation produced by a particle is the cause for a verbal cognition in which a noun-referent is the qualifier and difference is the relation. This is the meaning.

Nor should it be argued that there would be excessive complexity (gaurava) if one were to include "other than particles" in some derivations and include the term "particle" in others; for once it is established by the reasoning of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) that particles possess denotative power (vācakatva), such complexity must be accepted as unavoidable. Moreover, precisely because they are denotative, we observe that upon the utterance of the mere word "not," there arises both the cognition of absence and a desire to know whose absence it is, just as occurs with the word "absence" itself.

If, however, they are indicators (*dyotaka*), then indication is impossible without their co-occurrence with another word. If it is objected that if particles (*nipāta*) were denoters (*vācaka*), there would be the undesirable consequence of their being used alone, we say no. This is because some particles are restricted by the rule "they [occur] before the verbal root" (*te prāgdhātoḥ*); others, such as *na*, etc., are intended to be used even alone; and for the rest, even though they are denoters, they are not used in isolation—just as a root or a suffix is never used alone.

This has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "Even though the suffix is expressive, it is not used in isolation; even when expressing a collection [of meanings], there is no independence [from the base]. Although these [suffixes] are not traditionally taught as being subsequent (*para*) in the same manner as verbal suffixes (*pratyaya*), nevertheless, because they lack a connection with a relatum—such as excellence (*prakarpa*) and so forth—without which the cognition [of the meaning] would be incomplete, their isolated usage is impossible. Even when expressing a collection, since the cognition remains incomplete without the specific presentation of those two [the base and the suffix], they are eternally dependent (*nitya-paratantra*); thus, they do not occur in isolation.

Thus, although there may be no fault in particles being denotative according to their respective cases, in some instances their status as indicators must also be accepted; otherwise, in the case of "pratiṣṭhate," the cognition established by experience in the form of the speed of movement would not occur.

Since it is not established that there is a grammatical connection (*anvaya*) between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root due to their difference, even if the restriction [of the rule] "in the case of a particle" (*nipāta*) is applied by excluding non-particles, and even if the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the root is accepted in the absence of the prefix *pra*, the understanding would still result in "the absence whose counter-positive is the cessation of motion"—that is, the meaning of the root as "cessation of motion" connects with the absence expressed by the prefix *pra* through the relation of being a counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*). Thus, the cognition would occur only in the form of "the absence of the absence of the cessation of motion."

However, if they are indicators (*dyotaka*), since the verbal root *tiṣṭhati* itself conveys the sense of "going" through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the cognition of it in the form of "motion" is established without effort. The phrase "not thus" means that the distinction made by the Naiyāyikas—that prefixes (*prādi*) are indicators while particles (*cādi*) are denoters—is also not tenable. As for what has been said by some: "If all particles were denoters, the rule prescribing the nominal stem designation (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) for 'a meaningless particle' would be redundant."

Since the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is already established by the *arthavat-sūtra* itself, even if all [words] were merely indicative (*dyotaka*), the status of being a nominal stem would be established by the rule "of a particle" (*nipātasya*) alone; thus, the portion "of that which is meaningless" (*anarthakasya*) would be entirely redundant. Therefore, it must be stated that only some [words] possess meaning. Consequently, it follows that only prepositions (*upasarga*) are indicative, whereas particles such as *ca* and others are expressive (*vācaka*).

That is incorrect; for it is clear from Kaiyaṭa and other sources that this statement [of Patañjali] was made for the purpose of including those particles understood to be meaningless (*anarthaka*) from various authorities: from the *Amara-kośa* ("*tu*, *hi*, *ca*, *sma*, *ha* are used for filling the verse-line"), from the *Nirukta* ("*kam*, *īm*, *id* are used for filling the verse-line"), and from the rule "*adhi-parī* are meaningless" (*anarthakau*). Furthermore, regarding the question of which are the denoters (*vācaka*), there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamanābhāva*), and one could just as well argue the opposite—that the *ca*-type particles are the denoters while the *pra*-type prefixes are the indicators (*dyotaka*).

In reality, since this Vārttika has been rejected by the authors of the Bhāṣya, it appears that what is based upon it is indeed not to be trusted. [The word] "useless" (vyartham) means that, according to the view that [particles] are indicators (dyotaka), all particles are devoid of meaning; thus, there is nothing to be excluded [by the rule]. [The phrase] "because it has been rejected" refers to the rule *adhiparī anarthakau*, by which the designation of *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed for the words *adhi* and *pari* when they are meaningless, in order to set aside their designations as *gati* and *upasarga*.

Furthermore, by the two rules "Prepositions [are designated as such] when connected with a verb" (*upasargāḥ kriyāyoge*) and "And [the words] *gati* [are so designated]" (*gatiśca*), it is established that the designations *gati* and *upasarga* apply only when there is a connection with a verb. In that case, since the words *adhi* and *pari* are devoid of meaning (in this context), a connection with a verb is impossible; thus, the application of the designations *gati* and *upasarga* cannot even arise. Consequently, the prescription of the designation *karmapravacanīya* for the purpose of overriding those [other designations] would be redundant.

Nor should it be argued that the rule prescribing the designation *karmapravacanīya* for the sake of the second case (*dvitīyā*)—namely, "the second case occurs when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*"—would otherwise be purposeless. For, since [the particle] is devoid of meaning, it is impossible to determine its being "joined with a *karmapravacanīya*. Thus, the rule prescribing the *karmapravacanīya* designation, having become redundant, indicates the following: that one must perform the grammatical operations occasioned by particles even after accepting their meaningfulness, despite their being [otherwise considered] meaningless.

Furthermore, since a verbal action (*kriyā*) is possible [in such cases], the designations *gati* and *upasarga* would apply; therefore, the prescription of the designation *karmapravacanīya* serves its purpose by precluding those two. Consequently, in examples such as *kuto 'dhyāgacchati*, the elision (*nighāta*) prescribed by the rule *gatir gatau* does not occur. This is the result [of the rule]: even for particles (*nipāta*) that lack meaning, the designation *prātipadika*—which is triggered by meaningfulness—still applies, thereby effecting the required grammatical operation.

The meaning is that, in that case, the statement "of a particle which is meaningless" (*nipātasyānarthakasya*) need not be formulated, because it has been rejected [as unnecessary]. Regarding the plural form "Mīmāṃsakas": the intention is that the plural is used because there is a plurality among Mīmāṃsakas due to the distinctions between the authors of the Bhāṣya and others. He sets forth the Mīmāṃsaka position with the words beginning with "only" (*kevala*). He refutes the Mīmāṃsaka position with the passage beginning with "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and ending with "nor is there the assumption of two powers" (*na śaktidvayakalpanāpi*). Regarding the phrase "for us" (*asmākam*):...

The meaning is: for those who accept the two positions—that particles (nipātas) possess both denotative power (*vācakatva*) and indicative power (*dyotakatva*). Regarding the phrase "upon grasping the secondary signification" (*lakṣaṇāgraha*): when it is maintained that the word *ca* and others function as indicators of intention (*tātparyagrāhaka*), just like context and so forth, after one has grasped the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of words such as *ghaṭa* in the sense of conjunction and so on, then—since the cognition of the meaning of conjunction and so forth arises from the word *ghaṭa*—the knowledge of the secondary signification as determined by the word *ghaṭa* becomes the cause of the verbal cognition whose object is the meaning of the jar and so forth as qualified by conjunction and so forth.

The causal relationship between the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) and verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is necessary. This means that when the indication of a word used in co-occurrence with others is grasped with respect to a qualified meaning, the indicated meaning is understood; thus, the knowledge of *lakṣaṇā* is the cause for the understanding of the indicated meaning, and this causal relationship between the understanding of the indicated meaning and the grasp of *lakṣaṇā* must necessarily be accepted. The same applies to the grasp of *śakti* (denotative power).

In the view that [prefixes and particles] are expressive (*vācakatva*), the cognition of the expressive power (*śakti*) residing in words such as *vṛkṣa* is the cause of the verbal cognition whose object is the meaning of *vṛkṣa* and so forth; likewise, the cognition of the expressive power residing in prefixes and particles (*prādi-nipāta*) is the cause of the cognition of meanings such as conjunction (*samuccaya*). Thus, the causal relationship between the cognition of expressive power and the verbal cognition must necessarily be accepted. The phrase "due to the absence of any other postulated [factors]" means that there is no need to postulate anything additional compared to the two established causal relationships in both the view that they are expressive and the view that they are illuminative (*dyotakatva*). The phrase "both of them" refers to these two views.

The meaning is that both expressiveness (*vācakatva*) and suggestiveness (*dyotakatva*) are appropriate because there is no [theoretical] burden (*gaurava*). "For this very reason" means precisely because both positions are logically sound due to the absence of such a burden. "That is expressive" means that the particle in the form of a prefix (*upasarga*) is expressive.

Regarding the term *pratiṣṭhā*: according to Pāṇini’s rule (*smṛti*) "ṣṭhā gatinivṛttau" (DhP 1.96), the root *sthā* denotes the cessation of motion; however, the prefix *pra-* indicates the absence of that [cessation]. Thus, by the maxim "the negation of an absence is the nature of presence," Puñjarāja has explained that [the compound] denotes motion. "In another system" means: according to the method of the Naiyāyikas. "It is indeed denotative" should be understood as referring to particles such as *ca* and so forth. "It is indeed indicative" refers to prefixes and the like. The word "restriction" (*niyama*) [is used here].

Indicating that the restriction—that prefixes and the like are exclusively indicators (*dyotaka*) while [verbs] are exclusively denoters (*vācaka*)—is not tenable, he says: "That very opinion is not [our own]. Or rather (*vā*): the meaning is that the opinion of others, namely the Mīmāṃsakas, that all particles (*nipāta*) are exclusively denoters, is precisely our own opinion. This is because, in the case of the word *pratiṣṭhate*, it has been established by the principle that the absence of a cognition in the form of "going" is itself of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*). || 47 ||

The meaning of "it is concluded" (*paryavasitam*) is as follows: the Naiyāyika position—that prefixes (*upasarga*) are merely indicative (*dyotaka*) while particles (*nipāta*) are expressive (*vācaka*)—is not tenable, because there is no justification for such a disparity; thus it is established at the conclusion. "Summarizing" (*upasaṃharan*) means "concluding. He says—that is, he states—"the status of being a particle belongs to others. Now, if both prefixes and particles were expressive, there would be the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) regarding the delimiters of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) for the properties of being a prefix and being a particle; therefore, he says: "the status of being a particle belongs to others."

Now, if one were to assume that in the rule *cādayo’sattve* ("*ca* and so on [are called *nipātas*] when not denoting a substance"), the term *asattve* functions as a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), there would be the complexity of either an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound) or a split in the sentence structure; therefore, for the sake of parsimony, he states the definition of a *nipāta* by resorting to an exclusion (*paryudāsa*): "provided that it has the meaning of a non-substance. The meaning is this: *nipātatva* (the state of being a *nipāta*) consists in being listed in the group beginning with *ca* while being co-referential with the property of having a non-substantial meaning.

The point is that in cases such as "because of existence while being distinct from quality and action" (*guṇakarmānyatve sati sattvāt*), the meaning understood is "because of existence which is co-referential with being distinct from quality and action"; for it is well-established that the locative case in the sense of *sati* (i.e., *satī-saptamī*) signifies co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Now, one might object that this definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*) regarding prefixes (*prādi*); therefore, he says: "by way of the relation of power" (*śaktisaṃbandhena*). The meaning is: *nipātatva* (the state of being a particle) consists in being the substratum of the word *nipāta*, or [equivalently] being denoted by the word *nipāta*, by means of the relation called "power" (*śakti*), which is of the nature of the signifier-signified relationship (*vācyavācakabhāva*).

Furthermore, since this status of being a particle (*nipātatva*) is common to both the *prādi* and *cādi* groups, that very [status] should be accepted as the delimitor of denotative capacity (*vācakatāvacchedaka*) due to parsimony (*lāghava*). Thus, the aforementioned complexity does not arise; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "or it is a universal" (*jātir vā*): An objection may be raised that the status of being a particle cannot be a universal, because it would result in a confusion (*saṃkara*) with [other universals] such as "being a root" (*dhātutva*), etc., and it is accepted that such confusion is a subverter of universality. To illustrate: the status of being an element (*bhūtatva*) exists in the five—earth, water, fire, air, and ether. [Similarly, the status of being a particle would exist in] *pṛ*, *ā*, *te*, *vā*, and *ca*.

Including the mind (*manas*), corporeality (*mūrtatva*) exists in these five. Corporeality is defined as possessing a limited dimension (*apakṛṣṭa-parimāṇavat*). Here, "confusion" (*saṃkara*) refers to the coexistence of two properties that are mutually exclusive (*parasparātyantābhāva-samānādhikaraṇa*). Indeed, there is such a coexistence in the four elements beginning with earth, where corporeality—existing in the mind while excluding the state of being an element (*bhūtatva*)—and the state of being an element—existing in space while excluding corporeality—both reside together.

Therefore, it is the established doctrine of the Naiyāyikas that both *abhūtatva* (the state of not having come into being) and *bhūtatva* (the state of having come into being) are not universals (*jāti*). Similarly, in the word *ha* occurring in such forms as *hasati*, *hatva* exists but *nipātatva* (the state of being a particle) does not; in the particle *ca*, *nipātatva* exists but *hatva* does not. However, in the particle *ha*, since both *hatva* and *nipātatva* coexist in one and the same locus, [the author] states "or it is an adventitious property" (*upadhir vā*) with the intention that *nipātatva* is not a universal.

Among the Naiyāyikas, the conventional usage of the term "limiting adjunct" (*upādhi*) generally applies to properties that are distinct from genus (*jāti*). This [adjunct] is also of two kinds: the delimited adjunct (*sakhaṇḍopādhi*) and the undelimited adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*). That property which can be defined is a delimited adjunct; for example, the nature of ether (*ākāśatva*) as the inherent cause of sound, or the nature of direction (*digatva*) as the cause for the conventional usage of "east" and so forth—such are the cases of *ākāśatva* and the like. And that property which cannot be defined is the undelimited adjunct.

And it has been said: "The nature of being an *anuyogi* (the related term), the nature of being a *pratiyogi* (the counter-correlate), the nature of being an object (*viṣayatā*), and so forth. Similarly, although the nature of being a particle (*nipātatva*)—defined as being listed in the group beginning with *ca* while having non-existence as its meaning—is also a *sakhaṇḍa* (composite) property, nevertheless, because this *sakhaṇḍa* property of being a particle does not pervade both the *prādi* and *cādi* groups, it must be accepted as an *akhaṇḍopādhi* (indivisible, unitary property).

The meaning is this: whatever nature—as a genus (*jāti*) or as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—the *nipātatva* (status of being a particle) is intended by others such as the Mīmāṃsakas, that very same nature, whether as a genus or as an adjunct, is also intended by us. In that regard, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that particles such as *pra* and others possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), just like particles such as *ca*. Other grammarians, however, maintain that particles such as *ca* and others possess indicative power (*dyotakatva*), just like particles such as *pra*.

This being the case, since both schools must assume that prefixes (upasargas) are either denoters (*vācaka*) or indicators (*dyotaka*), the property that serves as the delimitor of denotation (*vācakatāvacchedaka*) or the delimitor of indication (*dyotakatāvacchedaka*) residing in *pra* and other such items must be stated as "prefixhood" (*nipātatva*) itself, and not "the state of being an upasarga" (*upasargatva*). Regarding this point, there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamaka*) [to prefer one over the other]. Alternatively, the delimitor of indication residing in *pra* and others must be stated as "prefixhood" itself, and not "the state of being an upasarga. Regarding this point... [repetition of the final clause].

He dispels the doubt that there is a lack of a decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*) with the words "But on the other hand" (*paraṃ tu*), and so forth. "A general property" (*sāmānyadharma*) means a pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*). "In the absence of a subverting factor" (*asati bādhake*) and so on [is the meaning]. Thus, when there is no subverting factor, the "partiality," "inclination," or "insistence"—meaning the bias—of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) toward assuming a general (pervading) property as the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) [is established].

Thus, when it is accepted that prefixes (*upasarga*) function either as denoters (*vācaka*) or as indicators (*dyotaka*), one must consider that the status of being a particle (*nipātatva*)—which is a pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*) common to both—is the very determinant of their denotative capacity (*vācakatāvacchedaka*) or their indicative capacity (*dyotakatāvacchedaka*). This is because of the maxim that "proofs favor the general. Consequently, the distinction asserted by the Naiyāyikas—that prefixes like *pra* are indicators while particles like *ca* are denoters—is not tenable; such is the sense.

"Because of pervasiveness": the meaning is that *nipātatva* (the state of being a particle), whether in the form of a genus (*jāti*) or an adjunct (*upādhi*), is a general property (*sāmānyadharma*) because it resides in both [categories], namely *prādi* (prepositions) and so forth. "Of the capacity" (*śaktatāyāḥ*): the meaning is "of the denotative power" (*vācakatāyāḥ*). "An illustration of 'capacity'" (*śaktatāyā upalakṣaṇam*): the analysis of the compound is "that from which there is the knowledge (*lakṣaṇaṃ jñānam*) of what is proximate and of its own related object. The meaning is that a word is that which conveys both itself and something other than itself through the function of indication (*ajahatsvārthalakṣaṇā*).

The sense is this: just as in the expression "let curd be protected from crows" (*kākebhyo dadhi rakṣyatām*), the word *kāka* (crow) denotes itself, others [than itself] such as dogs, and so forth; similarly, the word *śaktatā* (capacity) denotes its own capacity (*śaktatā*) and that which is other than it, namely *dyotakatā* (indicative function), through a lakṣaṇā (indication) that does not abandon its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*). And thus, the intended meaning is that the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of both expressive function (*vācakatā*) and indicative function (*dyotakatā*) is the twofold nature of being a particle (*nipātatva*). || 48 ||

Thus ends the determination of the indicative (*dyotaka*) and expressive (*vācaka*) nature of particles (*nipāta*) in the *Śāṅkarī*, a commentary on the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, composed by Śaṅkara, the son of Raṅgabhaṭṭa. In this work, the determination of the meaning of particles has been completed in the first chapter. || 8 ||
Now follows the determination of the meaning of abstract suffixes (bhāvapratyaya).

In the context of defining names and their referents, intending to define the meaning of primary (kṛt) and secondary (taddhita) suffixes included within names, [the author] first states the definition of the meaning of abstract (bhāva) suffixes, saying: "of abstract suffixes" (*bhāvapratyaya*). This means the meaning of suffixes such as *tva*, *tal*, and so forth.
