Regarding the phrase "from primary derivatives, secondary derivatives, and compounds": the abstract suffixes such as *tva* and *tal*, which are applied after primary derivatives, secondary derivatives, and compounds, express a relationship (*sambandha*).

Since one experiences understanding in cases such as *kṛṣṇasarpatva* (the state of being a black snake) and *gaurakharatva* (the state of being a white donkey) precisely by way of a specific universal (*jāti*), he says "elsewhere," and so forth. The meaning is that, apart from conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), from a non-different form, and from those [words] with an invariable relation—excluding words such as *rūḍhi* and the like—the suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) expresses the relation itself. Among *rūḍhi* and the others, it has been stated that in the case of conventional usage, understanding occurs precisely by way of a specific universal.

The form is non-different as in "white" (*śukla*) and so forth. In such cases, although the suffix *matup*—derived by the rule "the suffix *matup* is added in the sense of 'this belongs to him' or 'this exists in this'"—is elided according to the statement "the elision of *matup* is desired after words denoting qualities," the word remains a derivative (*taddhita*). Nevertheless, through the cognition "the jar is white" (*ghaṭaḥ śuklaḥ*), which means "the jar is non-different from that which possesses the quality of whiteness," the relation of difference between the quality and the possessor of the quality is suppressed. Consequently, in expressions such as "whiteness" (*śuklatvam*), it is the quality itself that functions as the qualifier (*prakāra*), not the relation. In this regard, the form of the word "white" (*śukla*) is identical whether it denotes the quality or the possessor of the quality.

An example of an inseparable relation (*avyabhicarita-sambandha*) is: "the state of being existent is existence" (*sato bhāvaḥ sattā*). Here, the abstract suffix (*bhāva-pratyaya*) arises from the very word *sat* (existent). The relation between the existent (*sat*) and existence (*sattā*) never deviates; since the relation exists from the moment of the existent's production until its destruction, the sense is that it is an "inseparable relation. Such is the meaning of the rule concerning *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compound words. To dispel the misconception of the Mīmāṃsakas—who hold that this rule belongs to the author of the *Vārttika*—he states: "In the *Ṭīkā*."

To that end, he says "by Bhartṛhari," and so forth. The intention is that Mīmāṃsakas mistakenly believe this [work] to be a *vārttika* on the words of Hari (Patañjali). Regarding the phrase "merely a suffix expressing a state" (*bhāvapratyayamātra*): the word *mātra* signifies "entirety. Thus, the meaning is "all secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) prescribed with the sense of a state (*bhāva*). By this, the inclusion of suffixes such as *ṣyañ* and *vuñ* is established, since they too convey a state consisting of a relationship. He states the meaning of Hari’s statement with the words "this meaning," and so forth. "This" means "that which is about to be stated. "Meaning" (*artha*)...

The meaning is that this is the intended sense (*tātparyārtha*). Although in cases such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s man), *aupagavaḥ* (the son of Upagu), and *pācakaḥ* (the cook), the mere relation is not the denoted meaning, nevertheless, when a primary expressive power (*śakti*) is postulated for the compound and so forth, it is postulated precisely by including within its scope the meaning of the genitive case and other such elements present in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*). For this very reason, the traditional doctrine that the compound (*vṛtti*) and the analytical sentence have the same meaning (*samānārthatva*) is consistent. Regarding the phrase "the relation of the king and so forth": the meaning is that the primary expressive power of the compound *rājapuruṣa* and others resides in the man and so forth, who possess the relation as determined (*nirūpita*) by the king and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "it has been said": the meaning is that since the power (*śakti*) in a compound is indeed distinct [from the powers of its constituent parts], this refers to the occasion for defining the power of the compound. Regarding the phrase "and likewise": the meaning is by way of the method of postulating the power of the compound in that which is qualified by the relation with the king and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the suffix denoting a state following that": [this refers to the abstract suffix added after the compound].

In cases such as *rājapuruṣatvam* (the state of being a king’s man), *aupagavatvam* (the state of being Upagu’s descendant), and *paktṛtvam* (the state of being a cooker), the suffixes expressing abstract states (*bhāvapratyaya*), such as *-tva*, signify or convey a relation—namely, the relation of owner and owned, the relation of offspring and progenitor (i.e., the relation of produced and producer), or the relation of action and agent. This is because, in these instances, one understands [the meaning] as such. The point is that the relation of the preceding member's referent appears precisely as a qualifier (*prakāra*) within the referent of the subsequent member. "This too" refers to this very point.

The meaning is that abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*), such as *tva*, also convey a relation. This is because it is impossible [for them to do so] under the theory of difference (*bheda*) as stated in the verse: "The denotable object is established as being either difference, relation, or both. Under that [theory of difference], since a relation does not appear as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by compounds such as *rājapuruṣa* (the king’s man), in the expression *rājapuruṣatva*, the suffix *tva* has only difference as its meaning.

The meaning is as follows: in the view that [the relation] is distinct (*bhedapakṣe*), in the case of "king's man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), there arises the cognition "a man distinct from one who does not belong to a king"; thus, because the distinction appears as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*) within the referent of the subsequent word, the man. "And so forth" (*evam ca*) means: in the various alternative views, when the relation (*saṃsarga*) is the expressed meaning (*vācyatva*) in compound formations (*samāsa*) and the like. "The relation of owner and owned" (*svasvāmibhāvasambandha*) means: in the view that [the relation] is the expressed meaning (*saṃsargapakṣe*), in cases such as "king's man," there arises the cognition "a man who possesses ownership as determined by the lordship residing in the king."

"Upagu-apatya-sambandha" means the relationship between Upagu and his offspring, consisting of the nature of the relation between progenitor and progeny. "Ityanvayabodhaḥ" means verbal cognition (śābdabodha). The point is that even in a compound ending in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix, since a specific unitary power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) is admitted, there is no separate presentation [of the meanings]. Because there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) in a complex formation (*vṛtti*)—since the connection would merely be the relation between two meanings that are not separately presented—the statement "ityanvayabodhaḥ" is utterly impossible. This is the intended meaning.

And likewise, in the view that [the meaning] arises from association (*saṃsarga*), just as the aggregate "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*) is accepted as having a specific power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*)—namely, the power to denote a man who possesses a relation defined by the king—in the same way, since "kingliness" (*rājapuruṣatva*) is also a derivative formation (*vṛtti*), the aggregate "kingliness" (*rājapuruṣatvam*) is accepted as having a specific power in the sense of "the state of being a king's man," which is to say, the relation of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*). Thus, [the cognition arises] precisely through the power residing in the derivative formation consisting of "kingliness."

The intended meaning is that one should not be deluded into thinking that the statement "from *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compounds" (*kṛttaddhitasamāsebhyaḥ*)—which belongs to the Vārttikakāra—is something unprecedented; for it is established that the suffix occurring within the compound *rājapuruṣatvam* conveys the relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*). Regarding the phrase "but when the relationship is invariable" (*avyabhicaritasaṃbandhe tu*), the meaning is: "but when the relationship between offspring and progenitor is an invariable relationship. *Aupagavatvam* is the state of being an *aupagava*.

In this context, from the word *aupagava*, the suffix *tva* is applied in the sense of "state" (*bhāva*) according to the rule *tasya bhāvas-tvatalau*. Regarding the term "state," Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita states in the *Kaumudī*: "State is the mode (the qualifier) in the cognition produced by the base. The meaning of this is as follows: by proximity, that which is the base of the suffixes *tva*, *tal*, etc.—that is, the word which serves as the basis for the prescription of those suffixes—the object perceived as a mode, that is, as a qualifier, in the cognition produced by such a word, is "state."

In this regard, in the case of the word *aupagava*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the word *upagu* in the sense of offspring according to the rule "its offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*). The relationship between Upagu’s offspring and [Upagu] himself is the relation of producer and produced (*janyajanakabhāva*). Upagu is the producer, and the offspring is that which is produced. The state of being produced (*janyatā*) resides in the produced, and the state of being a producer (*janakatā*) resides in the producer; this alone constitutes the relation of producer and produced, based on the etymological derivation "the state (*bhāva*) of the produced and the producer. This very relation of producer and produced is what is called the relationship between offspring and progenitor.

The meaning is that "apatyatā" (the state of being offspring) refers to the relationship between the offspring and the possessor of offspring, as well as the state of possessing offspring itself. In this context, "apatyatā" corresponds to the status of being produced (*janyatā*), while "apatyavattā" corresponds to the status of being a producer (*janakatā*). Thus, in the case of *aupagavaḥ*, there arises the cognition: "one who possesses the state of being offspring as defined by the state of possessing offspring residing in Upagu. Consequently, because the relationship between offspring and the possessor of offspring appears there as a qualifier, the sense is that the very relationship between offspring and the possessor of offspring is what constitutes *aupagavatva* (the state of being an Aupagava), and this is the meaning of the suffix *-tva*.

The meaning is that the relationship between offspring and the progenitor is an invariable relationship; just as the relationship between existence and the existent is never subject to deviation, so too the relationship between offspring and the progenitor is never subject to deviation. Since this relationship exists from the moment of the existent's birth until its destruction, and since the relationship of being offspring exists from the moment of the offspring's birth until its destruction, it is therefore an invariable relationship.

The point is this: by the statement "and the *yotra* [lineage] together with the feet," the fact that being an offspring (*apatyatva*) is a genus (*jāti*) is made known. Because the relationship of difference between the genus and the possessor of the genus is obscured, the genus itself is the qualifier (*prakāra*) there; thus, it is that very genus which is the meaning of suffixes such as *tva*. Regarding the phrase "functioning with respect to another meaning" (*arthāntaravṛtti*): "another meaning" (*arthāntara*) means a different object. The meaning is: that whose function—its expressive power (*śakti*)—lies in another meaning. The sense is that one should cite a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix as an example when it is expressive of a meaning other than "offspring," such as in the word *dīvyati* ("he plays/shines").

For example, from the word *akṣa* with the suffix *ṭhak* in the sense of "one who plays" (*dīvyati*), there arises the form *ākṣika*. Here, because the understanding is that [the person] is one who possesses the action of playing where the dice (*akṣa*) are the instrument, the action of playing appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) within the meaning of the suffix *ṭhak*—namely, the agent (*kartṛ*) in the relation of action and its factor (*kriyākārakabhāva*). Therefore, in the expression *ākṣikatvam*, that very action of playing is the meaning of the abstract suffix *tva*.

In cases such as *gaurakharaḥ* (a wild ass) and *kṛṣṇasarpaḥ* (a black snake), because they possess the status of being compounds (*samāsa*), it would follow that the expression of the relation [between the members] would occur through a case-ending suffix (*sup*) expressing a state (*bhāva-pratyaya*) in the latter member; refuting this, he says "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) and so forth. By the phrase "conventional usage has been stated," the meaning is: by the passage of the text which states that in examples such as *dāmodaratvam*, there is an experienced cognition based on the specification of a particular genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*). The meaning of "the second" is: an example of an undifferentiated form (*abhinnarūpa*).

By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even though it ends in a *taddhita* suffix," it is implied that the expression of a relationship with the subsequent abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) was previously considered problematic. Regarding the phrase "due to the cognition of non-difference" (*abhedapratyayāt*): because the common worldly cognition of non-difference—expressed as "this is that"—obscures the relationship of difference between quality and qualified (which is what is denoted by the suffix *matup* prescribed for the sense of the genitive case), in expressions such as "whiteness" (*śuklatvam*), the abstract suffix does not denote a relationship, but rather the quality itself.

The rule for the elision (*luk*) of the suffix in the word *matura* (as in *ghaṭasya śuklaḥ*) should be understood as intended to prevent the undesirable usage *ghaṭaḥ śuklavān*, since the linguistic practice of treating quality and the possessor of quality as distinct (*guṇaguṇinor bhedavyavahāraḥ*) still exists. The same should be understood regarding universals (*jāti*) such as *sattā* (existence). In the expression *sato bhāvaḥ* (the state of being existent), because one experiences the cognition that the word *sat*—derived from the root *as* with the suffix *śatṛ*—means "that which possesses existence" (*sattāvān*), existence (*sattā*) appears as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*) in relation to the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix *śatṛ*. Therefore, by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) following it, that very [existence] is denoted. This applies to the universal (*jāti*).

In expressions such as "this is a Brāhmaṇa," because there is an experienced cognition of identity between the physical body denoted by the word "this" and the specific caste denoted by the word "Brāhmaṇa," the relationship of difference between the genus and the individual possessing the genus is obscured; therefore, in terms such as "brāhmaṇatva" (Brāhmaṇahood), the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) does not denote a relationship, but rather denotes the specific caste itself—this is the meaning.

Just as there is a conventional usage of difference between a quality and its possessor, such as "the cloth is white," the absence of any usage like "this [person] is a Brāhmaṇa" (meaning "the specific caste related to this body") with reference to the universal (*jāti*) implies that there is never a conventional usage of difference between the universal and its possessor (*jātimat*). Since they are understood only through non-difference, the meaning of the subsequent abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is the universal itself as it appears as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*) in the individual instance of a Brāhmaṇa; this is the intended sense. || 49 ||

Desiring to refute the Mīmāṃsaka position regarding the meaning of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) such as *tva* and *tal*, he first restates it with the words "In cases such as *daṇḍī*" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "qualified by the meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyarthaviśiṣṭa*): the sense is that the secondary suffix (*taddhita*), such as *-in*, denotes merely that substance which is, in reality, qualified by a staff or the like through a relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*). The intended meaning is that the syntactical construction of the words is: "by the secondary suffix *-in* and others, because they denote merely the substance qualified by a staff and so forth."

Here, by the word *mātra* (only), the exclusion of relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is intended. The meaning is that a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) such as *-in* denotes only a substance, and not a relation such as conjunction. This is the underlying point: in cases such as *daṇḍī* ("staff-bearer"), the relation of conjunction appears through the force of the relational context (*saṃsargamaryādayā*), and thus there is no expressive power (*śakti*) for it; rather, the expressive power of the base (*prakṛti*) lies in the staff, while the expressive power of the suffix (*pratyaya*) such as *-in* lies in the substratum (*āśraya*).

Precisely because a relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth is not denotable, even in cases such as "the cook" (*pācaka*), a relation consisting of the connection between action and its factor (*kriyā-kārakabhāva*) is not denotable. As stated by the Bhaṭṭas: "The root *pac* denotes the cooking, and the suffix *aka* denotes the agent; however, the agent as connected with the cooking is not denotable by either one [of them] alone."

And thus, in cases such as *daṇḍī* ("staff-bearer"), since the staff (*daṇḍa*) and so forth are perceived as qualifiers (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by the base (*prakṛti*), the Mīmāṃsaka—who maintains that the meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) following that [base] is that very staff and not the relation—being countered, [the author] says: "In this case, there is the fallacy of the 'half-old woman' (*ardhajaratīya*). He explains the meaning of the word *atra* (in this case) found in the verse: "by the abstract suffix" (*bhāvapratyaya*). This means: within the scope of abstract suffixes such as *tva*, *tal*, and so forth.

One might ask: "What would happen in the case of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) such as *tva* and *tal*? To this he replies: "It would be like the 'half-old-woman' rule" (*ardhajaratīyam*). The meaning is that there would be the fault known as the "half-old-woman" (*ardhajaratīya*). "Half of an old woman" is *ardhajaratī*; the compound is formed according to the rule "the neuter [word] is used in the sense of a half. That which resembles this is *ardhajaratīyam*. The suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule "and from a compound denoting that [resemblance]."

The sense is that it is utterly unreasonable to accept—as one does in the case of an old woman who desires one half [of her body] but not the other, which is inconsistent—that although the two words *dāmodara* and *daṇḍin* are equal in their failure to denote a relation, the suffix following the former denotes a universal (*jāti*) in the expression *dāmodaratvam*, while the suffix following the latter denotes a relation in the expression *daṇḍitvam*. Thus, in the one case there is no denotation of a relation, whereas in the other there is; this is highly improper.

He says "by not denoting the relation" (*saṃbandhānabhidhāyakatvena*) in order to demonstrate precisely this state of being "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīyatva*). The meaning is that because the relation is not perceived as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*) in the cognition produced by the base form (*prakṛti*)—such as the words *dāmodara* or *ghaṭa*—there is an absence of the denotation of the relation. The word "of the Mīmāṃsakas" implies the ellipsis "in the opinion [of the Mīmāṃsakas]". Thus, there would be no denotation of that [relation].

The meaning is that there would be no expression of the relation; rather, there would be the expression of the staff and so forth alone, and that is not desired. Just as in the case of the cognition produced by the base-words *dāman* (rope), *udara* (belly), or *ghaṭa* (pot), because the relation does not appear as a qualifier (*prakāra*), the relation between the pot and potness appears through the mode of the "relational juncture" (*saṃsarga-maryādā*). In that case, since there is no postulation of a separate denotative power (*śakti*) for the word *ghaṭa*—as there is for [the word *ghaṭatva*]—it denotes only the pot as qualified by potness. Consequently, the suffix following it [denotes the universal].

The point is this: just as [the suffixes] do not denote a relation, so too in the cognition produced by the base words *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer) and *pācaka* (cook), since the relation is not perceived as a qualifier (*prakāra*), the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) following them would likewise not denote a relation.

One might object: "In cases such as *dāmodarasya bhāvo dāmodaratvam* ('the state of Dāmodara is dāmodaratva'), the word *bhāva* (state/nature) refers to a specific property residing in Dāmodara and the like; thus, it is logical that the relation is not denoted. However, in cases such as *daṇḍino bhāvo daṇḍitvam* ('the state of the staff-bearer is daṇḍitva'), the *bhāva* is simply the conjunction [of the staff] and so forth. Therefore, what obstacle is there to the relation being denoted by the suffix *-tva* in that case? To dispel this doubt, he defines the meaning of the term *bhāva*: "prakṛti... [and so on].

The meaning is this: *bhāvatva* (the state of being a *bhāva*) consists in being a category that inheres in the referent of its own base (*prakṛti*), while simultaneously possessing the property of being a qualifier in the cognition produced by the base of suffixes such as *tva* and *tal* when they are intended to be used. To demonstrate the purpose for excluding [certain cases] regarding the two parts—the qualifier and the qualified—he says "otherwise" (*anyathā*). This means that in the formal definition of the category of *bhāva*, there would be an absence of the inclusion of both the qualifier and the qualified portions; that is to say, if only one of them were included. Alternatively, it means that the category of *bhāva* would consist merely of whatever property resides in that [referent].

Regarding the phrase "of substanceness, etc.": if one were to state that "existence" (*bhāvatva*) consists merely in inherence in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), while omitting the qualifying portion "provided it exists," then since substanceness (*dravyatva*) subsists in a jar by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), the suffix *-tva* in the word *ghaṭatva* would result in denoting substanceness itself. This is the meaning.

However, if the qualification "being a qualifier in the cognition produced by the base" (*prakṛtijanyabodhe prakāratve sati*) is included, then although *dravyatva* (substanceness) occurs in the pot—the meaning of the base—by way of inherence (*samavāya*), it is not denoted by the suffix following the word "pot," because it lacks the status of being a qualifier in the cognition produced by the base-word "pot. Since it lacks the status of being a *bhāva* (abstract property), it is not what is expressed; rather, it is precisely that *ghaṭatva* (potness) which is denoted by the suffix following it. This is the intended meaning.

In all these cases, "inherence" (samavetatva) does not mean existing by way of the relation of inherence (samavāya-sambandha); for if it did, then in instances such as "the nature of potness" (ghaṭatvatva) or "the nature of absence" (abhāvatva), since the nature of potness and so forth do not inhere [in their respective substrata], it would be impossible for suffixes such as -tva to denote them. Rather, it should be understood that inherence means existing there by whatever relation whatsoever.

If it is objected: "Since substanceness (*dravyatva*) is likewise inherent in a jar just as jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) is, why is it that from the word 'jar' there is not also the possibility of a cognition having substanceness as its qualifier, just as there is a cognition having jar-ness as its qualifier? We reply: No. For one who has not grasped the word's convention (*vṛtti*), no comprehension of meaning is observed from a word whose convention has not been grasped. Therefore, the causal relation must necessarily be stated as follows: "The knowledge of the expressive power (*śakti*) denoted by a property delimited by a certain attribute is the cause for a verbal cognition whose object is delimited by that same attribute."

For example, with respect to a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) whose object is a cloth delimited by the property of clothness (*paṭatva*), the cause is the knowledge of that power (*śakti*) residing in the word "cloth" which is defined by the cloth delimited by the property of clothness; the effect, however, is the verbal cognition whose object is the cloth delimited by the property of clothness. Only for that person who has known the power residing in the word "cloth"—namely, that the power of the word "cloth" resides in that which is delimited by clothness—does a cognition having as its object that which is delimited by clothness arise from the word "cloth."

The meaning is as follows: when a word has the capacity to denote a particular thing as possessing a certain property, then from that word arises a cognition having that property as its qualifier; that is to say, when the word "cloth" (paṭa) is uttered, a cognition arises from the word "cloth" having the property of cloth-ness (paṭatva) as its qualifier.

One might object: "Just as the word 'cloth' produces a cognition in which cloth-ness (*paṭatva*) is the qualifier because cloth-ness exists in the cloth, so too, since there is the conventional usage of identity in the form 'the cloth is a substance,' and substance-ness (*dravyatva*) also exists in the cloth, the word 'cloth' should produce a cognition in which substance-ness is also the qualifier—namely, a cognition such that the cloth is the qualificandum as determined by a qualifier-status residing in substance-ness. If this is argued, we say no. For the phrase "having that property as its qualifier" means "having the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) as its qualifier. Since substance-ness is not the delimitor of the denotable capacity for the word 'cloth,' it does not function as a qualifier in that cognition.

And here, the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is precisely "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*), not "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*). This is because only a property that occurs neither less nor more [than the objects denoted] can be the delimitor of denotability. Since cloth-ness exists in all cloths denotable by the word "cloth," it does not occur less [than those objects]; nor does it occur more than the cloths, as it does not reside in pots and other things distinct from cloths. Therefore, that alone is the delimitor of denotability here; substance-ness, however, cannot be the delimitor of denotability because it resides in pots and other things distinct [from cloths].

That property (*dharma*) by which the power (*śakti*) of a word is delimited when its referent is delimited is the "delimitor of denotability" (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Since the power of the word "cloth" (*paṭa*) resides in a cloth delimited by the property of "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*), "cloth-ness" is the delimitor of denotability. Furthermore, regarding that property, it should be understood—according to the position stated in the *Bhāṣya* that "the application of words is fourfold"—that in some cases it is a genus (*jāti*), a quality (*guṇa*), an action (*kriyā*), or a proper name (*yadṛcchā-śabda*).

Objection: If the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word "cloth" is postulated with respect to a cloth delimited by the property of being a substance (*dravyatva*) which resides in the cloth, then it follows that "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) also ought to be a delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "cloth. Reply: This is not so. For the denotative power of a particular word must be postulated as residing in that which is delimited by a property whose extension is neither less nor more than [the extension of the object denoted]. Objection: What is the proof for this very point? Reply: Know that the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra* itself is the proof.

For this is what that commentary states: "Indeed, when 'jaggery' (guḍa) is mentioned, sweetness is not understood as a qualifier (*prakāra*). The meaning of this is: because when "jaggery" is mentioned, sweetness is not understood as a qualifier. Although sweetness exists in jaggery by virtue of being invariably concomitant with it, it is indicated that sweetness lacks the status of being the delimitor of the denotable object (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "jaggery," since it does not appear as a qualifier. The underlying point is that sweetness resides not only in jaggery but also in honey and other such things.

Now, if it is asked, "What then is the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word 'guḍa' (jaggery)? we reply: "It is *guḍatva* (the property of being jaggery). And that property which subsists in only a single part of the [referent] does not become a delimitor of denotability. For example, "yellow-cowness" (*pītagotva*). Indeed, yellow-cowness exists only in a yellow cow and not in all cows, such as blue ones; therefore, it is not a delimitor of denotability because its occurrence is too restricted (*nyūnavṛttitvāt*).

Even a property that resides in that [referent] but also occurs in what is distinct from it cannot be the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). For example, "hornedness" (*śṛṅgitva*): although hornedness exists in all cows, it also exists in buffaloes and other animals distinct from them; therefore, it cannot be the delimitor of denotability because it has an over-extended occurrence (*atiriktavṛttitvāt*). Indeed, only that property which is neither under-extended (*nyūnavṛtti*) nor over-extended can be the delimitor of denotability.

Just as, for example, having horns [is the delimitor] when there is possession of a dewlap. Since "candied sugar-ness" (guḍatva) exists in all and only in candied sugars, it does not have a narrower extension nor a wider extension; therefore, that alone becomes the delimitor of the denotability of the word "guḍa. The meaning is: because of its having neither less nor more extensive occurrence.

The sense is that by the Blessed One prohibiting sweetness (*madhurattva*) as having a wider extension than molasses (*guḍa*), it is also indicated that molasseness (*guḍatva*)—which has neither less nor more extension—is alone the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "molasses. This should be understood in the same way for all cases, such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*), "cloth" (*paṭa*), and so forth. Therefore, the cognition produced by the word "molasses" is one whose qualifier is the universal (*jāti*), specifically: "that which is delimited by the universal of molasseness is the denotation of the word 'molasses'."

And the state of being a delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*) consists in appearing as the locus of a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) that is itself defined by a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the denotation (*śakya*). Furthermore, in the apprehension of the denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), it is potness (*ghaṭatva*) alone that is the delimitor of denotability, not substanceness (*dravyatva*) and so forth.

And this accords with what has been stated in the *Laghumañjūṣā*: that even when there is a cognition of co-referential connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in sentences such as "The jar is a substance," there is no cognition from the word "jar" etc. having substanceness as its qualifier, nor is there a cognition from the word "substance" etc. having potness as its qualifier.

Thus, since [the suffix] occurs in the sense of the base (prakṛti) in words such as *ghaṭa* (pot), and because it is that which appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by the base, it is the "being" (*bhāva*) of pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth; for this is the meaning of the word *bhāva*. Therefore, it should be understood that pot-ness and the like are denoted by the suffix following that [base], and not substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and so forth. This is the intended meaning.

Now, if one were to set aside the qualifying portion—"being inherent in the meaning of the base"—and instead state only "being the qualifier in the cognition produced by the base," then he points out the undesirable consequence (aniṣṭāpatti) in cases such as *daṇḍitva* ("the state of being staff-bearing") with the words "of the staff, etc. (daṇḍādeśca). The meaning is this: since the verbal cognition [from *daṇḍin*] takes the form "one who possesses a qualificandumhood determined by a qualifierhood residing in the staff," the staff would be a qualifier in the verbal cognition produced by the word *daṇḍin*. Consequently, in cases such as *daṇḍitva*, the suffix *-tva* would result in denoting the staff itself and so forth.

[Objection: But surely, since in the verbal cognition produced by the word *daṇḍin* (the staff-bearer), the relation between the two—just as between the staff and the bearer—is also manifested, and since that [relation] functions as a qualifier (*prakāra*), the denotation of the relation is established without effort simply by the suffix *tva*. To this, he says: "And not in his view."

In the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, since the relation between the staff and the bearer of the staff is manifested through the very constraint of syntactic relation (*saṃsargamaryādā*), no power (*śakti*) is postulated for the relational aspect. Rather, the base (*prakṛti*) has power with respect to the staff, and the suffix *tva* has power with respect to the locus (*āśraya*). Consequently, from the cognition "the person is the locus of the staff," the staff is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the person is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Thus, in the cognition produced by the word *daṇḍin*, there is no manifestation of the relation at all; how much less could it possess the status of being a qualifier?

And likewise, in cases such as *daṇḍitvam* ("the state of being a staff-bearer"), it is all the more difficult for the suffix *-tva* to denote a relation; with this intention, he says: "The relation is the qualifier" (*prakāra*). The meaning of the phrase "and not" (*na ca*) is that a relation cannot possibly be a qualifier by virtue of being a relation itself, such that it could be expressed by suffixes like *-tva* or *-tal*. Now, regarding the expression *daṇḍitvam* and others, he restates the argument put forward by the Mīmāṃsakas concerning the denotation of a relation by the suffixes *-tva*, *-tal*, etc., beginning with "As for what [was said]" (*yattu*) and "When" (*yadā*).

In this context, in examples such as *daṇḍitva* ("the state of being a staff-bearer"), [the property] "inhering in itself" means inhering in that which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the cognition produced by the base (*prakṛti*). "Expressible" (*vācya*) means, in short, being the qualifier (*prakāra*) of the cognition produced by the base. "There is no other quality"—as in *śuklatva* ("whiteness") and so on—it is not possible [for it to be a quality] like the quality of whiteness and the like. "At that time" [means]: because there is no other alternative, even though the staff and so forth are qualifiers in the cognition produced by the base, they cannot constitute the referent of an abstract noun (*bhāvapadārtha*) because they do not inhere in the base's meaning, just as the property of potness (*ghaṭatva*) does not inhere in the pot [itself]. Therefore, "the relation is expressible."

The meaning is that even a relation which is not a qualifier in the cognition produced by the base (*prakṛti*), yet is inherent in itself, is accepted as being denotable by suffixes such as *tva* and so on. It should be understood that the words *yadā* and *tadā* terminate in the sense of "wherever" (*yatra*) and "there" (*tatra*).

The purport of the statement of the Mīmāṃsakas is this: where a quality—which is a qualifier in the cognition produced by the base and a qualifier in the cognition produced by the base—is impossible, there even a relation which is not a qualifier in the cognition produced by the base, yet resides in the qualificand of the cognition produced by the base, must be accepted as being denotable by suffixes such as *tva*.

And thus, he refutes the statement of the Mīmāṃsakas—that in expressions such as *daṇḍitva* (the state of being a staff-bearer), it is the relation itself that is denoted by suffixes like *tva* and *tal*, and not the staff (*daṇḍa*) and so forth—by saying "that is not [so]"; [he does so] by [stating] "because [the suffix] denotes the relatum."

Even though in the analysis (*vigraha*) of words such as *daṇḍin* ("staff-bearer")—as in "this man has a staff" (*asya daṇḍo'sti*) or "the cows belong to him" (*asya gāvaḥ santi*)—one observes that the explanation (*vivaraṇa*) in phrases like "of this" (*asya*) emphasizes the predominance of the relation between the meaning of the suffix and its base, it follows that the relation (*saṃsarga*) is primary. Thus, suffixes such as *matup* (the possessive suffix *-in*) are prescribed specifically for the relation itself, in the sense of "this belongs to him" or "it exists in this. And it is stated in the *Vārttika* on the *Āruṇādhikaraṇa*: "The possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is applied when there is a relation [expressed] as 'this belongs to him' (*asya ayam*) or 'it is in this' (*atra ayam*)."

Nevertheless, since the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*) and "Caitra who possesses cows" (*gomāṃścaitraḥ*) is understood from the word itself even without reflecting upon the impossibility [of such coreferentiality] otherwise, one must accept that suffixes such as *matup* denote substances (*dravya*), in accordance with that understanding. And it has been said by the Mīmāṃsakas: "In all cases, substance alone is denoted by derivative (*yaugika*) words; for it is not possible for the relation to be the denotation, because that would entail excessive complexity (*atigaurava*). Regarding the term "derivative" (*yaugika*): that which is capable of producing a connection (*yoga*) is "derivative."

In the expression *yogādyacca*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is employed. A word is that which denotes a meaning obtainable through the combination of a base (*prakṛti*) and a suffix (*pratyaya*). The mention of "base and suffix" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the preceding and following parts that denote meanings and constitute a derivative (*yaugika*) word; by this, it is established that even a compound (*samāsa*) is a derivative word. For this very reason, the statement of the learned authorities is consistent: "A derivative word is a name that conveys only a meaning obtained through etymological derivation (*yoga*); it is of three kinds: compounds, words ending in secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), and words ending in primary suffixes (*kṛt*)."

The meaning of the first half [of the verse] is that, in all cases, it is the substance (*dravya*) alone that is primarily denoted by derivative (*yaugika*) words. He states the meaning of the second half with the words beginning "for not" (*na hi*), etc. The underlying intention (*bhāva*) is as follows: if, in an analysis such as "one who has cows" (*gāvo yasya santi*), the predominance of the relation—which is the meaning of the suffix in "whose" (*yasya*)—is observed, and if, accordingly, the suffixes *matup* and so on were to denote only the relation and not the substance, then...

Since a relation that depends on two relata in the form of the *anuyogin* (the substratum) and the *pratiyogin* (the counter-correlate) cannot be established if either one is absent, it would follow that in expressions such as *gomān* ("cow-possessor"), the relation of even a single relatum—namely, the cow—would have to be denoted. This would result in the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating two distinct powers (*śakti*). Now, if it is accepted that suffixes such as *matup* denote the relation, then in cases like *gomān*, there would be no cognition of the relation.

By the word *go*, the relatum in the form of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is expressed; by the suffix *-mat*, the relatum in the form of the sub-correlative (*anuyogin*) is denoted; however, the relation itself is not denoted by anything. If the relation were denoted by the suffix *-mat*, then only a bhāva-suffix such as *-tva* or *-tal* arising from a nominal stem like *gomat* would be capable of denoting the relation, and not otherwise. And yet, the relation is perceived everywhere in cases such as *pācakatva* (the state of being a cook) or *pāṭhakatva* (the state of being a reciter). If this is argued, it is not so.

For the comprehension of the relation is established through implication by that very related entity which must necessarily be denoted. And it has been said: "If the relation can be understood through the related entity itself, who would then attribute a further denotative power to the word?"

The sense is that, because the linguistic usage "the possessor" (*saṃbandhī*) is untenable without a relation (*saṃbandha*), a relation is postulated—just as eating at night is postulated from the fact that fatness would otherwise be inexplicable—and thus, due to the fear of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), one need not postulate a separate denotative power (*śakti*) for the possessive suffix *matup* with respect to the relation itself, just as it has been postulated for the possessor. Furthermore, since derivative (*yaugika*) words everywhere denote the substance primarily, the application of the section concerning the "Red [Cow]" (*āruṇādhikaraṇa*) becomes logically consistent.

Otherwise, if even by the words *piṅgākṣī* (tawny-eyed) and *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old) the connection itself were denoted primarily, then because qualities such as tawny color, eye-ness, oneness, and one-year-old-ness are incorporeal (*amūrta*), they could not possibly serve as instruments (*karaṇa*) for the act of buying; consequently, the status of being an instrument for the act of buying would not be obtained from this sentence at all. Thus, since there would be no possibility of even suspecting a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) regarding the quality of redness (*āruṇya*), the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) would never arise, and it should be understood that the commencement of such a section (*adhikaraṇa*) would be untenable.

The sense is this: if, because the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) such as *-tva* denotes a relatum, the relation can be understood through that very relatum—provided that the apprehension of the relation is thus established according to the reasoning already stated—then, due to the absence of any other alternative, the reason previously mentioned simply does not exist. As for the phrase "it has been explained in detail": the point is this—that if the relation were not denotable in cases such as *daṇḍī* ("the man with a staff"), then the relation would likewise not be denotable in the case of *daṇḍitvam* ("staff-ness").

Nor should it be argued that the capacity for denoting a relation is postulated for words such as *tvad* (you) in accordance with experience; for rather than postulating a new capacity (*śakti*), one should—just as with the substratum itself—postulate that words like *ini* possess the quality of having a relation as their object within their already established capacity. That is to say, just as the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas), based on the experiential cognition "the person possesses a relation defined by the staff" (*daṇḍa-nirūpita-sambandhavān puruṣaḥ*), have accepted that words like *ini* denote a substance possessing a relation (*sambandhavaddravyavācitva*), so too the Mīmāṃsakas must likewise accept that [words like *tvad*] denote a substance possessing a relation. It is not [otherwise].

[The suffix] denotes only the substance (*dravya*). Thus, since the relation (*sambandha*) is a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by the base *daṇḍin* (‘staff-bearer’), it is that very [relation] which would be denoted by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) following it. Since this assumption allows for the suffix *tva* and others to denote the relation in cases such as *daṇḍitva*, it is cumbersome to postulate a separate primary denotative power (*śakti*) for the suffixes *tva* and so on with respect to the relation.

Others, however, maintain that although words such as *hanti* do not express a relation, words like *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer) are applied only through the cognition of a relation with a staff; thus, since the relation itself serves as the ground for the application of the word (*śabda-pravṛtti-nimitta*), it is possible for suffixes such as *tva* to denote the relation. They assert that in the rule *tasya bhāvaḥ*, the meaning of the term *bhāva* (abstract state) is precisely the ground for the application of the word. This has been explained in detail in the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*. Such is the sense. He raises an objection with "Now [it may be objected]... (*nanu*). [He replies with] "In your view also... (*tavāpi*).

The meaning is: "even for you, the grammarian"; this is the point of disparity. The meaning is that in cases such as *dāmodaratvam* (the state of being Dāmodara) or *ghaṭatvam* (the state of being a pot), the relation is not denoted (*vācya*), whereas in cases such as *daṇḍitvam* (the state of being a staff-bearer), it is denoted; such is the disparity. [The opponent asks] "How?"—in what manner can this be established? To this he replies: "But in our established doctrine (*siddhānta*)... By the rule *tasya bhāvaḥ*, suffixes such as *tva* and *tal* are prescribed in the sense of "state" (*bhāva*). And the referent of the word "state" (*bhāvapadārtha*) is that which serves as the qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by the base (*prakṛti*).

When the inquiry arises as to what constitutes the qualifier (*prakāra*) in a cognition produced by a base (*prakṛti*), two positions have been stated therein; the sense is that, having determined the meaning of the abstract noun (*bhāvapadārtha*) according to those [positions], the suffixes *tva*, *tal*, and so forth, should be prescribed in their respective instances. || 50 ||

Regarding what was stated—that there are two positions concerning the point that "the [meaning] is the qualifier (prakāra) in the cognition produced by the base (prakṛti)"—he says "those two positions" in order to demonstrate them. The phrase "relying on the adjunct (upādhi) in usage" means "an adjunct in the act of usage. When a word such as *ghaṭa* or *paṭa* is to be employed, that which serves as the adjunct—the cause for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—is its meaning; this is the sense. He then asks, "What kind of adjunct is that? and replies, "the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*)."

"In the meaning of the base of suffixes such as *tva* (*tvādipratyayaprakṛtyarthe*)" means in the cognition produced by the base of suffixes such as *tva*. The phrase "having become a qualifier" (*prakāratām*) has the ellipsis "having attained the state of being a qualifier" (*prakāratām āpannam*). "Having resorted to" (*āśritya*) means having resorted to that property which, appearing as a qualifier, constitutes the ground for the application of the word (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*), by virtue of its being the denotable object (*śakyatā*) of suffixes such as *tva*. "They arise" (*jāyante*) means that suffixes such as *tva* and *tal* are prescribed with respect to that property which constitutes the ground for the application of the word and appears as a qualifier in the cognition produced by the base of suffixes such as *tva*.

Now, one might object: since the inclusion of the adjunct (*upādhi*) is already established by the very statement that it "attains the status of a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by the base (*prakṛti*)," for what purpose is it mentioned separately? To this, he says: "It is a qualifier in the cognition produced by the base. And that qualifier is an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) residing in the meaning of the base.

In that context, uniqueness (*asādhāraṇya*) is apprehended as existing in all its own instances while not existing in anything other than itself; by the term "self" (*sva*), individual instances such as a jar or a cloth are to be understood. Thus, because it exists in all jars while not existing in anything other than a jar, "non-jar-ness" (*aghaṭatva*) is the unique property residing in a jar. By the inclusion of the qualifying phrase "while existing in all its own instances" (*nikhilasvavṛttitve sati*), properties such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) do not become unique properties residing in a jar, since substance-ness exists in earth and other substances as well.

Furthermore, because [the term] is used as a qualifier (*viśeṣya*), that "individuality" (*tadvyaktitva*) and so forth do not constitute the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of the jar; for that individuality, by virtue of residing only in that specific individual, lacks the quality of residing in all jars. Therefore, the meaning is that a property expressed by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*)—such as "being" (*tva*) and so forth—is denoted in its unique form. When a word is employed for a certain object based on the cognition of a particular property, that property is the cause (*nimitta*) for the application of that word.

And *dharma*, which serves as the ground for the application of a word (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*), is in some cases a genus (*jāti*), in some cases a quality (*guṇa*), and in some cases an action (*kriyā*). Among these, in cases such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) or "Dāmodara-ness" (*dāmodaratva*), the genus is the referent of the suffix *tva* and so on. Words such as "white" (*śukla*) are denotative of both the quality and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*). In those words like "white" that refer to the quality, the genus residing therein is the ground for the application of the word; thus, in expressions such as "such whiteness" (*tādṛśaśuklatva*), the genus residing in the quality is the referent of the suffix *tva*.

In words such as *śukla* ("white") when they refer to the possessor of a quality (*guṇin*), the quality itself is the basis for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Thus, in expressions such as *tādṛśa-śuklatva* ("that such whiteness"), the universal (*jāti*) residing in the quality is the meaning of the suffix *tva*. In words such as *śukla* when they refer to the possessor of a quality, the quality is the basis for their application; thus, in expressions such as *tādṛśa-śuklatva*, the quality itself is the meaning of the suffix *tva*. In the case of words such as *pācaka* ("cook"), there is a primary denotative power (*śakti*) directed toward the agent who possesses the connection with the act of cooking. The action is the denoted object of the root *pac*; the agent is the denoted object of the suffix *aka*; and the relation is the denoted object of the whole complex. Furthermore, this relation is the relationship between action and its factor (*kriyākārakabhāva*).

And since that very [action] is the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) in such cases as "the state of being a cook" (*pācakatva*), the suffix *tva* and so forth have the sense of a relation (*sambandha*). Thus, the meaning of the statement "a word whose basis for application is an action is an action-word" (*kriyāśabda*) should be understood as "a word whose basis for application is a relation with an action."

[Objection: "In that case, let it be assumed that in words whose basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is a genus (*jāti*), the denotative power (*śakti*) resides in individuals possessing the connection with that genus; likewise, let it be assumed that in words whose basis for application is a quality (*guṇa*), the power resides in things such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) possessing the connection with that quality. Consequently, since in both genus-words and quality-words the relation itself is the basis for application, even in cases such as 'jar-ness' (*ghaṭatva*) or 'whiteness' (*śuklatva*), let the meaning of the suffix *-tva* and so on be the relation itself. [Response: This is not so.

The *pravṛttinimitta* (the ground for the application) is that knowledge by which the application of a word occurs. In the rule [Pāṇini 5.1.119], "tasya bhāvaḥ," the word *bhāva* refers precisely to the ground for the application of a word; and it is clearly stated in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary that the application of a word sometimes arises from the knowledge of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a property, and sometimes from the knowledge of a relation (*saṃbandha*). Thus it is said in the *Laghumañjūṣā*.

In this regard, in cases such as "this Brāhmaṇa" or "the jar is white," because the relation of difference between the universal and the possessor of the universal, or between the quality and the possessor of the quality, is obscured by the worldly-established cognition of non-difference expressed as "this is that," a relation cannot possibly serve as the ground for the application [of the word] there. Therefore, the relation is not denoted by the suffix *tva* and the like. Rather, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) applies to the property—whether a universal or a quality—which serves as the ground for the application of the word.

In the case of words ending in *kṛt* suffixes, since a distinction [between action and its agent] is invariably perceived through the verbal action (*kriyā*), the application of the word occurs precisely through the cognition of that relationship; therefore, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied there alone. However, according to the view that there is both difference and non-difference between the action and its factors (*kāraka*), in the case of words ending in *tiṅ* suffixes—as in the rule "when *yuṣmad* or *asmad* are coreferential with a proximate term"—there is a concealment of the distinction. And in this matter, the very nature of the expressive power of words (*śabdaśaktisvabhāva*) is the underlying cause.

For this very reason, after stating that "the relation [of the base] is denoted by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) following primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*)," Hari cited *pācakatva* as an example. It was previously stated that the phrase "having action as the cause for its application" means "having the relation to action as the cause for its application. Thus, in the statement that "the application of words is fourfold—based on genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and convention (*yadṛcchā*)," the word "action" is an indicator for words whose application is caused by a relation; therefore, there is no deficiency.

Arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*) include names such as *ḍittha*, as well as [verbal roots] like *kv* and [nominal suffixes] like *bh*. Among these, in the case of words like *ḍittha*, which function as designations applied to a single substance, the individual (*vyakti*) alone is the denoted meaning, because there is an absence of both infinity (*ānantya*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Since no understanding of the meaning arises from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone, and since number and so forth appear as qualifiers (*prakāra*) precisely when the word ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*), no indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) arises from it. Nor should it be argued that in cases such as *ḍitthatvam*, since there is no qualifier in the cognition produced by the base (*prakṛti*), the suffix *tva* would be untenable due to the absence of a referent for the suffix-meaning; this is not so.

Because the individual itself appears through two types of objectivity (*viṣayatā*)—namely, as the qualifier (*prakāra*) and as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)—the individual, as delimited by its own status as a qualifier, is precisely what is denoted by suffixes such as *tvā*. Alternatively, in that context, the base word (*prakṛti*) refers to the word-form itself, and the meaning that serves as the qualificand is indeed the referent of suffixes like *tvā*; thus, "being-Ḍittha" (*ḍitthatva*) means "that which is denotable by the word 'Ḍittha'. Consequently, the words "Ḍittha" and "Ḍitthatva" become synonyms.

As for the claim that the universal "Ditthatva" (the property of being Dittha) resides in the body because the body differs according to states such as childhood or youth—that is incorrect due to a lack of evidence. However, in the case of space (*ākāśa*), since there is common worldly usage of distinctions such as "the space of a cloth" or "the space of a hut," a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is established there; this is made clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *tasya bhāvaḥ*. Regarding words such as "ka" and so forth, if one holds that the phonemes "k" and so on are single entities, the word's expressive power (*śakti*) resides in five individual phoneme-manifestations; if one holds they are not single, it resides in five individual phoneme-manifestations belonging to five universals. In the latter case, the universals serve as secondary indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*).

In that case as well, because there is an absence of infinity [of forms], the suffix denoting the abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) applies; thus, *kutva* and the word *ku* are indeed synonyms. However, in the case of words such as *bha*, since there is an infinity of individual instances capable of being denoted—such as *yūṣṇaḥ* and *rājñaḥ* from *yūṣan* and *rājan*—one must rely on a delimiter of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Therefore, the word *bha* itself is the delimiter of the denotable capacity, and that very word is the meaning of the suffixes *tva* and so forth that follow it. It is precisely with this intention that it was stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *vṛddhir ādaic*: "Why does *kutva* not occur [in *rājñaḥ*] by the rule *coḥ kuḥ padasya*? [The answer is: "Because it is a *bha*."

"What is meant by the term *bha*? By this, it is clearly stated that the terms *kutva* and *kupada*, as well as the terms *bhatva* and *bhasaṃjñā*, are synonyms. And thus, this is the response to the objection raised by the Mīmāṃsakas against the Grammarians—namely, "How is there such a discrepancy even in your own system?": In the rule *tasya bhāvaḥ*, the word *bhāva* refers to a property (*dharma*) which serves as the ground for the application of a word (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*), appearing as the qualifier (*prakāratayā*) in the cognition produced by the base form (*prakṛti*).

The application of a word occurs sometimes from the knowledge of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a property (*dharma*) and sometimes from the knowledge of its relation (*saṃbandha*). Thus, in cases such as *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness) or *dāmodaratva* (Dāmodara-hood), since no relation is apprehended, the abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) such as *-tva* and *-tā* denote the property that serves as the ground for the application of the word (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*), namely the universal (*jāti*). However, in cases such as *pācakatva* (cook-ness) or *daṇḍitva* (staff-bearer-ness), because a relation is apprehended, the abstract suffix denotes the relation itself; this is the intended meaning.

Now, if it is argued that by the term "bhāva" (abstract property) is meant a property serving as the ground for the application of a word (*śabda-pravṛtti-nimitta*), which appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by the base of suffixes such as *tva* and so on—then, since even "pot-ness-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*) and the like appear as qualifiers, the suffix *tva* following the word "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) would also have to have "pot-ness" itself as its denotation. With this intention, he raises an objection starting with "nanu" (now, surely), using the phrase "because of being a qualifier."

Although the word "pot" (ghaṭa) expresses the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), namely "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), by means of that very word—since it is said that the word "pot" has its denotative power (*śakti*) in the pot as delimited by pot-ness—nevertheless, it is expressed by the word "pot" as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). This is because we experience from the word "pot" a cognition in which the pot is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and pot-ness is the qualifier (*prakāra*). However, for the sake of a cognition [of it] as the qualificandum, that very same delimitor of denotability is denoted by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), such as *-tva*.

According to the maxim that "between the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix, the meaning of the suffix is predominant," in expressions such as *ghaṭatvam* (pot-ness), the suffix *tva* expresses that [meaning] as the primary element; thus, it is logical that the abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) such as *tva* are prescribed for the delimitors of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

When there is a desire to employ a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) for the word "ghaṭatva" (pot-ness), such as *tva* or *tal*, the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)—namely, *ghaṭatvatva* (the nature of pot-ness)—must be expressed. Although that [delimitor] is already expressed by the word "ghaṭatva" itself, it is expressed therein only as a qualifier; therefore, for the sake of cognition as the primary object, that very same thing must be denoted again by the suffix *tva*. Thus, it should be understood that the property appearing as the qualifier in the cognition produced by the base is precisely *ghaṭatvatva*, the delimitor of the denotable capacity.

However, the status of that [ghaṭatvatva] as the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*) is not accepted; for when a simpler [property] is possible, there is an absence of that [complex one]. The meaning of this is: when it is possible to postulate the status of being a delimitor for a simpler property, one should not postulate the status of being a delimitor for a complex property, due to the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*).

For this very reason, in the case of the cognition "this possesses the absence of a knowable fire" (*prameyavahnayabhāvavān*), the Naiyāyikas—on account of parsimony (*laghutva*)—abandon the property of being a knowable fire (*prameyavahnitva*) as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absence, and instead accept a property co-extensive with it, namely the nature of fire (*vahnitva*), as the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of the absence.

Even if this were so, if one were to accept that the property of being a "heavy duty" (*gurudharma*) is the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*), that would be incorrect because it contradicts established logic (*nyāyaviruddhatva*). Since the property of being "pot-ness-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*) lacks the status of being a delimitor of denotability, it is impossible for it to be the denotability residing in the suffix following the word "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Thus, by the phrase "there would be denotability," the undesirable consequence of such denotability is indicated.

Although there is complexity (gaurava) in postulating that "potness-ness" (ghaṭatvatva) is the delimitor of the denotability (śakyatāvacchedaka), this is nonetheless swallowed by the acceptance of what is desired; thus he says, "merely a property" (dharmamātram iti). A mere property, such as "cowness" (gotva) or "cowness-ness" (gotvatva), is denoted by abstract suffixes (bhāvapratyaya) like *tva* in the form of "property-ness" (dharmitva), but not in its specific individual forms, because that would entail an infinite number of denotative powers (śakti).

Others, however, maintain that since the universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*) is a property residing in a substance such as a cow, and the quality such as "blueness" (*nīla*) is a property residing in a substance such as a jar, and likewise the action such as "cooking" (*pāka*) is a property residing in a substance such as Caitra—since it is possible for there to be a single expressive power based on the commonality of these universals, qualities, and actions being properties residing in substances—it would be more cumbersome to postulate three separate powers for the three categories of universals and so forth; therefore, let the abstract suffixes (*tva*, etc. denote universals and the like by way of their nature as properties (*dharmitva*).

And thus, there is no infinity of powers (*śakti*). Furthermore, that property (*dharma*) such as "genus" (*jāti*) which resides in a substance is called "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) because, while not occurring in any substance other than those capable [of being denoted], it occurs in all substances capable [of being denoted]. Similarly, a property such as "cowness-ness" (*gotvatva*) is also called "uncommon" because it resides in a substance through a mediated relation (*paramparayā*). Thus, they maintain that in cases such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) or "pot-ness-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*), the cognition is that the uncommon property residing in the pot and so forth is [the object of the suffix].

The meaning is that a mere property (*dharmamātra*) which has attained the status of a qualifier (*prakāratā*) with respect to the meaning of the base of suffixes such as *tv-* is held to be what is expressed by the abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) such as *tva-*. By the phrase "mere property of the entire referent" (*kṛtsnārthakamātraśabdena*), there is an inclusion of both types of properties that serve as the delimiters of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka-dharma*).

The point is this: whether the property that delimits the possibility (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is heavy or light, it does not matter; one cannot make a distinction there because of the capacity of the word's denotation (*śaktigraha*). This is because, by accepting that "possessing a conch-like neck" (*kambugrīvādimattva*) is the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) in the cognition "there is no [thing] possessing a conch-like neck," there is no obstacle to accepting even a heavy property as a delimitor. Thus he says: "But here there is no consideration of light or heavy."

In reality, however, there is no complexity at all in postulating the state of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) within the property of the Guru; thus he says: "tattadvya-kti... (with respect to each particular individual). Just as a snake is [superimposed] upon a rope, so too, through the superimposition of the entire world upon Brahman, it is the existence of Brahman alone that shines forth everywhere. And that existence of Brahman, being delimited by specific individuals such as cows, jars, and so forth, becomes the object of linguistic usage in the form of "cowness," "jarhood," "the nature of cowness," "the nature of jarhood," and so on. As it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*: "Due to the difference of related entities (*saṃbandhibhedāt*)."

The universal (*jāti*) is said to be that very *brahman*-existence which resides in individual cows and the like—the substrata of properties such as "cowness"—which, though distinct due to the difference between those individuals, appears as if divided by its presence in all cows while simultaneously not residing in non-cows. The meaning is that all words are established as denotative with respect to that existence, which is expressed by the term "universal. This view is favorable to the position of those who maintain that the universal is the word-meaning (*padārtha*).

He clarifies that the very existence of Brahman (brahmasatta) is what is denoted by all words with the words "tām" (that). The meaning is: "the existence of Brahman as qualified by this or that particular individual. They declare it to be the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha), the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), and action (kriyā)—that is to say, they describe it according to the logic of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* [of the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtras]. It is eternal, being devoid of modifications such as origination and destruction; for this very reason, that same existence is called the "Great Self" (mahān ātmā), and the suffixes expressing abstract state (bhāvapratyaya), such as *-tva* and *-tal*, denote it—this is the construction.

The sense is this: since all phenomena (*dharmas*) consist of the reality of Brahman (*brahmasattā*), and since that reality of Brahman is eternal, there is no occasion for considering their relative weight or lightness. Regarding the fact that a *dharma*—which serves as the ground for the application of a word—is expressed by abstract suffixes such as *-tva* and *-tal*, he cites the consensus of the author of the *Vārttika* with the words "And it has been said," etc. He restates what was stated by the authors of the *Vārttika* in the rule *tasya bhāvastvatalau* (Pāṇini 5.1.119) with the passage beginning "Of which quality... and ending with "...the suffixes -tva and -tal. [He says: "Of which quality... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.]

In this context, the word *guṇa* (quality) does not refer to qualities such as color (*rūpa*) or taste (*rasa*), but rather intends to mean "that which assists" (*upakāraka*). With this intention, he says: "appearing as a qualifier. And Kaiyaṭa has stated: "By the word *guṇa*, whatever differentiator dependent on another—be it a genus (*jāti*) or anything else—is all included here. Thus, in the present instance, the word *guṇa* means, in effect, that which expresses a subordinate meaning (*upasarjana-bhūta-artha*). He explains the meaning of the word *bhāvāt* (from existence) as "because of being the substratum" (*āśrayatvāt*). He states the meaning of the word *dravye* (in the substance) as "the qualificand" (*viśeṣya*).

He explains "the application of a word" (*śabdaniveśa*) as "the operation of a word" (*śabdapravṛtti*). The meaning is: that genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which is subordinate, and having placed which before it, a word proceeds to denote an object. "In that [object] being denoted" (*tasmin vācye*) means: when such an object—the genus and so forth—which has become a qualifier, is the thing to be expressed. "The suffixes *tva* and *tal*"—the ellipsis is that the suffixes *tva*, *tal*, and others are *bhāva*-suffixes (denoting abstract states).

And so, among words such as *jāti* (genus) and others, he demonstrates which suffix, such as *tva*, is applied to which meaning by saying "tathā ca" (and thus). Regarding "rūpādi" (form, etc.): by the word "etc.," there is the inclusion of taste, smell, and so forth, as well as qualities like white and the like. Regarding "jātāv" (in the genus): the meaning is "in the genus such as *rūpatva* (form-ness) and *śuklatva* (whiteness). The remainder of the sentence is that "the suffix *tva* and others [function] as *bhāvapratyaya*s (abstracting suffixes). Regarding "guṇe" (in the quality): the meaning is "as a quality, [the suffix is applied] after words like 'white' that refer to the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*). However, it should be understood that when those [words] refer to the quality itself, [the suffix is applied] "in the genus."

Words such as *aṇu* (minute) and so forth always refer primarily to the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*); therefore, from these words, the abstract suffix *tva* and others denote only the quality that is the measure (*parimāṇa*). Measure is of four kinds—minute, large, long, and short—and it should be understood that the meaning is that the fourfold measure, such as minuteness (*aṇutva*) and so on, resides in objects such as the minute and the like. Regarding the phrase "from *pācaka* and so forth": it should be understood that from action-words (*kriyāśabda*), the abstract suffix *tva* and others occur in the sense of the action, whereas from genus-words (*jātiśabda*) such as *ghaṭa* (pot), they occur in the sense of the genus. Regarding the phrase "of words such as *rūpa* (color/form) and so forth": [the abstract suffix occurs in the sense of the quality].

The point is this: since words such as *rūpa* (form) generate a cognition whose qualifier (*prakāra*) is the universal (*jāti*), the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied to them to denote that universal. Regarding the example "cook" (*pācaka*) and so forth: when words denoting action generate a cognition of an action as the qualifier of its substratum—such as "Caitra is the locus of the act of cooking"—the abstract suffix is applied to those action-words to denote the action itself. [Regarding the phrase] "having a relation as its qualifier" (*saṃsargaprakāraka*).

The sense is this: since a distinction is invariably perceived through action in words ending in *kṛt* suffixes—given that in cases such as *pācaka* ("cook"), one experiences a cognition whose mode is a relation, namely "Devadatta is one who possesses a connection with the act of cooking"—the application of words like *pācaka* arises solely from the knowledge of the relationship between action and its factors (*kāraka*). Thus, for those who maintain that a word generates a cognition whose mode is a relation (*saṃsarga*), the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) after verbal roots denotes precisely that relation. This [view] is easily established.

The intention is that there is no restrictive rule stating that suffixes such as *tva* (denoting abstract properties) apply only to genus (*jāti*). In this context—among those words ending in abstract suffixes that denote genus and so forth—he states an alternative position: "of those denoting genus," meaning "of words such as *ghaṭatva*. This amounts to saying: "primarily of those denoting genus."

Although words such as *ghaṭa* (pot) are also denoters of universals (*jāti*), nevertheless they do not denote the universal primarily; rather, the sense is that they do so as a qualifier (*prakāra*). And thus, the phrase "of those denoting universals" results in the meaning: "of the abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) such as *-tva*, which denote universals primarily. [The conclusion is: "only the individuals" [are denoted by the suffixes]. That is to say, the abstract suffixes such as *-tva* are the denoters (*śakta*), while the universal is the denotable object (*śakya*) of such abstract suffixes.

The delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) for such a genus (*jāti*) as "pot-ness" is not "pot-ness-ness" (*ghaṭatvatva*) and so forth; rather, because they are present [in cognition], the individual entities (*vyakti*) such as pots, which are denoted by the base (*prakṛti*) of the suffixes *tva* and *tal*, themselves become the delimiters of denotability. The meaning is that the genus "pot-ness," which consists of the existence of Brahman (*brahmasattā*), is the denotable object (*śakya*) of the word "pot-ness"; denotability resides in it, but the delimiter of such denotability is indeed the individual pot-entity itself. This is because of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that the differentiation of the existence of Brahman occurs only through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the form of individual entities.

Objection: Is it not observed everywhere that only that which resides in the denotable (śakya) possesses the status of being the delimitor of denotability (śakyatāvacchedakatva)? For example, the individual cow is the denotable, and the "cowness" residing in it is the delimitor of its denotability. This is because [the property] does not reside in anything other than itself, while residing in all its own instances; thus, by taking the word "self" (*sva*) to refer to the individual cow, the definition is consistent. If it is argued: "Since a universal (*jāti*) resides in individuals, but individuals do not reside in a universal, how can individuals be the delimiters of the universal?"—we say no.

Since there is no evidence that only that which is the denotatum (śakya) can be the delimitor of denotability (śakyatāvacchedaka), and since there is no obstacle to that which has the denotatum as its locus also being the delimitor of denotability, the point is this: it is easily stated that individuals are the delimiters of the universal (jāti) through the relation of "being contained" (ādheyatā), which consists in residing in all [the individuals] while not residing in anything other than itself. Here, by the term "self" (sva), the individual is to be understood.

It should be noted that this alternative view is stated in consideration of what was previously asserted regarding words denoting universals—such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and the like—where *ghaṭatvatva* (the property of being pot-ness) was said to be the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Having thus explained the meaning of the suffix *tva* and others for each of the four types of words—namely those denoting universals, qualities, and so forth—he states the resulting verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) with the words "And so... (*tathā ca*).

In the expression "ghaṭatvam" (potness), with the intention that the property of potness—the meaning of the base—attains the status of an uncommon property because it functions as a qualifier through the relation of being inherent in all its own instances while not being inherent in anything other than itself, he says: "the cognition is that 'it is an uncommon property residing in a pot'. The sense is that the cognition occurs by way of its being an uncommon property, and not by way of its being a genus (*jāti*) or the like.

Since from the word "ghaṭa," which denotes a genus, there arises the cognition "the jar is delimited by jar-ness" (ghaṭatvāvacchinnaḥ) with jar-ness appearing as a qualifier (prakāratayā), the abstract suffix -tva and so forth apply precisely to that [jar-ness]. However, the intention is that the cognition of jar-ness is not desired as being in the form of a specific particular (viśeṣa-rūpa) consisting of jar-ness itself, nor in the form of a universal (sāmānya-rūpa) consisting of the genus, but rather as an uncommon property (asādhāraṇadharma-rūpa); with this in mind, he says: "The cognition is that 'it is an uncommon property residing in the jar'."

Regarding the term "bodha" (cognition), the phrase "from the word *ghaṭatva*" (*ghaṭatvaśabdāt*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
