When there is a desire to employ a second abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) after the word *ghaṭatva*, the individual jar (*ghaṭavyakti*) serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the universal of jar-ness (*ghaṭatvajāti*), which is the primary meaning expressed by that abstract suffix. Thus, the second abstract suffix occurs precisely with respect to that [individual]. Consequently, it should be understood that because the meaning of *ghaṭatvatva* is the individual jar, the individual jar is cognized as the primary referent.

Regarding what was stated—“But listen to the two positions established in our own system (siddhānta) concerning [words like] *tvad* and so forth”—the author says “another position” (*pakṣāntaram*) with the intention of stating the second position. The meaning is that since the word itself appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by the base form (*prakṛti*), just like a genus (*jāti*) or a quality (*guṇa*), it is precisely that specific word which is denoted by the abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) such as *-tva*; this is the "other position. He explains that the word *yadvā* occurring in the verse is intended to indicate the *vārttika* containing the word *yadvā*, saying: "it also has the purpose of indicating that [vārttika]."

The meaning is that it has as its purpose (*sūcanam*) the indication of that *vārttika* which contains the words "or else" (*yadvā*). The word "api" (also) includes the previously mentioned position that the uncommon property residing in jars and so forth is denoted by the suffix *tv*. He restates the *vārttika* containing the words "or else" as: "Or else, all entities... By the statement "because of the utterance of the *vārttika*," it is indicated that this position is approved by the author of the *vārttika*; thus, not even a suspicion of lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) should be entertained here.

He states the commentary on the *Vārttika* as expressed in the *Bṛhadbhūṣaṇa*: "They signify" (*vanti*). "By way of denotation" (*vācakatvena*) means by the relation of being a denoter (*vācakatā-sambandhena*). To the word "they function" (*pravartante*), the phrase "toward objects" (*artheṣu*) is to be supplied. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *bhū* here has the sense of "functioning. And "functioning" here takes the form of usage. Thus, the meaning is: "those entities which are used toward objects by way of denotation"—therefore, he says that the word *bhāva* here signifies "words," stating "the *bhāvas* are words. "By their own meaning" (*svenārthena*).

"In its own object," is the meaning. He states the meaning of the word "bhavanti" (they exist) as "pravartante" (they function). And thus, all words exist by means of their own expressed object; that is to say, they function therein as denoters. For since words are employed solely for the purpose of conveying an object, the sense is that the third case ending (*svenārthena*) is used with the intention of expressing the object's status as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the functioning of the word. Furthermore, the object which serves as the basis (*nimitta*) for the functioning of a word is of two kinds.

The denotable object (*vācya*) and the ground for the application of the word (*pravṛttinimitta*) [are to be distinguished]. The denotable object is either a substance (*dravya*) or a word (*śabda*). As for the ground for the application of the word: in the case of genus-words such as "pot" or "cloth," it is the genus (*jāti*) such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*); in words such as "cook" (*pācaka*), it is the action (*kriyā*); in words such as "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*), it is the relation (*saṃbandha*); and in proper names such as "Dittha," it is the name (*saṃjñā*)—all of this is to be understood in accordance with experience. Regarding the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*): the meaning is that because there exists an object in the form of a substance, a word, a genus, and so forth, which serves as the cause for the application of a word, for that reason. Regarding the word "that" (*sa*): [it refers to the aforementioned object].

The meaning is that the "object" (artha) consists of substance, word, genus, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of them" (teṣām), the meaning is "of all words. Regarding the term "state" (bhāva), the meaning is "the ground for the application [of a word]" (pravṛttinimitta); such is the collective sense. And thus, since a word itself serves as the ground for the application of another word—just like a genus and the rest—a word also becomes the ground for the application of a word. In the *Sāra*, however, with the intention that in the expression "by its own object" (*svenārthena*), the word "own" (*sva*) denotes the self (*ātman*) and not what belongs to oneself (*ātmīya*), it was stated: "by its own form" (*svena rūpeṇa*).

The own form (*svarūpa*) of a word is the word itself, not its meaning, because that [meaning] belongs to it [as an external object]. Thus, it has been explained that words function as denoters with respect to their own forms—that is, with respect to the meaning which consists of the word's own form. In accordance with this, regarding the expression "their state" (*teṣāṃ bhāvaḥ*), it is stated that "that" refers to the meaning consisting of the word's own form; "of them" means "of the words"; and "state" means the ground for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*).

The point is that by this, it has been clearly stated that for all words, the word itself is the ground for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Now, one might ask: how can a word be the ground for its own application? For it is only a qualifier (*prakāra*)—that is, a property as determined by the denoted object—that serves as the ground for application. For example, the denoted object of the word "jar" is an entity possessing a neck with a conch-like shape; since the "jarness" (*ghaṭatva*) resides in the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) as determined by the subjecthood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in that [object], jarness alone is the ground for the application of the word "jar. To dispel this doubt, he says: "This is the meaning," and so forth.

In cases such as "the jar," "the cloth," "white," and "cook," since it is established by universal experience that universals (jāti), qualities (guṇa), and actions (kriyā) possess a modehood (prakāratā) relative to substances (dravya) like jars, one may, by an analogous reasoning, establish that words also possess a modehood relative to substances. To this end, he says: "like the meaning" (arthavat). This means "like the meanings such as universals."

Just as it is well known from common examples that an object such as "birth" (*jāti*) and so forth is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) defined by a substance (*dravya*), so too is the word itself a qualifier defined by a substance. To provide a well-known example of this, he says: "Hari, Hara, Nala... [and so on]. Regarding the phrase "from words": the meaning is "from words beginning with 'Hari' and ending with 'Vaśiṣṭha'. [The phrase] "there was someone denoted by each of those" means...

Since words such as *hari* (lion/green) do not fall within the range of the senses, there is an absence of sense-object contact; consequently, because the specific form of "greenness" (*haritva*) and so forth is not presented, there is no apprehension of the word's denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to that which is delimited by the specific property of greenness. Thus, since it is impossible for there to be a verbal cognition having "greenness" as its qualifier, it must be admitted that the cognition occurs only in a general form. This is because there exists a grasp of the denotative power in the form of a general inference: "This word *hari*, *hara*, *nala*, etc., possesses a denotative power somewhere, because it is a correct word."

The point is this: when an object is presented in a general way and there is a requirement for a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), since other [qualifiers] such as "tawny-ness" (*haritva*) are impossible, one must accept that the word itself which has been presented serves as the qualifier. Thus, a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) must be admitted in which the word is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the general object is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), in the form: "There was some object denoted by the word 'tawny' (*hari*)," and so on. The phrase "otherwise" (*anyathā*) means: if one does not accept the word as the qualifier of the object.

Because there is proximity for villagers due to forest herbs being within the range of their senses, it is possible for them to grasp the word-potency (*śakti*) with the delimitor of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) as the qualifier; therefore, the term "city-dwellers" (*nāgarika*) was used. The implication is that for city-dwellers, since there is generally no such proximity, it is impossible to grasp the potency with the universal (*jāti*) as the qualifier, and thus they cannot know the forest herbs in their specific forms. The mention of "city-dwellers" refers to those who are ignorant of the specific forms; consequently, there is no contradiction even if some particular city-dweller should have knowledge of them in their specific form.

"Because it would result in a lack of cognition. This means that due to the absence of a grasp of the word's denotative power (*śakti*) in its specific form, words such as *kākajaṅghā*, *ākhuparṇī*, and *aśvakarṇa*—which are conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for specific medicinal plants—would not produce cognition [of their referents]. However, if one accepts that the word has a substance (*dravya*) as its qualifier (*prakāra*), then there is indeed the production of a general cognition of the object in the form: "There is some particular medicinal plant denoted by the word *aśvakarṇa*," and so forth. This is the intended meaning. "In this very way" [refers to the following].

"It has the form 'denotable by this word' (etad-padavācya), meaning that it has the word as its qualifier (padaprakāraka). It does not, however, have the form of those respective universals (jāti) and so forth; that is to say, it does not have specific forms such as 'pot-ness' (ghaṭatva) or 'cloth-ness' (paṭatva). He states the consequence of accepting a cognition where the word is the qualifier: "And thus, both [are the denotable]" (tathā cobhayam). This means that both the universal and so forth, as well as the word, are the delimiters of the denotable (śakyāvacchedaka).

In this context, it should be understood that for a word, the state of being the delimitor of the denotable (śakyatāvacchedakatva) occurs through the relation of power (śakti), whereas for a genus (jāti) and so forth, it occurs through relations such as inherence (samavāya), as appropriate. "Of whom" refers to the person. "Thus, the apprehension of power" means that the apprehension of power has occurred in the form of specific universals (jāti) and so forth, such as "pot-ness" or "cloth-ness. "Of him" refers to that person. Regarding "the genus and so forth," the meaning is that since the presentation of the object occurs only in the form of specific universals and so forth, the cognition also occurs only in that specific form. "Having the word as its qualifier" (padaprakāraka).

"Is not required in its specific form" means that it is not required in its specific forms such as "pot-ness," "cloth-ness," and so forth. Although, in the phrase *svenārthena*, the word *sva* does not denote "one's own" but rather "self," and thus—following Sāri’s commentary which maintains that all entities and all words function by their own form, i.e., by the form of the word as the object—it follows that the word itself is the ground for the application of all words; nevertheless, for a person who has grasped the expressive power [of a word] in its specific forms such as "pot-ness" and so on...

Since the cognition of a jar as qualified by "jar-ness" (ghaṭatva) arising from words such as "jar" is established by experience and is universal among all people, it is impossible to deny it; furthermore, in cases involving words with well-known meanings, a cognition having the word itself as its qualifier is generally not experienced. Therefore, even in the view that follows Śarīraka’s commentary, one must accept that universals (jāti) and so forth are the grounds for the application of words (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*). The point is that it is only in cases of words with unfamiliar meanings that a cognition having the word as its qualifier is generally observed.

Now, if the apprehension of the word’s expressive power (*śaktigraha*) does not require [the object] in its specific form, then in what form is it required? To this he says: "But rather... (*kiṃtviti*). "In such a form" (*ityādirūpa eva*) means: in the form "there is some object denoted by this word"; that is to say, it is required in the form of a universal, namely "being denotable by this word. "Not grasped specifically" (*viśiṣyāgṛhītā*) means: those whose expressive power has not been grasped in specific forms such as "Nala-ness" (*nalatva*); [this refers to] words such as "Nala" and so on. "In that very same way" (*tathaiva*).

The meaning is that [the word] has only the word as its qualifier (*prakāraka*). The sense is that because there is a grasp of the expressive power (*śakti*) of words such as "Nala" by way of their being denotable by those words—namely, the general cognition that "there is some object denoted by the word Nala"—there is a difference in the resulting cognition due to this difference in the grasp of expressive power. "And so" (*tathā ca*): the meaning is "and when the word is a qualifier in the cognition produced by the stem. "In the word as well" (*śabdo 'pi*): the particle *api* includes universals (*jāti*) and so forth. "The meaning of the suffix *-tva*" (*tvapratyayārtha*): [this refers to the abstract property of being a word].

The meaning is that the word and [the categories] such as genus (*jāti*) are the objects denoted by abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) such as *tva* and *tal*. However, according to others, for those who hold that the word itself is the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), the word is the meaning of the abstract suffixes like *tva*; whereas for those who hold that the object consisting of genus and so forth is the ground for application, they say that genus and so forth are the meaning of *tva* and the other suffixes.

Others, however, explain the meaning of the Vārttika passage beginning with “Or rather, all things (*bhāvāḥ*) exist by means of their own object (*svārthena*”) as follows: here, the word *sva-* refers to "one's own" (*ātmīya*), and not to "self" (*ātman*). A word has two kinds of meanings: the denoted object (*vācya*), such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), and the form of the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). When either of these is expressed, the suffix *-tva* (or *-tā*) is used to denote the abstract state (*bhāva*). Of these, the latter occurs in cases such as *ghaṭatvam* ("jar-ness"). In that instance, the base (*prakṛti*) refers exclusively to the object; for it is possible for the object—the jar and so forth—to be construed with the meaning of the suffix, which consists of the universal (*jāti*) and the like.

In examples such as *ḍitthatvam*, the first [type of bhāva-pratyaya] applies. Therein, because the meaning of the suffix would otherwise be untenable, the base (*prakṛti*) refers solely to the word-form; from the word *kuta-* and others, which refer to the word-form, the bhāva-suffixes such as *-tva* arise to denote the object in its specific individual form (*vyakti-rūpa*). Thus, there is synonymy between *ḍitthatva* and the word *ḍittha*, and between *kutva* and the word *ku*. It has been stated that the relationship between the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix is the denotable power (*śakya*) of the entire aggregate consisting of the beginning and the end [of the word]. "It has been elaborated" means it was explained in detail in the *Bṛhad-bhūṣaṇa*. || 51 ||

Thus ends the determination of the meaning of abstract suffixes (bhāvapratyaya) such as *tva* and others, in the *Śāṅkarī*, a commentary on the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, composed by Śaṅkara, the son of Raṅgabhaṭṭa;
in this exposition, the determination of the meaning of *tva* and other suffixes is complete. (9)
Now follows the determination of the meanings of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) such as those denoting deities (*devatā*) and so forth.

In the context of determining the meaning of abstract (bhāva) taddhita suffixes such as *tva* and *tal*, he also defines the meanings of other taddhita suffixes denoting deities (*devatā*) and so forth that have been traditionally recorded, beginning with the rule: "That is its deity" (*sā'sya devatā*). If it is asked: "What is the reason for disregarding the taddhita suffixes denoting offspring (*apatya*), which were mentioned first, and instead taking care to determine the meaning of the taddhita suffixes denoting deities?"—the answer is as follows:

In the case of the expression *tasyāpatyam* ("his offspring"), because the meaning of the suffix—namely, the offspring—is singular, and because it is easy to understand that the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) functions as a qualifier (*prakāratā*) toward the meaning of the suffix (the offspring) through a relation such as the relationship between the produced and the producer (*janyajanakabhāva*), there is no doubt in that regard, and thus no need for a formal determination. However, it should be understood that in the case of *taddhita* suffixes denoting a deity (*devatā*), since various alternative views are possible, the primacy of the suffix-meaning and the way the base-meaning functions as its qualifier are difficult to ascertain; therefore, a careful determination of that meaning is undertaken.

"The object to be given (*deyam*) is qualified by the deity (*devatāviśiṣṭam*). This means that the meaning of the suffix denoting the deity is "the object to be given" as qualified by the deity, either through the relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*), or through the relationship of being the object of a renunciation (*tyāga*) directed toward oneself. In this context, the "object to be given" is the meaning of the suffix precisely as a related entity (*saṃbandhitvena*). The point is that in the expression *asya* ("of this"), by reversing the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, the meaning of the pronoun *asya* signifies a related entity, because the meaning of the genitive case—the relationship—is subordinate to the primary sense of the stem *idam*.

The phrase "it is to be given" (*deyam*) is also an elliptical reference to the mantra. By means of words such as *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) and so forth, the specific nature of that very object to be given—which has already been cognized as being connected [to the action]—is provided. Consequently, the meaning is either: "the object to be given is that which possesses a relation of ownership (*svatva*) defined by a lordship (*svāmitā*) residing in a deity non-different from Indra," or "the object to be given is that which possesses a relation of being the object (*karmatva*) defined by a renunciation (*tyāga*) directed toward a deity non-different from Indra. In this manner, there is a general cognition of the connection with the deity non-different from Indra.

Regarding the nature of a deity (*devatātva*): according to the commentary on the *sūtra* "devāt tal" (Pāṇini 5.4.27), which states that a deity is so called because of its sovereignty over divine actions, a deity is that which is the object of a sacrifice performed with a mantra—specifically, that which is intended as the recipient of the offering and is the locus of the fruit other than heaven produced by that act, and which is praised by the mantra. This is also stated in the *Anukramaṇikā*: "He whose [name] is in the verse is the seer (*ṛṣi*); that which is expressed by it is the deity. For this very reason, both types of usage are established: "a mantra addressed to Indra" (*aindro mantra*) and "an oblation for Indra" (*aindraṃ haviḥ*).

It should be understood that this result consists precisely of the desire (pīti) in the form "May this fruit belong to the deity" or "May this fruit be for the deity. Now, one might object: since in cases such as *aindra* and *vaiśvadeva*, Indra and the others are invariably deities, the meaning of the deity is already obtained from the words *indra* and so on themselves; therefore, what is the purpose of describing the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix as having a power (*śakti*) whose meaning includes the deity? To this, he says: "by other [means] that bring about the cognition of deityhood" (*devatātvopasthāpakāntara*).

Even though the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) is never absent in Indra and the other [deities], from the word "Indra" alone, there arises a presentation of Indra and the others solely in the form of "Indra-ness" (*indratva*), and not in the form of "deity-ness. However, if one postulates a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) in the sense of a deity, then because Indra and the others are construed non-differently with the meaning of "deity," there arises a cognition that "the deity is non-different from Indra"; thus, Indra and the others are presented in the form of "deity-ness" as co-located with "Indra-ness. This is just as earth and the other [elements] are presented, but not in the form of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*).

The point is this: if one were to say "the substance [consisting of] earth and so forth" (*pṛthivyādidravyam*), because earth and the others would be construed as non-different from the substance, there would arise the cognition that "the substance is non-different from earth and so forth. Consequently, it would be necessary to assume a *taddhita* suffix’s denotative power (*śakti*) by internalizing the deity within the meaning of "earth" and the other terms. To support this assumption of the *taddhita* suffix’s power through the inclusion of the deity, he cites the consensus of the Mīmāṃsakas with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). This means: precisely because a *taddhita* suffix derived from a deity-name has the sense of "that which is to be given (*deya*) in relation to the deity."

"This is the statement of the author of the *Tantravārttika*: 'The curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) is connected with a deity. In the expression *vaiśvadevī āmikṣā*, the word *vaiśvadeva* is established by adding the suffix *aṇ* according to Pāṇini’s rule *sā'sya devatā* [4.2.24], which prescribes that suffix in the sense of a pronoun (meaning "this belongs to it"), and then adding the feminine suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*. In this context, since pronouns generally denote the specific object presented [in the mind], the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) prescribed in their sense also denotes a qualifier."

And thus, the meaning is this: the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) in the word *vaiśvadevī* indeed conveys even the specific object consisting of curd-mixture (*ikṣu*) associated with the deity. By the use of the particle *eva* (indeed) connected with the verb "it expresses" (*vadati*), there is an exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*); therefore, the sense is that it is not the case that it never conveys the specific meaning. Consequently, a specific qualification is obtained in the form of strengthening the contextual meaning.

Although that deity is the qualified meaning of the suffix in the sense of "this belongs to her," nevertheless, because the deity is perceived there as a qualifier for the referent of the pronoun "this" (asya), the primary status in the meaning of the secondary derivative (taddhita) belongs to the referent of the pronoun itself. Alternatively, the suffixes such as *aṇ* may occur after a word in the nominative case (*sā*) in the sense of "this belongs to her" (*asya*), provided that which is in the nominative case is a deity; in this connection, the word "deity" (*devatā*) serves to indicate the base form (*prakṛti*). However, the meaning of the suffix is simply "this belongs to" (*asya*). This is according to the opinion of the ancients.

Regarding the phrase "the word *āmikṣā*": "of that very [suffix]" means of that very taddhita suffix. "The presentation of the object" means that a specific object in the form of *āmikṣā* is presented. The sense is this: when there is a desire to know what specific object is denoted by the word *vaiśvadevī*, it is understood from the proximity of the word *āmikṣā* that the specific object is of the nature of *āmikṣā*. However, that specific object is not restricted to being "this particular thing"; rather, the comprehension of a restricted specific meaning arises from that taddhita suffix itself.

In this regard, the proximity of the word *āmikṣā* functions as a cooperative factor. Thus, one should not be deluded into thinking that while the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix conveys only the general meaning, the cognition of the specific [meaning] arises solely from the word *āmikṣā*. For the intended sense is that although the word *āmikṣā* itself expresses a meaning that is inherently specific, it brings about definiteness within the meaning of the secondary derivative, which otherwise would be of an indefinite particular form. [The phrase] "from the word alone" [is used].

The meaning is as follows: a taddhita suffix denoting a deity, which arises—that is, appears—after the word *agni* when that word is devoid of proximity to words such as *soma*, is incapable of conveying the object to be given as intended for a deity consisting of *agni* joined with another [deity] such as *soma*. Since it is stated that "that which is dependent [on another] is as if incapable," the taddhita formation in expressions such as *āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ* would not even occur due to this lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*).

By the statement "not joined with another [deity], having Agni as its deity," and so forth, it is indicated that [the suffix] is capable of establishing a deity that is exclusively Agni. Furthermore, bearing in mind the intention that this is also the consensus of Mīmāṃsakas such as the author of the Tantravārttika—that the meaning of a taddhita suffix denoting a deity is the object to be given (deya) as qualified by that deity—he says: "of one part of the meaning of the suffix. And here, non-difference is the relation (*saṃsarga*). [He says] "of the meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyartha*).

The meaning is that the referent of the base (*prakṛti*), such as Indra and so forth—characterized by attributes like "thousand-eyed"—is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for one part of the meaning of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*), namely the deity-form, which constitutes the object to be given as distinguished by the deity. The sense is that the referent of the base, Indra and so forth, possesses the quality of being a qualifier relative to the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the referent of the word "deity. Thus, Indra and so forth are the qualifier and the referent of the word "deity" is the qualificand. To the question of by what relation that qualifier is connected, he says: "And here there is non-difference (*abheda*)."

The meaning is that the sense of the base (prakṛti) is a qualifier of the deity through a relation of non-difference (*abheda*). Now, one might object: "But it is not possible for the sense of the base, such as *agni*, to be construed with the deity, which is the sense of the suffix, either as non-different or as different, according to the maxim that 'a word-meaning is construed with a word-meaning, but not with a part of a word-meaning'. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Now, [regarding] the deity... He uses the word "also" (*api*) to indicate that while a construction as different is impossible—because it is contradicted by fact—it is indeed possible as a construction of non-difference.

And thus, since there is no syntactic connection whatsoever between Agni and other [names] and the deity, he says: "In the case of the deity and the offering. "Fragmentarily" means that the power is distinct; that is to say, there are two powers. Consequently, the meaning is that the deity cannot even be a part of the referent of the word. And so, the point is that there is no obstacle whatsoever to the non-differential connection of Agni and others with the deity, which is the meaning of the suffix. || 52 ||

One might object: "Since the deity Agni and others are obtained from the very words 'Agni' and so forth, there is no need to postulate a denotative power (*śakti*) for the *taddhita* suffix in reference to a deity, as that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). This is the objection raised by the phrase "nanvaganyādidevasya. The reason given is "because it is obtained through the base itself" (*prakṛtyaiva lābhāt*). The sense is that the deity Agni and others are already presented by the word 'Agni' and so forth—which denote the actual fire and such—since the state of being a deity is never absent from Agni and the like.

[Objection: "But surely, even though Agni and the others are presented by the base-words *agni* etc. through their nature as fire (*agnitva*) and so forth, the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) must be assumed to have a denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the deity in order to present Agni and the others as deities (*devatātvena*). To this, he says: "By means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone on the part of the base. The meaning is that the base-word *agni* and so forth is indicative (*lākṣaṇika*) with respect to the deity Agni and so forth. That is to say, by means of non-abandoning indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*), it conveys the deity Agni and so forth as qualified by the property of deityhood (*devatātva*) which resides in the same substratum as firehood (*agnitva*) and the like. [This is] according to the theory of being a suggestor (*dyotakatva*).

Regarding the view that [prefixes] possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), it was stated that "dyotakatve" (in the case of being indicative) there is no possibility of a supporting example, because excellence (*prakarṣa*) is held to be the meaning of the prefix, and one does not accept that the verbal root has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to that which is qualified by it. This is illustrated by the phrase "just like the cognition of excellent victory. The underlying point is this: in the expression *prajayati*, an excellent victory is experienced; however, that is not the meaning of the verbal root. For if it were, then even in the case of *jayati* alone, there would be the undesirable consequence of cognizing an excellent victory. Nor is it the meaning of the prefix.

If that were the case, then even in the word *praharati* ("he strikes"), there would arise the cognition of a "superior victory" (or excellence). Nor can it be a qualified meaning (*viśiṣṭārtha*). For if that were so, since the qualified object would possess both forms, one would have to postulate a separate expressive power (*śakti*) for both [the prefix and the root], which would result in the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, it is the verbal root itself, whose power to denote victory is already established, that conveys the sense of "superior victory" through indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The prefix (*upasarga*), however, merely serves to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya-grāhaka*). It is by this much alone that the convention exists of calling prefixes "illuminators" (*dyotaka*).

And thus, just as the understanding of "supreme victory" arises from the verbal root *ji* through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), so too in the present case, the presence of deities such as Agni may arise from the very words "Agni" and so forth—which serve as the bases—through secondary indication; with this intention, he says: "Or rather, the power [of denotation] resides in that which is to be offered."

The capacity of the *taddhita* suffix resides solely in the substance to be offered (*pradeya-dravya*); however, let there be a conventional (*nirūḍha*) secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the base word for the deity. Alternatively, the word "deity" may serve merely to indicate the base; thus, by the rule "from that which is in the nominative case [and] capable [of being qualified], the suffixes *aṇ* and others occur in the sense of 'belonging to this'," it follows by implication that whatever is in the nominative case must be the deity. All these positions are established in the treatises of the Mīmāṃsakas and others—this is the construction [of the argument]. By the restrictive particle *eva* ("solely") in the phrase "in the substance to be offered," the capacity of the *taddhita* suffix for the deity is excluded.

The meaning is that the sense of the base (prakṛti) will be construed with the sense of the suffix (pratyaya)—namely, "that which is to be given"—by way of the relation of being the specifier of the divinityhood residing in its own function. By the term "established" (nirūḍha), it is stated that the indication (lakṣaṇā) possesses beginningless intentionality. One might object: "Since the substance to be given is already obtained from the word 'curd' (dadhi) and so forth occurring in immediate proximity, to postulate a further denotative power (śakti) for the taddhita suffix there is contrary to the maxim that 'the meaning of a word is not something other than what can be indicated by other means'. To this, he objects with the words: "And [it is] not [the case] in examples such as *aindraṃ dadhi*," etc., ending with "because of obtaining [the meaning]."

The meaning is that [the meaning of the suffix] is obtained from another word, such as "curd" (*dadhi*), which is uttered with equal status [to the base]. Regarding the phrase "therein the expressive power" (*tatra śaktiḥ*): why is the expressive power postulated "therein"—that is, in the substance to be given? The expressive power should not be postulated in the substance to be given, because the substance is obtainable through other means. Rather, the expressive power of the *taddhita* suffix must be postulated in the deity alone, and not in the substance to be given as qualified by the deity; such is the intention of the objector.

Even in the absence of a postulation of a power (*śakti*) in the substance, since the deity obtainable from the secondary suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*) can be construed with the substance obtainable from words such as "curd" (*dadhi*) through a relation such as being the qualifier of the deityhood residing in itself, the meaning "the curd is that which qualifies Indra and other deities as their deityhood" is established; thus, it is possible to arrive at the sense that the object to be given is qualified by the deity.

If it is argued that in this view there is no fault of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) being construed with only a portion of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), and that this is another favorable point, [the author] says "even when other words are not heard" to show that this is not tenable. The meaning is that even where another word such as *dadhi* is not heard, the cognition of the substance is established by experience, because it is cognized from a *devatā*-suffix (*taddhita*) ending [in the word *saumya*, for instance].

The point is that in cases where other words such as *dadhi* (curd) are not heard, the postulation of the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the *taddhita* suffix with respect to the substance to be offered is necessary, because the cognition of the substance arising there would otherwise be inexplicable. He states another proof for postulating the primary power of the *taddhita* suffix with respect to the substance to be offered: "And because of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyāt*). If the *taddhita* suffix denoted the deity alone, then the word *aindra*, which has the meaning "the deity non-different from Indra," would lack grammatical coreferentiality with words such as *dadhi*.

It should be understood that since there is a co-referential (sāmānādhikaraṇya) connection between "Aindra" and "dadhi" (curd) by way of non-difference (abheda), it is necessary to assume that the *taddhita* suffix has its denotative power (*śakti*) residing in the substance (*dravya*), in order to conform to that [co-referentiality]. Furthermore, a connection between the referents of two nouns—namely, the deity and the curd—by means of a relation such as "qualifier-qualified" (*nirūpakatva*) and so forth, is extremely difficult to maintain. This is because it contradicts the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that the connection between the referents of two nouns is one of non-difference (*abheda*). Consequently, the burden of assuming that the *taddhita* suffix has its denotative power in the substance to be offered falls upon your own neck as well; this is the intended meaning.

If it is argued: "Let there simply be a conventional secondary function (lakṣaṇā) of the base word (*prakṛti*) with respect to the substance qualified by the deity; what is the point of postulating a denotative power (*śakti*) for the *taddhita* suffix in relation to the offering-substance (*pradeya*)?"—this is not so. For if that were the case, since the meaning of the base word would be the substance to be offered and the *taddhita* suffix would merely serve to indicate it, the substance to be offered would fail to attain the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) as determined by the meaning of the base word. This is because there is a rule that the meaning indicated [by a suffix] must appear as a qualifier (*prakāra*).

For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *striyām*, regarding examples such as *ajā-khaṭvā* (goat-mat), it is raised as an objection that since the femininity (*strītva*) understood through suffixes like *ṭāp* is the meaning of the suffix and thus primary, and because it is of the nature of a non-substance (*asattva*), the expression of number (*vacana*) with respect to it is untenable. In response, it is argued that since femininity is indicated (*dyotya*), femininity appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the form "a goat qualified by femininity" (*strītvaviśiṣṭā ajā*). Therefore, there is no untenability: the expression does not denote the number residing in that [femininity], but rather denotes the number residing in the individual goat (*ajā-vyakti*) which serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

[The author] says "otherwise" (anyathā), having reflected that if [the deity] were to appear as the qualificand even while being the object to be illuminated, then the inconsistency of the resolution would be quite evident. The meaning is: "if one does not accept the primary denotative power of the taddhita suffix in the *pradeya* (the substance to be offered) in order to conform to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). The phrase "it would not be so" refers to the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*).

For the grammarians (vaiyākaraṇas), when it is accepted that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) expresses the agent and the object—as in "Devadatta cooks" (*pacati devadattaḥ*) and "the rice is cooked" (*pacyate taṇḍulaḥ*)—there arises a lack of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the agent and object expressed by the suffix and the words *Devadatta* and *rice*. Consequently, in accordance with that [requirement], they maintain that the verbal suffix denotes the agent and the object. Coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), moreover, consists in the denotation of a single entity qualified by two modes [of expression].

When a verb expresses the agent or the object, then whatever individual (vyakti) is understood as an agent or as an object from such a verbal suffix, that very same individual is understood as "Devadatta-ness" from the word *devadatta*, and as "rice-ness" (*taṇḍulatva*) from the word *taṇḍula*; thus, in both cases, the individual functioning as the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is one and the same. Therefore, the intention is that the justification for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) lies in accepting that the verb possesses a denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the meanings of agent and object.

The intention is as follows: if, however, in deference to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the denotative power (*śakti*) of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is not admitted to reside in the substance to be offered (*pradeya*), then by the same logic, the denotative power of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) would likewise fail to be established in respect to the agent and the object. Consequently, the coreferentiality experienced in such cases as "Devadatta cooks" (*pacati devadattaḥ*) would be difficult to explain; likewise, the coreferentiality well-established by universal experience in instances such as "curd for Indra" (*aindraṃ dadhi*) would also be untenable.

In the case of *bhāvanā* (the efficient force), since its existence is impossible without a substratum (*āśraya*), one takes that substratum by means of implication (*ākṣepa*) based on the impossibility of its being otherwise; likewise, in the expression *sā 'sya devatā* ("that is its deity"), setting aside the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) of the word ending in the genitive suffix in *asya*, and by postulating a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in relation to the deity within the connection expressed by the genitive, one takes the implied substratum through the implication of a property-bearer (*dharmin*) consisting of a relatum connected to its own substratum, based on the impossibility of the connection [of the deity] otherwise.

Furthermore, the Mīmāṃsaka claim that the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [of "Devadatta" and "curd"] is possible because of the non-difference (*abheda*) of Devadatta with the curd and so forth is all the more difficult to maintain. This is because an object obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*) or other means does not appear as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and there is no evidence for its participation in the verbal relation (*śābdānvaya*). Otherwise, from the sentence "Bring the jar," one would have the undesirable consequence of the cognition "Bring space," since space would also be verbally related through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), as it is present [in the world] by that relation. This should be carefully considered.

Having thus stated the undesirable consequence (āpatti) against the Grammarians—that the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) lacks the capacity to denote the agent or the object—he now addresses the Mīmāṃsakas with the words "But for the Mīmāṃsakas... Regarding the suffix (pratyaya): it refers to the secondary derivative suffix (taddhita) prescribed in the sense of "this is its deity" (*sā'sya devatā*). "Only deityhood" (*devatātvam eva*): rather than postulating a linguistic potency (*śakti*) for the secondary derivative suffix in the deity as qualified by the property of deityhood, it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to postulate the potency of the secondary derivative suffix in deityhood itself. The word "only" (*eva*) excludes the deity [as the denotatum].

Since it has already been stated that the substance (*dravya*) is indeed obtained from another word, the intention is that the "deity-ness" (*devatātva*) will be construed with the substance through the relation of being its own qualifier (*svanirūpakatva*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "The oblation is the qualifier of the deity-ness residing in Indra. [The author adds: "Let there be no denotability (*vācyatva*) for the agent, just as in the Mīmāṃsā view, where the agent is not the denotation of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), but rather the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) alone is the denotation due to parsimony (*lāghava*), since the substratum (the agent) can be obtained from other words such as 'Devadatta'."

The point is that, since the substratum is obtainable from another word, the substratum would be understood as qualified by agency through the very connection (*anvaya*) of the agency consisting of *bhāvanā*. Similarly, in the present case, since the object to be offered (*pradeya*) is obtainable from another co-occurring word, the object to be offered can acquire its qualification by being the deity (*devatātva*) through the very connection of the deityhood denoted by the secondary suffix (*taddhita*); thus, the claim that the secondary suffix has a direct denotative power (*śakti*) toward the object to be offered is not established. If it is argued, "Is it not the case that the absence of a denotative power of the secondary suffix toward the object to be offered is precisely what we desire?"—the answer is no.

Since it has been clearly stated by the Mīmāṃsakas in the statement, "This *taddhita* suffix expresses the curd (*āmikṣā*) as being connected with the deity," that the denotative power (*śakti*) of the *taddhita* resides in the substance to be offered, it should be observed that if the power of the *taddhita* is postulated here [in *saumyaḥ*] to reside in the substance to be offered in order to conform to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), then the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) must likewise denote the agent; for in the case of "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), coreferentiality is experienced between the agent and Devadatta.

Now, one might ask: "Since the deity such as Agni is already established through the primary power (*śakti*) of the word 'Agni' and so forth, what is the purpose of resorting to indication (*lakṣaṇā*)? To this he replies: "By way of being a deity. The meaning is that indication is resorted to for the sake of presenting Agni and the others in their capacity as deities. The point is that although the bank is invariably connected with the Ganges, the referent "bank" would not be presented without indication; likewise, although the nature of being a deity is invariably present in Agni and the others, the referent "deity" would not be presented from the words "Agni" and so forth without indication—thus, indication is necessary.

And that indication (lakṣaṇā) is not [always] purpose-driven; thus he says: "established" (nirūḍha). He explains the nature of the established [indication] with the words "non-justification" (anupapatti): the meaning is that its essence is either the state of being devoid of the cognition of non-justification regarding syntactic connection (anvaya) and so forth, or the state of possessing beginningless intentionality (tātparya); this is what constitutes being "established. || 54 ||

In the context of defining the meaning of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) used for deities, he states that the same method follows even regarding other meanings of secondary suffixes mentioned in the traditional grammatical treatises (*smṛta*), saying: "The suffix *ṇa* [is applied] in the sense of 'sport' when [the meaning] is 'this belongs to him'. Regarding the phrase "in this case": the meaning is a word such as *dāṇḍa*, which ends in the suffix *ṇa* prescribed by the specific rule *tadasyāṃ praharaṇam*. "Sport qualified by a weapon" means that the qualification of sport by a weapon occurs through the relationship of locus and located; the sense is that sport is the locus, and the weapon is what is located therein.

The word "its" (*asya*) is construed with "the meaning" (*arthaḥ*). Regarding the term "meaning": the meaning of the suffix *ṇa* in the word *dāṇḍā*—which refers to a game characterized by a weapon—is "the meaning. In that context, the base-meaning, "staff," is construed non-differently with the "weapon," which is a constituent part of the meaning of the suffix *ṇa* (namely, the game characterized by a weapon). Thus, the meaning is: "a game whose locus is a weapon non-different from a staff."

Since it contradicts the logical principle that "a word-meaning connects with a word-meaning, but not with a part of a word-meaning," [the author], unable to tolerate connection with a single part, says: "in striking and in play" (*praharaṇakrīḍe*). The meaning is that the suffix *ṇa* has a distributive power (*khaṇḍaśaḥ śaktiḥ*) with respect to both striking and play. Consequently, the fault of connection with a single part does not arise; this is the intended sense. In this view, the striking qualified by the staff connects with the play through the relation of being its locus (*āśrayatva-sambandha*).

Considering that it would be cumbersome to postulate two separate powers for both cases, [the author] says "mere play" (*krīḍāmātram*) out of regard for parsimony (*lāghava*). By the word *mātra*, it is stated that the suffix *ṇa* does not denote the instrument of striking (*praharaṇa*). The sense is that the act of striking with a staff or similar object can be obtained through the power (*śakti*) itself by means of the word "staff" (*daṇḍa*), etc. "Striking" (*praharaṇa*) means the instrument of a blow; for the word *praharaṇa* is derived from the root *hṛ* with the prefix *pra* and the instrumental *ghañ* suffix, in the sense of "that by which one strikes" (*prahriyate 'nena*).

If it is argued that even though the instrument is obtained through the property of being a staff (*daṇḍatva*), the suffix *ṇa* must still possess the power (*śakti*) to obtain it specifically as an instrument (*praharaṇatva*)—then let it be accepted that the word "staff" and so forth has a conventional (nirūḍha) secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for the act of striking with a staff and so forth. On this view, since the primary meaning—the act of striking with a staff—is connected to the game by a relation such as being the specifier of the instrumenthood residing in itself, the meaning becomes "a game characterized by the act of striking with a staff," and thus the characterization of the game by the instrument is obtained.

In this regard, the following should be understood: when the suffix *ṇap* (denoting an agent) is postulated to have distinct potencies for both "striking" (*praharaṇa*) and "sporting" (*krīḍā*), then—even though it would be necessary to postulate a causal relation such that "the presentation of a word-meaning by another word is a cause for the comprehension of a relational connection whose object is delimited by a property produced by that [first] word"—in order to prevent the mutual relation of locus and located between the horse and the sun presented by the word *hari*, such a causal relation is indeed required.

Since it is unestablished that there can be a mutual syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between two meanings presented by a single word, the mutual connection between the two meanings presented by the suffix *ṇa*—namely, "striking" (*praharaṇa*) and "play" (*krīḍā*) [in the form of] "play qualified by striking"—is difficult to justify; nevertheless, due to the diversity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), a mutual connection between two meanings presented even by a single word does occur.

Just as in the view of the ancients, although the root possesses distinct potencies for both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*), the result is construed with the operation by way of the relation of "conduciveness" (*anukūlatā*), and the operation is construed with the result by way of the relation of "being produced" (*janyatva*)—this being due to the diversity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*)—so too should it be understood in the present case. Regarding the verse, the phrase "this very method" means that the same method which was stated regarding the meaning of the *taddhita* suffixes denoting deities (*devatātaddhita*) is to be followed in the case of the meaning of the *ṇa* suffix.

He demonstrates what is included by the word "etcetera" (ādipada) with the phrase "that is his abode" (so'sya nivāsaḥ), and so forth. Here, the word *nivāsa* (abode), derived from the root *vas* (to dwell) with the suffix *ghañ*, should be understood as having an instrumental sense (*adhikaraṇasādhana*), meaning "that in which one dwells."

Regarding the word *asya* (of this), although the relation denoted by the genitive case—which has the meaning expressed by the base-word *idam* (this) as its subordinate element—is perceived as the qualificand, and thus it would follow that the genitive meaning itself is the primary referent of the suffix; nevertheless, according to the maxim, "This *taddhita* suffix indeed expresses *āmikṣā* as conjoined with the deity," the meaning of the base-word, having the genitive relation as its subordinate element, is accepted as the primary sense.

And thus, according to the principle that "the meaning of the base (prakṛti) possesses a relation," the meaning of the genitive ending in the word *asya* (of this) results in "that which is related. For this very reason, it was stated previously that in the expression *sā'sya* ("this belongs to her"), the object to be given (*deyadravya*) denoted by the word *idam* is the meaning of the deity-suffix (*devatā-pratyaya*). In this way, both the residence and the related party constitute the meaning of the suffix prescribed by rules such as *so'sya nivāsaḥ*. Here too, the meaning of the suffix is the related party qualified by the residence.

The qualification of the locus of residence (*nivāsādhikaraṇa*) as being related to the relatum (*saṃbandhin*) is to be understood through relations such as that of the container and the contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). Both "residence" and "relatum" are the meanings of the suffix individually; or, the relatum alone may be the meaning of the suffix—these three positions should be understood as before. For example, Devadatta is called *sraughna* because Strughna is the locus of his residence.

In this regard, according to the first view, the base-meaning *srughna* is construed non-differently (*abheda*) with the locus of residence, which is one part of the meaning of the suffix—namely, the relation qualified by the locus of residence; and that locus of residence is construed with the relatum through the relation of being the locus of inherence (*ādheyatā*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "Devadatta is non-different from the relatum that possesses the state of being the locus of inherence as determined by the locus of residence non-different from Srughna."

In the second alternative (*pakṣa*), there is a connection, as before, with that which is related to the locus of residence (*nivāsādhikaraṇa*) as qualified by *srughna* through non-difference (*abheda*). In the third alternative, it should be understood that the word *srughna* possesses a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) referring to the locus of residence in *srughna*. Everything else is to be understood exactly as before. The verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) common to all three alternatives is: "one who is related to the locus of residence non-different from *srughna*. Furthermore, the "residence" (*nivāsa*) must be understood as having an agent (*kartṛ*) who is related to the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) present by proximity (*pratyāsatti*).

The rule "sā'smin paurṇamāsī" means that after a word ending in the nominative case denoting a *paurṇamāsī* (full moon day), a suffix such as *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "in this [month]. The meaning is that the combination of the base and the suffix becomes a conventional term (*rūḍha*). For example, the full moon day conjoined with the asterism Puṣya is called *pauṣī*; when one says "the month in which the *pauṣī* full moon occurs," it is the *pauṣa* month. Here, the word *paurṇamāsī* is both the conventional term itself and the meaning related to the suffix.

There are three possible positions to be considered: that the meaning of the suffix is the relatum qualified by the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*); that the full moon and the relatum are separate meanings; and that the meaning of the suffix is the relatum alone. In this context, words such as *pauṣī* are formed with the feminine suffix *ṅīp* attached to a base ending in the suffix *aṇ*, as prescribed by the rule "time joined with a lunar mansion" (*nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ*). Among these, the word *puṣya* refers to the moon conjoined with its respective lunar mansion.

Otherwise, since all constellations exist at all times, there would result the improper usage of expressions such as "today is Caitra-maha" (the festival of Caitra) and so forth. In this context, it is precisely the meaning of the suffix that is appropriate, and not time itself; for, by parsimony (*lāghava*), it is more fitting that only the real entity (*vastusat*) serves as the cause for the production of the suffix. Furthermore, time can be obtained through words such as "day" (*ahar*). Thus, the cognition produced by the word *pauṣī* is [of the form] "that which is conjoined with the moon when Puṣya is present."

The meaning of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*) following words such as *pauṣī* is "that which has such a full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) as its locus" and so forth. Although there is no rule that the moon must be in conjunction with the Puṣya constellation on every specific full moon day, in expressions such as *pauṣī paurṇamāsī* ("the Pauṣa full moon"), it is precisely the *fitness for conjunction* with that respective constellation that is intended. This is because usage occurs even in the absence of actual conjunction with those respective constellations, as in *caitrī paurṇamāsī* ("the Caitra full moon") and *caitraḥ vaiśākhaḥ* ("the month of Caitra [or Vaiśākha]"). Furthermore, this fitness consists in being conjoined with either its own constellation or one adjacent to it.

The distinction is as follows: for the months beginning with Caitra and ending with Śrāvaṇa, the application of any of the [asterism] pairs starting with Citrā is the determinant for such conventional usage; for Bhādrapada and Āśvayuja, it is the application of any one of the triads beginning with Śatabhiṣaj or Revatī; for the months beginning with Kārtika and ending with Māgha, it is the application of any one of the pairs beginning with Kṛttikā; and for Phālguna, it is the application of any one of the triads beginning with Pūrvā-phalgunī. As it has been said: "The last two [months] are to be known as having three [asterisms], and Phālguna is considered to have three."

"The remaining months are to be known as divided into two [halves] according to the arrangement beginning with Kṛttikā. Thus, the last two [months] are Bhādrapada and Āśvayuja. *Bha* means a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). The term "Caitra" and so forth has its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) in the aggregate of the period from the first day of the bright fortnight until the new moon; however, it does not have a conventional meaning for the aggregate beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight until the full moon, because there is no widespread common usage for it in that sense.

Since a month defined by the full moon is lunar (*cāndra*), and because of such traditional legal texts (*smṛti*) as "The lunar month begins with the bright fortnight and ends with the new moon," as well as due to the abundance of the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), it is appropriate to accept only that which begins with the bright fortnight and ends with the new moon. It should be understood that the usage [of the term] for a month beginning on the first day of the dark fortnight and ending with the full moon is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*). [The suffix -mat] is used in the sense of "that belongs to this" or "this contains that."

The meaning [of the rule] is this: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "it belongs to him" (*tad asya asti*) or "it exists in this" (*tad asmin asti*), the suffix *matup* occurs after a word ending in the nominative case that stands in grammatical apposition with the verb "to be," in the sense of the genitive—that is, in the sense of a related object (*saṃbandhin*) denoted by "his"—and in the sense of the locative, denoted by "in this. Although it might be understood from the expression "it belongs to him" (*asya*) that the prescription of *matup* applies only to the relation of the genitive, nevertheless, because of the requirement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in examples such as "Caitra has cows" (*gomāṃś caitraḥ*), it is logical that the prescription of *matup* applies specifically to the related object itself.

And thus, in cases such as *gomān* ("possessing cows"), the resulting cognition of the syntactic connection (*anvayabodha*) is that "one who possesses the relation of ownership as characterized by a cow. Here, both the relatum (*saṃbandhī*) and the relation (*saṃbandha*), along with its locus, constitute the meaning of the suffix. In this context, the present tense—as in "he exists"—is intended; otherwise, the word would simply be "cow" (*gavādi*). Consequently, the cognition is: "one who possesses a cow whose existence is present."

In cases such as *gomān āsīt* ("he was possessed of cows"), however, it is established in the works of Kaiyaṭa and others that the word *gomat* has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the object of the usage denoted by the pronoun *tat*. Regarding the statement in the *Ślokavārttika*, "in cases of abundance, censure, and praise," although the inclusion of the meanings "abundance" (*bhūmā*) and so forth alongside "relation" (*saṃbandha*) suggests that these meanings are also directly expressed (*vācya*) by the suffix *matup*, nevertheless, since the sūtra does not establish that the meanings of abundance and so forth constitute the primary denotation of *matup*, it is more appropriate to regard them merely as conditions for the employment of the suffix, just like the meaning of "existence" (*asti-artha*).

The term "being a condition for the application [of a word]" (*prayogopādhitva*) means that even in the absence of being directly denotable (*vācyatva*), it serves as the cause for the employment of a word by virtue of its mere conceptual existence (*ārthikasattāmātra*). This is to say that they are expressed by the suffix *matup*. Thus, the meaning is that words such as *go* (cow), which serve as the base (*prakṛti*) for *matup*, possess a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to meanings qualified by abundance (*bhūman*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādikam*): by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should include [the following]: the suffix *pūraṇa* (denoting ordinal numbers), the suffix *īṣadasamāpti* (denoting slight incompleteness), the suffix *thāl* (denoting manner), and [the formation] "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*) and so on. For example: "the filler of five" (*pañcānāṃ pūraṇaḥ*) is *pañcamaḥ* (the fifth).

In this context, regarding the suffix *ḍaṭ* prescribed by the rule "in the sense of its completion" (*tasya pūraṇe*), there is the augment *maṭ* [added] after a stem ending in *n*, provided it is not a numeral. The meaning of the rule "of that" (*tasya*) is as follows: when the completion of a number denoted by the base—specifically a number expressed in the genitive case which signifies the object to be numbered—is to be expressed, the suffix *ḍaṭ* occurs. That which completes is called "completion" (*pūraṇa*); it refers to a constituent part, and that is the meaning of the suffix. The meaning of the base (the number itself) connects with the meaning of the suffix through the relation of being the completer of the number five residing in itself.

The understanding is that [the suffix] completes the number five residing in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). For example, in the expression "as Hari, so Hara," the suffix *thāl*—introduced by the rule *prakāravacane thāl*—has as its meaning the possessor of a mode (*prakāravat*), in accordance with the requirement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And in this context, a "mode" (*prakāra*) is a particularity that differentiates a universal. Thus, the understanding is: "Hara possesses those same specific attributes that Hari possesses. When the identity of the two attributes is apprehended through the correlative pronouns *yat* and *tat*, the similarity of Hara to Hari results.

Objection: Let similarity (*sādṛśya*) itself be the meaning of the suffix *thāl*. In that case, the verbal cognition established by experience—having similarity as its qualifier, namely "Hara is similar to that which is similar to Hari"—would be accounted for. Response: No, because in expressions such as *sarvathā* ("in every way"), *anyathā* ("otherwise"), and *itarathā* ("elsewise"), no similarity is perceived.

In the expressions *guḍakalpā drākṣā* ("grapes that are almost like molasses") and *bahuguḍā drākṣā* ("grapes that are mostly molasses"), the suffixes *kalpa*, *deśya*, and *deśīya* are applied by the rule *īṣadasamāptau kalpab-deśya-deśīyaraḥ*, and the suffix *bahu* is applied optionally before a nominal ending by the rule *vibhāṣā supo bahuca purastāttu*. Thus, these two suffixes—*kalpa* and *bahu*—occur in their own sense (*svārthe*) after a nominal stem (*subanta*) that denotes a meaning qualified by "slight incompleteness" (*īṣadasamāpti*). In this context, the word *guḍa* refers to something similar to molasses; the suffix, however, is merely indicative (*dyotaka*).

Precisely because the suffix (*pratyaya*) is indicative (*dyotaka*), the forms *guḍakalpā* (feminine) and *bahuguḍo drākṣā* (masculine) are established in their respective genders; for it is an inherent property of suffixes added in the sense of identity (*svārthika*) whether they deviate from or do not deviate from the gender and number of the base (*prakṛti*). However, if similarity (*sādṛśya*) were the meaning of the suffix, then in the case of *bahuguḍo drākṣā*, the feminine gender belonging to the substantive (*viśeṣya*) would necessarily follow.

In this case, sweetness (*mādhurya*) and other qualities that serve as the basis for similarity are perceived through the completion of the word-form; therefore, a cognition of only partial similarity does not arise. The understanding is "the grape is similar to jaggery," and thus the simile (*upamā*) is apprehended. In examples such as *pācakakaḥ*, the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *kutsite* (Pāṇini 5.3.74) to the word *pācaka*, which conveys a meaning qualified by contempt. The resulting understanding is "one who possesses the state of being a contemptible cook."

However, when a deprecation of the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is impossible, since the suffix *kan* is attached to the word itself—which is already complete in its own meaning—through a connection with deprecation and so forth, the deprecation residing in the substance, gender, and other properties of the object denoted by the stem ending in *sudhān* (e.g., *sudhān-kaḥ*) is conveyed by the suffix *kan*.

In the expression *śuklakaṃ rūpam* ("a white form"), there is a disparagement of the substance (*dravya*). In "Behold the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow; know the Kauravas as women," there is a disparagement of gender (*liṅga*). In *putrakaśatam* ("a hundred sons"), there is a disparagement of the number one (*ekatvasaṃkhyā*), because of the understanding that "the suffering involved in supporting a hundred is the same as that in supporting just one. In cases such as *aupagavaḥ* ("the offspring of Upagu"), the meaning of the suffixes prescribed by rules such as *tasyāpatyam* ("his offspring") is "offspring" and so forth; the meaning of the genitive case and so on is understood through the whole word (*samudāyagamya*).

In other words, this is understood through *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning), which consists in the capacity of a single [compound] to produce a single presentation (*upasthiti*) of a qualified object. The cognition arises in the manner of "the offspring related to Upagu. In cases such as *cūrṇaiḥ saṃsṛṣṭāścūrṇino'pūpāḥ* ("flour-cakes mixed with flour"), the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), such as "flour," is construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*) within the relation (*saṃsarga*), which is a part of the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) prescribed by the rule *saṃsṛṣṭe-cūrṇādiniḥ*. The resulting cognition is: "flour-cakes characterized by a mixture having flour as its cause."

And thus, because it would involve the complexity of having the meaning of the base (prakṛti) relate either to a portion of the meaning of the secondary derivative (taddhita) or to the entire meaning of the secondary derivative itself, he sets that aside and—on the basis of parsimony—resorts to the view of *jahatsvārthā* (the abandonment of the primary meaning), stating: "In every type of compound formation (*vṛtti*), there is a distinct power (*atirikta-śakti*). The five types of formations (*vṛtti*) are: those ending in *kṛt* suffixes, secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), compounds (*samāsa*), *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one of several synonyms), and verbal roots ending in *san*, etc. (*sanādyanta-dhātu*).

In this context, "function" (*vṛtti*) is the expression of another meaning; thus, it is the general definition of function, as is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*. The meaning of this is as follows: in the word *abhidhāna*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). It is neuter because it denotes a general category. The "expression of another meaning" refers to the inclusion of the meaning of another word as a qualifier by means of a principal word (*pradhānaśabda*). That which is the instrument for this is the function. Thus, a *vṛtti* is that [compound formation] by which, through its principal member, there arises the presentation of its own meaning precisely as qualified by the other [member].

This presentation of its own meaning as conjoined with the meanings of other [constituent] elements is accomplished by the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*), assisted by the power of the parts (*avayavaśakti*). The power of the parts is established by common usage (*loka*) and is also postulated by the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*). The latter occurs in the case of suffixes such as *taddhita*. Regarding the former, the ancients employ the term "function" (*vṛtti*) metaphorically for these [parts], since they serve as the substrata for the function of the whole. Furthermore, the power of the whole is obtained through the governing rule (*paribhāṣā*): "The prescription of words applies to those that are semantically connected" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*). And its meaning is as follows: "that which is prescribed" (*vidhīyate*) is the "prescription" (*vidhi*), i.e., the grammatical operation (*kārya*); the suffix *kip* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*).

"Padasya vidhā" means "the prescription for a word"; this is a compound formed with a genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). It should be understood that whatever rule pertains to a word is dependent upon semantic competency (*sāmarthya*). Here, semantic competency is *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning). This is because the *Bhāṣya* states that semantic competency is the unification of meanings that were previously distinct; for example, in the sentence "rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ" (the king's man), the meanings are distinct, whereas in the compound "rājapuruṣaḥ" (king-man), they are unified.

Thus, it follows that *ekārthībhāva* (the state of having a single unified meaning) is the capacity of words—which are observed in common usage to denote distinct objects when presented separately during the stage of grammatical derivation—to convey a single qualified meaning through their collective power (*samudāyaśakti*). This is based on the etymological derivations: "that whose meanings are conjoined (*saṃgata*) is *samartha*," and "that whose meanings are fused (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) is *samartha*. Conjunction (*saṃgati*) and fusion (*saṃsarga*) are indeed nothing other than unification (*ekībhāva*). For example, as in the expression "the ghee has been mixed with oil," it is understood to mean "it has become one."

Or as it is said in the Bhāṣya: "Just as when fire is mixed [with other elements], it is understood to have become one"; this is that "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), which occurs only in *vṛtti*s such as compounds (*samāsa*). Thus, it is designated as "*vṛtti*" and also as "the *vṛtti* that abandons its own meanings" (*jahatsvārthā vṛtti*). The intention behind the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) in the Bhāṣya statement "in a compound, [the members] have a single meaning" is that the term "compound" serves as an illustration for all *vṛtti*s in general.

In this regard, since it is clear that the rules concerning *samāsa* (compound) and *taddhita* (secondary derivative) have as their domain the word (*pada*), and because establishing many properties of *vṛtti* through explicit statements would involve great complexity (*mahāgaurava*), and because the principle of *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning) must necessarily be accepted as being simpler than that, the application of the *paribhāṣā* is indeed evident. Furthermore, for certain *kṛt* suffixes—such as those caused by an *upapada* under the rule "karmaṇyaṇ" (Pāṇini 3.2.1)—the status of being a *padavidhi* (a rule whose domain is the word) is clear. By association with those, other instances such as *pācaka* are also considered *padavidhi*. The term *kṛt* refers to a *kṛdanta* (a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix).

The term *taddhita* refers to a word-group containing that [suffix]; for this very reason, there is no fault regarding the suffixes *bahu* and *aka*. Furthermore, even in the case of *ekaśeṣa*, because the word *dvandva* is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), since *ekaśeṣa* is prescribed specifically in the domain of *dvandva*, *ekārthībhāva* (syntactic unification) certainly exists there. In the case of *san* and other affixes, the status of *kyac* and others as being governed by the rules of word-formation (*padavidhi*) is quite clear. As for the suffix *san*, since its occurrence or non-occurrence is established by its very nature, the option (*vāvacana*) need not be applied; this is based on the authority of the *Bhāṣya* which rejects that [option].

In this manner, because the rule *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.1) establishes that in all types of *vṛtti* there exists a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) of the whole—distinct from the individual powers of the parts—that qualifies the respective meanings of the base elements, the aforementioned investigation into the meaning of *taddhita* suffixes has been stated by those belonging to other systems, such as the Mīmāṃsakas, according to the very methodology of those other systems. The underlying intention is that, according to the Vaiyākaraṇa view, since words are devoid of meaning within compounds and other forms of *vṛtti*, an investigation into their meaning would be inappropriate.

Alternatively, one might argue that the analysis of the meaning of suffixes should be established by superimposing their respective meanings onto the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya). To this he says: "superimposed," and so forth. In reality, however, it is through a specific power alone—that is, through the power of the whole (samudāyaśakti) residing precisely in that which is qualified by the meaning of the respective base and its relation [to it]—that the presentation of the meaning occurs; that is, the presentation of the qualified meaning. The word "is produced" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Having reflected on this, he says: "In fact, it is simply a function (vṛtti); therefore, no great effort is made here."

The meaning is that because there is a state of "single-unity" (*ekārthībhāva*) in a compound (*vṛtti*), there is no mutual connection at all between the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). Therefore, regarding the question of whether there is partial connection (*ekadeśānvaya*), or connection through difference (*bheda*) or non-difference (*abheda*), no special effort is made. For further details, one should refer to what was previously stated in the investigation of the power of compounds (*samāsaśaktivicāra*). || 54 ||

Thus ends the determination of the meaning of the suffixes for deities and so forth, in the *Śāṅkarī*, a commentary on the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, composed by Śaṅkara, the son of Raṅgabhaṭṭa; herein, the meaning of the suffixes for deities and other categories has been ascertained in this exposition of the essence. 10.
Now follows the determination of the number one as non-difference.

In compound formations (*samāsa*) and other types of *vṛtti*, because there is no case-ending following the subordinate member (*upasarjana*), specific numbers such as singularity and so forth are not perceived in their specific forms, such as "singularness" (*ekatvatva*). Rather, all numbers appear in their general form as "numberness" (*saṃkhyātva*); this is what is called "non-dual number" (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*). Regarding this point, he cites Bhartṛhari as authority, stating "and it has been said," referring to specific numbers—that is, numbers such as singularity and so forth as qualified by "singularness" (*ekatvatva*) and the like.

"Without division" means without distinction; the meaning is that they remain as they are. This is the point: in a sentence, subordinate words are indeed endowed with case-endings, and thus they convey their own meanings as qualified by specific case-relations and numbers.

In a compound (*vṛtti*), however, [the word] expresses the primary meaning while having its own specific meaning as a qualifier; thus, since there is an absence of case-endings in that subordinate member (*upasarjana*), the specific numbers—such as oneness and so forth—are not perceived in their respective forms. Consequently, [the author], reflecting that this implies the existence of those [numbers] in an undifferentiated state, composes the introductory remark—"In connection with the discussion of compounds"—in order to determine the number "one" for the qualifier within the compound.

And thus, the point is that the description of the number "identity and oneness" (abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā), which was brought to mind in the context of defining the function (vṛtti), is not irrelevant. The word "therein" (tatra) means "in the subordinate member (upasarjana) that constitutes the function. "The established conclusion" (siddhāntam) means the established conclusion consisting of the cognition of the number "identity and oneness. "By way of an illustration" (dṛṣṭāntena) means by way of the illustration of the meaning of the sentence concerning the *kapiñjala* birds. He "establishes" (upapādayati)—that is, supports—this [point] regarding the number "identity and oneness" through reasoning.

He explains the meaning of the term "number" (*saṃkhyā*) as distinct from "oneness through non-difference" (*abhedaikatva*) according to different philosophical views, beginning with the words "of the specific numbers" (*saṃkhyāviśeṣāṇām*). Regarding the phrase "the medicinal juices": this refers to the honey in a secondary sense.
