Regarding "having deposited their powers" (*āhitaśaktayaḥ*): the meaning is that by them [the juices], powers—which are differentiated by the various effects consisting of the pacification of specific humors such as wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and so forth—have been deposited or established. In other words, they have abandoned their distinctions. "Without division" (*avibhāgena*) means in an undifferentiated form; that is to say, without distinction. "That number" (*tāṃ saṃkhyām*) refers to the number of oneness through non-difference (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyām*).

The syntactical construction is: "They know [it] to be like that"—that is, similar to the state in which all flavors exist as distinct from one another yet are present within honey. Just as all medicinal juices, having deposited all their potencies into a single substance, honey, exist as if they have attained non-distinction and unity by virtue of being based on a single common property—the nature of being a flavor that pervades them all; in the same way, within a compound or other *vṛtti*, all numbers in the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) are perceived as if they have attained unity through non-difference, by virtue of being based on a single common property—the nature of being a number that pervades them all.

This is the meaning. Just as all tastes appear as "tasteness" in honey, so too all numbers appear as "numberness" in a subordinate term; this is what is intended. Having thus stated one sense of the word *abhedaikatva-saṃkhyā* (the number of non-different unity), he states another: "or that which has abandoned its particularity. The word *vā* ("or") indicates an alternative position.

With the intention that there is no evidence for postulating the existence of all specific numbers here—despite the postulation of the coexistence of all tastes in honey based on the experience of a result consisting in the cessation of various diseases and so forth which arises from the presence of all tastes—he says: "abandoned" (*parityaktā*). For number is of two kinds: particular and general. Among these, the particular kind consists of unity, duality, and so forth, because they are endowed with specific properties such as "unity-ness" and "duality-ness" which reside exclusively in those respective [individuals].

Number (*saṃkhyā*) is characterized by the general property of "number-ness" (*saṃkhyātva*), which is its common form; this is because it is delimited by the universal property of number-ness that pervades all [numbers] such as unity (*ekatva*) and so forth. Although, according to the maxim "there is no universal devoid of particulars," a number in its purely general form cannot be shown separately—since there is no such thing as a "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*) alone, stripped of particularities like *plakṣa*-ness (*plakṣatva*)—nevertheless, when, for some reason, the particularities such as unity and so forth are set aside...

When number remains as delimited by the general property of "number-ness" (*saṃkhyātva-sāmānya-dharma*) alone, then that [number], being of a general form, can be known separately. And it is precisely this number, in its general form, that is designated as "number-universal" (*saṃkhyā-sāmānya*).

The sense is as follows: just as in the case of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and other cases denoting "relation-universal" (*saṃbandha-sāmānya*), when specific relations such as agency (*kartṛtva*) or objecthood (*karmatva*) are not intended and are thus set aside, the relation that remains—delimited by the general property of "relation-ness" (*saṃbandhatva-sāmānya-dharma*)—is called "relation-universal"; it is the same here.

And thus they are "abandoned"—that is, not perceived for some reason. "Whose particularities" refers to that number-generality (*saṃkhyāsāmānya*)—meaning the number in its general form—which possesses particular properties such as "oneness-ness" (*ekatvatva*) and so forth; the meaning is that this very thing is denoted by the term "non-differentiated oneness-number" (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*). To support this point as well, he cites the *Vākyapadīya*: "Or of the particulars. "Of the particulars" means of the specific properties such as "oneness-ness," "duality-ness," and so forth. "Due to abandonment" means due to non-apprehension; that is to say, due to non-appearance.

That [oneness] consists of unity and so forth. Its nature as number means that its essential form is the generality of number (*saṃkhyāsāmānya*), because it is delimited by the general property of being "number-ness" (*saṃkhyātva*). Such a thing is designated by the term "non-dual oneness" (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*). The word "it is" is to be supplied. Regarding its being designated by the term "non-dual oneness," the reason stated is "its nature as number."

The point is this: since that [number] which has abandoned specific properties such as oneness and so forth is perceived precisely as "the general category of number" (*saṃkhyāsāmānya*) because it is delimited by the general property of being a number (*saṃkhyātva*), it is therefore designated by such a term. Now, one might ask: "Since there is no universal (*sāmānya*) devoid of particulars (*nirviśeṣa*), how can this be? To this he says: "Because of the operation of the generic portion. This means that in the case of a subordinate word (*upasarjana*) within a compound, because of the operation of the genus itself—namely, the nature of being a number—it functions by way of the manifestation of the number in the form of "number-ness" (*saṃkhyātvena*).

Regarding the phrase "by the exclusion of difference" (*bhedāpohena*): the exclusion (*apoha*) of "difference"—that is, the specific qualifying attributes such as oneness and so forth—is the removal (*vyāvṛtti*). By means of that [exclusion], it exists; the meaning is that it exists in the form of a universal devoid of particulars. The underlying intention is this: since even the meanings of subordinate words in a compound possess the nature of existence (*sattvabhūtatva*), they necessarily involve a connection with number.

Furthermore, due to the absence of a specific number, there arises the manifestation of a general number—namely, a non-dual unity (*abhedaikatva*) which consists in the exclusion of distinctions (*bhedāpoha*) that pervade all specific numbers. Consequently, in both philosophical systems regarding expressions such as *rājapuruṣa* ("the king's man"), it is understood merely that the referent of the word "king" possesses a number; however, unlike the meaning of an indeclinable (*avyaya*), it does not lack number, nor, like a jar (*ghaṭa*) or similar entities, is it delimited by a specific number.

The intended meaning is that since the number "one" and so forth are not perceived as distinct numbers, and since the specific particulars are perceived in their respective forms, the exclusion of difference (*bhedāpoha*) is to be understood here. Previously, non-difference (*abhedaikatva*) was described as the state of all specific numbers existing through a conjunction within the subordinate term (*upasarjanapada*), like the conjunction of all specific medicinal juices in a single honey. In this view, the specific numbers appear as "number-ness," just as specific tastes appear as "taste-ness" in honey.

But now, the distinction from the previous [view] is that it has been stated that there is a unity of difference consisting in the exclusion of differences (bhedāpoha), which is accompanied by all specific numerical particulars. In this position, it should be understood that there is the manifestation of the universal of number itself in its form as "being all numbers," and not of the particular. He supports precisely this point—that there is the manifestation of the universal of number alone and not of the particular—with the words beginning "by that whose particular... By the phrase "agṛhītaviśeṣeṇa" and so forth: "agṛhīta" means ungrasped; "viśeṣa" refers to a particular such as whiteness and the like; "yasya" means of which [the universal]; "yaniṣṭha" means residing in which; [thus,] "tādṛśena rūpeṇa" means by such a form.

The meaning is: by means of a universal form (*sāmānyarūpa*) which is the object of a cognition delimited by "having color" (*rūpatva*), occurring at the same time as the non-cognition of specific qualities such as whiteness. Thus, one says of a cloth or the like that "it has color. Regarding the phrase "whiteness and so forth": the meaning is that the exclusion (*apoha*) consisting of a particularity such as whiteness—the nature of which is a property that excludes what is not that—is not apprehended and is not perceived.

Just as a form is perceived from a distance as "form" (*rūpa*) without its specific qualities such as white or black being apprehended, so too in expressions such as *rājapuruṣa* (the king's man), within the subordinate member of the compound, only a general number is perceived as "numberness" (*saṃkhyātva*), and not specific numbers such as oneness or duality; this is the intended meaning. Having thus described the word-meaning of non-dual oneness (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*), he explains the meaning of the verse containing that term with the words "of this" (*asyāḥ*). This means: of the number of non-dual oneness.

The sense is that the term "non-dual unity number" (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*) is used as a conventional designation for a number whose distinctions have dissolved. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the meaning is that its manifestation—that is, its cognition—is established by reasoning within a *vṛtti*, such as a compound (*samāsa*). Regarding the phrase "the established view": since such a number is not accepted in other philosophical systems (*darśana*), the words "of the Grammarians" (*vaiyākaraṇānām*) have been supplied. He states the reasoning that serves as the proof for the manifestation of non-dual unity number within a *vṛtti* with the words beginning "this is the sense."

The meaning is as follows: when the term "rājapuruṣa" (the king's man) is uttered, there is an experience-based certainty that a desire for specific knowledge arises—namely, whether [the king] is one, or the king, or the kings; and since there is an invariable rule that a desire for specific knowledge is preceded by a general cognition, it is necessary that a general cognition of number must arise from the word. "Sāmānyajñānapūrvikā" means having a general cognition as its cause. "Tatpratītiḥ" means a cognition in the form of a generality—that is, in the form of "number-ness"—which is to say, a cognition of number. "Āvaśyakī" means necessary.

The sense is that without the knowledge of the general property (*sāmānya*) which serves as the cause, the desire to know the specific (*viśeṣa*) cannot arise. Thus, the intended meaning is that—just as the king’s eating is inferred from the impossibility of [the servant] being fat otherwise—the cognition of number as a numerical category is postulated to arise from the subordinate word within the compound, due to the impossibility of the desire to know the specific otherwise. Furthermore, in some cases, even a specific number is perceived, as for example in "one who has two sons" (*dviputra*) or "one who has three sons" (*triputra*). And in the absence of any indicator of a specific number, non-differentiated oneness (*abhedaikatva*) is understood.

The meaning is this: that which is perceived as number, namely number itself, is the universal of number (*saṃkhyāsāmānya*). This very thing is the number of non-different unity (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*). Because it is permeated throughout all instances of unity and so forth by the single form of "number-ness," the universal of number—which has attained, as it were, non-difference due to its unitary nature—is designated by the term "the number of non-different unity."

By means of the etymological derivation of the term *abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā* (the number of non-distinct unity), he demonstrates that the general category of number itself is indeed "non-distinct unity. The etymology is as follows: *bheda* is a specific number such as duality, triplicity, and so forth; *abheda* is the absence thereof; and *abhedaikatva* is "unity" (*ekatva*) qualified by that [absence]. Thus, the meaning is that which is the presence of unity at the same time as the non-appearance of specific numbers like duality and so forth—this alone is "non-distinct unity. Consequently, through this definition, it is understood that within the subordinate member of the compound, it is precisely this "unity" that is designated as "number."

Regarding the cognition of unity when a general number whose distinctions have dissolved occurs in a function, he provides an example: "The *kapiñjala* [partridge]... In the *Aśvamedha*, by the sentence "One sacrifices *kapiñjala*s for the sake of Spring," the act of sacrificing *kapiñjala*s qualified by plurality is enjoined with reference to the deity Spring. And this plurality is a specific property that pervades numbers from three and four up to the highest number (*parārdha*), but it is not the state of being any one of those [specific numbers] such as three or four.

Consequently, since it is impossible to perform all those [numbers] simultaneously through a collective application (*samuccaya*) upon their attainment, the act of touching (*ālambhana*), which falls under those numbers, must rest upon specific instances such as three or four. Thus, having raised the doubt that one might touch three, four, five, or any other number according to one's own whim, [the author notes: for one who adopts a number such as four, it is not possible to exclude the "three" contained within it; however, by adopting the number "three," it is possible to exclude the "four" and so forth contained therein.

Therefore, because it is inevitable, because it is the first to present itself in the enumeration of plurality, and because of parsimony, it was determined that only three are to be sacrificed; thus, in the eighth section of the first quarter of the eleventh chapter of the Mīmāṃsā, it was established as a final conclusion (siddhānta) that, by virtue of its multiplicity, "three" alone is the meaning of the plural suffix. This is expressed as: "appearing in that very form."

The meaning is as follows: in the enumeration of a plurality, since the number three is the first to be presented, the plural suffix expresses that very number three; likewise, in the present case, where there is no indicator of a specific number, unity is the first to be presented in every instance, and since there is no evidence for abandoning it, unity alone is perceived as a number. This is because unity, stripped of its specific attributes, is precisely what constitutes the referent of the term "non-dual unity" (*abheda-ekatva*).

Thus, the view that all numbers appear as numberhood (*saṃkhyātva*) in subordinate members (*upasarjana*) within a compound (*vṛtti*) according to the aforementioned etymological method has already been refuted due to a lack of evidence. Now, he refutes the view that the cognition of number in general (*saṃkhyāsāmānya*) from the subordinate member in a compound is necessary because the desire to know the specific [number] would otherwise be inexplicable.

In the case of a compound (vṛtti), when there is the cognition of the number "one" in the form of a general number, that specific inquiry which was stated as being the means of proof does not first enter the path of experience; for if it did, one would have to postulate the appearance of the aforementioned non-differentiated number "one" in the compound in accordance with that inquiry.

Since it has been stated that "a substance (dravya) is that which is endowed with gender and number," and because a substance is invariably accompanied by number—such that wherever there is substantiality (dravyatva), there is possession of number—an inferential knowledge of the generality of number arises. Consequently, the aforementioned desire to know [the specific] is possible. Furthermore, since a desire for a particular [instance] is not established by its own natural force (*svarasataḥ*) in that context, it is merely imagined through one's own latent impressions (*vāsanā*); and because there is no rule that a desire for a particular must necessarily be preceded by a general knowledge produced by a linguistic function (*vṛtti*), [the objection does not hold].

Such a desire for specific knowledge is capable of establishing that number is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) of a compound (*vṛtti*). He says, "Or else, if that were the case," because if one does not accept that the desire for specific knowledge is established by experience, the maxim "one who desires the branches loses even the root" would apply. The phrase "rājapuruṣa" and so forth refers to the meaning: if one accepts that the desire for specific knowledge regarding number is established by experience in a compound such as "the king's man. The expression "by virtue of the cognition and the desire having the same mode of presentation" (*samānaprakārakatvena*) [is used].

The meaning is as follows: one first knows, and then desires; thus, based on experience, knowledge is the cause of desire, because such desire is impossible without that knowledge. Furthermore, the knowledge that arises—having a particular property (*dharma*) as its qualifier (*prakāra*) and a particular object (*viśeṣya*)—produces a desire that has that same property as its qualifier and that same object as its qualificand. Likewise, whatever desire has a particular property as its qualifier and a particular object as its qualificand, the cause of such a desire is precisely a knowledge that has that same property as its qualifier and that same object as its qualificand.

Just as it is observed that the causal relationship (the relation of cause and effect) between knowledge and desire consists in their having the same mode of presentation—such that a desire whose qualificandum is pleasure and whose mode of presentation is "pleaseness" has as its cause a cognition whose qualificandum is pleasure and whose mode of presentation is "pleaseness"—so too, in the present case, since the desire for knowledge (the *jijñāsā*) has as its mode of presentation specific properties such as "oneness-ness," one must necessarily admit that the causal cognition which precedes it also has as its mode of presentation those same specific properties, such as "oneness-ness."

The meaning is as follows: since in a compound (vṛtti), when the specific properties such as singularity and so forth are already understood from the subordinate member (upasarjana) alone, it is absolutely impossible for such a desire to know [the specific] to arise; and because the general knowledge—which is the root of the desire to know the specific—has perished, the desire to know the specific, which depends upon it, also perishes. Thus, the assumption that number is perceived as "number-ness" from the subordinate member in a compound is merely a mimicry of the maxim: "He who desires the branches has lost even the root."

The sense is that because we experience a rule of causal relation based on the requirement that knowledge and desire must have identical modes (*samānaprakārakatva*)—that is, they must take the same specific form—it must be stated that number is denoted by the word only in its respective specific forms such as "oneness-ness" (*ekatvatva*) during the process of *vṛtti* (word-meaning application). Consequently, it is all the more difficult to maintain that during *vṛtti*, a general cognition of number (a cognition having number as its qualificandum and "number-ness" as its mode) arises from a subordinate term (*upasarjana*). This is the intended meaning.

Having considered all this, Bhaṭṭanāgeśa stated in the *Laghumañjūṣā*: "Precisely by the force of *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning) in a compound (*vṛtti*), since there is no nominal stem (*prātipadika*) expressive of number regarding the subordinate member's referent, there is no cognition of specific numbers such as singularity and so forth. The inclusion of the phrase 'expressive of number' and so on is for the purpose of avoiding defects in cases such as *dviputra* ('having two sons')."

The meaning is that since the cognition of a specific number depends upon the knowledge of a word that presents it separately, and since in compound (*samāsa*) and other types of *vṛtti* there is an absence of that cause—namely, the hearing of a case-ending (*vibhakti*) that presents a separate number with respect to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), as occurs in a sentence—there is no comprehension of a specific number. As it has been said: "Whether they are expressive (*vācikā*) or indicative (*dyotikā*) of numbers, those case-endings [which convey them]—when they are elided in a *vṛtti* [such as a compound], the distinction of number ceases. This very non-comprehension of a specific number is what constitutes the number of "undifferentiated unity" (*abheda-ekatva*).

The meaning of the term *abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā* (non-differentiation and unity number) is the non-appearance of any specific number, such as unity, that is accompanied by differentiation; it does not mean that there exists some other general category of number (*saṃkhyāsāmānya*) denoted by the word *abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*. By this, it is clearly understood that even the cognition of a general category of number does not arise from a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) in a compound.

If it is asked, "How then is there the manifestation of one or many individuals (*vyakti*) in a compound (*vṛtti*)?"—the answer is: just as from expressions such as *ghaṭāḥ* ("pots"), there is sometimes the manifestation of three or four [individuals] precisely through their plurality due to the force of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), but never as "three-ness," "four-ness," and so on; likewise, in a compound such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("king's man"), it should be understood that there is the manifestation of one or many individuals solely through the property of being a king (*rājatva*), etc., due to the force of the intention, and never through singularity (*ekatva*), etc.

For this very reason, the Bhāṣya states only the non-comprehension of a specific number (*saṃkhyāviśeṣa*), and not the non-comprehension of one or many objects. And for this same reason, the statement in the Bhāṣya on the *prakṛtigrahaṇa* rule—that in compounds such as *kumāryagāram*, although the analysis (*vigraha*) contains a dual ending, there is no cognition of duality in the derivative form (*vṛtti*) due to the force of "becoming a single referent" (*ekārthībhāva*), but rather a cognition of two girls by way of their being "girls"—is thus consistent; this is the intended meaning. || 55 ||

Thus ends the determination of the number "non-dual unity" in the *Śāṅkarī*, a commentary on the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*. In this work composed by Śaṅkara, the son of Raṅgabhaṭṭa, the determination of the number "non-dual unity" has been completed. (11)
Now follows the determination of whether number is intended to be expressed.

According to the maxim that "what has been brought to mind cannot be neglected," he prepares the introductory stage for the purpose of determining whether the number of the two recollections (*smṛti*) is intended or not, by means of a contextual connection (*prasaṅga*), stating: "In connection with the discussion of number. This means: because of the commencement of the determination of the number one as non-difference. That is to say, it refers to the context of observing the intention to express the number three by means of the plural suffix in the example "the *kapiñjala* birds" (*kapiñjalān*). An objection might be raised: "But surely, where a singular suffix or the like is heard, there such a number is indeed intended."

Since the use of the singular number and so forth is prescribed precisely when one intends to express that specific number, it follows by implication that any other number is not intended there; thus, how could there even be an occasion for a debate regarding the intention or non-intention of a number? To this, he says: "In the case of the subject and the predicate."

The meaning is that there arises a necessity for determining whether the number associated with the subject (*uddeśya*) is intended or not intended, as well as whether the number associated with the predicate (*vidheya*) is intended or not intended; this is because such intention or non-intention is observed only in the case of numbers explicitly expressed by the words, which gives rise to doubt. The phrase "of the number, according to the requirements of the context" indicates the non-intention of the specific number of the subject, as shown in the example: "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*). This is heard in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*: "He cleanses the cup with the *daśāpavitra* [filter]."

*Dasāpavitram* is a piece of cloth; *graha* is a soma-vessel; *saṃmārjanam* is cleansing. Accordingly, some maintain that this injunction prescribes the meaning: "one should cleanse the vessel sprinkled with soma using a piece of cloth. Others, however, say it means that at the time of drawing [the soma], one should wipe away the droplets adhering to the outside of the vessel. Wiping (*proñchanam*) is the action designated by the word *pusarṇe* in the Marathi language.

In that context, by the accusative singular form "graham," the number one associated with the cup (*graha*) is understood. There are ten cups, beginning with the *aindravāyava*. Since this is the case, and because there is no reason to abandon the number already employed once it has been taken up, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that only one among them should be wiped. However, by the accusative case in "graham," the cup is the objective (*uddeśya*) as that which is most desired to be attained; for that which is most desired to be attained is the objective.

Likewise, from the statement "one offers with the cups" (*grahair juhoti*), the instrumental case ending conveys the status of an instrument; thus, because the cups serve as the means for accomplishing the nature of the oblation, they possess purposefulness in the form of being connected to a result. Since it is observed in the verse that whatever is the objective (*uddeśya*) and whatever possesses a result is primary, the cup is understood to be the principal element because it is the objective and because it possesses a result. Consequently, the act of wiping (*saṃmārjana*) becomes subordinate in relation to the cup.

And likewise, in the case of the injunction "one should wipe the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), once it is established that the cup (*graha*) is the primary object (*pradhāna*) and the wiping (*saṃmārga*) is the subordinate quality (*guṇa*), the principle that "the subordinate quality must recur for each primary object" applies. When it is thus determined that as many cups as exist must be wiped, there is no desire to know how many cups are to be wiped; therefore, the singularity inherent in the subject, although heard in the text, is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). This was the conclusion reached by Jaimini in the seventh section of the first quarter of the third chapter of his *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*.

And thus, just as there is the rule among Mīmāṃsakas that the singularity residing in the subject (*uddeśya*) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), so too for Grammarians there is no such rule that the qualification of the subject is not intended to be significant. He states this with the words "not for us" (*nāsmākam*). The meaning is "for us Grammarians. He provides the reason for the absence of a rule regarding the non-intentionality of the qualification of the subject with the words "of the singularity of the verbal root" (*dhātorityekatvasya*).

The meaning is that, since singularity is intended (*vivakṣita*) in the grammatical system as a qualifier of the word "root" (*dhātu*) found in the rule *dhātoḥ*—which serves as the subject (*uddeśya*) in the formulation of suffixes—there is a violation of such a restrictive rule [if one were to ignore it]. The point is that if singularity were not intended there, it would follow that suffixes could arise even from a collection of roots (*dhātusamudāya*). He states that the intention of singularity in the word "root" (*dhātoḥ*) is also agreed upon by the Mīmāṃsakas with the verse beginning "utpadyeta. This is a verse from the *Tantravārtika*.

Regarding the phrase "arising from a *dvandva*": the meaning is that just as when a suffix is applied after a *dvandva* compound, all the word-meanings contained within that *dvandva* are qualified by the number and other properties of the nominal stem-meaning (i.e., they are made to possess a predication-ness [viśeṣyatā] determined by a qualification-ness [viśeṣaṇatā] residing in the number of the nominal stem-meaning), so too, if a suffix were to arise after a collection of verbal roots, then that many root-meanings would be connected with the meaning of the suffix. This refers to the section concerning "other words" (*śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*).

The meaning is: "In the case of a different word, there is a difference in action because of the connection with what has been performed" (Jaimini Sūtra 2.2.1). By "the venerable Bhaṭṭas," it is meant Kumārila Bhaṭṭa. Having reached the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that—in instances such as *yajati* (he sacrifices), *dadāti* (he gives), and *juhoti* (he offers)—since the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denoting the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) produced after each distinct root is one and the same, it is logical that the productive activities of sacrificing, giving, and offering are also one—the author states the reply: "In the case of a different word," and so forth.

When there is a difference in words—that is, a difference in verbal roots—there is a difference in action; that is, a difference in the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) of actions such as sacrifice (*yāga*), and so forth. The word "becomes" is to be supplied [as the verb]. He states the reason for the difference in productive activity: "because of having an established connection" (*kṛtānubandhitvāt*). It is called "having an established connection" because by this [word], a delimitation (*vyavaccheda*) of the productive activity is established. The meaning is that when the meaning of one root is connected with one productive activity, the productive activities of sacrifice, giving, and offering become mutually distinct due to the delimitation of the other productive activities.

It should also be understood that if a suffix were to arise from a collection of verbal roots (*dhātu-samudāya*) when that collection is designated as a "member" (*aṅga*), then the *aṭ* augment, reduplication (*dvirvacana*), and so forth would also belong to the collection as a whole. Now, one might object: since the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*)—defined as denoting an action that is co-located with what is listed in the *bhvādi* group—is present in each individual member, the collection of roots lacks the status of being a verbal root (just as a collection of body parts lacks the status of being a single body part). Therefore, it is utterly impossible to claim that a suffix arises from such a collection.

The stated reasoning does not prove the intention (*vivakṣā*) to restrict the qualifier of the subject (*uddeśya*), nor is there any utility for such an intention in that context; therefore, he says: "of the *ārdhadhātuka*, the augment *iṭ*. [He explains: "as a subject-qualifier" means that in the rule prescribing *iṭ*, the qualifier of the *ārdhadhātuka* which is taken as the subject—namely, "beginning with a consonant" (*valādi*)—is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*). The point is that if there were a fixed rule that a qualifier of the subject is never intended to be significant, then the qualifier of the *ārdhadhātuka*, namely "beginning with a consonant," would result in being redundant.

The intended meaning is that, in this way, the rule in the science of grammar (vyākaraṇa-śāstra) that "the qualification of the subject (uddeśya-viśeṣaṇa) is never intended to be significant" cannot be accepted. The word "evam" (in this way) means: just as the rule that the qualification of the subject is never intended to be significant is not accepted. The word "paśunā" (with an animal) [is used as an example].

Just as in the case of the injunction "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ samārṣṭi*), the singularity inherent in the cup (*graha*) which is the object of the injunction is not intended to be significant, so too, it was argued in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), that the singularity inherent in the animal (*paśu*)—which is conveyed by the suffix (*pratyaya*) in *paśunā*—should likewise not be intended to be significant. However, [the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) states]: in the sentence "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), the sacrifice already established by the *agnīṣomīya* passage is referred to by the root *yaj* (in *yajeta*). The animal is then enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that sacrifice, such that the meaning is "one should effect the sacrifice by means of an animal" (*paśunā yāgaṃ bhāvayet*). Thus, since the animal is enjoined as a subordinate factor with respect to the sacrifice—which is the primary element (*pradhāna*) as the object of the injunction—the animal is indeed a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*).

In this regard, there is no logical principle whatsoever to suggest that "the primary [element] recurs with each subordinate," as opposed to the rule that "the subordinate recurs with each primary. Since the sacrifice is the primary element by virtue of being the objective (*uddeśya*), and since there is a desire to know by how many animals the sacrifice is to be performed, the singular number is introduced by the use of the singular suffix. Because there is no reason to abandon the number already expressed, the singularity residing in the object of the injunction—which is perceived through the singular suffix—is indeed intended as a qualifier of the thing to be enjoined; such is the established rule of the Mīmāṃsakas.

We cannot rely upon the grammatical treatise (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*). Why? To this he says: "Because of [the rule] *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhātaḥ*. This means that because of the prescription of two *nakāra*s, there would be no attainment [of the desired result]. The meaning is as follows: since the rule *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhātaḥ* prescribes a *nakāra* for the *takāra* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix following *repha* and *dakāra*, and since the singular number (*ekatva*) conveyed by the word *naḥ* (the nominative singular of *nadī*) is intended as a qualifier of the thing to be prescribed (*vidheya-viśeṣaṇa*), when that intention is applied, only one *nakāra* is prescribed; therefore, the prescription of two *nakāra*s would not occur.

To the objection, "Let there be no rule for two *n*s; what is the harm? he replies with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*). The meaning is that if the qualifier of the prescribed element were intended [to apply universally], then two *n*s would not be obtained in cases such as *bhinnam*; thus, there is a fault.

Now, one might object: if the rule were enjoined as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*)—meaning that "the *na* occurs in place of both the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix characterized by *r* or *d*, and the *d* preceding it"—then even if two *na*s were not obtained, it would still follow that the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* becomes *na*, and the *d* preceding it also becomes *na*. On the other hand, if the rule is enjoined through a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*)—meaning "the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* becomes *na*, and the *d* preceding it also becomes *na*"—then the obtaining of two *na*s is easily explained. Moreover, because of the inclusion of the word *ca* ("and") in the rule *pūrvasya ca daḥ*, a split in the sentence is indeed the intention of Pāṇini.

Even if one accepts the rule that "an attribute of the thing to be enjoined (vidheya-viśeṣaṇa) must necessarily be intended," there is no fault [in our position]; therefore, what is the reason for not relying on such a rule in the grammatical treatise? To this, he says: "ādguṇaḥ. In the example *upendra* and others, the word "one" (*eka*) is included in the sūtra "ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ" so that, in place of both the preceding and the following sounds, only a single substitute (the *guṇa*) may arise, and not two [substitutes] due to the difference in their original bases (*sthānin*).

Furthermore, if the Mīmāṃsaka rule—that a qualifier of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) must necessarily be intended—is to be strictly maintained in the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), then in the rule *ādguṇaḥ*, since the *guṇa* is the thing to be enjoined, the singularity perceived through the singular number would be its qualifier. And because of the rule that a qualifier of the thing to be enjoined must necessarily be intended, there would be only a single *guṇa* substitute in place of both the preceding and following sounds in cases such as *upendra*; thus, the explicit mention of the word "single" (*eka*) being made again [in the rule *eko yaṇaci*] would be redundant.

Therefore, the meaning is that Pāṇini does not intend a restrictive rule (niyama) stating that "only a qualifier of the thing to be enjoined (vidheya-viśeṣaṇa) is intended [to be significant], while a qualifier of the subject (uddeśya-viśeṣaṇa) is never intended. Now, one might object: "In this way, let there be a rule in the science of grammar (vyākaraṇa-śāstra) that is the reverse of the Mīmāṃsaka position—namely, that only a qualifier of the subject is intended to be significant, and a qualifier of the thing to be enjoined is never intended. To that, we reply: that too is not so.

This should be understood as follows: because in the rule *upeyivānanāśvānanūcānaśca*, it is seen that the qualifier of the subject (*uddeśya*), namely *upeyivān*, is not intended to be significant (i.e., its number is not restricted); whereas in the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, it is seen that the qualifier of the predicate (*vidheya*), namely the singular number, is intended to be significant. Otherwise, forms such as *īyivān* and *samīyivān* would fail to be established, and in cases like *sudhyupāsya*, there would result an *ananta* (non-final) *y* in place of the vowel *i*. Having kept all this in mind, he says: "But the meaning of the word... The meaning is that the intention or non-intention regarding number is the meaning of the word.

Regarding the phrase "of number" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ*) and so forth: in the *Tantra* (the system) and the *Atantra* (the non-system), there is the intention (*vivakṣā*) or lack of intention (*avivakṣā*) regarding the number of the subject (*uddeśya*) and the number of the predicate attribute (*vidheya*). (*Tantra* means intention; *atantra* means lack of intention. *Vivakṣā* is the desire to express; its absence is *avivakṣā*. This is according to the observed examples and in accordance with the grammatical targets, because—this being the reason—it is the accepted view of the desired [authorities]. The words "of the teachers who founded the science of grammar" (*vyākaraṇaśāstrapravartakācāryāṇām*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.)

In the rule *dhātoḥ*, the singular number (*ekatva*) qualifying the subject (*uddeśya*) is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*), whereas in *upeyivān*, the prefix *upa-* is not so intended. Likewise, in *iko yaṇ*, the singular number qualifying the predicate (*vidheya*) is intended to be significant, while in *jvaratvara-*, the singular number qualifying the predicate is not intended to be significant; for this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya that "there are two *ūṭh*s—one for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) and one for the letter *v*. The point is that whether a grammatical feature is intended to be significant or not depends on conformity with the linguistic data (*lakṣya*). The meaning of the phrase *ato hetoḥ* is "for this reason."

Regarding the section on the "singularity of the animal" (*paśvekatvādhikaraṇa*): for there, because of the employment of the instrumental case-ending in the singular number in the word *paśunā*, three factors—the instrument as a grammatical participant (*kāraka*), singularity, and masculinity—are understood from a single nominal suffix (*pratyaya*). Among these, singularity and masculinity are subordinate (*aṅga*), while the instrument as a grammatical participant is the principal (*aṅgin*) or primary element.

Since the instrumental *kāraka* is expressed by the same suffix as the singular number (*ekatva*) and the masculine gender (*puṃstva*), there is a syntactic connection between the gender and number—being proximate due to being conveyed by the same suffix—and the instrumental *kāraka* which is the meaning of the case-ending. However, according to the method stated in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, the singular number, the masculine gender, and the animal (the meaning of the case-ending) first connect individually with the sacrificial productive operation (*yāgabhāvanā*).

And thus, the understanding is that the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of the sacrifice has the triad beginning with the animal as its instrument, expressed as: "one should effect the sacrifice by means of the animal, its singularity, and its masculinity. Subsequently, the connection of masculinity and singularity occurs with the animal, which is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prakṛti*). This is because, seeing that gender and number do not exist independently without a substratum, there arises an expectancy for a locus for singularity and masculinity—asking "on what do these rest?"—and through proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the animal itself is understood as their locus.

It has been stated that the mental cognition (*pārṣṭhika-bodha*) is that [realization] wherein the animal which serves as the means for the sacrifice is understood as being "one" and "male. For example, in the injunction "One purchases Soma with a ruddy, tawny-eyed, one-year-old cow," because there is a rule that syntactical factors (*kārakas*) must necessarily connect only with the action, the four attributes—being ruddy, being tawny-eyed, and so forth—which are not yet connected to the other [substantives], are connected individually to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) of the purchase.

The understanding is that the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of purchase has as its objective factors (*karaṇa*) redness (*āruṇya*), tawny-eyedness (*piṅgākṣī*), one-year-old-ness (*ekahāyanī*), and cow-ness (*go*). Then, when the inquiry arises as to what the redness and other qualities are directed toward, there arises—by virtue of proximity—a subsequent mental cognition (*pārṣṭhika-mānasa-bodha*) that the very cow which serves as the means for the purchase is the same one qualified by the quality of redness, and that she is likewise tawny-eyed and one-year-old; however, this is not a verbal (*śābda*) cognition. This is the sense. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the singularity of the vessel (*graha-ekatva*) is included.

In the injunction "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), cleansing is prescribed with reference to the cups, which contradicts the number nine enjoined by the sentence beginning "There are nine cups for Prajāpati. In that case, because of the contradiction with the number nine found in another sentence, the singularity mentioned in this sentence cannot be included within the scope of the subject matter (*uddeśya*); rather, that [singularity] would also have to be something enjoined.

And thus, in the interpretation of the statement "one should cleanse the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmṛjyāt taṃ caikam*), the split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is indeed evident; therefore, it is said that the singularity of the cup (*grahaikatvam*) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣitam*). As it has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "But elsewhere, cups have been enjoined with various numbers, individually, such as 'nine for Prajāpati' and so forth, endowed with such distinctions. When they are understood as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) in the act of cleansing, how could the number mentioned in reference to those principal entities (*aṅgin*) be intended to be significant?"*1* *1 Vāk. III. 14.58–59. (Cf. Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita, Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakaumudī, paribhāṣāprakaraṇa, paribhāṣā 72: *ekavacanam asamartham*. The meaning is as follows: In other scriptural injunctions, cups are prescribed with plural numbers, such as "nine cups for Prajāpati. Since these cups are already established as subsidiaries through their specific numbers, when they are subsequently mentioned in the context of the cleansing (*saṃmārga*), which is itself a subsidiary, the singular number used there cannot be intended as a restrictive qualification. If it were intended, it would result in a syntactical split, because one would then have to understand two distinct meanings: first, that the cleansing applies to all the cups, and second, that it applies to only one. Therefore, the singular number is merely a conventional usage (*autsargika*) and is not meant to restrict the scope of the action. This principle is applied here to show that the singular number in the word "self" (*ātman*) in the phrase "the self is to be known" (*ātmā jñātavyaḥ*) is likewise not intended to be significant. Thus, the knowledge of the Self is enjoined for every individual soul without exception. This concludes the discussion on the non-intentionality of the singular number. Now, the author proceeds to refute the objection that the Self is not an object of the act of knowing. To do this, he first presents the opponent's view. The opponent argues: "The Self is not an object of the act of knowing, because it is the agent of that very act, just as the knower is not the object of his own act of knowing. This is the formal syllogism (*prayoga*). The Self is the subject (*pakṣa*). "Not an object of the act of knowing" is the probandum (*sādhya*). "Because it is the agent of that act" is the reason (*hetu*). "Just as the knower is not the object of his own act of knowing" is the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*). The opponent further provides a counter-argument (*prasaṅga*) against the proponent: "If the Self were an object of the act of knowing, then it would follow that it is something produced (*janya*), just like a pot. This is the formal syllogism. The Self is the subject. "It would follow that it is something produced" is the probandum. "If it were an object of the act of knowing" is the reason. "Just like a pot" is the corroborative instance. The meaning is: if the Self were an object of the act of knowing, then—since no other cause for its production is possible—it would necessarily follow that it is produced by that very act of knowing. And if it were produced by the act of knowing, it would be impermanent, like a pot. However, the Self is eternal. Therefore, it cannot be an object of the act of knowing. Furthermore, the opponent states: "Moreover, the Self is not an object of the act of knowing, because it is consciousness (*caitanya*), just as the nature of consciousness itself is not an object of the act of knowing. This is the formal syllogism. The Self is the subject. "Not an object of the act of knowing" is the probandum. "Because it is consciousness" is the reason. "Just as the nature of consciousness itself is not an object of the act of knowing" is the corroborative instance. The meaning is: if the Self were an object of the act of knowing, then it would lose its nature as consciousness, just as a pot loses its nature as consciousness when it becomes an object of cognition. But since the Self does not lose its nature as consciousness, it is not an object of the act of knowing. Moreover, the opponent says: "Furthermore, the Self is not an object of the act of knowing, because it is the witness (*sākṣin*) of that act, just as the witness of an act is not itself an object of that act. This is the formal syllogism. The Self is the subject. "Not an object of the act of knowing" is the probandum. "Because it is the witness of that act" is the reason. "Just as the witness of an act is not itself an object of that act" is the corroborative instance. The meaning is: if the Self were an object of the act of knowing, then it would cease to be the witness of that act, just as a pot, being an object of an act, is not its witness. But since the Self remains the witness of the act of knowing, it is not an object of that act. Furthermore, the opponent says: "Also, the Self is not an object of the act of knowing, because it is the illuminator (*prakāśaka*) of that act, just as light is not an object of its own illumination. This is the formal syllogism. The Self is the subject. "Not an object of the act of knowing" is the probandum. "Because it is the illuminator of that act" is the reason. "Just as light is not an object of its own illumination" is the corroborative instance. The meaning is: if the Self were an object of the act of knowing, then it would cease to be the illuminator of that act, just as darkness, being an object of illumination, is not its illuminator. But since the Self remains the illuminator of the act of knowing, it is not an object of that act. Moreover, the opponent says: "Furthermore, the Self is not an object of the act of knowing, because it is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) of that act, just as the enjoyer is not an object of his own enjoyment. This is the formal syllogism. The Self is the subject. "Not an object of the act of knowing" is the probandum. "Because it is the enjoyer of that act" is the reason. "Just as the enjoyer is not an object of his own enjoyment" is the corroborative instance. The meaning is: if the Self were an object of the act of knowing, then it would cease to be the enjoyer of that act, just as food, being an object of enjoyment, is not its enjoyer. But since the Self remains the enjoyer of the act of knowing, it is not an object of that act. Furthermore, the opponent says: "Also, the Self is not an object of the act of knowing, because it is the locus (*āśraya*) of that act, just as the locus of an act is not itself an object of that act. This is the formal syllogism. The Self is the subject. "Not an object of the act of knowing" is the probandum. "Because it is the locus of that act" is the reason. "Just as the locus of an act is not itself an object of that act" is the corroborative instance. The meaning is: if the Self were an object of the act of knowing, then it would cease to be the locus of that act, just as a pot, being an object of an act, is not its locus. But since the Self remains the locus of the act of knowing, it is not an object of that act. Moreover, the opponent says: "Furthermore, the Self is not an object of the act of knowing, because it is the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) of that act, just as the seer is not an object of his own seeing. This is the formal syllogism. The Self is the subject. "Not an object of the act of knowing" is the probandum. "Because it is the seer of that act" is the reason. "Just as the seer is not an object of his own seeing" is the corroborative instance. The meaning is: if the Self were an object of the act of knowing, then it would cease to be the seer of that act, just as a pot, being an object of seeing, is not its seer. But since the Self remains the seer of the act of knowing, it is not an object of that act. Furthermore, the opponent says: "Also, the Self is not an object of the act of knowing, because it is the hearer (*śrotṛ*) of that act, just as the hearer is not an object of his own hearing. This is the formal syl
The meaning is that it is the recourse to the reasons already stated. "Not our established doctrine" means that it is not established by the doctrine set forth in the Mahābhāṣya. || 56 ||

Now, in order to introduce the *kārikā* stating that "the differentiator is the *tantra* (governing factor) with respect to the predicate," he prepares the introductory context with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely). The phrase "vidheyaviśeṣaṇa" means "of the singularity which is a qualifier of the predicate. He says "anyathā" (otherwise) precisely to demonstrate the necessity of intending such singularity; the meaning is: in the absence of the intention to express the singularity of the predicate-qualifier. The example given is "sudhyupāsyaḥ" (to be worshipped by the wise).

The meaning is as follows: since the singular number (*ekatva*) qualifying the *yaṇ* to be enjoined in the rule *iko yaṇ* is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), there would be no injunction characterized by a specific number such that "a *yaṇ* occurs in place of an *ik*. Consequently, just as a single *y* might occur in place of an *ik*, two *y*s or even three *y*s would also result. Regarding the phrase "of others" (*anyeṣām*): just as in examples such as *bhinnam*, where two *n*s occur in place of the *t* and *d*, so too in place of an *ik*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of two, three, or more *y*s occurring instead of a single *y*.

If the singular number were intended as a qualifier of the element to be prescribed (*vidheya*), then the mention of "one" (*eka*) in the rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* would be redundant; he dispels this doubt with the words "and the mention of 'one'" (*ekagrahaṇam ca*). [He explains: "because of the difference in the substituends" (*sthānibhedāt*).

In the rule *pūrvaparayoḥ*, although it would have been simpler to use the compound *pūrvaparasya* by means of a collective (*samāhāra*) *dvandva*, the author has instead employed the cumbersome method of using the distributive (*itaretara-yoga*) *dvandva*—*pūrvaparayoḥ*. By doing so, he indicates that both the preceding and the following elements are individually the substituends (*sthānin*). Consequently, because there is a difference in the substituends, and in accordance with that, the qualifier of the element to be prescribed (*vidheya*) is not intended to be restricted, there might arise two separate substitutions of *guṇa* for the two [substituends]. To prevent this, the word "one" (*eka*) was included; having reflected on these points, [the author] composed the rule.

He says: "In the case of the predicate, the differentiator is the *tantra*. Regarding "the differentiator in the predicate": the differentiator—that is, the qualifier—is defined by the predicate. He states through the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) that what is intended is that which possesses the status of being a qualifier, namely, "the qualifier of the predicate. The meaning is: let that which possesses the property of being a mode (*prakāratā*) as defined by the subject-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the predicate be intended. He explains the meaning of the second quarter of the verse, beginning with "even so," starting from the word "from another" (*anyataḥ*). "Of the thing to be restated" (*anuvādyasya*) means: of the qualifier of the subject (*uddeśya*).

The meaning is: "possessing a qualification (*viśeṣaṇatā*) determined by a subject-locus (*uddeśyaniṣṭha*) ultimate qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*). "There is no restriction" means that the rule—that a qualifier of the subject (*uddeśyaviśeṣaṇa*) is invariably unintended—is not present in the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇaśāstra*). He states the purport of this absence of restriction: "In some cases, it is governed by the principle of *tantra*. The sense is that, in accordance with the illustrative examples (*lakṣya*) supported by the *Bhāṣya* and other authorities, a qualifier of the subject is sometimes intended (*vivakṣyate*) and sometimes not. "Such as syntactic split (*vākyabheda*), etc. refers to these consequences.

The doctrine of the split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) has just now been described above. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), it is understood that the cup (*graha*) possesses primacy because, through the accusative case ending in the word "graham," the cup is intended as the most desired object (*īpsitatama*).

Furthermore, by the principle that "the subordinate element (guṇa) repeats with each principal element (pradhāna)," since all the cups (grahas) present must be cleansed, the cleansing of every cup is established by implication; thus, even though singularity is heard [in the text], it is not intended to be significant. This acceptance is based on the reason that there is no fruit resulting from such an intention. This very point has also been explained at length previously under the heading of "splitting of the sentence" (vākya-bheda), and should therefore be consulted there. The phrase "of that" (tasya) means: of the aforementioned reason regarding the non-intentionality of the qualification of the subject (uddeśya-viśeṣaṇa).

"Anākaram" means that its acceptance in the grammatical treatises (*vyākaraṇaśāstra*) is not established by authoritative source-texts (*ākaragrantha*) such as the *Bhāṣya*, or is even contrary to them. Now, one might raise the objection: "In the case of *dhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.162], just as the singularity [of the root] is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣā*), so too in *ārdhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.35], the state of being preceded by *bal* (the *valāditva*) would likewise be unintended. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The root qualified by singularity," and so forth.

The point is this: just as there exists an obstacle such as a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) when the act of cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) is enjoined with reference to a cup (*graha*) qualified by singularity, so too here there is no such obstacle; therefore, it is possible to enjoin the augment *iṭ* and [the substitution of] *guṇa* with reference to a verbal root (*dhātu*) qualified by singularity and an *ardhadhātuka* suffix qualified by having a *valādi* beginning. Thus, there is no syntactical split, nor is it possible for singularity and the like to be unintended (*avivakṣā*) merely on the strength of referring back to what is already qualified by singularity and so forth.

In the case of "paśunā" (with an animal) and similar expressions, because the number one is conveyed by the nominal suffix (-nā), and because there is no reason to abandon a number that has already been conveyed, the number one—due to its proximity as being conveyed within the same word—is construed with the meaning of the verbal root itself. Thus, since this constitutes a qualified injunction in the form "one should effect the sacrifice by means of an animal qualified by oneness," the oneness is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*). Furthermore, precisely because it is a qualified injunction, there is no risk of the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākya-bheda*).

Since the scripture (śruti) teaches that the qualified [entity] is a subordinate element (aṅga), it is established that just as there is a deficiency of the sacrifice when there is a deficiency of the qualifier "animal-ness" (paśutva) and so forth, there is likewise a deficiency of the sacrifice when there is a deficiency of "oneness" (ekatva). Similarly, in the science of grammar, in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*, because the substitution of *yaṇ* and so forth is prescribed as qualified by oneness, there is neither the contingency of multiple *y*-sounds nor the contingency of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, the intention is that for the grammarians, there is no obstacle whatsoever to adopting the restriction that the qualifier of the thing to be prescribed (*vidheya*) is indeed intended (*vivakṣita*). || 57 ||

One might raise the objection: "But surely the qualifier of the *niṣṭhā* [the suffix] is intended to be significant; thus, if one resorts to such a restrictive rule (*niyama*), would there not be a fault in certain cases? This is expressed by the phrase "nanvevam" (but if this were so). The phrase "nakāradvayalābho na" (there would be no acquisition of two *n*s) means as follows: In the rule *niṣṭhāto naḥ*, the number "one" (*ekatva*)—which is conveyed by the singular form of the predicate (*vidheya*)—is intended to be significant. If that singularity qualified by "one" is indeed intended, then the meaning would be that a single substitute *n*, characterized by oneness, occurs in place of both *t* and *d*. Consequently, in a word like *bhinnam*, two *n*s would not be obtained; rather, only a single *n* would appear in place of both, just as happens with [substitutes for] *guṇa* and other operations.

To dispel such a doubt, he says: "by the two [sounds] *ra* and *da*, through a split in the sentence" (*radābhyāṃ vākyabhedena*). Furthermore, because of the simplicity of not having to employ the word *ca* (and) due to the brevity of the non-splitting of the sentence—specifically, the excellence of simplicity consisting in the absence of the word *ca*—there is the following: in the view that prescribes [the rule] as a single sentence, namely that "the *na* occurs in place of the *ta* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix which follows *ra* and *da*, and also in place of the *ta* preceding that [suffix] when it is preceded by *da*," although one does not obtain two *na*s in examples such as *bhinnam* because of the intention to express the singularity of the *na* to be prescribed, nevertheless, the *na* occurs in place of the *ta* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix which follows *ra* and *da*.

The meaning is as follows: if one were to establish two separate rules by stating, "then [the final *n*] occurs," and "furthermore, in view of the completion [of the word], the *d* of the preceding [element] becomes *n*," then indeed two *n*s would be obtained. Moreover, since Pāṇini intends a split of the sentence precisely by formulating the sūtra with the particle *ca*, there is no obstacle to accepting the restriction that the qualifier of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya-viśeṣaṇa*) is intended to be significant. || 58 ||
Thus ends the determination regarding the intention or non-intention of number in the *Śāṅkarī*, a commentary on the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*.
This determination concerning the intention or non-intention of number has been composed by Saṅkara, the son of Raṅgabhaṭṭa, within this commentary. (12)
Now follows the determination of the meaning of the suffixes *ktvā* and others.

By way of the "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokana*) method—due to the occasion of recollecting the determination of the meaning of the suffixes included within the nominal stem—he says "of the *ktvā* suffix, etc. He explains [this]—that is, he sets forth—the statement "the indeclinable *kṛt* [suffixes]" because of that expression. Regarding "the *tumun* suffix, etc.": it should be understood that although the *ktvā* suffix was mentioned in the introductory commentary by virtue of being specifically prescribed (*pratipadokta*), its inclusion here is intended to highlight its predominance according to the "Brāhmaṇa-Vasiṣṭha" maxim (*brāhmaṇavasiṣṭhanyāya*), owing to the great volume of matters to be stated concerning its scope.

Now, since suffixes such as *tumun* are prescribed after verbal roots (*dhātu*), and because the fruit of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha-phala*) is likewise the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), these suffixes would also apply to that [fruit]. To this he says: "In the sense of *bhāva*. This means: in the sense of the operation (*vyāpāra*) which is primary to the root-meaning. The word "etc. (*ādi*) is for the purpose of including *ktvā* and others. He states the authority for *tumun* and the other suffixes having the sense of operation by saying: "The indeclinable *kṛt*s" (*avyayakṛtaḥ*). This refers to the Vārttika. The meaning of the Vārttika is: those *kṛt* suffixes which cause the designation "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) denote *bhāva*.

The authors of the Bhāṣya also accept that the suffixes *tumun* and others denote only "action" (*bhāva*). However, the meaning of *tumun* and the like is action in its non-substantialized state (*asattvabhūta*), because one does not experience the application of gender or number to the meaning of *tumun* and so forth, as one does in cases such as *pākaḥ*. Thus, it follows that *tumun* and the other suffixes merely restate the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The rule prescribing *tumun* is: *tumun-ṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.10). Its meaning is: that which has an "object" (*artha*)—that is, a purpose—is "for the sake of an action" (*kriyārthā*).

When there is an *upapada* consisting of an action [performed] for the sake of such an action—that is, when there is an *upapada* denoting an action whose fruit is another action—then, from the root (meaning: from the root denoting the action that constitutes the fruit), the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* occur in the sense of the future. Here, because it is stated "for the sake of an action" (*kriyārthāyāṃ kriyāyām*), the sense of being for the sake of something (*tādarthya*) in the form of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) is also expressed by *tumun*. And that is a relation (*saṃsarga*). Furthermore, here, by the force of the expression, the fact of having the same agent (*samānakartṛtva*) is also obtained as a relation, just like the sense of being for the sake of something between the meanings of the base and the *upapada*.

However, there is no manifestation [of the suffix] by way of a specific difference (*vaijātya*) that serves as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) for the non-arising of an expectancy for another action (*kriyāntarākāṅkṣā*), because an expectancy for another action is observed even when the suffix *tumun* has that meaning. There is, however, indeed manifestation by way of a specific difference that serves as the delimitor for the fitness (*yogyatā*) of connection with a *kāraka*. The *ṇvul* prescribed by this [rule] occurs only in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

In expressions such as "he goes to see Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇaṃ draṣṭuṃ yāti*) or "the seer goes [to see] Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇaṃ darśako yāti*), the understanding occurs in this manner: "going, which has Kṛṣṇa as its object, which has as its agent the agent of seeing, and which has seeing as its purpose," or "going, which has as its agent the agent of a future seeing that has Kṛṣṇa as its object, and which has that seeing as its purpose. The *bhāva* (action/state) expressed by suffixes such as *ghañ* exists only in a state of completion (*siddhāvasthāpanna*), because in cases such as "cooking" (*pākaḥ*), we observe its connection with all numbers and so forth.

It was stated previously that being an accomplished entity (*siddhatva*) consists in possessing that specific generic nature (*vaijātya*) which serves as the delimiting factor for the arousal of an expectancy for another action. Even in that case, there is the presentation of the object itself as being in a state of being accomplished (*sādhyāvasthāpanna*). For this very reason, in the expression *odanasya pākaḥ* ("the cooking of the rice"), the word *odanasya* functions as a genitive of the agent (*kāraka-ṣaṣṭhī*), and the use of the suffix *tumun* in expressions such as *bhoktuṃ pākaḥ* ("cooking in order to eat") is justified.

One might object: since the operation conducive to the softening (viklitti) that has reached the state of being an effect (*sādhya*)—as presented by the *ghañ*-affix in words such as *pāka* ("cooking")—is but a single part [of a larger complex], how can there be a grammatical connection (*anvaya*) therein with factors (*kāraka*) such as "of the rice" (*odanasya*), according to the maxim that "a word-meaning connects with a word-meaning, but not with a part of a word-meaning"? If this is raised, we say no; for that maxim is accepted only in regard to objects other than the action (*kriyā*).

For this very reason, the observed syntactic connection of the *kārakas* with a subordinate action in such expressions as *bhoktuṃ gataḥ* ("gone to eat"), *devadattena grāmo gataḥ* ("the village was gone to by Devadatta"), and *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat") becomes coherent. In reality, however, forms such as *bhoktuṃ pākaḥ* ("cooking in order to eat") are simply ungrammatical.

Because it has been stated that [the rule applies] "when there is an action for the sake of another action," proximity (*pratyāsatti*) ensures the attainment of a commonality of kind between the causal action and the effectual action. Thus, just as the effectual action—presented by the verbal root which is the base of the *tumun* suffix—is understood as being subordinate to the meaning of the *tumun* suffix inherent in its own base and as being in a state of being to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*), so too the causal action, when functioning as an *upapada*, is understood only as being subordinate to the meaning of the suffix inherent in its own base and as being in a state of being to-be-accomplished.

Having kept this very point in mind, Bhaṭṭanāgeśa stated in his *Śabdenduśekhara* under the rule *tumunṇvulau* that "the subordinate action (*upapada-kriyā*) which serves as the cause here must be presented by a finite verb (*tiṅanta*). In examples such as *bhoktuṃ gataḥ* ("he went to eat"), the subordinate action that serves as the cause is presented by the verbal root *gam-* (to go). Since this action is subordinate with respect to the agent, who is the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix whose base is that [root], the suffix *tumun* is not grammatically correct when such an action is present as the subordinate element. Thus, the sense is that *tumun* merely restates the meaning of the verbal root itself.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *tum-arthe* that the action (*bhāva*) denoted by suffixes such as *ghañ* is external to the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), whereas that denoted by suffixes such as *tumun* is internal. Having said this, it follows that for suffixes such as *aṇamul* as well, the meaning is indeed an action that has not yet attained the status of a substance (*asattvabhūta*). One might object: "If it is accepted that the *ktvā* suffix denotes only an action that has not yet attained the status of a substance, then rules such as *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle* (Pāṇini 3.4.21) would become redundant. This is the doubt raised by the words beginning with "nanu. [The questioner asks: "What is the solution? (*kā gatiḥ*)?

From the inclusion of terms such as "prior time" (*pūrvakāla*) and so forth, it is understood that prior time and the like are denoted by the *ktvā* suffix. However, if the *ktvā* suffix were to denote merely the abstract action (*bhāva*), that would be inconsistent. Therefore, it must be accepted that agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth are denoted by the *ktvā* suffix. Precisely because the *ktvā* suffix expresses an agent as its meaning, in the sentence "Having cooked the flatbread, I shall eat," the third case ending does not appear after the word "I" (*asmad*). This is because the agent of the cooking is already expressed by the *ktvā* suffix.

With the intention that "the state of having a common agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*) is also obtained because the agent of the cooking (*pākakartṛ*) is construed with the act of eating (*bhojana*) through the relation of being the specifier of the agency residing in itself (*svaniṣṭhakartṛtvanirūpakatā*), he says: "Because of the state of having a common agent, etc. The rule prescribing the suffix *ktvā* is the sūtra: "When there are two actions having a common agent, [the suffix is used] for the one occurring at the earlier time" (*samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle*). Its meaning is as follows: in the phrase "of two having a common agent," the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*); "at the earlier time" (*pūrvakāle*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound.

The suffix *ktvā* occurs after a verbal root that denotes an action qualified by prior time, between two actions whose agents are identical (*samānakartṛka*). Thus, "prior time" is a qualifier of the meaning expressed by the base of the *ktvā*-suffix. The term "past" (*bhūta*) was stated instead of "prior time" out of disregard for brevity, and because there is no experience of cognition [of the action] as being merely "past."

The action expressed by the base of the *ktvā* suffix, being a subordinate element (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to another action, serves as a qualifier for that other action because of the governing rule concerning the connection between verbal roots (*dhātu-sambandha*). Since the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) is untenable without a relation, the meaning of the *ktvā*-base is construed with the meaning of the other verbal root through the relation of immediate succession (*ānantarya*). Thus, the modern grammarians (*navīna*) maintain that just as the genitive case expresses a relation, the *ktvā* suffixes and others can also be said to express relations such as having the same agent (*samāna-kartṛkatva*).

The ancient [grammarians], however, hold that the meaning of *ktvā* is "from a verbal root denoting an action related to an earlier time, between two actions of the same agent whose objects are of the nature of buying. Their intention is that the term "earlier time" (*pūrvakāla*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Consequently, intending to show that suffixes such as *ktvā* indicate the intended relation expressed by the syntactic unity (*vākyaśakti*), he says: "This is the sense. [He then states: "It is a single sentence" (*ekavākyatā*).

The meaning is that "unity of sentence" (*ekavākyatā*) refers to the predominance of a cognition whose primary qualificand is a single action—such as the present act of cooking which has eating as its future fruit, and the present walking which occurs after the meal. This is established for all and proven by universal experience. The point is that it does not mean a split sentence where two actions are the primary qualificands—such as "eating performed by a single agent" and "cooking performed by a single agent"—as would be the case in a construction like *bhuṅkte pacati ca* ("he eats and he cooks").

And that state of being a single sentence (ekavākyatā) between the acts of eating and cooking is not possible without the relationship of qualifier and qualified; thus he says, "otherwise. The meaning is: the acceptance of the status of a single sentence even without the relationship of qualifier and qualified. [He says] "because of the consequence of [absurd] unity of sentence."

The meaning is that the cognition established by experience possesses two primary objects of predication (viśeṣya): namely, "the act of eating performed by a single agent at the present time" and "the act of cooking performed by a single agent at the present time"; however, a syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) characterized by a single primary object of predication is not established by experience there. And so, he says "tathā ca" (and thus), stating that a relation which accounts for the qualifier-qualified relationship must necessarily be stated. The phrase "tayoh" means "of the two acts," namely, the acts of eating and cooking.

The relationship that defines the qualifier-qualified (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya) relation is manifold; like the relations of having a common agent (sāmāna-kartṛkatva) and priority-subsequence in time (pūrva-uttara-kālitva), others are also possible. With the intention that such [other relations] are also expressed by the suffix *ktvā* and others, he says "janyatvam" and so forth. "Sāmānādhikaraṇyam" means "subsisting in a single locus"; that is to say, "having a single agent. "Pūrvottarabhāva" means "the collection of subsistence in a prior time and subsistence in a subsequent time. "Vyāpyatvam" [means] "being produced by eating," etc.

In the expression "he cooks in order to eat" (*bhoktuṃ pacati*), the relationship between the acts of eating and cooking is that of the produced and the producer (*janyajanakabhāva*); this is what is indicated by the suffix *tumun*. In the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyām...* (Pāṇini 3.3.10), it is stated that [the suffix is used] when [the action] is for the sake of another action (*kriyārthāyām*). The sense is that being "for the sake of an action" consists in the nature of the relationship between the produced and the producer. Others, however, hold that the purposefulness (*tādarthya*)—which consists in being the specifier of the object of desire (*uddeśyatvanirūpakatva*)—is what is indicated by *tumun* and the like, and it appears as a relation (*saṃsarga*); and that [purposefulness] is the state of being the object of a desire dependent upon a desire for that [other action].

Since cooking is the object of a desire subordinate to the desire for food, it possesses the property of being the specifier of the "intendedness" (uddeśyatva) residing in the food. Furthermore, futurity is also expressed by the suffix *tumun*, because the word "bhaviṣyati" (in the future) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*) in the sūtra *tumunṇvulau*. Thus, the resulting cognition is: "cooking, which has as its intended object future eating and which is performed by the agent of that eating. Regarding the phrase "produced by eating": in the expression "having eaten, he is satiated," the meaning is "the substratum of that satisfaction which is produced by eating," based on the relation of producer and produced between eating and satisfaction.

This is because the suffix *kta* is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) by the rule *gatyarthākarmaka-* (Pāṇini 3.4.72). Now, one might object: in the case of "having eaten, he is satiated" (*bhuktvā tṛptaḥ*), let there be the manifestation of only immediate succession and common agency as the relation—namely, that the satiation is that which follows immediately after the eating performed by that same agent—rather than accepting the manifestation of the property of being produced (*janyatva*) as the relation, since its body is cumbersome. To this, he says: "For this very reason. This means: precisely because of the acceptance of the manifestation of the property of being produced as the relation. [The phrase] "there is no usage" [is explained as follows].

Even though the drinking of water immediately follows the satisfaction produced by eating, the expression "having drunk, [he is] satisfied" (pītvā tṛptaḥ) does not occur. The meaning is that the aforementioned satisfaction lacks the quality of being produced by the drinking of water. It should be understood that since the substratum of the eating is the very same as the substratum of the satisfaction, there is a perception of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—in the form of both residing in a single substratum—as the relation (*saṃsarga*) between eating and satisfaction; thus, "having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*) is also obtained. Furthermore, this co-referentiality constitutes the relation.

And likewise, in the case of "having eaten, he goes" (*bhuktvā vrajati*), the cognition is that "the act of going, performed by that same agent, occurs at a time subsequent to the act of eating which occurred at a prior time. Since both the occurrence at prior and subsequent times and coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) appear as the relation [between the two acts], he states the form of the resulting cognition in the words "coreferential with eating" (*bhojana-samāna-*). The meaning is: that act of going whose substratum is coreferential with the act of eating.
