The sense is that the very same [agent] who is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the act of eating is also the substratum of the act of walking. "Occurring at a time subsequent to that" means that the act of walking occurs at a time subsequent to the eating that took place in the prior period. Regarding the verse from the *Raghuvamśa* (1.77), "She cursed you, saying 'O son, without honoring my progeny, you shall have no offspring,'" the first half is: "Since you despise me, therefore it shall not be yours. Here, the word "of one standing" (*sthitasya*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).

The meaning is that this is a curse pronounced by Surabhi, with the king as its object, stating: "If you remain without having propitiated my offspring, you shall have no progeny. Thus, since the action of "remaining" (*sthiti*) is taken as the basis for establishing the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) and other such requirements, there is no logical inconsistency regarding the use of the suffix *-ktvā*. And so, by taking the action of remaining as the basis, the establishment of the identity of the agent and so forth ensures that the suffix *-ktvā* is not untenable.

And thus, the understanding is as follows: there is an absence of the act of becoming pregnant by me, which is co-located with the absence of [my husband's] service; and there is an absence of the act of becoming pregnant performed by the future offspring, which stands in a relation of non-difference from that which is the locus of such a state. Furthermore, the aspect of "immediacy" must also be included in the occurrence during the preceding and succeeding times. By this, the expression "having eaten at the father-in-law’s house, he goes" is not used when referring to eating at the father-in-law’s house produced in the previous year and going, whose locus is the current year.

The meaning is that there is an intervention (*vyavadhāna*) caused by a long duration of time between such acts as eating and going. Furthermore, this "non-intervention" (*avyavadhāna*), depending on the intended sense (*tātparya*), should be understood accordingly as occurring in some cases after a moment, in others after an hour, and in yet others after a day or so. Consequently, there is no logical inconsistency in the usage: "Having eaten today, he will go tomorrow. [Objection: But if temporal priority and posteriority (*pūrvottarakālatva*) and the like are accepted as being part of the relation (*saṃsarga*), then the usage "He sleeps with his mouth open" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti*) would not be possible.

The opening of the mouth occurs at the very time of sleep; thus, since the opening does not precede the sleep, the usage "having studied, he remains" (*adhītya tiṣṭhati*) is likewise untenable. This is because study and remaining exist simultaneously, and thus there is no sequence of study immediately preceding the state of remaining. With this intention, [the author] says: "Having studied, he remains," and so forth. Here, the understanding is that he remains together with the act of studying; it does not mean that he first performs the study and only at a subsequent time remains.

For when the persistence of the agent of that [study] is intended to be conveyed as occurring subsequent to the study performed by that same agent, then the usage "having studied, he remains" (*adhītya tiṣṭhati*) indeed occurs. The point here is that the usage in this context intends to convey the meaning: whenever he remains, he does so only in concomitance with the act of studying.

Similarly, in the case of the expression "he sleeps having opened his mouth," it should be understood that the intended meaning is that whenever he sleeps, he does so precisely accompanied by the opening of his mouth. Thus, the sense is that because such expressions are not used at times when [the action] is absent, the two aforementioned usages were not employed with the desire to convey the meaning that the actions of remaining and sleeping occur respectively after the prior acts of studying and sleeping; however, the point is not that such expressions would be improper for such meanings.

Here, by the repetition "whenever... whenever" (*yadā yadā*), the pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) of staying and sleeping is indicated; and by "then... then" (*tadā tadā*), the pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) of studying and keeping the mouth open is likewise suggested. Thus, the meaning is that one never remains [awake] without the pervasive activity of studying, but rather possesses continuous study; similarly, one never sleeps without the pervasive activity of keeping the mouth open, but rather possesses sleep characterized by continuous mouth-opening. This is the intended sense. [The phrase] "delimited by specific times" (*kālaviśeṣāvacchinna*) refers to this.

The meaning is as follows: that study and mouth-opening which are delimited by their respective specific times possess a pervadedness (*vyāpyatā*) defined by a pervasiveness (*vyāpakatā*) residing therein; thus, the staying and sleeping performed by those agents are understood [to be pervaded]. In this context, the relation is pervadedness (*vyāpyatva*) and co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And so, because they are the counter-positives (*pratiyogin*) of absolute non-existences (*atyantābhāva`) that are co-located with themselves, study and mouth-opening are the pervaders (*vyāpaka*).

One's own "abiding" (*sthiti*) and "sleeping" (*svāpa*) are delimited by their respective specific times; the locus of these is Devadatta in such a state. The absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) residing in that [locus]—namely, the absolute non-existence of studying and opening the mouth—does not occur, because those two [activities] exist in Devadatta.

Rather, there is the absolute non-existence of a jar; the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is the jar, while studying and opening the mouth are the non-counter-positives (*apratiyogin*). Since they are non-counter-positives, the pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) defined by abiding and sleeping resides in studying and opening the mouth. Likewise, being non-existent in a locus where its own non-existence occurs is "pervadedness" (*vyāpyatva*).

One's own study (*sva-adhyayana*) is the opening of the mouth (*mukhavyādāna*). One's own absence (*svābhāva*) is the absence of both study and the opening of the mouth. One who possesses that absence (*svābhāvavān*) is Devadatta of such a kind. Motion (*gamana*), cooking (*pacana*), and so forth, reside in him (*tadvṛtti*); staying (*sthiti*) and sleeping (*svāpa*) do not reside in him (*tadavṛtti*). Since staying and sleeping do not reside in him, it follows that one should understand that staying and sleeping possess the property of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*) as defined by the opening of the mouth for the purpose of studying.

And thus, the meaning of the passage beginning with "delimited by a specific time" (*kālaviśeṣāvacchinna*) is as follows: the pervasion (*vyāpyatva*), which consists in co-existence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that which has the nature of the opening of the mouth for study—a nature whose non-pervading factor (*anavacchedaka*) is the absolute absence residing in its own locus (*svādhikaraṇa*) as delimited by that [specific] time—is located in the states of standing and sleeping; this is because of the cognition of that [pervasion]. "And in this way" (*evañca*) means: when [properties] such as being produced (*janyatva*) appear as relations (*saṃsarga*). "Because it is obtainable from another" (*anyalabhyatvāt*)— [The rest of the sentence continues: ...because [the relation] is already established by other means. In the case of the word *svapiti* ("he sleeps"), the relation of the state of sleeping with the subject is not expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), because that relation is already obtained through the denotation of the root (*dhātu*) itself. Therefore, the verbal suffix expresses only the universal (*sāmānya*) aspect of the action. However, in the case of the word *tiṣṭhati* ("he stands"), since the relation of the state of standing with the subject is not obtainable from elsewhere, the verbal suffix expresses that very relation. Thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) [in the definition of verbal suffixes expressing relations], nor is there over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [to nouns], because the relation of the state of standing with the subject is not expressible by the nominal suffix (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, the relation of the state of standing with the subject is not expressible by the nominal suffix because it is not a quality (*guṇa*), and the relation of the state of sleeping with the subject is not expressible by the verbal suffix because it is not a universal (*sāmānya*). Therefore, the distinction between the two words is established. This is the intention. The meaning is that because they are obtainable through the power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*), they do not constitute the denotation of the suffix *ktvā*; thus, what is stated in the *Paramamūla*—that "the indeclinable *kṛt* suffixes occur in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*)"—is indeed correct. Furthermore, it should be understood here that in instances involving a construction ending in *ktvā* as prescribed by the rule *samānakartṛkeṣu...* (Pāṇini 3.4.21), the relation of having a common agent and the relation of preceding and succeeding [actions] appear universally as the relational content (*saṃsarga*). However, relations such as being produced (*janyatva*) and so forth appear in that manner only occasionally, depending on the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).

He states the result that follows from this description of the sentence-meaning with the words "If it is thus" (*evaṃ ceti*). This means: even in the absence of common agency (*samānakartṛkatva*) and so forth being denoted by suffixes such as *ktvā*. Regarding the phrase "of the base-meaning and the action" (*prakṛtyarthakriyayoḥ*): it is a *dvandva* compound meaning "the base-meaning and the action. Alternatively, one may take "base" (*prakṛti*) to refer to both the base of the *ktvā* suffix and the *tap* suffix contained within the word expressing the co-occurring action. Thus, the meaning is "of those two actions which are the meanings of the two bases," and there is no inconsistency.

The meaning is that suffixes such as *ktvā* are indicators (*dyotaka*)—by virtue of making known the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*)—of the relationship described as "co-occurrence" (*saṃsarga*), which consists of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) and so forth, through the expressive power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*). The point is that suffixes like *ktvā* possess only the capacity to indicate the aforementioned relationship, but not the capacity to denote it (*vācakatva*). "For this very reason" means: precisely because suffixes such as *ktvā* indicate relationships such as having a common agent. "A fragment of the Bhāṣya" (*bhāṣyapratīkam*)... [refers to the following].

Regarding the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.21), one asks: "Why does [the suffix] *ktvā* not apply here in the example *pūrvaṃ bhuṅkte paścād vrajati* ('first he eats, afterwards he goes'), given that eating and going have the same agent and occur in a temporal sequence? To resolve this, it is replied: "Because [the sequence] has been expressed by its own word (*svaśabdenoktatvāt*), [the suffix does not apply]."

The meaning of this is as follows: "one's own" (*svam*) refers to the meaning understood from the suffix *ktvā*, namely the prior and posterior time; the words expressing that [time] are "before" (*pūrvam*) and "after" (*paścāt*). Since the prior and posterior time have already been expressed by those [words], the suffix *ktvā* does not occur, according to the maxim: "that which has already been expressed need not be used again. Thus, it is said that the prior and posterior time is to be indicated (*dyotya*), and not the object (*viṣaya*). Kaiyaṭa also states that the suffix *ktvā* and others are not prescribed when the priority and posteriority are conveyed by words forming part of the actual usage, but rather they are prescribed when [the priority and posteriority] are to be indicated.

The meaning here is that because priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) have already been expressed by the words "prior" (*pūrva*) and "subsequent" (*paścāt*), the suffix *ktvā* is not required. By this passage from the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, it is clearly indicated that suffixes such as *ktvā* merely serve to indicate (*dyotaka*) priority, posteriority, and so forth, but do not denote (*vācaka*) them; thus, the intention is that their manifestation occurs solely as a relation (*saṃsargatā*), which is the view agreed upon by the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa. He restates another opinion regarding the meaning of the *ktvā* suffix in order to refute it, beginning with "As for [the claim] that... The term *samānakartṛkayoḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

The meaning of the word *kriyā* (action) is the meaning of another constituent (*anyapadārtha*). Furthermore, in the compound *pūrvakāla*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* in the sense of a genitive case, meaning "that whose time is prior. Thus, between two actions denoted by verbal roots that have the same agent, the suffix *ktvā* must be understood to signify "having the same agent" in the form of "having the same agent as the agent of that specific action," since the action itself is already obtained through the verbal root. Therefore, it must be accepted that the state of having the same agent—consisting in having the same agent as the agent of that respective action—is the expressed meaning of the *ktvā* suffix.

The point is that because the term *samānakartṛka* (having the same agent) is employed, it is understood that having the same agent is expressed (*vācya*) by the suffix *ktvā*. He states the objection (*bādhaka*) to the view that rejects having the same agent as being expressed and instead accepts it as being merely indicated (*dyotaka*): "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). This means: if one does not accept that having the same agent is expressed by the suffix *ktvā*. "The consequence of [using] the third case" (*tṛtīyā-prasaṅga*) means: since the agent is not denoted (*anabhidhāna*) by the suffix *ktvā* in the example *odanaṃ paktvā* ("having cooked the rice"), there would be the consequence of using the third case for the word *asmat* ("I") when used as an agent, as in *ahaṃ*.

One might object: "In the rule *anabhihite*, if one adopts a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (a simple negation) such as 'when [the agent] is not expressed,' then in the case of *bhokṣye* ('I shall eat'), since the agent is already expressed by the *tiṅ*-suffix, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would incorrectly apply to *yayā* ('by which'). To this he replies: "And not by the verb. In the rule *anabhihite*, it is impossible to adopt a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* in the form "when [the agent] is expressed," because that would be beset by faults such as the splitting of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).

And likewise, in the case of *bhokṣye* ("I shall eat"), although the agent of the act of eating (*bhujikriyā*) is expressed by the *tiṅ* suffix following the root *bhuj*, the agent of the act of cooking (*pacikriyā*) is not expressed. Consequently, because he is distinct from one who has already been expressed (*abhihitabhinnatva*), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) in *mayā* is unavoidable. Even though the agent is one and the same, there is a distinction between agents due to the difference in the actions that define their agency; thus, the agent of the act of cooking remains unexpressed. This is what is meant by the statement: "it occurs when [the agent] is unexpressed" (*anabhihite bhavati*). For this very reason—namely, for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*), the term *anabhihita* is understood here as a restrictive exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

Regarding the term *anabhihita*, he states that by resorting to a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), there is not only brevity but also a specific result, namely: *prāsāde āste*. [In this case,] the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *sad* preceded by the prefix *pra* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), according to the rule *hal-śca*. By the rule *upasargasya ghañ-i*, the long vowel is substituted for the final letter of the preceding member.

The meaning is that although the status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) as determined by the action of sitting (*āsikriyā*) is not expressed by the suffix *ghañ*, the locative case in *prasāde* is justified because the status of being a locus as determined by the action of lying down (*śayikriyā*) is not expressed; this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *anabhihite*. He concludes with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He refutes the view that the suffix *ktvā* denotes the agent (*kartṛvācitva*) with "That is not so" (*tan na*). To clarify that the denotation of the agent for *ktvā* is not obtained from the sūtra, he states the meaning of the sūtra: "Of two actions having the same agent," and so forth.

The term *ktvā* [is applied] when there is another word denoting an action (*kriyā-rūpa-anyapadārthe*), and when two actions have the same agent (*samāna-kartṛkayoḥ*) and [one occurs] at a prior time (*pūrva-kāle*); thus, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Consequently, the meaning is that the suffix *ktvā* is attached to a verbal root (*dhātu*) which denotes an action occurring at a prior time (*pūrva-kāla-sambandhin*) between two such actions that possess the same agent (*samānaḥ kartā yayos-tādṛśa-kriyayoḥ*). Therefore, the sense is that both the state of having the same agent and the state of occurring at a prior time are understood as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇatā*) of the action denoted by the verbal root, and not as qualifiers of the suffix *ktvā* itself which is to be enjoined (*vidheya-ktvā-viśeṣaṇatā*). This is the intended meaning.

The intention is as follows: just as in the expression "the owner of brindled cows" (*citraguḥ gauḥ*), the brindled cows are merely qualifiers of the referent of the other word (the cow-owner), and do not qualify the existence (*sattā*) residing in that cow-owner as the cow itself does; likewise, the agent cannot in any way be established as the denotation of the suffix *-ktvā*. This is the essential meaning.

Now, one might object: "If the agenthood of the *ktvā* suffix is not intended to be expressed, then since [properties] such as having the same agent would be understood through the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth—as relations—just like [properties] such as being produced (*janyatva*), their mention in the Sūtra would be entirely redundant. Therefore, following the previously stated method, one must accept that having the same agent is what is expressed by *ktvā*. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). This means: if, according to the previously stated method, the agent were intended to be expressed by *ktvā*. [He then states: "having the same agent" (*samānakartṛka*).

The meaning is that one should say "samānakartṛkayoḥ" (of two having the same agent) after removing [the restriction], and in its place say "samānakartari" (when there is a single agent), just as in the rule "kartari kṛt" (kṛt-affixes occur when the agent is expressed). The phrase "samānakartari" means "ekakartari" (when there is one and the same agent). The ellipsis to be supplied is "asya ktvā bhavati" (the suffix *ktvā* occurs for this). When the question arises as to with which agent the agent of the *ktvā*-meaning is identical, it is understood—by virtue of proximity—that it is identity with the agent of the action denoted by the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) co-occurring [with the gerund], which serves as the qualificand.

And thus, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in the expression "having eaten, he goes" (*bhuktvā vrajati*) is that the subsequent act of going has as its agent one who is non-different from the agent of the prior action of eating. Since the Sūtra was not formulated in such a manner, the implication is that Pāṇini did not intend for the agent to be the direct denotation (*vācya*) of the suffix *-ktvā*.

Now, one might object: "If it is not accepted that the agent (*kartṛ*) is denoted by the suffix *-ktvā*, then in the sentence 'Having cooked rice, I shall eat' (*odanaṃ paktvā'haṃ bhokṣye*), the occurrence of the third case ending after the word *asmad* (I) would remain inevitable. Anticipating this objection, he says "But the induction of the third case... (*tṛtīyāpādanaṃ tu*). Regarding the phrase "of the action which is the meaning of the finite verb" (*ākhyātārthakriyāyāḥ*): according to Yāska’s statement that "the finite verb has the action as its primary meaning" (*bhāvapradhānamākhyātam*), the action presented by the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is the qualificand; and in this context, that refers to the action of eating, namely "I shall eat" (*bhokṣye*). The phrase "because of the denotation of the agent" (*karturabhidhānāt*) [is explained as follows].

The meaning is that since the agent of such a primary action is already expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), and since the agent of the cooking action—which serves as a qualifier for that primary action and is presented by the verbal root that is the base of the *ktvā* suffix—is likewise already expressed, it is impossible for the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) to arise in that context.

The sense is this: although there is a difference between the two actions of cooking (*pāka*) and eating (*bhojana*) which define the agency, and consequently a difference between the two types of agency defined by them, nevertheless, when the agent qualified by the agency defined by the primary action of eating is denoted, it is—according to the *Bhāṣya* and other authorities—also accepted that the agent qualified by the agency defined by the subordinate action of cooking is thereby denoted. Therefore, in the present example, it is all the more difficult to justify the introduction of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*). To substantiate this point, he cites the verses of Hari, saying: "And it has been said."

Regarding the phrase "of the primary and the other": its connection is with the word "of the two actions" (*kriyayoḥ*). And the two actions are connected to the *kāraka*-capacity (*kāraka-śakti*) by way of the relation of being defined (*nirūpitatva*). Furthermore, the *kāraka*-capacity is connected to the substance (*dravya*) by way of the relation of substratum (*āśrayatā*). Thus, the implication is that the two *kāraka*-capacities, which are themselves defined by the two actions standing in the relation of qualifier and qualified, reside together in a single substance. [The statement] "the capacity resides in the quality" (*śaktir guṇāśrayā*) [is explained as follows].

In this context, the meaning is that the *kāraka*-capacity determined by the qualifying action conforms to—that is, follows—the *kāraka*-capacity determined by the qualified (principal) action. He clarifies this very conformity with the words "with respect to the principal object. When the *kāraka*-capacity determined by the principal action is expressed by the suffix—namely, the *tiṅ* suffix—then the *kāraka*-capacity determined by the subordinate action, even if not expressed by the suffix following it, is perceived as if it were expressed, just like the former.

By the same logic, when the kāraka-śakti (case-role power) defined by the principal action has not been expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the kāraka-śakti defined by a subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*)—even if it is expressed by a suffix following its own denoting root—is to be understood as unexpressed. By the word "its own" (*sva*), the subordinate action is to be understood.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya that in the expression *prāsāde* (in the palace), although the locative power (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*) relative to the subordinate action of sitting (*sādī-kriyā*) is expressed by the suffix *ghañ*, the locative power relative to the primary action of sitting (*āsikriyā*)—which is presented by the finite verb ending in *tiṅ* (*āste*)—is not expressed by the *tiṅ*. Consequently, because the locative power relative to the action of sitting is perceived as if it were unexpressed, the seventh case (*saptamī*) occurs in *prāsāde āste*.

Furthermore, one must necessarily accept that the kāraka-power (kāraka-śakti) as determined by a subordinate action (guṇakriyā) must conform to the kāraka-power as determined by the principal action (pradhānakriyā). Otherwise, although the occurrence of the instrumental case would be avoided in the sentence "Having cooked rice, I shall eat" (*odanaṃ paktvā 'haṃ bhokṣye*) by accepting that the suffix *ktvā* denotes the agent, the occurrence of the accusative case after the word *odana* in the sentence "The rice, having been cooked, is eaten by me" (*paktvaudano mayā bhujyate*) would be difficult to prevent; with this intention, he says "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*). He explains the phrase "Otherwise" (*anyathā*) as follows:

The meaning is that it is not accepted that the *kāraka*-capacity defined by a subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*) must conform to the *kāraka*-capacity defined by the principal action (*pradhānakriyā*). Regarding the consequence of [the suffix] *ktvā* being the meaning [of the accusative]: in the sentence "Having cooked, rice is eaten" (*paktvaudano bhujyate*), two instances of objecthood (*karmatva*) are perceived—one defined by the action of eating (*bhujikriyā*) with respect to the rice, and likewise one defined by the action of cooking (*pacikriyā*).

In that case, although the status of being an object (*karmatva*) as defined by the action of eating (*bhujikriyā*) is expressed by the *ktvā* suffix following the root *bhuj*, the status of being an object as defined by the action of cooking (*pacikriyā*) is not expressed by the *kta* suffix following the root *pac*. Consequently, a second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would result after the word *odana* (rice). To prevent this, it must be admitted that the *ktvā* suffix also expresses the object; thus, the meaning is that the object would necessarily become something denoted by the *ktvā* suffix. "By another method" (*prakārāntareṇa*)... [refers to the following].

The meaning is that it is not possible to prevent the occurrence of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) by accepting that the *ktvā* suffix possesses the power to denote the agent. The underlying intention is that the objecthood (*karmatva*) residing in the cooked rice (*odana*), as determined by the action of cooking (*pacikriyā*), is not expressed by the *ktvā* suffix. Furthermore, it is impossible to argue that—just as the *ktvā* suffix denotes the agent—it might also be accepted that it denotes the object; for there is no evidence for such a hypothesis, and it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

The summarized meaning is as follows: since the capacity of a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) as determined by a subordinate action must follow the capacity as determined by the principal action, and because the capacity for "objecthood" (*karmatva*) as determined by the principal verbal action denoted by the *tiṅ*-suffix is expressed by that *tiṅ*-suffix itself, there is no occurrence of the second case (*dvitīyā*)—even though that same capacity as determined by the subordinate action of cooking (*pacikriyā*) is not expressed by the suffix *-ktvā*—because it is perceived as if it were already expressed.

Furthermore, on the view that [the suffixes] denote [the action], there would be the consequence of multiple meanings for *ktvā* and other such suffixes, such as "being produced" (*janyatva*) and "being pervaded" (*vyāpyatva*). If "being produced" and so forth were the denoted meanings, then by the rule that "between the meaning of the stem and the meaning of the suffix, the meaning of the suffix is predominant" because it is the meaning of the suffix, these [meanings] would result in being the qualificands (*viśeṣya*). Consequently, in the case of *bhuktvā bhuktvā vrajati* ("having eaten repeatedly, he goes"), the doubling [of the suffix]—which occurs when repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is to be denoted—would not apply, because the predominance of the action [as the primary element] would be absent.

Nor should it be argued that even in the Siddhānta, because actions presented by forms ending in *ktvā* serve as qualifiers for the action conveyed by the finite verb (*tiṅanta*), the predominance of the action is absent; consequently, the problem of the non-occurrence of reduplication—as in *bhuktvā bhuktvā*—remains exactly as it was.

The point is this: although the rule "the verb denotes the primary state" (*bhāvapradhānamākhyātam*) is set aside by the principle that the meaning of the suffix is primary, what is actually intended here is the opposite—that the meaning of the verbal root, which is the base of the suffix, is primary in relation to the meaning of the suffix. Therefore, even though these actions expressed by the *ktvā* suffix function as qualifiers with respect to another action, there is no loss of the primacy of the action itself. However, if [properties] such as "being produced" (*janyatva*) were the meanings expressed by the *ktvā* suffix, then because they would be the meanings of the suffix, they would become the qualificands (*viśeṣya*), and thus the primacy of the action would be lost. This is the underlying sense.

In this regard, the following should be understood: by the statement "the verb (ākhyāta) has action as its primary meaning," which sets aside the general rule that the meaning of the suffix is primary, it is made known that the action conveyed by a finite verb (tiṅanta) is predominant. Consequently, in expressions such as *snātvā bhuktvā pītvā vrajati* ("having bathed, eaten, and drunk, he goes"), the suffix *ktvā* is used everywhere by taking the state of being prior relative to the action of going (*vrajanakriyā*), and not by taking the state of being prior relative to actions such as eating.

That being the case, just as in expressions such as "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*), there is a lack of intention to express the singularity and so forth of the base even when it is not intended, so too—when it is said, "Of these Brahmins, let the one who is first be brought," the very first among all is brought, and not someone who is merely prior to some middle one; likewise here, the suffix *ktvā* would belong only to the act of bathing (*snāna*) and not to eating (*bhuj*) and the rest. Thus, the actions beginning with bathing and ending with drinking are construed only with the action of going (*vrajana*).

But [this does not apply] to the act of bathing in relation to eating and so forth; the meaning is that, according to the maxim "qualities are for the sake of another" (*guṇānāṃ ca parārthatvāt*), there is no mutual connection between the actions beginning with bathing and ending with drinking. For this very reason, even the reversed construction "having eaten, having drunk, having bathed, he goes" (*bhuktvā pītvā snātvā vrajati*) is justified. In the case of the statement "having invoked, one should worship with the sixteen services" (*āvāhya ṣoḍaśopacāraiḥ pūjayet*), the phrase "with the sixteen services" functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the worship qualified by the invocation; or else, the qualification of the worship by the invocation occurs through an internal relationship.

And thus, since the meaning understood is that worship consists of the performance of the sixteen services subsequent to the invocation, it should be noted that there is no fault even if the invocation itself is included within those sixteen services; enough of this. 59.

Thus ends the determination of the meaning of *ktvā* and other suffixes in the *Śāṅkarī*, a commentary on the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, composed by Śaṅkara, the son of Raṅgabhaṭṭa; in this exposition of the *Sāra*, the determination of the meaning of *tumun*, *ktvā*, and others has been completed. (13)
Now, the investigation of *sphoṭa*.

In order to suggest that the analysis of the meanings of bases, suffixes, and so forth, previously mentioned, is unreal, he says: "siddhānta... (regarding the established doctrine). This means the firm conviction of the established doctrine that the *sphoṭa* alone is the expressive agent. He states—meaning he declares—the *vākya-sphoṭa* and so forth. "Eight positions" refers to these very eight positions which he points out in sequence by name, beginning with "varṇa-sphoṭa" and so on. "Akhaṇḍa-pada-vākya" means the pair consisting of the indivisible word-*sphoṭa* and the indivisible sentence-*sphoṭa*. "Jāti-sphoṭāḥ" means...

The meaning is that there are three [types]: the *sphoṭa* of the class of phonemes (*varṇajāti-sphoṭa*), the *sphoṭa* of the class of words (*padajāti-sphoṭa*), and the *sphoṭa* of the class of sentences (*vākyajāti-sphoṭa*). One should not think that because a word or a sentence is indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*), there is no universal (*jāti*) therein; for this very reason, the latter two positions have been set forth. By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that from which the meaning bursts forth (*sphuṭati*) or is manifested (*prakāśate*)," it is concluded that *sphoṭa* is the word that causes the cognition of meaning.

The sequence is as follows: from the articulated manifesting sound (vyañjaka-śabda), there arises the cognition of the word called *sphoṭa* which resembles it; and from that [cognition of the *sphoṭa*], there arises the cognition of the meaning. In the investigation into the eternality of the word, it is the word called *sphoṭa* alone that is eternal, and that alone possesses the meaning. Since this is accepted by authoritative sources such as the Bhāṣya, and since there is no other [entity] to be excluded among the eight positions [regarding the nature of the word], he says "useless" (*anarthakam*)—meaning that the mention of "sentence" (*vākya*) would be redundant. He further says "and meaningless" (*durarthakam*), because [the term "sentence"] serves to exclude *sphoṭas* other than those established in the Bhāṣya's own doctrine, such as the *dhvani*-type *sphoṭa*.

Now, for what purpose then is the mention of "sentence" (vākya)? To this he says: "of those [sphoṭas] other than the sentence-sphoṭa. Regarding their "unreality": among the eight types of sphoṭas, the sentence-sphoṭa alone is primary. This is because, through the usage of elders—which is the crest-jewel among the means of grasping linguistic capacity (śakti)—the capacity is first grasped in relation to the sentence as a whole; thus, in common worldly usage, it is the sentence-sphoṭa alone that conveys meaning.

The meaning is that the acceptance of *varṇasphoṭa* and the others is solely for the purpose of establishing the grammatical system (*sāstra-prakriyā*). With this very intention, he says: "in the ultimate analysis" (*atiniṣkarṣe*). "This is the established view" (*iti mata-sthitiḥ*) means the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), such as the author of the Mahābhāṣya and others. Since the word *sphoṭa* possesses both etymological and conventional meanings (*yogarūḍhatva*), like words such as *paṅgaja*, the term *vākyasphoṭa* means that the sentence is the signifier (*vācaka*). Similarly, for *varṇasphoṭa* and the rest, the meaning is that the phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth are the signifiers.

In that regard, while examining all of them in sequence, he first states the *varṇasphoṭa* [the phoneme-sphoṭa] with the words "within the correct word" (*sādhuśabde’ntar*). "Disagreement" (*vipratipatti*) means dispute. Here, the Naiyāyikas say this: the suffixes such as *la*, *karmaṇi*, *ca*, and *o*, as well as the case-endings such as *su*, *au*, *jas*, and *am*, which are evoked by the correct words *ghaṭati*, *bravīti*, *visarga*, and so forth, are themselves the expressive agents (*vācaka*), because it is precisely their status as expressive agents that has been established by rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi ca* and *svaujasam*.

However, the case of *tib*, *visarga*, and so forth is like that of written characters (*lipi*): they convey meaning through the recollection of the substituends, such as the letter *l*. Thus, the positive position—that the letter *l* and so on are the expressive units (*vācaka*)—belongs to other Naiyāyikas; this is the meaning. The negative position—that the *l*-suffixes and so on are not expressive—belongs to us, the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*); this is the meaning. Consequently, it results that the body of the dispute (*vipratipatti*) is whether or not the *l*-suffixes and *sva*-suffixes, which are the substituends (*sthānin*) residing within correct words (*sādhuśabda*) by way of their substitutes (*ādeśa*), are expressive.

If, however, the body of the dispute were accepted as being whether the *tiP* suffix, the visarga, and so forth, contained within correct words (*sādhuśabda*) are expressive (*vācaka*) or not, then the subsequent passage—which states that the affirmative position belongs to others and the negative position to the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*)—would be utterly inconsistent. This is because the Naiyāyikas do not accept that the *tiP* suffix and so forth are expressive, whereas the Grammarians have established as their own tenet (*siddhānta*) that the *tiP* suffix and so forth alone are expressive.

Therefore, students are taught by their teachers that "the point of contention is whether or not expressive words are included within correct words (*sādhuśabda*). In this context, the phrase "not included within correct words" should be understood to mean those elements such as *l*-affixes and *sva*-affixes which, being the substitutes for the actually heard *ti*, *visarga*, and so forth, are consequently not included within the [actual] correct forms to be derived.

Thus, against the Naiyāyikas who maintain that only the *l*-suffixes and so forth possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), and not the *tiP*, visarga, and other elements contained within actual usage, he says: "For it is those [sounds] internal to the correct word (*sādhuśabda*) that are denotative, not those merely remembered as such. He explains this meaning word by word: "In the correct word"—that is, when words such as *pacati* or *rāmaḥ* are employed—"those internal constituent parts," namely the *tiP*, visarga, and so on, "are themselves the conveyors"—the meaning is that they are the denoters (*vācakāḥ*). To the question of how the status of being a denoter is obtained from the term "conveyor" (*bodhaka*), he replies: "Of those very [parts]."

The meaning is: "only those [phonemes] which are properly internal and are actually heard," such as the *t* and the *visarga*. "Power" (*śaktatva*) means "denotative capacity" (*vācakatva*). This is because, as stated previously—in the thirty-seventh verse beginning with "of the sense organs with respect to their own objects"—the view that "power is simply the capacity to produce cognition" has been established. "Because it has been settled" means: because it has been determined through an investigation of supporting and subverting arguments.

Even in the view that "potency (*śakti*) is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*)," it should be understood that the potency postulated because the capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatva*) would otherwise be inexplicable is co-extensive with that very capacity to convey meaning. Thus, once it is established that there is no capacity to convey meaning in those [forms] not included among correct words (*sādhuśabda*), the absence of potency is also established by implication. "But not... means that the *la*-suffixes and *sva*-suffixes, which are merely recalled (*smārita*) by the heard *tiP*, visarga (*visarga*), and so forth contained within correct words, are not at all the expressive agents (*vācaka*). || 60 ||

He introduces the view of the Naiyāyikas, who are adherents of other philosophical systems, in order to refute it—beginning with the words "But those who... He states the reason for the lack of denotative power (*vācakatva*) in *tiṅ*, visarga, and so forth, which occur in grammatical usage, with the words "Of these," etc. This means: of *tiṅ*, visarga, and so on, which are components of grammatical usage. "By way of multiplicity" means: by way of being more numerous than their respective substituends (*sthānin*), such as *la* and the suffixes beginning with *su*. "An infinity of powers" means: because one would have to postulate a separate power for each of those many elements, there would result an infinity of powers.

The sense is that because "plurality" (*bahutva*) is undelimited and thus infinite, there would be an infinity of powers (*śakti*). The phrase "infinity of power" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); by it, one should understand another defect in this position: the cumbersome requirement (*gaurava*) that the property of being the delimitor of capacity (*śaktatāvacchedakatva*) must also be postulated in the numerous serial orders (*ānupūrvī*) residing in the various substitutes (*ādeśa*).

Furthermore, in cases where substitutes such as *l* and others take the form of non-existence (*abhāva*) through elision (*luk*) and so forth, since it is never observed that non-existence generates cognition, it is all the more impossible for such substitutes to possess the capacity to convey meaning; therefore, he says: "edhāṃcakre. Here, by the rule "āmaḥ," there is elision (*luk*) of the *liṭ* suffix. Regarding the phrase "of the elision and so forth which consists of non-existence": the term "consisting of non-existence" is a qualification intended to provide a reason (*hetugarbha*). Since a substitute in the form of elision and so forth is of the nature of non-existence, it follows that its capacity to convey meaning is impossible.

The point is that since the power consisting of the capacity to convey meaning (bodhakatva) resides in positive entities, an absence can never produce cognition anywhere. In the case of *edhāṃścakre*, it is clear from the treatises that the understanding of time, agent, and other factors arises solely through the substitute *tiṅ* affix heard after the subsequently employed root (*anuprayujyamāna-dhātu*).

Although the meaning of that [verbal root]—such as its object, time, and agent—enters into a syntactic relation (*anvaya*) only with the meaning of the auxiliary verbs *kṛ* and so forth that are subsequently employed, nevertheless, it is indeed possible for that meaning to appear implicitly (*ārthika-bhāna*) even in the sense of roots like *edh*, through a relation of non-difference (*abheda*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kaumudī* on the rule "The root *kṛ* is also employed as an auxiliary" (*kṛñ cānuprayujyate*): "Because those [auxiliaries] express general action (*kriyā-sāmānya*), while the original verbal bases (*āmaprakṛti*) express specific action (*viśeṣa-vācitva*), there is a relation of non-difference between their respective meanings."

Regarding the relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*): words such as *edh-* (to increase) signify an activity conducive to their respective results; the root *kṛñ* signifies an activity conducive to production (*utpatti*); and the roots *bhū* and *as* denote activities conducive to existence (*sattā*). Due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), production and so forth must reside in the result that constitutes the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛti*). Thus, from the sentence *aidhāṃścakre* ("he grew"), the understanding to be derived is: "an activity conducive to a past, non-present, remote production, which is non-different from an activity conducive to growth, having a single agent."

Thus, even in the view that substitutes (ādeśas) possess denotative power, there is no fault here; this is what is meant by the statement "it is Brahman. The word "etcetera" (ādi) is for the purpose of including [forms such as] *vāri*, *pacati*, *apaḥ*, *apāt*, and so on. By the phrase "of elision, etc. (*lugādeḥ*), elision (*lup*) and disappearance (*lopa*) are included. The point here is that since elision and the like are of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), and since non-existence lacks the capacity to produce cognition, the understanding of number, object, and so forth would not occur; thus, the fault remains as it was in the view that substitutes possess denotative power.

[Objection: "But even here, according to the maxim that 'that which remains expresses the meaning of what has been elided,' it is the base (prakṛti) itself that generates the cognition of the meaning of the elided suffix. [Reply: This is not so. Rather than postulating a power (śakti) in the base for each respective meaning of those suffixes, it is simpler to postulate the recollection of the suffix—which is already established as the expressive agent in cases such as *atra pauṣamahaḥ*, *rāmeṣu*, *payasā*, *payase*, *lihau*, and *duhau*. Thus he says: "But by them," meaning "by the substitutes consisting of *tiP*, the visarga, and so forth."

The meaning is that *la* and so forth, as well as *sva* and so forth, are expressive only when they function as substituends (*sthānin*). He states "of the quality of being *l*" (*latvasya*) because there is also a parsimony of the delimitors of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka-lāghava*) when the substituend possesses expressiveness.

Just as the universal "potness" (*ghaṭatva*) is postulated for the sake of accounting for the inclusive cognition that arises regarding many individual pots—namely, the cognition "this is a pot," "this is a pot," which takes a single property as its qualifier—in the same way, the status of "la-ness" (*latva*) as a universal is established for that which is postulated for the sake of establishing the inclusive cognition arising everywhere with respect to the *la*-suffixes and others, namely, the cognition "this is *la*," "this is *la*. The point is that inclusive cognition alone is the basis for postulating a universal.

And thus, it is appropriate to postulate that the property of being a *la* (the letter *l*) alone is the delimitor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedakatva*), just as the property of being a *ghaṭa* is; and since that delimitor of expressibility (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is one and the same in the form of a universal (*jāti*), there is a parsimony (*lāghava*) regarding the delimitor of expressive power—this is the meaning. The point is that if the substitutes (*ādeśas*) were themselves the denoters, then because they possess various forms, it would be impossible to postulate a single, recurring property [as their delimitor]; consequently, the delimiters of expressibility would also be manifold, resulting in a complexity (*gaurava*) regarding the delimiters of expressibility.

He states another argument for the fact that the *l*-suffixes are the expressive agents (vācaka): "and because of non-deviation" (*avyabhicārāt*). Deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is the violation of the rule governing the relationship between cause and effect; its absence is non-deviation. Therefore, for this reason as well, it is logical that the expressive agency belongs to the *l*-suffix itself, which denotes the tense (stānin). For instance, with respect to the cognition whose object is the meaning of the word "jar," the cognition of the word "jar"—which possesses that meaning—is the cause.

For this very reason, since it is observed in the world that for one who does not know the word "jar" (ghaṭa), the knowledge of its meaning does not arise even when that [word] is known—thereby establishing through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) the causal relationship between the knowledge of the word and the knowledge of the word-meaning—it follows that in this case, the knowledge of the word signifying that object is the cause, and the knowledge of that object is the effect.

Thus, since the knowledge of the suffixes *la* and so forth, which possess those meanings, is the cause for the knowledge of the meanings such as the agent (*kartṛ*), wherever there is knowledge of the meaning such as the agent, there—prior to that knowledge of the meaning—the knowledge of the suffix possessing that meaning necessarily exists. Therefore, because the causal relationship between the word and the knowledge of its meaning—which is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in the form "when this exists, that exists; when this is absent, that is absent"—is not subject to deviation in the negative instance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), for this reason as well, the expressive power (*vācakatva*) belongs only to the substituendum (*sthānin*), namely the suffix *la* and so forth.

The sense is that this is logical. He states "of the substitutes" (*ādeśānām*) because, in the view that substitutes possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), there is the fault of deviation through negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*). If the substitutes such as *tiP*, the visarga, and so forth, which are heard in established usages like *pacati* and *rāmaḥ*, were themselves denotative, then—since those substitutes such as *tas* and others are distinct—the substitute *tas* would be different from the substitute *tiP*, and the substitute *tiP* would be different from the substitute *tas*. Thus, *tas* would possess a difference relative to *tiP*, and *tiP* would possess a difference relative to *tas*.

Thus, because there is multiplicity due to mutual opposition (*pratiyogika-bheda*), it must be stated that with respect to the cognition of the meanings such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, the cognition of the substitutes *ti* and *ba* signifying those meanings, as well as the cognition of the substitutes *tas* and *āt* signifying those meanings, are the causes.

The point is that in both cases—*bhavati* and *bhavataḥ*—although there exists knowledge of the meaning of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, in the case of *bhavati*, there is no knowledge of the substitution of *-tas* which serves as the cause for the knowledge of the agent-meaning; and in the case of *bhavataḥ*, there is no knowledge of the substitution of *-tiP* which serves as the cause for such knowledge. Thus, even though the effect (the knowledge of the meaning) is present, the absence of the cause establishes a clear instance of "deviation in negative concomitance" (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*). This is also because [the rule] is consistent [with this view].

Furthermore, following the meaning of sūtras such as *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), it is clearly understood that the *lakāras* themselves possess the expressive power (*vācakatva*). Just as the authority of Pāṇini and others, the founders of the science of grammar, is found regarding the expressive power of the *lakāras*, no such authority is found regarding the expressive power of the substitutes (*ādeśas*) such as the *tibs* and the *visarga*. Thus they say. And so, their intention is that the expressive power belongs only to the *lakāras*, which are the original forms (*ādeśins*) to which the substitutes belong, and this is supported by authoritative evidence (*prāmāṇika*).

Nor should it be argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of understanding [the meaning] even from "bhū-la" (the substitution form *la* for *liṭ*). This is because we accept that a specific co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*), such as with the word "bhavati," serves as the cause for such an understanding. Otherwise, in your own view as well, the consequence of understanding [the meaning] from "bhū-ati" and so forth would arise. As for the understanding of those who lack knowledge of the original element (*sthānin*) *lakāra*, it is accounted for by a misconception of the expressive power (*śakti*) residing in the substitute (*ādeśa*). The point is that, just as in the case of corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), the capacity to convey meaning is postulated through a misconception of expressive power.

The sense is that the *sphoṭa*—which is devoid of denotative power residing solely in the path of what is merely heard—is not tenable. "Those [logicians, etc. refers to the Naiyāyikas and others. "By means of arguments supporting their own position" means by means of arguments that nourish their own view that the *ti*, *t* (the *tit*), visarga, and so forth are the denoters. He refutes or sets aside [this view] by stating, "because of the established usage. How is the agent [of the action of denoting] understood? It is "in accordance with the established order" (*vyavasthā*). "Established order" (*vyavasthā*) means the determination of meaning through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); the sense is "by following that."

Regarding the term "vācakāḥ" (expressive): only the audible [sounds] such as the *ti* and *visarga*, which constitute the connection with correct words (*sādhuśabda*), are expressive; the meaning is that the *l*-substitutes (*la-ādeśa*) remembered by those [audible sounds] are not themselves expressive. Thus, the word ending in the ablative case, "evam vyavasthiteḥ" (because of this established state), is to be construed with "bodhakāḥ" (the indicators) mentioned in the preceding verse. It should be understood that the two phrases beginning with "evam vyavahṛteḥ" (because of such usage) are likewise to be construed in that same place.

Regarding this, those who know the tradition say as follows: if the substitutes (*ādeśas*) possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), then the established rule (*vyavasthā*) that in the word *rāmaḥ*, the *visarga* denotes singularity is maintained. If the original forms (*smartāni*) possessed denotative power, there would be no such fixed rule. For instance, in the case of *rāmaḥ*, by means of the *visarga*, should *su* be remembered [as the original], or *rū*, or *si*? By the followers of Pāṇini, *su* is prescribed; by others, *rū*; and by those versed in the Kālāpa-tantra, *si*.

As for the argument that one who is conversant with all the grammatical treatises (*tantra*) would, due to the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamanā*), lack the recollection of any particular rule because of cognitive obstruction—this is not correct. Just as there is no obstruction to the simultaneous mental presence of multiple words when one knows many scripts, so too there is no obstruction to the recollection of substitutes (*ādeśa*) for one who is proficient in all the grammars.

However, there is memory for all [words], and by that [memory] there is the presentation of the object; and that [presentation] is non-distinct (*avilakṣaṇā*), meaning it is not distinct—that is, not different—but rather uniform. Therefore, even from various synonyms such as *ghaṭa*, *kalaśa*, and so on, a non-distinct cognition is logically established. For this reason, he explains otherwise with the words "For instance" (*tathāhi*) and so forth. [The phrase] "from the cognition" (*bodhāt*).

Since even those common people who lack knowledge of the *l*-suffixes and so forth are observed to have a cognition of the meanings such as the agent (*kartṛ*) in cases like "he cooks" (*pacati*), it is not appropriate to postulate that the *l*-suffixes possess denotative power (*vācakatva*). Thus, because there is a deviation from the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*)—namely, that the effect [the cognition of meaning] occurs even in the absence of the cause [the suffixes]—the impossibility of the *l*-suffix having denotative power is all the more evident. Consequently, the intended sense is that the very non-occurrence of the cognition [of meaning] constitutes the meaning of the term "lack of determination" (*avyavasthā*) in this context.

Regarding what was stated by those who maintain that the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix) is the expressive unit—that in cases such as *pacati*, understanding occurs for those devoid of knowledge of the *lakāra* which serves as the *sthānin* (the original element), due to a misconception of its expressive power (*śaktibhrama*), just as it does with corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*)—he refutes this, saying "And not... and so forth. "Of them" means of ordinary people who lack knowledge of the *lakāra* in expressions such as *pacati*. "Due to a misconception of its expressive power" [is the meaning].

The meaning is as follows: just as there is an error regarding the nature of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell due to seeing its shimmering appearance, so too, because the *tiṅ* suffix is observed in every usage such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), whereas the *lakāra* (the verbal root marker) is never observed in any established usage, those [opponents] mistakenly hold that the expressive power resides in the *tiṅ*s alone. Regarding the word "tasya" (of that): it means of the expressiveness (*vācakatva*) which arises from the heard *tiṅ* substitutes in *pacati* and so forth, and which is the cause for the cognition of the meanings of the agent and so on. Regarding "mānābhāvāt": it means because there is an absence of any valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for [proving] that this is an error.

The rule is that error (bhramatva) exists only where there is a sublation (bādha) of the object [of cognition]. For example, because the silver-ness in a mother-of-pearl shell is sublated, the cognition of it is an error; likewise, in the present case, since expressiveness (vācakatva) is not sublated, it is impossible to say that the cognition of it is an error. Since the cognition of the meaning of the agent and so forth arises from the *tiṅ* suffixes and other elements contained in words such as *pacati*, and because the power of expressiveness is uncontradicted therein, it is all the more impossible to speak of error; thus, the sense is that there is no evidence for its being an error.

One might object: "Since there are many substitutes (ādeśa) such as *tiP* and others, if one accepts their power to denote meaning (*vācakatva-śakti*), then that very multiplicity would be an obstacle. To this, he says: "Of the substituends (*ādeśin*) as well. This means: of the bases (*sthānin*) for the substitutes such as *tiP*, *visarga*, and so forth. "By various grammarians" means: by Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, Śākaṭāyana, Apiśali, and other etymologists (*śābdika*). "Of distinct [forms]" means: because they have been stated according to their own respective preferences in various ways, such as *suḥ*, *siḥ*, *ruḥ*, *laṭ*, *kaṭ*, or some other form.

The meaning is that this is because the teachers who promulgate the treatises act according to their own independent will (*svatantra-icchā*). In that regard, since it is impossible to determine which substitute (*sthānin*) is expressive (*vācaka*) and which is not, the conclusion is reached that "this alone is the expressive substitute"; such is the sense. Now, one might object: "Since there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanā-viraha*), let all substitutes be expressive. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of all" (*sarveṣām*). This means: "of all those various substitutes belonging to the different grammarians who follow their own independent will."

"Even if the capacity to denote is accepted"—this is the ellipsis (*iti śeṣaḥ*). "Excessive complexity" (*gauravam*) means that because one must necessarily postulate a separate denotative power for each of the many substituends (*sthānin*), there is excessive complexity due to the multiplicity of powers. Now, even so, since the substituends are fewer in number than the substitutes (*ādeśa*), one might argue that the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) favors the substituends alone as being the denoters; to this, he says: "And there would be deviation" (*vyabhicāraśca*). For instance, the cognition of meanings such as singularity in the word *rāma* is established by universal experience.

To account for such an experience, one must state the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) that a cognition of the substituend (*sthānin*) is the cause of a cognition whose object is the meaning of "oneness" (*ekatva*) and so forth. In this regard, in the system of Pāṇini, although there exists a cognition of the substituend *sup* suffix in the word "rāma," there is no cognition of the *si* suffix; likewise, in the system of Kālāpa, although there exists a cognition of the *si* suffix, there is no cognition of the *sup* suffix.

The meaning is as follows: since the cognition of meanings such as "oneness" (ekatva) indeed exists even in both philosophical systems, there is a deviation from the rule of negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyabhicāra); for even when one [of the two] is absent, the other produces the understanding of the meaning such as oneness, and thus the effect exists despite the absence of the cause. Consequently, the sense is that those two defects—which led to the abandonment of the position that the substitutes (ādeśas) possess denotative power—remain unavoidable even under the position that the original bases (stānins) possess denotative power.

Since there is no deviation from the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)—given that the knowledge of the substitutes (*ādeśa*) necessarily exists prior to the knowledge of the meanings such as singularity (*ekatva*)—it is logical that the expressive power (*vācakatva*) belongs only to the substitutes occurring within actual usage; thus he says: "of the substitutes in usage" (*ādeśānāṃ prayoge*). In this way, although the two positions are equal in terms of the faults of complexity (*gaurava*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*), there is greater complexity in the position that the original bases (*sthānin*) possess the expressive power, because it involves the additional burden of postulating the recollection of the original base. In the position that the substitutes possess the expressive power, however, that [burden] does not exist; thus there is simplicity (*lāghava*). This is what he expresses with the passage beginning "And so" (*tathā ca*) and ending with "simplicity" (*lāghavam*).

Now, since Bhaṭṭanāgeśa stated in the *Mañjūṣā* that the relationship between a word and its meaning—consisting of the nature of the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*)—is what constitutes "potency" (*śakti*), it would be appropriate to accept that potency only where such a signifier-signified relationship is established by a grammatical rule (*śāstra*). Since the signifier-signified relationship is specified for the *l*-suffixes and others specifically by rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), it follows that the capacity to signify belongs to the *l*-suffixes alone.

Considering the lack of conviction that the complexity (gaurava) of postulating the recollection of substitutes (*ādeśa*) is not a fault because it is based on authoritative sources, [the author] sets forth another argument for accepting that the *tiṅ* and other substitutes heard in actual usage are themselves expressive (*vācaka*), beginning with the words "from usage" (*vyavahṛteḥ*). Regarding the phrase "primary": the elders state that the apprehension of word-power (*śaktigraha*) occurs through grammar, comparison, lexicons, the statements of reliable persons, usage, the remainder of a sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), explicit explanation (*vivṛtti*), and the proximity of a known word (*siddhapada*). [The verse: "The elders say that the apprehension of power comes from grammar, comparison, lexicons, the speech of trustworthy people, and from usage; from the remainder of a sentence, from explicit explanation, and from the vicinity of a word whose meaning is already established."

Thus, "usage" (*vyavahāra*), which is the crest-jewel among the factors that apprehend word-potency as recited by the learned, is the primary one; the meaning is that it is the most important. Its primacy consists in its independence from other means of apprehending potency when the apprehension of that potency is to be produced. Grammar and the like, however, do not possess such primacy.

The point is this: when the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) of suffixes such as *aṇ*—generated by [rules] such as "the offspring of that" (*tasyāpatyam*)—is to be produced, the apprehension of the expressive power of words such as "offspring" (*apatya*) is required. If one were to maintain that this [apprehension] occurs through another word, and that the apprehension of the power of that [other word] likewise occurs only through yet another word, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. Therefore, since linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is required as the means for accomplishing the apprehension of the power of words like "offspring," grammar and the like do not hold the status of being the primary means (*mukhya-upāyatva*) among those that apprehend power; rather, the nature of the primary means belongs solely to linguistic usage.

And linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) consists in the employment of specific words by authoritative persons (*āpta*), such as teachers and others, for the purpose of communicating various objects; for example, elders employ the word "jar" in the sentence "Bring the jar" in order to communicate an object possessing a shell-like neck and a mountain-like belly. An authoritative person (*āpta*) is one who possesses complete certainty regarding the reality of words and their referents through direct experience. Alternatively, he is one who possesses knowledge of the reality of objects. "Attainment" (*āpti*) is the knowledge of the reality of objects; one who is recognized by that is an "authoritative person" (*āpta*), according to this etymological derivation. And he [is as follows]:

The meaning is that the apprehension of word-meaning power (*śaktigraha*) arises from the linguistic usage of elders. "Those very [elements]" means that since the aforementioned apprehension of power exists only in the case of the substitutes (*ādeśa*)—such as *tiP*, visarga, and so on—which are actually heard in the employment of correct words (*sādhuśabda*) in the present context, the intention is that these substitutes for *tiṅ* and so forth alone are the denoters of meanings such as the agent and the object. By the use of the restrictive particle *eva* ("only"), there is the exclusion of the *lakāra*s and other elements which serve as the original bases (*sthānin*) for those substitutes.

Now, an objection may be raised: even though the expressive power (*śakti*) is apprehended in the case of *tiṅ* suffixes by the usage of elders—which is the preeminent means for grasping such power—that power is nonetheless established as residing in the substitutes (*ādeśin*), rather than in the *tiṅ* suffixes themselves, due to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*). This is just as, although the expressive power is initially apprehended in the entire sentence through usage, it is postulated to reside in the individual words due to parsimony.

Alternatively, since everyday transactions such as bringing and taking away are untenable without the employment of verbal suffixes denoting injunctions (vidhi) such as the imperative (*loṭ*), and although the denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) of those phonemes included within such injunctive suffixes is established by that very usage, one must nevertheless accept that the denotative capacity of the phonemes constituting usages devoid of injunctive suffixes is prescribed solely by grammatical rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi ca*.

Since the treatise states that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides only in the substitutes (*ādeśin*) such as *la* and so on, once the denotative capacity of the phonemes contained within the injunctive suffixes is established, one might object that this capacity should be postulated for other substitutes as well. To avoid this dissatisfaction, he states another proof, beginning with "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*). Regarding the phrase "by the maxim of the cause of that" (*taddhetunyāyataḥ*): the nature of the maxim is "let that [effect] arise from its own cause; what is the use of that [intermediary]? The analysis of the compound is: "that which has that as its cause is *taddhetu*; [the maxim] belonging to that *taddhetu*."

The meaning is: let that causality of the pot and so forth belong to its cause—namely, the clay and so forth alone; what is the use of that "internal goiter" (antargaḍu) which is the effect in the form of the shards and so forth? This principle is rooted in parsimony (*lāghava*). By postulating the causality of the pot and so forth for the clay and so forth—which are the causes of the shards and so forth—one achieves parsimony by having a single causality in one place. However, if one were to further postulate the causality of the pot and so forth for the shards and so forth as well, there would be complexity (*gaurava*) due to postulating causality in both places; this is the intended sense.

The *taddhetunyāya* (the maxim of "for that very reason") refers to a logical principle whose form begins with the words "taddhetoḥ" (for that reason). The intended meaning is that the two terms *taddhetu* and *nyāya* form a *karmadhāraya* compound preceded by the word *saṃbhāvanā* (possibility). He applies this maxim to the present context with the words "of the *lakāra*" (*lakārasya*). This means "of the original element (*ādeśin*). The phrase "if its capacity to convey meaning (*bodhakatve*)"—that is, if it possesses the power of denotation (*vācakatāśakti*)—is to be understood as being followed by the word "being accepted" (*abhyupagate sati*). The expression "even from 'bhū-la'" means even from an unorthodox (*alaukika*) procedural sentence (*prakriyāvākya*). The result is the "undesired consequence of cognition" (*bodhāpattiḥ*).

The meaning is that there would result the cognition of existence (*sattā*) as having an agent (*kartṛka*). The point is that the claim that the substituendum (*sthānin*) is the expressive word (*vācaka*) contradicts experience, for such a cognition of that kind of meaning does not arise from such a sentence for people in the world. "Such a cognition" means the cognition brought about in the form: "an operation conducive to existence at the present time having a single agent. This also applies to the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word *bhavati*.

The meaning is: if it is argued that even the co-utterance of the word-form *bhavati*—which is composed of the verbal root *bhū* qualified by the relation of "immediately following"—is to be accepted as a cause [of meaning]; and thus, the very substitute *lakāra* (the letter *l*) which is presented by the immediately preceding substitute *ati* and so on, is the expressive element (*vācaka*), and not the directly uttered form. [This is said] because it is necessary.

The meaning is as follows: just as the eating at night is accepted [as the cause] because otherwise corpulence would be inexplicable (*pīnatvānyathānupapattyā*), so too, since the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of words such as "bhavati" is necessary and absolutely required because otherwise the generation of the understanding of the word "bhū" would be inexplicable, let the expressive power (*śakti*)—in the form of denotative capacity—be attributed to that very co-occurrence for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*). He states "otherwise" (*anyathā*) to show that there is prolixity (*gaurava*) for one who accepts the denotative capacity of the substituend (*sthānin*); that is to say, in the acceptance of the substituend as the denoter.

He demonstrates this very complexity: "of the letter *l*" (*lakārasya*). Since this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), the meaning is "of the letter *l* and so forth. "Denotative capacity" (*vācakatva*) refers to the power (*śakti*) consisting in denotation; and there is also the causality of co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*). Thus, both must be postulated, which constitutes complexity (*gaurava*)—this is the meaning.

And thus, since the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) itself—being the cause of the knowledge of the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix), which in turn is the cause for the cognition of the meanings such as the agent (*kartṛ*)—should be accepted as the expressive unit (*vācaka*), because there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating expressiveness in one thing alone; what is the use of that cumbersome internal growth (*antargaḍu*) consisting in the postulation of the expressiveness of the *lakāra*? This is the sense. Now, even if by this much logical analysis the expressiveness of the co-occurrence is established, it is not thereby established for the phonemes contained within the roots and suffixes that constitute a correct word (*sādhuśabda*). To this he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*).

The meaning is: "and [this applies] when the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) itself is the expressive unit. Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of a decisive criterion" (*vinigamanāvirahāt*): this means that since there is no evidence to determine which of the two alternatives is correct—whether the expressive power belongs to the co-occurrence (such as the word *bhavati*) or to the individual phonemes constituting such a co-occurrence—it is established that the phonemes occurring together also possess expressive power.

However, some argue that if co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) were the expressive unit, one would have to postulate that the multiple phonemes constituting it possess the status of being the delimitors of expressiveness (*vācakatāvacchedakatva*), which results in complexity (*gaurava*). On the other hand, if the phonemes themselves are the expressives, then only a single specific sequence (*anupūrvī*) as previously described serves as the delimitor of expressiveness, resulting in parsimony (*lāghava*). Thus, parsimony alone is the supporting argument for the view that phonemes are the expressives.

Others, however, argue as follows: "In the view that the substituendum (ādeśin) is reminded by the substitute (ādeśa), and the meaning is understood through that [remembrance], those factors which are the delimiters of denotative capacity (*vācakatāvacchedaka*) in our own system must be considered the delimiters of the reminding function (*smārakatāvacchedaka*) in their system. Consequently, according to the principle of 'the cause being present' (*taddhetunyāya*), let it be granted that only the delimiters of the reminding function are the delimiters of denotative capacity, due to parsimony (*lāghava*). What is the use of further postulating the status of being a delimiter of denotative capacity for the *lakāra*s and so forth, which are like internal tumors (*antargaḍu*) and involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*)? Thus they say.

It should be understood that since expressiveness (*vācakatā*) is accepted as residing in the collection of phonemes (*varṇa*) as they are uttered together, there is no contingency of the cognition of those respective meanings arising from each individual phoneme that does not constitute that collection. Furthermore, if the letter *l* were the expressive unit, it would result in the subversion of the doctrine you have stated; therefore, for that very reason, it is established that only the substitutes (*ādeśa*) possess expressiveness—this is what he states with the words "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*).

The point is this: the Mīmāṃsakas and the ancient Naiyāyikas maintain the established doctrine that in forms such as *paktṛ* (cook), the *kṛt* suffix denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), whereas in forms such as *pacati* (he cooks), the *tiṅ* suffix denotes the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). However, if the denotative power belonged to the *lakāra* alone, then because the *lakāra* as the substituendum (*sthānin*) is one and the same in both cases, it would be impossible for it to denote the agent when appearing in the form of a *kṛt* suffix like *śatṛ*; consequently, the aforementioned doctrine—that the *lakāra* denotes only the productive activity—would be difficult to justify and thus undermined.

And thus, the sense is that for you, who maintain that the letter *l* is the expressive element (*vācaka*), there is a contradiction with your own statement. It should be understood that in the view of the modern Naiyāyikas, this contradiction does not arise, because they accept that only the audible suffixes (*vibhakti*) and so forth occurring in established usage (*siddhaprayoga*) are expressive. Now, if the substitutes (*ādeśa*) are expressive, one might ask: how is the distinction between *kṛt* and *tiṅ* suffixes as denoters of the agent and the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) maintained? In response to this expectation, he says: "And if the substitutes are expressive... [and so forth].

The sense is that because there are many verbal suffixes (ādeśas), the property of being the delimitor of denotative power (vācakatāvacchedakatva) residing in them is also manifold; thus, it is established that *tiṅ*-ness is the delimitor for the denotation of *bhāvanā* (efficient force), while the state of being a *śānac* suffix and so on is the delimitor for the denotation of the agent (*kartṛ*), and this systematic distinction is thereby justified. Now, the proponent of the view that the *lakāra* suffixes denote [the agent] raises an objection in order to prove that the *śānac* suffix and others denote the agent: "And not... [He states: "Action (*kṛti*) is the meaning of the *lakāra*. This is because the ancient Naiyāyikas maintain that the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the *lakāras* resides in action, as it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*).

But it is not [denoted] as the agent (*kartṛ*), because there is prolixity (*gaurava*) in positing the expressive power (*śakti*) for that [agent] in its capacity as an agent, which possesses an action (*kṛtimat*). This is his intention: for according to his view, agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being the substratum (*āśrayatva*) of an action (*kṛti*). That being the case, if the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) were to denote the agent, one would have to state the actions (*kṛtis*) that delimit the denotative capacity; and since those actions are infinite—even though "action" is a single term serving as a general indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for an infinity of instances—there is prolixity due to the infinity of actions.

However, if the *l*-suffix denotes effort (*kṛti*), then even though efforts are infinite, since the universal "effort-ness" (*kṛtitva*) is one, it is possible to postulate that this single universal alone serves as the delimitor of denotative capacity; thus, the economy [of the theory] is quite evident. The mention of "effort" (*kṛti*) is merely illustrative of "productive activity" (*bhāvanā*). For the Mīmāṃsakas accept that the *l*-suffix denotes productive activity alone, out of deference to parsimony, having abandoned the view that it denotes the agent who possesses productive activity—since, according to the aforementioned method, that would involve complexity (*gaurava*). This is the intended meaning.

The intention of the objection is as follows: in instances such as *pacamānaḥ* (cooking), where suffixes like *śānac* occur, the meaning of the *l*-suffix is the *kṛtya* (the action/task) and so forth; however, the substratum (i.e., the agent) is the meaning of the *śānac* suffix, because of the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) stating "the *kṛt* suffixes denote the agent" (*kartari kṛt*). Thus, since both meanings are established by two separate rules of grammar, the conclusion is that the suffix *śānac* and others possess a distinct expressive power (*śakti*) to denote the agent.
