Thus, if there is no grasping of the power of the sentence with respect to the sentence-meaning—which consists of the connection of word-meanings—then [the same would apply].

The meaning is as follows: if it is argued that because the relation between word-meanings does not exist prior to the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, the apprehension of the sentence’s power (vākyaśakti) with respect to that [relation] would be impossible; having thus stated the impossibility of apprehending the sentence’s power regarding the sentence-meaning—which consists of the relation—under the theory of Abhihitānvaya, he states "the same applies to the word" (pade 'pi samam), showing that under the theory of Anvitābhidhāna as well, the impossibility of apprehending the sentence’s power is equally present in the case of the word.

Now, one might object: since it is possible to grasp the expressive power (*śakti*) of a word in relation to an object presented by the senses—such as the eye—prior to verbal comprehension, how can it be said that the grasping of power in a word is impossible prior to verbal comprehension? To clarify the intention behind this [objection], the author states: "The factor of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) resides in the word itself. This means, according to the view of the proponents of *Anvitābhidhāna* (the theory that words denote meanings as already connected), the power of words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*) lies in the object "pot" as connected with other factors.

This is indeed their intention: when an instigator, such as a teacher, utters the sentence "O student, bring the cow," and having heard it, the person being prompted, such as a disciple, brings the cow; then a bystander—a child who does not yet know the word-potencies of "cow" and so forth—observing the act of bringing the cow performed by the prompted agent, concludes that this very act of bringing the cow is prompted by the utterance of the words "bring the cow."

Furthermore, in sentences such as "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*) and "Bring the horse" (*aśvam ānaya*), through the methods of presence (*āvāpa*) and absence (*udvāpa*), one grasps the denotative power (*śakti*) of words like "cow" with respect to objects such as those possessing a dewlap that are associated with other factors. This is established by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): when the word "cow" is present, there is the cognition of the object possessing a dewlap; and in the absence of the word "bring," there is no cognition of the object possessing a dewlap. Thus, one understands that the power of words like "cow" resides in objects such as those possessing a dewlap as related to something else.

Thus, because the apprehension of the word's denotative power (*śaktigraha*) occurs precisely with respect to a qualified entity through the initial linguistic usage such as "bring the cow," the referent of words like "cow" is indeed the object possessing a dewlap and so forth, as conjoined with the act of bringing and the like. Furthermore, if the relation of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) were incapable of being denoted, it could not be the object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), since the apprehension of the denotative power is the determining factor for being an object of verbal cognition; otherwise, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of even that which is incapable of being denoted becoming an object of experience.

And thus, the meaning of a sentence is indeed the meaning of a word—a category that possesses a general form conforming to all its particular sub-varieties, yet which finds its ultimate rest in a specific variety due to the proximity of other particulars; for a sentence consists of words alone, with other words being merely implied. Just as "clay-ness" is a general form conforming to all particular varieties such as jars, bowls, and the like, so too "word-ness" (*śabdatva*) and the like are general forms conforming to all particular varieties such as "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*), and so forth; this is the intended meaning.

Thus, their intention is that the power (*śakti*) of words resides in their relation to the specific qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) precisely in the form of being word-meanings (*padārthatva*). That is to say, even in the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), which consists of the relation, the power of the words resides [in that relation]. And so, the sense is that one need not postulate a power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*) with respect to the sentence-meaning, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). "The impossibility of grasping that" means that even in the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhānavāda*), the impossibility of grasping the power of words with respect to the relation is equally [present].

The meaning is that the sentence-meaning, which consists of a positive concomitance (*anvaya*), is not present prior to the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). According to the theory of "crooked" power (*kubjaśaktivāda*), he says "if," and so forth. Regarding the "theory of crooked power": this is its underlying intention—the individual qualified by the universal (*jāti*) alone is the denotable object (*śakya*). However, only when there is the manifestation of the power residing in the universal does the cognition of the sentence-meaning arise from the word after the recollection of the object; it does not arise otherwise. And thus, there is no utility in knowing the power with respect to the individuals, because they are infinite in number.

Thus, the individual (vyakti) is the cause for the recollection of the word-meaning by virtue of its own existence as a real entity; it is not necessary to have knowledge of it [at that time]. Furthermore, regarding the causal relationship in the apprehension of power (śaktigraha), for the purpose of understanding an individual qualified by a universal (jāti), the apprehension of power having the universal as its qualifier (jātiprakāraka-śaktigraha) is the cause. In this way, only the status of having the universal as the qualifier is introduced, and not the status of having the individual as the qualificand (vyaktiviśeṣyaka). For this very reason, the power is "crooked" (kubjā) with respect to the individual portion; this is because there is no requirement for the knowledge of power with respect to the individual portion.

The point is this: the doctrine that in some respects the known power (*śakti*) is the cause, while in other respects the unknown [power] is the cause, is precisely what is called the "crooked power theory" (*kubja-śakti-vāda*). Accordingly, according to the crooked power theory, with respect to the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), the power of the word is known; because the meanings of words are already established and have been presented prior to verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), it is possible to grasp the power there, and thus the known [power] is utilized.

If it is argued that regarding the aspect of relation (*anvaya*), since the relational component in the form of the sentence-meaning is not present prior to the verbal cognition, it is precisely when unknown that it is useful—then for me, the proponent of the theory of sentential power (*vākyaśaktivādin*), the power of the sentence is likewise useful toward the sentence-meaning in the form of a relation precisely when it is unknown. Thus, the acceptance of this "crooked" theory of power (*kubjaśaktivāda*) is equal [for both sides], and therefore one should not raise the objection that the apprehension of the sentence's power with respect to the sentence-meaning is impossible. This is the intended meaning.

"Is it not the case that power (*śakti*) is unknown, yet it is said to be useful? Since it is impossible for something unknown to perform any function, there is a lack of firmness in this position. Bearing this weakness in mind, he introduces another method with the words "Is it not the case... and so forth. "Beholding" means: when a teacher or the like says "Bring the cow," a child who does not know the word's power beholds the cow being brought by the pupil or the like. "Like the meaning of a word" means: [like understanding the object].

The intended meaning is as follows: according to the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (the expression of meanings followed by their connection), for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), words possess power (*śakti*) only with respect to the word-meanings themselves, and not with respect to other aspects as well, because that would involve prolixity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, because [the connection] is obtainable through expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, it is obtainable from another source. Thus, first there is the presentation of the mere word-meanings from the words; subsequently, there is the presentation of the sentence-meaning, which consists of the connection of those word-meanings acting as qualifiers. With this intention, he says: "like the word-meanings."

Here, the suffix *vati* is applied according to the rule *tatra tasyeva*, because the locative case is observed in the object of comparison (*upameya*), which is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Thus, if it is argued that—just as a child acquires the grasp of word-power (*pada-śakti*) regarding an object possessing a dewlap and so forth through the mind, so too there should be such a grasp regarding the sentence-meaning, i.e., the sentence-meaning in the form of a syntactic relation (*anvaya*)—then he says "lakṣaṇādi" (beginning with indication) to show that this is equal [to the other case]. By the words "it is indicated" (*lakṣyate*) and so forth, he expresses the meaning required in the present context, since the word *lakṣaṇa* has multiple meanings.

The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of instrument (*karaṇe*) for the word *lakṣadhātu*. "Bhāna" means a sense organ that is an instrument of cognition. In the *Paramamūla*, regarding the phrase "let it be [used] for the word (*pade*) as well as for the meaning (*arthe*)," the word "meaning" (*artha*) refers to that which conveys the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Since there would be an inconsistency if the word "api" (also) following the word "artha"—which has such a meaning—were intended to include the word-meaning (*padārtha*), as the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) with respect to the word-meaning is not being rejected, he says: "The word 'api' [is used] after the word 'pada'. [Note: This passage clarifies a grammatical point concerning the interpretation of the compound *pade'rthe'pyastu* from the *Mūla* text.]

The meaning is that the word "api" (also) should be construed even after the word "pade" (in the case of a word), following a different order [of the sentence]. He states this purpose with the words "pade 'pi" and so forth. The sense is: if it is maintained that the apprehension of the power (śakti) determined by the meaning is possible even in the case of a word through the mind by means of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), then let the apprehension of the power determined by the sentence-meaning also occur in the case of a sentence through the mind alone.

The point is this: just as the primary apprehension of the power (śakti) of words denoting word-meanings arises through the mind from the linguistic usage of elders in the form of a sentence such as "Bring the jar," so too, when the word-meanings are presented by the constituent words upon hearing that sentence, the presentation of their mutual relation (saṃsarga) through the mind is not untenable. Thus, the meaning is that the power of the sentence with respect to the sentence-meaning, which consists of that relation, is likewise not untenable.

By this extensive discussion, he states—beginning with "In reality" (*vastutastu*)—that first there is the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) regarding the individual word-meaning; then, once the word-meanings have been presented by that [word], there is subsequently the apprehension of the power regarding the relation (*saṃsarga) presented to the mind; and finally, through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*), there is the apprehension of the power of each specific word in its respective meaning. Here too, the phrase "of one observing the linguistic usage of elders" (*vṛddhavyavahāraṃ paśyataḥ*) should be supplied. Consequently, there is no contradiction even if the power of the word is apprehended prior to the apprehension of the power of the sentence, by means of a lexicon (*kośa*) or other such sources.

And thus, by the elder’s usage (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), which is the crest-jewel among those that apprehend linguistic capacity (*śaktigrāhaka*), the apprehension of the capacity [of words] as determined by the sentence-meaning first arises with respect to the sentence itself; in some cases, the apprehension of the sentence-capacity also arises first through instruction (*upadeśa*). "The apprehension of that" means the apprehension of the capacity as determined by the specific sentence-meaning. Now, one might object: even if the sentence-sphoṭa (*vākyasphoṭa*) is established in this way, the word-sphoṭa (*padasphoṭa*) is not established. To this he says: "by insertion and deletion" (*āvāpodvāpābhyām*), meaning by the bringing in and taking away [of words].

"Each one is the apprehension of that": the sense is that for each individual word, there occurs an apprehension of the expressive power (śakti) as determined by the meaning of that specific word. Furthermore, the intended meaning should be understood as resulting in two positions: when the verbal cognition of the sentence-meaning arises from a word through the force of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) and other factors assisted by the expressive power of each individual word, then it is the *padasphoṭa*; but when the power of the sentence produces the qualified cognition independently of the power of each individual word, then it is the *vākyasphoṭa*. Thus, these two positions follow. || 65 ||

"This very [is it]" means that the capacity for the meaning of the whole resides in the qualified sentence alone; this is the sense of "this very. "Of the Mīmāṃsakas" means of the Bhāṭṭas and others who accept figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) everywhere in a sentence. "Of certain Vedāntins" means of those following the Mīmāṃsakas, such as Vācaspati, the author of the *Kalpataru*, and others. All of these maintain that there is figurative indication at the level of the sentence, just as there is at the level of the word. Furthermore, without a sentence-capacity (*vākya-śakti*) analogous to the word-capacity (*pada-śakti*), figurative indication at the level of the sentence is not possible.

Since it is universally accepted that *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is a relation with what is directly denoted (*śakya*), he says "in all cases indeed. The sense is this: even those Mīmāṃsakas such as the Bhāṭṭas who claim that in every instance the sentence-meaning is exclusively indicated—that is, produced solely by the function of indication—also maintain that the apprehension of *lakṣaṇā* depends upon the sentence-potency (*vākyaśakti*) regarding the collective meaning as the means (*gati*). Without sentence-potency, sentence-indication (*vākyalakṣaṇā*) cannot be explained, because the established doctrine accepted by all is that *lakṣaṇā* is a relation with the directly denoted.

In the systems of Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika, there is no *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in a sentence. It is stated that *lakṣaṇā* is a relationship with what is directly denotable (*svaśakyasaṃbandha*). Since a sentence, which is a collection of words, possesses no denotative power (*śakti*) toward any meaning whatsoever, how could a relationship with what is denotable by that sentence—namely *lakṣaṇā*—be possible? This is the point. "The two aforementioned positions" means the two positions established through the distinction between word and sentence: namely, that the word is the denoter or that the sentence is the denoter.

He clarifies the very impossibility [of simultaneous production] with the words "because of production" (*utpatteḥ*). According to the view that phonemes (*varṇa*) are produced, [the phrase refers to] "because of production"; according to the view that phonemes are eternal, however, it refers to "because of manifestation" (*abhivyakteḥ*). In the system of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), there is this distinction: for words (*śabda*), there is production; but for the *sphoṭa*, there is manifestation. With the words "due to the impossibility at one time," he means that the simultaneous production or manifestation of all the phonemes constituting a word is not possible.

The meaning is as follows: because the conjunctions of air with the various articulatory points (*sthāna*) that manifest [the phonemes] occur sequentially, their production is also sequential; consequently, since it is impossible for letters (*varṇa*)—which perish very rapidly—to coalesce simultaneously, there is an absolute impossibility of cognizing a word (*pada*) consisting of a collection of such produced and manifested letters. "And thus" (*tathā ca*) means: and given the impossibility of cognizing a word consisting of a collection of those many letters. "That collection" (*tatsamūha*)... [refers to the aforementioned].

The sense is that the cognition of a sentence, which consists of a collection of such words, is even more impossible. Therefore, if it is argued that the theories of *pada-sphoṭa* (word-sphoṭa) and *vākya-sphoṭa* (sentence-sphoṭa) are in every way untenable, he says "no," beginning with the words "the perception of the subsequent phoneme" (*uttaravarṇapratyakṣa*), and so on. The meaning is as follows: in the word *ghaṭa*, there is first the utterance of the phoneme *gha*, then the utterance of the phoneme *a*, then the utterance of the phoneme *ṭa*, and finally the utterance of the phoneme *a*; this is the sequence.

In that context, the meaning is as follows: at the time of the cognition of the letter *a* which follows the letter *gha*, there is the property of possessing such a letter *gha*—wherein the preceding letter *gha* is presented (or remembered) in the subsequent letter *a* by way of the relation of being immediately followed; and likewise, at the time of the perceptual cognition of the letter *ṭa* following that [letter *a*], there is the property of possessing such a word *gha*—wherein the second letter, qualified by the first letter, is presented in that letter *ṭa* by way of the relation of being immediately followed.

The connection [of the words] is with "asya sugraham" (this is easy to grasp). The meaning is that the specific quality of the letter *gha* in the following letter *a*, and the specific quality of the letter *a*—as qualified by the letter *gha*—in the following letter *ṭa*, can be easily grasped, i.e., known with ease and without effort.

The intended meaning is as follows: in this manner, when perceiving the fourth and subsequent phonemes, the qualification of the third phoneme by the second phoneme—which itself is qualified by the first phoneme already remembered—is easily grasped. By this process, the perception of the final phoneme comes to have all the phonemes constituting the word or sentence as its object; thus, there is no logical inconsistency in the cognition of word-meanings or sentence-meanings. The word-meaning is now pointed out in the passage beginning with "the subsequent phoneme," etc., referring to the time of the utterance of each successive phoneme following the preceding phonemes within words such as *ghaṭa*.

"In that subsequent phoneme" (*tasmin-uttaravarṇe*): the meaning is "presented" (*upasthite*), which is to say "remembered" (*smṛte*). "Unintervened" (*avyavahite*): the meaning is that the relation between the preceding and subsequent phonemes is the state of the subsequent phoneme being immediately after the preceding one. "Possessing the preceding phoneme" (*pūrvavarṇavattvam*): the meaning is "being qualified by the preceding phoneme" (*pūrvavarṇavaiśiṣṭyam*). This connects with the phrase "is easily grasped" (*asya sugraham*). "Qualified by the presented" (*upasthitaviśiṣṭa*): the meaning is the second phoneme qualified by the first phoneme which has been presented, i.e., remembered.

Just as the status of being a word (*padatva*), which consists of a collection of phonemes (*varma*), is easily understood, so too is the status of being a sentence (*vākyatva*), which consists of a collection of words, easily understood; thus he says: "just like the status of being a word constituted by such a sequence."

The meaning is as follows: the qualification by the preceding word resides in the subsequent word; the qualification by the subsequent word—already qualified by the preceding word—resides in the third word. In this manner, the qualification of each preceding word in the final word of a sentence can be understood in each successive word. Thus, since the nature of a sentence (*vākyatva*) is also easily apprehended, both the *pada-sphoṭa* (word-essence) and the *vākya-sphoṭa* (sentence-essence) are free from contradiction. Thus ends the section on the *pada-sphoṭa* and *vākya-sphoṭa*. Now begins the determination of the indivisible *pada-sphoṭa*.

Now, at the occasion of establishing the indivisible sphoṭa (akhaṇḍasphoṭa), he says "now" (idānīm). This means immediately after the explanation of the divisible sphoṭa (sakhaṇḍasphoṭa). "The position of the indivisible" (akhaṇḍapakṣam) means the position regarding the indivisible word-sphoṭa and sentence-sphoṭa; the sense is that "indivisibility" (akhaṇḍatvam) consists in being devoid of the conceptualization of parts. He explains—i.e., defines it—by saying "there are no phonemes in a word. He states the meaning of the locative-ending word "in a word" (pade) found in the verse by saying "in [words such as] 'pacati' and so forth."

Anticipating the objection that it is irrelevant to the present topic to say "parts do not exist in phonemes," he says: "by way of an illustration" (*dṛṣṭāntavyājena*). This means "under the guise of an example. A reading is seen in some places: *kvacid varṇeṣv avayavā iva*, which is indeed highly appropriate. Just as it is well known even to children that there is no conceptualization of parts in phonemes such as the letter *ka*, so too it should be understood that there are no parts consisting of phonemes in a word either. Thus, the point is that what was stated regarding the "illustration" is entirely logical.

[Objection: But surely, parts are indeed perceived even in the case of certain phonemes (*varṇa*). To this, he says: "they are merely perceived" (*pratīyamānāḥ*). Although parts such as the *ikāra* and *repha* are perceived in [complex sounds] like *ekāra* and *arkāra*, nevertheless, because they are not clearly apprehended, that perception is nothing but an illusion produced by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the coloring (*uparāga*) of specific sounds (*dhvani-viśeṣa*) having the same form as those respective phonemes. The meaning is that parts do not exist as real entities within phonemes. The point is that there is no stronger evidence for postulating parts in *ekāra* and so forth, and thus it would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Just as there is an absence of phonemes (*varṇa*) in a word (*pada*), he says [in the verse] "from the sentence" (*vākyāt*) in order to state that the sentence likewise lacks words as its constituent parts; he explains the meaning of the term *praviveka* in that verse as "distinction" (*bheda*). The meaning is that, following the root-meaning of the verbal root *vi-ci* (to separate/divide), the word *praviveka* signifies distinction. Now, one might object: since the phonemes—which are the constituents of words—are perceived when a word or the like is cognized, how can there be an absence of phonemes and an absence of words? To this he replies: "This is the point. [The word] "entirely indivisible" (*akhaṇḍam eva*) [is used].

The meaning is that [the word] is indeed not composed of phonemes, forms, or parts. By the use of the restrictive particle *eva* ("indeed"), he demonstrates what is excluded: namely, that it is "not a collection of phonemes. The underlying intention is that one should not postulate constituent parts for either a sentence or a word. This is because there is no evidence for postulating infinite phonemes, and because such a view would result in an ungrounded theoretical complexity (*gaurava*).

Anticipating the objection that the very fact that the cognition "I hear the letter *kha*" cannot otherwise be explained—given the perception of the letter *ka*—serves as the proof for postulating an infinite number of properties (*dharma*) therein, he refutes this with the words "by being the producer of those respective letters," and so forth. The meaning is: it resides in that conjunction of air which is intended to be the producer of each respective letter, such as *ka*, *kha*, and so on. The word "residing" (*niṣṭha*) is to be construed with the "delimiting factor" (*avacchedaka*). [The phrase] "of the productivity of those respective properties" [is explained as follows].

The meaning is: that generativity (*janakatā*) which resides in each respective phoneme beginning with the letter *ka*. This refers to the position of the Naiyāyikas, because phonemes are non-eternal and thus possess the qualities of production and destruction. "Of the manifestor-ship" (*vyañjakatāyāḥ*): this refers to the position of the Grammarians (*Vaiyākaraṇa*), according to whom phonemes are eternal, and therefore only their manifestation is to be expressed. "The delimiting factor" (*avacchedaka*): the meaning is that which possesses the status of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*), whether as defined by generativity or as defined by manifestor-ship. "Heterogeneity" (*vijātīyam*).

The meaning is that it refers to a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) that is mentally constructed (*parikalpita*). Regarding the phrase "due to a difference in cognition" (*pratītivailakṣaṇya*): the point is that the *sphoṭa* manifests through forms such as *katva* (the quality of being *ka*) and *khatva* (the quality of being *kha*) residing in the contact with the air; thus, a distinct cognition such as "the letter *ka*" or "the letter *kha*" can be established. He states that this very point has been clearly expressed in the work of Vācaspati by saying "in the *Bhāmatī*"; the meaning is: in the commentary named *Bhāmatī*, composed by Vācaspati, which is an exposition of Śaṅkara’s commentary on the *Brahmasūtras*.

"It is superimposed" means that qualities such as high pitch (*tāratva*) residing in the air are superimposed upon the phonemes (*varṇa*); this is clearly stated in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (Brahma-sūtra 1.3.26). This is the sense. For this very reason, the cognition and linguistic usage regarding a single phoneme—as "high" or "low"—are accounted for. Indeed, the linguistic usage that "this [phoneme] is high relative to something else" or "this is low relative to something else," even with respect to a single phoneme, is established by the experience of all people. However, if one accepts superimposition (*āropa*), this objection does not arise.

This is because it is a rule that the connection of two contradictory properties in something not [previously] superimposed necessitates a difference in the substratum of those properties. He raises the objection, "But if this were so," suggesting that the conjunction of air produced by the striking of the throat, palate, and other organs might itself be the denoter. He says, "The denoter too... meaning that in that case, the conjunction of air itself would consist of the letter *ka*, the letter *kha*, and so forth. To refute the idea that the conjunction of air has the nature of the letter *ka* and other such phonemes, he says, "perceived through direct perception..."

The meaning is that the denotative capacity belongs precisely to that which is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), such as the letter *ka* and so forth, which is the object of a perceptual cognition characterized by the mode (*prakāra*) of being the letter *ka*; for it is this [the letter] alone whose denotative capacity is established by experience. Since sound is perceivable by the sense organ of hearing, it is an object of direct perception; however, because the conjunction with air is not perceivable by a sense organ, it lacks the status of being an object of direct perception, and thus it is not logical for it to possess denotative capacity—this is the intended point. Now, concluding and stating the essential conclusion, he says: "And so... (*tathā ca*).

The meaning is: "and because the conjunction of air lacks denotative power. Regarding the phrase "by the impossibility of explaining denotative power otherwise": if the word (*pada*) and the sentence (*vākya*) were not something over and above a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*), then—since phonemes are sequential and perish very rapidly—it would be impossible for them to conjoin simultaneously; consequently, their denotative power could not be asserted. Thus, by the necessity of explaining it otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*), it becomes essential that the word and the sentence are distinct from the collection of phonemes, and thereby the denotative power of words and sentences is established. This is the meaning.

He states that this recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—namely, "this is that"—is correctly established within this theory of the eternity of sound, by saying: "this is that very same [thing]. The three expressions beginning with "this is that" are to be construed with the word "by means of cognition" (*pratītyā*). The meaning is that since the identity of the individual manifestation is experienced in recognition, the indivisible *sphoṭa* is established. By the cognition "this is that *ga*-sound," the eternity of phonemes (*varṇa*) is asserted.

The point is this: if phonemes (*varṇa*) were impermanent, then words and sentences composed of those impermanent phonemes would also be impermanent, and thus the phenomenon of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) could not be accounted for; consequently, the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) of the *sphoṭa* would not be established. Nor should it be argued that even when there is a difference between individual instances, the aforementioned cognition is possible by relying on generic similarity (*sājātya*), as in the case of "this is that same medicine. For if that were so, one would also have to accept the usage "this word belongs to that class," which is not desired. Nor should it be argued that such usage is indeed accepted.

This is because the linguistic usage that takes the identity of the individual manifestation as its object—namely, "this very word is that"—is established by direct experience. By this [phrase], the meaning is: by establishing the status of the indivisible *sphoṭa* as the signifier (*vācaka*), which is rooted in recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Regarding the phrase "of the audible phonemes" (*śrūyamāṇavarṇānām*): those who claim that the phonemes themselves are the signifiers because there is no experience of a *sphoṭa* distinct from the *ga*, *au*, and *visarga* in the word "cow" (*gauh*) are thereby refuted. Regarding the phrase "of them" (*teṣām*): it means of the phonemes such as *ga*. Regarding the phrase "because of the absence of being distinct from the *sphoṭa*" (*sphoṭātiriktatvābhāvāt*): [it refers to the fact that the phonemes are not separate from the *sphoṭa*].

The sense is that the sphoṭa alone is manifested by the universals such as *gatva* (the "g-ness") residing in the conjunctions with the manifesting air-currents (*vyañjakavāyusaṃyoga*). He restates the portion to be refuted with the words "As for [the claim]... and so forth. Having raised the dilemma—whether the denotative power belongs to the letters individually or to their collection—he states that the first alternative is not tenable with the words "Of the letters individually. "The consequence of the cognition of meaning" means the consequence of the repeated occurrence of the cognition of meaning. He states that the second alternative is not tenable with the words "But of the collection... "Arising more rapidly" (*āśutarotpannānām*)... [refers to the letters].

This is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for those things that perish very quickly. Thus, the meaning is that since phonemes—whether uttered in a sequence of prior and posterior [moments] and perishing immediately after their utterance, or manifested in such a sequence—are not experienced as merging simultaneously, the cognition [of them as a whole] is simply impossible. In the view that phonemes are produced (janya), the cognition of them is impossible because their collection (samudāya) itself cannot exist.

The point is that, under the view of the eternality [of phonemes], even if a collection [of phonemes] were possible, the cognition of it would be impossible. Now, one might object: in the word "ghaṭa," at the time of the utterance of the second phoneme, the vowel *a*, there exists—by way of the relation of immediate succession—the property of being preceded by the preceding phoneme, which is remembered through the force of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of uttering that phoneme; likewise, at the time of the utterance of the third phoneme, in that third phoneme, there is that which is qualified by the first phoneme as remembered.

The second phoneme possesses that qualification [of the first] by way of the relation of immediate succession (*avyavahitottaravartitva*). Thus, since it is possible to state the qualification of each preceding phoneme up to the final phoneme, a cognition of all the phonemes in the form of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) is indeed possible; nevertheless, in cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*, or *nadī* and *dīnaḥ*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) of generating a comprehension of the meaning qualified by "being *dīna*" from the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of the phonemes *na*, *i*, *da*, and *i* that constitute the word *nadī*, even when they are experienced in the reverse order.

Having stated that Kaiyaṭa’s claim—that the *sphoṭa* alone, which is indivisible, not composed of phonemes, and manifested by the phonemes contained within the sound (*dhvani*), is the signifier—is incorrect, [the author] says: "That is trivial. "Complete knowledge" means the knowledge of the entire word. "Common to *nadī*, *dīna*, and so on" means that although there is a sequence among the phonemes, there is no fixed rule regarding the cognition that arises from their collective apprehension.

This is because it is established by experience that there can be a cognition of word-meanings through a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*), even for those [cognitions] devoid of some part [of the sequence], or even without a sequential order. Thus, if a cognition were to arise from the phonemes constituting the word *nadī* with their anterior-posterior order reversed, the meaning of the word *nadī* would be understood from that [reversed] word; likewise, the meaning of the word *nadī* would result from the word *dīna*. This is the sense. A cognition characterized by multiple modes and possessing multiple primary object-ness (*mukhya-viśeṣyatā*) is called a collective apprehension.

For example, the cognition "this is a jar," "this is a pillar," and "this is a pot" constitutes a single unit of knowledge. Thus, according to Kaiyaṭa—and likewise in this view—it should be understood that from the conjunctions with air (vāyu-saṃyoga), phonemes (varṇa) possessing properties such as *katva* and *khatva* arise; from these, the indivisible sphoṭa is manifested, and from the manifested indivisible sphoṭa, the comprehension of meaning occurs. [The author states: "That is trivial."

The cognition of an entire word, which arises from the experience of the final phoneme assisted by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experiences of each preceding phoneme, is common to both the words *nadī* and *dīna*. Since there is no rule that memory must occur in the same sequence as the objects appeared during experience, it may sometimes occur in reverse order; thus, when the two syllables of *nadī* are remembered in reverse order, and likewise the two syllables of *dīna* are remembered in reverse order, the resulting cognition is common to both the words *nadī* and *dīna*.

The meaning is that Kaiyaṭa’s statement—that it is a cognition consisting of such recollection—is trivial. He states the reason for this with the words "of the knowledge of the word" (padajñānasya). This means: of the knowledge of a word composed of phonemes characterized by a sequence of preceding and succeeding order. The phrase "because it has been established" refers to what was previously demonstrated.

The point is that, as established during the commentary on the sixty-seventh verse at the time of explaining the *sakhaṇḍasphoṭa* theory, it has been demonstrated that in the cognition of a word—produced by the experience of the final phoneme assisted by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of each preceding phoneme—the phonemes appear precisely with their specific sequential order; therefore, there is no defect in cases such as *saroruṣaḥ* and *nadīdīnaḥ*. He demonstrates the fault in accepting a *sphoṭa* distinct from the phonemes as the expressive agent with the words "of the phonemes" (*varṇānām*) and "because of being swallowed by dilemma" (*vikalpagrāsāt*).

If each [letter] were individually the manifester, then since the manifestation would be accomplished by the first letter alone, the other letters would be useless. Furthermore, it is impossible for them to be manifesters as a collective; for at the time of the manifestation of the final letter, it is impossible for the preceding manifestations of the successive earlier letters to persist, and thus their simultaneous conjunction is impossible, which renders the very notion of a "collection" untenable. Even if the final letter were the manifester, the other letters would still be useless.

If the experience of each successive letter, accompanied by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experiences of the preceding letters, serves as the manifestor [of the word], then let that very thing be the conveyor of meaning; there is no need for the postulation of a separate *sphoṭa*. This is the sense. The Naiyāyika raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). "Even in your view" means even in the doctrine of those who maintain that the *sphoṭa* is distinct from the letters; that is to say, in the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*). "This defect" means a defect consisting of a dilemma. He clarifies that very defect with the words "of those respective letters" (*tattadvarṇa*).

According to the view of the Naiyāyikas who maintain that color arises [from conjunction], it is considered to be produced [by conjunction]. Having raised the dilemma as to whether the conjunctions with the air are individually manifesting agents or collectively so, if each individual conjunction with the air were a manifesting agent, then since manifestation would be accomplished by the very first conjunction with the air, the employment of subsequent conjunctions with the air would be redundant.

It should be understood that because the air rising from the region of the navel produces conjunctions in various locations sequentially, those [articulations], being successive, cannot possibly exist simultaneously like a pair of yokes; thus, since their combination is impossible, it is all the more remote for their collective aggregate to be the manifestor. Even if each were individually a manifestor, one would manifest the *sphoṭa* in the form of the letter *ga*, another in the form of the letter *au*, and another in the form of the *visarga*.

And thus, since it is only that [sphoṭa] manifested by the specific nature of each [letter-sound] that possesses the capacity to convey meaning, no conjunction with air (vāyusaṃyoga) is redundant; this is the intention of the author, who provides the solution: "Each individually. "For this very reason" means: because the conjunctions with air manifest the sphoṭa by means of their own inherent properties, such as being a *ga*-sound (*gatva*), and so forth. "Even if one does not accept anything additional to that" means: even if one does not accept letters (*varṇa*) as distinct from the sphoṭa.

The intention [of the author] is this: if one does not accept that the conjunctions of air (vāyusaṃyoga) manifest the sphoṭa through properties such as "ga-ness" (gatva), then it would necessarily be required to admit letters (varṇa) distinct from the sphoṭa in order for such manifestation to occur. Now, one might raise the objection: "If letters are not admitted as distinct entities in this way, then in the absence of words (pada), the claim that the cognition of a word is the cause of the comprehension of meaning would be utterly untenable. Anticipating this doubt, the author states "And thus" (evaṃ ca) in order to refute it. The meaning is: even when the sphoṭa is manifested by the various forms residing in the conjunctions of air, such as "ga-ness" and so forth.

The phrase "are apprehended" implies the ellipsis "in which [cognition]. Thus, the meaning is: of that causal efficacy belonging to the cognition of a word-sound (*yatpadajñāna*) in which the property of being a *dhava* (the tree) appears in the word *ṭa*. "Because there is no dispute" means because it is accepted by everyone.

The point is this: having thus apprehended a distinction created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the word "ghaṭa" is applied to that very same entity consisting of the sound *ṭa*—which is the object of a cognition characterized by the universal "ghatva" and is the object of an immediate apprehension; therefore, it is universally accepted that the knowledge of such a word is the cause of the comprehension of meaning. Now, one might object: let it be granted that the property of being a "gha" exists in the single entity consisting of the sound *ṭa* due to the difference in limiting adjuncts, but in what manner does the property of "being immediately followed by itself" (*svāvyavahitottaratva*) exist there? To this, he says: "immediate succession" (*avyavahitottaratvam*).

Regarding the phrase "svajñānādhikaraṇa" (the locus of its own cognition): "sva" refers to the sphoṭa appearing as jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth; that which is the locus of the cognition of that [sphoṭa] is the moment capable of being such, and "immediate succession" (*avyavahitottaratva*) consists precisely in being the object of a cognition produced at that very moment. It does not mean, however, that it is produced in a moment subsequent to the destruction of the moment that was the locus of its own production. Thus, immediate succession belongs to the cognition itself, not to the production. The point is that in all cases, immediate succession is perceived only in relation to cognition.

Anticipating the objection that such "immediate succession" (avyavahitottaratva) is not observed anywhere else, he says: "For this very reason. This means: precisely because the aforementioned immediate succession is the cause for the conventional usage of the term "sequence" (ānupūrvī). The point is that the usage of elders and Naiyāyikas—such as "the sequence is that which consists in the cognition of the letter *ya* following the cognition of the letter *gha*"—is thus logically consistent. "There is no fault whatsoever."

The meaning is that even though the phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal, because their manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is non-eternal, the property of "immediately following the manifestation of one phoneme" exists in the manifestation of another phoneme; thus, the cognition of words such as *ghaṭa* is established, and since it is easy to state that the knowledge of the word is the cause of the comprehension of the meaning, there is no defect whatsoever. With the words "by this," [the author] refutes the refutation of *sphoṭa* stated by the author of the *Parimala*; the meaning is: by establishing that the *sphoṭa*, characterized by a specific sequence (*ānupūrvī*) consisting of priority and posteriority, is the signifier (*vācaka*).

Having raised the alternative as to whether the sphoṭa is one and the same or manifold across synonyms such as *ghaṭa* and *kalaśa*, he states that the first [position] is not tenable—namely, "not the first. This means that there is not a single sphoṭa. He states the fault in accepting that the sphoṭa is indeed one: "in the word *ghaṭa* alone," meaning that the sphoṭa is manifested by the word *ghaṭa* as characterized by its specific sequence [of phonemes]. "From the word *kalaśa*" means from the sphoṭa manifested by the word *kalaśa* as characterized by its specific sequence, [provided] its expressive power (*śakti*) has not been grasped.

The meaning is as follows: if there were only one single *sphoṭa* for synonymous terms such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), "vessel" (*kalaśa*), and so forth, then for a person who has grasped the expressive power (*śakti*) of the *sphoṭa* manifested by the word "jar," there would follow the cognition of the object even upon hearing previously unknown synonyms like "vessel" and the like—because the *sphoṭa*, whose power had not yet been grasped, would be manifested by those previously unknown synonyms. Thus, the object would be cognized despite the fact that the power of the new words had not been previously learned.

The meaning is as follows: because of the consequence of [immediate] comprehension of the object (*arthabodhaprasaṅgāt*). Since the apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*) occurs within the single *sphoṭa* manifested by the word "ghaṭa," there would follow the consequence that the comprehension of the object would arise even from the *sphoṭa* manifested by the word "kalaśa," even though its potency has not been apprehended. However, this fault does not apply to the view that the word, in the form of a collection of phonemes (*varṇasamudāya*), is the expressive agent (*vācaka*). This is because, in that view, the apprehension of the potency for that specific sound is the cause in the production of the comprehension.

The point is that because the cause—the apprehension of the power (*śakti*) residing in the *sphoṭa* manifested by the word "kalaśa"—is absent, there is no possibility of the comprehension of meaning from the word "kalaśa. To refute the objection that for a person who has grasped the power in the *sphoṭa* manifested by the word "ghaṭa," the comprehension of meaning would undesirably follow even from the *sphoṭa* manifested by the word "kalaśa" (since the *sphoṭa* is one and the same), the author raises the doubt with the words "And not... (*na ca*). "The cause of the cognition of meaning" means the instrumental cause of the understanding of meaning. He explains what kind of causal relationship this is with the words "manifested by its synonyms" (*tatparyāyābhivyakte*).

The meaning is that when the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) has occurred with respect to a *sphoṭa* manifested by a particular synonym (*paryāya*), then upon hearing that same synonym, the comprehension of the object arises from the *sphoṭa* thus manifested.

Just as, when a sphoṭa is manifested by a synonym for "pot" (ghaṭa), the apprehension of its expressive power (*śaktigraha*) occurs in the form: "this sphoṭa is the designator of the object possessing a conch-like neck and so forth"; therefore, in the sentence "bring the pot," because there is the hearing of a synonym for the form "pot," the cognition of the object possessing a conch-like neck and so forth arises from the manifested sphoṭa—this is indeed logical. For the apprehension of expressive power exists in a sphoṭa manifested by whatever synonym is heard within a sentence.

The meaning is as follows: if, however, instead of the sentence "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), the sentence "bring the pot" (*kalaśam ānaya*) were employed, then—since the sphoṭa which manifests such synonyms as exist within the sentence has not yet had its power grasped in the form "this [sphoṭa] denotes an object possessing a shell-like neck and so forth"—there would be no occurrence of the cognition of the meaning from it due to the absence of the cause, which is the grasping of that power (*śaktigraha*). Thus it is said, "in this way."

The meaning is that the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in the *sphoṭa* manifested by such synonyms as are heard in a particular sentence, because this [apprehension] is accepted as the cause for the understanding of the meaning. Here, based on the etymology "that which is manifested (*sphuṭyate*) by the phonemes (*varṇaiḥ*)," the word *sphoṭa* should be understood as referring to the sound (*śabda*). Regarding the phrase "by the necessity of the apprehension of the expressive power": the meaning is that the aforementioned causal relationship is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Regarding the phrase "pertaining to each respective synonym":...

The sphoṭa manifested through the mode (paryāya) consisting of "jar" (ghaṭa) is the denoter of the object possessing a conch-like neck and so forth; likewise, the sphoṭa manifested through the mode consisting of "pitcher" (kalaśa) is also the denoter of the object possessing a conch-like neck and so forth. Thus, the meaning is that it is appropriate for the apprehension of the power residing in each respective mode to be the cause [of the cognition]. He states the reason why the apprehension of the power residing in each respective mode is appropriately the cause of the cognition of the object: "tathā sati" (when that is the case), and "śaktigrahatvenaiva" (precisely by way of being the apprehension of power).

The meaning is: "precisely by way of grasping the capacity residing in each respective synonym. Regarding the phrase "and because of parsimony" (*lāghavāt ca*): the word *ca* (and) indicates a reason. The sense is that since there is parsimony in the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), it is therefore appropriate to state the causality only in the aforementioned form. Regarding the phrase "otherwise" (*anyathā*): the meaning is "in the case of the opposite of what was stated. He demonstrates this very opposition with the words "manifested in each respective synonym" (*tattatparyāyābhivyakta*).

The meaning is that if the apprehension of a power residing in a *sphoṭa* manifested through various synonyms were the cause of the comprehension of meaning, there would be a complexity (*gaurava*) in the delimiting condition (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) of that causality; this is because this delimiting condition would be more cumbersome than the previously mentioned one. "Not the second" means that even the second position—that there are multiple *sphoṭas* in the case of synonyms—is not tenable. He states the reason for its untenability with the word "infinite" (*ananta*).

The meaning is as follows: since there are infinite synonyms for each individual object, one must postulate as many words as there are synonyms—this constitutes the infinity of words (*padānantya*). Furthermore, one must postulate that these infinite words possess the expressive power (*śakti*) to denote their respective meanings—this constitutes the infinity of powers (*śaktyānantya*). Consequently, this results in extreme theoretical complexity (*gaurava*). In comparison to that, it is simpler (*lāghava*) to postulate that the expressive power resides only in those phonemes (*varṇa*), which are already established and perceptible by the auditory organ.

"Therefore, the theory of *sphoṭa* as something distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*) is untenable"—this refers to what was stated by the author of the *Parimala*. The meaning is that it was stated by the author of the *Parimala* and others. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the work *Nyāyarakṣāmaṇi* is included. "It has been discarded" means that the refutation of the theory of *sphoṭa* as distinct from the phonemes, as set forth in the *Parimala* and other texts, has been rejected. The underlying sense is that [we] accept that the *sphoṭa*, consisting of the phonemes qualified by a specific sequence such as "gha-ṭ-a," is the expressive agent (*vācaka*).

Anticipating the objection that in the case of synonyms, the assumption of multiple powers (śakti) under the theory of multiple sphoṭas would entail unnecessary complexity (gaurava), the author provides the following resolution: "Because it is established for all" (*sarvasiddhatvāt*). This means that even in the systems of the Naiyāyikas and others who do not accept a transcendent sphoṭa, a difference in power is established according to the difference between synonymous words. Thus, since the infinity of powers is agreed upon by everyone, including the Naiyāyikas and others, the proponents of a transcendent sphoṭa should not raise the charge of an "infinity of powers" as a defect against us; this is the underlying sense.

Synonymy (*paryāyatva*) consists in having different word-orders while possessing the same basis for application (*samānapravṛttinimittakatva*), or alternatively, in having different determinants of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) while the determinant of the denotable object (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) remains identical. For example, "ghaṭa" and "kalaśa" are synonyms. An objection might be raised: "In the case of synonyms, if the *sphoṭa* were multiple, there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*); but if it were one, how could there be a difference in their expressive powers? Anticipating this, he says: "tadavacchedaka... (the determinant of that). This means the determinant of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*).

And thus, even though the *sphoṭa* is one, a difference in its powers (*śakti*) should be understood to arise from the difference in the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) that delimits those powers; the sense is that this is like a difference in the denotable object (*śakya*) resulting from a difference in the delimiter of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Regarding the phrase "because it has been established previously": the meaning is that this was established by such passages as the *Sāra* commentary, which states: "But [the relation of] 'immediately following' consists in being the object of a cognition produced in a moment that has the cognition [of the preceding element] as its locus. Demonstrating the argument for a distinct *sphoṭa* stated in the *Kaustubha*, he says: "In the *Kaustubha*, however..."

The meaning is: "in the *Śabdakaustubha* composed by Bhaṭṭojī Dīkṣita. One should understand that this applies to the *Smṛtikaustubha*, the *Saṃskārakaustubha*, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the series of phonemes" (*varṇamālāyām*), the meaning is "in a collection of phonemes. The mention of "the cognition [of] a word" (*padam iti pratīteḥ*) is an elliptical expression (an *upalakṣaṇa*) for "the cognition [of] a sentence" (*vākyam iti pratīteḥ*). "Precisely distinct" (*atirikta eva*) means "precisely distinct from the phonemes. This is because a collection is distinct from its constituent members; otherwise, cognitions such as "this is a word" would be untenable.

Because each individual phoneme lacks the nature of being a word, and because, according to the reasoning already stated, the cognition that "this is one word" would otherwise be untenable. The phrase "otherwise" means: in the absence of accepting a *sphoṭa* distinct from the phonemes. The phrase "distinct from the pot-sherds" [is used] as an illustration.

If you argue that the cognition "word" (*padam*) can be accounted for by referring simply to those phonemes residing in the intellect—since such a cognition is capable of being explained [by them] alone—it is therefore not possible to postulate a *sphoṭa* distinct from the phonemes, because the cognition is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhatvāt*), then it would follow as a consequence that even the cognition "jar" (*ghaṭaḥ*) could be accounted for by those very potsherds which are accepted as the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the jar; thus, the existence of a jar or similar object as something distinct from the potsherds and so forth, as maintained by the Naiyāyikas and others, would be unestablished. This is the meaning.

Therefore, the sense is that since the cognition of "word" and "sentence" cannot otherwise be accounted for, one must accept the sphoṭa as something distinct from the phonemes, just as a jar is distinct from its shards and so forth. || 67 ||

Now, having raised the objection that the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*) would be useless, he prepares the introductory framework by demonstrating its utility, beginning with the words "nanvevam" (But if this were so). The meaning is that one accepts that only the indivisible *sphoṭa*—whether of a word or a sentence—is the expressive agent. "Śāstrāprāmāṇya" means that the science of grammar, as initiated by the three sages beginning with Pāṇini, would face the consequence of being invalid, i.e., it would result in futility. The underlying thought is that a word, consisting of suffixes (*sup*) and verbal endings (*tiṅ*), is indivisible. [The author continues] with the words "śāstrasya" (of the science...).

The meaning is "of the science of grammar" (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*). Regarding the phrase "by means of base and suffix" (*prakṛti-pratyayābhyām*): the base (*prakṛti*) is the verbal root *bhū* and so forth; the suffix (*pratyaya*) is *tiP* and so forth. The meaning is that [grammar] has as its sole fruit the derivation of words through the prescription of these two. Thus, the implication is that if one were to accept the indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) of the word, this science—which establishes the denotation of word-meanings through the division into base and suffix—would lack authority. Keeping such a doubt in mind, he says "like the five sheaths" (*pañcakośādivat*) in order to dispel it.

The phrase "up to the words 'for the sake of attaining the goal'" (upeyapratipattyarthā ityantena) means "this conceptualization" (eṣākalpanā). The meaning is: the conceptualization of stems, suffixes, and so forth. One should understand that in the expression "for the sake of attaining the goal," there is a change of number (vacanavipariṇāma) and a change of gender (liṅgavipariṇāma), because of its grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the word "conceptualization" (kalpanā). The meaning of "by this which has such a form within" (antaratenaitadrūpaḥ) is as follows: the word "since" (yataḥ) is to be supplied from what follows. The syntactical connection (anvaya) is: "Since, for whatever reason, the means (upāyāḥ) for attaining the goal (upeyapratipattyarthāḥ) are unstable (anavasthitāḥ), that is, indefinite (aniyatāḥ)."

The meaning is the attainment (*pratipatti*)—that is, the reaching or the knowledge—of that which is to be reached (*upeya*). He establishes the analogy of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) and so forth with the words "this is the point" (*ayaṃ bhāvaḥ*), etc. Regarding the word "just as" (*yathā*): in the *Bhṛguvallī*, Bhṛgu Vāruṇi questioned his father Varuṇa about Brahman. That Varuṇa declared, "Food is [Brahman]. Having reflected upon the origin and other aspects of food, he questioned him again. Thereupon, he replied, "Prāṇa is Brahman."

After determining that it was not so, he asked again, and [the teacher] replied once more: "It is the mind. Since the scripture states regarding that [mind] as well—"The food that is eaten becomes threefold; that which is coarse becomes feces, that which is middling becomes flesh, and that which is subtle becomes the mind"—he asked again when [the teacher] said, "It consists of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*). Having understood that this too is not so because it is merely conditioned by its own functions (*vṛtti*), he questioned him yet again.

Then, when it is stated that "Bliss is Brahman," after the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), the Brahman to be known is presented as "the tail, the support. In this context, the exposition of the five sheaths is for the purpose of leading one to the realization of the pure Brahman. This is just as in the *Ānandavallī*, where there is a copulative compound ending with the word "bliss" (*ānanda*), such as "food, breath, mind, understanding, and bliss. Following that, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of abundance and so forth; it is connected to each member individually, according to the maxim: "That which is heard at the end of a copulative compound is connected with each member."

Thus, the meaning is that there is an exposition—that is, a demonstration—of the five sheaths (kośas), consisting of the *annamaya*, *prāṇamaya*, *manomaya*, *vijñānamaya*, and *ānandamaya*, which serve as the means for the knowledge of the pure Brahman. Here, the term *ānandamaya* does not refer to the primary Brahman, but rather to the individual soul (*jīva*). However, the word "Brahman" heard in the phrase "Brahman is the tail, the support" (*brahmapucchaṃ pratiṣṭhā*) is indeed what designates the primary Brahman; it is for this very reason that the use of the word "tail" (*puccha*), signifying the support of the universe, is appropriate.

Because the primary meaning of "tail" (the literal object) is sublated in that context, he says with this intention: "real" (*vāstavam*). The meaning is: for the purpose of making known that which is the tail—Brahman—which is uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time and is the support of the universe. By stating the reality of this Brahman, who is the primary support of the universe, the unreality of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) is indicated; and this is indeed clear from the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* and other works. Using this illustration, he states the point relevant to the present subject as established: "In the same way" (*evam*).

Here too, by asserting the reality of the *sphoṭa*, it is indicated that the conceptualization of the division between base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) and so forth is unreal. One might object: "Is the science of grammar not an alternative means for establishing the knowledge of the *sphoṭa*? For such knowledge is possible even without it. To this, he raises the doubt beginning with "nanu" (but surely). Regarding the phrase "of perception" (*pratyakṣasya*): the meaning is that because sound is grasped by the sense organ of hearing, it is perceptible. The word "ādi" (and so forth) in the phrase "from hearing and so forth" includes reflection (*manana*). [The phrase] "because of the possibility of cognition" (*bodhasaṃbhavāt*) refers to this.

And thus, since understanding can occur through other means even without the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), grammar is not the sole means for that knowledge; therefore, he says: "The means [of knowledge] are for those who are learning. Demonstrating the reasoning—accompanied by an illustration—for why one means does not invalidate another means, he says: "And likewise, grammar..."

Regarding this, they say: "This grammatical treatise is not a means for the knowledge of *sphoṭa* in the manner of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), because even a common person (*pāmara*) who has merely mastered the usage of a sentence such as 'bring the cow' experiences verbal comprehension even without knowledge of the treatise. Consequently, since comprehension is possible for him without the knowledge of *sphoṭa*, and that knowledge [of *sphoṭa*] exists even without the treatise, the causal relationship between the grammatical treatise and the knowledge of *sphoṭa* is not invariable. Anticipating this objection, he says: "A distinct class (*vaijātya*) is postulated."

The meaning is that [the property] is postulated as a specific universal (jāti) established by being the delimitor (avacchedaka) of the state of being produced by the practice of grammar. And thus, there is no fault because of the difference in the delimiters of the effect (kāryatāvacchedaka). In this regard, he provides an illustration: "as if produced by a mantra."

The sense is as follows: Just as in the case of the recollection of an object that is an integral part of the ritual performance (*prayogasamavāyin*), since it can be accomplished by various means, when one desires to recall the object by some other method while setting aside the mantra, the rule is established that "the object must be recalled by the mantra alone. Consequently, the Mīmāṃsakas postulate a specific "extraordinary nature" (*vaijātya*)—in the form of a particular universal (*jāti*)—which serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for being produced by the mantra within the recollection of the object generated by the mantra; the same applies here as well. [This refers to the phrase] "vedānta... and so forth.

The sense is as follows: since it is possible for the knowledge of Brahman to arise even from hearing non-Vedic texts on the nature of speech, the Vedāntins postulate a specific "extraordinary nature" (*vaijātya*)—which consists of a particular genus established as the delimitor of being produced by the hearing of Vedānta—in order to exclude such deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Regarding the utility of such knowledge, he says: "And of that knowledge... and so forth.

The meaning is: "of the knowledge of *sphoṭa* produced by the study of the science of grammar. Regarding the phrase "for the purification of the body": just as sacrifices such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* are useful for the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), so too the knowledge of *sphoṭa* is useful for the purification of the body and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "body and so forth," speech and mind are included. Thus, the implication is that the treatise is not useless. Regarding the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*): the meaning is that it is a direct cause of heaven, while it is a cause of liberation (*mokṣa*) through a mediated succession.

The intended meaning is as follows: it is true that the *sphoṭa* alone, common to both spoken and refined (Sanskrit) language, is the signifier (*vācaka*), and that its cognition takes the form of auditory perception and so forth. However, it is also [presented] as consisting of stems and suffixes, just like the phonemes (*varṇas*). And thus, the knowledge of that [sphoṭa] preceded by the analysis of stems, suffixes, and so on, becomes a cause for the purification of the body through its application preceded by that [analysis], just as sacrifice and other rites are for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). To support this stated point, he cites the *Vākyapadīya*: "That has been said," and "that is the door."

The science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*) is that which expresses that *sphoṭa*. Regarding the phrase "of liberation" (*apavargasya*): according to Amara, *mokṣa*, *apavarga*, and *artha* are synonyms for liberation. Regarding the word "door" (*dvāram*): it means a door in the sense of being its cause, like a gateway. The qualifying attribute in the form of its cause is "the treatment of the impurities of speech" (*vāṅ-malānāṃ cikitsitam*). The meaning is: "that in which treatment has arisen. From the root *kit* (meaning "remedy for disease") with the suffix *san* and then the suffix *kta*, the final meaning is "the agent of the removal of the impurities of speech. Regarding the term "pertaining to knowledge" (*adhividyam*).

The term *avyayībhāva* [is used] in the sense of a case ending (*vibhaktyarthe*). The meaning is that, among all branches of knowledge (*sarvavidyā*), it shines forth preeminently because of its extreme purity. Regarding the word *idam*: the meaning is that this science of grammar (*vyākaraṇaśāstra*) is exceedingly pure because it was initiated by great seers (*maharṣi*) such as Pāṇini and others. Regarding the phrase *siddhisopāna*: the meaning is that, among those steps (*sopānaparvan*) which constitute the ladder (*sopāna*) to perfection (*siddhi*), that is, liberation (*mokṣa*), it is the first station for placing one's feet. Regarding the word *iyam*: it is the straight royal road (*rājapaddhati*), meaning the main highway, for people who desire liberation.

Regarding this: "consisting of *sphoṭa*" is the meaning. Regarding "past": the meaning is "one for whom error—that is, delusion—is past"; that is to say, one who is free from illusion. "Solely" means "the speech known as Parā. "Perceives" means he directly realizes [it] through the power born of yoga. Now, an objection is raised: since the division between stem (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) is merely conceptual and thus like the horn of a hare, it is impossible to have knowledge of a reality consisting of *sphoṭa* by means of that [division]. To this, he says: "And not by means of what is false. [The opponent asks: "How then can it be real?"

The point is that, since one does not observe the production of the cessation of thirst by means of illusory deer or water, the perception of a real *sphoṭa* cannot occur through the postulation of an illusory nature (*prakṛti*) and so forth. "Of that" refers to the postulation of the nature and other categories. "Because its falsity is unestablished" means that even if it is of the nature of *māyā*, like the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) and so on, it is not as utterly non-existent or void as a rabbit's horn; this is the sense. "Because it will be stated later."

The meaning is that by the verse beginning with "manifested by many individuals" (*anekavyaktyabhivyaṅgyā*), the distinction of [Brahman] from both the existent and the non-existent is intended to be indicated, just as in the case of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*). By the phrase "from the five sheaths," etc., the analogy of the "line-drawn cow" (*rekhāgavaya*) is included.

Just as it is well known in the world that the knowledge of a conventionally real gavaya arises through a figure of a gavaya variegated with lines such as horns and so forth, in the same way, even by means of an unreal conceptualization of primordial matter (prakṛti) and the like, the knowledge of the sphoṭa—which exists as a reality—is by no means impossible; thus, everything is faultless—this is the intended meaning. || 68 ||

He states the grounds for accepting [the phoneme as the object]: "even accent, length, and so forth. By "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of production, destruction, and other such properties is intended. Accentuation (udāttatva) and the like do not reside in the phoneme (*varṇa*), because that [phoneme] is unitary and eternal. This is due to the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is that very same [phoneme]. Nor is the object of that [recognition] the absence of difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by the universal *gatva* (phonemic-ness); for it is impossible to discard the non-difference of the individual aspect (*vyakti-aṃśa*), which also appears [in cognition], unless there is a subverting proof (*bādhaka*). Furthermore, the perception of production is not a subverting proof.

Since origination, which consists in the coming into being of what was previously non-existent, would contradict experience with respect to phonemes (*varṇa*), for this very reason the cognition and linguistic usage are "he utters a phoneme" and not "he produces a phoneme. Furthermore, "utterance" (*uccaritva*) is the state of being characterized by manifestation produced by the contact of the palate, lips, and so forth. Moreover, since it is possible to explain the origination and other properties residing in the manifesting sound (*dhvani*) as having the phoneme as their locus through a causal chain (*paramparā*), that [origination] does not prove the existence of a distinct phoneme.

Furthermore, because it is accepted that there is a commitment to the persistence of the sound through a series (*paramparā*), there is no error [in the cognition]. What remains is the claim that there is error regarding the aspect of direct connection (*sākṣāt-sambandha*). But even that is equal to your own position regarding the aspect of non-difference between individuals in the case of the judgment "this is that" (*so 'yam*); however, for me, the parsimony (*lāghava*) is superior, as I do not have to postulate additional phonemes, their antecedent non-existences (*prāgabhāva*), or their destructions (*dhvaṃsa*). Nor should it be argued that in the case of sound-persistence there is a lack of evidence, or that such persistence is impossible due to the absence of conch-shells or other sources that produce sound.

In the case of the utterance of sounds beginning with the letter *ka*, it is observed that at each respective place of articulation, no varṇa is produced within the slight interval of the tongue, yet a sound (*dhvani*) is produced; therefore, it is postulated that the contact between the air-current generated by the striking of the tongue and the throat, and so forth, is the producer of the sound.

Furthermore, since that [quality] exists even at the site of the production of the phoneme (*varṇa*), the postulation of a relationship of counteracted and counteractor (*pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva*) would be without proof for you alone; thus, there is indeed the opposite burden of complexity (*gaurava*). Likewise, due to mutual contradiction, it is not logical that properties such as acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), short (*hrasva*), and long (*dīrgha*) reside in the phoneme. This is their intention. And so, the resolution of the cognitions of production and so forth, as well as their status as valid knowledge, is equal for others [the Mīmāṃsakas] as well; the sense is that the reply is by way of a *pratibandyā* (reductio ad absurdum). || 10 ||
Thus, there are five types of *vyakti-sphoṭas*. Now, he states the *jāti-sphoṭa*:
"Just as [the universal] is regarded as the denotatum (*śakya*), let the parsimony (*lāghava*) of the universal be observed regarding its being the signifier (*śaktatva*).
Or, let there be a distinction among phonemes based on adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*), like [the difference between] high and low pitches. (11)

The point is this: phonemes (*varṇa*) are indeed necessary according to the reasoning already stated; otherwise, just as one might say "this is that *ga*-phoneme," one could also say "that which was heard as this *ga*-phoneme is this *ha*-phoneme," because the *sphoṭa* is unitary. Furthermore, there would be no basis for the cognition "this is a *ga*-phoneme, not a *ha*-phoneme. Moreover, must one accept the property of being a *ga*-phoneme (*gatva*) and so forth in the *sphoṭa*, or not? In the first case, let that very thing be the *ga*-phoneme itself, since proponents of the eternity of phonemes do not admit a separate *gatva*.

Thus, there is indeed complexity (gaurava) in postulating an additional *sphoṭa*; furthermore, in the latter case, there is a contradiction with the perception of the phonemes such as 'ga'. If it is argued that the cognition occurs by superimposing a specific generic quality (*vaijātya*) residing in the conjunctions of air or the sound itself, we say no; for a cognition cannot be considered an error in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*). Or, let the conjunction of air itself be the letter 'ga'; if it is objected that its being beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*) is a defect, we reply that this is like the manifestation of a property, so there is no need for a *sphoṭa*. Therefore, the phonemes certainly exist, but they are not the expressers (*vācaka*), because that would involve unnecessary complexity.

Furthermore, it is logical that the denotative capacity (vācakatva) belongs to the universal (jāti) alone, just as its denotedness (vācyatva) does, according to the principle of the *ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*. This is because, based on the uniform cognition "this is the word *hari*," the knowledge of the word *hari* is the cause for the presentation of the object *hari*, being delimited by the status of being the presentation of *hari*; and since a specific universal must necessarily be postulated as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of that [causal relation].

Nor can the determination of the relatum and the delimiter be accounted for by the mere sequence of phonemes (*varṇa*), because that would lead to the undesirable consequence (*anyathāsiddhi*) that even a jar or "jar-ness" could be established otherwise—namely, through the clay particles qualified by specific conjunctions and by shapes such as the belly and so forth. Therefore, it is that very genus (*jāti*) which is the expressive [signifier], and it delimits [the object] through identity (*tādātmya*). Now, one might object: in cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*, since those two genera are present [in both words], there would be no cognition of a difference in meaning. To this, he says: "Or it is adventitious (*aupādhikaḥ*). The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "but" (*tu*).

The meaning is that the distinction lies in the fact that the sequential order itself is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) which manifests the specific universal (*jāti*); thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the cognition that serves as the cause. He provides an illustration for this difference in cognition conditioned by an adjunct with the words "of the phonemes" (*varṇānām*). || 11 ||
Now, one might object that since the universal (jāti) exists in each individual phoneme once it has been produced, the meaning should be understood from each individual phoneme. To this he says:
"The universal, manifested by many individuals, is known as the sphoṭa;
by some, the individuals themselves are conceived as its 'sounds' (dhvani). (12)

The universal (*jāti*) itself, manifested through various individual instances (*vyakti*), is known as *sphoṭa*; that is to say, it is the means of cognition by virtue of its connection [to the instances]. By this, the objection that because *sphoṭa* is eternal, there would be the consequence of constant comprehension of meaning, is refuted. This is the sense: although the aforementioned defect exists in the view that the *dhvani* (sound) is the *sphoṭa*, it does not exist in the views regarding the word (*pada*) or the sentence (*vākya*), because in those cases, its existence as a quality distributed across multiple substrates (*vyāsajyavṛttitva*) is established by the very means of cognition that apprehend the substrates themselves. The remaining point is that some maintain that the individuals are merely *dhvanis*, since there is no difference between *dhvani* and *varṇa* (phoneme).
For it is said in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: "The learned grammarians have designated as 'dhvani' that sound which manifests the sphoṭa, which is the primary element. (12)
Now, what is that genus? To this he says:
"In every individual object there exist two parts, one real and one unreal;
that which is real therein is considered the genus, while the individuals are regarded as unreal. (13)

In every cognition and for every object, the universal (*jāti*) is real while the individuals (*vyakti*) are unreal; the meaning is that Brahman itself, as qualified by each respective individual, is the universal.
