And it has been stated by Kaiyaṭa: "The meaning is that the reality of Brahman, delimited by unreal limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is what is denoted by the word 'substance' (*dravya*). And: "The very reality of Brahman appears in the form of the word."

How, then, is Kaiyaṭa’s statement—that even the universal such as "cowness" (gotva) is impermanent because it does not exist in the vision of Brahman, according to the Vedic declaration "All this is indeed the Self"—to be reconciled? It should be understood that this refers to an alternative position, namely that [the universal] is either a particular property of ignorance (avidyā) or something produced by ignorance (āvidyaka). || 13 ||
He clarifies that very element of truth:
"The essence of sound, which is thus being extracted as stainless, they call the imperishable Brahman itself; salutation to that Perfect Self. (14)
Thus ends the exposition on the *padādi-sphoṭa* (the sphoṭa of words and so forth) within the *Kārikās* composed by Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita. The *Sphoṭavāda* is complete.
Thus end the Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakārikās composed by Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita.

The intended meaning is this: there is a twofold creation established by the Śruti text, "I shall unfold name and form"; therein, the reality (tattva) of name is the very same as that of form. The aspect of grammatical derivation (prakriyā), however, is merely the manifestation of ignorance (avidyā).
And it is said in the Vākyapadīya:
"In the scriptures, it is ignorance itself that is described through various distinctions of grammatical derivation."
"But the undertaking of entities is beginningless; Brahman is eternal."

By the phrase "Brahman alone," he indicates that the nature of being self-luminous and illuminating others—established by such scriptural passages as "In this state, this person is his own light," "Everything shines after Him alone," and "By His light all this shines"—is the meaning made manifest (*sphuṭati*). Thus, he indicates that the word *sphoṭa* is used in its etymological sense (*yaugika*) as that which is the object of manifestation. At the end of the collection of verses, he utters an auspicious benediction in the form of praise and salutation, beginning with the words "To the Full Self" (*pūrṇātmane*), etc. (Verse 73).

Thus ends the exposition of the eight types of *sphoṭa* in the *Śāṅkarī*, a commentary on the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, composed by Śaṅkara, the son of Raṅgabhaṭṭa; herein, the determination of *sphoṭa* is complete in this explanatory work on the *Sāra*. (17)
Now, the Sphoṭacandrikā.
Having bowed at the pair of feet of his parents, Jānakī and Raghunātha, Mauni Śrī Kṛṣṇabhaṭṭa composes the Sphoṭacandrikā. || 1 ||

Among grammarians, the term *sphoṭa* is used for words that convey the expressed (*vācya*), indicated (*lakṣya*), or suggested (*vyaṅgya*) meanings—namely, denotative (*vācaka*), indicative (*lākṣaṇika*), and suggestive (*vyañjaka*) words—or for the universal (*jāti*) residing in them. The word *sphoṭa* is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍha*), based on the derivation "that from which the meaning bursts forth" (*sphuṭati arthaḥ yasmāt*), similar to the word *paṅkaja* ("born in mud," i.e., a lotus). If one were to accept only the etymological sense, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to gestures and other such things, since they too convey suggested meanings. Furthermore, it is not the case that the word *sphoṭa* is unknown as a synonym for "denotative" and the rest.

As it is seen in the *Harivaṃśa*: "Among letters you are the letter 'a', you are the *sphoṭa*, and you are that which rests upon the phonemes. Thus, there are five types of *vyakti-sphoṭas*: those consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), sentences (*vākya*), indivisible words (*akhaṇḍapada*), and indivisible sentences (*akhaṇḍavākya*). According to the view that the universal (*jāti*) which delimits the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is the denoted (*vācya*), just as the universal which delimits the denotative capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) is the denoter (*vācaka*), there are three types of *jāti-sphoṭas* distinguished by phoneme, word, and sentence. In this way, there are eight *sphoṭas*.

Just as in the *Ānandavallī*, for the sake of knowing the pure Brahman, the method employed is the presentation of the non-ultimate nature of Brahman within the five sheaths (*kośas*)—consisting of food, vital breath, mind, intellect, and bliss; or just as, for the sake of knowing the star Arundhatī, one is led to it by first identifying a gross star as being non-ultimately the Arundhatī; so too, for the sake of attaining the knowledge of the ultimate, indivisible sentence-meaning, these—letters, words, sentences, indivisible words, and *sphoṭa*—are merely means.

As it has been said: "The means [of instruction] for those in training are the caresses of children; by standing upon the path of the unreal, one subsequently strives for the real. The *padāsphoṭa* (word-sphoṭa) is the denotative capacity of a collection of phonemes—such as *pat*, *pit*, and so forth—which, though not encompassed by the definitions of a "word" (*pada*) as "that which ends in a nominal or verbal suffix" or a "sentence" (*vākya*) as "that whose primary qualificand is the meaning of a single finite verb," have their expressive power grasped through grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). This refers to the phonemes themselves in the form of roots (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*).

Furthermore, those [elements] such as the *visarga* and *tiP* are inherent in the application (*prayoga*), but not the *l*-sounds, *s*-sounds, and so forth, which are merely postulated as their substitutes (*sthānin*). This is because the latter are not fixed; for instance, the *r* is remembered through the *visarga*, and through that, the *su*; likewise, the *tip* is remembered through the *ṇal*, and through that, the *l*-sound. Thus, the complexity (*gaurava*) is quite evident. Moreover, it would lead to the undesirable consequence that a non-grammarian, who lacks knowledge of the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*), would understand only the substitute.

Thus, the claim of the logicians—that the *sthānin* (the original form) alone is the expressive unit (*vācaka*) due to parsimony (*lāghava*), whereas the substitute (*ādeśa*) is not because of its complexity (*gaurava*)—is refuted; for that would result in the opposite burden of complexity. This is what the logicians intend by the "word-sphoṭa" (*padasphoṭa*), since they accept that "a word is that which possesses expressive power" (*śaktam padam*). However, the grammarians (*śābdikas*) maintain that this is incorrect because it lacks proof, lacks utility, and contradicts their own treatises. To illustrate: a word possessing expressive power is fourfold—conventional (*rūḍha*), etymological (*yaugika*), conventional-etymological (*yogarūḍha*), and etymological-conventional (*yaugikarūḍha*).

"Ox," "cook," "lotus," and "horse-ear" are, in order, the examples. Among these, regarding the derivative example "cook" (*pācaka*), that word which is expressive—namely *pac* and *aka*—is not derivative; for although the whole (*pācaka*) is derivative, it is not expressive. Thus, the statement that "an expressive word is derivative" is an unexamined assertion. In the absence of a specific [inherent] power (*viśiṣṭaśakti*), the status of being a derivative word consists in being a word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), which is a composite of stem and suffix as taught by grammar.

The inclusion of the term "satya" (truth/real) is for the purpose of excluding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to [words like] *yoga-rūḍha* (conventional-derivative), because in those cases, the apprehension of the word's power (*śakti-graha*) occurs with respect to the qualified whole. Likewise, the example of *gaura* as a conventional (*rūḍhi*) word is also inconsistent. For a word is conventionally fixed (*rūḍha*) when it conveys a meaning through its aggregate form as a *subanta* (inflected noun), provided there is no cognition of the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) as postulated by grammar—just as in the case of words such as *maṇi* (jewel) or *nūpura* (anklet). A word is *yogarūḍha* (conventional-derivative) when it conveys a meaning through the power of its aggregate preceded by a recollection of the meanings of its constituent parts as postulated by the technical treatises (*śāstra*).

Just as in the case of "lotus-born" (*paṅkaja*) and so forth, it is appropriate that [the word] possesses both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍha*) meanings due to its being occupied by both. Furthermore, the distinction asserted by the logicians—that there is a category called "etymologically-conventional" (*yaugika-rūḍha*)—is also untenable. This is because of the maxim that "that which is uttered once conveys its meaning only once"; thus, the word *maṇḍapa* is conventionally fixed (*rūḍha*) in the sense of a specific type of house, and distinct from its separate etymological sense as "one who prepares a festive pavilion. Since there is no evidence for accepting an additional category of meaning, the example of "skilled in ritual action" (*karmaṇi kuśalaḥ*) as an instance of conventional indication (*rūḍhi-lakṣaṇā*) is likewise incorrect.

According to the reasoning stated, since the quality of being conventionally established (*rūḍhatva*) in the sense of "one who gathers *kuśa* grass" applies to the agent of that action, the term *dvirepha* is indeed conventionally established in the sense of a "bee. This is because it is included in the lexicon (*kośa*) as a synonym for "bee"; for in a lexicon, there is no inclusion of terms used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) among synonyms. Thus, through the relation of being denotable by a word whose own denotation [is "two *rephas*"], the word *dvirepha* refers to the bee; and according to the one-syllable lexicons (*ekākṣara-kośa*), all individual phonemes (*varṇas*) possess the status of the *sphoṭa*.

This is because the *Bhāṣya* establishes that phonemes (*varṇas*) possess meaning by stating, "phonemes are meaningful. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that words such as *dhanaṃ* (wealth) and *vanaṃ* (forest) would fail to receive the designation of *prātipadika* (nominal stem). This is because the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) acts as an obstacle to any grammatical operation whose purpose is to destroy the sequential order (*kānupūrvī*) that serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the power residing in its own constituents. As for the claim in the *Bhūṣaṇa* that the word *sphoṭa* is used purely etymologically—as in "that from which meaning bursts forth (*sphuṭati arthaḥ yasmāt*)"—meaning "the signifier"—that is not correct.

Since corrupt words (*asādhu-śabda*) possess expressive power (*śakti*) just like correct words (*sādhu-śabda*), they would indistinguishably become *sphoṭa* as well. This is not an acceptable consequence, for grammarians do not admit it; furthermore, it would result in the failure to include metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*) and suggestive (*vyañjaka*) words. Nor should one be misled by the statement "the word here is threefold—[denotative, indicative, and] suggestive"—into thinking that the suggester exists only in poetry and not in grammar. For those who maintain that the indivisible *sphoṭa* is manifested by the word (*pada*) accept this very point.

Objection: In the view of the Naiyāyikas, *śakti* (expressive power) is the will of God (*īśvarecchā*). In the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, it is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) over and above the others. The modern Naiyāyikas accept it as either the will of God, knowledge, or form (*ākṛti*), due to the lack of a decisive reason [to choose otherwise]. In both cases, however, that power resides only in correct words (*sādhu*) and not in incorrect ones (*asādhu*). Otherwise, since the definition of correctness is "the possession of expressive power" (*śaktimattva*), it would follow that even incorrect words are correct, as they too would be subject to that definition. Furthermore, there is an absence of grammar, lexicons, and other means for grasping expressive power in the case of incorrect words. Response: This is not so.

In that case, since comprehension would not arise from those [corrupt forms] due to the absence of expressive power (*śakti*), the argument of the Naiyāyikas—that comprehension arises either from an error regarding power or from the recollection of the correct word—is not tenable. This is because comprehension is established by experience even for those who are linguistically proficient, even without the recollection of the correct word, and because such an assumption involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, the claim that comprehension arises from an error is also untenable; for just as a piece of mother-of-pearl perceived through the error of being silver does not produce the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) of "silver," so too, comprehension known to have arisen from an error regarding power would fail to produce practical usage.

For it is impossible to assert the absence of the Lord’s will—which has pure existence (*sanmātra*) as its object—at that time. Furthermore, whose error regarding power (*śakti-bhrama*) is it? Is it the Lord’s, the agent of all worldly transactions, or someone else’s? It cannot be the former, because it is logically untenable for the Lord to be subject to error. Nor can it be the latter, because at the beginning of creation, there exists no one other than the Lord who could be the agent of the usage of correct or incorrect words, nor the instigator or the one being instigated.

Just as the creation of objects that produce merit and demerit has God as its creator, so too the creation of both types of words—correct and incorrect—has God alone as its creator. Consequently, the claim that this is an error is entirely untenable. Furthermore, the inference of a child standing by the roadside is not an error regarding either correct or incorrect words; for, since the causal complex that leads to the inference of expressive power (*śakti*) is present and there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), it cannot be considered an error.

[Objection: If it is accepted that even incorrect words (*asādhu*) possess denotative power (*śakti*), then by the definition of the logicians—that correctness (*sādhutva*) consists in possessing denotative power—it would follow that they are correct. And if that were so, there would be no scope for the prohibition: "One should not speak barbarously (*dhlecchitavai*), nor should one use corrupt forms (*apabāṣitavai*). [Reply: This is not so, because it would result in the incorrectness of words used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*). Nor can correctness be defined as "possessing a function" (*vṛttimatva*), for if one were to include either *śakti* or *lakṣaṇā* [as the specific type of function], there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Therefore, correctness (*sādhutva*) is a specific genus that delimits the capacity to produce merit, while incorrectness (*asādhutva*) is that which delimits the capacity to produce transgression. Alternatively, correctness is the state of being understood through grammar, and incorrectness is the state of being other than that. Thus, according to the [Vedic] statement, "A single word, when correctly known and properly employed, becomes a cow of plenty (*kāmadhuk*) in the heavenly world," a word is understood as having been derived through its base and suffix by means of grammar for a specific meaning; and it is employed for such a specific meaning.

Therefore, the word *gauṇī* is correct only when applied to the cow *goṇī*, and not to the animal *gavaya*. Nor is it correct to argue that there is a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), for a determining factor is indeed a reason that favors one side over another; and such a reason exists here in the form of the prior manifestation of the cognition. For this very reason, the teacher Vardhamānopādhyāya maintains that the power (*śakti*) is the knowledge of God. Grammarians (*śābdika*), however, hold that power is the capacity to produce understanding (*bodhajanakatva*). And that consists in possessing a property that delimits the capacity to produce understanding from time immemorial (*anādibodhajanakatāvacchedakadharmavattva*).

This has been stated by Hari: "Just as there is a beginningless capacity (*yogyatā*) of the sense organs toward their respective objects, so too is the relationship between words and their meanings beginningless; such is their capacity. This capacity consists in possessing a property that delimits the status of being a generator [of the cognition]. Nor is there a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*)—such that because verbal comprehension does not arise for one who has not grasped the word-power (*śakti*), the grasp of power is a cause of verbal comprehension, and thus the grasp of power follows comprehension, while comprehension follows the grasp of power—because the grasp of power occurs through grammar, lexicons, and other means.

Otherwise, even in the position that the Lord’s will is the expressive power (*śakti*), there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) identical [to the previous case]: the comprehension of meaning follows the apprehension of the power, and the apprehension of the power follows the comprehension of meaning. Alternatively, the power is the beginningless relationship between word and meaning. However, it occurs to me that power is simply capacity (*sāmarthya*); just as in a lamp or similar light there is the capacity for being perceived and perceiving, or in fire the capacity for burning, or in the sense organs the capacity for manifesting objects—this [capacity] is effective by its very existence (*svarūpasat*), not by being known.

Nor does it follow that there would be comprehension even for one who has not grasped the word’s capacity (*śakti*), because—as in the case of sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) and other factors—the absence of the grasp of intention (*tātparya*) serves as the counter-positive of the absence that is the cause of the non-occurrence of comprehension. If it is argued that the grasp of intention is a causal factor only in the case of words with multiple meanings (*nānārtha*), that is true; however, according to the view of the Grammarians (*Śābdika*), all words possess multiple meanings. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *vṛddhir ādaic*: "of a word that has many capacities" (*anekaśakteḥ śabdasya*). The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is: "one whose capacity is manifold (aneka) across many (anekesu)," or "one who possesses many (anekā) capacities."

The established doctrine of the Naiyāyikas and others is that there is a difference in power (*śakti*) due to the difference in delimiters (*avacchedaka*). The established doctrine of the Grammarians (*Śābdikas*), however, is that there is only one single power on account of parsimony (*lāghava*). Nor should it be argued that "it is improper for a word to have multiple meanings," for this objection applies equally to your own position as well. The only difference is this: in your view, [the meanings are conveyed] by different functions (*vṛtti*), whereas in my view, they are conveyed by a single function. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of the abolition of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), for that is actually desired. Just as you yourselves do not accept *suggestion* (*vyañjanā*), even though it is established by universal experience, on account of parsimony.

And in that case, just as the consequence of the elimination of *vyañjanā* (suggestion) is not a defect [in your view], so too in my view, because of parsimony (*lāghava*), since the matter can be resolved by *śakti* (denotative power) alone, the consequence of the elimination of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is not a defect. In reality, the meaning of that [statement] is simply that when a matter can be resolved by this very function (*vṛtti*), it is improper for there to be multiple functions; for the word "meaning" (*artha*) here refers to the function (*vṛtti*). And the principle "it is improper" is rooted in parsimony. Nor should it be said that "the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained otherwise."

The meaning is not that it is improper to postulate a power (*śakti*) for that which is obtainable through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); rather, the point is that it is inappropriate to postulate a power for what is already established by the very nature of the relation (*saṃsargamaryādā*). Thus, while the Grammarians accept an additional power in fire as they do in the word, the Logicians' acceptance of a power in the word but not in fire—like the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīya*) approach—is improper. Nor should it be argued that since the phenomenon is explained by the absence of the jewel qualified by the absence of the stimulator (*uttejaka*), the postulation of such a power is entirely useless.

This is because it is more appropriate to accept a relationship of a distinct power (*śakti*), which is a simpler assumption, than to accept that the property of being a cause is delimited by a quality (*guṇatva*) or substance-ness (*dravyatva*) that is superior to the guru-mut [the teacher’s tradition]. Furthermore, in the view of the Grammarians (*Śābdika*), identity (*tādātmya*) is a non-difference that tolerates difference. Even though there is a difference between quality and substance in terms of their respective properties of quality-ness and substance-ness, they possess identity because a substance is never perceived without its quality, nor are qualities ever perceived without a substance. Thus, wherever there is inherence (*samavāya*), there is the conventional usage of "identity."

And thus, since it is impossible for the jar to exist prior to its quality [of being produced], it lacks causality with respect to that quality; therefore, by the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*), they accept that the qualified entity alone serves as the delimiting condition of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), and consequently maintain that the potsherd qualified by the quality is the cause of the jar qualified by that quality.

However, the logicians (tārkikas), because the qualified [entity] cannot be the delimiting factor of causality and because it is impossible for the qualified to be the cause, have accepted the production of a jar devoid of qualities; and since that [jar] is not pervaded by the definition of substance (*dravyatva*)—which consists in being the substratum of qualities—they have formulated the essential definition as "the possession of a genus subordinate to substance which is co-locative with qualities. This, I believe, is incorrect.

For instance, although the power (*śakti*) in fire is known through both the obstructing factor (*pratibandhaka*) and the stimulating factor (*uttejaka*), the existence of a separate power has been refuted by accepting that the cause is the absence of the magnet (*maṇi*) qualified by the absence of the stimulating factor; yet, in the case of sound, that [separate power] is accepted. Likewise, having accepted that the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) there, one says "not here" and accepts the production of a pot devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), like a sky-flower. Since all these [claims] lack the support of experience, they are all untenable; such is the direction [of the argument].

The grammarians (Śābdikas), however, accept an additional power (*śakti*) residing in fire as well as in the space within the cavity of the ear, just as there is a power in sound; this very power, or the ether qualified by that power, is the auditory organ (*śrotra*). Thus, even though the auditory organ remains in its own place, it possesses the capacity to manifest the sound of a distant drum, like a ray of light. Consequently, the view that the sound of a drum travels to the location of hearing according to the analogy of waves and ripples is not appealing, as it would entail the denial of the direct experience: "I am hearing the sound of the drum right here."

Furthermore, there is the burden of postulating multiple sounds. Nor is it reasonable to claim that the auditory organ itself travels there, because space cannot move, and because it would follow that there would be no space within the ear-cavity. The auditory organ produces the direct perception of the quality alone. Some, however, assert that like the auditory organ, the gustatory and olfactory organs also produce the direct perception of the quality alone; others, however, maintain that this is incorrect.

For instance, since sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*), a direct relationship exists by way of inherence (*samavāya*); thus, while direct perception of it is possible, the case of taste and smell is different. Their means of contact is "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyukta-samavāya*). This is an indirect relationship (*paramparā-sambandha*) based on a connection with a substance, such as a jar. In that case, since the direct perception of a substance is possible through that contact, and because a quality cannot exist in isolation from a substance, the direct perception of a quality alone is impossible.

Therefore, those two [the sense of sight and the sense of touch] produce the direct perception of a quality as qualified by its substance; they do not, however, produce the direct perception of a substance as qualified by its qualities. This is because their capacity is determined precisely in that manner through experience. As for the sense organs of sight and smell, they produce the direct perception of both types: a substance qualified by a quality, or a quality qualified by a substance. A detailed account should be seen in my *Tarkāmṛta*; it is not elaborated here for fear of prolixity. This is the direction [of the argument]. Let us return to the subject at hand.

Although an incorrect word (*asādhuśabda*) possesses denotative power, it lacks the status of *sphoṭa* because it is not what is propounded by grammar. As for the phonemes (*varṇa*) contained within it, if they possess a power determined by a monosyllabic lexicon (*ekākṣarakośa*) and manifest a different meaning, this is the "word-sphoṭa" (*padasphoṭa*), which will be analyzed under the section on word-sphoṭa. In the case of imitative words (*anukaraṇaśabda*), however, because there is a desire to express the distinction between the object of imitation and the imitation itself, they possess the status of *sphoṭa* due to their conveying the meaning in the form of the object being imitated.

If it is objected: "Granted that there is the designation of *sphoṭa* for the imitation of a correct form because of its correctness; however, since the imitation of an incorrect form is itself incorrect, how can the designation of *sphoṭa* apply to it?"—we say no. For even the imitation of an incorrect form is accepted as being correct. When the Daityas ought to have used "he 'arayah," they used "he 'alayaḥ"; by imitating that, saying "helayo helayaḥ," they did not suffer defeat. Thus, its incorrectness does not extend to the sentence as well. As the saying goes: "Whatever [the original] was, so [is the imitation]."

In the sense of "let there be," the expression *yarvāṇas tarvāṇas* was employed; those who performed an imitation of that became the sages named *yarvāṇas tarvāṇas*. No one accepts that this [imitation] is ungrammatical even within a sentence. Therefore, the grammatical correctness of an imitation of what is ungrammatical is universally accepted. In that case, when there is an intention to express non-difference between the two, there is no status as *sphoṭa* because of the absence of the manifestation of meaning.

For the sake of the knowledge of pure Brahman, just as the *annamaya-kośa* (the sheath consisting of food) is external to all, so too for the purpose of awakening to the indivisible sentence (*akhaṇḍa-vākya*), there is the *varṇasphoṭa* (the phoneme-sphoṭa); such is the direction [of the argument]. Thus ends the discussion on the *varṇasphoṭa*. Now, the *padasphoṭa* (the word-sphoṭa), which is more internal than the *varṇasphoṭa*—just as the *prāṇamaya-kośa* (the sheath consisting of vital breath) is more internal than the *annamaya-kośa*—is described. Its internality consists in its being a direct constituent of the sentence. The externality of the phoneme (*varṇa*) consists in its being a constituent of the sentence only by way of producing the word (*pada*). The *padasphoṭa* is of two kinds: *sakhaṇḍa* (with parts) and *akhaṇḍa* (without parts).

Since the apprehension of the word-potency (*śakti*) occurs through linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) and the like precisely at the level of the word, that which for us is the "divisible word-sphoṭa" (*sakhaṇḍapadasphoṭa*)—consisting of forms such as *pacati* (he cooks) or *rāmaḥ* (Rāma), namely inflected words ending in *su*-suffixes or *tiṅ*-suffixes—is, according to the view that "the word is the locus of potency," the very same thing that the logicians call the "sentence-sphoṭa" (*vākyasphoṭa*). Now, the indivisible word-sphoṭa (*akhaṇḍapadasphoṭa*) is described. It is manifested by all the phonemes (*varṇa*) existing within the word, and it is the conveyor of meaning; this is the established tenet of the Grammarians (*śābdika*).

Nor is it the case that what is already known lacks the capacity to convey meaning; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (pratyayāpatti) of understanding the word "artha" (meaning) in the expression "śabdaṃ vetti" (he knows the word). This would contradict the Bhāṣya on the rule *aṇudit* (Pāṇini 1.1.69). The meaning of that [Bhāṣya] is not that something generally known lacks the capacity to convey meaning; rather, it means that a word known by way of a technical grammatical designation (*saṃjñā*) lacks such capacity. This is because the general rule is restricted by the context.

Thus, the argument of the Navya (Neo-logicians) who claim that even when one is reading a book in private, there is indeed a subtle articulation (*sūkṣmoccāraṇa*) because they fear the non-attainment of the cognition of meaning otherwise, is refuted. This is because it contradicts actual experience. Furthermore, regarding this point, the Logicians (*Tārkika*) and Vedāntins [propose]: Is the sphoṭa manifested by all the phonemes (*varṇa*), or by any particular phoneme, or by the final phoneme? It cannot be the first, because a conjunction of things that perish instantly is impossible. Nor can it be the second, because once the sphoṭa has been manifested by the phoneme *pa*, the phoneme *ṭa* would be redundant.

The third [alternative] is not tenable. For if the comprehension of meaning is established by the final phoneme alone, accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding phoneme, what is the use of *sphoṭa*? That is not correct, because there is no evidence for the instantaneous destruction of phonemes. Nor is the cognition "the letter *ga* has arisen" or "the letter *ga* has perished" such evidence; for that can be explained as a manifestation and disappearance, just as in the case of the statement "space was produced. Furthermore, it would involve the unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating infinite prior non-existences (*prāgabhāva*) and subsequent non-existences (*pradhvaṃsa*).

Even if the letters are impermanent, it is possible for them to coalesce within a memory produced by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) generated from the experience of those letters. Furthermore, in the second case as well, there is no pointlessness to the utterance of the second and subsequent letters; for they serve a purpose by removing doubts such as whether, upon the pronunciation of the word *paśu*, what is manifested is *pa-sphoṭa*, or *pa-ṭa-sphoṭa*, or "the letter *pa* is the *sphoṭa*."

In the third [view], just as a cloth is accepted as a distinct whole (*avayavin*) even though the final conjunction—characterized by the conjunctions of threads of the same genus—is alone capable of producing the effect that is the cloth, so too do I accept it. Nor is there a distinct entity [there] based on experience, for the same applies to the word-sphoṭa (*padasphoṭa*). Furthermore, [the view of the whole] involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). If you ask how there is simplicity (*lāghava*) regarding the sphoṭa, listen: the sphoṭa is manifested by the sounds (*dhvani*) themselves.

Furthermore, there is great parsimony [in our view]: one need not postulate an infinite number of phonemes (*varṇa*), nor their prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), as one would have to in cases such as *nadī*, *dīna*, *sara*, *rasa*, *jarā*, and *rāja* for the sake of perceiving distinct meanings. Nor need it be asserted that the final phoneme—conjoined with the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of the preceding phonemes—is the cause [of word-cognition]. For you, however, all of that must be asserted, which constitutes a burden of complexity (*gaurava*).

Thus, by this brief glance, the sphoṭa as something distinct from phonemes (*varṇa*)—which is manifested by phonemes and constitutes the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) in all beings—has been explained according to my view, following the refutation of the fallacious arguments of the logicians and others. It is also stated in another way: the indivisible word-sphoṭa is not something distinct [from the phonemes].

Where logicians and others speak of a word as being either etymological (*yaugika*) or both etymological and conventional (*yogarūḍha*), such as *pācaka* (cook) or *paṅkaja* (lotus), that very same thing is by us designated as the "divisible word-sphoṭa" (*sakhaṇḍapadasphoṭa*), because the apprehension of its collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) occurs through dictionaries and other means preceded by the consideration of the powers of its parts. However, for one who lacks knowledge of grammar and whose apprehension of the collective power arises solely through common usage, that very same entity is intended as the "indivisible word-sphoṭa" (*akhaṇḍapadasphoṭa*).

In that regard, because the apprehension of the power (of a word) resides in the whole [the *sphoṭa*], as evidenced by the linguistic usage of all people characterized by a lack of knowledge regarding the meaning of the individual parts; and thus, since the words "conventional" (*rūḍhi*) and "etymological" (*yaugika*), as well as the "divisible" (*sakhaṇḍa*) and "indivisible" (*akhaṇḍa*) *sphoṭas*, are synonyms, the dispute is merely over names—this is the direction [of the argument]. Furthermore, the fallacious refutations of the Logicians (*tārkika*) and others are struck down even before birth, such is the direction [of the argument]. For there is no rule that the reasoning of the Logicians and others is necessarily sound reasoning (*sattarka*), since many instances of unsound reasoning are observed therein that do not accord with experience.

For instance, it was previously stated that since a qualified entity is established only by virtue of being an effect or a cause, the production of a cloth devoid of qualities is untenable. Likewise, the hypothesis that there exists a distinct variegated color (*citra-rūpa*)—postulated because the perception of a jar would otherwise be inexplicable—is also entirely unjustified, because there is no evidence for such a restrictive rule (*niyama*) that color must be pervasively present (*vyāpyavṛtti*). Or, even if such a rule were to exist, [the objection remains].

Nevertheless, the direct perception of a jar (*ghaṭasākṣātkāra*) is established solely by the final sensory contact with the final part as delimited by the final color, accompanied by the sensory contacts with the respective parts as delimited by their respective substances; for there is the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a distinct variegated color (*citrarūpa*). Likewise, since the knowledge of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is the cause of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*), and since such [prior] knowledge is impossible in cases like "this is a jar," the postulation of an indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpakajñāna*) that does not apprehend the relation between the jar and its jar-ness is also improper, as it is untenable.

The postulation of that [conjunction] occurs only in cases such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*), where there is a relation of conjunction distinct from an eternal relation; however, it does not occur in cases such as "this is a jar" (*ayaṃ ghaṭaḥ*). This is because in the latter case, only a determinate cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) arises. And thus, there is great parsimony in not having to accept indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpakajñāna*). Likewise, the postulation of a twofold division of time based on the distinction between the indivisible and the divisible is also improper, because the indivisible does not serve as a basis for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).

Nor can it be maintained that time is accepted as the generator of produced things and the substratum of the worlds; for its status as both the generator and the support of the universe is well-established as belonging to God (Īśvara) alone. Furthermore, one should not argue that we have already stated—by saying "space and time do not exceed God" and so forth—that space and time are not distinct from God. For in that context, the identity of space and time with God was asserted specifically [as a logical category], and that contradicts the Vedic scripture which declares, "All this, indeed, is Brahman."

Likewise, according to such scriptural passages as "From which indeed these beings are born" and "In that all are established," the status of being the creator of the world and the support of the world belongs to the Lord (Īśvara) alone, and not to time. Therefore, the statement "time is the progenitor of produced things" is improper, because it would imply a non-difference between time and the Lord even with respect to the seven categories beginning with earth; thus, to specifically establish the non-difference of both [time and the Lord] from that [Lord] is untenable. In this way, "limited time" (khaṇḍakāla) is also improper, for limited time is merely a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of specific movements of the sun.

In this way, let the specific movement of the sun itself be the "fractional time" (*khaṇḍakāla*); what is the use of something additional to that? And thus, the fractional time would possess the nature of an action (*kriyātva*). Likewise, those who maintain the theory of baking in a mass (*pīlupākavādin*) accept that baking occurs within the atom, thereby accepting the destruction of the dark pot and the production of a red pot. In that case, since there is an absence of instrumental causes such as the wheel and the stick, how can there be production? Yet, they accept it even without an instrumental cause. [The opponent asks: "In that case, since there is an absence of instrumental causes such as the wheel and the stick, how can there be production?"

If that [status of being a cause] were accepted even in the absence of an efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), then the status of the staff, the crookedness, and so forth as efficient causes would be utterly destroyed. Thus, resorting to such heavy arguments that are not supported by multiple experiences constitutes "simplicity" (*lāghava*). It is improper to refute the indivisible sphoṭa—which is distinct from these—with fallacious refutations; this is the general direction. Since the knowledge of word-meanings is the cause for the knowledge of sentence-meaning, after defining the word-sphoṭa, the sentence-sphoṭa is now defined. And that is twofold, distinguished as indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) and divisible (*sakhaṇḍa*).

In that regard, an indivisible [sphoṭa] distinct from the word is accepted because it is more parsimonious, and this has been explained in the section on the indivisible word-sphoṭa (*akhaṇḍapadasphoṭa*). Furthermore, there is great parsimony in that expectancy, semantic competency, and contiguity need not be posited as causes [of comprehension]. As for the divisible [sphoṭa], it is already well-known. Alternatively, in cases such as *hare 've* (O Hari, come), once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has occurred, the division of words becomes unavoidable; therefore, the distinction is that the indivisible sentence-sphoṭa (*akhaṇḍavākyasphoṭa*) applies there, while elsewhere the divisible [sphoṭa] applies. And thus, the objections [against the sphoṭa theory] are like a miscarriage.

In this context, a sentence (*vākya*) is that which has as its primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) the meaning of a single finite verb (*tiṅanta*). For example: "pac" (cook) and "bhavati" (is). Even in such cases, although the word "pacati" (he cooks) is a qualifier, there is no lack of definition (*avyāpti*), because it lacks the status of being the primary qualificand.

The logicians (tārkika), however, in order to establish that preceding and succeeding [sentences] form a single syntactical unit, cite the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra: "A sentence is one because of the unity of its purpose, provided that there is mutual expectancy if it were divided. Having set aside their own interpretation of "unity of purpose" as "the unity of the productive operation (bhāvanā) which serves as the qualificand," they instead explain its meaning as "the oneness of the intended object (tātparya-viṣaya-ekya)," thereby asserting the status of a single sentence for both perception and inference.

In an independent [sentence], it must be stated that whatever possesses a connection [of meaning] constitutes a single sentence; however, it is neither appropriate nor faultless to assume just any meaning whatsoever. For instance, in the case of the intention to teach recitation—such as "Just as Devadatta recites, so does your son recite"—there would follow the undesirable consequence of this also being a single sentence. Nor is such a conclusion desirable, because it would entail the occurrence of grammatical substitution (*ādeśa*) due to the sentences being syntactically identical.

Likewise, "I prepare a pleasant seat for you; I fashion it well with a stream of clarified butter" is the mantra that establishes the seat (*sadanapratipādaka*), similar to a perceptible object. "Sit upon this, O immortal one; stand firm, O essence of rice, being well-disposed" is the mantra that establishes the [deity] upon the seat (*sādanapratipādaka*), similar to inference. Just as the determination of the auxiliaries of sacrifice is the intended subject matter for one who investigates the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too, although inference depends upon perception, the establishing [mantra] does not depend upon it.

And thus, these two [sentences] would also result in being a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*). Nor is this an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it contradicts your own cited counter-example regarding "on account of the identity of meaning" (*arthaikyāt*). Furthermore, is this unity of sentence (*vākyaikavākyatā*) a unity of words (*padaikyavākyatā*), a unity of sentences (*vākyaikavākyatā*), or a unity of texts (*granthaikavākyatā*)? Not the first, because that [unity of words] is possible only between a verb and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), since mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is possible only between those two. For such unity occurs only when there is expectancy for both, and not when there is expectancy for only one of the two.

Not the second [alternative], because syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) consists in the connection of a sentence that is independent of others with another sentence that requires it; and in the present case, such unity exists only between the two parts of the work in the form of a textual composition (*vākya-saṃdarbha*), not between individual sentences. This is because sentences such as "Inference is the cognition produced by the consideration (*parāmarśa*) of the three marks" have no requirement for a perceptual sentence, and because there is an absence of proximity (*āsatti*). Furthermore, syntactic unity of sentences is indeed "context" (*prakaraṇa*), since its definition is "the requirement of one of the two."

If one accepts that even this [sentence] constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), there would be a contradiction with the section on the relative strength of the means of proof—*śruti*, *liṅga*, *vākya*, *prakaraṇa*, and so forth—which establishes that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is weaker than the sentence (*vākya*). Nor is it the third [alternative]; for the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) between perception and inference is semantic (*ārthī*), not verbal (*śābdī*). Therefore, the composition of a sūtra here and the postulation of some arbitrary meaning is improper. As for the work of Śiromaṇi, it is already established by the principle that "whatever possesses mutual connection constitutes a single syntactical unit. This is the direction of the argument. Let us now return to the subject at hand.

Because the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) occurs through usage (*vyavahāra*) with respect to the sentence, and because the sentence alone is the signifier, there is the theory of the sentence-sphoṭa (*vākya-sphoṭa*). Nor should it be argued that although the expressive power in the sentence was previously apprehended, it is abandoned through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpa-udvāpa*) and then apprehended in the word; for if that were so, the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence would become the cause of the knowledge of the word-meaning, which would result in the collapse of the universally established doctrine that the knowledge of the word-meaning is the cause of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning. The sentence-sphoṭa is of two kinds: *sakhaṇḍa* (with parts) and *akhaṇḍa* (without parts). The *akhaṇḍa* is of two kinds.

[The sphoṭa] is both distinct from and non-distinct from the phonemes (varṇa). When phonemes are not accepted because of their complexity (gaurava), and the view is held that the indivisible sentence-sphoṭa is manifested by sounds (dhvani) alone due to parsimony (lāghava), then [the sphoṭa] is distinct. In this position, fallacious objections such as "it is manifested by as many phonemes as there are" are refuted by a miscarriage of their own. However, when the view is held that phonemes are manifested by sounds, then there is the divisible sentence-sphoṭa, as in the case of "Bring the jar."

Because it is possible to effect a division between the action (*kriyā*) and its factors (*kāraka*), [the view that they are distinct is maintained]. However, in cases such as *hareḥ* or *viṣṇoḥ*, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, a division between the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the suffix (*ākhyāta*) cannot be made; thus, there is the non-distinct sentence-sphoṭa (*anatiriktavākyasphoṭa*). For a non-grammarian who lacks knowledge of actions and their factors, even the expression *ghaṭam ānaya* (bring the jar) is nothing but the non-distinct, indivisible sentence-sphoṭa. "In a word (*pada*), phonemes (*varṇa*) do not exist; nor do parts exist within phonemes. There is no absolute distinction whatsoever between words and the sentence."

Thus ends the exposition of the indivisible sentence-sphoṭa as distinct [from its parts]. The meaning is that just as there are no constituent parts in a phoneme (*varṇa*), so it is here. In examples such as *paśya mṛgo dhāvati* ("See, the deer runs") and *pacati bhavati* ("He cooks and exists"), one should understand—as before—that the indivisible [sentence] is neither more nor less than the sum of its parts. The action of running, performed by the deer, is construed with the act of seeing through the relation of being its object (*karman*). The action of cooking, performed by Devadatta, is construed with the present action of existing.

As it has been said: "Just as a single inflected noun (*subanta*) may serve as an attribute for many finite verbs (*tiṅanta*), so too they say that a finite verb may serve as an attribute for another finite verb. However, in the view that the verbal cognition has the nominative-terminated (*prathamānta*) "deer" as its qualificand—namely, "the deer possesses an effort conducive to running"—there arises the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the accusative case for the deer, because the deer would then be the object (*karman*) relative to the meaning of the root *dṛś* ("to see").

Anticipating the objection that supplying the word "him" (tam) would result in a syntactical split (vākyabheda), some have resolved this by arguing that, as in passages such as "Look, Lakṣmaṇa, at the supremely righteous crane on Lake Pampā," the meaning of the entire sentence functions as the object, and thus there is no syntactical split. That, however, is quite mistaken.

Since the deer possesses agency (kartṛtva) as defined by the internal action of running, and since that [agency] is expressed by the verb (ākhyāta), the nominative case arises. Furthermore, although [the deer] is the object (karman) as defined by the meaning of the root *dṛś* (to see), which involves many factors, there is no evidence to sublate the grammatical refinement (saṃskāra) already produced on account of its being the more internal factor; for this is logically consistent, just as it is said, "Hunger can be assuaged even by dog-meat and the like."

Thus, even in this view where the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*) ends in the nominative case, although the grammarians' objection does not apply, there arises the problem that the syntactic unity of the expression *pacati bhavati* ("he is cooking") cannot be established in the sense of "the becoming [of that which] has as its agent the act of cooking whose agent is Devadatta. Nor can it be argued that once the meaning "Devadatta, who possesses an effort conducive to cooking, exists" is established, the principle *saviśeṣaṇe vidhiniṣedhau viśeṣaṇam upasaṃkrāmataḥ sati viśeṣye bādhe* (restrictions and prohibitions involving a qualified subject apply to the qualifier when there is a contradiction regarding the qualified subject) would allow agency to belong to the action itself.

And because there would be no purpose [for the rule] if they were part of a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*). Nor can it be argued that the result [of the rule] is the substitution of *nighāta* (anudātta accent), the forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, etc., [only] in a "single sentence" (*samānavākya*), since the substitution of *nighāta* is already precluded by the inclusion of the term *atiṅ* (not a finite verb) in the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*. True; however, in the case of the usage *devadattaḥ pacati te bhavati* with the meaning "the act of cooking, performed by Devadatta, belongs to you," the substitutions would not occur because there is no status as a "single sentence. This is because the sense is "the act of cooking related to you is being performed by Devadatta. Thus, due to the absence of *samānavākyatva* (being within the same syntactic unit), the substitutions would not be applicable.

Furthermore, in the sense that "there is a single act of cooking performed by multiple Devadattas," the usage *devadattāḥ pacanti* ("the Devadattas cook") would also not be possible; for since there is multiplicity of agents, the plural number would necessarily apply to the verb *bhavati*. Moreover, there is the presence of a purposeful factor in the form of the *nighāta* (elision of accent) in the expression *paśya mṛgo dhāvati* ("look, the deer runs"). Furthermore, the claim of the Logicians (*Tārkikas*) that the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) functions as the object (*karman*) is not logical. To explain: is the sentence-meaning something distinct [from the word-meanings] or non-distinct?

Not the first [alternative], because since that [Self] is not presented by a mental mode (*vṛtti*), its connection as the object of the act of seeing (*dṛśi-kriyā*) is untenable; for there is a rule that only what is presented by a mental mode can be the object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Otherwise, space (*ākāśa*), which is presented from the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), would also result in being an object of verbal cognition. Not the second either, because the connection of the meaning of a noun with the meaning of a verb through a relation of difference, without mediating the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhakti*), is unestablished in linguistic usage. Otherwise, it would follow that one could say "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*).

Nor should it be said that in such cases the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is the object (*karman*) and not the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); for if that were so, the sentence "The rice is delicious; he cooks" (*ramaṇīya odanaḥ pacati*) would be untenable. In examples such as "Behold Pampā, O Lakṣmaṇa" (*paśya lakṣmaṇa pampāyām*), there is indeed a syntactic split (*vākyabheda*) through the ellipsis of the word "it" (*tam*); thus, the claim that the sentence-meaning is the object is an unexamined assertion. Likewise, the statement in the *Vyutpattivāda* that in the sentence "The pot becomes blue" (*nīlo ghaṭo bhavati*), the meaning is "the pot is the locus of the becoming whose agent is blue," is also not logical.

This is because there is no sublation of the grammatical derivation [of the compound] such as "the existence of the object denoted by the name" (*nāmārthasya bhavana*), and because the cognition "the blue pot is the locus of existence" is possible. For when an injunction or a prohibition concerns something with a qualifier, they apply to the qualifier provided that the qualified object is understood; thus, in the case of the qualifier, the connection with "existence" will occur in the blue itself—this is the general direction. In the same way, in cases such as "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*) and "This is that Devadatta," the distinction between being with parts (*sakhaṇḍa*) and without parts (*akhaṇḍa*) should be understood as before.

Regarding the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the traditional teachers maintain that because it is impossible for the consciousness qualified by omniscience and other attributes denoted by the word *tat* (That) to be identical with the consciousness qualified by the internal organ denoted by the word *tvam* (thou), one must employ the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (indication that both excludes and includes) in order to establish their identity. Now, what is the proof for the identity of these two? Nor can it be the grammatical rule regarding the meaning of nouns (*nāmārthavyutpatti*). For does that rule mean that there is only a syntactic connection of non-difference between the meanings of two nouns, or that there is indeed non-difference between the meanings of two nouns?

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because of the deviation [of the rule] in cases such as "he cooks a little" (*stokaṃ pacati*) and "the curdled milk is for Viśvedevas" (*vaiśvadevī āmikṣā*). Nor is the second, because of the deviation in cases such as "the jar and the cloth" (*ghaṭapaṭau*). Therefore, since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, syntactic non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is improper; this is based on the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*). True. There is the scriptural authority establishing non-difference preceded by a condemnation of difference: "He goes from death to death who perceives here [in this world] as if there were multiplicity" (*mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyumāpnoti ya iha nāneva paśyati*).

Nor should it be argued that even there, the statement "he who perceives as if there were diversity goes from death to death, but he who perceives [it] as reality does not" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.12.2)—by means of the word "as if" (*iva*) and the use of the particle *iti*—implies that only difference is being perceived; for in the Chāndogya, beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" and concluding with "That is the Self, That art thou, Śvetaketu," the identity [of the Self and Brahman] is determined through the uniformity of the opening and the conclusion, which establishes the purport of the Veda.

This is because identity is established even by the Śruti text: "Brahman would desert him who knows Brahman as other than the Self. In this view, there is the manifestation of a sentence through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). However, in reality, this is indeed the manifestation of a sentence through direct denotation (vācaka). For instance, although the syntactic relation of identity between the referents of the words *tat* and *tvam*, as presented by their specific powers, is untenable, there is no obstacle to the syntactic relation of identity between the two substrata (*viśeṣya*) as presented by those same powers.

Just as in the case of "the jar is impermanent," although the property of jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*), which is one part denoted by the word "jar," is unfit for connection with impermanence, the connection with impermanence occurs with the individual jar that is fit; or rather, the denotative power (*śakti*) resides in the substantive alone, while the qualifier is merely an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). In this view, there is no fault whatsoever. Or again, just as in cases of multiple meanings (*nānārtha*) the denotative function is restricted by factors such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), so too, in accordance with the requirement for the connection of difference (*bhedānvaya*), the denotative function is restricted to the substantive alone.

Or, let there be indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and let that be "indication with exclusion" (*jahallakṣaṇā*); by that, there is merely the abandonment of the qualifying aspect (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*), but it has no utility regarding the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) either, since its establishment is possible through primary denotation (*śakti*) alone. This is likewise the case in the sentence "This is that Devadatta. Thus, the example of "indication with both exclusion and non-exclusion" (*jahadajahallakṣaṇā*) is inconsistent; such is the direction of the argument. Similarly, in the sentence "One tree becomes five boats," whether [the identity] is with parts (*sakhaṇḍa*) or without parts (*akhaṇḍa*), it should be understood as before.

On this point, the logicians (*tārkika*) say: "The expressive word (*vācaka*) takes on the number of the base (*prakṛti*), not that of the derivative (*vikṛti*)," according to this statement; thus, they claim that after the root *bhū*, it is only the singular number belonging to the base-word *vṛkṣa* that occurs. That is incorrect, because the word *gṛhṇāti* refers specifically to cases involving the suffix *cvy-anta*. This is seen, for example, in such instances as *saṃghībhavanti brāhmaṇāḥ* ("the Brahmins become a group"), *tvadbhavāmi aham* ("I become you"), and *madbhavasi tvam* ("you become me"), where both number and person belong exclusively to the base. [Objection: But what is the authority for this restriction?

The very usage in the *Mahābhāṣya*—"the lump of gold becomes two earrings resembling charcoal from the *khadira* tree"—is an instance of this. Furthermore, regarding cases of the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), if the grammatical treatises are authoritative, then the number residing in the subject is [conveyed] by the verbal suffix, as in such examples. Again, a sentence is of two kinds: poetic (*kāvyātmaka*) and non-poetic (*akāvyātmake*). The second has already been described. The first, however, is defined by the verse: "That which consists of word and meaning, free from defects, possessing qualities, and sometimes even without ornaments."

In this regard, it is impossible to state the absence of all defects, because such an absence is impossible. If the meaning were merely the absence of some defect or other, the term *adoṣa* (absence of defects) would be redundant. Therefore, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) here is "scarcity" (*alpatva*), as in the expression "a girl with a small belly" (*anudarā kanyā*). And this "scarcity" refers to the absence of those defects that are clearly perceived. This definition of poetry has been refuted in the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, on the grounds that if poetry were a property residing collectively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) in both word and meaning, the common usage—"the poem has been heard, but its meaning is not understood"—would be impossible. Thus, that [definition] is inconsistent.

For, as in the case of saying "the cloth is burnt" even when only one part is burnt, the application [of the term] is possible even for a single part; this is because the *Bhāṣya* states that words whose primary denotation is a whole may also apply to a part thereof. However, that definition itself is not tenable. For instance, the definition is: "Poetry (*kāvyam*) is a word that conveys a beautiful meaning (*ramaṇīya-artha*)," and "beauty" (*ramaṇīyatva*) is "being the object of a cognition that produces extraordinary delight. This definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*), as it applies to such statements as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). Nor is there a distinct class (*vaijātya*) of delight [in the case of the Upanishadic statement]. What follows from that?

This is because the quality of being the object of a knowledge that produces supramundane bliss is equal in both cases, and because it is described by all as being the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*). Furthermore, does the word *ramaṇīya* (delightful) possess the capacity to convey a delightful meaning or not? Not the first alternative; for if it did, even the word "delightful" itself would possess the capacity to convey a delightful meaning, and thus it would follow that it is poetry (*kāvyatva*). This point is implied by the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "If it is argued that a word which conveys the meaning of an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) is itself an incorrect word, then [we reply] no, because it would follow that even an incorrect word would be an incorrect word."

Not the latter [alternative], because it is untenable as a definition since it would apply to anything that conveys a pleasant meaning. Therefore, the definition stated by Prakāśa alone is correct. In this way, in cases such as "the fire sprinkles," there is indeed only the sentence-sphoṭa (vākya-sphoṭa).

If it is objected: "Is it not the case that the certainty of incompatibility (*ayogyatā-niścaya*) acts as an obstacle to the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, while the knowledge of compatibility (*yogyatā-jñāna*) is its cause—a principle established in the systems of the Naiyāyikas and others? In the present case, since there exists the obstacle consisting of the certainty of incompatibility in the form of a contradiction regarding the object—namely, 'fire is not the instrument of pouring'—and since the knowledge of compatibility in the form of non-contradiction regarding the object is absent, how can this [sentence] possess the nature of *vākya-sphoṭa*? [Response: True. Compatibility is the non-contradiction of the intended object (*tātparya-viṣaya-abādha*). Its absence is incompatibility.

In the present context, the intended meaning is "he sprinkles with extremely hot water. For example: "The ill-fames of this lord of the earth—counted by numbers exceeding a parārdha, appearing as if deaf to those who observe with the eye of wisdom—are indeed sung in the eight musical notes (*aṣṭasvara*) by the multitude of the dumb born from the wombs of the wives of prisoners on the shore of the milk-ocean of the beloveds of the enemy. The sky is like the sky; the oceans are comparable to the oceans; the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa is like the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa."* *Note: This verse is a famous example of *anvaya-virodha* (contradiction in the syntactical connection), where the literal meaning is impossible, thus necessitating a figurative interpretation.*

"On the first peak of Kailāsa, hearing his fame being sung by the celestial nymphs with the melodies of flutes, the elephants of the quarters—casting aside their sidelong glances and suspecting them to be the stalks of lotuses in a lake—wave their trunks upon the sandy banks of their ears. Behold, sharp arrows issue forth like a stream of blue lotuses. In the case of the first type of ornament (metaphor) within single sentences, such as "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) and so forth, as well as in cases where there is a cognition of identity (*tattvapratīti*), the established consensus is that "compatibility" (*yogyatva*) consists in the non-sublation of the intended meaning (*tātparyaviṣayābādha*).

Likewise, here too, the ascertainment of incompatibility (*ayogyatā-niścaya*) does not act as an impediment to verbal cognition; for even when such an ascertainment is present, satisfaction is experienced from a complimentary statement such as "You are Bṛhaspati," and anger is experienced from a statement such as "You are the son of a barren woman," even when there is the ascertainment of sublation (*bādha-niścaya*) that "I am not the son of a barren woman."

This is untenable in the absence of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). Furthermore, in cases of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) such as "Behold the pair of blue lotuses," where there is a determination of incompatibility—namely, that "the arrows do not have a pair of blue lotuses as their point of departure"—does this determination of incompatibility occur after hearing the sentence and following the understanding of the sentence, or does it occur prior? It cannot be the first, because when there is a certainty of sublation (*bādha*), there is no absence of sublation. Nor can it be the latter, because in the absence of sublation, there is no non-occurrence of syntactic connection (*anvaya*).

Indeed, it is not the actual existence of the incompatibility of connection (*anvayānupapatti*) that is the seed of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), but rather its cognition. Nor should it be argued that such a cognition already exists because there was previously a certainty of incompatibility; for the cognition of the incompatibility of connection produced by the understanding of the sentence-meaning did not exist prior [to the sentence being heard]. For when the common worldly knowledge that "the Ganges is not the locus of the hamlet" exists, the incompatibility of connection is established by experience following the understanding from the sentence "The hamlet is on the Ganges" that "the hamlet has the Ganges as its locus."

Furthermore, no prior knowledge of that [fitness] is possible; nor is the view of the logicians—that cognition is essentially erroneous—tenable. For they must postulate that the ascertainment of unfitness acts as an impediment and that the knowledge of fitness acts as a cause, while also having to postulate that cognition is essentially erroneous; thus, there is great complexity (gaurava). For the proponents of *sphoṭa*, not even this triad needs to be postulated, which constitutes simplicity (lāghava), since that [fitness] is accepted only in relation to the activity generated by the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.

Furthermore, when there is a subverting certainty that "I am not the Supreme Lord," the sentence "That thou art" cannot produce a valid cognition (pramā), or at best it produces a cognition consisting of error; for a cognition consisting of error is incapable of generating a valid cognition. This is likewise the case with the statement, "You are the tenth."

If it is asked, "What is the referent (*padārtha*) that is the indivisible sentence-sphoṭa (*akhaṇḍavākyasphoṭa*), which is distinct from multiple phonemes (*varṇa*) and manifested by multiple sounds (*dhvani*)?"—then listen: Just as the logicians (*tārkika*), despite the possibility of other alternatives, accept a distinct "variegated color" (*citrarūpa*) according to the method previously stated; or just as the grammarians (*śābdika*) accept, in the *Vārttika* on the rule *ṛti ṛ vā*, *lṛti lṛ vā*, a single phoneme (*varṇa*) characterized by two *repha*s (the *r* sound) and the *ajbhāga* (the vowel portion); or just as it is established in the *Vārttika* on the rule *sasthānatvādaicoścottarabhūtvāt* regarding polysyllabic vowels (*anekācām*).

The state of consisting of a single phoneme (*ekavarṇātmakatva*) has been stated; likewise, it is accepted by me as well that the word (*śabda*), which is of the nature of a sentence, is manifested by multiple sounds (*dhvani*). And that [word] is of the nature of *Śabdabrahman*. Regarding this, there are three views: some say "it is *Śabdabrahman*," others say "it is the meaning of the word (*śabdārtha*)," and still others have declared "it is the word (*śabda*). "In my view, *Śabdabrahman* is the consciousness (*caitanya*) of all beings. Even from the etymological derivation of the term *Śabdabrahman*, its status as a phoneme (*varṇatva*) is established. This is also established through inference.

For instance: the indivisible sentence-sphoṭa is of the nature of a single phoneme, because it is audible, or because it is manifested by sound; for what is not so is not so, like earth and the other elements. As for the positive example, however, it consists of phonemes and the like as established in other systems. In reality, however, the inference based on positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireki) is redundant, since its purpose is already served by "presented cognition" (upanītabhāna).

For instance, just as the perception of a piece of sandalwood is ordinary (*laukika*) while its fragrance is extraordinary (*alaukika*), so too the perception of smoke is ordinary while that of fire is extraordinary; this is the distinction in this view regarding [the cognition] "by means of the presented appearance" (*upanītabhānena*). Alternatively, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), because there is no fault, and because there is no other [manifested entity] manifested by sound (*dhvani*), the status of being a phoneme (*varṇatva*) is accepted. Nor should it be argued that, since the property of being manifested by sound occurs even in the case of what is implied by intonation (*kāku*)—which is a sub-variety of "subordinate suggestion" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*)—there might be some other [manifested entity] as well.

This is because, although it is suggested by the modification of sound (*dhvani*) and by intonation (*kāku*), it is not suggested by *dhvani* itself. Furthermore, although the scripture—"Desire, volition, doubt, faith, lack of faith, fear, and shame—all this is indeed the mind"—establishes that desire and the rest are attributes of the mind, the logicians have asserted that they are attributes of the self (*ātman*), and this has been accepted by all; however, that [assertion] is based on error. The cause of that error is like the cognition that a crystal is red when in proximity to a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*).

In the case under discussion, however, there is no proximity of the mind; the seed [of the cognition] would reside in the property of the self, and there would be a contradiction with the Śruti. But this is not so in the case of the sphoṭa. Therefore, it is established that the indivisible sentence-sphoṭa, consisting of a single phoneme, is the signifier. Thus ends the *Sphoṭacandrikā* composed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa, son of Raghunātha Bhaṭṭa—who was the son of Janakījāni, daughter of Govardhana Bhaṭṭa, who was like a crest-jewel of the Mauni lineage.
